In the APG III classification system, it is placed in the family Asparagaceae, subfamily Convallarioideae. Beaucarnea is sometimes treated as a synonym of the genus Nolina, with the species being then transferred to that genus. However, recent research shows that Beaucarnea should be treated as an independent genus.

items.name: Devil's herb
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn in cold frames as they require winter chilling to break dormancy before spring.
Grow in moist well-drained alkaline soil by adding garden lime to neutral UK garden borders.
Wear heavy gloves when handling to avoid absorbing toxic alkaloids through your skin during pruning.
Cut stems back to the ground in late autumn after the black berries have fallen to prevent self-seeding.
Watch for the deadly nightshade flea beetle which skeletonises foliage in warm UK summer months.
items.description: Atropa bella-donna, commonly known as deadly nightshade or belladonna, is a toxic perennial herbaceous plant in the nightshade family Solanaceae, which also includes tomatoes, potatoes and eggplant. It is native to Europe and Western Asia, including Turkey, its distribution extending from England in the west to western Ukraine and the Iranian province of Gilan in the east. It is also naturalised or introduced in some parts of Canada, North Africa and the United States.

items.name: Poet's laurel
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist well-drained humus-rich acidic to neutral soil in deep shade to mimic UK woodlands.
Water weekly during dry UK summers until established to prevent the glossy evergreen foliage drying.
Prune out old damaged stems at the base in late spring to encourage fresh bright green new shoots.
Propagate by dividing the slow-growing rootball in spring or sowing ripe red berries in autumn cold frames.
Watch for slug and snail damage on tender new shoots emerging from the soil in damp British springs.
items.description: Danae is a monotypic genus of flowering plants. The single species, Danae racemosa, is native to west Asia. It is a slow-growing evergreen shrub about 60 cm in diameter and its common names are Alexandrian laurel and poet's laurel. In the APG III classification system, Danae is placed in the family Asparagaceae, subfamily Convallarioideae.

items.name: Datura quercifolia
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in March at five millimetres deep using a heated propagator to mimic desert heat.
Grow this tender annual in pots of gritty, free-draining soil placed against a south-facing wall.
Water deeply only when the top five centimetres of soil is dry to prevent root rot in wet summers.
Wear thick gloves when handling this highly toxic plant and prune dead stems only in late autumn.
Position near French marigolds to deter spider mites, which thrive on Datura in dry UK glasshouses.
items.description: Datura quercifolia, commonly known as the oak-leaved thorn-apple and also the Chinese Thorn-Apple, is a small shrub in the genus Datura that is native to Mexico and the Southwestern United States. It grows equally well in dry and moist soils and requires full sun. It contains a mix of alkaloids that are poisonous and can be potentially lethal when ingested.

items.name: Elephant's Ear
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender South African tuber in a gritty loam-based compost with at least fifty percent sand.
Plant the tuber in late August with the growing tip positioned just below the gritty soil surface.
Water only from September to April when the single leaf is active, keeping it dry during summer.
Overwinter pots on a sunny indoor windowsill or heated greenhouse keeping temperatures above five C.
Watch for vine weevil grubs in autumn which will chew through the tuber and destroy the root system.
items.description: Eriospermum is a genus of tuberous flowering plants. It contains 114 species native to sub-Saharan Africa.

items.name: Eriospermum paradoxum
items.growersTips:
Grow in a heated greenhouse or sunny windowsill as this South African tuber cannot survive UK frosts.
Plant the tuber in autumn in extremely gritty, free-draining soil with the growing tip just exposed.
Water only from September to April when the fuzzy leaf is active, keeping it totally dry in summer.
Position in the brightest south-facing spot possible to mimic winter sun and prevent leaf stretching.
Watch for mealybugs nestled inside the dense, complex leaf hairs during the winter growing season.
items.description: Eriospermum paradoxum ("haasklossie") is a species of geophytic plant of the genus Eriospermum, indigenous to the Cape region of South Africa. Its habitat is sandy or rocky clay soils in arid winter-rainfall areas. It is a bit peculiar in having a true leaf that is like the scale-leaves of some junipers, from which emerges an enation up to 15 cm (5.9 in) in height and half as wide. but is semisucculent in nature.

items.name: Peliosanthes violacea
items.growersTips:
Grow under glass in a heated greenhouse as this tropical Asian native cannot survive UK winters.
Use a peat-free compost mixed with one-third perlite to ensure the sharp drainage this plant needs.
Water only when the top two inches of soil are dry to prevent root rot in cool British weather.
Keep in dappled shade or indirect light to mimic its natural forest floor habitat and avoid scorch.
Maintain a minimum winter temperature of fifteen degrees Celsius to keep the evergreen foliage alive.
items.description: Peliosanthes is a genus of flowering plants found in eastern Asia. In the APG III classification system, it is placed in the family Asparagaceae, subfamily Convallarioideae.

items.name: Eriospermum capense
items.growersTips:
Grow this tuberous South African native in a gritty, free-draining loam to prevent winter wet rot.
Keep the soil completely dry during its summer dormancy, starting watering only when leaves emerge.
Provide a minimum winter temperature of 5C in a bright greenhouse or conservatory to prevent frost.
Plant the tuber with its growing tip just below the soil surface in a deep, narrow terracotta pot.
Watch for mealybugs in the leaf axils during the autumn and winter active growing season.
items.description: Eriospermum capense is a species of geophytic plant of the genus Eriospermum, indigenous to the Western Cape Province, South Africa.

items.name: Eriospermum dregei
items.growersTips:
Grow in a heated greenhouse or indoors as this South African tuber is not hardy in the UK climate.
Plant the tuber in a highly gritty, free-draining loam-less compost with the crown at soil level.
Water only from autumn to spring during its active winter growth phase and keep dry in summer.
Position in a south-facing window or under grow lights to prevent leggy winter leaf growth.
Watch for mealybugs in the fibrous leaf sheath and treat with an organic contact insecticide.
items.description: Eriospermum dregei is a species of geophytic plant of the family Asparagaceae.

items.name: Iochroma arborescens
items.growersTips:
Plant in late May after frosts in rich loamy soil mixed with grit for essential winter drainage.
Water deeply once a week in summer but keep the root zone barely damp during cold winter months.
Prune back hard in early spring to encourage vigorous new wood which produces the best blooms.
Overwinter in a pot indoors or wrap the base in thick fleece to survive wet UK winter freezes.
Check regularly for glasshouse whitefly and red spider mite when keeping sheltered under glass.
items.description: Iochroma arborescens is a species of flowering plant in the genus Iochroma, belonging to the nightshade family Solanaceae. Formerly it was considered the single species in the monotypic genus Acnistus. Common names include gallinero, mata-gallina, fruta-de-sabiá, hollowheart, wild tobacco, siyou, bastard sirio, galán arbóreo, tabaco de monte, nigüito, marieneira, güitite, and tabak djab.

items.name: Maianthemum
items.growersTips:
Plant in autumn at a depth of five centimetres in moisture-retentive, humus-rich acid to neutral soil
Position in full or dappled shade to mimic their natural UK woodland habitat and prevent leaf scorch
Water weekly during dry British summers to keep the soil consistently damp but never waterlogged
Mulch annually in late winter with leaf mould or composted bark to mimic natural woodland floor decay
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using beer traps or organic wool pellets
items.description: Maianthemum includes the former genus Smilacina and is a genus of perennial herbaceous flowering plants with fleshy, persistent rhizomes. It is widespread across much of North America, Europe and Asia, and may be terrestrial, aquatic or epiphytic. It is characterized by simple, unbranched stems that are upright, leaning or hanging down and have 2–17 foliage leaves. Leaves are simple and may clasp the stem or be short-petiolate. The inflorescence is terminal and either a panicle or a raceme with few to many pedicelate flowers. Most species have 6 tepals and 6 stamens; a few have parts in 4s. Te

items.name: Dasylirion acrotrichum
items.growersTips:
Plant in a raised bed of 50 percent grit and loam to survive wet UK winters without root rot.
Position in full south-facing sun against a brick wall to maximize essential summer heat.
Protect the crown with a fleece jacket or removable glass cloche from November through March.
Water deeply once a fortnight in summer but keep completely dry during the damp winter months.
Prune dead lower leaves in late spring by cutting close to the trunk to maintain a clean shape.
items.description: Dasylirion acrotrichum, the great desert spoon and green sotol, is a plant native to the Chihuahuan Desert and other xeric habitats in northern and central Mexico.

items.name: Hyoscyamus aureus
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at a depth of two millimetres in free-draining gritty compost during early spring
Grow this tender Mediterranean native in a terracotta pot to move indoors before autumn frosts hit
Water sparingly only when the top five centimetres of soil is dry to prevent root rot in UK damp
Wear gloves when handling to avoid skin contact with its highly toxic tropane alkaloid sap
Position in your sunniest south-facing spot or unheated greenhouse to mimic its dry native climate
items.description: Hyoscyamus aureus, the golden henbane or yellow henbane, is a species of plant in the family Solanaceae native to the Eastern Mediterranean and Iraq.

items.name: Sansevieria
items.growersTips:
Water only when the compost is bone dry, usually every three to four weeks during the UK winter.
Repot in spring using a free-draining mix of two parts peat-free compost to one part coarse grit.
Keep plants above ten degrees Celsius near bright, indirect light but away from cold UK drafts.
Wipe the upright leaves with a damp cloth monthly to remove dust and check for mealybug pests.
Use heavy terracotta pots to prevent top-heavy mature specimens from tipping over on windowsills.
items.description: Sansevieria is a historically recognized genus of flowering plants, native to Africa, notably Madagascar, and southern Asia, now included in the genus Dracaena on the basis of molecular phylogenetic studies. Common names for the 70 or so species formerly placed in the genus include mother-in-law's tongue, devil's tongue, jinn's tongue, bow string hemp, snake plant and snake tongue. In the APG III classification system, Dracaena is placed in the family Asparagaceae, subfamily Convallarioideae ; before that it was placed in family Ruscaceae. It has also been placed in the former family Dracaenac

items.name: Streptosolen
items.growersTips:
Overwinter indoors or in a heated greenhouse as this tender shrub will not survive UK winter frosts.
Prune back by half in early spring to encourage bushy growth and more orange flowers on new wood.
Water copiously in summer but allow the top inch of compost to dry out before watering again.
Feed weekly from May to September with a high-potash liquid tomato food to boost the bloom cycle.
Plant in a loam-based John Innes No 3 compost mixed with plenty of grit to ensure rapid drainage.
items.description: Streptosolen is a monotypic genus of flowering plants in the family Solanaceae. It is closely related to the genus Browallia, within which it was originally placed. The single species, Streptosolen jamesonii, the marmalade bush or fire bush, is an evergreen shrub bearing loose clusters of flowers which change gradually from yellow to red as they develop, resulting in an overall appearance resembling orange marmalade, found in open woodlands in Colombia, Venezuela, Ecuador, and Peru. The plant has become naturalized in certain localities in Hawaii.

items.name: Datura ceratocaula
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in March at 5mm deep using bottom heat of 21C to counter the cool UK spring.
Grow in a heavy clay soil mix or boggy container to mimic its natural Mexican wetland habitat.
Keep the soil constantly saturated or submerge the pot base in shallow water during summer.
Position in the sunniest, most sheltered south-facing spot to maximize the short UK heat window.
Wear thick gloves when handling any part of this highly toxic plant to prevent skin absorption.
items.description: Datura ceratocaula is a species of Datura. It is weed-like in its natural habitat, but is grown in gardens and yards as an ornamental plant. The flower has a sweet smell. It is an annual plant that originally came from Mexico.

items.name: Datura leichhardtii
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in early March at five millimetres deep using a heated propagator set to twenty-one Celsius.
Grow in pots of loam-based John Innes Number Two compost to restrict roots and encourage earlier flowering.
Water only when the top two centimetres of soil are dry to prevent root rot in cool British summers.
Move pots inside a heated greenhouse or conservatory by mid-September before the first autumn frosts.
Wear thick gloves when pruning seed pods in October to avoid contact with toxic tropane alkaloids.
items.description: Datura leichhardtii is a species of thorn apple in the genus Datura. In 1844, Ludwig Leichhardt discovered this species in Australia. Ferdinand von Mueller gave it the name Datura leichhardtii when he published his first description of it in 1855.

items.name: Datura wrightii
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in March at five millimetres deep using a heated propagator to mimic desert heat.
Grow in a terracotta pot with fifty percent grit to survive wet UK winters and prevent root rot.
Water deeply only when the top five centimetres of soil is dry, then keep completely dry in winter.
Cut back dead stems to ground level in late autumn and mulch heavily with bark to protect from frost.
Position in your garden's hottest south-facing spot to ensure enough summer heat for night blooms.
items.description: Datura wrightii, commonly known as sacred datura, is a poisonous perennial plant species and ornamental flower of the family Solanaceae native to the Southwestern United States and northwestern Mexico. It is sometimes used as a hallucinogen due to its psychoactive alkaloids. D. wrightii is classified as an anticholinergic deliriant.

items.name: Dasylirion leiophyllum
items.growersTips:
Plant in a gritty loam at a depth of fifteen centimeters to ensure rapid drainage in wet UK winters.
Water only once a week in summer and keep completely dry from October to March to prevent root rot.
Position in full south-facing sun against a brick wall to maximize heat and protect from cold winds.
Wrap the crown in fleece during prolonged UK frosts below minus eight to prevent freezing damage.
Grow in a terracotta pot using a mix of three parts John Innes number three to one part grit.
items.description: Dasylirion leiophyllum is a species of flowering plant in the asparagus family known by the common names green sotol, smooth-leaf sotol, and smooth sotol. It is native to North America, where it occurs in Chihuahua and Coahuila in Mexico and New Mexico and western Texas in the United States. It was first collected by Valery Havard in 1880 and was described by William Trelease in 1911.

items.name: Iochroma fuchsioides
items.growersTips:
Grow in a pot of peat-free loam-based compost so you can move it into a heated greenhouse for winter.
Water copiously daily in summer but keep the soil barely damp from November to March to avoid rot.
Prune back hard by half in early spring just as new growth starts to maintain a bushy shrub shape.
Check the undersides of leaves weekly in summer for glasshouse whitefly and red spider mite pests.
Feed weekly with high-potassium liquid tomato fertilizer from May to September to boost flowering.
items.description: Iochroma fuchsioides is an Iochroma species found in Ecuador and Colombia. It was first described in 1848. In addition to the known withanolide D {1}, three new withanolides have been isolated from Iochroma fuchsioides.

items.name: Dracaena
items.growersTips:
Bring potted Dracaena indoors by October before UK frosts damage the foliage of this tropical plant.
Water only when the top two inches of compost dry out to prevent root rot in damp UK winters.
Wipe the strap-like leaves with a damp cloth monthly to remove dust and maximise low UK winter light.
Repot in spring using a free-draining peat-free compost mix with added grit to ensure good drainage.
Place in bright indirect light near an east or west window to avoid leaf scorch from summer sun.
items.description:
Dracaena can mean:Drakaina (mythology), a Greek mythological entity
Dracaena (plant), a genus of plants
Cordyline australis, a plant commonly known as the Dracaena palm
Dracaena (lizard), a genus of lizard
Dracena, a town in Brazil
Dracaena, a fictional dragon-woman in Percy Jackson & the Olympians
Drakaina (model), a French actress and model.

items.name: Beaucarnea pliabilis
items.growersTips:
Bring this tender Mexican shrub indoors by October to protect it from wet and freezing UK winters.
Grow in a gritty loam-based compost with fifty percent perlite to prevent root rot in damp weather.
Water only when the soil dries out completely in summer, and keep it totally dry throughout winter.
Position in your brightest south-facing window or conservatory to maximise scarce UK winter light.
Prune leggy stems back in late spring to encourage a bushier habit and stimulate fresh new growth.
items.description: Beaucarnea pliabilis is a tree in the family Asparagaceae, native to the Yucatán Peninsula. It grows up to 10 metres (30 ft) tall.

items.name: Nicotiana attenuata
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds on the soil surface in spring as they need light to germinate in cool UK climates.
Grow in poor well-drained soil to prevent excessive leafy growth and encourage better flowering.
Water sparingly once established to mimic its native dry habitat and prevent root rot in UK rain.
Watch for slugs and aphids which target young Solanaceae foliage during damp British spring weather.
Plant near night-scented stock to enhance evening fragrance and attract native UK pollinating moths.
items.description: Nicotiana attenuata is a species of wild tobacco known by the common name coyote tobacco. It is native to western North America from British Columbia to Texas and northern Mexico, where it grows in many types of habitat. It is a glandular and sparsely hairy annual herb exceeding a meter in maximum height. The leaf blades may be 10 centimetres (4 in) long, the lower ones oval and the upper narrower in shape, and are borne on petioles. The inflorescence bears several flowers with pinkish or greenish white tubular throats 2 to 3 centimetres long, their bases enclosed in pointed sepals. The flower

items.name: Maianthemum gigas
items.growersTips:
Plant in moisture-retentive, humus-rich acid to neutral soil in partial to full woodland shade.
Mulch annually in spring with leaf mould or composted bark to mimic its native forest floor.
Water weekly during dry UK summer spells to keep the soil consistently moist but never waterlogged.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit or beer traps in April.
Propagate by dividing the creeping rhizomes in early autumn after the red berries have finished.
items.description: Maianthemum gigas is a perennial flowering plant. It is found in Mexico and Central America, growing in forest openings and along roadsides or sometimes as an epiphyte on trees.

items.name: Maianthemum scilloideum
items.growersTips:
Plant in autumn at a depth of five centimetres in moisture-retentive, humus-rich acidic soil.
Position in dappled shade under deciduous trees to mimic its native cool woodland habitat.
Water weekly during dry UK spring spells to keep the soil consistently damp but never waterlogged.
Mulch annually in late winter with leaf mould to protect emerging shoots from late spring frosts.
Divide congested clumps in early autumn after foliage dies back to propagate and maintain vigour.
items.description: Maianthemum scilloideum is a perennial flowering plant. It is a terrestrial forest herb from southern Mexico and Guatemala and also reported from Honduras.

items.name: Dasylirion wheeleri
items.growersTips:
Plant in a raised bed of 50% grit and 50% loam to survive wet UK winters without rotting.
Position in full south-facing sun against a brick wall to maximize summer heat and light.
Water only during dry summer spells and keep completely dry from October through March.
Wrap the crown in fleece during prolonged freezing UK temperatures to prevent frost damage.
Prune dead lower leaves in late spring by cutting close to the trunk to maintain shape.
items.description: Dasylirion wheeleri is a species of flowering plant in the asparagus family (Asparagaceae), native to arid environments of northern Mexico and the southwestern United States.

items.name: Datura inoxia
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in March at five millimetres deep using a heated propagator to mimic warm climates.
Grow in pots of free-draining gritty compost placed in the sunniest, most sheltered patio corner.
Water deeply only when the top two inches of soil are dry, as wet UK winters will rot the roots.
Wear thick gloves when pruning dead stems in autumn to protect against highly toxic plant sap.
Move pots into a frost-free greenhouse or conservatory by October to overwinter the tender roots.
items.description: Datura innoxia, known as pricklyburr, recurved thorn-apple, downy thorn-apple, Indian-apple, lovache, moonflower, nacazcul, toloatzin, toloaxihuitl, tolguache or toloache, is a species of flowering plant in the family Solanaceae. It is more rarely called sacred datura, a common name which is applied more often to the closely related Datura wrightii. It is native to the Southwestern United States, Central and South America, and introduced in Africa, Asia, Australia and Europe. The scientific name is often cited as D. innoxia. When English botanist Philip Miller first described the species in 17

items.name: Pleomele
items.growersTips:
Grow in a heated greenhouse or conservatory as this tropical plant cannot survive UK winter frosts.
Water only when the top two inches of compost dry out to prevent root rot in cool UK light levels.
Keep in bright indirect light near a south-facing window but shade from intense midsummer midday sun.
Wipe the broad leaves with a damp cloth monthly to remove dust and prevent red spider mite attacks.
Repot in spring every two years using a free-draining peat-free loam mixed with one-third perlite.
items.description:
Pleomele is used a common name for several cultivated ornamental plants and may refer to:Species of Pleomele (genus), a former plant genus in the family Ruscaceae now included in Dracaena
Dracaena reflexa (pleomele), a widely cultivated plant previously classified in the genus Pleomele

items.name: Physalis viscosa
items.growersTips:
Plant this spreading perennial in a buried bottomless bucket to restrict its invasive underground runners.
Sow seeds indoors in March at five millimetres deep, keeping them at twenty degrees to germinate.
Water deeply once a week at the base rather than daily to prevent root rot in damp UK summers.
Apply a thick layer of straw mulch in late November to protect the crown from severe British frosts.
Watch for red spider mites under leaves when growing this plant inside a UK greenhouse or polytunnel.
items.description: Physalis viscosa is a species of flowering plant in the nightshade family known by many common names, including starhair groundcherry, stellate ground-cherry and grape groundcherry in English, and arrebenta-cavalo, balãozinho, and camambú in Portuguese and Spanish. It is native to South America, and it is known on other continents as an introduced species and sometimes a weed. It can grow in many types of habitat, including disturbed areas.

items.name: Physalis virginiana
items.growersTips:
Plant rhizomes 5cm deep in spring in well-drained sandy loam to prevent winter root rot in UK clay.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells, allowing the top 3cm of soil to dry out between.
Watch for red spider mites under leaves in dry greenhouse borders or warm south-facing UK patios.
Cut dead stems back to ground level in late autumn and mulch with leaf mould to protect from frost.
Grow in buried bottomless buckets to restrict the invasive running rhizomes from overtaking borders.
items.description: Physalis virginiana, the Virginia groundcherry, is a rhizomatous perennial with a deeply buried stem base. It is found mostly in eastern North America as far west as Wyoming.

items.name: Physalis angulata
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in March at three millimetres deep using a heated propagator set to twenty degrees.
Harden off and plant out in late May only after the very last frost in a sheltered south-facing spot.
Water consistently at the base to keep soil moist but never waterlogged to prevent split lanterns.
Grow in pots of free-draining loam-based compost to restrict root run and encourage earlier fruiting.
Watch for glasshouse red spider mite under cover and apply biological controls at the first sign.
items.description: Physalis angulata is an erect herbaceous annual plant belonging to the nightshade family Solanaceae. Its leaves are dark green and roughly ovate, often with serrate margins. The flowers are five-sided and pale yellow; the yellow-orange fruits are borne inside a balloon-like calyx. The exact native range is uncertain. The species may be naturally endemic to Australia or the Americas or the native range may encompass both the Americas and Australia. It is now widely distributed and naturalized in tropical and subtropical regions worldwide.

items.name: Schwenckia curviflora
items.growersTips:
Grow in pots using free-draining loam to easily move this tender Solanaceae indoors before frost.
Water only when the top two inches of soil dry out to prevent root rot in cool UK summers.
Position in your warmest south-facing spot or greenhouse to mimic its tropical light needs.
Prune back leggy stems by half in early spring to encourage bushy growth and more purple flowers.
Watch closely for aphids and glasshouse whitefly which target this family in humid UK conditions.
items.description: Schwenckia curviflora is a species of flowering plant in the family Solanaceae. It is native to southeastern and southern Brazil as well as southeastern Uruguay. It is a perennial plant that grows primarily in seasonally dry tropical biomes. The species belongs to the genus Schwenckia, a group of herbaceous plants and subshrubs mainly distributed in tropical regions of the Americas.

items.name: Sansevieria eilensis
items.growersTips:
Grow this slow-growing Somali succulent in a gritty, free-draining cactus mix with 50% pumice.
Keep the plant completely dry from November to March in a heated room or greenhouse above 10C.
Water only when the cylindrical, channelled leaves begin to slightly wrinkle during summer.
Position on a south-facing UK windowsill to maximise winter light and prevent rot in damp air.
Repot only every three to four years in spring, using a heavy clay pot to prevent tipping.
items.description: Dracaena eilensis, synonym Sansevieria eilensis, is a species of succulent plant native to a small region of Somalia near the town of Eyl. The species was collected in 1973 by John Lavranos.

items.name: Solanum grandiflorum
items.growersTips:
Grow in a large pot with loam-based compost so you can move it into a heated greenhouse for winter.
Water copiously in summer to support the huge leaves but keep the soil barely damp during winter.
Prune hard in early spring to control size and encourage new flowering wood on this vigorous shrub.
Watch out for glasshouse red spider mite and whitefly when overwintering this plant indoors.
Feed weekly with high-potassium tomato fertiliser from May to September to boost the blue blooms.
items.description: Solanum grandiflorum is a species of evergreen tree or treelet in the family Solanaceae. It is native to the wet lowland forests of the Amazon Basin; currently reported in Bolivia, Brazil, Colombia, Ecuador and Peru at 150–1600 meters above sea level.

items.name: Solanum myriacanthum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in warm propagators by March to counteract the short, cool UK growing season.
Wear thick leather gloves when handling this plant to protect your hands from its sharp, dense spines.
Grow in large pots of peat-free loam-based compost to easily move them under glass during wet autumns.
Water deeply at the base once the top inch of soil dries, keeping foliage dry to prevent blight.
Prune lower leaves in late August to maximize sunlight exposure and ripen the decorative berries.
items.description: Solanum myriacanthum, the Himalayan nightshade, is a species of flowering plant in the family Solanaceae. It is native to Mexico and Central America, and has been introduced to Cuba, Nepal, Assam and Myanmar. It may be invasive in the southeastern United States

items.name: Solanum pachyandrum
items.growersTips:
Grow in a heated greenhouse or south-facing conservatory to survive cool UK summer temperatures.
Sow seeds indoors in February at twenty-one degrees Celsius using a heated propagator for success.
Water deeply once a week at the base to prevent blossom end rot without wetting the foliage.
Support the heavy climbing stems using sturdy bamboo canes or a trellis system by midsummer.
Apply a high-potassium liquid tomato feed every fortnight once the first flower trusses set fruit.
items.description: Solanum pachyandrum, known as bombona, is a spine-forming vine of the Solanum genus. It is native to southwestern Ecuador and northwestern Peru where the large juicy fruit is commonly eaten and considered a treat by children. Although the plant has been known and consumed by the indigenous people of that land, it was only published scientifically in 1914 by German botanist Friedrich August Georg Bitter.

items.name: Withania riebeckii
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in early March at five millimetres deep using a heated propagator at twenty degrees
Grow in pots of gritty, free-draining loam to easily move plants indoors before first autumn frosts
Water only when the top two centimetres of soil are dry to prevent root rot in damp UK summers
Apply a high-potassium liquid tomato feed fortnightly once the first star-shaped flowers appear
Check foliage weekly for red spider mites which thrive on this plant in dry greenhouse conditions
items.description: Withania riebeckii is a species of plant in the family Solanaceae. It is endemic to the islands of Socotra and Samhah in Yemen's Socotra Archipelago. It is widespread in succulent shrubland and drought deciduous woodland from sea-level to 800 metres elevation.

items.name: Polygonatum arisanense
items.growersTips:
Plant in partial shade using humus-rich, moist, well-drained acidic soil to mimic woodland conditions.
Mulch annually in autumn with leaf mould to protect rhizomes from severe UK winter frosts.
Water consistently during dry summer spells to keep the soil evenly moist but never waterlogged.
Watch for Solomon's seal sawfly larvae in May and handpick them immediately to prevent defoliation.
Propagate by dividing the creeping rhizomes in early spring just as new growth begins to emerge.
items.description: Polygonatum arisanense is a flowering plant in the family Asparagaceae. The species is endemic to Taiwan and is found in areas around 1,500 meters in elevation. Its Chinese common name and the species epithet refer to the Alishan Range.

items.name: Physalis minima
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in March at three millimetres deep using a heated propagator to offset UK cold.
Transplant outdoors in late May only after the final frost into free-draining soil facing south.
Water the base deeply once weekly to prevent fruit splitting while keeping the foliage dry.
Construct a sturdy bamboo tripod support in June to prevent heavy fruiting stems from snapping.
Watch for glasshouse red spider mite under leaves and mist with water to raise local humidity.
items.description: Physalis angulata is an erect herbaceous annual plant belonging to the nightshade family Solanaceae. Its leaves are dark green and roughly ovate, often with serrate margins. The flowers are five-sided and pale yellow; the yellow-orange fruits are borne inside a balloon-like calyx. The exact native range is uncertain. The species may be naturally endemic to Australia or the Americas or the native range may encompass both the Americas and Australia. It is now widely distributed and naturalized in tropical and subtropical regions worldwide.

items.name: Fabiana imbricata
items.growersTips:
Plant in free-draining, acidic to neutral soil, adding grit to the planting hole to prevent rot.
Position in full sun against a south-facing wall to protect it from cold, drying UK winter winds.
Water sparingly once established, allowing the soil to dry out completely between summer waterings.
Prune lightly immediately after flowering in early summer to maintain shape and prevent legginess.
Protect young plants with horticultural fleece during severe, prolonged winter frosts below -5C.
items.description: Fabiana imbricata, vernacular names pichi, palo piche, or false heath, is a species of flowering plant in the family Solanaceae. It is native to dry upland slopes in the foothills of the southern Andes of Chile and Argentina. Growing to 2.5 m tall and wide, it is a frost-hardy, heath-like evergreen mound-forming shrub. It has needle-like leaves and small white, tubular flowers in early summer.

items.name: Physalis pubescens
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in March at 3mm depth using a heated propagator to combat cool UK spring soil.
Transplant outdoors in late May after frosts, spacing plants 50cm apart in a sheltered, sunny spot.
Water deeply at the base twice weekly during dry summer spells to prevent fruit drop and splitting.
Support the sprawling stems with a short pea brush or low trellis by July to keep husks off damp soil.
Harvest only when the papery calyx turns completely straw-coloured and drops naturally to the ground.
items.description: Physalis pubescens is a species of flowering plant in the nightshade family known by many common names, including husk tomato, low ground-cherry and hairy groundcherry in English, and muyaca and capulí in Spanish. It is native from Brazil, but also found in southern half of the United States, Mexico, Central and much of South America. It can be found elsewhere as an introduced species and sometimes a weed. It can grow in many types of habitat, including disturbed areas. This is an annual herb producing a glandular, densely hairy stem up to about 60 cm (24 in) in maximum height from a taproot.

items.name: Withania frutescens
items.growersTips:
Grow in a terracotta pot with grit-heavy compost to protect roots from wet UK winter rot.
Move the pot to a frost-free greenhouse or conservatory from November to April to survive UK cold.
Water deeply only when the top five centimetres of soil are bone dry, mimicking Mediterranean heat.
Prune back leggy stems by one third in late April to stimulate bushy new growth and more flowers.
Inspect the undersides of leaves weekly in summer for glasshouse red spider mite and whitefly pests.
items.description: Withania frutescens is a plant species belonging to the family Solanaceae. It is native to the western Mediterranean region, including southern Iberia, the Balearic Islands, Northwest Africa and the Canary Islands.

items.name: Polygonatum humile
items.growersTips:
Plant rhizomes shallowly at five centimetres deep in autumn using moisture-retentive leaf mould soil.
Water weekly during dry UK spring spells to establish the running carpet before summer dormancy.
Watch for Solomon's seal sawfly larvae in May and handpick them immediately to prevent defoliation.
Divide congested clumps in autumn after the foliage dies back to propagate and maintain plant vigour.
Plant alongside hostas and ferns in dappled shade to create a weed-suppressing woodland groundcover.
items.description: Polygonatum humile, the dwarf Solomon's-seal, is a species of plant in the family Asparagaceae. The plant is said to possess scars on the rhizome that resemble the ancient Hebrew seal of King Solomon. This is a perennial species of the genus Polygonatum native to China, Japan, Kazakhstan, Korea, Mongolia and parts of Russia.

items.name: Withania somnifera
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in early spring at five millimetres deep using a heated propagator at twenty degrees
Grow in pots of free-draining sandy loam so you can move them indoors before the first autumn frost
Water sparingly once established, allowing the compost to dry out completely between waterings
Prune back by half in late spring to encourage bushy growth and increase root yield for autumn harvest
Check regularly for red spider mites when growing under glass or in warm greenhouse conditions
items.description: Withania somnifera, known commonly as ashwagandha, is an evergreen shrub in the Solanaceae family that is native to the Middle East and North Africa, other African regions, southern Europe, Indian subcontinent, and across Southeast Asia. Several other species in the genus Withania are morphologically similar. Other common names include Indian ginseng and winter cherry.

items.name: Disporopsis
items.growersTips:
Plant in partial shade in humus-rich, moist, well-drained acidic soil to mimic UK woodland conditions.
Water weekly during dry UK summer spells to keep the soil consistently damp but never waterlogged.
Apply a five-centimetre mulch of leaf mould or well-rotted manure each spring to retain soil moisture.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using beer traps or organic wool pellets.
Propagate by dividing the creeping rhizomes in early spring just as new growth begins to show.
items.description: Disporopsis is a genus of plants in the Asparagaceae. It is native to China, Indochina and the Philippines.

items.name: Comospermum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in March at five millimetres deep using a heated propagator to beat UK chills.
Grow in a greenhouse or against a south-facing wall to maximise essential British summer sunshine.
Water deeply at the base twice a week during dry spells to prevent blossom end rot in the fruit.
Support the climbing vines with sturdy bamboo canes or a trellis as soon as active growth begins.
Apply a high-potash liquid tomato fertiliser every fortnight once the first flower trusses appear.
items.description: Comospermum is a genus of one species of flowering plant found in southern Japan. In the APG III classification system, it is placed in the family Asparagaceae, subfamily Convallarioideae.

items.name: Sansevieria stuckyi
items.growersTips:
Grow in free-draining cactus compost with added grit to prevent root rot in damp UK winter air.
Water only when the soil is bone dry, reducing to once every six weeks during dark winter months.
Keep on a south-facing windowsill to maximise limited UK sunlight and maintain a warm microclimate.
Wipe the upright cylindrical leaves with a damp cloth monthly to remove dust and improve light intake.
Repot in spring only when the thick rhizomes begin to crack or push against the sides of the pot.
items.description: Dracaena stuckyi, synonym Sansevieria stuckyi, is a species of succulent plant native to Africa including Mozambique, Tanzania, and southern Kenya. It is a member of a group of related Dracaena including Dracaena angolensis and Dracaena pearsonii, that grow upright, cylindrical foliage and are native to dry biomes.

items.name: Physalis acutifolia
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in March at 5mm deep using a heated propagator to overcome the cool UK spring.
Grow in pots of free-draining sandy loam to restrict roots and encourage early summer flowering.
Water only when the top two inches of soil are dry to prevent root rot in damp British summers.
Position in your sunniest south-facing spot or greenhouse to ensure the green husks ripen fully.
Check weekly for red spider mites and aphids which thrive on this species under glass or fleece.
items.description: Physalis acutifolia is a species of flowering plant in the nightshade family known by the common names sharpleaf groundcherry and Wright's ground-cherry. It is native to the southwestern United States from California to Texas, and northern Mexico, where it can be found in many types of habitat, including disturbed areas. It is sometimes a weed when it springs up in agricultural fields, but it is generally not weedy in wild habitat. This is an annual herb producing a branching stem up to a meter tall. The lance-shaped to oval leaves are up to 12 cm long and have edges lined with shallow, smooth

items.name: Physalis hederifolia
items.growersTips:
Plant in well-drained, gritty soil to prevent winter root rot in wet UK clay.
Sow seeds indoors in March at a depth of 6mm, keeping them at 20C before late May planting.
Water deeply once a week in summer, allowing the top 5cm of soil to dry out between waterings.
Cut back dead stems to ground level in late autumn and apply a thick straw mulch to protect roots.
Check plants weekly in June for red spider mites, which thrive in dry UK greenhouse conditions.
items.description: Physalis hederifolia is a species of flowering plant in the nightshade family known by the common name ivyleaf groundcherry. It is native to the southwestern United States and northern Mexico, where it can be found in rocky, dry desert and mountain habitat. This is a rhizomatous perennial herb producing a hairy, branching stem 10 to 80 centimeters long. The gray-green oval leaves are 2 to 4 centimeters long and have smooth or bluntly toothed edges. The flowers growing from the leaf axils are bell-shaped and just over a centimeter long. They are yellow with five brown smudges in the throats. Th

items.name: Physalis peruviana
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in early March at five millimetres deep using a heated propagator for UK warmth.
Grow in pots of poor soil to restrict root space and force the plant to produce fruit over foliage.
Water sparingly once fruit lanterns form to prevent the berries from splitting in damp UK weather.
Pinch out the growing tips in July to encourage branching and speed up ripening before autumn frosts.
Overwinter containers in a frost-free greenhouse or conservatory to get an early harvest next year.
items.description: Physalis peruviana is a species of plant in the nightshade family (Solanaceae) native to Chile and Peru. Within that region, it is called aguaymanto, uvilla or uchuva, in addition to numerous indigenous and regional names. In English, its common names include Cape gooseberry, goldenberry and Peruvian groundcherry.

items.name: Physalis walteri
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in March at five millimetres deep using a heated propagator to offset UK cold.
Plant out in late May in a south-facing border with free-draining sandy soil to prevent root rot.
Water deeply once a week at the base rather than daily sprinkles to encourage deep taproot growth.
Check weekly for red spider mites under leaves when growing in UK greenhouses or polytunnels.
Prune the stems back to ground level in late autumn and mulch heavily to protect roots from frost.
items.description: Physalis walteri, commonly known as Walter's groundcherry or dune groundcherry, is a species of flowering plant. Its native distribution is Alabama, Florida, Georgia and Virginia in the United States as well as Northeast Mexico. Its habitat is pinelands and open coastal areas.

items.name: Mandragora autumnalis
items.growersTips:
Plant in deep gritty loam to accommodate the long taproot and prevent winter wet rot in UK soils.
Sow fresh seeds in autumn and expose them to winter cold outdoors to break their natural dormancy.
Position in full sun but protect the delicate autumn blooms from heavy rain using a cloche.
Water sparingly in summer during their dormant phase to mimic their native dry Mediterranean climate.
Protect young foliage from slugs and snails which are highly attracted to the toxic leaves in spring.
items.description: Mandragora autumnalis, known as mandrake or autumn mandrake, is recognized by some sources as a separate species from Mandragora officinarum, although with different circumscriptions. Others regard it as merely part of this very variable species. Plants given the name Mandragora autumnalis consist of a rosette of leaves up to 60 cm (2 ft) across, close to the ground, with a central group of usually purplish flowers followed by yellow or orange berries. The large tap-roots as well as the leaves contain alkaloids and are toxic. They have traditional uses as herbal medicines.

items.name: Physalis crassifolia
items.growersTips:
Grow this desert native in a terracotta pot using free-draining sandy loam to prevent winter rot.
Sow seeds indoors in March at five millimetres deep using a heated propagator set to twenty degrees.
Water only when the top five centimetres of soil is bone dry to mimic its arid natural habitat.
Overwinter pots indoors or in a heated greenhouse as this species cannot survive wet UK frosts.
Prune back leggy stems by half in early spring to encourage bushy growth and more lantern fruits.
items.description: Physalis crassifolia is a species of flowering plant in the nightshade family known by the common names yellow nightshade groundcherry and thick-leaf ground-cherry. It is native to the southwestern United States and northern Mexico, where it can be found in rocky, dry desert and mountain habitat. This is a perennial herb producing a ridged, angular, branching stem approaching 80 cm long, taking a clumped, matted, or erect form. The fleshy oval leaves are 1 to 3 cm long and have smooth, wavy, or bluntly toothed edges. The herbage is glandular and coated in short hairs. The yellow flowers growin

items.name: Withania coagulans
items.growersTips:
Grow in a heated greenhouse or indoors as this tender shrub cannot survive UK winter frosts.
Sow seeds in spring at a depth of five millimetres using a heated propagator set to twenty degrees.
Water sparingly only when the top two inches of sandy, free-draining soil mix have dried out completely.
Prune lightly in late spring to maintain a bushy shape and encourage new berry-bearing growth.
Monitor indoor plants closely for red spider mites and whiteflies in dry summer conditions.
items.description: Withania coagulans is a plant in the Solanaceae or nightshade family, native to Afghanistan and the Indian subcontinent. Within the genus Withania, W. somnifera (Ashwagandha) and W. coagulans are economically significant, and are cultivated in several regions for their use in Ayurveda. It is claimed to help control diabetes. The berries contain a rennet-like protease that can be used to clot milk for cheese production. The plant is prone to leaf spot disease caused by Alternaria alternata.

items.name: Speirantha gardenii
items.growersTips:
Plant in early spring in rich, moisture-retentive soil, burying the root crown exactly 5cm deep.
Water deeply once a week at the base during dry UK summer spells to prevent blossom end rot.
Watch for potato beetles and aphids from June; handpick them or use organic insecticidal soap.
Prune lower yellowing leaves in late August to improve air circulation and speed up fruit ripening.
Grow alongside basil or marigolds to naturally deter pests and boost pollination in UK plots.
items.description: Speirantha is a genus of one known species of flowering plants found in south-east China. In the APG III classification system, it is placed in the family Asparagaceae, subfamily Convallarioideae.

items.name: Eggplant
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in warm propagators by early March to ensure a long enough growing season in the UK.
Grow plants in a greenhouse or polytunnel as UK outdoor summers are rarely warm enough for success.
Pinch out the main growing tip when the plant reaches thirty centimetres to encourage bushy growth.
Limit each plant to four or five fruits and remove later flowers to ensure the remaining crop ripens.
Water the compost consistently to keep it moist and mist the foliage daily to deter red spider mites.
items.description: Eggplant, aubergine, brinjal, or baigan is a plant species in the nightshade family Solanaceae. Solanum melongena is grown worldwide for its edible fruit, typically used as a vegetable in cooking.

items.name: Scopolia japonica
items.growersTips:
Plant in partial shade in humus-rich, moist, well-drained alkaline soil to mimic woodland conditions.
Sow seeds in cold frames in autumn, as they require winter chilling to break dormancy for spring.
Water consistently during the spring growing phase, but keep the soil drier during summer dormancy.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.
Wear thick gloves when handling this highly toxic plant to prevent skin absorption of alkaloids.
items.description: Scopolia japonica, also Japanese belladonna or Korean scopolia, is a flowering plant species in the genus Scopolia - one of the eight genera in tribe Hyoscyameae of the nightshade family Solanaceae.

items.name: Sansevieria ehrenbergii
items.growersTips:
Grow in gritty cactus compost with fifty percent perlite to prevent root rot in damp UK winters.
Water only when soil is bone dry, reducing to once every two months from November through March.
Keep on a south-facing windowsill to maximise limited UK sunlight and maintain a warm microclimate.
Protect from drafts and ensure indoor temperatures never drop below twelve degrees Celsius in winter.
Repot only when the fan-shaped leaves literally begin to crack or push out of the plastic pot.
items.description: Dracaena hanningtonii, synonym Sansevieria ehrenbergii, is a flowering plant which grows in northeastern and eastern tropical Africa and the Arabian Peninsula. It occurs notably in proliferation along the Olduvai Gorge in northern Tanzania.

items.name: Saint George's Sword
items.growersTips:
Position on a bright UK windowsill but keep dry in winter to prevent root rot in unheated rooms
Plant in a free-draining mix of two parts peat-free compost to one part grit or perlite
Only water when the compost has completely dried out to cope with cool and damp UK climates
Wipe the broad leaves with a damp cloth monthly to remove dust and improve light absorption
Repot in spring only when the roots start cracking the plastic pot as they prefer being tight
items.description: Dracaena trifasciata is a species of flowering plant in the family Asparagaceae, native to tropical West Africa from Nigeria east to the Congo. It is most commonly known as the snake plant, Saint George's sword, mother-in-law's tongue, and viper's bowstring hemp, among other names. Until 2017, it was known under the synonym Sansevieria trifasciata. This plant is often kept as a houseplant due to its non-demanding maintenance; they can survive with very little water and sun.

items.name: Physalis pruinosa
items.growersTips:
Sow indoors in March at 5mm deep using a heated propagator to overcome cool UK spring temperatures.
Grow in pots of peat-free compost on a south-facing patio to maximise essential summer sun and heat.
Water consistently at the base to prevent split fruit, avoiding overhead watering to stop blight.
Support the sprawling, brittle stems with a short cane teepee as the heavy fruit trusses develop.
Harvest only when the papery husks turn completely straw-coloured and drop naturally to the ground.
items.description: Physalis pruinosa is a plant in the genus Physalis in the nightshade family Solanaceae, often referred to as ground cherry or husk tomato. It is a native species in a range extending from northern Mexico through Central America. The plant has a low, spreading habit, and fruits develop in a papery husk, as is characteristic of the genus. While most parts of the plant are toxic to humans due to the presence of solanine and solanidine, the fruit becomes edible once it has ripened to yellow. The fruit's flavor is similar in some respects to that of a ripe tomatillo, but notably has a strong flavor

items.name: Physalis heterophylla
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in March at 6mm deep using a heated propagator to overcome the cool UK spring.
Plant out in late May in a sheltered, south-facing spot with free-draining, low-nitrogen soil.
Water deeply once a week at the base rather than daily to prevent root rot in damp British summers.
Check regularly for red spider mites under leaves when growing in a UK greenhouse or polytunnel.
Prune the growing tips in July to restrict vegetative growth and force energy into ripening husks.
items.description: Physalis heterophylla, colloquial name clammy groundcherry, is species of herbaceous plant in the family Solanaceae. It is native to North America, occurring primarily in the eastern United States and Canada. It is known to occur in all contiguous states except for Nevada and California. It is found mainly in habitats such as dry or mesic prairies, gravel hills and rises, sandy or rocky soils, and waste places such as roadsides.

items.name: Downy Solomon's seal
items.growersTips:
Plant in autumn at a depth of five centimetres in moisture-retentive, humus-rich soil in deep shade.
Water weekly during dry spring spells to establish rhizomes, keeping the soil damp but not sodden.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.
Cut the yellowing stems back to ground level in late autumn once the foliage has completely died.
Divide congested clumps in early spring just as the new growth buds begin to show above the soil.
items.description: Polygonatum pubescens, the hairy Solomon's seal or downy Solomon's seal, is a species of flowering plant in the family Asparagaceae, native to the north-central and eastern US and eastern Canada. It is a forest gap specialist.

items.name: Anthotroche myoporoides
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender Australian shrub in a container to overwinter indoors when UK temperatures drop.
Plant in a free-draining loam-based compost mixed with plenty of grit to prevent winter root rot.
Position in your sunniest south-facing spot or unheated greenhouse to maximise essential summer heat.
Water sparingly once established, allowing the top five centimetres of soil to dry out completely.
Prune lightly in late spring after frost risk passes to maintain a compact shape and boost growth.
items.description: Anthotroche myoporoides is a plant species in the family Solanaceae, native to Western Australia. It was first described in 1943 by Charles Gardner.

items.name: Anthotroche pannosa
items.growersTips:
Grow in a gritty, free-draining loam-based compost mix inside a terracotta pot to prevent root rot.
Position in the sunniest unheated greenhouse or conservatory to survive damp UK winters and frost.
Water only when the soil dries out completely, reducing to once a month from November to March.
Prune lightly in late spring after flowering to maintain its compact, woolly shrub shape.
Monitor closely for aphids and glasshouse whitefly which target the dense, felted silver foliage.
items.description: Anthotroche pannosa is an erect or sprawling shrub in the family Solanaceae. It is found in Western Australia.

items.name: Reineckea carnea
items.growersTips:
Sow Reineckea seeds indoors in early March at a depth of six millimetres using a heated propagator.
Keep soil consistently damp but never soggy to prevent damping off in cool British spring weather.
Apply a high-potassium liquid feed every fortnight once the first yellow flowers begin to open.
Watch for tomato hornworms and aphids under leaves during humid UK midsummer afternoons.
Stake the main stem early with a bamboo cane to support heavy fruit during wet and windy Augusts.
items.description: Reineckea is a genus of plants in the Convallarioideae. Several species names have been proposed within the genus, but only one is widely accepted: Reineckea carnea, native to China and Japan.

items.name: Solomon's seal
items.growersTips:
Plant rhizomes 10cm deep in autumn in moisture-retentive, humus-rich soil in partial or full shade.
Water weekly during dry spring spells to establish strong stems before the summer canopy closes.
Check leaves daily in May for Solomon's seal sawfly larvae and handpick them to prevent defoliation.
Cut the dying stems back to ground level in late autumn after the foliage turns yellow and papery.
Mulch annually in March with leaf mould or well-rotted manure to mimic a damp UK woodland floor.
items.description: Polygonatum multiflorum, the Solomon's seal, David's harp, ladder-to-heaven or Eurasian Solomon's seal, is a species of flowering plant in the family Asparagaceae, native to Europe and temperate Asia. In Britain it is one of three native species of the genus, the others being P. odoratum and P. verticillatum.

items.name: Calibanus hookeri
items.growersTips:
Grow in a heated greenhouse or indoors as it is a Mexican succulent, not a Solanaceae vegetable.
Use a gritty, free-draining cactus compost with fifty percent perlite to prevent caudex rot.
Water thoroughly only when the soil is bone dry, keeping it completely dry throughout winter.
Position in the brightest south-facing window or greenhouse spot to mimic its desert habitat.
Watch for mealybugs hiding in the dense, grass-like foliage clumps and treat with isopropyl alcohol.
items.description: One of only two species in its genus, Calibanus hookeri is a member of the family Asparagaceae native to Tamaulipas in Mexico, which can easily be mistaken in the wild for a boulder overgrown with grass tufts.

items.name: Sansevieria masoniana
items.growersTips:
Grow in a heavy clay pot with gritty, free-draining cacti compost to prevent top-heavy tipping.
Water only when the soil is bone dry, reducing to once every six weeks during damp UK winters.
Position in bright, indirect light near a south window, keeping temperatures strictly above 10C.
Wipe the single large leaf monthly with a damp cloth to remove dust and maximise winter light.
Propagate in spring by dividing the rhizome with a sterile knife, leaving one leaf per section.
items.description: Dracaena masoniana, synonym Sansevieria masoniana, is a species of Dracaena native to Africa and originally collected in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. It was initially known in cultivation under the cultivar name 'Mason Congo'. Commonly grown as a houseplant for its striking foliage, it can survive in bright filtered light or shade and with infrequent watering. Often grown as a single large, stiff leaf in pots, the plant's other common names include "whale fin" or "shark's fin".

items.name: Mini angel's trumpet
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in early March at five millimetres deep using a heated propagator for UK warmth.
Grow in pots of peat-free compost with added grit to ensure the sharp drainage this plant requires.
Water only when the top two inches of soil are dry to prevent root rot in cool British summers.
Overwinter containers in a frost-free greenhouse or conservatory as this species cannot survive frost.
Watch for glasshouse whitefly and red spider mite when growing under glass in the UK climate.
items.description: Eriolarynx australis, called mini angel's trumpet or blue angel's trumpet, is a species of flowering plant in the genus Eriolarynx, native to Bolivia and northwest Argentina. It is widely listed in the horticultural literature under the synonym Iochroma australe. It has gained the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit.

items.name: Arborescent sansevieria
items.growersTips:
Bring indoors before October frosts as this tender African plant cannot survive wet UK winters.
Grow in a heavy terracotta pot with 50% grit to prevent root rot in damp British humidity.
Water only once a month from November to March keeping the compost almost entirely dry.
Position on a south-facing windowsill to maximise limited winter sunlight in the UK.
Repot in spring only when roots crack the pot as they thrive when tightly bound.
items.description: Dracaena arborescens, synonym Sansevieria arborescens, is a succulent plant native to Kenya and Tanzania.

items.name: Sansevieria bagamoyensis
items.growersTips:
Grow in a heated greenhouse or indoors as this tender African succulent cannot survive UK winters.
Water only when the gritty compost dries out completely to prevent root rot in damp UK climates.
Provide bright indirect light on a south-facing windowsill to mimic its native tropical habitat.
Use a free-draining cactus mix with added perlite or grit to ensure excellent drainage in pots.
Repot in spring only when the plant becomes root-bound to encourage upright stem growth.
items.description: Dracaena bagamoyensis, synonym Sansevieria bagamoyensis, also known as snake plant is a succulent plant native to Kenya and Tanzania.

items.name: Physalis infinemundi
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in early March at five millimetres deep using a heated propagator at twenty degrees.
Grow in pots of peat-free loam-based compost to easily move plants indoors before autumn frosts hit.
Water consistently at the base to keep soil damp but never soggy to prevent root rot in cool summers.
Pinch out the growing tips in June to encourage bushy growth and increase the yield of lantern fruit.
Watch for glasshouse whitefly and red spider mite when growing under glass in humid UK midsummers.
items.description: Physalis infinemundi is an extinct species of the genus Physalis known from two fossilised fruit found in the Laguna del Hunco Formation of Chubut Province, Argentina dating to the Eocene, around 52 million years old. The species name derives from "in fine mundi" means "at the end of the earth" referring to the fact that it grew in the far south. The fossil was considerably older than the diversification ages predicted by previous molecular clock studies of Solanaceae, which estimated that the family as a whole originated 30 million years ago. The fossils are very similar to modern Physalis sp

items.name: Polygonatum biflorum
items.growersTips:
Plant rhizomes shallowly at five centimetres deep in autumn using humus-rich moisture-retentive soil.
Water weekly during dry UK spring spells to establish roots before the summer canopy closes in.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.
Cut yellowing stems back to ground level in late autumn after the foliage dies back naturally.
Divide congested clumps in early spring just as new growth buds begin to show above the soil.
items.description: Polygonatum biflorum is an herbaceous flowering plant native to eastern and central North America. The plant is said to possess scars on the rhizome that resemble the ancient Hebrew seal of King Solomon. It is often confused with Solomon's plume, which has upright flowers.

items.name: Polygonatum ×hybridum
items.growersTips:
Plant rhizomes shallowly at five centimetres deep in autumn using humus-rich, moist, acid-to-neutral soil.
Water deeply during dry UK spring spells to keep the woodland soil consistently damp but not soggy.
Check leaves daily in May for sawfly larvae and pick them off immediately to prevent defoliation.
Cut the dying stems back to ground level in late autumn once the foliage turns yellow and collapses.
Mulch annually in late winter with leaf mould to mimic a natural forest floor and retain moisture.
items.description: Polygonatum × hybridum, the garden Solomon's-seal, is a hybrid flowering plant, which is a cross between common Solomon's-seal and angular Solomon's-seal.

items.name: Solanum galapagense
items.growersTips:
Start seeds indoors in February using a heated propagator to mimic the warm Galapagos climate.
Grow in a greenhouse or polytunnel as UK summers are too cold and wet for outdoor success.
Water sparingly once fruit sets to prevent the small orange tomatoes from splitting in damp air.
Prune lower foliage in August to maximize sunlight penetration and airflow in humid UK weather.
Support the sprawling, highly branched wild habit using a sturdy multi-stem stake or cage system.
items.description: Solanum galapagense is a wild tomato in the family Solanaceae section Lycopersicon and is one of two tomato species endemic to the Galápagos Islands, 500 miles west of Ecuador.

items.name: Solanum esuriale
items.growersTips:
Grow this Australian native in a terracotta pot with 50% grit to survive wet UK winters outdoors.
Position in your sunniest south-facing spot or unheated greenhouse to meet its high heat requirement.
Water deeply only when the top five centimetres of soil are bone dry, then leave to dry out again.
Prune back the dieback in late spring once new shoots appear at the base to keep the habit tidy.
Sow seeds in early spring using a heated propagator set to 22 degrees Celsius to trigger germination.
items.description: Solanum esuriale is a species of perennial herbaceous plant native to Australia.

items.name: Solanum ditrichum
items.growersTips:
Plant this tender perennial in a deep container to easily move it indoors before first autumn frosts.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells, allowing the top two inches of soil to dry out.
Prune back leggy stems by one third in early spring to encourage bushy growth and more flowers.
Incorporate grit into heavy UK clay soil to ensure the sharp drainage this root-rot prone plant needs.
Watch for aphids on new spring shoots and wash them off with a sharp blast of water from the hose.
items.description: Solanum ditrichum, commonly called forest nightshade, is a low growing herbaceous perennial native to the east coast of Australia, found north of Dungog on the coast and tablelands.

items.name: Fabiana patagonica
items.growersTips:
Plant in free-draining gravelly loam in full sun to mimic its native dry Andean slopes.
Protect from wet UK winters by planting against a south-facing wall or in a container moved indoors.
Water sparingly once established, allowing the soil to dry out completely between waterings.
Prunt lightly after flowering in late summer to maintain its compact, heather-like shape.
Propagate via semi-ripe cuttings in late summer using a gritty, low-nutrient compost mix.
items.description: Fabiana patagonica is a species of plant in the nightshade family, native to Patagonia. This plant species is native to South America.

items.name: Physalis longifolia
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in March at five millimetres deep using bottom heat of twenty degrees Celsius.
Plant out in late May in a sun-baked, south-facing border with poor, sharply draining soil.
Water sparingly once established to restrict leafy growth and encourage heavy fruit production.
Erect a sturdy stake early to support the brittle, sprawling stems against strong UK winds.
Apply a thick straw mulch in late autumn to protect the underground rhizomes from wet winter rot.
items.description: Physalis longifolia, known by the common names common groundcherry, longleaf groundcherry, and wild tomatillo, is a species of flowering plant in the nightshade family, Solanaceae. It is native to North America, where it is native to eastern Canada, much of the continental United States, and northern Mexico. It has also been noted as an introduced species in other regions, including parts of the United States outside its native range. In some areas, such as California, it is an occasional noxious weed.

items.name: Sansevieria pinguicula
items.growersTips:
Grow in a gritty, free-draining cactus mix with fifty percent pumice to prevent winter root rot.
Keep dry at room temperature in winter and only water when the rosette leaves begin to wrinkle.
Place on a south-facing windowsill to maximise limited UK winter sunlight and maintain variegation.
Propagate by letting aerial stolons touch the soil surface in spring to root before cutting free.
Maintain indoor temperatures above twelve degrees Celsius to prevent cold-induced collapse and rot.
items.description: Dracaena pinguicula, synonym Sansevieria pinguicula, also known as the walking sansevieria, is a xerophytic CAM succulent native to the Bura area of Kenya, near Garissa. The species was described by Peter René Oscar Bally in 1943.

items.name: Semele androgyna
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in March at ten millimetres deep using bottom heat of twenty-one degrees Celsius.
Grow in a greenhouse or polytunnel as this Solanaceae crop demands more summer heat than UK climates.
Water deeply at the base twice weekly to keep soil moist but prevent blight on the foliage.
Support the climbing vines with sturdy bamboo canes or trellis as soon as active growth begins.
Apply a high-potassium liquid tomato feed every fortnight once the first flowers start to open.
items.description: In Greek mythology, Semele, or Thyone, was the youngest daughter of Cadmus and Harmonia, and the mother of Dionysus by Zeus.

items.name: Sansevieria kirkii
items.growersTips:
Keep this Sansevieria dry in winter by watering only when the potting mix has completely dried out.
Grow in a free-draining mix of two parts pumice to one part peat-free compost to prevent root rot.
Position on a bright south-facing windowsill but shade from intense midsummer afternoon sun.
Maintain indoor temperatures above 10C in winter to prevent cold damage and scarring on leaves.
Repot in spring only when the thick rhizomes begin to crack or distort the plastic nursery pot.
items.description: Dracaena pethera, synonym Sansevieria kirkii, also known as the star sansevieria or the snake plant, is a succulent plant native to Tanzania and the surrounding region in East Africa.

items.name: Physalis coztomatl
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in March at five millimetres deep using a heated propagator set to twenty degrees.
Grow in pots of peat-free compost with added grit to ensure the sharp drainage this species needs.
Move plants to a sunny greenhouse or south-facing patio only after all risk of May frosts has passed.
Water sparingly once established to prevent root rot and encourage the development of sweet fruit.
Watch for glasshouse whitefly and red spider mite when growing under glass in the humid UK summer.
items.description: Physalis coztomatl is a plant species in the genus Physalis. It produces edible orange-yellow fruits, but is rarely cultivated. The leaves are oval-shaped. It is native to America; the Aztecs used it medicinally. It contains labdane diterpenes, and was the first species in Physalis in which they were found.

items.name: Sansevieria cylindrica
items.growersTips:
Keep this African succulent in a free-draining cactus compost mix with added grit to prevent rot.
Water only when the soil is bone dry, reducing this to once every six weeks during UK winters.
Position on a south-facing windowsill to maximise light, as UK overcast days slow its growth.
Maintain indoor temperatures above 12C to protect this tender plant from cold draughts and shock.
Wipe the cylindrical leaves with a damp cloth monthly to remove dust and improve photosynthesis.
items.description: Dracaena angolensis, commonly known as African spear or the spear sansevieria, is a succulent plant native to Angola in Southern Africa. For years, it was placed within the genus Sansevieria (snake-plants), a specific name which is still used synonymously by some; in the 21st century, Sansevieria became part of Dracaena (dragon-trees), after improved testing methods, physical comparisons, and other analyses found sufficient commonalities between the two genera to warrant subsumption.

items.name: Solanum wendlandii
items.growersTips:
Grow in a large pot of peat-free loam-based compost so you can move it indoors before first autumn frost
Provide a sturdy trellis or wires to support the vigorous, scrambling stems armed with sharp thorns
Water deeply once a week in summer, allowing the top two inches of gritty soil to dry out completely
Prune hard in late winter to healthy buds to control size and encourage fresh flowering wood
Watch for glasshouse whitefly and red spider mite when overwintering in a heated conservatory
items.description: Solanum wendlandii, the giant potato creeper, potato vine, Costa Rican nightshade, divorce vine, or paradise flower, is a species of flowering plant in the family Solanaceae. It is native to Mexico, Central America, and northwest South America, and has been widely introduced as an ornamental to other tropical locales, including the Caribbean, Africa, Nepal, Java, and many islands in the Indian and Pacific Oceans. A robust vine reaching 15 ft (4.6 m), its long-lasting dark purple flowers eventually fade to white.

items.name: Tobacco weed
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender shrub in a large pot so you can move it into a frost-free greenhouse for winter.
Prune hard in early spring to encourage vigorous new growth and keep its rapid spread contained.
Wear gloves and a mask when handling to avoid irritation from the fine, dusty hairs on the leaves.
Water deeply once a week in summer, allowing the top two inches of gritty, free-draining soil to dry.
Check foliage weekly for aphids and glasshouse red spider mite when overwintering indoors.
items.description: Solanum mauritianum is a small tree or shrub native to South America, including Northern Argentina, Southern Brazil, Paraguay and Uruguay. Its common names include earleaf nightshade, woolly nightshade, flannel weed, bugweed, tobacco weed, tobacco bush, wild tobacco and kerosene plant.

items.name: Solanum laxum
items.growersTips:
Plant against a south or west-facing wall in fertile, well-drained soil to survive UK winter frosts.
Prune hard in early spring by cutting back overgrown stems to a strong framework to boost summer bloom.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells rather than giving daily light sprinkles.
Tie new shoots regularly to a sturdy trellis or wires as this scrambler lacks self-clinging tendrils.
Apply a thick layer of organic mulch around the base in November to protect roots from freezing soil.
items.description: Solanum laxum, commonly known as potato vine, potato climber or jasmine nightshade, is an evergreen vine in the family Solanaceae. It is native to South America and commonly grown as an ornamental garden plant.

items.name: 'Solanum pyracanthon' Jacq. (1804)
items.growersTips:
Grow in a large pot of loam-based compost so you can move it into a heated greenhouse for UK winters.
Water sparingly in winter but keep soil consistently moist during the active summer growing season.
Wear thick leather gloves when pruning in spring to protect your hands from the sharp orange thorns.
Position in the sunniest, most sheltered south-facing spot possible to encourage summer flowering.
Check regularly for aphids and red spider mites which thrive on this plant in dry conservatory air.
items.description: Solanum pyracanthos, also known as the porcupine tomato, is an evergreen shrub native to tropical Madagascar. It belongs to the genus Solanum, a diverse and cosmopolitan genus with over 1,500 species including the tomato, potato, and eggplant.

items.name: Chamaesaracha sordida
items.growersTips:
Grow in gritty, sharply draining neutral soil to prevent winter root rot in wet UK climates.
Sow seeds in autumn and leave pots outdoors to experience natural winter chilling for germination.
Plant in your warmest, south-facing border or against a sunny wall to mimic its native dry habitat.
Water sparingly only during dry summer spells, letting the soil dry out completely between waterings.
Protect young spring shoots from slugs and snails which target tender Solanaceae growth in damp UKs.
items.description: Chamaesaracha is a genus of perennial herbs in the nightshade family which are known commonly as five eyes. There are around nine species of five eyes, and they are native to the southwestern and western United States and parts of Mexico. These are hairy plants growing low to the ground and covered in crinkly dull green leaves. The flowers are star-shaped to wheel-shaped and their dried remnants can be found around the fruits, which are spherical berries filled with flat, kidney-shaped seeds.

items.name: Solanum pseudocapsicum
items.growersTips:
Bring indoors to a frost-free windowsill by October as this tender shrub cannot survive UK winters.
Water thoroughly when the top inch of soil dries out, but reduce watering in winter to avoid rot.
Hand-pollinate indoor spring flowers with a soft brush to ensure a heavy crop of autumn berries.
Prune stems back by half in early spring to maintain a bushy shape and encourage fresh fruiting wood.
Watch for aphids and red spider mites when keeping this plant in dry, heated indoor winter air.
items.description: Solanum pseudocapsicum is a nightshade species with mildly poisonous fruit. It is commonly known as the Jerusalem cherry, Madeira winter cherry, or, ambiguously, "winter cherry". These perennials can be grown decoratively as house plants, but in some areas of South Africa, India, Australia and New Zealand it is regarded as a weed.

items.name: Border grass
items.growersTips:
Cut back old foliage hard to the ground in March to allow fresh new growth to emerge undamaged.
Plant in well-drained soil as wet UK winters will rot the crown if the ground remains waterlogged.
Watch for slugs and snails in damp spring weather as they love to eat the emerging new flower spikes.
Divide congested clumps in spring to propagate and maintain the plant's vigorous flowering habit.
Plant alongside autumn-flowering cyclamen or ferns for excellent dry shade tolerance in UK gardens.
items.description: Liriope muscari is a species of flowering plant from East Asia. Common names in English include big blue lilyturf, lilyturf, border grass, and monkey grass. This small herbaceous perennial has grass-like evergreen foliage and lilac-purple flowers which produce single-seeded berries on a spike in the fall. In some parts of the United States, it is an invasive species.

items.name: Bad woman
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in March at five millimetres deep using bottom heat to mimic warm native soils.
Grow this prickly annual in terracotta pots to restrict roots and prevent invasive garden spreading.
Water only when the top two inches of soil dry out to prevent root rot in damp UK summers.
Wear thick leather gauntlets when handling to protect your hands from the extremely sharp spines.
Plant alongside marigolds to deter whiteflies and aphids which are highly attracted to this host.
