items.description: Solanum rostratum is a species of nightshade that is native to the United States and northern and central Mexico. Common names include buffalobur nightshade, buffalo-bur, spiny nightshade, Colorado bur, Kansas thistle, bad woman, Mexican thistle, and Texas thistle.

items.name: Bar-room plant
items.growersTips:
Position the plant in a draft-free, north-facing room to mimic its natural deep shade habitat.
Water only when the top five centimetres of compost are dry to prevent root rot in damp UK winters.
Wipe the broad leaves with a damp cloth monthly to remove dust and prevent red spider mite attacks.
Repot every three years in spring using a peat-free loam-based compost with added grit for drainage.
Feed monthly from April to September with a weak liquid seaweed fertilizer to boost slow growth.
items.description: Aspidistra elatior, the cast-iron-plant or bar-room plant, also known in Japanese as haran or baran (葉蘭) is a species of flowering plant in the family Asparagaceae, native to Japan and Taiwan. Tolerant of neglect, it is widely cultivated as a houseplant, but can also be grown outside in shade where temperatures remain above −15 °C (5 °F). It is used as training material for the seika form of ikebana.

items.name: Jaltomata lojae
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in March at five millimetres deep using a heated propagator set to twenty degrees.
Grow in large pots of peat-free compost in a sunny greenhouse to protect from cool UK summer nights.
Water consistently at the base to keep soil damp but not soggy to prevent blossom end rot in pots.
Support the sprawling stems with a sturdy tripod of bamboo canes as the heavy green berries develop.
Watch closely for aphids and glasshouse whitefly, using yellow sticky traps to catch them early.
items.description: Jaltomata lojae is a plant species native to Peru and Ecuador.

items.name: Scopolia carniolica
items.growersTips:
Plant in autumn in moisture-retentive, humus-rich soil under deciduous trees to mimic woodland shade.
Sow seeds in cold frames during UK winter as they require a prolonged cold period to trigger growth.
Keep soil consistently damp during spring but allow it to dry slightly when the plant goes dormant.
Wear thick gloves when handling this highly toxic plant to avoid absorbing alkaloids through skin.
Watch for slugs and snails in early spring as they target the emerging bell-shaped purple flowers.
items.description: Scopolia carniolica, the European scopolia or henbane bell, is a poisonous plant belonging to tribe Hyoscyameae of the nightshade family Solanaceae. It bears dark brownish-violet nodding flowers on long, slender pedicels. It grows to 60 centimetres (24 in) in height. Its toxicity derives from its high levels of tropane alkaloids, particularly atropine. The concentration of atropine is highest in the roots.

items.name: Winter cherry
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in March at five millimetres deep using a heated propagator set to twenty degrees.
Grow in pots of free-draining sandy loam so you can move them into a greenhouse before autumn frosts.
Water sparingly once established, allowing the top two inches of compost to dry out between drinks.
Watch for greenhouse whitefly and red spider mite, treating early with organic insecticidal soap.
Harvest the roots in October of the second year after the berries turn bright red and leaves yellow.
items.description: Withania is a genus of flowering plants in the nightshade family, Solanaceae, with 19 to 23 species that are native to parts of North Africa, western Asia, south Asia, southern Europe, the Mediterranean, and the Canary Islands. Withania was initially included within Physalis by Linnaeus in 1753 but has since become its own genus. This grouping was due to the shared feature of an inflated calyx that surrounds and protects the fruit.

items.name: Jaltomata procumbens
items.growersTips:
Start seeds indoors in warm propagators in March to combat the cool UK spring before outdoor planting.
Plant out in late May after frosts pass into free-draining soil enriched with well-rotted manure.
Water deeply at the base twice weekly during dry summer spells to prevent blossom end rot in fruit.
Support the sprawling brittle stems with sturdy pea sticks or a low trellis to keep fruit off soil.
Watch for potato aphids and flea beetles in June, using physical barriers or insecticidal soap.
items.description: Jaltomata procumbens, the creeping false holly, is a plant species native to Arizona, USA, Mexico, Central America, Colombia, Ecuador, and Venezuela. It grows as a weed in agricultural fields and other disturbed locations, but in many places the people protect it because of the edible fruits it produces.

items.name: Nothocestrum latifolium
items.growersTips:
Grow this rare Hawaiian native in a heated greenhouse or conservatory to survive cool UK summers.
Plant seeds 5mm deep in a well-draining, peat-free compost mix with added perlite for drainage.
Water only when the top two inches of soil dry out to prevent root rot in damp British winters.
Inspect leaves regularly for glasshouse whitefly and spider mites, common pests in UK indoor setups.
Feed fortnightly in spring and summer with a high-potassium liquid tomato fertiliser to aid growth.
items.description: Nothocestrum latifolium, commonly known as broadleaf ʻaiea, is a species of flowering plant in the nightshade family, Solanaceae, that is endemic to Hawaiʻi. It can be found in dry and mesic forests at elevations of 460–1,530 m (1,510–5,020 ft) on the islands of Maui, Molokaʻi, Lānaʻi, Oʻahu, and Kauaʻi. Broadleaf ʻaiea is threatened by habitat loss. The CDP of ʻAiea on Oʻahu was named after this species.

items.name: Jaltomata chihuahuensis
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in March at five millimetres deep using a heated propagator to mimic Mexican heat.
Grow in pots under glass or against a south-facing wall to protect from cool UK summer nights.
Water consistently at the base to prevent blossom end rot, keeping the compost damp but not soggy.
Watch for glasshouse whitefly and red spider mite, treating early with biological controls.
Support the sprawling Solanaceae stems with canes as the heavy green-to-black berries develop.
items.description: Jaltomata chihuahuensis is a plant species native to the Mexican States of Chihuahua and Durango.

items.name: Tzeltalia amphitricha
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in March at five millimetres deep using a heated propagator set to twenty degrees
Grow in a greenhouse or polytunnel to provide the high heat and humidity this Mexican native needs
Water consistently at the base to keep soil damp but never waterlogged to prevent root rot issues
Support the sprawling stems with canes or a small trellis as the heavy lantern fruits develop
Watch for glasshouse whitefly and red spider mite under glass and use biological controls early
items.description: Tzeltalia is a genus of flowering plants belonging to the family Solanaceae.

items.name: Solanum prinophyllum
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender Australian native in a pot of gritty loam to move indoors before first autumn frost.
Water deeply once a week in summer, allowing the top two inches of soil to dry out between waterings.
Prune back leggy stems by one third in early spring to promote bushy growth and more purple flowers.
Wear thick gloves when handling to protect your hands from the sharp yellow spines on stems and leaves.
Watch for aphids and glasshouse red spider mite when overwintering the plant in a heated greenhouse.
items.description: Solanum prinophyllum, known as the forest nightshade or Grin Whiskers, is a accepted species of small plant native to the east coast of East Victoria to Southeast Queensland, Australia. S. prinophyllum is a short lived herb, annual or perennial.

items.name: Solanum pungetium
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in warm propagators during March to counter the cool UK spring temperatures.
Plant out in late May after the final frost in well-drained soil enriched with organic compost.
Water deeply at the base twice a week during dry summer spells to prevent blossom end rot.
Stake the heavy fruiting stems by mid-July to prevent them from snapping in strong UK winds.
Apply a high-potassium liquid tomato feed every fortnight once the first flower trusses set.
items.description: Solanum pungetium, known as the eastern nightshade is a small, low spreading plant native to the east coast of Australia.

items.name: Solanum quadriloculatum
items.growersTips:
Overwinter this tender Australian native indoors as it will not survive UK frosts below five degrees.
Grow in pots of free-draining sandy loam to prevent root rot during wet British summers and autumns.
Wear thick gloves when pruning in spring to protect your hands from its sharp, dense yellow spines.
Water sparingly once established, letting the compost dry out completely between light waterings.
Position in your hottest, most sun-drenched south-facing spot to encourage purple star-shaped blooms.
items.description: Solanum quadriloculatum commonly known as tomato bush or wild tomato, is a flowering plant in the family Solanaceae. It is an upright perennial with hairy, grey-green thick leaves and purple flowers and grows on mainland Australia with the exception of Victoria.

items.name: Hawai'i horsenettle
items.growersTips:
Grow in a heated greenhouse or large pot moved indoors by October to survive UK winter frosts.
Sow seeds in March at five millimetres deep using a heated propagator kept at twenty-one degrees.
Water deeply once a week to keep soil damp but never soggy, preventing root rot in cool UK summers.
Prune lightly in late spring to remove dead wood and maintain a compact shape for patio containers.
Check foliage weekly for aphids and glasshouse whitefly, common pests in humid UK growing spaces.
items.description: Solanum sandwicense is a rare species of flowering plant in the nightshade family known by the common names Hawai'i horsenettle and popolo 'aiakeakua. It is endemic to Hawaii, where it occurs today on the islands of Kauai and Oahu. It is threatened by the destruction and degradation of its habitat. It is a federally listed endangered species of the United States.

items.name: Solanum sodiroi
items.growersTips:
Start seeds indoors in warm propagators by March to counter the short, cool UK growing season.
Grow in large pots of rich, free-draining loam so you can move them under glass when frosts threaten.
Water deeply at the base twice a week to keep soil damp but never waterlogged in cool UK summers.
Prune lower leaves in late August to maximize sunlight exposure and ripen the fruit before autumn.
Watch for potato blight during warm, wet July spells and apply copper-based organic sprays early.
items.description: Solanum sodiroi is a species of plant in the family Solanaceae. It is possibly endemic to Ecuador.

items.name: Rapistrum rugosum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in spring at a depth of five millimetres into poor, well-drained soil to limit wild spread.
Water seedlings weekly until established, then withhold water entirely to prevent leggy, weak stems.
Hand-pull plants in June before the yellow flowers set seed to stop aggressive self-seeding in lawns.
Grow alongside mint or rosemary in pots to contain its invasive roots and mask cabbage white butterflies.
Check foliage weekly in June for flea beetles and crush them to protect nearby vegetable brassicas.
items.description: Rapistrum rugosum is a species of flowering plant in the mustard family commonly known as bastard cabbage or annual bastard cabbage, as well as "common giant mustard", "turnipweed", "ball mustard", "wild turnip", "wild rape", or "tall mustard-weed". It is native to parts of Eurasia and Africa, but is present throughout the world as an introduced species and a common weed. It is an invasive species in many areas. It is an annual herb producing an erect stem reaching up to about a meter tall. The leaves are variable in shape and size and the proximal blades are generally cut into lobes or divide

items.name: Horseradish
items.growersTips:
Plant in spring placing root cuttings at a forty-five degree angle under five centimetres of soil.
Grow in large heavy-duty pots to prevent the invasive taproots from taking over your garden borders.
Water deeply once a week during dry UK summer spells to prevent the roots from becoming woody.
Watch for cabbage white butterfly caterpillars and flea beetles which target this brassica family member.
Lift and replant the main roots every autumn to maintain the best pungent flavour for horseradish sauce.
items.description: Horseradish is a perennial plant of the family Brassicaceae. It is a root vegetable, cultivated and used worldwide as a spice and as a condiment. The species is likely native to Southeastern Europe and Western Asia.

items.name: Coralroot bittercress
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbils in late summer just below the soil surface in moist shaded spots under deciduous trees
Incorporate leaf mould into heavy clay to mimic the ancient woodland soils of the Chilterns and Weald
Collect the dark purple aerial bulbils from leaf axils in July before they drop to propagate easily
Control local slug and snail populations in early spring as they eagerly eat the emerging shoots
Plant alongside native wood anemones and wild daffodils for a synchronized spring woodland display
items.description: Cardamine bulbifera, known as coralroot bittercress or coral root, is a species of flowering plant in the family Brassicaceae. It is a perennial with upright, mostly unbranched, stems to 70 cm (28 in) tall, and leaves made up of between three and 13 leaflets. At the base of each leaf there are bulbils which can fall off and grow into new plants. The flowers have petals that are 10–15 mm (0.4–0.6 in) long collected in corymbose few-flowered racemes and are generally light purple, pink or almost white. It is found in damp places.

items.name: Aethionema saxatile
items.growersTips:
Plant in gritty, free-draining alkaline soil to prevent winter root rot in wet UK climates.
Position in full south-facing sun next to limestone rock garden companions like Campanula carpatica.
Sow seeds shallowly at a depth of two millimetres in cold frames during early spring.
Cut back the spent flowering stems by half in late summer to maintain a compact, bushy habit.
Protect young spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic ferrous phosphate pellets.
items.description:
Aethionema saxatile, the burnt candytuft, is a species of flowering plant in the family Brassicaceae.
It is found in the European Alps.

items.name: Rapeseed
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in late August or September at a depth of one to two centimetres for overwintering.
Incorporate well-rotted manure into heavy clay soils to improve drainage before autumn sowing.
Net young plants immediately to protect them from wood pigeon damage during UK winter months.
Apply a nitrogen-rich organic fertiliser in early spring to boost rapid leafy growth and flowering.
Monitor closely for cabbage stem flea beetle damage on seedlings during dry autumn spells.
items.description: Rapeseed, also known as rape and oilseed rape and canola, is a yellow-flowered member of the Brassicaceae family.

items.name: Cardamine trifolia
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist, humus-rich, acidic to neutral soil under the canopy of deciduous trees or shrubs.
Water regularly during dry UK summers to keep the soil consistently damp, mimicking woodland floors.
Divide congested clumps in early autumn or immediately after the white flowers fade in late spring.
Plant alongside shade-loving companions like Athyrium ferns, Galanthus, and Hostas for contrast.
Watch for slugs and snails in damp spring weather, protecting the delicate emerging flower buds.
items.description: Cardamine trifolia, the trefoil cress, trifoliate bittercress, or three-leaved cuckoo flower, is a species of flowering plant in the family Brassicaceae. It is native to central and southern Europe, and has been introduced to Great Britain. It appears to have survived in several glacial refugia in the Alps, the western Carpathians and Dinaric Alps from where it spread to nearby area. A creeping perennial, in the garden it is recommended as a ground cover in shady areas.

items.name: Chamois cress
items.growersTips:
Plant in sharply drained, gritty soil or scree to prevent winter wet rot in damp UK climates.
Sow seeds shallowly at a depth of two millimetres in autumn to allow natural winter cold stratifying.
Water sparingly only during dry summer spells, keeping the grit mulch around the crown bone dry.
Shear back lightly by half after spring flowering to maintain a tight, cushion-like growth habit.
Protect young spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers in damp UK gardens.
items.description: Hornungia alpina is a flowering plant in the family Brassicaceae. It is native to the mountains of Southern and Central Europe, as far south as northern Spain, central Italy and North Macedonia , and is sometimes grown as an ornamental plant in gardens .

items.name: Alyssum chondrogynum
items.growersTips:
Plant in gritty, sharply draining alkaline soil to prevent winter wet rot in damp UK climates.
Position in full south-facing sun against a warm stone wall to mimic its native Cypriot cliffs.
Water sparingly only during dry summer spells once established, keeping the crown completely dry.
Pruneback lightly by one third after summer flowering to maintain a tight, cushion-like habit.
Protect from slugs and snails in damp British springs when tender new growth first emerges.
items.description: Odontarrhena chondrogyna is a species of perennial flowering plants in the family Brassicaceae. It was previously included in the genus Alyssum, and hence named Alyssum chondrogynum, but was assigned to the newly established Odontarrhena after molecular phylogeny studies from the 2010s. It is endemic to the island of Cyprus, where it grows on rocky serpentinised slopes.

items.name: Alyssum serpyllifolium
items.growersTips:
Plant in gritty sharply draining alkaline soil to survive wet UK winters and prevent root rot
Position in full south facing sun to mimic its native dry Mediterranean limestone habitat
Water sparingly only during prolonged summer droughts once the established root system is mature
Prune back lightly by one third after summer flowering to maintain a compact tidy cushion habit
Protect from slugs and snails in damp UK springs when young tender shoots are most vulnerable
items.description: Alyssum serpyllifolium, the thyme-leaved alison, is a species of flowering plant in the family Brassicaceae, native to the western Mediterranean region. It is adapted to serpentine soils. The Royal Horticultural Society recommends it for rock gardens.

items.name: Alyssum minutum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at three millimetres deep in April using free-draining gritty soil to avoid rot
Water sparingly only during dry summer spells as this alpine Brassicaceae dislikes wet UK winters
Watch for flea beetles in spring by using yellow sticky traps around these low-growing crucifers
Plant alongside carrots to attract predatory hoverflies that naturally control destructive aphids
Avoid rich fertilisers which cause floppy growth and instead topdress with fine limestone grit
items.description: Alyssum minutum is a species of flowering plant in the genus Alyssum, family Brassicaceae, native to the Mediterranean and Eastern Europe.

items.name: Alyssum desertorum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at a depth of two millimetres in April to prevent damp-off in cool UK springs.
Grow in poor, sharply drained chalky soil to prevent the leggy growth caused by rich UK garden loam.
Water only during prolonged summer droughts as this annual easily rots in damp British conditions.
Position near early-flowering brassicas to attract hoverflies that control spring aphid outbreaks.
Shear back by half after the first June flush to trigger a second wave of blooms before autumn.
items.description: Alyssum desertorum is a species of flowering plant in the family Brassicaceae known by the common name desert madwort. It is native to Europe, North Africa and Asia, and it is found in parts of western North America as an introduced species and sometimes a weed. This is a hairy annual herb producing upright stems up to about 20 centimeters tall. The leaves are linear to oblanceolate-linear in shape, 0.5-4 millimeters long and 0.3-3 millimeters wide. The entire plant is covered by 8-20 rayed stellate trichomes, giving the plant a grayish appearance. It produces small yellowish flowers with peta

items.name: Rapistrum perenne
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn in well-drained, gritty soil at a shallow depth of five millimetres.
Grow in full sun and avoid watering once established, as this plant thrives in dry UK soils.
Cut back the flowering stems to the base in late summer to prevent aggressive self-seeding.
Check regularly for cabbage white butterfly caterpillars and flea beetles in damp UK springs.
Plant alongside drought-tolerant UK natives like wild marjoram to create a resilient gravel garden.
items.description: Rapistrum perenne is a species of flowering plant in the mustard family commonly known as the perennial bastard cabbage. It is natively found between east, central, and southeast Europe and the Caucusus, but has also been introduced to a number of other European countries. It was first collected in 1922 from southeastern Saskatchewan, but has not been seen there since 1932; it was introduced to North America, but unlike Rapistrum rugosum did not persist as a naturalized population.

items.name: Hairy bittercress
items.growersTips:
Hand-pull before spring seed pods explode to stop rapid spread in damp UK borders and gravel paths.
Mulch bare soil with five centimetres of bark in autumn to block light and prevent seed germination.
Hoe young seedlings on a dry breezy UK morning in early spring so the roots dehydrate and die fast.
Grow dense groundcover like Ajuga reptans as a companion to crowd out this light-loving weed.
Check container compost bought from UK garden centres for tiny rosettes before potting up plants.
items.description: Cardamine hirsuta, commonly called hairy bittercress, popping cress, common bittercress, hoary bittercress, hairy wood-cress, small bittercress, pepperweed, shotweed, or snapweed, is an annual or biennial species of plant in the family Brassicaceae, and is edible as a salad green. It is common in moist areas around the world.

items.name: Alyssum propinquum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in spring at 2mm depth in well-drained, gritty soil to prevent dampening off in UK damp.
Water sparingly once established, allowing the soil to dry out fully between waterings to avoid rot.
Shear back by half after the first summer flush to encourage a second wave of blooms in autumn.
Watch for flea beetles in dry spells, using fine insect mesh to protect the young brassica foliage.
Plant alongside rosemary or thyme in sunny, south-facing rockeries to mimic its alpine habitat.
items.description: Alyssum propinquum is a species of flowering plant in the family Brassicaceae native to southern Turkey. Typically 7.5 cm (3 in) tall and spreading to 30 cm (12 in) wide, it is hardy in USDA zones 7 through 10 and is recommended for rock gardens.

items.name: Drooping bittercress
items.growersTips:
Plant in late autumn at a depth of five centimetres in moisture-retentive, humus-rich deciduous shade.
Water weekly during dry spring spells to mimic damp UK woodland soils and prevent early dormancy.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.
Cut back yellowing foliage to ground level in midsummer once the plant has naturally died back.
Incorporate well-rotted leaf mould into the planting hole to replicate British forest floor soils.
items.description: Cardamine enneaphyllos, the nine-leaved toothwort, nine-leaved coralwort, or drooping bittercress, is a species of flowering plant in the family Brassicaceae, native to east-central Europe, and on into Italy and the Balkans. A spreading rhizomatous geophyte, it prefers shady situations.

items.name: Hornungia procumbens
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn on the surface of gritty, well-drained soil as they need cold to trigger growth
Water only during prolonged dry spells in summer to mimic its natural dry coastal habitat
Plant in full sun in a raised bed or rockery to prevent winter wet from rotting the roots
Keep surrounding soil free of aggressive weeds that will easily smother this tiny low-growing herb
Grow alongside Sedum or Sempervivum which share its need for sharp drainage and poor soils
items.description: Hornungia procumbens is a species of herb native to the temperate zone of the northern hemisphere. Common names include oval purse, slenderweed and prostrate hutchinsia.

items.name: Aethionema grandiflorum
items.growersTips:
Plant in sharply draining, gritty, alkaline soil to survive wet UK winters and prevent root rot.
Position in full south-facing sun, tucked into a raised bed, rockery, or gravel garden crevice.
Water sparingly only during dry summer spells, keeping the crown dry to mimic alpine conditions.
Prune back by half immediately after summer flowering to keep the plant compact and prevent legginess.
Protect young spring shoots from slugs and snails using beer traps or grit barriers in damp weather.
items.description: Aethionema grandiflorum, commonly known as Persian stonecress or Persian candytuft, is a flowering plant in the family Brassicaceae, preferring to grow at 750 to 2600 m on limestone slopes. It is sometimes kept as a garden plant, and occasionally naturalizes outside its original range of eastern Turkey, the southern Caucasus and northern Iran. It is a recipient of the RHS's Award of Garden Merit.

items.name: Sand bittercress
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at a depth of two millimetres in early spring using a moisture-retentive loam.
Keep the soil consistently damp but not waterlogged by watering lightly at the base every morning.
Watch for flea beetles in June and protect young leaves using fine insect mesh covers.
Grow alongside mint or chives to deter common brassica pests that target small bittercress.
Hand-weed surrounding soil weekly to prevent fast-growing weeds from smothering this small annual.
items.description: Cardamine parviflora, commonly known as small-flowered bittercress or sand bittercress, is a species of flowering plant belonging to the family Brassicaceae.

items.name: Sea kale
items.growersTips:
Plant in deep gritty free-draining soil to mimic UK shingle beaches and prevent winter root rot.
Sow seeds outdoors in autumn at 2cm depth so winter cold naturally breaks their dormancy.
Protect young spring shoots from slugs and snails using beer traps or grit barriers.
Force early tender stems in January by covering the crown with a dark bucket or forcing pot.
Cut back faded flower stems in late summer to encourage a fresh flush of blue-green foliage.
items.description: Crambe maritima, common name sea kale, seakale or crambe, is a species of halophytic (salt-tolerant) flowering plant in the genus Crambe of the family Brassicaceae. It grows wild along the coasts of mainland Europe and the British Isles.

items.name: Succowia balearica
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in spring at a depth of five millimetres directly into well-drained, gritty soil.
Grow this Mediterranean annual in full sun to mimic its native Balearic light levels in the UK.
Water sparingly once established, allowing the top two centimetres of soil to dry out completely.
Protect young seedlings from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.
Harvest the edible leaves before the plant produces its distinctive spiny, spherical seed pods.
items.description: Succowia is a monotypic genus of flowering plants belonging to the family Brassicaceae. It only contains one known species, Succowia balearica (L.) Medik.

items.name: Shepherd's purse
items.growersTips:
Sow Capsella bursa-pastoris seeds in early spring at a shallow depth of just two millimetres.
Keep the soil consistently moist but not waterlogged to prevent early bolting in dry UK summers.
Watch out for flea beetles in May and protect young seedlings with fine insect mesh covers.
Grow Capsella near onions or garlic to naturally deter common Brassicaceae pests from the crop.
Incorporate well-rotted garden compost into light sandy soils to retain essential spring moisture.
items.description:
Capsella may refer to:Capsella (bivalve), a mollusc genus in the family Donacidae
Capsella (plant), a plant genus in the family Brassicaceae

items.name: Crambe cordifolia
items.growersTips:
Plant taproots deeply in autumn or spring to accommodate their massive, carrot-like root systems.
Stake the giant flowering stems early in May to prevent heavy summer winds from snapping them.
Apply a thick layer of well-rotted manure in late winter to satisfy this heavy feeder's appetite.
Watch out for cabbage white butterfly caterpillars and slugs which target this brassica family giant.
Cut the faded flower stems right back to the ground in August to encourage fresh basal foliage.
items.description: Crambe cordifolia, the greater sea-kale, colewort or heartleaf crambe, is a species of flowering plant in the family Brassicaceae, native to the Caucasus. It has gained the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit.

items.name: Wild cabbage
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in spring at a depth of 1.5cm in firm, alkaline soil to prevent clubroot disease.
Net plants with 7mm mesh from May to October to block cabbage white butterflies and wood pigeons.
Water deeply once a week at the base during dry summer spells to prevent premature bolting to seed.
Plant mint or sage nearby to mask the brassica scent and deter destructive flea beetles.
Apply a high-nitrogen organic mulch in early spring to boost leafy growth in damp UK weather.
items.description: Brassica oleracea, also known as wild cabbage in its uncultivated form, is a plant of the family Brassicaceae.

items.name: Tropidocarpum gracile
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at a depth of three millimetres in early spring once the frost risk has passed
Grow in sharply draining sandy loam to mimic its native habitat and prevent winter wet root rot
Water sparingly at the base only when the top two centimetres of soil have dried out completely
Watch for flea beetles and cabbage white caterpillars which target this Brassicaceae family member
Position in the sunniest south-facing spot of your garden to maximise the short UK summer heat
items.description: Tropidocarpum gracile is a species of flowering plant in the family Brassicaceae known by the common name dobie pod. It is native to California and Baja California, where it can be found in many types of habitat from coastal canyons to inland mountains and deserts in chaparral, scrub, woodlands, beaches, valleys, and washes. It is an annual herb producing a decumbent to erect, spreading, branching stem 10 to 50 centimeters in length. It is coated in short and long rough hairs. The basal leaves are up to 10 to 15 centimeters long and are divided into elongated lobes along the edges; leaves high

items.name: Aethionema retsina
items.growersTips:
Grow in sharply draining gritty soil or a raised scree bed to survive wet UK winters without rotting
Plant in full south-facing sun to mimic its native Greek habitat and ensure compact flowering cushions
Water sparingly only during dry summer spells once established as this alpine dislikes wet foliage
Protect from slugs and snails in early spring when the delicate new shoots first begin to emerge
Trim back lightly by one third after summer flowering to maintain a tight habit and prevent legginess
items.description: Aethionema retsina is a species of flowering plant in the family Brassicaceae. It is a subshrub endemic to Greece, where it is native to the islands of Skyros and Skyropoula in the central Aegean. Its natural habitats are Mediterranean-type shrubby vegetation and rocky shores. It is threatened by habitat loss.

items.name: Zilla spinosa
items.growersTips:
Grow in a heated greenhouse or conservatory to mimic its native desert heat and prevent winter rot
Use a potting mix of three parts coarse grit to one part loam to ensure the rapid drainage it needs
Water only when the soil is completely dry then drench thoroughly and never let the pot sit in water
Position in the absolute brightest south-facing spot possible to maximise scarce UK summer sunlight
Sow seeds in spring at a depth of five millimetres using a heated propagator set to twenty degrees
items.description: Zilla is a genus of plants in the family Brassicaceae. It includes a single species, Zilla spinosa, that grows in the Sahara-Arabian deserts of northern Africa and the Arabian Peninsula.

items.name: Cardamine amara
items.growersTips:
Grow in permanently wet, poorly drained soil or shallow pond margins up to ten centimetres deep.
Propagate by division in spring or take stem cuttings in summer to easily increase your stock.
Plant in partial to full shade to mimic its natural UK woodland stream habitat and prevent leaf scorch.
Watch for orange tip butterfly caterpillars in spring as this plant is a key larval food source.
Cut back hard after flowering in midsummer to encourage fresh, lush edible foliage for salads.
items.description: Cardamine amara, known as large bitter-cress, is a species of flowering plant in the family Brassicaceae. It is a perennial with upright, mostly unbranched, stems to 70 cm (28 in) tall, and leaves made up of between three and 13 leaflets. The flowers have petals that are 8–14 mm (0.3–0.6 in) long and are generally white, although sometimes pink or purple. It is found in damp places.

items.name: Hornungia petraea
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in autumn on well-drained gravelly soil to mimic UK limestone habitat.
Water sparingly only during prolonged dry spells as this winter annual dislikes damp summer soil.
Grow alongside limestone lovers like wild thyme to provide the sharp drainage and low competition.
Leave seed heads intact in late spring to allow natural self-seeding before the plant dies back.
Clear surrounding weeds in autumn to give the tiny overwintering rosettes enough light to grow.
items.description: Hornungia petraea is a small flowering plant in the family Brassicaceae. It is native to Europe and parts of North Africa and the Middle East.

items.name: Dyer's woad
items.growersTips:
Sow Isatis tinctoria seeds in spring at a depth of 5mm in well-drained, alkaline to neutral soil.
Water young plants weekly until established, then only during prolonged dry UK summer spells.
Watch for cabbage white butterfly caterpillars and flea beetles, netting the crop in midsummer.
Cut back flowering stalks in July before they set seed to prevent invasive self-seeding in lawns.
Grow alongside rosemary or mint to help deter the brassica pests that commonly attack Isatis.
items.description: Isatis is a genus of flowering plants in the family Brassicaceae, native to the Mediterranean region east to central Asia. Its genus name, Isatis, derives from the ancient Greek word for the plant, ἰσάτις. The genus includes woad. Due to their extremely variable morphology, the Asian species in particular are difficult to determine; the only reliable diagnostic feature is the ripe fruit. They are (usually) biennial or perennial herbaceous plants, often bluish and hairless or downy hairy with the upright stem branched.

items.name: Long-stalked rape
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in spring at 1cm depth in a sunny, well-drained bed with a high pH of 6.5 to 7.5.
Firm the soil thoroughly around transplant roots to prevent wind rock during wet UK winters.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells rather than daily light sprinkling.
Protect young spring shoots from cabbage white butterflies using a fine insect mesh.
Grow alongside mint or sage to deter flea beetles which target this specific brassica.
items.description: Brassica elongata, the elongated mustard or long-stalked rape, is a species of the mustard plant that is native to parts of Central Europe, Eastern Europe, the Balkan Peninsula, the Caucasus, Morocco and parts of Central Asia. Through plant invasion this species has become naturalized in many other parts of the world. Some of these naturalized regions include South Africa, North Western Europe, Australia and North America. Given the wide range of climate and ecological conditions of these regions, B. elongata has been able to disrupt the ecosystems of their native plant habitats and has been l

items.name: Rhamphospermum pubescens
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn in well-drained, alkaline soil to mimic UK chalk downland habitats.
Water young plants weekly during dry spring spells, but keep established roots dry in winter.
Hand-pull competing perennial weeds around the base to prevent this wild brassica being choked out.
Watch for cabbage white butterfly caterpillars in summer and net plants with fine insect mesh.
Prune back the faded flowering stems in late autumn to encourage healthy basal growth for spring.
items.description: Rhamphospermum pubescens is a species of flowering plant in the family Brassicaceae. It is native to the central Mediterranean; France, Italy, Sardinia, Sicily, Albania, Algeria, Tunisia, and Libya, and it has been introduced to Madeira and the Canary Islands. A perennial, its chromosome count is 2n = 18.

items.name: Garden cress
items.growersTips:
Sow garden cress seeds shallowly at five millimetres deep in moisture-retentive, fertile soil.
Grow pepperwort in partial shade during hot UK summers to prevent premature bolting and bitter leaves.
Water the soil consistently at the base to prevent damping off disease in damp British weather.
Protect young seedlings from flea beetles using fine insect netting or fleece from early spring.
Sow seeds every two weeks from March to September for a continuous harvest of fresh salad leaves.
items.description:
Lepidium is a genus of plants in the mustard/cabbage family, Brassicaceae. The genus is widely distributed in the Americas, Africa, Asia, Europe, and Australia. It includes familiar species such as garden cress, maca, and dittander. General common names include peppercress, peppergrass, pepperweed, and pepperwort. Some species form tumbleweeds.
The genus name Lepidium is from Greek meaning 'small scale', which is thought to be derived from a folk medicine usage of the plant to treat leprosy, which cause small scales on the skin. Another meaning is related to the small scale-like fruit.

items.name: Garden rocket
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds directly from March to September at a shallow depth of one centimetre to avoid taproot damage.
Water plants consistently at the base in summer to prevent premature bolting caused by dry UK soil.
Cover young crops with fine insect mesh to block flea beetles, a major pest in British gardens.
Grow alongside mint or rosemary to deter pests and mask the peppery scent of the foliage.
Harvest the outer leaves regularly when young to encourage continuous growth and milder flavour.
items.description: Eruca vesicaria is a species of Eruca native to Spain, Morocco, and Algeria. Some botanists consider Eruca vesicaria and E. sativa (arugula) to be conspecific. However, they are different in many morphological aspects such as sepal persistence, silique shape, and habit. Most importantly, they do not hybridize freely with each other as there is partial reproductive isolation between them. Plants of the World Online has accepted them as two distinct species.

items.name: Lady's smock
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn on the surface of damp, peat-free compost as they need winter cold to germinate
Grow in boggy soil or beside a garden pond in partial shade to mimic its natural damp meadow habitat
Leave foliage uncut until July to allow the orange-tip butterfly to lay eggs and caterpillars to feed
Divide established clumps in spring after flowering to maintain vigour and increase your stock easily
Choose the double-flowered Flore Pleno cultivar if you want longer-lasting blooms that do not self-seed
items.description: Cardamine pratensis, the cuckoo flower, lady's smock, mayflower, or milkmaids, is a flowering plant in the family Brassicaceae. It is a perennial herb native to Eurasia.

items.name: Cordylocarpus muricatus
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in spring at 1cm depth in well-drained, alkaline soil to prevent clubroot in UK gardens.
Water consistently at the base to keep soil moist but not waterlogged, avoiding powdery mildew.
Protect young seedlings from slugs and snails using beer traps or physical barriers in damp weather.
Cover plants with fine insect netting to exclude cabbage white butterflies and flea beetles.
Incorporate well-rotted manure into the bed a month before planting to provide essential nitrogen.
items.description: Cordylocarpus is a genus of flowering plants belonging to the family Brassicaceae. It includes a single species, Cordylocarpus muricatus, which is native to Algeria and Morocco.

items.name: Cardamine flexuosa
items.growersTips:
Hand-weed early in damp spring soil to remove the entire taproot before the explosive seed pods pop.
Sow seeds just 2mm deep in moist, shaded clay-loam borders to mimic natural UK woodland edges.
Water weekly during dry summer spells to keep the soil consistently damp but never waterlogged.
Watch for orange tip butterfly caterpillars in May and hand-pick them to protect young foliage.
Plant alongside hostas and ferns in damp shade to create a natural ground cover that deters weeds.
items.description: Cardamine flexuosa, commonly known as wavy bittercress or wood bitter-cress, is an herbaceous annual, biennial, or short-lived perennial plant in the cabbage family (Brassicaceae).

items.name: Pachyphragma macrophyllum
items.growersTips:
Plant in damp shade under deciduous trees where autumn leaves naturally mimic its woodland habitat
Sow seeds in cold frames during autumn as they require winter chill to germinate in UK climates
Divide congested clumps immediately after the white spring flowers fade to maintain plant vigour
Keep soil consistently moist during dry UK summers but ensure good drainage to prevent winter rot
Pair with hostas and ferns to cover the bare ground when those companion plants die back in winter
items.description: Pachyphragma is a genus of flowering plants belonging to the family Brassicaceae. It includes a single species, Pachyphragma macrophyllum, a perennial or rhizomatous geophyte native to eastern Turkey and the Caucasus.

items.name: Fast plants
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds 1cm deep in multi-purpose compost from April to July for reliable UK summer harvests.
Water consistently at the base to prevent bolting during dry spells or sudden UK summer heatwaves.
Protect young seedlings from flea beetles using fine insect mesh immediately after sowing outdoors.
Plant alongside mint or sage to deter cabbage white butterflies from laying eggs on the leaves.
In wet UK autumns, harvest the leafy greens early as annuals before winter frosts rot the crowns.
items.description: Brassica rapa is an annual to biennial plant species native to Eurasia that is from the Brassicaceae family. The B. rapa subspecies oleifera is an oilseed commonly known as turnip rape, field mustard, bird's rape, and keblock.

items.name: Muricaria prostrata
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in spring at a depth of five millimetres into free-draining sandy loam to prevent rot.
Water sparingly at the base only when the top two centimetres of soil are completely dry.
Protect young seedlings from slugs and cabbage white caterpillars using fine insect netting.
Grow in full sun in a south-facing border or container to mimic its native Mediterranean light.
In wet UK winters move container-grown plants under a cold frame to protect roots from waterlogging.
items.description: Muricaria is a genus of flowering plants belonging to the family Brassicaceae. It includes a single species, Muricaria prostrata, which is native to Algeria, Libya, Morocco and Tunisia in North Africa.

items.name: Crambe abyssinica
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds directly outdoors in late April at a depth of 1.5cm once the UK spring soil has warmed up.
Grow in free-draining, low-nitrogen soil to prevent excessive leaf growth at the expense of seeds.
Water young plants weekly during dry spells, but let established plants rely on natural UK rainfall.
Net the crop early in summer to protect the young brassica foliage from cabbage white butterflies.
Harvest the seed pods in late August once they turn a dry golden-brown color before autumn rains.
items.description: Crambe abyssinica is an annual oilseed crop of the family Brassicaceae. It is mainly cultivated due to the high levels of erucic acid that are contained in its seeds. The crambe oil is used for industrial purposes and its side products can be partly used as animal feed.

items.name: Cardamine impatiens
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in late summer on moist, weed-free soil to mimic natural autumn germination.
Keep the soil consistently damp but not waterlogged, mimicking its native UK damp woodland habitat.
Hand-pull plants in early summer before seed pods explode to prevent aggressive self-seeding.
Grow in partial to deep shade under deciduous shrubs where soil remains cool during dry spells.
Watch for orange-tip butterfly caterpillars in spring and tolerate light foliage damage for wildlife.
items.description: Cardamine impatiens, the narrowleaf bittercress or narrow-leaved bitter-cress, is a plant species in the genus Cardamine of the family Brassicaceae. It is a slender, biennial herb, that produces sterile leaves in the first year, one to several flowering stems during the next. Its leaves are pinnate with several pairs of lanceolate, dentate leaflets and a terminal, slightly longer leaflet. The short petals surpass the calyx by half of its length. The seeds are arranged in one row on each side of the central membrane of the narrow pod and are ejected out in a shower due to the tension formed as

items.name: Chinese violet cress
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at a depth of 2mm in late summer for natural winter vernalisation in UK soils.
Grow in dappled shade under deciduous trees to mimic its native woodland edge habitat in the UK.
Water weekly during dry spring spells to prevent premature bolting and prolong the purple blooms.
Watch for cabbage white butterfly caterpillars in summer and net plants to protect the foliage.
Plant alongside early spring bulbs like daffodils to mask their fading foliage as this plant grows.
items.description: Orychophragmus violaceus, the Chinese violet cress, is a species of flowering plant in the family Brassicaceae. It is native to northern and southeastern China and North Korea, and it has been introduced to Japan and the U.S. state of Virginia. An annual or biennial herb typically 60 cm (24 in) tall, it is found in a wide variety of habitats, including anthropogenically disturbed ones. Hardy in USDA zones 7 through 10, in China it is cultivated as a vegetable for its stalks. The Royal Horticultural Society considers it "potentially harmful".

items.name: Tropidocarpum californicum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in early spring at a depth of five millimetres to protect them from late frost damage.
Grow in well-drained, gritty soil with neutral pH to prevent winter root rot in wet UK climates.
Water sparingly at the base only when the top two centimetres of soil are completely dry.
Protect young seedlings from slugs and snails using beer traps or physical copper barriers.
Position in full sun to maximise warmth and mimic its native dry Californian habitat.
items.description: Tropidocarpum californicum, the king's gold, is a plant species endemic to a small region in California. It is known from only Kern and King counties in the southern part of the San Joaquin Valley.

items.name: Aurinia saxatilis
items.growersTips:
Plant in gritty, sharply draining soil to prevent winter root rot in wet UK climates.
Position in full, baking sun next to south-facing stone walls or in gravel scree beds.
Cut back by half immediately after spring flowering to keep the mound compact and neat.
Propagate by taking softwood cuttings in early summer rather than sowing seeds in wet soil.
Watch for cabbage white butterfly caterpillars and flea beetles which attack this brassica.
items.description: Aurinia saxatilis is an ornamental plant native to Asia and Europe.

items.name: Psychine stylosa
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in early spring under fleece to protect young seedlings from late UK frosts and slugs.
Grow in well-drained, alkaline soil, adding grit and lime to heavy UK clay to prevent root rot.
Water deeply once a week at the base rather than daily to encourage deep, drought-resistant roots.
Net the plants from May to September to exclude cabbage white butterflies and prevent caterpillar havoc.
Plant alongside mint or sage to deter flea beetles, which frequently target this brassica family member.
items.description: Psychine is a genus of flowering plants belonging to the family Brassicaceae. It includes a single species, Psychine stylosa, which is native to Algeria, Morocco, and Tunisia.

items.name: Rytidocarpus moricandioides
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in early spring under cloches to protect young seedlings from late UK frosts and slugs.
Grow in fertile, well-drained alkaline soil, adding garden lime if your UK garden has acidic soil.
Net plants securely from transplanting onwards to exclude cabbage white butterflies and pigeons.
Water deeply at the base once a week during dry summer spells to prevent premature bolting to seed.
Interplant with mint or sage to help deter flea beetles, which heavily target Brassicaceae crops.
items.description: Rytidocarpus is a genus of flowering plants belonging to the family Brassicaceae. It includes a single species, Rytidocarpus moricandioides, which is endemic to Morocco.

items.name: Brassica juncea
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds directly in July or August at a depth of 1cm to prevent premature bolting in summer heat.
Net crops immediately with 7mm mesh to exclude cabbage white butterflies and flea beetles.
Water consistently at the base to keep soil damp but not waterlogged, preventing a bitter taste.
Grow alongside mint or sage to deter pests, avoiding planting near other brassicas to limit disease.
Harvest outer leaves continuously when 10cm long to encourage fresh, tender growth through winter.
items.description: Brassica juncea, commonly mustard greens, brown mustard, Chinese mustard, Indian mustard, Japanese mustard, Korean green mustard, leaf mustard, Oriental mustard and vegetable mustard, is a species of mustard plant.

items.name: Cardamine occulta
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn at a depth of two millimetres in damp compost to match UK winter stratification.
Water the soil consistently to keep it moist but never waterlogged during dry spring spells.
Hand-weed surrounding soil early in spring before this invasive brassica flings its seeds.
Grow it in partial shade alongside damp-loving companion plants like hostas and astilbes.
Watch for the cabbage white butterfly caterpillars which target this Brassicaceae family member.
items.description: Cardamine occulta, the hidden bittercress, is a species of flowering plant in the family Brassicaceae, native to the Indian Subcontinent, China, Taiwan, Southeast Asia, most of Malesia, and Japan. It has been introduced many locales around the world, including most of Europe, the South Island of New Zealand, central Mexico, Costa Rica, El Salvador, Cuba, the US state of Maryland, and Newfoundland. An annual or biennial, it is typically found in ruderal situations.

items.name: Armoracia sisymbrioides
items.growersTips:
Plant in autumn in deep fertile soil to allow the taproot to establish during the wet UK winter.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells to prevent the root from becoming woody and bitter.
Grow in large heavy containers to prevent this vigorous Brassicaceae root from invading your lawn.
Watch for cabbage white caterpillars and use fine insect netting to protect the foliage in summer.
Harvest roots in late autumn after the first UK frost has concentrated the pungent mustard oils.
items.description: Armoracia sisymbrioides is a species of flowering plant in the mustard family, Brassicaceae. It is native to Asia.

items.name: Aethionema armenum
items.growersTips:
Plant in sharply draining, grit-amended soil to prevent winter root rot in wet UK climates.
Position in full south-facing sun against a brick wall to mimic its native dry alpine habitat.
Cut back by half immediately after flowering in July to maintain a compact, bushy shrub habit.
Water sparingly only during prolonged summer droughts, as this plant is highly drought-tolerant.
Protect from slugs and snails in damp spring weather when tender new shoots first emerge.
items.description: Aethionema armenum, also called rock cress, stonecress, or Persian candytuft, is a low-growing evergreen shrub in the family Brassicaceae native to the Mediterranean. There, it is typically found on rocky slopes above 800 meters.

items.name: Cardamine concatenata
items.growersTips:
Plant tubers 5cm deep in autumn in humus-rich, damp soil under deciduous trees to mimic woodland.
Water weekly during spring active growth if UK rainfall is low, then keep dry during summer dormancy.
Watch for garlic snails and flea beetles in spring, which target Brassicaceae foliage in damp gardens.
Do not prune or cut back dying foliage in summer; let leaves yellow naturally to feed the tuber.
Incorporate leaf mould and grit into heavy UK clay before planting to ensure drainage yet retain moisture.
items.description: Cardamine concatenata, the cutleaved toothwort, crow's toes, pepper root or purple-flowered toothwort, is a flowering plant in the family Brassicaceae. It is a perennial woodland wildflower native to eastern North America.

items.name: Cardamine diphylla
items.growersTips:
Plant this woodland perennial in moist, humus-rich, acidic to neutral soil under deciduous trees.
Sow seeds in cold frames during autumn, barely covering them with compost to mimic forest leaf litter.
Keep soil consistently damp but not waterlogged, mimicking wet UK woodland floors in spring.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit or beer traps.
Divide established clumps in late summer after the foliage dies back to propagate new plants.
items.description: Cardamine diphylla is a flowering plant in the family Brassicaceae. It is a spring flowering woodland plant that is native to eastern North America.

items.name: Brassica carinata
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in April or May at a depth of 1cm to avoid early frosts and ensure rapid germination.
Water deeply once a week at the base to prevent downy mildew in damp UK summer conditions.
Net the crop immediately after planting to protect the leaves from cabbage white butterflies.
Grow alongside mint or sage to deter flea beetles which heavily target young carinata leaves.
Incorporate well-rotted manure into neutral soil before sowing to meet its high nitrogen demand.
items.description: Brassica carinata is a species of flowering plant in the Brassicaceae family. It is referred to by the common names Ethiopian Kale, Ethiopian rape or Ethiopian mustard. It is believed to be a hybrid between Brassica nigra and Brassica oleracea.

items.name: Sinapis
items.growersTips:
Sow Sinapis alba seeds directly from March to September at a depth of one centimetre in firm soil.
Grow mustard as a quick green manure to dig into clay soil before it flowers in autumn.
Watch for flea beetles in dry spring weather by using yellow sticky traps near the young seedlings.
Water the crop consistently at the base to prevent premature bolting during dry UK summer spells.
Interplant Sinapis with potatoes to help suppress soil-borne pests and wireworms naturally.
items.description:
Sinapis is a genus of plants in the family Brassicaceae. As of July 2025, three species are accepted by Plants of the World Online:Sinapis alba L. – white mustard, formerly Brassica alba
Sinapis flexuosa Poir.
Sinapis pubescens L.

items.name: Cardamine maxima
items.growersTips:
Plant in autumn in moist soil rich in leaf mould to mimic UK woodland conditions for best growth.
Keep soil consistently damp but not waterlogged during dry spring spells to prevent early dormancy.
Watch for orange tip butterfly caterpillars in May which feed on the foliage but support biodiversity.
Sow seeds immediately after harvesting in summer as they lose viability quickly if stored dry.
Grow alongside wild garlic or primroses in partial shade to create a natural woodland ground cover.
items.description: Cardamine maxima is a species of flowering plant in the mustard family Brassicaceae.

items.name: Cardamine angulata
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist acidic to neutral soil enriched with leafmould to mimic UK woodland conditions.
Position in partial to full shade under deciduous shrubs to prevent summer leaf scorch.
Water weekly during dry UK spring spells to keep the soil consistently damp but not waterlogged.
Divide the creeping rhizomes in autumn after flowering to control spread and propagate new plants.
Watch for flea beetles in spring and protect young foliage with fine mesh or organic sprays.
items.description: Cardamine angulata is a species of perennial rhizomatous forb known by the common names angled bittercress, seaside bittercress, and angle-leaved bittercress. The species is endemic to the western United States and British Columbia.

items.name: Hirschfeldia incana
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn or spring just below the soil surface in poor, well-drained chalky or sandy soil.
Water seedlings sparingly during dry UK spells, then leave established plants to survive on rainfall.
Cut back the tough flowering stems in late summer to prevent aggressive self-seeding in your borders.
Watch for cabbage white butterfly caterpillars and flea beetles which target this brassica family member.
Grow alongside rosemary or thyme in sunny, dry gravel gardens to mimic its natural maritime habitat.
items.description: Hirschfeldia incana is a species of flowering plant in the mustard family known by many common names, including shortpod mustard, buchanweed, hoary mustard and Mediterranean mustard. It is the only species in the monotypic genus Hirschfeldia, which is closely related to Brassica. The species is native to the Mediterranean Basin but it can be found in many parts of the world as an introduced species and often a very abundant noxious weed. This mustard is very similar in appearance to black mustard, but is generally shorter. It forms a wide basal rosette of lobed leaves which lie flat on the gro

items.name: Brassica fruticulosa
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in spring at a depth of 1cm in free-draining, alkaline soil to prevent clubroot disease.
Grow in full sun but protect young autumn crops from heavy frost using horticultural fleece.
Water deeply once a week at the base rather than daily misting to discourage downy mildew.
Net the crop with 7mm mesh from May to October to block cabbage white butterflies and pigeons.
Interplant with mint or sage to mask the scent of the crop from destructive cabbage root flies.
items.description: Brassica fruticulosa, the Mediterranean cabbage or twiggy turnip, is a member of the agriculturally significant genus Brassica. It was described by Domenico Maria Leone Cirillo in 1792.

items.name: Brassica macrocarpa
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in March at a depth of 1cm to protect this rare Sicilian wild cabbage from UK frost.
Grow in free-draining limestone-rich soil with a high pH of 7.5 to mimic its native coastal cliffs.
Position in the sunniest south-facing spot possible to cope with cool, damp British summer weather.
Protect young plants from cabbage white butterflies and snails using fine insect netting in June.
Water sparingly once established as this drought-tolerant brassica is highly prone to winter rot.
items.description: Brassica macrocarpa is a species of Brassica found in Sicily.

items.name: Brassica cretica
items.growersTips:
Plant in free-draining, gritty alkaline soil to mimic its native Greek cliffside habitat in the UK.
Sow seeds in spring at a depth of five millimetres in modular trays to protect delicate seedlings.
Position in full sun and shelter from cold, wet winter winds which cause root rot in UK gardens.
Protect young leaves from cabbage white butterflies and pigeons using fine insect netting.
Water sparingly once established, allowing the soil to dry out completely between waterings.
items.description: Brassica cretica is a species of flowering plant in the family Brassicaceae, native to the Eastern Mediterranean, particularly to Greece and the Aegean Islands. It was first described by Jean-Baptiste Lamarck in 1785. A 2021 study suggested that it was the origin of cultivated Brassica oleracea, with later admixture from other Brassica species.

items.name: Cardamine heptaphylla
items.growersTips:
Plant in autumn at a depth of 8cm in moisture-retentive, humus-rich soil under deciduous trees.
Water weekly during dry spring spells to mimic damp UK woodland floors and prevent early dormancy.
Mulch annually in late autumn with leaf mould to replicate natural British beechwood soil conditions.
Divide congested clumps immediately after flowering in late spring before the foliage dies back.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.
items.description: Cardamine heptaphylla, common name pinnate coralroot, is a species of flowering plant in the family Brassicaceae.

items.name: Brassica narinosa
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in mid to late summer to prevent bolting caused by the long daylight hours of UK spring.
Plant seeds exactly one centimetre deep in fertile soil enriched with well-rotted garden compost.
Water the soil consistently at the base to keep it moist and prevent the leaves from turning bitter.
Cover crops with fine insect netting immediately after sowing to block cabbage root fly and beetles.
Grow alongside mint or rosemary to deter pests and avoid planting near other brassica family crops.
items.description: Tatsoi is an Asian variety of Brassica rapa grown for greens. Also called tat choy, it is closely related to the more familiar bok choy. This plant has become popular in North American cuisine as well and is now grown throughout the world.

items.name: Alliaria petiolata
items.growersTips:
Uproot garlic mustard manually in early spring before seed pods form to prevent aggressive spreading
Sow seeds in autumn at five millimetres depth in damp shady spots to mimic natural UK winter chilling
Water young plants weekly during dry spring spells to establish healthy leaves for culinary use
Grow in containers to easily contain the vigorous self-seeding habit of this biennial herb
Interplant with wild garlic in moist woodland soil to create a productive native salad corner
items.description: Alliaria petiolata, or garlic mustard, is a biennial flowering plant in the mustard family (Brassicaceae). It is native to Europe, western and central Asia, north-western Africa, Morocco, Iberia and the British Isles, north to northern Scandinavia, and east to northern Pakistan and Xinjiang in western China. It has now become a tenacious invasive plant across the northern U.S., in particular because of its earlier springtime emergence than many native species, often in the forest understory.

items.name: Brassica rupestris
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in late spring at a depth of 1cm in free-draining, alkaline soil to prevent clubroot.
Water deeply once a week at the base during dry summer spells to establish the deep taproot system.
Net plants with 7mm mesh from May to October to block cabbage white butterflies and wood pigeons.
Plant alongside rosemary or mint to deter flea beetles and mask the brassica scent from pests.
Prune yellowing lower leaves in autumn to improve air circulation and prevent grey mould in damp UK winters.
items.description: Brassica rupestris is a species of flowering plant in the family Brassicaceae, native to southwestern Italy and Sicily. The plant is known to grow on vertical limestone cliffs. In the past it was proposed, based on morphology, that Brassica rupestris contributed to the ancestry of either kale or kohlrabi, but DNA evidence shows that it did not.

items.name: Brassica hilarionis
items.growersTips:
Grow this rare Cypriot native in sharply draining, gritty alkaline soil to survive wet UK winters.
Sow seeds in spring at a depth of five millimetres in a cold frame to protect young seedlings.
Position in full sun against a south-facing wall to mimic its natural warm cliffside habitat.
Water sparingly only during dry summer spells to prevent root rot in the damp British climate.
Protect the evergreen foliage from cabbage white caterpillars and slugs using fine insect netting.
items.description: Brassica hilarionis is a species of perennial cruciferous plant in the family Brassicaceae. It is endemic to Northern Cyprus and is classified as endangered. This species flowers from March to May. Its common name is St. Hilarion Cabbage.

items.name: Cardamine nuttallii
items.growersTips:
Plant this woodland perennial in partial shade using humus-rich, moist but well-drained acidic soil.
Sow seeds in autumn in cold frames to allow natural winter chilling for spring germination in the UK.
Keep the soil consistently moist during spring growth but reduce watering when the plant goes dormant.
Apply a leaf mould mulch in autumn to mimic its native forest floor and protect shallow rhizomes.
Watch for slugs and snails in early spring as they target the tender emerging edible shoots.
items.description: Cardamine nuttallii is a species of cardamine known by the common name Nuttall's toothwort. It is native to western North America from British Columbia to California, where it grows in moist mountain habitats.

items.name: Cardamine douglassii
items.growersTips:
Plant in autumn at a depth of five centimetres in moist, humus-rich soil under deciduous shrubs.
Water weekly during dry spring spells to mimic the damp woodland conditions of its native habitat.
Hand-weed around the delicate spring foliage to prevent vigorous garden grasses from smothering it.
Divide the fibrous root clumps immediately after flowering in late spring to propagate new plants.
Position next to Galanthus or Eranthis as companion plants that share its early damp shade needs.
items.description: Cardamine douglassii, the limestone bittercress or purple cress, is a perennial forb that produces white to pink or purple flowers in early spring. It is native to Ontario, Canada, as well as the eastern and central United States.

items.name: Cardamine constancei
items.growersTips:
Plant this Californian woodland native in deep shade under deciduous shrubs to mimic forest canopies.
Incorporate leaf mould into heavy UK clay to create the damp, acidic, well-drained soil it requires.
Water weekly during dry spring spells to keep the soil consistently moist but never waterlogged.
Protect the delicate emerging spring foliage from slugs and snails using organic wool pellets.
Propagate by dividing the creeping rhizomes in early autumn once the summer dormancy period ends.
items.description: Cardamine constancei is a rare, narrow-ranged species of perennial rhizomatous forb known by the common name Constance's bittercress. It is endemic to select tributaries of the Clearwater and Coeur d'Alene Rivers in Idaho.

items.name: Cardamine angustata
items.growersTips:
Plant in autumn at a depth of 5cm in moist, humus-rich soil under deciduous trees to mimic woodlands.
Water weekly during dry spring spells to keep soil damp but avoid waterlogging during winter dormancy.
Hand-pick orange-tip butterfly caterpillars in early summer rather than using chemical pesticides.
Clear away fallen autumn leaves from the crown to prevent crown rot in damp UK winter conditions.
Grow alongside Galanthus nivalis and Primula vulgaris which share its early spring shade preferences.
items.description: Cardamine angustata is a perennial forb native to the eastern United States, that produces white to pink or purple flowers in early spring.

items.name: Cardamine flagellifera
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade to mimic its native woodland habitat.
Propagate by dividing the creeping runners in autumn or early spring to control its spreading habit.
Water consistently during dry UK summer spells to keep the soil damp but avoid waterlogged conditions.
Watch for flea beetles and cabbage white caterpillars which target this Brassicaceae family member.
Grow alongside shade-loving Astilbe or Hostas to complement its delicate white spring blooms.
items.description: Cardamine flagellifera, commonly known as Blue Ridge bittercress, is a species of herbaceous plant in the mustard family. It is native to eastern North America, where it is found primarily in the southern Blue Ridge. It is a perennial that produces white flowers in the spring.

items.name: Cardamine rotundifolia
items.growersTips:
Grow this native of wet woods in moisture-retentive, humus-rich soil that mimics UK stream banks.
Plant divisions in early autumn at a depth where the crown sits level with the damp soil surface.
Water deeply twice a week during dry UK summers to keep the soil consistently boggy and cool.
Watch for flea beetles in spring, protecting young leaves with fine insect mesh if damage occurs.
Cut back faded flowering stems in midsummer to encourage fresh green foliage and prevent self-seeding.
items.description: Cardamine rotundifolia, also known as American bittercress or mountain bittercress, is a perennial herbaceous brassica native to eastern North America. It was first described by André Michaux in his publication Flora Boreali-Americana (1803).

items.name: Cardamine depressa
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at a depth of two millimetres in early spring to match cool UK temperatures.
Keep the soil consistently damp but not waterlogged by watering lightly every two to three days.
Protect young leaves from slugs and snails using organic wool pellets during damp British springs.
Grow in partial shade to mimic its natural alpine habitat and prevent the delicate foliage burning.
Plant alongside wild garlic or mint to help deter common Brassicaceae pests like flea beetles.
items.description: Cardamine depressa, commonly known as bitter cress, is a plant in the Brassicaceae family, found in the Antipodean Islands.

items.name: Cardamine quinquefolia
items.growersTips:
Plant this woodland perennial in autumn under deciduous shrubs to mimic its native damp forest floor.
Incorporate well-rotted leafmould into clay soils to create the humus-rich, moist conditions it loves.
Water weekly during dry spring spells to keep the soil consistently damp before summer dormancy.
Leave the dying foliage alone in early summer as it naturally dies back to underground rhizomes.
Watch for slugs and snails in damp UK springs as they quickly devour the emerging tender shoots.
items.description: Cardamine quinquefolia, the five-leaved cuckoo flower or whorled coral-root, is a species of flowering plant in the family Brassicaceae, native to an area from south eastern Europe to northern Iran.

items.name: Bivonaea lutea
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at three millimetres deep in early autumn to match UK cool-season germination.
Grow in sharply draining gritty soil to prevent winter root rot during wet British winters.
Position in full south-facing sun to maximise the limited light levels of UK spring months.
Water sparingly only when the top two centimetres of soil are dry to avoid damping off disease.
Plant alongside early-flowering Aubrieta to attract pollinators to this low-growing annual.
items.description: Bivonaea is a genus of flowering plants belonging to the family Brassicaceae. It includes a single species, Bivonaea lutea, an annual native to Algeria, Sardinia, Sicily, and Tunisia in the central Mediterranean region.

items.name: Cardamine bellidifolia
items.growersTips:
Grow in a gritty alpine trough with 50% horticultural grit to mimic UK mountain scree drainage.
Water from below in winter to prevent crown rot in damp, humid UK cold seasons.
Sow seeds in autumn on the soil surface as they require cold stratification to germinate in spring.
Position in a north-facing rockery or light dappled shade to prevent summer leaf scorch.
Watch for flea beetles in early summer and protect young leaves with fine insect mesh.
items.description: Cardamine bellidifolia is a species of perennial rhizomatous forb known by the common name alpine bittercress. This species is a circumboreal alpine plant endemic to North America, Europe, and Asia.

items.name: Pterygostemon spathulatus
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in early spring under cloches to protect young seedlings from late UK frosts and slugs.
Grow in free-draining neutral to alkaline soil to prevent clubroot, a common Brassicaceae disease.
Water consistently at the base to keep soil moist but not waterlogged, preventing premature bolting.
Net the crop with fine mesh from May to October to exclude cabbage white butterflies and pigeons.
Apply a high-nitrogen organic mulch in June to support rapid leafy growth in cool maritime summers.
items.description: Pterygostemon is a genus of flowering plants belonging to the family Brassicaceae. It includes a single species, Pterygostemon spathulatus, which is native to Kazakhstan and Xinjiang.

items.name: White mustard
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds directly outdoors from March to September at a depth of one centimetre in firm soil.
Water consistently during dry summer spells to prevent early bolting and keep the leaves tender.
Watch out for flea beetles in spring by using fine insect mesh to protect young emerging seedlings.
Incorporate the crop into the soil as green manure before it flowers to boost organic matter.
Grow as a companion plant near brassicas to act as a sacrificial trap crop for cabbage butterflies.
items.description: White mustard, also called yellow mustard, is an annual plant of the cabbage family. It is sometimes also referred to as Brassica alba or B. hirta. It is native to the Mediterranean region, Europe and Tropical Asia, but is now widespread worldwide. Grown for its seeds, it is used to make the condiment mustard, as a fodder crop, or as a green manure.

items.name: Berteroa incana
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at a depth of two millimetres in autumn to mimic natural UK self-seeding cycles.
Grow in poor, sharply draining sandy soil to prevent winter root rot in wet UK climates.
Water seedlings sparingly once established, allowing the gritty soil to dry out fully between feeds.
Cut back flowering stems in late summer before seed pods explode to control its invasive spreading.
Watch for cabbage white butterfly caterpillars and flea beetles which target this brassica family weed.
items.description: Berteroa incana is a species of flowering plant in the mustard family, Brassicaceae. Its common names include hoary alyssum, false hoary madwort, hoary berteroa, and hoary alison. It is a biennial herb native to Eurasia and it has been introduced to western Europe and North America. It is listed as an invasive noxious weed in some areas of United States and Canada

items.name: Fourraea
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn in a cold frame to mimic alpine winter chill for successful spring germination.
Grow in gritty, alkaline soil with sharp drainage to prevent winter root rot in wet UK climates.
Water sparingly from below during summer, keeping the foliage dry to prevent downy mildew attacks.
Protect young spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.
Plant alongside wild thyme or saxifrages in a raised scree bed to mimic its natural alpine habitat.
items.description: Fourraea alpina is a species of flowering plant in the family Brassicaceae, and the only member of the genus Fourraea. It is native to Europe, where its range extends from Spain in the west to Croatia in the east, and from Belgium and Czechia in the north to Italy in the south.

items.name: Brassica tournefortii
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in spring at a depth of 6mm in free-draining sandy soil to mimic its native dry habitat.
Water sparingly once established as this drought-tolerant weed-like brassica rots in soggy UK clay.
Cover crops with fine insect netting in May to block the inevitable cabbage white butterfly larvae.
Grow in full sun in a dedicated container to prevent its aggressive self-seeding habit in borders.
Harvest the young tender flowering shoots in early summer before the plant becomes tough and bitter.
items.description: Brassica tournefortii is a species of plant known by the common names Asian mustard, pale cabbage, African mustard, Sahara mustard, and Aslooz.

items.name: Pale madwort
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at three millimetres deep in April directly into poor well-drained UK soils.
Water young seedlings sparingly only during dry spells to prevent dampening off in damp UK springs.
Plant alongside cabbages to attract hoverflies whose larvae voraciously consume brassica aphids.
Hand-weed around the delicate shallow roots instead of hoeing to avoid disturbing the plants.
Collect the small seed pods in August before they split to prevent unwanted self-seeding nearby.
items.description: Alyssum alyssoides is a species of flowering plant in the mustard family known by several common names, including pale madwort and yellow alyssum. It is native to Eurasia, but it can be found throughout much of the temperate world as an introduced species and sometimes a common weed. For example, it has been noted as a weed in the western United States. It often appears in arable fields, sandy tracks, pits, and docks.

items.name: Selenia aurea
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in early spring at a depth of 5mm in free-draining, neutral to alkaline soil.
Keep soil consistently moist but never waterlogged to prevent root rot in damp UK springs.
Protect young seedlings from slugs and cabbage white butterflies using fine insect netting.
Grow alongside mint or sage to deter common Brassicaceae pests naturally in UK plots.
Harvest the peppery leaves when young and tender before the yellow flowers appear in summer.
items.description: Selenia aurea, the golden selenia, is a flowering plant in the mustard family (Brassicaceae). It is endemic to the southern United States where it grows in sunny prairies, barrens, and glades of Arkansas, Kansas, Missouri, and Oklahoma. It flowers between March and May.

items.name: Isle of Man cabbage
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in spring 5mm deep in well-drained, sandy soil to mimic its native UK coastal habitat.
Water sparingly once established, allowing the gritty soil to dry out fully between waterings.
Protect young leaves from cabbage white butterflies and slugs using fine mesh netting in summer.
Grow in full sun and avoid acidic soils by adding lime to reach a neutral to alkaline pH of 7.0.
Do not over-fertilize this wild cabbage relative, as rich soil causes floppy, weak growth.
