items.description: Coincya monensis subsp. monensis, the Isle of Man cabbage, is a species of plant in the family Brassicaceae that is found in coastal habitats on the west of the island of Great Britain and around the coasts of the Isle of Man.

items.name: Rorippa gigantea
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at two millimetres deep in early spring using a moisture-retentive compost.
Keep the soil consistently damp but not waterlogged to mimic its natural wet woodland habitat.
Protect young seedlings from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers during damp UK springs.
Grow alongside water-loving companion plants like native ferns and marsh marigolds in partial shade.
Clear away the dying annual foliage in late autumn to prevent rot and encourage self-seeding.
items.description: Rorippa gigantea is a species of plant in the cabbage family Brassicaceae. The forest bitter-cress is usually seen as an annual plant, growing to 120 cm high, found in Australian east coast forests.

items.name: Rorippa sessiliflora
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at two millimetres deep in early spring using a moist seed compost under glass
Keep the soil constantly wet or boggy to mimic its natural UK riverbank and wetland habitat
Grow in full sun to partial shade in acidic to neutral clay soil to ensure rapid leaf development
Watch for flea beetles and cabbage white caterpillars which target this Brassicaceae family member
Harvest the peppery leaves continuously before the yellow flowers appear in midsummer to stop seeding
items.description: Rorippa sessiliflora, commonly known as stalkless yellowcress, is a species of flowering plant in the family Brassicaceae.

items.name: Cardamine corymbosa
items.growersTips:
Uproot this highly invasive weed immediately before its explosive seed pods scatter across borders.
Grow it in containers of poor soil if you must cultivate it, to prevent it suffocating alpines.
Hand-pull plants in early spring before white flowers appear to stop rapid self-seeding in damp soil.
Apply a thick organic mulch over cleared soil to block light and stop dormant seeds from germinating.
Check newly purchased nursery pots carefully to avoid accidentally introducing this weed to your garden.
items.description: Cardamine corymbosa, commonly known as the New Zealand bitter-cress, is a flowering plant in the family Brassicaceae. Native to the subantarctic islands of Australasia, it has become an invasive species in plant nurseries. The specific epithet refers to the structure of the inflorescence.

items.name: Descurainia pinnata
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at a depth of two millimetres in early spring once the UK soil begins to warm.
Grow in well-drained, sandy or chalky soil with a neutral to alkaline pH to prevent root rot.
Water seedlings lightly until established, then allow the soil to dry out fully between waterings.
Watch for flea beetles and cabbage white butterflies which frequently target this brassica family.
Position in full sun to mimic its native open habitat and ensure strong, upright stem development.
items.description: Descurainia pinnata is a species of flowering plant in the family Brassicaceae known by the common names southeastern tansymustard and western tansymustard. It is native to North America, where it is widespread and found in varied habitats. It is especially successful in deserts and dry fields. It is a hardy plant which easily becomes weedy, and can spring up in disturbed, barren sites with bad soil.

items.name: Spring cress
items.growersTips:
Plant in damp acidic to neutral clay loam in a partially shaded woodland border or bog garden edge.
Sow seeds in cold frames during autumn or divide the bulbous rhizomes in late summer after dormancy.
Keep the soil consistently moist but not waterlogged to mimic its native wet meadow habitat.
Watch for orange tip butterfly caterpillars which feed on the foliage but cause minimal damage.
Position alongside native UK moisture-lovers like Primula vulgaris and Caltha palustris.
items.description: Cardamine bulbosa, commonly called bulbous bittercress or spring cress, is a perennial plant in the mustard family. It is native to a widespread area of eastern North America, in both Canada and the United States. Its natural habitat is moist soils of bottomland forests and swamps, often in calcareous areas.

items.name: Crucihimalaya wallichii
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in early spring at 5mm depth in free-draining, gritty soil to mimic alpine scree conditions.
Water sparingly from below to prevent crown rot, keeping the compost damp but never waterlogged.
Protect young shoots from slugs and cabbage white caterpillars using fine mesh netting in May.
Grow in full sun in a cold frame or alpine house to protect the foliage from heavy winter rain.
Top-dress the pot with horticultural grit to keep the foliage off wet soil and prevent damping off.
items.description: Crucihimalaya is a genus of flowering plants belonging to the family Brassicaceae. Its native range is Sinai to China, and western and subarctic North America.

items.name: Wild rape
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in spring at a depth of one centimetre into poor, well-drained soil to limit wild spread.
Water seedlings weekly until established, then rely solely on UK rainfall to prevent root rot.
Hand-pull plants before yellow flowers fade in July to stop aggressive self-seeding in borders.
Check leaves weekly for cabbage white butterfly caterpillars and flea beetles to protect crops nearby.
Grow as a green manure, digging the foliage into heavy clay soils in autumn to improve structure.
items.description: Rhamphospermum arvense, the charlock, sometimes also called field mustard, wild mustard, or charlock mustard, is an annual or winter annual plant in the family Brassicaceae. It is found in the fields of North Africa, Asia, Europe, and some other areas where it has been transported and naturalised. Pieris rapae, the small white butterfly, and Pieris napi, the green veined white butterfly, are significant consumers of charlock during their larval stages.

items.name: Lemphoria andraeana
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at 3mm deep in early spring once UK soil temperatures reach 10C for best growth.
Grow in free-draining, gritty soil to prevent root rot during wet, cool British summer periods.
Water the base consistently during dry spells to prevent premature bolting and early seed setting.
Net plants with fine mesh to protect the Brassicaceae foliage from cabbage white butterfly larvae.
Position in full sun to maximise the short annual lifecycle before autumn frosts arrive in the UK.
items.description: Lemphoria andreaeana is a species of flowering plant in the Brassicaceae family. It is an annual found throughout inland Australia.

items.name: Cardamine californica
items.growersTips:
Plant in autumn at a depth of 5cm in moisture-retentive, humus-rich soil under deciduous tree shade.
Water weekly during dry spring active growth, then stop watering completely when it goes dormant.
Protect emerging spring foliage from slugs and snails using organic beer traps or copper tape.
Propagate by dividing the fragile rhizomes in late summer while the plant is fully dormant.
Grow alongside early shade-lovers like Galanthus or Hepatica to mark its spot during dormancy.
items.description: Cardamine californica, or milkmaids, is a flowering plant in the family Brassicaceae, native to western North America from Washington to California and Baja California. It is common in a variety of habitats including shady slopes, open woodlands, chaparral and grasslands in the winter and early spring. In the San Francisco Bay Area, it is one of the first wildflowers to bloom, with blossoms from January to May.

items.name: Moricandia arvensis
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at five millimetres deep in spring once UK soil warms to fifteen degrees.
Grow in free-draining chalky or sandy soil to mimic its native Mediterranean limestone habitat.
Water sparingly once established as this drought-tolerant brassica dislikes wet winter roots.
Protect young spring shoots from slugs and cabbage white butterflies using fine insect netting.
Plant alongside rosemary or thyme to deter pests and match its preference for dry sunny spots.
items.description: Moricandia arvensis, the purple mistress, is a species of flowering plant in the family Brassicaceae. It has a broadly western Mediterranean distribution, from the Canary Islands to northern Africa including Mauritania and Chad, the Iberian Peninsula, Italy and as far as Greece, and has been introduced to France, Corsica, and Sardinia. It has an intermediate C3–C4 carbon fixation system, known as C2 photosynthesis.

items.name: Descurainia bourgaeana
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at a depth of two millimetres in early spring using free-draining sandy loam.
Water sparingly once established, allowing the gritty soil to dry out fully between waterings.
Position in the sunniest south-facing spot possible to mimic its native hot volcanic habitat.
Protect young plants from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers during damp UK springs.
Grow in containers to easily move indoors or under a cold frame to survive wet winter frosts.
items.description: Descurainia bourgaeana is a species of flowering plant in the family Brassicaceae endemic to Las Cañadas del Teide on Tenerife and La Palma in the Canary Islands.

items.name: Descurainia incana
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in late summer at a depth of two millimetres to mimic natural UK autumn drop.
Grow in sharply draining sandy loam to prevent root rot during wet British winters and springs.
Water sparingly only during prolonged summer dry spells once the deep taproot has established.
Watch for flea beetles in spring which chew small holes in the greyish felted Brassicaceae foliage.
Position near spring-flowering honesty to attract beneficial pollinators to your wildlife garden.
items.description: Descurainia incana is a species of flowering plant in the mustard family known by the common name mountain tansymustard. It is native to much of North America, including most of Canada, the western United States, and Baja California. It is known from many types of habitat. It is a biennial herb with a slender, greenish, often hairy stem sometimes exceeding a meter tall. The leaves are narrowly to widely oval in shape, the lower ones lobed and sometimes compound, the upper generally unlobed. The mustardlike inflorescence is a series of developing fruits beneath an elongating cluster of small br

items.name: Rapeseed
items.growersTips:
Firm the soil thoroughly by treading before planting to prevent wind rock in wet UK winters.
Cover crops with ultra-fine insect netting immediately after planting to block cabbage root fly.
Apply garden lime in autumn to raise soil pH above 6.8 to prevent the devastating clubroot fungus.
Water deeply at the base once a week during dry summer spells rather than daily light sprinkling.
Plant companion nasturtiums nearby to act as a trap crop for hungry large and small white butterflies.
items.description: Brassica is a genus of plants in the cabbage and mustard family (Brassicaceae). The members of the genus are informally known as cruciferous vegetables, cabbages, mustard plants, or simply brassicas. Crops from this genus are sometimes called cole crops—derived from the Latin caulis, denoting the stem or stalk of a plant.

items.name: Alyssum wulfenianum
items.growersTips:
Plant in gritty, sharply draining alkaline soil to survive wet UK winters and prevent root rot.
Position in full south-facing sun against a stone wall to mimic its alpine scree habitat.
Water sparingly only during dry summer spells once established, as damp soil will kill the plant.
Trim back by half after the yellow spring blooms fade to maintain a tight, cushion-like habit.
Protect young shoots from slugs and snails during damp UK springs using organic grit barriers.
items.description: Alyssum wulfenianum, the madwort, is a species of flowering plant in the family Brassicaceae, native to the southeastern Alps. Preferring dry, porous soils, it is hardy in USDA zones four through nine. There is a cultivar, 'Golden Spring'.

items.name: Wild Radish
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in well-drained UK soil at a depth of 1.5cm from March to August for continuous harvests.
Water consistently at the base twice a week to prevent the roots from splitting or becoming woody.
Net crops early in spring to protect against cabbage white butterflies and flea beetle damage.
Incorporate well-rotted manure into heavy UK clay soils before planting to prevent root fanging.
Grow alongside mint or rosemary to deter common Brassicaceae pests like the cabbage root fly.
items.description: Raphanus raphanistrum, also known as wild radish, white charlock or jointed charlock, is a flowering plant in the family Brassicaceae. The species is native to western Asia, Europe and parts of Northern Africa. It has been introduced into most parts of the world and is regarded as a habitat threatening invasive species in many areas, for example, Australia. It spreads rapidly and is often found growing on roadsides or in other places where the ground has been disturbed. The cultivated radish, widely used as a root vegetable, is sometimes considered to be one of its subspecies as Raphanus rapha

items.name: Descurainia sophia
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at 2mm deep in autumn or early spring directly into well-drained, sandy UK soil.
Water seedlings sparingly only during dry spells, as this plant thrives in dry, nutrient-poor soil.
Hand-pull plants before they set seed in late summer to prevent aggressive self-seeding in borders.
Watch for cabbage white butterfly caterpillars and flea beetles which target this brassica family weed.
Grow alongside spring-flowering bulbs to fill dry, sunny gaps where other plants struggle to survive.
items.description: Descurainia sophia is a species of flowering plant in the cabbage family Brassicaceae. Common names include flixweed, herb-Sophia and tansy mustard. It is an annual plant that reproduces by seeds. It is a dominant weed in dark brown prairie and black prairie soils of southern Alberta. Its stem is erect, branched, and 4–30 in (10–76 cm) high. It was once given to patients with dysentery and called by ancient herbalists Sophia Chirurgorum, "The Wisdom of Surgeons". It is the type species of the genus Descurainia and of the rejected genus Sophia Adans.

items.name: Cardamine breweri
items.growersTips:
Grow this UK-hardy bittercress in wet, acidic soil or shallow pond edges to mimic its stream habitat.
Sow seeds in autumn just under the soil surface in a cold frame to benefit from winter stratification.
Keep the soil constantly saturated or water daily during dry summer spells to prevent early bolting.
Protect young spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic beer traps or copper barrier tape.
Plant alongside water mint or marsh marigold in boggy areas to create a natural damp-loving community.
items.description: Cardamine breweri is a species of cardamine known by the common name Brewer's bittercress. It is native to western North America from British Columbia to California to Colorado, where it grows in coniferous forests, particularly in wet bog habitats.

items.name: Cardamine micranthera
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn 5mm deep in damp, acidic to neutral soil to mimic UK stream-side habitats.
Keep soil constantly wet but not stagnant, watering daily with rainwater during dry summer spells.
Grow in partial to deep shade to prevent the delicate foliage from scorching in midday UK sun.
Protect young spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic wool pellets or beer traps.
Plant alongside water forget-me-not or marsh marigold in bog gardens for natural shade and support.
items.description: Cardamine micranthera is a rare species of flowering plant in the mustard family known by the common names small-anthered bittercress and streambank bittercress. It is endemic to the Piedmont region around the border between Virginia and North Carolina, and is today restricted to the Dan River watershed. It is in decline mainly because its habitat has been disturbed and destroyed by a number of processes. By the 1960s the only known populations of the plant had disappeared and in the 1970s it was feared extinct. The plant was rediscovered in the 1980s and for a while was presumed to be a rare

items.name: Notothlaspi rosulatum
items.growersTips:
Grow in gritty, free-draining alpine compost to mimic scree and prevent winter rot in wet UK climates.
Sow seeds in autumn and leave pots outdoors to undergo natural winter chilling for germination.
Water sparingly from below to keep the foliage dry, preventing crown rot during humid UK summers.
Protect plants with a cloche or alpine house during persistent winter rain to keep them dry.
Watch for slugs and snails which target the fleshy leaves in damp British spring weather.
items.description: Notothlaspi, or penwiper, is a genus of flowering plants belonging to the family Brassicaceae.

items.name: Aethionema saxatile
items.growersTips:
Plant in gritty, free-draining soil with added horticultural grit to survive wet UK winters.
Position in full sun, ideally in a raised bed or rockery to prevent waterlogging and root rot.
Prune back lightly by one-third immediately after flowering in July to maintain a compact habit.
Water newly planted specimens sparingly, only during prolonged dry spells in the British summer.
Protect young shoots from slugs and snails during damp UK spring weather using organic barriers.
items.description: Aethionema is a genus of flowering plants within the family Brassicaceae. They are known as stonecresses. Stonecresses originate from sunny limestone mountainsides in Europe and West Asia, especially Turkey. It is the only genus in the subfamily Aethionemoideae.

items.name: Cardamine pensylvanica
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at a depth of two millimetres in damp, humus-rich soil during early spring.
Keep soil consistently wet by watering twice weekly to mimic its natural UK wetland habitat.
Position in partial shade to prevent the delicate edible leaves from scorching in summer sun.
Hand-weed surrounding soil regularly as this species easily gets choked out by aggressive grasses.
Harvest the peppery leaves before white flowers appear in May to prevent self-seeding and bitterness.
items.description: Cardamine pensylvanica is a species of Cardamine known by the common name Pennsylvania bittercress. It is native to most of Canada and the United States from coast to coast.

items.name: Cardamine glara
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade, mimicking its native UK woodland edge habitat.
Sow seeds in autumn at 2mm depth in cold frames to allow natural winter chilling for germination.
Water weekly during dry UK summer spells to keep the soil consistently damp but never waterlogged.
Hand-weed around the base in spring to prevent aggressive garden grasses from smothering the crown.
Divide mature clumps in early autumn every three years to maintain plant vigour and increase stock.
items.description: Cardamine glara is a species of flowering plant in the family Brassicaceae, native to New Zealand. A rhizomatous perennial herb, its specific epithet refers to the scree that it is often found growing in.

items.name: Cardamine lyrata
items.growersTips:
Grow this aquatic bittercress in a garden pond margin or boggy soil at a depth of 0 to 10cm.
Plant in partial shade to prevent the delicate foliage from scorching in hot UK summer sun.
Propagate in spring by taking stem cuttings and pushing them directly into wet, muddy pond edges.
Watch for aphids and flea beetles in summer, rinsing them off with pond water to avoid chemicals.
Trim back aggressive runners in late autumn to keep the plant from overtaking smaller pond plants.
items.description: Cardamine lyrata, known commonly as Japanese cress and Chinese ivy, is a species of aquatic plant in the mustard family. It is native to the marshes of eastern China and Siberia, as well as Korea and Japan. It flowers from May to June in the wild, with seeds ripening through September. The flowers are bisexual and are pollinated by insects, but are also self-fertile.

items.name: Alyssum montanum
items.growersTips:
Plant in gritty, free-draining soil with added horticultural sand to prevent winter root rot in UK wet.
Sow seeds shallowly at a depth of two millimetres in spring once the risk of frost has passed.
Water sparingly only during prolonged summer dry spells, allowing the soil to dry out completely.
Cut back the foliage by half immediately after flowering in July to maintain a neat, compact mound.
Position in full south-facing sun next to lavender or rosemary to thrive in poor, alkaline soils.
items.description: Alyssum montanum is a species of flowering plant belonging to the family Brassicaceae. It is an evergreen, prostrate perennial with small, hairy, greyish leaves. It typically grows to 10-15 centimeters tall and 30-45 centimeters across. It produces tiny, yellow, fragrant flowers from May to July. These flowers are typically 4-6 centimeters across and borne in dense racemes.

items.name: Cardamine pentaphyllos
items.growersTips:
Plant in autumn under deciduous shrubs to mimic UK woodland soil rich in leaf mould and organic matter
Keep soil consistently moist but free-draining during spring growth using a thick bark mulch layer
Divide congested clumps immediately after flowering in late spring before the foliage dies back
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps
Associate with Galanthus and Erythronium for a synchronized early spring shade garden display
items.description: Cardamine pentaphyllos, the five-leaflet bitter-cress or showy toothwort, is a flowering plant in the family Brassicaceae, native to Western and Central Europe in Slovenia and Croatia. It is an herbaceous perennial, growing to 30–50 cm (12–20 in), with palmate leaves and racemes of purple, pink or white flowers in late Spring and early Summer.

items.name: Coincya monensis
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in spring at a depth of 1cm in free-draining sandy soil to mimic UK coastal habitats.
Protect young plants from cabbage white butterflies and slugs using fine insect netting.
Water deeply once a week during dry UK summer spells rather than giving frequent light sprinkles.
Grow alongside mint or sage to help deter common Brassicaceae pests in your vegetable plot.
Avoid waterlogged winter clay by planting in raised beds or incorporating grit before sowing.
items.description: Coincya is a genus of flowering plant that belongs to the family Brassicaceae. Three species of the plant are endemic to the British Isles, these being Coincya wrightii, Coincya cheiranthos (nokkasinapit) and Coincya monensis, which has two subspecies, C. monensis subsp. monensis and C. monensis subsp. recurvata. Another four species are endangered and endemic to the south-central Iberian peninsula.

items.name: Morisia monanthos
items.growersTips:
Grow in sharply drained gritty soil or scree to prevent winter wet from rotting the deep taproot.
Plant in full sun in an alpine trough or raised bed to mimic its native Mediterranean grit habitat.
Water deeply but infrequently during dry summer spells, allowing the gritty topsoil to dry fully.
Protect the crown with a layer of horticultural grit or gravel to stop damp soil touching leaves.
Watch for slugs and snails in early spring as they target the low-growing rosettes of yellow blooms.
items.description: Morisia is a monotypic genus of ornamental plant in the family Brassicaceae. Its only species is Morisia monanthos, also called M. hypogaea. It is a perennial native to the Mediterranean islands of Corsica and Sardinia.

items.name: Iodanthus pinnatifidus
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn 5mm deep in moist, alkaline soil to mimic UK woodland edges for spring growth.
Water consistently at the base to keep soil damp but not waterlogged during dry UK summer spells.
Protect young spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.
Plant alongside wild garlic or mint to deter common Brassicaceae pests like flea beetles.
Cut back faded flower stems to ground level in late autumn to encourage healthy crown development.
items.description: Iodanthus pinnatifidus, commonly known as purplerocket, is a species of flowering plant in the mustard family. It is monotypic, with no other species in the genus Iodanthus.

items.name: Moricandia arvensis
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at five millimetres deep in spring using free-draining grit-amended compost.
Grow in full sun and alkaline soil to mimic Mediterranean cliffs, adding lime to acidic UK soils.
Protect young plants from slugs and cabbage white butterflies using fine netting or organic bait.
Water sparingly once established, allowing the soil to dry out completely between waterings.
Overwinter container-grown plants in a cold greenhouse to protect them from excessive winter wet.
items.description: Moricandia is a genus of plants of the family Brassicaceae. This genus is mainly distributed in North Africa, the Middle East, and Southern Europe. It is associated with arid and semi-arid environments. Flowers of this genus are actinomorphic-dissymmetrical and mostly lilac in color, although they vary from white to purple depending on the species and climatic conditions. Some species show extreme phenotypic plasticity for flower size, shape, and color. The fruits are two-valved dehiscent siliques with one or two sets of seeds per valve.

items.name: Descurainia sophia
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at three millimetres deep in early spring once UK soil reaches ten degrees.
Water seedlings sparingly only when the top two centimetres of gritty, well-drained soil feels dry.
Net young plants in May to block the cabbage white butterfly and prevent devastating caterpillar loss.
Sow alongside mint or sage to deter flea beetles which frequently target UK brassica crops.
Harvest the peppery young leaves before yellow flowers appear in June to prevent bitter tasting crop.
items.description: Descurainia is a genus of plants in the family Brassicaceae which are known commonly as the tansymustards. The genus name commemorates French botanist and herbalist François Descurain (1658–1749). The plants are similar in appearance to other mustards, sending up long erect stems and bearing small yellow or whitish flowers. Many species are noxious weeds. Some species are toxic to livestock and become a nuisance when they grow in grazing fields. Plants of this genus are found worldwide in temperate regions. Descurainia sophia,, is the type species of Descurainia.

items.name: Rorippa aquatica
items.growersTips:
Grow this semi-aquatic plant in a shallow pond margin with the crown submerged under 5cm of water.
Propagate in spring by taking stem cuttings and rooting them directly in wet, muddy ericaceous soil.
Keep containerized plants in a water-filled tray to mimic UK wetland conditions and prevent drying.
Watch for flea beetles and cabbage white caterpillars in summer, as they target this brassica.
Divide the root clumps every three years in March to maintain vigor and prevent overcrowding.
items.description: Rorippa aquatica, the lakecress or lake cress, is a species of freshwater aquatic flowering plant in the family Brassicaceae. It is found in eastern and central North America, generally in the Great Lakes and Mississippi watersheds. A submerged perennial, it has emergent flowering branches. It is typically found in slow-moving water, such as oxbow lakes. It is used as a foreground aquarium plant, as it is undemanding and very slow-growing.

items.name: Bog yellowcress
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at a depth of two millimetres in autumn to mimic natural UK riverbank conditions
Keep soil constantly damp by watering twice weekly during dry spells to simulate marshy habitats
Watch for flea beetles in spring by checking leaves for tiny holes and using fine mesh netting
Cut back spent flowering stems in late summer to prevent aggressive self-seeding across your lawn
Incorporate heavy organic compost into clay soil to retain moisture while ensuring adequate drainage
items.description: Rorippa palustris, marsh yellow-cress, bog yellow-cress or common yellow-cress, is a species of flowering plant in the family Brassicaceae. It is widespread and native to parts of Africa, and much of Asia, Europe and Eurasia, North America and the Caribbean. It can also be found in other parts of the world as an introduced species and a common weed, for example, in Australia and South America. It is an adaptable plant which grows in many types of damp, wet, and aquatic habitat. It may be an annual, biennial, or perennial plant, and is variable in appearance as well.

items.name: Malcolmia africana
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at five millimetres deep directly into well-drained soil from March to May.
Water sparingly once established as this Mediterranean native dislikes waterlogged UK winter soil.
Watch for flea beetles in spring which chew tiny holes in the leaves of this brassica family member.
Sow in successive batches every fortnight until July to extend the short three-week flowering window.
Grow alongside carrots to help deter carrot rust fly with the strong scent of these flowers.
items.description: Malcolmia is a genus of flowering plants from the family Brassicaceae. It includes 11 species native to the Mediterranean basin, Western Asia, the Transcaucasus, Central Asia, and Pakistan.

items.name: Rorippa austriaca
items.growersTips:
Control this highly invasive weed by digging up the deep taproots entirely in early spring.
Smother persistent patches with thick black polythene sheeting for at least two full growing seasons.
Never compost the roots or stems; dispose of them in council green waste to prevent re-sprouting.
Grow only in sturdy, submerged containers if you must cultivate this aggressive spreader in the UK.
Mow or cut back the yellow flowers in May before they set seed to stop wind-blown garden invasion.
items.description: Rorippa austriaca is a species of flowering plant in the family Brassicaceae known by the common names Austrian yellow-cress and Austrian fieldcress. It is native to parts of Europe and Asia, and it is known in North America as an introduced species and sometimes a noxious weed. It can grow in disturbed habitat, such as roadsides, and in very wet habitat such as mudflats. It is a perennial herb growing upright to erect, reaching a maximum height near one meter. The branching stem bears hairless blue-green lance-shaped leaves up to 10 centimeters long. The bases of the upper leaves clasp the st

items.name: Garden rocket
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds from March to September at a depth of one centimetre directly into moisture-retentive soil
Protect young spring sowings with fleece to prevent damage from flea beetles eating small holes
Water plants consistently at the base during dry summer spells to prevent premature bolting to seed
Grow in partial shade during July and August to keep the leaves tender and reduce the peppery heat
Sow small batches every three weeks for a continuous supply of fresh salad leaves until October
items.description: Eruca is a genus of flowering plants in the family Brassicaceae, native to the Mediterranean region, western and Central Asia, and China. It includes the leaf vegetable known as rocket or arugula.

items.name: Watercress
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in May after frosts, 1.5cm deep in poor soil to encourage flowers instead of just leaves.
Water young plants weekly, but once established only water during dry spells to avoid root rot.
Check under leaves weekly for large white butterfly caterpillars and hand-pick them off immediately.
Plant near runner beans or brassicas as a sacrificial trap crop to lure aphids away from vegetables.
Grow the compact cultivar Tom Thumb in pots to easily control its spread in damp UK weather.
items.description:
Nasturtium may refer to:Tropaeolum, a plant genus in the family Tropaeolaceae, commonly known as nasturtium
Nasturtium , a plant genus in the family Brassicaceae, which includes watercress
Nasturtiums  a 1912 painting by E. Phillips Fox
Nasturtiums, a 1903 painting by Tudor St. George Tucker
Nasturtium (horse) (1899–1916), an American Champion Thoroughbred racehorse
Senecio tropaeolifolius, a succulent plant that is known as "false nasturtium"

items.name: Borodinia macrophylla
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in early spring at a depth of 1.5cm in firm, alkaline soil to prevent clubroot disease.
Protect young crops from cabbage white butterflies using a fine insect mesh netting from May onwards.
Water deeply at the base once a week during dry summer spells to prevent the plants from bolting.
Grow alongside mint or sage to deter flea beetles and improve the overall health of the crop.
Apply a high-nitrogen organic mulch in autumn to protect roots from wet and freezing UK winters.
items.description:
Borodinia may refer to:Borodinia (plant), a genus of flowering plants in the family Brassicaceae
Borodinia (protist), a genus of foraminifers in the family Acervulinidae

items.name: Sea kale
items.growersTips:
Plant Crambe cordifolia in deep, fertile, well-drained soil to accommodate its massive taproot.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.
Water deeply during dry summer spells in the first year to help the deep root system establish.
Cut the large flower stems down to the base in late summer once they turn brown to keep it tidy.
Grow Crambe in full sun to prevent the heavy, cloud-like flower panicles from flopping over.
items.description: Crambe is a genus of annual and perennial flowering plants in the family Brassicaceae, native to a variety of habitats in Europe, Turkey, southwest and central Asia and eastern Africa. They carry dense racemes of tiny white or yellow flowers on stems above the basal leaves. Crambe hispanica subsp. abyssinica, formerly known as Crambe abyssinica, is grown for the oil from the seeds that has characteristics similar to whale oil.

items.name: Radish
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds every two weeks from March to September at one centimetre deep for a continuous UK harvest.
Water consistently in dry spells to prevent the roots from splitting and becoming woody or hot.
Cover crops with fine insect mesh immediately after sowing to block flea beetles and cabbage root fly.
Grow alongside mint or lettuce to deter pests and make efficient use of limited vegetable patch space.
Sow winter cultivars like Mooli in July or August so they mature in the cool British autumn weather.
items.description: Raphanus is a genus within the flowering plant family Brassicaceae.

items.name: Borodinia dentata
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds 1cm deep in early spring, using modular trays to avoid root disturbance when planting out.
Grow in moist, free-draining alkaline soil, adding garden lime if your UK garden has acidic soil.
Protect young plants from cabbage white butterflies and pigeons using a fine 4mm insect netting mesh.
Water consistently at the base to keep soil damp but not waterlogged during dry UK summer spells.
Grow alongside mint or sage to help deter flea beetles, which frequently attack Brassicaceae crops.
items.description: Borodinia dentata, commonly called Short's rockcress, is a species of flowering plant in the mustard family (Brassicaceae). It is native to the eastern North America, where it is found in Canada and the United States. In the United States, its range is primarily centered in the Midwest, and in Canada it is only known from Ontario. Its natural habitat is in nutrient-rich alluvial forests and loamy bluffs, often on calcareous substrate.

items.name: Ochthodium aegyptiacum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in April after frosts at a depth of 5mm directly into free-draining, gritty soil.
Position in the sunniest south-facing spot to mimic its native dry Mediterranean habitat.
Water sparingly only during prolonged dry spells to prevent root rot in damp UK summers.
Watch for flea beetles and cabbage white caterpillars which target this Brassicaceae family member.
Clear dying plants in autumn to prevent self-seeding and maintain neat borders in wet winters.
items.description: Ochthodium is a genus of flowering plants belonging to the family Brassicaceae. It includes a single species, Ochthodium aegyptiacum, an annual native to Cyprus, Egypt, the Levant, and Turkey in the eastern Mediterranean.

items.name: Morettia philaeana
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in early spring under fleece to protect young seedlings from late UK frosts and damp.
Grow in sharply draining, gritty soil with a neutral pH to prevent root rot in wet British winters.
Water sparingly at the base only when the top two inches of soil are dry to avoid downy mildew.
Net the crop securely from April onwards to block cabbage white butterflies and flea beetles.
Plant alongside mint or sage to deter common Brassicaceae pests naturally in small garden plots.
items.description: Morettia is a genus of flowering plants belonging to the family Brassicaceae.

items.name: Polyctenium fremontii
items.growersTips:
Plant in gritty, sharply draining alkaline soil to mimic its Great Basin home and prevent winter rot.
Position in full sun against a south-facing wall to maximise summer heat and protect from UK damp.
Water sparingly only during dry summer spells, keeping the root zone completely dry throughout winter.
Prune lightly in late spring after flowering to maintain a compact shape and prevent woody legginess.
Protect from slugs and snails in early spring when the delicate Brassicaceae foliage first emerges.
items.description: Polyctenium is a genus of flowering plants in the family Brassicaceae. It contains a single species, Polyctenium fremontii, the desert combleaf, a small and compact plant native to the northern Great Basin region of the Western United States. The plants are known by the common name combleaf, owing to the resemblance of their deeply lobed leaves to a comb. It grows in sagebrush shrub steppe in northeastern California, southeastern Oregon, southwestern Idaho, and northwestern Nevada.

items.name: Succowia balearica
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in early spring under cloches to protect young seedlings from late UK frosts.
Grow in free-draining sandy loam with a neutral pH to prevent clubroot common in Brassicaceae.
Water consistently at the base to keep soil moist but avoid waterlogging which causes root rot.
Net the crop with fine mesh in summer to block cabbage white butterflies and flea beetles.
Harvest the tender young leaves and seedpods before the yellow flowers fade and set tough seeds.
items.description: Succowia is a monotypic genus of flowering plants belonging to the family Brassicaceae. It only contains one known species, Succowia balearica (L.) Medik.

items.name: Sinapidendron frutescens
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds 1cm deep in early spring using cloches to protect young seedlings from late UK frosts.
Grow in fertile well-drained soil with a pH above 6.5 to prevent the devastating clubroot disease.
Net the crop securely from May to September to block cabbage white butterflies and wood pigeons.
Water deeply at the base once a week during dry summer spells to stop the plants bolting to seed.
Interplant with mint or sage to help deter flea beetles which riddle the leaves with tiny holes.
items.description: Sinapidendron is a genus of flowering plants belonging to the family Brassicaceae.

items.name: Rorippa sylvestris
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds 5mm deep in spring when UK soil warms, keeping the compost consistently moist for success.
Grow this invasive creeping yellowcress in containers to prevent its runners overtaking garden beds.
Water daily in dry UK summers to mimic its natural damp riverbank habitat and prevent bolting.
Hand-pull young plants before they flower in June to stop aggressive self-seeding in damp borders.
Plant alongside watercress or mint in boggy areas as they share similar high-moisture requirements.
items.description: Rorippa sylvestris is an invasive species of plant in the United States, likely entering from Europe before 1818 from ballast water and spreading throughout North America through contaminated nursery seed stock.

items.name: Nasturtiopsis coronopifolia
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in early spring at a depth of one centimetre once the risk of hard frost has passed
Keep the soil consistently moist but not waterlogged to prevent this brassica from bolting early
Protect young seedlings from slugs and cabbage white caterpillars using fine insect netting
Grow in moderately fertile well-drained soil with a neutral pH to encourage healthy leaf growth
Plant alongside mint or sage to help deter common brassica pests in the damp UK climate
items.description: Nasturtiopsis is a genus of flowering plants belonging to the family Brassicaceae.

items.name: Erucaria microcarpa
items.growersTips:
Sow Erucaria seeds in early spring at a depth of six millimetres directly into well-drained soil.
Keep soil consistently moist but not waterlogged to prevent this brassica from bolting prematurely.
Protect young Erucaria seedlings from UK slugs and flea beetles using fine insect mesh netting.
Incorporate well-rotted manure into the bed two weeks before sowing to provide essential nitrogen.
Grow Erucaria alongside mint or sage to help deter common British brassica pests naturally.
items.description: Erucaria is a genus of flowering plants of the family Brassicaceae, commonly known as Pink-mustard. Species are native to southern and eastern Mediterranean region, Arabian Peninsula, and Iran.

items.name: Descurainia paradisa
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at three millimetres deep in autumn to mimic natural UK cold stratification.
Grow in sharply draining sandy loam with added grit to prevent winter root rot in wet UK climates.
Water sparingly only during prolonged summer dry spells once the deep taproot is fully established.
Prune back the woody stems by one third in late spring to maintain a compact shrubby growth habit.
Protect young spring shoots from slugs and snails using beer traps or organic wool pellets.
items.description: Descurainia paradisa is a plant species native to eastern and northern California, southeastern Oregon, Box Elder County in northwestern Utah, and most of Nevada. It grows in shrub communities at elevations of 3,300–7,500 feet (1,000–2,300 m).

items.name: Columbia yellowcress
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in spring at a depth of 5mm in a cold frame to protect them from late UK frosts.
Grow in wet, poorly-drained acidic soil or bog gardens to mimic its native damp gravel habitat.
Water daily to keep the soil constantly saturated, as this wetland plant cannot tolerate drying out.
Watch for flea beetles and cabbage white caterpillars which target this Brassicaceae family member.
Plant alongside watercress or marsh marigold in pond margins to create a thriving damp community.
items.description: Rorippa columbiae is a species of flowering plant in the family Brassicaceae known by the common names Columbian yellowcress and Columbia yellow cress.

items.name: Poor man's mustard
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn at 5mm depth in moist, shady spots to mimic UK woodland edge conditions.
Keep soil consistently damp but not waterlogged, mimicking damp British spring weather.
Watch for green veined white butterfly caterpillars which feed heavily on Alliaria leaves in summer.
Harvest leaves in early spring before the white flowers appear to prevent bitter tasting foliage.
Grow alongside wild garlic in damp clay soils as they share identical light and moisture needs.
items.description: Alliaria is a genus of flowering plants in the family Brassicaceae.

items.name: Chinese violet cress
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in late summer directly into moist, free-draining soil to establish winter-hardy rosettes.
Plant seeds at a depth of five millimetres in partial shade to mimic its native woodland edge habitat.
Water consistently during dry spring spells to prevent early bolting and keep the leaves tender.
Watch for cabbage white butterfly caterpillars and use fine netting to protect the brassica foliage.
Grow alongside early spring bulbs like daffodils to create a vibrant purple and yellow colour contrast.
items.description: Orychophragmus is a genus of plants in the family Brassicaceae. It includes seven species native to China and Korea.

items.name: Fibigia clypeata
items.growersTips:
Sow Fibigia clypeata seeds in autumn in well-drained chalky soil to mimic UK limestone habitats.
Water young plants weekly until established then leave dry as they rot easily in wet UK winters.
Watch for cabbage white butterflies and caterpillars which target this Brassicaceae family member.
Cut back spent flower stems in late August to encourage a second flush of decorative silver pods.
Plant alongside rosemary or thyme in south-facing gravel beds to ensure the required sharp drainage.
items.description: Fibigia is a genus of flowering plants in the family Brassicaceae. It includes six species native to the eastern Mediterranean, Western Asia, and the Caucasus.

items.name: Maresia pulchella
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in early spring at a depth of five millimetres to match cool UK germination temperatures
Grow in well-drained sandy loam with a neutral pH to prevent clubroot common in Brassicaceae crops
Water consistently at the base to keep soil damp but not waterlogged to prevent early bolting
Protect young seedlings from flea beetles and slugs using fine insect mesh or cloches in spring
Plant alongside mint or sage to deter cabbage white butterflies from laying eggs on the foliage
items.description:
Maresia is a genus of plants in the family Brassicaceae. The species can be found along the Mediterranean Sea and towards Iran and Afghanistan. There are two species in this genus:Maresia nana (DC.) Batt.
Maresia pulchella (DC.) O.E.Schulz

items.name: Carrichtera annua
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at five millimetres deep in early spring once UK frosts have fully passed.
Grow in sharply draining sandy soil to prevent root rot during wet British summer periods.
Water sparingly only when the top two inches of soil are dry to mimic its native arid habitat.
Protect young seedlings from slugs and cabbage white butterflies using fine netting or cloches.
Position in the brightest south-facing spot of your garden to maximise essential sun exposure.
items.description: Carrichtera is a genus of flowering plants belonging to the family Brassicaceae.

items.name: Berteroa incana
items.growersTips:
Sow Berteroa seeds in early spring at a depth of 5mm in free-draining, poor to average alkaline soil.
Keep soil barely damp during germination, then water only during dry spells to prevent root rot.
Watch for flea beetles in May, protecting young seedlings with fine insect mesh or horticultural fleece.
Grow Berteroa alongside rosemary or thyme to deter common Brassicaceae pests with strong scents.
Cut back the seed heads in late summer to prevent aggressive self-seeding across your garden beds.
items.description: Berteroa, the false madworts, is a genus of flowering plants of the family Brassicaceae, native to temperate Eurasia. Its best known member is the weedy invasive hoary alyssum, Berteroa incana.

items.name: Cusickiella douglasii
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn at five millimetres deep to allow natural UK winter cold to break dormancy.
Grow in a gritty, alkaline scree mix to mimic alpine scree and prevent winter wet root rot.
Water only during dry spring spells, allowing the gritty soil to dry out completely between feeds.
Protect young foliage from slugs and snails using copper tape around pots during damp UK springs.
Plant alongside wild thyme in stone troughs to provide excellent drainage and mimic alpine habitats.
items.description: Cusickiella is a small genus containing two species of plants in the family Brassicaceae which are native to the western United States. These are mat-forming perennials with a stumpy, branching caudex covered in rounded clusters of tiny, thick leaves. A short stem bears white or yellowish flowers that yield silicles.

items.name: Hirschfeldia incana
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in spring just 2mm deep in poor, well-drained soil as excessive nutrients reduce flavor.
Water sparingly only during prolonged summer droughts to prevent root rot in damp UK winters.
Cut back yellowing flower stalks in late summer to prevent aggressive self-seeding across lawns.
Check young leaves in spring for flea beetle damage and use fine mesh nets to protect the crop.
Grow alongside mint or rosemary to deter cabbage white butterflies from laying eggs on the foliage.
items.description: Hirschfeldia incana is a species of flowering plant in the mustard family known by many common names, including shortpod mustard, buchanweed, hoary mustard and Mediterranean mustard. It is the only species in the monotypic genus Hirschfeldia, which is closely related to Brassica. The species is native to the Mediterranean Basin but it can be found in many parts of the world as an introduced species and often a very abundant noxious weed. This mustard is very similar in appearance to black mustard, but is generally shorter. It forms a wide basal rosette of lobed leaves which lie flat on the gro

items.name: Peltaria angustifolia
items.growersTips:
Plant Peltaria alliacea in moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to mimic UK woodland edges.
Sow seeds in autumn in cold frames to allow natural winter stratification for spring germination.
Divide established clumps in early spring to control its vigorous, invasive-leaning root spread.
Water consistently during dry UK summers to prevent the leaves from becoming excessively bitter.
Watch for flea beetles in spring, protecting young foliage with fine insect mesh or fleece.
items.description: Peltaria is a genus of flowering plants in the family Brassicaceae. Their distribution ranges from Southeast Europe, Near East to Central Asia. They prefer rocky slopes.

items.name: Rapistrum rugosum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in spring at a depth of five millimetres into poor, well-drained soil to limit wild spread.
Water young seedlings weekly until established, then rely solely on natural UK rainfall to avoid rot.
Uproot plants manually before yellow flowers set seed in July to prevent aggressive self-seeding.
Grow alongside heavy feeders like cabbage to draw away flea beetles, acting as a sacrificial trap.
Hand-pull taproots from damp soil in autumn to clear beds without leaving root fragments to regrow.
items.description: Rapistrum, the bastard cabbages, is a genus of the family Brassicaceae with a distinctive cross like arrangement of its petals. It is also known as wild-turnip or turnipweed. Species of Rapistrum are annual to perennials. The yellow petals are accompanied by sepals that stand vertically at near right angles (erecto-patent). Leaf shape and arrangement varies from rough toothed (dentate) to a configuration of opposingly lobed pairs along the plant stalk, pinnately lobed.

items.name: Diplotaxis tenuifolia
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at five millimetres deep from March to September for continuous UK harvests.
Grow in free-draining, poor soil to prevent lush, weak growth and intensify the peppery flavour.
Water consistently at the base during dry summer spells to stop plants bolting and becoming bitter.
Protect young leaves from flea beetles using fine insect mesh immediately after sowing outdoors.
Cut back flowering stems promptly in summer to encourage fresh leaf growth and prevent self-seeding.

items.name: Erucastrum gallicum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in spring at a depth of five millimetres into well-drained alkaline soil to avoid clubroot.

Sow seeds indoors in April at 2cm deep using a heated propagator to ensure the required 21C minimum.
Grow inside a greenhouse or polytunnel as UK summers are too cold and wet for outdoor survival.
Water the soil consistently at the base to prevent powdery mildew on the highly sensitive foliage.
Train the vigorous vines up sturdy trellises and pinch out the growing tips to encourage lateral fruiting.
Harvest only when the spikes turn bright orange as unripe green fruits lack the signature banana flavor.

items.name: True melon
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in April on their sides 1.5cm deep in 9cm pots using a heated propagator set to 21C.
Grow in a greenhouse or polytunnel as UK summers are rarely warm enough for outdoor success.
Pinch out the main growing tip at the fifth leaf to encourage side shoots that bear the fruit.
Water the soil around the base of the plant daily but keep the main stem dry to prevent rot.
Place a tile or piece of wood under developing melons to stop them rotting on the damp soil.

items.name: Cucumber
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds on their edge 2cm deep in April indoors to prevent rotting in damp UK spring compost.
Water the soil around the base daily, never the leaves, to prevent powdery mildew in humid weather.
Grow all-female greenhouse varieties like Carmen to avoid bitter fruits caused by cross-pollination.
Pinch out the main growing tip at the top of the support to encourage heavy-fruiting side shoots.
Plant alongside dill or marigolds to deter aphids and attract pollinators to your outdoor crops.
items.description: The cucumber is a widely-cultivated creeping vine plant in the family Cucurbitaceae that bears cylindrical to spherical fruits, used as culinary vegetables. Considered an annual plant, there are three main types: slicing, pickling, and seedless.

items.name: Gac
items.growersTips:
Start seeds indoors in April at 25C using a heated propagator to survive the short UK summer.
Plant in a deep container of rich, free-draining loam and place in your warmest, sunniest greenhouse.
Hand-pollinate the distinct male and female yellow flowers daily as UK insects ignore them.
Water deeply at the base twice a week to keep soil damp but never let the roots sit in cold mud.
Provide a sturdy trellis or overhead netting to support the heavy, vigorous climbing vines.

items.name: Thladiantha dubia
items.growersTips:
Plant tubers ten centimetres deep in spring using large pots to restrict their highly invasive roots.
Water deeply once a week during dry UK summers to support the rapid growth of this vigorous climber.
Provide a sturdy two-metre trellis or wires against a south-facing wall to maximise summer sun.
Hand-pollinate the yellow flowers in August as UK native insects often ignore this dioecious plant.
Cut all vines back to ground level in late autumn and mulch heavily to protect tubers from hard frost.

items.name: Bitter gourd
items.growersTips:
Start seeds indoors in April at 2.5cm deep using a heated propagator set to 22C to ensure germination.
Grow in a greenhouse or against a south-facing brick wall to survive the cool UK summer nights.
Water deeply at the base twice a week to keep soil moist but avoid wetting leaves to prevent mildew.
Pinch out the main growing tip when it reaches 1.5 metres to encourage productive side branches.
Hand-pollinate the yellow flowers using a small paintbrush because UK pollinator activity can be low.

items.name: Trichosanthes kirilowii
items.growersTips:
Start seeds indoors in April at 20C in deep pots to protect the taproot before late May planting.
Grow against a south-facing wall or in a greenhouse to provide the high summer heat this vine needs.
Water deeply at the base twice a week during dry spells to keep the moisture-loving roots damp.
Provide a sturdy trellis at least two meters high to support the heavy climbing vines and fruits.
Apply a thick mulch of well-rotted manure in June to feed the plant and retain soil moisture.

items.name: Great Fringed-Flower Vine
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in April at 2cm depth using a heated propagator to overcome cool UK spring soils.
Grow this vigorous climber inside a polytunnel or greenhouse to ensure the high heat it requires.
Water deeply at the base twice a week to keep soil moist but avoid wetting leaves to prevent rot.
Train vines onto strong trellis support and pinch out growing tips to encourage lateral fruiting.
Hand-pollinate the nocturnal white flowers using a small brush since UK night pollinators are rare.

items.name: Cucurbita pepo var. clypeata
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in April at 2cm deep in 9cm pots using a heat mat to guarantee 20C germination.
Plant out in late May after frosts, burying the stem up to the first leaves to boost root growth.
Water deeply at the base twice weekly in dry spells, keeping water off leaves to prevent mildew.
Place a slate or tile under developing crown-shaped fruits to protect them from damp UK soil rot.
Pinch out the main vine growing tip after four fruits form to force energy into ripening before frost.

items.name: Dendrosicyos
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender desert tree in a gritty loam-based cactus compost with fifty percent perlite.
Keep the plant above twelve degrees Celsius year-round in a heated greenhouse or bright indoors.
Water only when the soil is bone dry in summer and keep completely dry throughout the winter.
Position in the brightest south-facing spot possible to mimic the intense light of Socotra.
Watch for glasshouse red spider mite under glass and treat immediately with biological controls.

items.name: Honeydew
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in April at two centimetres deep using individual pots on a warm windowsill.
Plant out in late May after frosts, spacing sixty centimetres apart in rich, moisture-retentive soil.
Water deeply at the base twice weekly to keep soil damp but avoid wetting the leaves to prevent rot.
Pinch out the main growing tip after five leaves to encourage lateral fruiting branches to develop.
Support developing melons on raised tiles or nets to prevent ground rot in damp British summers.

items.name: Montreal melon
items.growersTips:
Sow indoors in April at 2cm deep using individual pots on a heated propagation mat set to 21C.
Grow on in a greenhouse or polytunnel as the UK climate is too cool for outdoor success.
Train the main stem up a vertical support and pinch out the growing tip at the fifth leaf.
Support the heavy, netted melons in individual net bags tied to the frame to prevent vine breakage.
Water deeply at the base keeping foliage dry, then reduce watering when fruits reach full size.

items.name: Watermelon
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in April at 2cm deep in 9cm pots using a heated propagator set to 21C.
Grow in a greenhouse or polytunnel, or plant outdoors in June against a south-facing brick wall.
Water the soil deeply around the base, keeping the foliage dry to prevent powdery mildew.
Pinch out the main growing tip after five leaves to encourage lateral fruiting side-shoots.
Raise developing fruits off the damp soil using a slate, tile, or straw to prevent rotting.
items.description: The watermelon is a species of flowering plant in the family Cucurbitaceae, that has a large, edible fruit. It is a scrambling and trailing vine-like plant, and is widely cultivated worldwide, with more than 1,000 varieties.

items.name: Trichosanthes scabra
items.growersTips:
Start seeds indoors in April at 20C in deep pots to protect taproots before late May planting.
Grow against a south-facing wall under glass or polytunnel to survive cool UK summer nights.
Water deeply at the base weekly keeping foliage dry to prevent powdery mildew in damp UK weather.
Prune lateral shoots after the fifth leaf to encourage female flowers and improve fruit set.
Incorporate well-rotted manure and grit into soil to ensure rich nutrients with sharp drainage.

items.name: Trichosanthes pentaphylla
items.growersTips:
Start seeds indoors in April at 20C in deep pots to avoid disturbing the sensitive taproot system
Grow this tender climber inside a polytunnel or greenhouse to ensure the high heat it needs in the UK
Water deeply at the base twice a week to keep soil moist but never waterlogged to prevent root rot
Train vines up a sturdy trellis and prune side shoots after the first flower to boost fruit yield
Watch for slugs on young spring shoots and use organic wool pellets around the base to protect them

items.name: Trichosanthes cochinchinensis
items.growersTips:
Start seeds indoors in April at 2cm depth using a heated propagator kept at 22C to ensure germination
Grow in a greenhouse or south-facing polytunnel to provide the high heat and humidity this vine needs
Water deeply at the base twice a week to keep soil moist but never waterlogged to prevent root rot
Train the vigorous vines up sturdy trellises and hand-pollinate the white night-blooming flowers
Protect young plants from slugs in May using organic beer traps or copper tape around container rims

items.name: Fevillea trilobata
items.growersTips:
Grow Fevillea in a heated greenhouse or conservatory to survive the cold, damp UK climate.
Sow seeds 2cm deep in individual pots of peat-free compost on a heated propagator mat in April.
Water the soil deeply only when the top 3cm dries out, keeping foliage dry to prevent rot.
Train the vigorous vines up a sturdy trellis or wires to support the heavy, oil-rich fruits.
Watch for glasshouse whitefly and red spider mite, treating early with biological controls.

items.name: Solena amplexicaulis
items.growersTips:
Start seeds indoors in April at 2cm depth using bottom heat of 21C before transplanting out in June.
Grow against a south-facing wall on a sturdy trellis to keep the climbing vines off wet UK soil.
Water deeply at the base twice a week to keep soil moist while keeping the dense foliage dry.
Prune the main growing tip at 1.5 metres to encourage lateral fruiting branches to develop.
Apply a high-potassium liquid tomato feed every fortnight once the yellow flowers begin to open.

items.name: Thladiantha dubia
items.growersTips:
Plant tubers ten centimetres deep in spring using rich, moisture-retentive soil in a sheltered spot.
Provide a sturdy trellis or wires for this vigorous climber to scramble up to three metres high.
Water deeply at the base twice a week during dry summer spells to keep the soil consistently moist.
Hand-pollinate the yellow flowers in summer because UK native insects rarely trigger fruit set.
Mulch heavily in late autumn with compost to protect the tender root system from wet winter frosts.

items.name: Cantaloupe
items.growersTips:
Start seeds indoors in April at 2cm deep using bottom heat of 21C to counter cool UK spring soils.
Grow in a greenhouse or polytunnel to provide the high heat and humidity these melons require in the UK.
Pinch out the main growing tip after five leaves to encourage the lateral fruiting branches to grow.
Water deeply at the base, keeping leaves dry to prevent powdery mildew in damp UK summer weather.
Place a slate or tile under developing melons to protect them from damp soil and prevent rotting.

items.name: Benincaseae

Sow wax gourd seeds indoors in April at 2cm deep using bottom heat of 22C to ensure UK germination.
Grow winter melon in a greenhouse or against a south-facing brick wall to maximize summer warmth.
Water the soil deeply at the base twice a week, keeping the hairy foliage dry to prevent mildew.
Train vines up a sturdy trellis and support heavy developing gourds with individual netting slings.
Prune the main stem after five leaves to force side shoots where female flowers and fruit form.
items.description: Benincaseae is one of 15 tribes in the family Cucurbitaceae.

items.name: Melothria pendula
items.growersTips:
Start seeds indoors in April at 1cm depth using a heated propagator to overcome the cool UK spring.
Grow in a greenhouse or against a south-facing wall in fertile, free-draining soil pH 6.0 to 6.8.
Provide a fine netting or trellis immediately as the delicate climbing tendrils need early support.
Water consistently at the base to keep soil moist but never waterlogged to prevent root rot.
Harvest fruits when small and light green, as older dark green fruits have a strong laxative effect.

items.name: Doyerea emetocathartica
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender caudiciform in a heated greenhouse or indoors to survive damp UK winter cold.
Use a gritty loam-based compost with fifty percent perlite to prevent root rot in humid UK air.
Water only when the caudex feels slightly soft, keeping it completely dry throughout winter.
Position on a south-facing windowsill to maximise scarce UK sunlight and encourage caudex growth.
Check the swollen base weekly for mealybugs which hide in the deep crevices of the corky bark.

items.name: Tinda
items.growersTips:
Start seeds indoors in April at 2cm depth using bottom heat of 21C to survive the cool UK spring.
Grow in a greenhouse or against a south-facing wall in rich soil with a pH of 6.0 to 6.8.
Water deeply at the base twice a week to keep soil moist but avoid wetting leaves to prevent mildew.
Hand-pollinate the yellow flowers using a cotton bud because UK pollinator activity can be low.
Pinch out the main growing tip when it reaches 1 metre to encourage productive lateral fruiting.

items.name: Sprite melon

Sow seeds indoors in April at 2cm deep using a heated propagator to combat cool UK spring soil.
Grow this compact variety in a greenhouse or polytunnel to ensure the high heat it needs to fruit.
Water the soil around the base daily but keep the foliage dry to prevent powdery mildew outbreaks.
Pinch out the main stem after five leaves to encourage the side shoots where melons actually form.
Harvest when the skin turns from green to ivory-yellow and a sweet fragrance is present at the stem.

items.name: Ecballium
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in April at two centimetres deep in free-draining compost using individual pots
Grow in the sunniest sheltered spot possible to mimic Mediterranean heat and prevent wind damage
Water sparingly at the base once established to prevent powdery mildew in damp UK summer weather
Wear thick gloves when handling to avoid contact with the toxic and highly irritating skin sap
Plant in poor sandy soil to restrict rapid leafy growth and encourage more explosive seed pods

items.name: Kedrostis nana
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender caudiciform in a gritty, free-draining loam mix with fifty percent perlite or pumice.
Position the pot on a sunny south-facing windowsill or heated greenhouse to mimic its native warmth.
Water only when the soil is dry, then stop watering completely in autumn when the vine dies back.
Expose the top third of the swollen caudex during spring repotting once the root system is robust.
Check the soft vine foliage weekly for red spider mites, which thrive in dry indoor UK conditions.

items.name: Bitter gourd

Train vines up a sturdy trellis and pinch out the main shoot at 1.5m to encourage fruiting side branches.
Hand pollinate the yellow flowers using a small paintbrush because UK greenhouse pollinators are scarce.

items.name: Ibervillea sonorae

Grow this Mexican caudiciform in a heated greenhouse or indoors to survive damp UK winter cold.
Use a soil mix of fifty percent grit or perlite with loam to prevent caudex rot in humid UK weather.
Water only when the caudex softens slightly in summer, keeping it completely dry from October to March.
Position the pot on a south-facing windowsill to maximise scarce UK sunlight for vine development.
Sow seeds in spring using a heated propagator set to twenty-five degrees Celsius for germination.

items.name: Schizocarpum parviflorum

Train the vigorous vines up a sturdy trellis or netting to keep the small fragile fruits off wet soil.

items.name: Benincasa hispida var. chieh-qua

Sow seeds indoors in April at 2cm deep using bottom heat of 21C to counter cool UK spring soils.
Grow in a greenhouse or against a south-facing wall in fertile soil rich in well-rotted manure.
Train the heavy vines up a sturdy trellis and support developing melons in nets to prevent rot.
Water copiously at the base to keep soil moist but keep water off leaves to prevent powdery mildew.
Hand-pollinate the yellow flowers in midsummer using a cotton swab to ensure successful fruit set.

items.name: Citrullus afer

Start seeds indoors in April at 2cm depth using bottom heat of 21C to counter cool UK spring soils.
Grow in a greenhouse or under cloches to provide the high summer heat this African melon requires.
Water deeply at the base weekly to keep soil moist but keep the foliage dry to prevent powdery mildew.
Pinch out the main growing tip at five leaves to encourage lateral fruiting branches to develop.
Place a tile or slate under developing melons to protect them from damp UK soil and prevent rotting.

items.name: Sicana odorifera

Start seeds indoors in April at 2cm depth using a heated propagator kept at a constant 22C.
Grow inside a polytunnel or greenhouse to provide the high heat and humidity this vine requires.
Water heavily at the base twice weekly once fruit sets, keeping the foliage dry to prevent rot.
Provide a heavy-duty trellis or overhead support capable of holding fruits weighing up to 4kg.
Prune lateral shoots after the first female flower appears to focus energy on fruit development.

items.name: Momordica foetida
items.growersTips:
Start seeds indoors in April at 2cm depth using a heated propagator kept at a steady 22C to 25C.
Grow in a greenhouse or south-facing polytunnel to match the high heat this African vine requires.
Water deeply at the base twice a week to keep soil moist but never waterlogged to prevent root rot.
Provide a strong trellis or netting by June to support the vigorous climbing tendrils of this vine.
Hand-pollinate the yellow flowers using a small paintbrush to ensure fruit set in UK greenhouses.

items.name: Delicata squash

Sow indoors in April at 2cm deep in 9cm pots using a heat mat to guarantee the 20C needed for germination
Plant out in late May after hardening off, spacing 90cm apart in soil enriched with garden compost
Water deeply at the base twice weekly in dry spells, keeping the highly susceptible foliage dry
Pinch out the growing tips after four fruits have set to ensure they ripen fully in the UK autumn
Harvest in October before the first frost once the skin resists a fingernail and the stem turns woody

items.name: Fevillea cordifolia

Grow this tender tropical climber in a heated greenhouse or conservatory to survive UK winters.
Sow seeds individually 2cm deep in pots of free-draining compost on a heated propagator mat at 25C.

Provide a sturdy trellis or overhead wires to support the heavy, vigorous climbing tendrils.

items.name: Trichosanthes pilosa

Water deeply at the base twice a week to keep soil moist but never waterlogged to prevent root rot.
Train the vigorous vines up a sturdy trellis and pinch out growing tips to encourage lateral fruit.
Hand-pollinate the nocturnal white flowers at dusk using a paintbrush as UK night pollinators vary.

items.name: Cucurbitoideae
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds on their sides 2cm deep in April indoors to prevent rotting in cold UK spring soil.
Water the soil around the base not the leaves to prevent powdery mildew in humid UK summers.
Sink a plastic pot next to the plant base and water into it to target the deep roots directly.
Pinch out the main growing tip after four true leaves to encourage fruiting side shoots in the UK.
Raise developing squashes off wet UK soil using tiles or bricks to prevent rot before harvest.

items.name: Trichosanthes dioica

Grow this dioecious vine in a heated greenhouse or polytunnel as UK summers are too cold outdoors.

Hand-pollinate the nocturnal white flowers in the evening using a paint brush to transfer pollen.
Train the vigorous vines up a sturdy trellis and pinch out the main growing tip at one meter.

items.name: Cucumis melo var. flexuosus

items.name: Momordica dioica

Water deeply at the base twice a week to keep soil moist but never waterlogged to prevent root rot.
Provide a sturdy trellis or netting for the climbing tendrils to support heavy fruit development.

items.name: Momordica cymbalaria

Provide a sturdy vertical trellis to support the climbing tendrils and keep fruits off damp soil.
Overwinter the dormant tuber indoors in dry compost above 10C once autumn frosts arrive.

items.name: Alsomitra macrocarpa

Grow this tropical vine in a heated greenhouse or conservatory to survive the cold UK climate.
Sow seeds in free-draining sandy loam at a depth of two centimeters with bottom heat of twenty-five C.

Provide a sturdy overhead trellis for the climbing tendrils to support its heavy canopy and fruit.
Prune back excess lateral shoots in late winter while the plant is dormant to control its size.

items.name: Yubari King

Start seeds indoors in April at 2cm deep using bottom heat of 21C to survive the cool UK spring.
Grow only in a greenhouse or polytunnel to mimic the high heat and humidity this melon requires.
Hand-pollinate the female flowers at midday by brushing them with male pollen to ensure fruit set.

items.name: Monk fruit

items.name: Oriental pickling melon

Start seeds indoors in April at 2cm deep using bottom heat of 21C to survive the cool UK spring.

Water the soil deeply around the base but keep the foliage dry to prevent powdery mildew in damp UK air.

items.name: Citrullus ecirrhosus

Water sparingly at the base only when soil is dry to prevent root rot in damp British weather.

items.name: Oriental sweet melon

Start seeds indoors in April at 2cm deep using bottom heat of 21C to counter cool UK spring soils.
Grow in a greenhouse or polytunnel to provide the high heat and humidity these Asian melons need.
Pinch out the main stem at five leaves to force side shoots where the female flowers will form.
Hand pollinate the small yellow flowers using a paintbrush if greenhouse insect activity is low.
Restrict water as the smooth yellow fruits reach full size to prevent splitting in damp UK weather.

items.name: Melothria scabra

Start seeds indoors in April at two centimetres deep using bottom heat to combat cool UK springs.
Plant out in late May only after frost passes, spacing thirty centimetres apart against a trellis.
Water consistently at the base to prevent powdery mildew, keeping soil moist but never waterlogged.
Pinch out the growing tips at one point five metres high to encourage heavy fruiting side shoots.
Harvest when fruits are the size of a grape and still firm, before they turn yellow and bitter.

items.name: Trichosanthes cucumerina

items.name: Sicana odorifera

Train the sprawling, spiny vines onto a sturdy vertical trellis to save space in small UK glasshouses.
Hand-pollinate the yellow flowers using a soft brush as UK insects will not recognise this species.

items.name: Cucumis myriocarpus
items.growersTips:
Start seeds indoors in April at 2cm depth using bottom heat of 21C to counter the cool UK spring.
Plant out in June in a south-facing spot with sandy, free-draining soil of pH 6.0 to 7.5.
Water deeply at the base weekly, keeping foliage dry to prevent powdery mildew in damp UK summers.
Grow against a trellis to keep the small, prickly fruits off wet soil and prevent rot.
Wear gloves when handling this plant as the foliage and unripe fruits contain toxic cucurbitacins.

items.name: Cucumis humifructus
items.growersTips:
Grow in a heated greenhouse or polytunnel as UK summers are too cold for outdoor geocarpic fruiting.
Sow seeds indoors in April at 2.5cm deep using a heated propagator kept at a constant 21C to 24C.
Plant in deep pots of loose sandy loam so the burying peduncles can easily push fruit underground.
Water the soil directly around the base to keep it moist but avoid wetting the subterranean fruit.
Provide a sturdy trellis for the vines to climb while keeping the main crown clear for burying.

items.name: Cephalopentandra ecirrhosa
items.growersTips:
Grow in a heated greenhouse or sunny windowsill keeping minimum winter temperatures above twelve Celsius
Sow seeds five millimetres deep in a free-draining mix of equal parts John Innes number two and grit
Water only when the caudex feels slightly soft then drench thoroughly and let dry out completely
Check weekly for red spider mite under leaves and maintain humidity with light misting in summer
Do not prune the annual climbing vines until they naturally die back to the caudex in late autumn

items.name: Cucurbitella asperata
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in April at 2cm deep in 9cm pots of peat-free compost to avoid late UK frosts.
Water deeply at the base twice weekly in dry spells to keep soil moist without wetting the foliage.
Protect young outdoor plants from slugs using copper tape or beer traps during damp May nights.
Pinch out the growing tips once five true leaves form to encourage productive side shoots to grow.
Mix plenty of well-rotted manure into the planting site to provide the rich soil nutrients needed.

items.name: Long-tailed silverfish
items.growersTips:
Start seeds indoors in April at 2cm depth using a heated propagator to survive chilly UK springs.
Grow this tender climber against a south-facing wall or inside a polytunnel to maximise summer heat.
Water deeply at the base twice a week to keep soil moist but avoid wetting leaves to prevent mildew.
Pinch out the main growing tip at 1.5 metres to encourage lateral fruiting branches to develop.
Train vines onto a sturdy trellis or netting to keep the delicate climbing tendrils off damp soil.

items.name: Corallocarpus epigaeus
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender caudiciform in a gritty, free-draining loam-based compost with fifty percent grit.
Keep the swollen caudex completely above the soil level when potting to prevent winter wet rot.
Water only when the soil dries out fully from April to September, then keep totally dry in winter.
Overwinter indoors on a south-facing windowsill at a minimum temperature of twelve degrees Celsius.
Watch for red spider mite in dry greenhouse conditions and mist the surrounding air to deter them.

items.name: Cucurbita andreana
items.growersTips:
Start seeds indoors in April at 2cm deep using bottom heat to overcome cool UK spring soil.
Plant out in June in a sun-facing, sheltered spot using a raised mound of compost to aid drainage.
Water deeply at the base twice weekly in dry spells, keeping the hairy foliage completely dry.
Hand-pollinate the yellow flowers early in the morning if UK pollinator activity is low in July.
Harvest before the first autumn frost, leaving a 5cm stem to prevent rot during winter storage.

items.name: Cucurbita ecuadorensis
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in April at 2cm deep in 9cm pots using a heated propagator set to 21C.
Plant out in June after the last frost into soil enriched with plenty of well-rotted manure.
Water deeply at the base twice a week to keep the soil moist but avoid wetting the wild foliage.
Train the vigorous vines onto a sturdy trellis to keep the rare, heavy fruits off damp UK soil.
Hand-pollinate the yellow flowers in the morning using a small paintbrush to ensure fruit set.

items.name: Cyclanthera pedata
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in April at two centimetres deep using individual pots to avoid root disturbance.
Plant out in late May after frosts in fertile soil enriched with plenty of well-rotted manure.
Provide a sturdy two-metre trellis or netting immediately as the vigorous tendrils climb rapidly.
Water copiously at the base during dry summer spells to prevent the shallow roots from drying out.
