Hand-pollinate the nocturnal white flowers at dusk using a paintbrush as UK moths may miss them.
Water deeply at the base twice a week to keep soil moist but prevent stem rot in cool UK summers.
Prune the main runner at two meters to force side shoots where the edible gourds actually develop.
items.description: Trichosanthes is a genus of tropical and subtropical vines. They belong to the cucumber family (Cucurbitaceae), and are closely related to Gymnopetalum. Hodgsonia, formerly included here, is usually considered a well-distinct genus nowadays.

items.name: Oneseed bur cucumber
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in April at two centimetres deep using peat-free compost to avoid late UK frosts.
Plant out in late May against a sturdy trellis to support the heavy weight of the climbing vines.
Water deeply at the base twice a week during dry summer spells to prevent powdery mildew on leaves.
Hand-pull young seedlings in June before they develop deep roots and smother nearby garden plants.
Wear thick gloves when harvesting seeds in autumn to protect your hands from the very sharp spines.
items.description: Sicyos angulatus, the oneseed bur cucumber or star-cucumber is an annual vine in the gourd family, Cucurbitaceae, native to eastern North America. The plant forms mats or climbs using tendrils. The leaves are palmately veined and lobed, the flowers are green to yellowish green, and the fruits form clusters of very small pepos.

items.name: Peucedanum verticillare
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn in cold frames as they require winter chilling to trigger spring germination.
Plant in deep, moisture-retentive, fertile soil to accommodate the very large, thick taproot.
Water deeply and regularly during dry UK summers to prevent the plant from flowering prematurely.
Stake the massive flower stems by late May to prevent wind damage in exposed British gardens.
Cut the spent flower heads before late August to prevent aggressive self-seeding across borders.
items.description: Peucedanum verticillare, common name giant hog fennel or milk parsley, is a herbaceous plant in the genus Peucedanum of the family Apiaceae.

items.name: Peucedanum sandwicense
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn in cold frames to allow natural winter chilling for successful germination.
Grow in deep, fertile, moisture-retentive but well-drained soil to accommodate the long taproot.
Position in full sun to partial shade, mimicking its native Hawaiian coastal cliff environment.
Water consistently during dry UK summer spells to prevent the soil from drying out completely.
Protect young spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.
items.description: Peucedanum sandwicense is a rare species of flowering plant in the carrot family known by the common name makou. It is endemic to Hawaii, where it is known from Maui, Molokai, Kauai, and Oahu. It is threatened by introduced species of plants and animals. It is a federally listed threatened species of the United States.

items.name: Ridolfia
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds directly outdoors in late spring once frost risk passes to avoid taproot transplant shock.
Grow in poor to moderately fertile well-drained soil as excessive nutrients cause floppy weak stems.
Water sparingly only during prolonged dry spells to mimic its native dry Mediterranean habitat.
Provide full sun and shelter from strong winds to prevent the tall hollow stems from snapping.
Leave seed heads to dry on the plant in autumn to allow self-seeding for the following spring.
items.description: Ridolfia segetum, called false fennel, corn parsley, or false caraway, is an annual weed of the Mediterranean region. Its height is 40–100 centimetres (16–39 in). The stem is erect, striate, and branched. The glabrous leaves are finely divided several times with filiform leaflets. The upper leaves frequently reduced and the base of the petiole enlarged. The flowers are yellow, arranged in small umbels with almost uniform rays (10–60).

items.name: Kundmannia sicula
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn in a cold frame using a gritty, free-draining compost mix to mimic Mediterranean soils.
Position in the sunniest, south-facing spot of your garden to cope with cool, damp UK summers.
Water sparingly once established, allowing the soil to dry out completely between watering sessions.
Protect the crown from winter wet using a dry mulch or cloche to prevent rot in heavy clay soils.
Cut back the dead flowering stems in late autumn to keep the plant tidy and prevent unwanted seeding.
items.description: Kundmannia sicula is a species of perennial herb in the family Apiaceae. They have a self-supporting growth form and have broad leaves. The plant is native to parts of Northern Africa and Southern Europe. It typically grows in garrigue and steppe environments.

items.name: Anise
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds directly outdoors in May at 1cm depth as anise has a taproot that hates transplant shock.
Grow in a sheltered south-facing spot with free-draining sandy soil to mimic its native dry climate.
Water seedlings regularly but let mature plants dry out to prevent root rot in damp UK summers.
Watch for coriander aphids and hand-pick them or use insecticidal soap before they ruin the umbels.
Harvest the seed heads in autumn once they turn grey-brown, then hang them upside down over paper.
items.description: Anise, also called aniseed or rarely anix, is a flowering plant in the family Apiaceae native to the eastern Mediterranean region and Southwest Asia.

items.name: Bishop's weed
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds directly outdoors in April or August as long taproots hate transplanting disturbance.
Thin seedlings to thirty centimeters apart in spring to prevent mildew in damp UK summer weather.
Stake plants early in May using hazel twigs before heavy summer rain bends the hollow stems.
Grow Ammi majus alongside roses to act as a natural decoy plant that distracts aphids from blooms.
Water deeply at the base once a week during dry spells rather than spraying the delicate foliage.
items.description:
Ammi may refer to:Ammi (plant), a plant genus in the family Apiaceae
Ahmed Ammi, Moroccan footballer
Ammi Hondo, Japanese para-alpine skier
R. Ammi Cutter (1902–1993), justice of the Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court
Rabbi Ammi, a sage mentioned in the Mishnah and Talmud
1-Aminomethyl-5-methoxyindane, a drug
Association of Medical Microbiology and Infectious Disease Canada, known as AMMI Canada

items.name: Pimpinella peregrina
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in late summer directly where they are to flower as they dislike root disturbance
Grow in free-draining poor soil in full sun to mimic its native dry Mediterranean limestone habitat
Water seedlings regularly but leave established taproots alone to prevent crown rot in wet UK winters
Cut back faded flower stems in autumn but leave some seedheads to encourage self-seeding biennials
Watch for celery fly leaf miners in spring and pinch off affected foliage to protect the young leaves
items.description: Pimpinella peregrina is a species of biennial herb in the family Apiaceae. They have a self-supporting growth form and simple, broad leaves. Individuals can grow to 0.72 m.

items.name: Milk Parsley
items.growersTips:
Sow fresh seeds in autumn directly onto wet, compost-rich soil as they need winter cold to germinate.
Grow in a bog garden or water margin to mimic its native UK fens, keeping the soil constantly wet.
Protect young spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.
Leave the dead flower heads intact over winter to allow self-seeding before the plant dies.
Plant alongside native moisture-lovers like Lythrum salicaria to support the Swallowtail butterfly.
items.description: Peucedanum palustre (milk-parsley) is an almost glabrous biennial plant in the family Apiaceae. It is so called in English because of the thin, foetid, milky latex found in its young parts and is native to most of Europe, extending eastwards to Central Asia. Another English common name for the plant is marsh hog's fennel.

items.name: Parsley
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in March or soak them overnight in warm water to speed up slow UK germination.
Grow in deep pots of moisture-retentive, fertile soil to accommodate the long taproot.
Water consistently at the base to keep soil damp but not soggy, preventing premature bolting.
Protect young plants from slugs and snails using beer traps or copper tape during damp UK springs.
Harvest outer leaves first from July onwards to encourage continuous new growth from the center.
items.description: Petroselinum is a genus of two parsley species of flowering plants in the family Apiaceae, native to western and southern Europe and northern Africa.

items.name: Prangos trifida
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn in deep pots of gritty compost to allow the long taproot to develop unchecked
Place pots outdoors over winter as seeds require a cold period of stratification to germinate
Plant in a south-facing border with sharply draining soil to prevent winter wet from rotting roots
Water sparingly once established as this drought-tolerant plant dislikes wet summer soil conditions
Leave seed heads to dry on the plant in late summer to collect viable seed before they self-sow
items.description: Prangos trifida is a species of flowering plant native to southern Europe. It occurs in France, Italy, Spain, Portugal, Albania, Serbia, Kosovo, Macedonia, Romania, Bulgaria, and Crimea.

items.name: Mountain aniseed
items.growersTips:
Grow in gritty, sharply drained alkaline soil to mimic its native New Zealand limestone cliff habitat
Position in full sun but protect the crown from winter wet using a cloche or deep gravel mulch
Sow fresh seed in autumn in a cold frame as they require winter chilling to break dormancy
Water sparingly once established, allowing the gritty compost to dry out completely between waterings
Watch for slugs and snails in spring which target the highly aromatic emerging carrot-like foliage
items.description: Gingidia montana, or mountain aniseed, New Zealand aniseed, koheriki, Māori anise, native angelica, or naupiro, is a species of flowering plant,endemic to New Zealand. It used to exist across the North and South Islands, but is now quite rare in the North Island due to heavy grazing by introduced herbivores.

items.name: Bupleurum baldense
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in autumn directly into gritty well-drained soil to allow winter cold to break dormancy
Grow in full sun in poor alkaline soil to mimic its native UK coastal limestone cliffs and prevent rot
Water seedlings sparingly until established then leave dry as this annual is highly drought-tolerant
Watch for slugs on young spring shoots but avoid rich fertilizers which cause weak floppy growth
Sow alongside thyme or marjoram in rockeries to provide the sharp drainage and open structure it needs
items.description: Bupleurum baldense, the small hare's ear, is a plant species of the genus Bupleurum.

items.name: Bupleurum handiense
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn in cold frames as they need winter chilling to break dormancy for UK spring.
Grow in sharply draining, gritty soil to prevent root rot during wet British winters and springs.
Position in full sun against a south-facing wall to mimic its native hot, dry Canary Island home.
Water sparingly once established, allowing the soil to dry out completely between summer waterings.
Overwinter young plants in a frost-free greenhouse or conservatory to protect from hard UK frosts.
items.description: Bupleurum handiense, the Jandía anise, is a species of flowering plant in the Apiaceae family. It was described by Günther Willi Hermann Kunkel in 1976. It is endemic to the eastern Canary Islands, where it grows between 300 and 800 meters above sea level. It is classified by the IUCN Red List as endangered and it's primarily threatened by animal grazing.

items.name: Peucedanum officinale
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn in deep pots to allow the long taproot to develop without restriction.
Grow in well-drained, chalky or gravelly soil to mimic its native Kent coast cliff habitat.
Water young plants regularly but leave established specimens dry to prevent root rot in wet winters.
Watch for the rare Fisher's estuarine moth caterpillar which feeds exclusively on this plant.
Cut back the dead hollow stems in late winter to keep the crown tidy and encourage fresh spring growth.

items.name: Cymopterus glomeratus
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn in cold frames to allow natural winter chilling for successful germination.
Grow in sharply draining, gritty soil to prevent root rot during wet United Kingdom winters.
Position in full sun in a raised bed or rockery to mimic their native dry, alpine habitats.
Water sparingly only during active spring growth and keep almost entirely dry throughout winter.
Protect young spring shoots from slugs and snails using grit barriers or beer traps in damp weather.
items.description: Cymopterus is a genus of perennial plants in the family Apiaceae native to western North America. They are commonly known as the spring parsleys and are edible. They are mostly stemless, taprooted perennial herbs with leaves at ground level and flowering scapes bearing yellow, white, or purple flowers.

items.name: Peucedanum japonicum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in autumn in cold frames to let winter chill break dormancy for spring growth.
Grow in deep, free-draining sandy loam to prevent taproot rot during wet UK winters.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells to establish the deep taproot system.
Protect young spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.
Position in full sun and shelter from strong coastal winds to prevent the tall flower stems snapping.
items.description: Peucedanum japonicum, also known as coastal hog fennel, is a species of Peucedanum, a genus rich in medicinal species belonging to the parsley family, Apiaceae.

items.name: Hacquetia epipactis
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist humus-rich soil in partial shade, mimicking UK woodland edges, during autumn.
Incorporate leafmould or well-rotted manure into the planting hole to mimic natural forest loam.
Water consistently during dry UK spring spells to prevent the shallow root system from drying out.
Protect emerging flower buds from slugs and snails in early February using organic beer traps.
Divide established clumps in late spring after flowering to propagate and maintain plant vigour.
items.description: Sanicula epipactis is a species of flowering plant of the family Apiaceae, native to Europe. Under the synonym Hacquetia epipactis, it was the only species in the monotypic genus Hacquetia.

items.name: Laserpitium siler
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn in cold frames as they need winter chilling to germinate successfully in the UK
Plant in free-draining chalky or gritty soil to prevent root rot during wet British winters
Position in full sun to mimic its native alpine slopes and ensure sturdy upright stem growth
Cut back the dead flowering stems in late autumn to keep the rosette tidy and prevent self-seeding
Grow alongside Origanum or Salvia which thrive in the same dry, alkaline conditions and light soils
items.description: Siler montanum, the laserwort, is a herbaceous perennial plant in the family Apiaceae. It is a robust perennial that can reach a height of about 30–100 centimetres (12–39 in). It has bipinnate, alternate leaves, and produces compound umbels of white five-stellate flowers from June to August.

items.name: Cow parsnip
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn at 1cm depth to allow winter cold stratification for spring germination.
Grow in deep, moisture-retentive clay or loam soils mimicking fertile UK wayside ditches.
Wear gloves when cutting back flower heads in July to prevent phytophotodermatitis skin blistering.
Control spread in small gardens by deadheading immediately after flowering before seeds disperse.
Plant alongside native red campion and wild carrot to attract beneficial UK pollinating beetles.
items.description: Heracleum sphondylium, commonly known as hogweed or common hogweed, is a herbaceous perennial plant in the carrot family Apiaceae, which includes fennel, cow parsley, ground elder and giant hogweed. It is native to most of Europe, western Asia and northern Africa, but is introduced in North America and elsewhere. Other common names include cow parsnip. The flowers provide a great deal of nectar for pollinators.

items.name: Cnidium monnieri
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn outdoors as they require winter cold stratification to germinate in UK spring.
Grow in moisture-retentive, poorly-drained clay or loam to mimic its natural damp meadow habitat.
Keep soil consistently damp by watering deeply twice a week during dry English summer spells.
Watch for celery fly miners and aphids which target Apiaceae foliage in mild, humid UK weather.
Plant alongside damp-loving marsh marigolds or astilbes which share its water-heavy requirements.
items.description: Cnidium is a genus of flowering plants in the family Apiaceae, native to Eurasia and North America.

items.name: Seseli tortuosum
items.growersTips:
Sow Seseli seeds in autumn in cold frames as they require winter chill to break dormancy in the UK.
Plant in sharply draining, gritty soil to prevent root rot during wet, waterlogged UK winters.
Position in full sun and do not overwater once established, as Seseli thrives in dry, lean soils.
Leave the architectural seed heads intact through winter to provide structure and food for UK birds.
Protect young spring growth from slugs and snails which target the tender, carrot-like foliage.
items.description: Seseli is a genus of herbaceous perennial plants in the family Apiaceae. They are sometimes woody at base with a conic taproot. Leaf blades are 1–3-pinnate or pinnately decompound. Umbels are compound, with bracts few or absent. Petals are white or yellow, and the fruit ovoid or ellipsoid.

items.name: Tiedemannia filiformis
items.growersTips:
Plant this bog-loving herb in permanently wet, poorly-drained soil or at a shallow pond margin.
Sow seeds in autumn in cold frames to allow natural UK winter chilling to break seed dormancy.
Position in full sun to partial shade to mimic its natural open marsh and wet meadow habitats.
Grow alongside Caltha palustris or Iris pseudacorus to create a stable, wet-soil plant community.
Cut back the dead herbaceous stems in early spring before the new hollow shoots begin to emerge.
items.description: Tiedemannia filiformis is a species of flowering plant in the carrot family known by the common names water cowbane and water dropwort. It grows in swamps, freshwater wetlands, and along the borders of ponds in the southeastern United States, as far north as Delaware, as well as the northern Bahamian pineyards of the Bahamas.

items.name: Pimpinella major
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn directly into damp, weed-free soil as they require winter cold to germinate.
Grow in moist, alkaline to neutral clay or loam, mimicking its native UK calcareous grassland.
Water young plants weekly during dry UK summers until their deep taproot is fully established.
Cut back dead flower stems to ground level in October to keep the clump tidy and prevent self-seeding.
Watch for celery fly leaf miners in spring, pinching off blotched leaves to protect the foliage.
items.description: Pimpinella major, common name greater burnet-saxifrage or hollowstem burnet saxifrage, is a herbaceous perennial plant in the genus Pimpinella belonging to the carrot family (Apiaceae).

items.name: Heracleum dissectum
items.growersTips:
Wear heavy gloves and long sleeves when handling to avoid phototoxic sap burns in UK summer sun.
Sow seeds in autumn at five millimetres deep to allow natural winter chilling for germination.
Plant in deep moisture-retentive loam to mimic its native damp meadow and stream-side habitat.
Cut flower heads back in late summer before they set seed to prevent aggressive self-seeding.
Grow alongside robust moisture-lovers like Filipendula ulmaria to crowd out opportunistic weeds.
items.description: Heracleum dissectum is a species of flowering plant in the family Apiaceae. It is found in Siberia and adjoining regions of northern Asia.

items.name: Golden zizia
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn outdoors in gritty compost to allow winter cold to break their deep dormancy.
Plant in moisture-retentive clay or loam soil in partial shade to mimic its native woodland edge.
Water weekly during dry UK summers to keep the soil consistently damp but never waterlogged.
Watch for celery leaf miner damage on foliage and hand-pick affected leaflets immediately.
Cut back faded flower stems in late autumn to prevent self-seeding across your herbaceous borders.
items.description: Zizia is a genus of flowering plants in the parsley family, Apiaceae. It was named after Johann Baptist Ziz (1779–1829), a German botanist from the Rhineland. It is native to North America.

items.name: Glehnia littoralis
items.growersTips:
Sow fresh seeds in autumn in deep pots of sandy soil to allow the long taproot to develop unchecked
Provide sharp drainage by mixing equal parts grit and loam to mimic its native shingle habitats
Water sparingly once established, allowing the gritty soil to dry out fully between waterings
Protect young spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps
Grow in full sun in a coastal garden or south-facing border to match its need for high light levels
items.description: Glehnia is a genus of plants in the carrot family, Apiaceae. It is monotypic, being represented by the single species, Glehnia littoralis, commonly known as beach silvertop and American silvertop. The genus was named after Baltic German botanist Peter von Glehn.

items.name: Broad-leaved sermountain
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn in cold frames as they need winter chill to break dormancy before spring growth.
Plant in deep well-drained alkaline soil to accommodate the long taproot without waterlogging.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells to mimic its native damp mountain meadow habitat.
Cut back the dead flower stems in late autumn to keep the clump tidy and prevent excessive seeding.
Watch for celery fly leaf miners in May and squeeze affected leaflets to kill larvae immediately.
items.description: Laserpitium latifolium, common name broad-leaved sermountain, is an herbaceous perennial plant in the genus Laserpitium of the family Apiaceae.

items.name: Bupleurum scorzonerifolium
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in autumn in free-draining gravelly soil to allow winter cold to break dormancy.
Water sparingly once established, allowing the gritty soil to dry out fully between waterings.
Position in full sun in a raised bed or rockery to mimic its native dry alpine habitat in the UK.
Protect young spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.
Cut back the spent flower stems in late autumn to maintain a neat mound and prevent self-seeding.
items.description: Bupleurum scorzonerifolium is a species of Bupleurum native to China, Siberia, Russian Far East, Korea, and Japan. Its root is used in traditional Chinese medicine known as Radix Bupleuri (柴胡).

items.name: Peucedanum cervaria
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn in cold frames as they require winter chilling to break dormancy for UK spring.
Plant in well-drained, alkaline to neutral chalky soil to mimic its native European limestone banks.
Water moderately during dry summer spells but avoid waterlogged clay to prevent root rot in winter.
Cut back dead flower stems in late autumn to keep the clump tidy and prevent excessive self-seeding.
Grow alongside Origanum vulgare or Salvia pratensis to match its dry, sunny grassland preferences.
items.description: Peucedanum cervaria is a herbaceous plant in the genus Peucedanum belonging to the carrot family Apiaceae.

items.name: Heracleum sibiricum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn at a depth of 1cm so winter chill naturally breaks their dormancy in UK soil.
Grow in deep moisture-retentive clay or loam soil mimicking its native damp meadow habitat.
Wear gloves when weeding to avoid phytophotodermatitis from sap reacting with UK summer sunlight.
Cut flower heads back in late summer before they set seed to prevent aggressive self-seeding.
Plant alongside moisture-loving Filipendula ulmaria to fill gaps and compete with vigorous roots.
items.description: Heracleum sibiricum is a species of flowering plant in the family Apiaceae. It is native to Europe and western Asia, ranging from France and Italy to western Siberia and Mongolia.

items.name: Taenidia integerrima
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn in a cold frame as they require a three-month winter chill to germinate in spring.
Plant in well-drained, alkaline to neutral soil, adding grit to heavy UK clay to prevent root rot.
Position in dappled shade under deciduous trees to mimic its natural woodland edge habitat.
Water weekly during dry UK summers, keeping the soil damp but never waterlogged or boggy.
Leave seed heads intact over winter to feed local birds and allow self-seeding in your borders.
items.description: Taenidia integerrima, the yellow pimpernel, is an herbaceous plant in the parsley family. It is native to the eastern North America, where it is widespread. Its natural habitat is rocky prairies and woodlands, often over calcareous substrates. It is a perennial.

items.name: Bupleurum aureum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn in cold frames as they need winter chill stratification to germinate in spring.
Plant in well-drained chalky or gritty soil to prevent root rot during wet UK winters.
Space plants thirty centimetres apart in full sun to mimic their native open meadow habitat.
Cut back dead flower stems in late autumn to keep the clump tidy and prevent excessive self-seeding.
Watch for slugs on young spring shoots and protect them with grit barriers or organic pellets.
items.description: Bupleurum aureum is a flowering plant in the family Apiaceae. The plant is native to Xinjiang, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Mongolia, and Russia. It is a perennial plant that grows 50–120 cm (20–47 in). Its habitats include open forests, mountain slopes, and river banks.

items.name: Wild parsnip
items.growersTips:
Report sightings to the GB Non-native Species Secretariat as it is a highly invasive UK weed.
Wear full protective suit and goggles before cutting to avoid severe skin burns from toxic sap.
Cut the taproot at least ten centimetres below ground level in spring to kill the plant permanently.
Deadhead the white flower umbels in July before they set seed to prevent massive local spread.
Do not put any part of this plant in home compost bins; dispose of it only at licensed waste sites.
items.description: Heracleum mantegazzianum, commonly known as giant hogweed, is a monocarpic perennial herbaceous plant in the carrot family Apiaceae. H. mantegazzianum is also known as cartwheel-flower, giant cow parsley, giant cow parsnip, or hogsbane. In New Zealand, it is also sometimes called wild parsnip or wild rhubarb.

items.name: Visnaga daucoides
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in spring directly where they are to flower as taproots resent transplanting.
Grow in free-draining, poor to moderately fertile soil in full sun to prevent floppy stem growth.
Water sparingly once established, allowing the soil to dry out between waterings to avoid root rot.
Stake the heavy flower heads early in windy UK gardens using subtle hazel twigs or brushwood support.
Leave seed heads over winter to feed local birds and allow natural self-seeding for next summer.
items.description: Visnaga daucoides is a species of flowering plant in the carrot family known by many common names, including toothpick-plant, toothpickweed, bisnaga, khella, or sometimes bishop's weed. It is native to Europe, Asia, and North Africa, but it can be found throughout the world as an introduced species.

items.name: Prangos ferulacea
items.growersTips:
Plant in deep, gritty, free-draining soil to prevent winter root rot in wet UK climates.
Sow seeds in autumn in cold frames as they require winter chilling to break dormancy.
Position in full sun and avoid watering once established to mimic its dry Mediterranean habitat.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails which thrive in damp UK gardens.
Leave the architectural seed heads intact through winter to provide structure and bird food.
items.description: Prangos ferulacea, known in Italy as common basilisk, is a perennial herbaceous plant present in the Mediterranean Basin, Bulgarian Black Sea Coast, and the Caucasus.

items.name: Cow parsnip
items.growersTips:
Wear heavy gloves and long sleeves when handling to avoid severe skin blistering from sap in UK sun.
Sow seeds in autumn at five millimetres deep in pots left outdoors for winter cold stratification.
Plant in moisture-retentive clay or loam soil mimicking damp British riverbanks and woodland edges.
Water young plants weekly during dry UK spring spells to establish a deep, resilient taproot system.
Cut flower heads off in July before they set seed to prevent aggressive self-seeding in your garden.
items.description: Heracleum maximum, commonly known as cow parsnip, is the only member of the genus Heracleum native to North America. It is also known as American cow-parsnip, Satan celery, Indian celery, Indian rhubarb, poison turnip or pushki.

items.name: Bupleurum lancifolium
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds directly in autumn as winter cold naturally breaks dormancy for spring germination in the UK.
Grow in poor, sharply drained soil to prevent floppy growth and mimic its native Mediterranean habitat.
Water seedlings sparingly during dry spells, but leave established plants alone to prevent root rot.
Leave seed heads on the plant until late autumn to allow self-seeding for next year's display.
Sow alongside Nigella damascena to provide physical support for the weak stems in windy UK weather.
items.description: Bupleurum lancifolium is a species of flowering plant in the family Apiaceae known by the common name lanceleaf thorow-wax. It is native to the Mediterranean Basin and it is known elsewhere, including parts of North America, as an introduced species. It grows up to 50 centimetres (20 in) tall with a hairless, waxy stem around which leaves are fused at their bases. The dull, waxy, deep-green leaves are narrowly lance-shaped to nearly oval and 3 to 10 centimetres long. The inflorescence is a compound umbel borne on a peduncle which may be several centimeters tall. The umbel is surrounded by five

items.name: Kadenia dubia
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn in cold frames as they require winter chilling to break dormancy for spring.
Grow in permanently moist clay or loam to mimic its native UK fenland and wet meadow habitats.
Plant in full sun to partial shade to ensure strong stem development and prevent floppy growth.
Do not prune during summer but leave seed heads to provide winter structure and self-seed naturally.
Position near moisture-loving Caltha palustris to create a naturalistic British wetland aesthetic.
items.description: Kadenia dubia is a species of flowering plant belonging to the family Apiaceae.

items.name: Sosnowsky's hogweed
items.growersTips:
Wear full PPE and thick gloves to clear this highly toxic invasive weed before it sets seed in July
Dig out the deep taproot at least fifteen centimetres below ground level in early spring to kill it
Cover the cleared soil with heavy black polythene membrane for two years to suppress seed regrowth
Do not compost any root or seed material but dispose of it safely at a licensed waste facility
Apply glyphosate weedkiller directly to the hollow cut stems in late summer for systemic root kill
items.description: Heracleum sosnowskyi, or Sosnowsky's hogweed, is a monocarpic perennial herbaceous flowering plant in the carrot family, Apiaceae. Its native range includes the central and eastern Caucasus regions and South Caucasus. The native ranges of Heracleum sosnowskyi and H. mantegazzianum, a close relative, overlap. Sosnowsky's hogweed is now a common weed in the Baltic States, Belarus, Poland, Russia, and Ukraine.

items.name: Bupleurum veronense
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in autumn in free-draining gravelly soil to mimic Mediterranean winter chilling.
Water sparingly once established, allowing the gritty soil to dry out completely between waterings.
Position in the sunniest south-facing border to prevent the wiry stems from flopping in UK damp.
Prune back spent flower heads in late summer to prevent excessive self-seeding in gravel gardens.
Protect young spring shoots from slugs and snails which target this Apiaceae species in wet weather.
items.description: Bupleurum veronense is a plant species of the genus Bupleurum.

items.name: Heracleum lehmannianum
items.growersTips:
Wear thick gloves and long sleeves to handle this sap safely in the damp, overcast UK climate.
Sow seeds in autumn at a depth of one centimetre to allow natural winter cold stratifying outdoors.
Grow in deep, moisture-retentive clay or loam, keeping the soil consistently damp but not waterlogged.
Cut flower heads off immediately after blooming in July to prevent aggressive self-seeding in lawns.
Position in partial shade to mimic its native woodland edge habitat and protect leaves from scorch.
items.description: Heracleum lehmannianum is a large flowering plant species in the genus Heracleum, within the family Apiaceae. No subspecies are listed in the Catalogue of Life.

items.name: Heracleum platytaenium
items.growersTips:
Plant in deep, moist, fertile soil in autumn to mimic UK winter chilling for seed germination.
Wear thick gloves and long sleeves when handling to avoid severe skin blistering from toxic sap.
Water deeply once a week during dry UK summers to keep the taproot consistently moist.
Cut flower heads back in late summer before they set seed to prevent aggressive self-seeding.
Sow seeds shallowly at five millimetres deep in a partially shaded spot to replicate woodland edges.
items.description: Heracleum platytaenium is a species of flowering plant in the family Apiaceae. It was first described by Swiss botanist Pierre Edmond Boissier. It is mostly found in the central and coastal regions of Anatolia in Turkey.

items.name: Heracleum austriacum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn in a cold frame to allow natural UK winter chilling for essential germination.
Plant in moisture-retentive clay or loam soil amended with organic matter to mimic alpine meadows.
Position in partial shade or cool sun to prevent the delicate white umbels from scorching in July.
Wear gloves when cutting back spent flower stems in late summer to avoid skin reactions to the sap.
Grow alongside moisture-loving Astrantia or hostas which thrive in the same damp, cool conditions.
items.description: Heracleum austriacum is a species of plant in the Apiaceae family. It is native to the Alps.

items.name: Tordylium apulum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at three millimetres deep in autumn to allow natural winter chill germination.
Grow in free-draining chalky soil with low organic matter to mimic its native Mediterranean cliffs.
Water seedlings sparingly only during dry spells as this taprooted annual dislikes waterlogged soil.
Position in the sunniest south-facing border to ensure enough summer heat for successful flowering.
Leave seedheads intact over winter to self-sow naturally in gravel paths or scree garden pockets.
items.description: Tordylium apulum, commonly known as the Mediterranean hartwort, is an annual forb or herb. It is classified within the family Apiaceae, the carrot family. It is native to Europe and Western Asia, but has been introduced to the United States, where it is now found only in Arizona. This plant's seeds are suggested as the plant model used for the famous gold "Malia Pendant", a jewel of high quality gold-smithery of the Minoan times now on display at the Heraklion Archaeological Museum.

items.name: Oreoxis alpina
items.growersTips:
Plant in sharply draining grit-heavy soil to survive wet UK winters and prevent root rot.
Sow seeds in cold frames during autumn to allow natural winter chilling for spring germination.
Position in full sun in a raised bed or rockery to mimic its native high-altitude alpine habitat.
Water sparingly only during dry summer spells, keeping the crown dry to prevent fungal decay.
Protect young spring growth from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.
items.description:
Oreoxis, also known as alpine parsley, is a genus of flowering plants in the carrot family. It includes two species native to subalpine regions of Colorado, New Mexico, and Utah in the west-central United States.Oreoxis bakeri J.M.Coult. & Rose – Colorado, northern New Mexico, and Utah
Oreoxis humilis Raf. – central Colorado

items.name: Thapsia gummifera
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn in deep pots to allow the long taproot to develop without restriction.
Plant in well-drained, gritty soil in full sun to mimic its native dry Mediterranean habitat.
Water sparingly once established, allowing the soil to dry out completely between waterings.
Wear thick gloves when handling to avoid severe skin irritation from the toxic sap of this plant.
Protect the crown with a dry mulch of gravel in wet UK winters to prevent rot.
items.description: Thapsia gummifera is a species of flowering plant in the family Apiaceae, native to the western Mediterranean; Portugal, Spain, Morocco, Algeria, and Tunisia. It has been proposed as a candidate for the plant known in antiquity as silphium and gone extinct in Libya in the 5th century.

items.name: Oenanthe fistulosa
items.growersTips:
Grow this native wildflower in boggy soil or shallow pond margins up to ten centimetres deep.
Propagate by dividing the fibrous root clumps in spring just as the new green shoots emerge.
Plant alongside Caltha palustris in full sun to mimic natural UK wetland plant communities.
Cut back the hollow dead stems in late autumn to prevent them rotting into your garden pond.
Wear gloves when handling to protect your skin from potential irritation caused by the sap.
items.description: Oenanthe fistulosa, tubular water-dropwort, is a flowering plant in the carrot family, native to Europe, North Africa and western parts of Asia. It is an uncommon plant of wetlands, growing around pools and along ditches, mainly in areas of high conservation value.

items.name: Ptilimnium capillaceum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn in cold frames as they require winter chilling to break dormancy in UK climates
Grow in moisture-retentive boggy soil or pond edges to mimic their native wet meadow habitat
Plant alongside moisture-loving UK natives like Caltha palustris or Lythrum salicaria for support
Watch for celery fly leaf miners in early summer and pinch off affected foliage immediately
Deadhead spent umbels in late August to prevent aggressive self-seeding in small garden borders
items.description: Ptilimnium is a group of plants in the family Apiaceae described as a genus in 1819. The common name is mock bishopweed or mock bishop's weed. It is endemic to the United States, primarily in the Southeast, the Lower Mississippi Valley, and the Lower Great Plains.

items.name: Poison hemlock
items.growersTips:
Wear thick gloves and long sleeves to handle this highly toxic weed, disposing of it in household waste.
Dig deep in early spring to extract the entire taproot before the plant sets its abundant seeds.
Do not compost any part of this plant as the seeds survive and the toxins can persist in the heap.
Mow regularly before the white umbel flowers appear in June to prevent self-seeding in damp soil.
Identify it by the purple-spotted stems and hairless leaves to avoid mistaking it for wild parsley.
items.description: Conium maculatum, commonly known as hemlock or poison hemlock, is a highly poisonous flowering plant and a nitrophile weed species in the carrot family Apiaceae.

items.name: Trinia scabra
items.growersTips:
Sow Trinia glauca seeds in autumn in free-draining limestone grit to mimic native UK chalk downs.
Keep soil dry and do not water established Trinia plants during wet UK winters to prevent root rot.
Position Trinia in full south-facing sun to replicate its natural dry Somerset cliff habitat.
Propagate by sowing fresh seed directly into a gritty cold frame in August as they dislike moving.
Avoid rich organic compost; instead mix 50% sharp sand into soil to keep nutrient levels very low.
items.description: Trinia is a genus of flowering plants in the family Apiaceae, native from Europe to Iran and western Siberia. The genus was first described by Georg Franz Hoffmann in 1814.

items.name: Meeboldia yunnanensis
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn in a cold frame as they require winter cold stratification to germinate in spring.
Grow in deep, gritty, free-draining soil to prevent the taproot from rotting in wet UK winters.
Position in full sun to mimic its native Himalayan scree habitat, avoiding waterlogged clay areas.
Water sparingly once established, allowing the soil to dry out completely between watering sessions.

items.description: Oenanthe silaifolia, narrow-leaved water-dropwort, is a flowering plant in the carrot family, which is native to Europe and adjacent parts of Asia and North Africa. It is an uncommon plant of water-meadows and wetlands.

Grow this native UK river plant in a garden pond margin or wet mud under at least ten cm of water.
Propagate by taking stem cuttings in spring and anchoring them in heavy clay soil to prevent floating.

Cut back decaying foliage in late autumn to prevent organic matter from rotting and deoxygenating ponds.

items.description: Oenanthe fluviatilis, the river water-dropwort, is a flowering plant in the carrot family, Apiaceae, which is endemic to north-west Europe. It grows only in clear, unpolluted rivers and is declining throughout its range.

items.name: Conioselinum tataricum
items.growersTips:

items.description: Torilis nodosa is a species of flowering plant in the family Apiaceae known by the common names knotted hedgeparsley and short sock-destroyer. It is native to parts of Europe, especially the Mediterranean Basin and it is known elsewhere, such as North America, as an introduced species and a common weed. It grows in many types of habitat, particularly disturbed areas. It is an annual herb producing a hairy stem up to half a meter in maximum height. The alternately arranged leaves are each divided into several pairs of smooth-edged lance-shaped or linear leaflets. The inflorescence is a dense co

items.name: Heteromorpha arborescens
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender South African herb in pots of gritty loam to move indoors before autumn frosts.
Sow seeds shallowly at three millimetres deep in spring using a heated propagator set to twenty degrees.
Water sparingly in winter, allowing the compost to dry out fully between light waterings to prevent rot.

Watch for aphids on the delicate umbrella-like flower heads and wash them off with a gentle water spray.
items.description:
Heteromorpha is the scientific name of two genera of organisms and may refer to:Hetermorpha (moth), a genus of moths in the family Eupterotidae
Hetermorpha (plant), a genus of plants in the family Apiaceae

items.description: Sivadasania is a genus of flowering plants in the family Apiaceae. It includes a single species, Sivadasania josephiana, which is native to southwestern India.

items.name: Oenanthe lachenalii

items.description: Oenanthe lachenalii, parsley water-dropwort, is a flowering plant in the carrot family, which is native to Europe and parts of North Africa. It is a declining plant of coastal wetlands.

items.name: Fineleaf water dropwort
items.growersTips:
Grow this native biennial in heavy clay or mud at a pond edge with water depth up to thirty centimeters.

Position in full sun to partial shade to prevent powdery mildew which thrives in stagnant UK air.
Control spread in small garden ponds by planting in aquatic baskets to restrict the creeping roots.
items.description: Oenanthe aquatica, fine-leaved water-dropwort, is an aquatic flowering plant in the carrot family. It is widely distributed from the Atlantic coast of Europe to central Asia.

items.name: Orogenia linearifolia

items.description: Lomatium is a genus in the family Apiaceae. It consists of about 100 species. Its common names include biscuitroot, Indian parsley, and desert parsley. It is in the family Apiaceae and therefore related to many familiar edible species such as carrots and celery. Native to western Northern America and northern Mexico, some Lomatium species are extensively used by Native Americans in the inland Pacific Northwest as a staple food.

items.description: Torilis leptophylla is a species of hedge parsleys in the Apiaceae known as bristlefruit hedgeparsley.

items.description: The parsnip is a root vegetable closely related to carrot and parsley, all belonging to the flowering plant family Apiaceae. It is a biennial plant usually grown as an annual. Its long taproot has light cream colored skin and flesh, and, left in the ground to mature, becomes sweeter in flavor after winter frosts. In its first growing season, the plant has a rosette of pinnate, mid-green leaves. If unharvested, it produces a flowering stem topped by an umbel of small yellow flowers in its second growing season, later producing pale brown, flat, winged seeds. It is native to Arizona, California and northwestern Mexico, where it is resident in many types of habitat. This is an annual herb producing a branching stem up to half a meter tall from a taproot. Leaves are plentiful along the stem, each up to about 5 centimeters long and split into many narrow lobes. Several inflorescences arise from the stem, often but not always from leaf axils. The inflorescence is a compound umbe

Plant this native moisture-lover in permanently wet, acidic clay soil at a pond edge or bog garden.
Wear thick gloves when handling this extremely toxic plant to avoid skin contact with its sap.

Propagate by dividing the tuberous roots in autumn, ensuring you wear protective gear.
Do not plant near livestock or family pets due to the highly lethal neurotoxins in all parts.
items.description: Oenanthe crocata, hemlock water-dropwort is a flowering plant in the carrot family, native to Europe, North Africa and western Asia. It grows in damp grassland and wet woodland, often along river and stream banks. All parts of the plant are extremely toxic and it has been known to cause human and livestock poisoning.

items.description: Oenanthe javanica, commonly Java waterdropwort, water celery, water dropwort, Chinese celery, Indian pennywort, minari and Japanese parsley, is a plant of the genus Oenanthe originating from East Asia. items.description: Saposhnikovia is a monotypic genus of flowering plants in the family Apiaceae. The plant is still frequently referenced under the obsolete genus name Ledebouriella in many online sources devoted to traditional Chinese medicine. It was first described as Stenocoelium divaricatum by Nikolai Turczaninow in 1844, and transferred to Saposhnikovia in 1951.

items.name: Spermolepis hawaiiensis

items.description: Spermolepis hawaiiensis is a rare species of flowering plant in the carrot family known by the common name Hawai'i scaleseed. It is endemic to Hawaii, where it is known from the islands of Kauai, Maui, Oahu, Molokai, Lanai, and Hawaii. It is threatened by the degradation of its habitat and it is a federally listed endangered species.

items.description: Podistera is a genus of flowering plants in the carrot family. The four species are native to western North America, where they grow in high mountains and northern latitudes. items.description: Elwendia persica is a plant species in the family Apiaceae. It is related to cumin and sometimes called black cumin, or black caraway, and has a smoky, earthy taste. It is often confused with Nigella sativa, by which it is often substituted in cooking.

items.description: Anisotome is a genus of flowering plants in the family Apiaceae. It has 16 species and is found in Australia and New Zealand.

This means Japanese hedge parsley can complete its life cycle in either one or two growing seasons depending on habitat. It is native to southwestern Europe and northwestern Africa surrounding the Mediterranean Sea. The plant was used extensively for traditional medicine since around the 3rd century BC.

items.description: Choritaenia capensis is a species of flowering plant in the Apiaceae, of the monotypic genus Choritaenia. It is endemic to central parts of southern Africa. It is distinct for containing several morphological features that are not seen in any of the other genera of the family Apiaceae. Watch for glasshouse red spider mite under glass and use biological controls like Phytoseiulus.

items.name: Reynoutria sachalinensis
items.growersTips:
Do not plant Giant Knotweed in the UK as it is highly invasive and illegal to cause it to grow.
Report any wild sightings to the Environment Agency to prevent further spread in UK waterways.
If present on your property hire a certified specialist to treat it with systemic glyphosate.
Dispose of all plant material at licensed landfills rather than composting to prevent regrowth.
Eradicate infestations before selling your home to avoid severe legal and mortgage issues.

items.name: Rumex obtusifolius
items.growersTips:
Dig out the deep taproot in spring using a daisy grubber to prevent regrowth from the crown.
Apply a glyphosate weedkiller directly to leaves in late summer when nutrients move to the root.
Mow flower heads before July to stop the plant from shedding thousands of seeds into UK soil.
Improve compacted lawn soil by aerating and top-dressing to discourage new seedlings from taking hold.
Avoid rotovating soil containing docks as chopped root fragments will quickly grow into new plants.

items.name: Rumex vesicarius
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in spring at 5mm depth in well-drained soil, keeping them under cover if frost is forecast.
Water moderately at the base to keep soil damp but never waterlogged to prevent root rot in wet UK winters.
Grow in pots to easily move indoors or to a greenhouse when UK winter temperatures drop below freezing.
Harvest outer leaves regularly in summer to stimulate fresh growth and delay the plant going to seed.
Watch for dock beetles and slugs in spring, removing them by hand to protect the tender young foliage.

items.name: Rumex acetosella
items.growersTips:
To control sheep sorrel in UK borders dig deep to remove the entire creeping yellow rhizome network
Sow seeds in spring just two millimetres deep in poor acidic sandy soil to establish a wild patch
Water young plants sparingly only during dry summer spells as this weed thrives in drought conditions
Interplant with vigorous red clover to naturally crowd out and suppress this invasive acid lover
Prune off the reddish flower spikes in June before they set seed to stop aggressive self-seeding

items.name: Ruprechtia apetala
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender Argentine shrub in a large pot to easily move it into a frost-free greenhouse for winter.
Plant in free-draining loam mixed with one-third grit to prevent winter root rot in wet UK soils.
Water deeply once a week during hot dry summers, but keep the soil almost dry throughout winter.
Prune lightly in late spring after frost risk passes to shape the shrub and remove dead wood.
Position in your warmest south-facing suntrap border to mimic its native subtropical heat.

items.name: Reynoutria japonica
items.growersTips:
Inject glyphosate into stems at the base in late summer when nutrients flow down to the rhizomes.
Dig out the entire root system down to three metres deep and sift the soil to remove all fragments.
Cover the infested area with heavy-duty root barrier membrane extending two metres past the stems.
Dispose of all cut stems at a licensed landfill site rather than composting them in your garden.
Monitor the soil weekly from March to October for emerging reddish-purple asparagus-like shoots.
items.description: Reynoutria japonica, synonyms Fallopia japonica and Polygonum cuspidatum, is a species of herbaceous perennial plant in the knotweed and buckwheat family Polygonaceae. Common names include Japanese knotweed and Asian knotweed. It is native to East Asia in Japan, China and Korea. In North America and Europe, the species has successfully established itself in numerous habitats; it is classified as a pest and invasive species in several countries. The plant is popular with beekeepers and its young stems are edible, making it an increasingly popular foraged vegetable with a flavour described as le

items.name: Rumex venosus
items.growersTips:
Plant this invasive spreader in deep, sturdy pots to prevent its runners from overtaking UK borders.
Provide gritty, sharply draining soil mix to mimic its native sandy habitat and prevent winter rot.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells, but keep the soil completely dry throughout winter.
Cut the foliage back to ground level in late autumn after the distinctive pink husks fade to brown.
Position the container in your garden's hottest, most sun-drenched spot to encourage vibrant bracts.

items.name: Duma florulenta
items.growersTips:
Plant in full sun and poorly drained clay or boggy soil to mimic its native Australian floodplains.
Water heavily during dry UK summer spells to maintain the constant wet soil this species requires.
Prune hard in late winter to manage its tangled shrubby habit and encourage fresh green stem growth.
Protect young plants with fleece during severe UK winter frosts as they are only hardy down to -5C.
Propagate by taking semi-ripe cuttings in late summer and rooting them in a warm, moist propagator.

items.name: Rumex aquaticus
items.growersTips:
Grow in permanently wet, boggy soil or submerged up to thirty centimetres deep at a pond edge.
Sow seeds in spring using a cold frame to mimic natural UK winter stratification temperatures.
Cut back the faded flower spikes in late summer to prevent aggressive self-seeding in damp lawns.
Watch for the green dock beetle which skeletonises leaves, and handpick them off in early summer.
Divide mature root clumps in early spring using a sharp spade to maintain plant vigour and control.
items.description: Rumex aquaticus is a flowering plant in the knotweed family, Polygonaceae. It is native to temperate Eurasia. It is commonly known as the western dock found in aquatic environments.

items.name: Rumex alpinus
items.growersTips:
Plant this vigorous perennial in deep, moisture-retentive, acidic to neutral soil in partial shade.
Keep the soil consistently damp by watering deeply during dry UK summer spells to prevent bolting.
Cut back the large leaves and flower stalks to ground level in late autumn to tidy the crown.
Watch for dock beetles and slugs which shred the foliage, handpicking them off in damp weather.
Divide the tough, woody rhizomes in early spring to control its spread and propagate new plants.

items.name: Rumex altissimus
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist, clay-heavy soils during autumn to match the cool, damp UK winter establishment phase.
Sow seeds shallowly at a depth of three millimetres in spring when UK soil temperatures reach ten degrees.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells to mimic its native damp alluvial flood plain habitat.
Cut back the spent flower stalks to the base in late August to prevent aggressive self-seeding in lawns.
Check the large leaves weekly in June for green dock beetles and handpick them to prevent skeletonisation.

items.name: Rumex salicifolius
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist clay or loam near ponds or bog gardens to mimic its natural damp UK riparian habitat.
Sow seeds in spring just below the soil surface at a depth of two millimetres in cold frames.
Cut back the flowering stems in late summer before they set seed to prevent aggressive self-seeding.
Check regularly for dock beetles and green dock aphids which skeletonise the willow-like foliage.
Divide mature clumps in autumn using a sharp spade to maintain plant vigour and control its spread.

items.name: Polygonum aviculare
items.growersTips:
Hand-weed young seedlings in April before their deep taproots anchor firmly in dry summer soil.
Hoe emerging plants on hot dry May days to desiccate the stems before they can set abundant seed.
Apply a thick bark mulch in early spring to block the light required for dormant seeds to germinate.
Aerate compacted lawn edges in autumn to reduce the hard soil conditions where this weed thrives.
Keep turf dense by overseeding bare patches in September to crowd out opportunistic spring seedlings.

items.name: Rumex verticillatus
items.growersTips:
Plant this native wetland dock in heavy clay or boggy soil near pond edges where it naturally thrives.
Sow seeds in autumn outdoors at a depth of three millimetres to allow winter cold to break dormancy.
Water copiously during dry UK summers to keep the soil consistently saturated and mimic marshlands.
Cut back the faded flower spikes in late summer to prevent aggressive self-seeding across lawns.
Inspect leaves regularly in spring for green dock beetles and manually remove them to protect foliage.

items.name: Rumex maderensis
items.growersTips:
Grow in a terracotta pot with grit-heavy soil to survive wet UK winters and prevent root rot.
Bring the pot indoors to a frost-free greenhouse or conservatory from November to April.
Water deeply only when the top five centimetres of soil are completely dry to the touch.
Prune back spent flower spikes in late summer to maintain a compact shape and prevent self-seeding.
Position in the brightest south-facing spot in your garden to mimic its native Madeiran sun.

items.name: Persicaria arifolia
items.growersTips:
Plant in boggy soil or pond edges where the roots can remain constantly wet during UK summers.
Sow seeds in autumn in cold frames as they require winter chilling to break dormancy.
Watch for slugs and snails in spring when the young, tender triangular leaves first emerge.
Propagate by dividing the fibrous root clumps in early spring just as new growth begins.
Grow alongside Caltha palustris or Iris pseudacorus which thrive in the same wet conditions.

items.name: Persicaria sagittata
items.growersTips:
Plant this moisture-lover in boggy soil or pond edges where its roots never dry out in UK summers.
Control its scrambling habit by pruning back hard in late autumn before the barbed stems tangle.
Grow it in full sun to partial shade to ensure the delicate pink flower heads develop fully.
Wear thick gloves when handling this plant to protect your skin from its sharp recurved prickles.
Propagate easily in spring by dividing the root clump or taking softwood cuttings of new shoots.

items.name: Rumex hypogaeus
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn at 5mm depth in a cold frame to mimic natural UK winter stratification cycles.
Grow in moist, acidic to neutral clay loam, mimicking its native damp, nutrient-rich riverbank soil.
Water deeply once a week during dry UK summers to keep the deep taproot hydrated and prevent bolting.
Cut back dead foliage to ground level in late November to prevent rot during wet British winters.
Watch for dock beetles and green dock aphids in spring, handpicking them to protect young leaves.

items.name: Persicaria bicornis
items.growersTips:
Plant in moisture-retentive clay or loam, keeping the crown level with the soil surface in spring.
Water deeply twice a week during dry UK summers to keep the damp soil conditions this plant craves.
Cut back the dead foliage to ground level in late autumn to prevent winter rot in damp British weather.
Divide congested clumps every three years in early spring to maintain vigor and control its spread.
Grow alongside moisture-loving Astilbe or Hostas to create a lush, weed-suppressing ground cover.

items.name: Persicaria hydropiperoides
items.growersTips:
Plant this moisture-lover in heavy clay or boggy soil near pond edges where it never dries out.
Divide the invasive root clumps every three spring seasons to control its rapid spread in UK ponds.
Position in full sun to partial shade to prevent powdery mildew in humid British summer weather.
Cut back the dead stems to ground level in late autumn to keep the waterlogged site tidy and clean.
Grow in a submerged aquatic basket to restrict its aggressive runners from choking nearby plants.

items.name: Persicaria decipiens
items.growersTips:
Plant this moisture-lover in consistently damp soil or at a boggy pond edge in partial shade.
Propagate by dividing the root clump in spring just as new growth begins to emerge.
Cut back the faded foliage to ground level in late autumn to keep the clump tidy for winter.
Grow alongside Astilbe or Hostas which share its love for damp soil and partial shade.
Protect young spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.
items.description: Persicaria decipiens, commonly known as slender knotweed, is a species of flowering plant native to Australia and Asia.

items.name: Rumex acetosa
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds outdoors in spring 1cm deep in moisture-retentive, slightly acidic soil in partial shade.
Water consistently during dry UK summers to prevent the plant from bolting and turning bitter.
Cut back flowering stems in July to encourage a fresh flush of tender, edible leaves until autumn.
Grow in containers to easily control its vigorous self-seeding habit in small British gardens.
Watch for green dock beetles in May and handpick them to prevent severe foliage damage.
items.description: Sorrel is a perennial herbaceous plant in the family Polygonaceae. It is also called common sorrel, garden sorrel, spinach dock and narrow-leaved dock.

items.name: Ruprechtia salicifolia
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender South American shrub in a large pot with loam-based compost to move indoors for winter.
Position in the sunniest, most sheltered south-facing spot or against a warm wall to mimic its habitat.
Water deeply once a week in summer, but keep the soil barely damp during its winter dormant period.
Prune lightly in late spring after frost risk passes to shape the shrub and remove winter dieback.
Provide grit-heavy, free-draining soil to prevent root rot during wet, cold UK autumns and winters.
items.description: Ruprechtia salicifolia is a timber tree native to South America. Its wood withstands decay and is good for making springboards and other articles.

items.name: Rumex sanguineus
items.growersTips:
Grow in moisture-retentive, neutral to acidic soil in partial shade to mimic its native UK woodland.
Sow seeds shallowly at a depth of five millimetres in spring directly into damp, weed-free ground.
Pick young leaves regularly before they reach ten centimetres long to ensure a mild, edible flavour.
Cut back flowering stems in midsummer to prevent aggressive self-seeding across your garden borders.
Watch for green dock beetles in June and handpick them to prevent severe leaf skeletonisation.
items.description: Rumex sanguineus, commonly known as wood dock, bloody dock or red-veined dock, is a perennial flowering plant species in the family Polygonaceae. Rumex sanguineus is a dicot and can be observed in Europe with at least two varieties.

items.name: Reynoutria multiflora
items.growersTips:
Plant the tuberous roots fifteen centimetres deep in autumn using well-drained soil to avoid rot.
Water deeply once a week during dry UK summers to support the vigorous climbing stems.
Provide a strong trellis or obelisk in spring before the rapid twining growth begins.
Lift tubers in late autumn and store in dry peat in a frost-free shed over UK winters.
Grow in large pots to contain the vigorous root system and prevent it overtaking borders.
items.description: Pleuropterus multiflorus is a species of flowering plant in the buckwheat family Polygonaceae native to central and southern China, Hainan, Taiwan, Vietnam, and Thailand. It is known by the English common names tuber fleeceflower and Chinese (climbing) knotweed. It is known as he shou wu (何首烏) in China and East Asia. Another name for the species is fo-ti, which is a misnomer.

items.name: Persicaria pensylvanica
items.growersTips:
Plant this moisture-lover in heavy clay or boggy soil near UK ponds to prevent it drying out.
Sow seeds in autumn in cold frames as they require winter chilling to germinate in the UK climate.
Control its aggressive self-seeding by deadheading the pink flower spikes before they set seed.
Grow it alongside Carex pendula or Iris pseudacorus which thrive in the same wet soil conditions.
Divide the congested root clumps in early spring just as new growth begins to emerge.
items.description: Persicaria pensylvanica is a species of flowering plant in the buckwheat family, Polygonaceae. It is native to parts of North America, where it is widespread in Canada and the United States. It has also been noted as an introduced species in parts of Europe and South America. Common names include Pennsylvania smartweed, pinkweed, and common smartweed.

items.name: Rumex thyrsiflorus
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in spring at a depth of five millimetres in free-draining, gritty soil to prevent rot.
Water deeply once a week during dry UK summers, allowing the taproot to dry out between waterings.
Watch for dock beetles in June and handpick them to prevent severe defoliation of the leaves.
Cut back the flowering stems to the base in autumn to prevent aggressive self-seeding in lawns.
Grow alongside wild marjoram in neutral to alkaline soil to mimic its native chalk grassland home.
items.description: Rumex thyrsiflorus, also known commonly as the compact dock or thyrse sorrel, is a perennial herb, which grows in meadows and wasteland in most parts of Europe. It is somewhat similar to common sorrel.

items.name: Rumex abyssinicus
items.growersTips:
Plant in spring in moisture-retentive, neutral to acidic soil, keeping the crown level with the surface.
Water deeply twice a week during dry UK summers to prevent the large leaves from wilting and flagging.
Cut back the tall flower spikes in late summer to prevent aggressive self-seeding around your garden.
Watch for dock beetles and slugs in spring, handpicking them to protect the tender emerging shoots.
Divide the large perennial clumps every three years in autumn to maintain vigor and control spread.
items.description: Rumex abyssinicus is a species of flowering plant in the family Polygonaceae, native to tropical Africa, including Madagascar.

items.name: Rumex hastatulus
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in early spring at a depth of three millimetres in free-draining sandy or gravelly soil.
Water sparingly once established, allowing the gritty soil to dry out fully between applications.
Watch for dock beetles and slugs on young spring foliage, using physical barriers to protect them.
Grow alongside drought-tolerant UK herbs like wild marjoram and thyme to match soil requirements.
Prevent unwanted self-seeding in your garden borders by cutting back flower spikes in late summer.
items.description: Rumex hastatulus, commonly known as the heartwing sorrel, is an annual flowering plant species in the family Polygonaceae otherwise known as the buckwheat family. It is found spread out throughout the eastern and southern United States.

items.name: Rumex hydrolapathum
items.growersTips:
Plant this native giant in heavy clay or boggy soil at the pond edge with the crown just submerged.
Water deeply during dry UK summers if grown in bog gardens to keep the soil consistently saturated.
Cut back the large spent flower spikes in late autumn to prevent aggressive self-seeding in lawns.
Watch for the green dock beetle in spring and handpick them to protect the ornamental foliage.
Divide the tough woody rootstocks in early spring using a sharp spade to propagate new plants.
items.description: Rumex hydrolapathum, the great water dock, water dock, or giant water dock, is a species of perennial herbaceous plants in the genus Rumex native to fens and freshwater banks of Europe and Western Asia. It is the tallest species in the genus, with flowering stems attaining a height of up to 2 m. It is one of the small number of decaploid organisms, containing two hundred individual chromosomes.

items.name: Rumex sagittatus
items.growersTips:
Grow this vigorous climber in a heavy pot to contain its highly invasive tuberous root system.
Prune vines hard to ground level in late autumn after frost kills the top growth to manage spread.
Plant tubers five centimetres deep in well-drained soil in a sheltered south-facing UK sun trap.
Cut off the greenish-pink papery seed heads before late summer to prevent aggressive self-seeding.
Water deeply once a week during dry UK summers but keep tubers barely damp in winter to avoid rot.
items.description: Rumex sagittatus, synonym Acetosa sagittata, commonly known as turkey rhubarb or rambling dock or potato vine, is a herbaceous perennial plant native to southern Africa, which has become a weed in Australia and New Zealand.

items.name: Rumex occidentalis
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in spring at a depth of 5mm in moisture-retentive, heavy clay soils common in UK gardens.
Water deeply twice a week during dry UK summers to mimic its natural damp, marshy habitat.
Cut back the flowering stalks in late summer to prevent aggressive self-seeding across your lawn.
Watch for dock beetles and green dock aphids, removing them by hand to protect the large foliage.
Grow alongside moisture-loving UK native companions like Filipendula ulmaria in boggy garden areas.
items.description: Rumex occidentalis is a flowering plant species belonging to the family Polygonaceae. Commonly known as western dock, Rumex occidentalis can be found in parts of Western North America.

items.name: Rumex rupestris
items.growersTips:
Grow this rare native in waterlogged neutral to acidic clay soil at a pond edge with full sun exposure
Sow seeds in autumn at five millimetres deep in wet peat-free compost left outdoors over winter
Water daily with rainwater to mimic UK coastal marshes and never let the potting medium dry out
Control aggressive garden weeds nearby to prevent them from smothering this slow-growing dock species
Grow alongside native Caltha palustris to provide compatible damp soil conditions and light shade
items.description: Rumex rupestris, commonly known as shore dock, is a species of flowering plant belonging to the family Polygonaceae. Its native range is Western Europe and is one of the world's rarest dock species.

items.name: Rumex paucifolius
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn in cold frames to mimic UK winter chill for natural stratification and germination.
Plant in moisture-retentive, acidic to neutral soil, adding grit to ensure winter drainage in wet clay.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells to mimic its native damp subalpine meadow habitat.
Watch for dock beetles and slugs in spring, handpicking them early to protect the tender young foliage.
Grow alongside moisture-loving UK natives like marsh marigolds to match its damp soil preferences.
items.description: Rumex paucifolius is a species of flowering plant in the knotweed family known by the common name alpine sheep sorrel.

items.name: Persicaria barbata
items.growersTips:
Plant this moisture-lover in boggy soil or shallow pond margins up to ten centimetres deep in spring.
Water daily during dry UK summers to keep the soil consistently wet and prevent leaf scorch.
Cut back the frost-damaged stems to ground level in late autumn to keep the crown tidy for winter.
Grow in full sun to partial shade to ensure the pink flower spikes develop their best colour.
Divide the root clumps every three years in March to control its spread and maintain plant vigour.
items.description: Persicaria barbata, commonly known as bearded knotweed, is a species of flowering plant in the family Polygonaceae. It is native to the Arabian Peninsula and much of tropical and subtropical Asia, and has also been introduced to parts of Africa and the Pacific islands. The plant typically grows in seasonally dry tropical regions, where it occurs as an erect or sometimes prostrate annual herb, 30–60 cm tall, with hairless, line-grooved stems and lance-shaped leaves up to 15 cm long. In some descriptions it is noted as a perennial, producing robust, loosely branched stems 40–90 cm tall from a cr

items.name: Rumex palustris
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in spring at a depth of 5mm in moisture-retentive, heavy clay soil to mimic UK marshlands.
Water copiously to keep the soil constantly soggy, simulating a British bog or pond-edge habitat.
Plant alongside Caltha palustris in bog gardens to create a balanced, moisture-loving community.
Cut back the spent flowering stems in late autumn to prevent aggressive self-seeding across lawns.
Watch for dock beetles in June, hand-picking them to protect the foliage from severe skeletonisation.
items.description: Rumex palustris, or marsh dock, is a plant species of the genus Rumex, found in Europe. The species is a dicot belonging to the family Polygonaceae. The species epithet palustris is Latin for "of the marsh" which indicates its common habitat.

items.name: Rumex patientia
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in spring at a depth of 1cm in moisture-retentive, deep soil to accommodate the long taproot.
Water deeply once a week during dry UK summers to prevent the leaves from becoming tough and bitter.
Cut back flowering stalks in July to encourage a fresh flush of tender leaves and prevent self-seeding.
Handpick dock beetles and green dock beetles in spring to protect the large edible leaves from holes.
Grow in partial shade to mimic its native damp habitat and delay bolting during hot UK spells.
items.description: Rumex patientia, known as patience dock, garden patience, herb patience, or monk's rhubarb, is a herbaceous perennial flowering plant belonging to the family Polygonaceae. In spring it is often consumed as a leaf vegetable and as a filling in pies in Southern Europe, especially in Bulgaria, North Macedonia, Turkey, Bosnia and Herzegovina and Serbia. It is also used in Romania in spring broths or sarmale.

items.name: Persicaria
items.growersTips:
Plant Persicaria amplexicaulis in moisture-retentive clay soil to prevent midsummer leaf scorch.
Divide congested clumps in March using two forks back-to-back to maintain vigorous flowering.
Cut back Persicaria microcephala Red Dragon in May to promote bushier growth and richer leaf colour.
Water deeply during dry UK July spells to stop lower leaves yellowing and dropping prematurely.
Associate Persicaria with Actaea simplex or ornamental grasses for reliable autumn structure.
items.description: Persicaria is a genus of herbaceous flowering plants in the knotweed family, Polygonaceae. Plants of the genus are known commonly as knotweeds or smartweeds. It has a cosmopolitan distribution, with species occurring nearly worldwide. The genus was segregated from Polygonum.

items.name: Harfordia macroptera
items.growersTips:
Plant in sharply draining gritty soil to survive wet UK winters and prevent root rot.
Position in full sun against a south-facing wall to mimic its native warm coastal habitat.
Protect from frost using fleece or move container-grown plants into a cold greenhouse by November.
Water sparingly once established, allowing the compost to dry out completely between soakings.
Propagate by taking semi-ripe cuttings in late summer to ensure backup plants survive the winter.
items.description: Harfordia macroptera is a woody perennial in the family Polygonaceae commonly known as rabbit's purse. It is the sole species in the genus Harfordia, which is endemic to the Baja California Peninsula. This plant is characterized by a unique, conspicuous bladder embellished with red to purple veins that surround the fruit. The sac-like structure is actually a dramatically modified bract, and assists in dispersal of the seeds through the wind.

items.name: Polygonum polystachyum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in March at five millimetres deep then transplant out after the May frosts
Grow in moist moisture-retentive soil amended with plenty of garden compost or well-rotted manure
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells to keep the soil consistently damp but not wet
Pinch out the growing tips in late May to encourage bushier growth and prevent the stems flopping
Plant alongside moisture-loving Astilbe or Hostas to create a lush bog-garden aesthetic in shade
items.description: Koenigia polystachya is a species of flowering plant in the knotweed family, known by the common names Himalayan knotweed and cultivated knotweed. It has several regularly used synonyms, including Polygonum polystachyum, Aconogonon polystachyum and Persicaria wallichii.

items.name: Polygonum shastense
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in early spring under glass to protect from late UK frosts before planting out
Grow in sharply draining gritty soil to mimic its native scree and prevent winter wet root rot
Water sparingly once established allowing the gritty soil to dry out fully between waterings
Position in the brightest spot possible to maximise the short UK summer sun and encourage blooms
Watch for slugs and snails on young spring shoots which can quickly decimate the tender seedlings
items.description: Polygonum shastense is a species of flowering plant in the knotweed family known by the common name Shasta knotweed. It is native to sections of southwestern Oregon, northwestern Nevada, and northern and central California, where it grows in rocky and gravelly mountainous habitat up to 3300 meters (11,000 feet) elevation. It is most common in the Sierra Nevada. The species name refers to its occurrence on Mount Shasta in Shasta County, California.

items.name: Persicaria maculosa
items.growersTips:
Hand-pull young plants in May before their taproots anchor deeply in damp UK clay soils.
Sow seeds shallowly at five millimetres depth in March under cold frames to get early summer blooms.
Water container-grown plants twice weekly in dry July weather to prevent lower leaves yellowing.
Position next to moisture-loving UK native ferns to create a naturalistic woodland edge display.
Snip off faded pink flower spikes in August to prevent aggressive self-seeding across your lawn.
items.description: Persicaria maculosa is an annual plant in the buckwheat family, Polygonaceae. Common names include lady's thumb, spotted lady's thumb, Jesusplant, and redshank. It is widespread across Eurasia from Iceland south to Portugal and east to Japan. It is also present as an introduced and invasive species in North America, where it was first noted in the Great Lakes region in 1843 and has now spread through most of the continent.

items.name: Persicaria amphibia
items.growersTips:
Plant the aquatic form in heavy clay loam in a submerged basket up to forty-five centimetres deep.
Grow the terrestrial form in moisture-retentive soil to prevent it from invading drier borders.
Prune back aggressive runners in autumn to contain its spread in small UK garden ponds.
Propagate by dividing the rhizomes in spring just as new growth begins to emerge.
Watch for aphids on young spring shoots and hose them off with water to protect the foliage.
