Grow this Australian desert shrub in a terracotta pot using a fifty-fifty mix of grit and loam.
Keep the plant dry in winter by moving the container into a cold greenhouse or unheated porch.
Water only when the soil is bone dry, soaking the pot fully then letting it drain completely.
Prune lightly in late spring after frost risk passes to maintain a compact, bushy shape.
Watch for root rot during wet UK autumns by ensuring the pot never sits in a drainage saucer.

items.name: Maireana erioclada
items.growersTips:
Grow this Australian shrub in a terracotta pot using a fifty-fifty mix of loam and grit for drainage
Bring the pot indoors to a frost-free greenhouse or conservatory from November to March in the UK
Water only when the compost is bone dry, then drench fully and let all excess water drain away
Place in your garden's hottest, most south-facing sun trap to mimic its native arid habitat
Prune lightly in late spring after frost risk passes to maintain a compact, bushy shrub shape

items.name: × Beallara
items.growersTips:
Position on a cool east-facing windowsill to avoid scorching summer sun and maintain humidity.
Water thoroughly with rainwater when the bark mix dries out, avoiding waterlogging in the saucer.
Repot every two years in spring using coarse bark mix to prevent root rot in damp UK winters.
Provide a winter temperature drop to twelve degrees Celsius to trigger the autumn flower spikes.
Wipe leaves weekly with a damp cloth to prevent red spider mite infestations in dry indoor air.

items.name: × Brassolaeliocattleya
items.growersTips:
Grow in coarse bark-based orchid compost in clear pots to monitor root health and allow light in.
Position on a south or east windowsill with sheer curtains to prevent leaf scorch in UK summers.
Water thoroughly with tepid rainwater only when the bark dries out, avoiding the pseudobulb crowns.
Maintain a minimum winter temperature of 12C and use gravel trays to boost dry indoor humidity.
Feed with high-nitrogen orchid fertilizer in spring, switching to high-potassium in late summer.

items.name: × Burrageara
items.growersTips:
Position on a cool east-facing windowsill to mimic the UK climate and prevent leaf scorch.
Water weekly using tepid rainwater when the bark mix feels dry, avoiding the central crown.
Repot every two years in spring using a coarse orchid bark mix to ensure excellent drainage.
Maintain winter temperatures above twelve Celsius and move outdoors to a shaded patio in summer.
Watch for spider mites under leaves in dry indoor winter heating and mist surrounding air daily.

items.name: × Degarmoara
items.growersTips:
Grow in medium bark mix and water only when the pot feels light to prevent root rot in UK damp.
Position on a east or west windowsill to provide bright filtered light without scorching the leaves.
Maintain a minimum winter night temperature of twelve degrees Celsius to prevent leaf spotting.
Flush the compost with rainwater monthly to prevent harmful mineral salt buildup from tap water.
Repot every two years in spring just as new growth begins to emerge to refresh the bark medium.

items.name: ×Heucherella alba
items.growersTips:
Plant in partial shade using humus-rich, moist but well-drained soil to prevent UK winter root rot.
Water deeply during dry summer spells to prevent leaf scorch, keeping the crown just above soil level.
Divide the woody crowns every three years in early autumn to maintain vigour and prevent center dieback.
Watch for vine weevil grubs in autumn, which chew the roots and cause the foliage to suddenly collapse.
Pair with hostas and ferns in damp woodland borders to highlight their semi-evergreen winter foliage.

items.name: × Oncostele
items.growersTips:
Grow in a bark-based orchid compost, never soil, to ensure the fast drainage these epiphytes need.
Position on a cool, bright east or west windowsill, keeping them out of direct mid-summer UK sun.
Water thoroughly with rainwater when the bark dries out, but never let the pot sit in standing water.
Maintain a winter minimum of twelve degrees Celsius, moving them away from cold window glass at night.
Feed with a weak half-strength orchid fertilizer every third watering during the active spring growth.

items.name: Acanthocarpus canaliculatus
items.growersTips:
Grow in free-draining sandy loam with added grit to prevent winter root rot in wet UK climates.
Position in full sun against a south-facing wall to maximize warmth and mimic its native habitat.
Protect from hard frost below minus five Celsius using a thick dry mulch of gravel around the crown.
Water sparingly only during dry summer spells once established to avoid waterlogging the roots.
Grow in a terracotta pot with drainage holes to easily move indoors to a greenhouse for winter.

items.name: Acanthocarpus preissii
items.growersTips:
Plant this tender Australian native in a terracotta pot using free-draining gritty loam-based soil.
Overwinter indoors or in a heated greenhouse as it will not survive wet UK winter frosts below zero.
Water sparingly from spring to autumn, allowing the compost to dry out completely between waterings.
Position in the brightest spot possible, such as a south-facing conservatory or sun-baked patio.
Wear thick gloves when handling to protect your hands from the sharp, needle-like leaf tips.

items.name: Acanthophyllum gypsophiloides
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in spring at a depth of three millimetres in free-draining gritty soil to prevent rot.
Water sparingly only when the top two inches of soil are dry to mimic their dry native habitat.
Position in the sunniest south-facing spot of your garden to maximise scarce UK summer warmth.
Protect young seedlings from slugs and snails using beer traps during damp British spring nights.
Incorporate plenty of horticultural grit into heavy UK clay soils to ensure excellent drainage.

items.name: Achyronychia parryi
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at two millimetres deep in April using a gritty, free-draining seed compost.
Grow in a terracotta pot to prevent waterlogging during wet and cool UK summer spells.
Water only when the top five centimetres of soil is dry to mimic its native arid habitat.
Position in your garden's hottest, most south-facing spot to maximise scarce UK summer sun.
Plant alongside Sedums in gravel beds to ensure the soil remains low in nutrients and dry.

items.name: Acianthinae
items.growersTips:
Grow these terrestrial orchids in a gritty, free-draining compost of peat substitute, sand and perlite.
Keep tubers completely dry during their summer dormancy from June to August to prevent them rotting.
Water sparingly from September when new shoots emerge, keeping the compost damp but never waterlogged.
Protect these frost-tender orchids by overwintering them in a cold greenhouse kept above five degrees.
Repot the small tubers annually in late summer at a shallow depth of two centimetres below the soil.

items.name: Pink Cedar
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in early spring at a depth of 1cm using bottom heat of 20C to boost germination.
Grow in a sheltered south-facing spot or greenhouse to protect from cool UK summer night chills.
Water deeply once a week at the base rather than daily light sprinkles to encourage deep rooting.
Pinch out the growing tips when seedlings reach 15cm high to promote a bushier flowering habit.
Feed fortnightly with a high-potassium liquid fertilizer once the first flower buds begin to form.

items.name: Acrothamnus colensoi
items.growersTips:
Plant in acidic, sandy, ericaceous soil with added grit to mimic its native New Zealand scree.
Position in full sun in a raised bed or rockery to ensure the sharp drainage this alpine needs.
Water with rainwater rather than tap water during dry summer spells to keep the soil slightly damp.
Prune lightly in late spring after flowering to maintain its compact, prostrate cushion shape.
Protect from wet winter slush using a pane of glass or cloche to prevent root rot in UK damp.

items.name: Acrothamnus hookeri
items.growersTips:
Plant in highly acidic soil with a pH of 4.5 to 5.5, mixing plenty of composted pine bark into the pit.
Water only with stored rainwater to prevent tapwater lime from raising soil pH and yellowing leaves.
Position in full sun to mimic Tasmanian alpine screes, ensuring sharp drainage to prevent root rot.
Prune lightly in late spring after flowering to maintain a compact dome and prevent woody legginess.
Protect young plants from harsh winter winds with a temporary fleece wrap during severe UK frosts.

items.name: Acrothamnus spathaceus
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist but well-drained acidic soil with a pH of 4.5 to 5.5, mixing in ericaceous compost.
Grow in full sun to partial shade, sheltered from harsh, drying winds in colder UK regions.
Water with harvested rainwater rather than tap water to maintain the necessary low soil pH.
Prune lightly in late spring after flowering to maintain shape and prevent the shrub from woody legginess.
Protect root zones in winter with a thick mulch of pine needles or composted bark to shield from frost.

items.name: Acrothamnus suaveolens
items.growersTips:
Plant in highly acidic soil with a pH of 4.5 to 5.5, mixing ericaceous compost into the planting hole.
Water only with stored rainwater, keeping the soil consistently damp but never waterlogged or soggy.
Position in full sun to partial shade, providing a sheltered spot to protect from harsh UK winds.
Prune lightly immediately after flowering in late spring to maintain its compact, bushy shrub habit.
Protect young plants with horticultural fleece during severe, prolonged winter frosts in colder areas.

items.name: Acrotriche aggregata
items.growersTips:
Grow in acidic soil with a pH of 4.5 to 5.5, mixing pine needles into the planting hole.
Water with harvested rainwater rather than tap water to keep the soil moist but never waterlogged.
Plant in a sheltered, semi-shaded spot to protect the delicate foliage from harsh UK winter winds.
Prune lightly immediately after spring flowering to maintain a compact shape and encourage berries.
Apply a thick mulch of composted bark annually in autumn to protect the shallow roots from frost.

items.name: Acrotriche depressa
items.growersTips:
Plant in acidic, sandy, ericaceous soil mixed with grit to mimic its native dry Australian heath.
Position in a sheltered, south-facing spot or unheated greenhouse to protect from wet UK winters.
Water sparingly with rainwater only, keeping the soil barely damp and never allowing it to waterlog.
Prune lightly immediately after spring flowering to maintain its prostrate, mat-forming habit.
Grow in a terracotta pot to ensure excellent drainage and allow easy relocation during hard frosts.

items.name: Acrotriche divaricata
items.growersTips:
Grow in acidic, sandy, well-drained soil mimicking its native heathland to prevent root rot in UK wet
Plant in a sheltered, south-facing spot or container to protect it from harsh UK winter frosts
Water with rainwater rather than tap water to keep the soil pH low and prevent chlorosis
Prune lightly immediately after spring flowering to maintain its compact, bushy shrub habit
Mulch with pine needles or composted bark to retain moisture and keep the root zone acidic

items.name: Acrotriche prostrata
items.growersTips:
Plant in acidic, sandy-loam soil mixed with pine needles to mimic its native Australian woodland.
Position in a sheltered spot with dappled shade to protect the prostrate foliage from UK frosts.
Water with rainwater rather than tap water to maintain the low soil pH this Ericaceae plant needs.
Avoid heavy pruning and only lightly trim wayward stems in late spring after the flowering period.
Protect the ground-hugging stems from slugs and snails during wet British spring and autumn days.

items.name: Acrotriche rigida
items.growersTips:
Plant in acidic, well-draining ericaceous soil mixed with grit to mimic its native sandstone habitat.
Grow in a container to easily move indoors to a frost-free greenhouse during wet, freezing UK winters.
Water sparingly with rainwater rather than tap water to maintain the essential low soil pH levels.
Position in full sun to partial shade in a sheltered spot away from cold, drying easterly winds.
Avoid hard pruning; only lightly trim wayward stems immediately after spring flowering finishes.

items.name: Acrotriche serrulata
items.growersTips:
Plant in acidic, sandy loam mixed with peat-free ericaceous compost to mimic its native habitat.
Position in a sheltered, partially shaded spot to protect it from harsh UK winter frosts and winds.
Water with rainwater rather than tap water to maintain the low soil pH this acid-lover requires.
Prune lightly immediately after spring flowering to maintain its compact, low-spreading shrub shape.
Mulch annually with pine needles or composted bark to retain moisture and keep roots cool in summer.

items.name: Actaea asiatica
items.growersTips:
Plant in partial to full shade in moisture-retentive, humus-rich, neutral to acidic soil.
Sow fresh seed in autumn in cold frames, as they require winter chilling to germinate in spring.
Apply a thick mulch of leaf mould or well-rotted manure each spring to retain essential moisture.
Keep soil consistently damp during dry UK summer spells to prevent leaf scorch and berry drop.
Wear gloves when handling or cutting back in autumn, as all parts of this plant are highly toxic.

items.name: Actaea biternata
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist, humus-rich, acidic to neutral soil in a sheltered, fully shaded woodland border.
Sow seeds in pots outdoors in autumn to undergo natural UK winter chilling for spring germination.
Water deeply during dry summer spells to keep the soil consistently damp but never waterlogged.
Mulch annually in early spring with leaf mould or well-rotted compost to retain crucial moisture.
Cut the faded flower stems and foliage back to ground level in late autumn after the first frost.

items.name: Tall bugbane
items.growersTips:
Plant in deep, moisture-retentive, humus-rich soil, adding leafmould to mimic woodland conditions.
Position in dappled shade to prevent leaf scorch from the intense midday summer sun in southern UK.
Water deeply during dry summer spells to keep the soil consistently moist but never waterlogged.
Cut the faded flower stems back to the base in autumn to maintain a tidy habit and promote vigor.
Watch for slugs and snails in spring as they can quickly decimate the emerging new shoots.

items.name: Actaea heracleifolia
items.growersTips:
Plant in moisture-retentive, humus-rich acidic to neutral soil in a sheltered, fully shaded spot.
Incorporate leaf mould deeply into the planting hole to mimic its native woodland floor habitat.
Water deeply twice a week during dry UK summers to prevent the large leaves from crisping at edges.
Cut the spent flower spikes to the base in late autumn, leaving foliage to die back naturally.
Watch for slugs and snails on emerging spring shoots, using beer traps or organic pellets early on.

items.name: Actaea japonica
items.growersTips:
Plant in moisture-retentive, humus-rich soil, incorporating leafmould to mimic UK woodland floors.
Position in partial to full shade, sheltered from harsh winds that dry out the delicate foliage.
Water deeply during dry summer spells to prevent leaf scorch and ensure late-season flowering.
Cut the spent flower stems back to the ground in late autumn after the foliage dies back naturally.
Divide congested clumps in early spring just as new growth emerges to maintain plant vigour.
items.description: Actaea japonica, the Japanese bugbane, is a species of flowering plant in the family Ranunculaceae. It is native to central and southern China including Hainan, Jeju Island in South Korea, and central and southern Japan. A perennial, the Royal Horticultural Society considers it to be a good plant to attract pollinators.

items.name: Actaea matsumurae
items.growersTips:
Plant in partial shade in moisture-retentive, humus-rich soil, incorporating leafmould before planting.
Set the crown just at the soil surface in autumn or spring, avoiding planting too deeply in heavy clay.
Water deeply during dry summer spells to prevent the foliage from scorching and drying at the edges.
Cut the faded flower spikes and foliage down to the ground in late winter before new spring growth.
Divide congested clumps in early spring every four years to maintain vigour and increase flower size.

items.name: Doll's eye
items.growersTips:
Plant in shade in moisture-retentive, humus-rich soil, adding leafmould to mimic UK woodland floors.
Keep soil consistently damp but not waterlogged, watering weekly during dry British summer spells.
Plant bare roots in autumn or spring with the crown positioned just below the soil surface.
Cut back the dead foliage to ground level in late winter before the new spring shoots emerge.
Wear gloves when handling this highly toxic plant, especially during autumn berry harvest.

items.name: Actaea podocarpa
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist, humus-rich soil in dappled woodland shade to mimic UK forest floors.
Incorporate leafmould or well-rotted manure deeply into the planting hole to retain summer moisture.
Water deeply during dry spring spells to support the development of the tall autumn flower spikes.
Cut the spent flower stems down to the ground in late autumn after the white berries have fallen.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.

items.name: Cimicifuga racemosa (L.) Nutt. (1818)
items.growersTips:
Plant in moisture-retentive, humus-rich soil, incorporating leafmould to mimic UK woodland floors.
Position in dappled shade to prevent the delicate white bottle-brush flowers from scorching in July.
Water deeply during dry summer spells to prevent the large foliage from crisping at the edges.
Cut the spent flower spikes down to the base in late autumn once the foliage dies back naturally.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit or beer traps in damp weather.

items.name: Actaea rubifolia
items.growersTips:
Plant in moisture-retentive, humus-rich soil, incorporating leaf mould to mimic UK woodland floors.
Position in deep or dappled shade to prevent the delicate, pale green foliage from scorching in summer.
Water deeply during dry summer spells to keep the soil consistently damp but never waterlogged.
Apply a thick mulch of well-rotted compost each spring to retain moisture and feed the crown.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.

items.name: Red baneberry
items.growersTips:
Plant in moisture-retentive, humus-rich soil in deep or partial shade to mimic UK woodland floors.
Sow fresh seed in autumn in cold frames, as they need winter chilling to germinate the next spring.
Water consistently during dry UK summer spells to prevent the delicate compound foliage from crisping.
Wear gloves when handling or pruning in autumn, as all parts of this native-relative are highly toxic.
Combine with ferns and hostas in damp shade to contrast the bright red autumn berries safely.

items.name: Actaea simplex
items.growersTips:
Plant in moisture-retentive, humus-rich soil in partial shade, incorporating leafmould before planting.
Keep soil consistently damp, watering deeply during dry UK summer spells to prevent leaf scorch.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit or beer traps.
Cut faded flower spikes to the base in late autumn, leaving foliage to die back naturally.
Position dark-leaved cultivars like Brunette near pale green ferns to highlight the foliage contrast.

items.name: Herb Christopher
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist, humus-rich, acidic to neutral soil in deep or partial shade to mimic UK woodlands.
Sow fresh seed in autumn in cold frames, as they require winter chilling to germinate the next spring.
Keep soil consistently moist during dry UK summers, watering deeply at the base to prevent drying out.
Wear gloves when handling or pruning in autumn, as all parts of this native plant are highly toxic.
Plant alongside ferns and hostas in shade borders to provide contrasting texture and foliage depth.
items.description: Actaea spicata, the baneberry or herb Christopher, is a species of flowering plant in the genus Actaea, native from Europe to western Siberia and northern Iran. It is often found on limestone edges and in deciduous woodland; key factors are shade, low competition, and a cool, protected root run.

items.name: Ada
items.growersTips:
Grow in a free-draining medium of medium-grade bark and perlite to mimic their cloud forest habitat.
Water weekly with rainwater to keep roots damp but never soggy, reducing slightly during winter.
Position in bright, indirect light in a cool room or greenhouse, avoiding any direct summer sun.
Maintain cool UK indoor temperatures of fifteen to eighteen degrees Celsius with high humidity.
Repot every two years in spring after flowering finishes to refresh the bark and prevent root rot.

items.name: ADA clade
items.growersTips:
Sow sweet peas in deep root trainers during October to encourage strong roots for winter survival.
Plant sweet pea seeds exactly two centimeters deep in well-drained, organic-rich soil in early spring.
Pinch out the growing tips of sweet peas when they reach ten centimeters to encourage bushy growth.
Water sweet peas deeply at the base twice a week during dry UK summers to prevent powdery mildew.
Tie sweet pea stems regularly to support structures using soft twine to prevent wind damage in autumn.

items.name: Ada keiliana
items.growersTips:
Grow this cool-growing orchid in a compost of fine bark and sphagnum moss to ensure rapid drainage.
Position in bright, indirect light near a north or east window, avoiding direct hot summer sun.
Water weekly with rainwater to keep the compost damp but never waterlogged, reducing in winter.
Maintain high humidity above fifty percent by placing the pot on a wet gravel tray in cool rooms.
Feed with a highly diluted orchid-specific fertilizer only during the active spring growth phase.

items.name: Adromischus cristatus
items.growersTips:
Grow in free-draining grit-heavy compost on a south-facing windowsill to maximize UK winter light.
Water only when soil is bone dry, keeping them completely dry from November to March to prevent rot.
Propagate in spring by gently twisting off a healthy leaf and laying it flat on dry gritty soil.
Watch for mealybugs in leaf crevices and treat with an alcohol-soaked cotton bud during active growth.
Keep indoors year-round or move outside only in peak summer when night temperatures stay above ten C.

items.name: Adromischus alstonii
items.growersTips:
Grow in a gritty free-draining cactus compost with fifty percent perlite or pumice to prevent rot.
Keep dry in winter and water only when the fleshy leaves start to wrinkle slightly from spring.
Place on a south-facing windowsill to maximise sunlight and maintain its deep purple leaf spots.
Overwinter indoors as this tender succulent cannot survive UK frosts and needs minimum five degrees.
Propagate in summer by gently detaching a mature leaf and laying it on dry grit to root.

items.name: Adromischus bicolor
items.growersTips:
Grow in a free-draining mix of two parts grit to one part peat-free compost to prevent winter rot.
Water only when the soil is bone dry from April to September, keeping it completely dry in winter.
Position on a south-facing windowsill to maximise light and maintain its deep purple leaf spots.
Keep indoors year-round as this tender succulent will not survive UK winter temperatures below 5C.
Propagate in late spring by gently twisting off a mature leaf and laying it on dry gritty compost.

items.name: Adromischus cooperi
items.growersTips:
Grow in a gritty cactus compost with fifty percent perlite or pumice to prevent winter root rot.
Keep on a south-facing windowsill indoors as they will not survive wet UK winters outside.
Water only when the soil is bone dry from spring to autumn, then keep completely dry in winter.
Propagate easily by gently detaching a mature leaf in spring and laying it on dry gritty soil.
Watch for mealybugs hiding in the tight crevices between the plump, spotted leaves in summer.

items.name: Adromischus cristatus
items.growersTips:
Grow in a gritty loam-based compost with fifty percent perlite or horticultural sand for drainage.
Water only when the soil is bone dry from spring to autumn, keeping it completely dry in winter.
Keep on a south-facing windowsill indoors as it needs protection from UK frost and winter wet.
Propagate by gently twisting off a mature leaf and laying it on dry soil to root in summer.
Watch for mealybugs hiding in the crinkled leaf tips and remove them with an alcohol-dipped swab.

items.name: Adromischus filicaulis
items.growersTips:
Grow in a gritty loam-free compost with fifty percent perlite or pumice to prevent winter root rot.
Keep dry on a bright windowsill from November to March and water only when the leaves start to wrinkle.
Propagate in late spring by gently twisting off a mature leaf and laying it on dry sandy soil.
Provide maximum winter light using a south-facing windowsill or a heated greenhouse kept above five C.
Watch for mealybugs hiding in the tight stem joints and treat immediately with organic neem oil spray.

items.name: Adromischus hemisphaericus
items.growersTips:
Grow in a gritty free-draining soil mix of two parts pumice to one part loam to prevent root rot
Water only when the soil is bone dry from spring to autumn and keep completely dry during winter
Overwinter indoors on a south-facing windowsill as this plant cannot survive UK frosts below five C
Propagate in late spring by gently twisting off a mature leaf and laying it flat on damp grit
Watch for mealybugs hiding in the tight crevices of the leaf joints during warm summer months

items.name: Adromischus maculatus
items.growersTips:
Grow in a gritty, free-draining cactus compost with fifty percent perlite to prevent winter rot.
Keep on a south-facing windowsill indoors to maintain the red leaf spots in weak UK winter light.
Water only when the soil is bone dry from spring to autumn, then keep completely dry all winter.
Propagate in late spring by gently twisting off a mature leaf and laying it flat on dry compost.
Protect from frost by keeping indoors or in a heated greenhouse as temperatures drop below five C.

items.name: Adromischus marianiae
items.growersTips:
Bring indoors by October to protect from cold damp UK winters as they require a minimum of ten Celsius
Water only when the gritty soil is bone dry from March to September then keep totally dry in winter
Grow in a mix of seventy percent horticultural grit and thirty percent loam-based compost in clay pots
Provide a south-facing windowsill or heated greenhouse to maximise essential UK winter sunlight hours
Propagate in late spring by gently twisting off a mature leaf and laying it on dry gritty compost

items.name: Aegiphila obducta
items.growersTips:
Overwinter Aegiphila in a heated greenhouse as they cannot survive UK frosts below ten degrees.
Grow Aegiphila in pots using peat-free loam-based compost mixed with one-third grit for drainage.
Water copiously in summer to keep soil damp but keep almost dry from November to March to stop rot.
Prune stems back by half in early spring to stimulate new flowering wood and maintain a neat shape.
Position pots in the sunniest south-facing spot possible to mimic their native tropical climate.

items.name: Aegiphila ferruginea
items.growersTips:
Bring this tender Lamiaceae indoors to a heated greenhouse before the first autumn frost hits the UK
Grow in a peat-free gritty loam mix with added perlite to ensure rapid drainage during wet winters
Water deeply once a week in summer but keep the soil almost dry from November through to March
Prune back leggy stems by one third in late spring to encourage a bushier habit and more blooms
Position in your sunniest south-facing sheltered spot to mimic its native warm South American climate

items.name: Aegiphila fluminensis
items.growersTips:
Overwinter in a heated greenhouse or indoors as this tender shrub cannot survive UK winter frosts.
Grow in a highly fertile loam-based compost mixed with plenty of grit to ensure rapid drainage.
Position in your sunniest south-facing conservatory or sheltered patio to maximise summer heat.
Water generously throughout the summer active growth phase but keep the soil barely damp in winter.
Prune back leggy stems by half in early spring to encourage a bushier habit and more flowers.

items.name: Aegiphila integrifolia
items.growersTips:
Overwinter container-grown plants in a frost-free greenhouse to survive damp UK winter freezes.
Grow in a highly fertile, loam-based compost mixed with grit to ensure rapid drainage in wet weather.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells, allowing the top two inches of soil to dry out.
Prune back hard in early spring to stimulate vigorous new growth and maintain a compact garden habit.
Position in the brightest spot possible, ideally against a south-facing wall to maximise summer heat.

items.name: Aegiphila lhotskiana
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender Brazilian shrub in a large pot to easily move it indoors before autumn frosts hit
Use a peat-free loam compost mixed with plenty of grit to ensure the sharp winter drainage it needs
Water thoroughly only when the top three inches of soil dry out to prevent root rot in cool weather
Prune stems back by a third in early spring to encourage bushy growth and more summer flowers
Position in your warmest south-facing sheltered spot or conservatory to mimic its tropical habitat

items.name: Aegiphila macrantha
items.growersTips:
Bring indoors or to a heated greenhouse by October to protect this tender shrub from UK winter frosts
Grow in a highly free-draining loam-based grit mix to prevent root rot during wet British winters
Water generously in summer but allow the top three inches of soil to dry out completely between feeds
Prune lightly in early spring after the last frost to shape the plant and encourage summer blooms
Position in a south-facing conservatory or against a warm sun-baked wall to maximise flowering heat

items.name: Aegonychon goulandriorum
items.growersTips:
Plant in autumn under deciduous shrubs to mimic UK woodland soils rich in leaf mould and organic matter.
Water weekly during dry spring spells to establish roots, then rely on natural UK rainfall patterns.
Prune back hard to ground level in late autumn to prevent the spreading stems from becoming woody.
Position alongside native Primula vulgaris as companions to create a classic British woodland floor.
Watch for slugs and snails during wet UK springs as they target the tender new emerging foliage.

items.name: Aeonium arboreum
items.growersTips:
Bring indoors to a frost-free greenhouse or windowsill from October to April to prevent rot.
Water only when the top five centimetres of gritty, free-draining compost is completely dry.
Take stem cuttings in May or June by letting the cut end calloused for a week before potting.
Watch for vine weevil grubs in autumn which eat the roots and cause the rosette to collapse.
Plant in a terracotta pot using a fifty-fifty mix of John Innes number two and horticultural grit.

items.name: Aeonium balsamiferum
items.growersTips:
Overwinter this tender succulent indoors on a south-facing windowsill to survive damp UK frosts.
Water only when the top two inches of gritty, free-draining loam-sand mix are bone dry to stop rot.
Propagate in spring by snipping leggy stems and letting them callus for three days before potting.
Watch for vine weevil grubs in container compost and pick off mealybugs with alcohol-soaked buds.
Position in full summer sun to stimulate the balsam-scented oils and encourage yellow spring blooms.

items.name: Aeonium canariense
items.growersTips:
Bring indoors to a frost-free greenhouse or windowsill from October to May to survive UK winters.
Grow in a gritty mix of equal parts peat-free compost and horticultural sand for sharp drainage.
Water thoroughly only when the top five centimetres of soil are bone dry during spring and summer.
Position in full sun on a south-facing patio to encourage the natural red leaf margins to develop.
Check leaf rosettes weekly for vine weevil grubs and mealybugs which thrive in damp UK conditions.

items.name: Aeonium ciliatum
items.growersTips:
Grow in a gritty loam-based compost with fifty percent perlite to prevent winter root rot in UK wet.
Sow seeds shallowly indoors in early spring at eighteen degrees to offset its tender annual habit.
Water only when the top two inches of soil are dry, reducing to a bare minimum during damp winters.
Move pots to a south-facing unheated greenhouse or porch by October to survive frost and damp cold.
Check leaf axils weekly for mealybugs, treating infestations immediately with organic insecticidal soap.

items.name: Aeonium cuneatum
items.growersTips:
Grow in a gritty, free-draining loam-based compost with fifty percent perlite to prevent winter rot.
Water thoroughly only when the soil is dry, then keep completely dry from November through March.
Bring pots indoors to a frost-free greenhouse or windowsill before the first autumn frost hits.
Propagate by detaching side rosettes in late spring, allowing the stem to callus before potting.
Watch for mealybugs in the leaf joints and treat immediately with organic insecticidal soap.

items.name: Aeonium glandulosum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in early spring on well-drained gritty compost, barely covering them with a fine grit layer.
Water only when the top two inches of soil are dry, reducing to almost nothing during winter dormancy.
Bring pots indoors to a frost-free greenhouse or windowsill by October to survive wet UK winters.
Watch for vine weevil grubs in the roots and treat with nematodes in late summer to prevent collapse.
Grow in terracotta pots with 50 percent perlite to ensure rapid drainage in damp British weather.

items.name: Aeonium glutinosum
items.growersTips:
Bring indoors before October frosts as this tender succulent cannot survive wet UK winter freezes.
Grow in a mix of equal parts John Innes number two and horticultural grit to ensure rapid drainage.
Water thoroughly only when the compost dries out completely, then keep almost dry through winter.
Propagate in spring by taking stem cuttings, letting the wounds callous for three days before potting.
Position in your sunniest south-facing spot or greenhouse to develop the characteristic sticky stems.
items.description: Aeonium glutinosum is a species of flowering plant in the family Crassulaceae endemic to Madeira, Portugal. It has fairly thick leaves and its appearance varies depending on its growing conditions. One characteristic is the very sticky stem of the inflorescence. The main flower is shown but small stalks with flowers continue to appear for several months.

items.name: Aeonium haworthii
items.growersTips:
Bring indoors to a frost-free greenhouse or windowsill from October to April to prevent wet rot.
Grow in a mix of two parts peat-free grit to one part John Innes number two for essential drainage.
Water only when the top five centimetres of soil is bone dry, keeping completely dry in winter.
Take stem cuttings in May by letting the wound callous for three days before potting in sharp sand.
Watch for vine weevil grubs in autumn which eat the roots and cause the rosette head to topple over.

items.name: Aeonium hierrense
items.growersTips:
Bring indoors before October frosts as this tender succulent cannot survive wet UK winter freezes.
Grow in a gritty mix of two parts horticultural sand to one part peat-free compost to ensure drainage.
Water only when the soil dries out completely in summer, and keep almost bone dry throughout winter.
Position in a terracotta pot on a south-facing patio to maximise summer sun and prevent root rot.
Watch for mealybugs in the leaf rosettes and treat immediately with organic insecticidal soap.

items.name: Aeonium holochrysum
items.growersTips:
Bring pots indoors by October to protect this tender succulent from wet UK winter frosts and rot.
Grow in a mix of two parts grit to one part peat-free compost to ensure rapid drainage in damp air.
Water only when the top five centimetres of soil is bone dry, keeping it completely dry in winter.
Inspect the leaf rosettes weekly for vine weevil grubs and mealybugs hiding in the tight crevices.
Take stem cuttings in May to propagate new plants as backups against cold British winter losses.

items.name: Aeonium lancerottense
items.growersTips:
Bring indoors before first frost as this tender Canary Island succulent cannot survive UK winters.
Water only when the top two inches of gritty soil are dry, reducing to once a month in winter.
Plant in a mix of two parts peat-free compost to one part horticultural grit for sharp drainage.
Position in the brightest south-facing spot possible to maintain the pink leaf margins in summer.
Propagate in late spring by taking stem cuttings and letting them callus for three days before potting.

items.name: Aeonium leucoblepharum
items.growersTips:
Bring indoors before October frosts as this tender succulent cannot survive cold UK winters.
Water only when the top two inches of gritty soil are dry, reducing to once a month in winter.
Grow in a mix of two parts peat-free compost to one part horticultural grit for sharp drainage.
Position on a south-facing windowsill or patio to bring out the distinctive red leaf stripes.
Propagate in spring by taking stem cuttings and letting them callous for three days before potting.

items.name: Aeonium lindleyi
items.growersTips:
Grow in a gritty, free-draining loam-based compost with fifty percent perlite to prevent root rot.
Water sparingly from autumn to spring, allowing the soil to dry out completely between waterings.
Protect from frost by overwintering indoors on a south-facing windowsill or in a heated greenhouse.
Propagate in spring by taking stem cuttings, letting the wounds callous for three days before potting.
Watch for mealybugs in the leaf axils during winter and treat immediately with organic insecticidal soap.

items.name: Aeonium nobile
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in spring using a heated propagator at twenty degrees to kickstart growth
Grow in ninety percent grit mixed with loam to prevent root rot during wet British winters
Water only when the rosette leaves feel soft then drench fully and let dry out completely
Bring indoors to a frost free windowsill by October as this tender succulent cannot survive frost
Protect the single large rosette from slugs and snails which disfigure the foliage in damp weather

items.name: Aeonium sedifolium
items.growersTips:
Grow in a gritty 50:50 mix of John Innes No 2 and perlite to prevent root rot in wet UK winters.
Bring indoors to a frost-free windowsill or heated greenhouse from October to April to avoid frost.
Water only when the soil is bone dry in summer, and keep almost completely dry during winter dormancy.
Prune leggy stems in spring by pinching out growing tips to encourage a bushy, compact shrubby habit.
Check leaf crevices regularly for mealybugs, the main pest in humid UK glasshouses and conservatories.

items.name: Aeonium smithii
items.growersTips:
Bring indoors before October frosts as this tender perennial cannot survive wet UK winters outside.
Grow in a gritty mix of fifty percent John Innes number two and fifty percent horticultural grit.
Water only when the soil is bone dry from spring to autumn and keep completely dry during winter.
Watch for vine weevil grubs in the compost which chew the roots and cause the rosette to topple.
Propagate in late spring by taking stem cuttings and letting them callus for three days before potting.

items.name: Aeonium tabuliforme
items.growersTips:
Plant this flat rosette on a slight slope in gritty soil so rainwater drains away from its crown.
Water only from the base during winter to prevent rot in the tight, plate-like leaf rosettes.
Position in partial shade rather than full sun to prevent the flat leaves from scorching in July.
Sow seeds annually in spring using a heated propagator as this monocarpic species dies after flowering.
Check regularly between the tightly packed leaves for mealybugs, using a cotton bud dipped in alcohol.

items.name: Aeonium undulatum
items.growersTips:
Overwinter your Aeonium indoors in a bright frost-free room as UK winters will kill this succulent.
Water only when the top five centimetres of gritty, free-draining soil mix has dried out completely.
Grow in terracotta pots rather than the ground to easily move them under cover before autumn frosts.
Position in full sun on a south-facing patio to prevent the large rosettes from becoming leggy.
Propagate by taking stem cuttings in late spring and letting the wound callous before potting up.

items.name: Aeonium urbicum
items.growersTips:
Bring indoors before first frost as this tender succulent cannot survive wet UK winter freezes.
Grow in a gritty, free-draining mix of two parts John Innes number two to one part horticultural grit.
Water only when the top five centimetres of soil are bone dry, keeping it completely dry in winter.
Inspect the leaf rosettes weekly for mealybugs, treating infestations with organic insecticidal soap.
Propagate by taking stem cuttings in late spring, allowing the cut end to callous before potting.

items.name: Aequatorium
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in April at a depth of five millimetres to protect them from late UK frosts.
Plant out in late May in well-drained soil enriched with grit to prevent winter root rot.
Water deeply once a week at the base rather than daily to encourage deep drought-resistant roots.
Pinch out the growing tips in June to promote a bushier habit and increase the number of flowers.
Watch for slugs and snails on young spring shoots by using beer traps or organic wool pellets.

items.name: Afzelia
items.growersTips:
Sow Afzelia seeds indoors in April at 2cm depth using a heated propagator kept at 21C to start early.
Grow Afzelia in a south-facing greenhouse or polytunnel to match the UK's cool summer temperatures.
Water the soil deeply once a week at the base to keep it moist but prevent waterlogged root rot.
Apply a high-potassium liquid feed every two weeks once the first flower buds begin to appear.
Watch for red spider mites in dry greenhouse air and spray the foliage with water to raise humidity.

items.name: Afzelia africana
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in April at a depth of two centimetres using a heated propagator set to twenty-four Celsius
Grow this tropical legume in pots of free-draining loam-based compost mixed with plenty of perlite
Water only when the top three centimetres of soil are dry to prevent root rot in cool wet UK summers
Position containers in your warmest south-facing suntrap or greenhouse to maximise summer heat units
Check regularly for glasshouse red spider mite under leaves when growing under glass in midsummer

items.name: Afzelia bipindensis
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in April at a depth of 2cm using bottom heat of 21C to counter cool UK springs.
Grow in pots of gritty, free-draining loam to easily move shelter during wet British summers.
Water only when the top 5cm of soil dries out to prevent root rot in humid UK weather.
Position in the sunniest south-facing spot or greenhouse to maximise limited UK summer heat.
Feed weekly with a low-nitrogen fertiliser to support pod development without overproducing foliage.

items.name: Afzelia quanzensis
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender African tree as a summer annual in pots using loam-based compost with extra grit.
Sow the thick-coated seeds in March after nicking the seed coat and soaking in warm water for 24 hours.
Bring pots indoors by September before UK night temperatures drop below 10C to prevent frost death.
Water deeply only when the top three inches of soil are dry to mimic dry-season conditions.
Position in the sunniest, most sheltered south-facing spot in your garden to maximise summer heat.

items.name: Afzelia rhomboidea
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in early spring at a depth of two centimeters using a heated propagator at twenty degrees.
Grow in large containers of free-draining loam-based compost to allow easy moving indoors for winter.
Water deeply once a week during summer, allowing the top five centimeters of soil to dry out fully.
Position in the sunniest, most sheltered south-facing spot to maximize limited UK summer warmth.
Apply a potassium-rich liquid fertilizer monthly from June to August to support container growth.

items.name: Afzelia xylocarpa
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender tropical annual in a heated greenhouse or conservatory to survive UK cool summers.
Sow seeds indoors in April at 2cm depth after soaking them in warm water for 24 hours to break dormancy.
Water deeply once a week to mimic monsoonal patterns, allowing the sandy potting mix to dry out fully.
Feed fortnightly with a low-nitrogen potassium fertilizer to encourage sturdy stems without excess sap.
Watch for glasshouse red spider mites under leaves and mist daily to maintain high local humidity.

items.name: Agarista populifolia
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist acidic soil enriched with pine needles or ericaceous compost to prevent chlorosis.
Position in a sheltered spot away from cold drying winds to protect the evergreen foliage in winter.
Water thoroughly with harvested rainwater rather than tap water to maintain the necessary low soil pH.
Prune lightly immediately after spring flowering to shape the shrub and encourage fresh new growth.
Mulch annually with leaf mould or chipped bark to keep the shallow ericaceous roots cool and moist.

items.name: Agrostemma
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds directly outdoors in March or April at a depth of five millimetres to avoid root damage.
Support the tall stems of Agrostemma githago with hazel twigs or brushwood before they start to flop.
Grow in poor to moderately fertile soil; overly rich soil produces lush foliage but fewer flowers.
Water seedlings weekly until established, then only during prolonged dry spells in the UK summer.
Deadhead regularly to prolong the blooming season and prevent aggressive self-seeding in borders.

items.name: Agrostemma githago
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds directly outdoors in March or April at a depth of five millimetres into poor, gritty soil.
Support the tall, floppy stems using hazel twigs or brushwood link stakes before flowers open in June.
Water seedlings sparingly during dry spells and completely avoid feeding to prevent excessive foliage.
Deadhead spent blooms weekly in summer to prolong flowering and prevent aggressive self-seeding.
Wear gloves when handling seeds and seed pods as all parts of this British native are highly toxic.

items.name: Agrostophyllinae
items.growersTips:
Grow these epiphytes in a heated greenhouse or conservatory keeping winter temperatures above twelve C
Pot in a free-draining medium of fine bark and perlite to prevent root rot in damp UK winters
Water with tepid rainwater only when the bark dries out to mimic their natural tropical wet-dry cycle
Position in bright indirect light avoiding direct summer sun which easily scorches the thin leaves
Inspect the dense clumps regularly for mealybugs hiding in the tightly overlapping leaf sheaths

items.name: Aichryson ×aizoides
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender succulent in pots of gritty, free-draining loam to easily move indoors by October.
Water sparingly from below only when the top two inches of soil feel bone dry to prevent stem rot.
Position in a bright, unheated porch or south-facing windowsill to mimic its native Canary Islands.
Pinch out the yellow spring flowers if you want to delay the plant dying after its monocarpic bloom.
Inspect the dense leaf rosettes weekly for mealybugs, treating infestations with organic neem oil.

items.name: Aichryson bollei
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in spring on the surface of gritty, free-draining compost without burying them deep.
Water only when the top two inches of soil are dry, reducing to a bare minimum during damp winters.
Bring pots indoors to a bright windowsill by October to protect this tender annual from UK frosts.
Watch for vine weevil grubs in the compost which chew through the delicate roots of this succulent.
Grow in shallow terracotta pots rather than deep plastic ones to prevent waterlogging in UK damp.

items.name: Aichryson divaricatum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in early spring on free-draining gritty compost under glass to start them early.
Water sparingly only when the top two inches of soil dry out to prevent root rot in damp UK weather.
Sow alongside Sedum album in shallow stone troughs to create a complementary dry-tolerant display.
Pinch out the growing tips of young plants in May to encourage a bushier habit before they flower.
Watch for vine weevil grubs in autumn which destroy the roots of these succulents in container soil.

items.name: Aichryson villosum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in spring on the surface of gritty compost without covering them as they need light to sprout
Water only when the top two centimetres of soil are bone dry to prevent winter rot in damp UK air
Bring pots indoors to a south-facing windowsill by October before the first autumn frosts arrive
Pinch out the growing tips of young plants in late spring to encourage a bushier branching habit
Discard the plant after it finishes flowering in summer as this species is a strict annual here

items.name: Ajuga
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist well-drained soil in partial shade to prevent leaf scorch in hot dry UK summers.
Space plants twenty centimetres apart and level with the soil line to encourage quick carpet cover.
Water deeply once a week during dry spring spells until the shallow root system is fully established.
Watch for powdery mildew in damp autumns and thin out dense foliage to improve air circulation.
Divide congested clumps every three years in early autumn to maintain vigour and vibrant leaf colour.

items.name: Ajuga chamaepitys
items.growersTips:
Grow this rare UK native in sharply draining, gritty, alkaline soil to prevent winter root rot.
Sow seeds in cold frames during autumn to allow natural winter chilling for spring germination.
Position in full sun, mimicking its open chalk downland habitat, to keep the pine-like foliage dense.
Water sparingly only during prolonged summer droughts as this species is highly drought-tolerant.
Keep surrounding soil free of aggressive weeds and vigorous plants that easily crowd this low grower.

items.name: Ajuga decumbens
items.growersTips:
Plant in autumn or spring at crown depth in moisture-retentive, humus-rich soil to prevent root rot.
Water weekly during dry UK summers, targeting the soil directly to avoid leaf mildew on the foliage.
Divide congested clumps every three years in autumn to maintain vigor and prevent center dieback.
Watch for vine weevil larvae in container-grown plants and treat with nematodes in late summer.
Pair with shade-loving UK native ferns or hostas to create a dense, weed-suppressing ground cover.

items.name: Ajuga genevensis
items.growersTips:
Plant in autumn or spring at a depth level with the soil surface to prevent crown rot in UK rain.
Water weekly during dry summer spells until established, then only during prolonged heatwaves.
Grow in moisture-retentive, humus-rich soil, incorporating well-rotted grit to improve drainage.
Divide congested clumps every three years in early autumn to maintain vigour and prevent mildew.
Plant alongside Primula vulgaris or Galanthus in partial shade for a classic British spring display.
items.description: A. genevensis is a herbaceous flowering plant native to Europe. It is less common than its relative, Ajuga reptans.

items.name: Ajuga iva
items.growersTips:
Plant in gritty, sharply draining soil to prevent winter root rot in wet UK autumn and winter months.
Water sparingly once established, allowing the top five centimetres of soil to dry out between feeds.
Position in full sun to mimic its native Mediterranean habitat and maximise summer flowering potential.
Protect young plants from slugs and snails during damp UK springs using organic grit barriers.
Divide congested clumps in early spring to maintain vigour and propagate new plants for the garden.

items.name: Ajuga japonica
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist well-drained humus-rich soil in partial shade to prevent summer leaf scorch in the UK.
Water weekly during dry UK summer spells to keep the shallow root system from drying out completely.
Divide congested clumps in early autumn to maintain plant vigour and prevent center-out dieback.
Watch for slugs and snails in damp British springs as they quickly damage the tender new foliage.
Grow alongside hostas and ferns in woodland borders for a contrasting shade-loving foliage display.

items.name: Ajuga pyramidalis
items.growersTips:
Plant in partial shade using humus-rich, moist but well-drained soil to prevent midsummer leaf scorch.
Water weekly during dry UK summers to establish young plants, keeping the crown just above soil level.
Divide congested clumps in autumn or early spring to maintain vigour and prevent crown rot in wet mud.
Watch for powdery mildew in late summer; space plants 30cm apart to improve airflow in damp weather.
Combine with native UK ferns and hostas in woodland borders to create a weed-suppressing ground cover.

items.name: Ajuga reptans
items.growersTips:
Plant in autumn or spring at the same depth as the pot in moist, well-drained soil to avoid crown rot.
Water weekly during dry UK summers until established, keeping the soil damp but never waterlogged.
Divide congested clumps every three years in autumn to maintain vigor and prevent powdery mildew.
Plant alongside yellow-flowered Primula vulgaris to create a striking spring colour contrast.
Grow the cultivar Burgundy Glow in partial shade to prevent the variegated leaves from scorching.
items.description: Ajuga reptans is commonly known as bugle, blue bugle, bugleherb, bugleweed, carpetweed, carpet bugleweed, and common bugle, and traditionally as St. Lawrence plant. It is an herbaceous flowering plant in the mint family Lamiaceae, native to Europe. It is also a component of purple moor grass and rush pastures, a Biodiversity Action Plan habitat in the United Kingdom.

items.name: Alchemilla alpina
items.growersTips:
Plant in gritty, free-draining soil to mimic its native UK mountain scree and prevent winter rot.
Position in full sun or partial shade, watering only during prolonged dry summer spells once settled.
Prune back faded foliage and spent flower stems in late summer to encourage fresh, compact growth.
Divide established clumps in early spring or autumn to maintain vigor and propagate new plants.
Grow alongside dwarf conifers or sedums in rock gardens to provide the sharp drainage it requires.

items.name: Alchemilla filicaulis
items.growersTips:
Grow in moisture-retentive clay or loam soil, adding grit to the planting hole to aid winter drainage
Water deeply once a week during dry UK summers, focusing on the root zone to prevent powdery mildew
Cut back foliage and faded flower stems to ground level in August to trigger a fresh flush of leaves
Divide congested clumps in early spring or autumn using a sharp spade to maintain plant vigour
Plant alongside hardy geraniums or pulmonarias in partial shade to create a classic cottage border

items.name: Alchemilla glabra
items.growersTips:
Plant in moisture-retentive UK clay or loam enriched with leafmould to mimic its native upland habitat
Water deeply during dry British summers to prevent the delicate leaf margins from scorching brown
Cut back foliage and faded flowers to ground level in August to trigger a fresh flush of clean leaves
Divide overgrown clumps in autumn or early spring using a sharp spade to maintain vigor and spread
Position in partial shade to protect the foliage from intense afternoon sun in southern UK gardens

items.name: Alchemilla glaucescens
items.growersTips:
Plant in free-draining UK soil with grit to prevent winter crown rot in wet clay.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells to keep the blue-grey foliage lush.
Shear back faded flowers and old leaves in August to trigger a fresh flush of foliage.
Divide congested clumps in autumn or early spring to maintain vigor and propagate.
Grow alongside purple-flowered salvias or lavenders for a classic UK cottage garden contrast.

items.name: Alchemilla mollis
items.growersTips:
Cut back faded foliage and spent flower stems to ground level in August to trigger fresh new growth.
Divide congested clumps in autumn or early spring by lifting and splitting with a sharp spade.
Plant bare-root divisions with the crown sitting exactly level with the soil surface in autumn.
Shake dried seedheads into a bucket in late summer to prevent aggressive self-seeding in borders.
Position in partial shade alongside hardy geraniums to prevent leaves from scorching in dry summers.
items.description: Alchemilla mollis, the garden lady's-mantle or lady's-mantle, is a species of flowering plant in the family Rosaceae. This herbaceous perennial plant is native to Southern Europe and grown throughout the world as an ornamental garden plant. It grows 30 to 45 cm tall, with leaves that are palmately veined, with a scalloped and serrated margin. The stipules are noteworthy in that they are fused together and leaf like. The chartreuse yellow flowers are held in dense clusters above the foliage. A. mollis has gained the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit. The plant self-seeds freel

items.name: Alchemilla xanthochlora
items.growersTips:
Plant in moisture-retentive clay or loam in partial shade to mimic its native UK damp meadow habitat.
Divide congested clumps in early spring or autumn using a sharp spade to maintain plant vigour.
Cut back faded foliage and spent flower stems to ground level in August to trigger fresh green growth.
Prevent self-seeding in damp UK borders by shearing off the chartreuse flowers before they set seed.
Grow alongside Astilbe or Hostas in damp soil to create a classic British semi-shade foliage contrast.

items.name: Aldina
items.growersTips:
Sow Aldina seeds indoors in April at 2cm depth using peat-free compost to beat late UK frosts.
Transplant outdoors in late May into free-draining sandy loam with a neutral to slightly acid pH.
Water deeply at the base once a week during dry summer spells to support the deep taproot system.
Grow near brassicas as a companion to fix nitrogen in the soil and boost their leafy development.
Watch for slugs on young spring shoots and use organic wool pellets to protect the tender foliage.

items.name: Alkanna
items.growersTips:
Grow Alkanna in sharply draining, gritty, alkaline soil to prevent winter root rot in wet UK climates.
Sow seeds shallowly at a depth of three millimetres in cold frames during the autumn or early spring.
Water established plants only during prolonged dry spells, allowing the soil to dry out completely.
Prune back the faded flowering stems in late summer to maintain a compact, tidy mound of foliage.
Plant alongside Mediterranean herbs like rosemary and thyme that share its need for dry, sunny spots.

items.name: Alsinidendron
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in March at a depth of two millimetres to protect them from late UK spring frosts
Grow in a gritty loam with neutral pH to mimic their native Hawaiian volcanic soil requirements
Water sparingly from below once a week to prevent damp-off in the damp British summer climate
Position pots in a south-facing conservatory or greenhouse to maximise essential sunlight hours
Check regularly for glasshouse red spider mite which thrives in dry indoor growing environments

items.name: Alsinidendron obovatum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at two millimetres deep in early spring under glass to protect from UK frosts.
Grow in a gritty, free-draining loam to mimic its native volcanic soil and prevent winter root rot.
Water sparingly from below once the top inch of soil dries out to avoid damping off in damp UK air.
Position in a south-facing cold frame or unheated greenhouse to maximise essential sunlight hours.
Watch closely for aphids and slugs which thrive in cool UK springs and quickly destroy young shoots.

items.name: Alsinidendron trinerve
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in spring under glass as this rare Hawaiian annual needs early warmth in the UK.
Keep compost consistently moist but never waterlogged to prevent stem rot in damp British summers.
Grow in a gritty, free-draining loam to mimic its native volcanic slopes and avoid root damage.
Position in a bright conservatory or south-facing sheltered patio to maximise crucial sunlight hours.
Monitor closely for glasshouse red spider mite and aphids which thrive on its delicate foliage.

items.name: Amana anhuiensis
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs in autumn at a depth of eight centimetres in gritty, sharply draining neutral soil.
Position in a sheltered rock garden or cold frame to protect delicate winter foliage from wet rot.
Water moderately during the active spring growing phase but keep the soil almost dry during summer.
Protect emerging early spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or traps.
Grow in pots alongside dwarf narcissus or crocus to provide companion interest in early spring.

items.name: Amana erythronioides
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs in autumn at a depth of 8cm in well-drained, gritty soil to prevent winter waterlogging.
Position in a partially shaded spot that mimics UK deciduous woodland, keeping soil moist in spring.
Incorporate leafmould and sharp sand into heavy clay soils to ensure the bulbs do not rot in winter.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.
Allow the foliage to die back naturally after flowering in May to feed the bulb for next year.

items.name: Amasonia
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender tropical in pots of peat-free loam compost to easily move indoors before autumn frost
Provide bright filtered light and maintain high humidity by placing the pot on a wet pebble tray
Water with tepid rainwater to keep soil evenly moist but never soggy to prevent root rot in winter
Feed fortnightly in spring and summer with a high-potassium liquid fertiliser to boost bract colour
Prune leggy stems by one-third in early spring to encourage bushy growth and more tropical blooms

items.name: Amasonia hirta
items.growersTips:
Grow in a heated greenhouse or conservatory as this tropical plant cannot survive UK winter frost.
Use a peat-free acidic loam compost mixed with plenty of perlite to ensure rapid root drainage.
Water with tepid rainwater to keep soil consistently damp but never waterlogged during summer.
Maintain high humidity by placing the pot on a tray of wet pebbles to prevent red spider mites.
Prune back leggy stems by one third in early spring just as new growth begins to encourage bushiness.

items.name: Amburaneae
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in April at 2cm depth using peat-free compost to counter cool UK spring soils.
Transplant outdoors in late May after the last frost into a sheltered south-facing border.
Water deeply at the base once a week during dry summer spells to support the taproot system.
Protect young plants from slugs using beer traps or copper tape during damp UK spring nights.
Incorporate well-rotted grit into heavy clay soils to ensure the sharp drainage this annual needs.

items.name: Amethystea
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in April under glass as this short-lived Lamiaceae needs warmth to germinate.
Grow in sharply draining gritty loam to prevent winter root rot in damp UK clay soils.
Position in full south-facing sun to intensify the signature metallic blue stem and flower colour.
Deadhead spent spikes in August to control its prolific self-seeding habit in small borders.
Protect young spring shoots from slugs and snails using beer traps or grit barriers.

items.name: Ammobium
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in March at a depth of two millimetres using free-draining compost on a windowsill.
Plant out in May after frosts into a gritty soil mix to prevent winter wet from rotting the roots.
Water sparingly once established to mimic dry Australian soils and prevent weak floppy flower stems.
Harvest the paper-like white blooms just as the yellow centres start to show for dry arrangements.
Support tall cultivars like Grandiflorum with brushwood twigs to protect them from strong UK winds.

items.name: Amphimas
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in April at 2cm depth using peat-free compost to counter cool UK spring soils.
Transplant outdoors in late May after frosts, spacing 40cm apart in a sheltered, south-facing border.
Water deeply at the base once a week during dry summer spells to support the deep taproot system.
Protect young shoots from slugs and snails using organic wool pellets or beer traps in damp weather.
Incorporate well-rotted manure into sandy soils before planting to boost nitrogen-fixing bacteria.

items.name: Amsinckia
items.growersTips:
Wear gloves to handle bristly stems and prevent skin irritation when weeding or pruning in summer.
Sow seeds in autumn directly into poor, well-drained soil to mimic natural UK winter stratification.
Grow in full sun and restrict watering to rainfall once established to prevent floppy, weak growth.
Deadhead immediately after flowering in July to prevent aggressive self-seeding across your garden.
Plant alongside red campion to create a vibrant wildlife border that thrives in dry UK soils.

items.name: Amsinckia calycina
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn at a depth of five millimetres to mimic natural UK winter cold stratification.
Grow in poor, sharply drained sandy soil to prevent winter root rot in wet British climates.
Water only during prolonged summer droughts, allowing the soil to dry out completely between feeds.
Wear thick gloves when weeding or pruning to protect skin from the irritating, bristly hairs.
Plant alongside red campion to create a vibrant colour contrast that thrives in dry, sunny borders.

items.name: Amsinckia douglasiana
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at 3mm deep in autumn to mimic natural UK winter chilling for spring germination
Grow in poor well-drained sandy soil to prevent floppy growth in wet British summers and winters
Water only during prolonged dry spells in summer as this plant is highly drought-tolerant once set
Wear thick gloves when weeding or handling to protect your skin from the irritating bristly hairs
Plant alongside native UK wildflowers like red campion to attract bees and support local pollinators

items.name: Amsinckia eastwoodiae
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn at 5mm depth in well-drained gritty soil to mimic cool UK winter stratification.
Water sparingly only during dry summer spells to prevent root rot in damp British clay soils.
Position in full sun and poor, alkaline soil to stop this wildflower from becoming overly leggy.
Wear thick gloves when weeding to protect your skin from the irritating, bristly hairs on stems.
Deadhead spent yellow blooms in late summer to control self-seeding in small cottage gardens.

items.name: Amsinckia grandiflora
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn in well-drained, gritty soil to mimic its native cool-season Mediterranean cycle.
Grow in full sun and poor, alkaline soil to prevent floppy growth and mimic its natural habitat.
Water sparingly once established, allowing the soil to dry out completely between watering sessions.
Protect young shoots from slugs and snails in early spring using grit barriers or organic pellets.
Avoid high-nitrogen fertilisers which cause excessive foliage at the expense of its yellow flowers.

items.name: Amsinckia lycopsoides
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at five millimetres deep in autumn to mimic natural UK winter cold stratification.
Grow in poor, sharply draining sandy soil to prevent the plant from becoming too floppy and weak.
Water only during prolonged summer droughts as this plant is highly adapted to dry British soil.
Wear thick gloves when handling to avoid skin irritation from the stiff, bristly hairs on stems.
Deadhead spent yellow blooms in late summer to prevent aggressive self-seeding around your garden.

items.name: Amsinckia menziesii
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in spring at a depth of 5mm directly into poor, well-drained soil in a sunny UK border.
Water seedlings sparingly during dry spells, then leave established plants to thrive on rainfall.
Wear thick gardening gloves when handling to protect your skin from the irritating, bristly hairs.
Deadhead spent yellow blooms in late summer to prevent aggressive self-seeding around your garden.
Grow alongside red campion to create a vibrant, wildlife-friendly contrast in dry cottage gardens.

items.name: Amsinckia spectabilis
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn at a depth of five millimetres to mimic natural winter chilling in UK soils.
Grow in poor, sharply drained sandy soil to prevent winter root rot in wet British climates.
Water seedlings sparingly only during prolonged dry spells to avoid promoting floppy, weak growth.
Wear thick gloves when weeding to protect your skin from the irritating, bristly hairs on stems.
Deadhead spent yellow blooms in late summer to prevent aggressive self-seeding across your borders.

items.name: Devil's lettuce
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at a depth of three millimetres in autumn to mimic natural UK winter chilling.
Grow in poor, sharply drained sandy soil to prevent root rot in wet British winters.
Water only during prolonged dry spells in summer, allowing the soil to dry out completely.
Wear thick gloves when handling to protect your skin from the irritating, bristly hairs.
Deadhead immediately after flowering in July to prevent aggressive self-seeding in your borders.

items.name: Amsinckia vernicosa
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at three millimetres deep in autumn to mimic UK wildflower meadow regeneration.
Grow in poor, sharply draining sandy soil to prevent winter root rot in wet British climates.
Water only during prolonged summer droughts, allowing the soil to dry out completely between feeds.
Deadhead spent yellow blooms in late summer to control aggressive self-seeding in small gardens.
Position in full south-facing sun to maximise flowering and prevent leggy growth in overcast weather.
items.description: Amsinckia vernicosa is a species of fiddleneck known by the common name green fiddleneck.

items.name: Amsinckiopsis kingii
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn in free-draining gritty soil to mimic its native dry habitat in UK winters.
Grow in a raised bed or alpine trough to prevent root rot from heavy UK winter rainfall.
Water only during prolonged dry spells in summer, allowing the soil to dry out completely between.
Protect young spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers around the crown.
Propagate by taking root cuttings in late autumn when the plant enters its winter dormancy.
items.description: Amsinkiopsis is a monotypic genus of flowering plants in the borage family consisting of the species Amsinckiopsis kingii. A. kingii was previously considered part of the genus Plagiobothrys, until phylogenetic study proved the genus to be polyphyletic.

items.name: Common bugloss
items.growersTips:
Plant Anchusa in sharply draining, gritty soil to prevent winter root rot in wet UK climates.
Sow seeds shallowly at a depth of three millimetres in spring under cover for reliable germination.
Cut back Anchusa azurea Loddon Royalist to ground level after flowering to encourage fresh growth.
Watch for powdery mildew in dry UK summers and water the soil directly at the base to prevent it.
Propagate by taking root cuttings in late autumn when the plant enters its winter dormant phase.
items.description: The genus Anchusa belongs to the borage family (Boraginaceae). It includes about 35 species found growing in Europe, North Africa, South Africa and Western Asia. They are introduced in the United States.

items.name: Ancipitia anthrax
items.growersTips:
Grow this cool-growing orchid in a fine bark and perlite mix to ensure rapid drainage in UK humidity.
Position in bright, indirect east-facing light, shielding leaves from scorching spring glasshouse sun.
Water weekly in active growth using harvested rainwater, keeping the roots barely damp during winter.
Maintain high humidity above fifty percent using gravel trays to prevent bud blast in dry UK winters.
Repot every two years in spring just as new root growth begins to prevent the potting mix from souring.
items.description: Pleurothallis is a genus of orchids commonly called bonnet orchids. The genus name is derived from the Greek word pleurothallos, meaning "riblike branches". This refers to the rib-like stems of many species. The genus is often abbreviated as "Pths" in horticultural trade.

items.name: Northern wild comfrey
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn in cold frames to let winter chill break dormancy naturally in the UK climate.
Plant in well-drained, alkaline to neutral soil, adding grit to prevent winter root rot in wet clay.
Water moderately during dry spring spells, but keep the crown dry in winter to prevent rot.
Watch for slugs and snails in damp UK springs, protecting young emerging shoots with grit barriers.
Position in partial shade mimicking woodland edges, pairing with native ferns or wild primroses.
items.description: Andersonglossum boreale, known as northern wild comfrey or just wild comfrey, is a species of flowering plant in the borage family, Boraginaceae. It is native to boreal coniferous and mixed forests in North America, from Nova Scotia to British Columbia and Yukon in Canada, south to New Jersey and Indiana in the United States. It is often found in rocky or sandy soils. It is extirpated from many of the southern parts of its range.

items.name: Andersonia aristata
items.growersTips:
Grow in extremely acidic, sandy, peat-free ericaceous compost mixed with plenty of grit for drainage.
Keep in a cold greenhouse or sheltered patio container to protect from wet, freezing UK winters.
Water exclusively with rainwater to maintain the low soil pH this sensitive Australian native needs.
Avoid pruning the woody stems as this slow-growing shrub does not regenerate well from old wood.
Position in full sun with excellent air circulation to prevent fungal rot in damp British weather.
items.description: Andersonia aristata, commonly known as rice flower, is a species of flowering plant in the family Ericaceae and is endemic to the southwest of Western Australia. It is a slender, erect or spreading shrub with linear to lance-shaped leaves and white, tube-shaped flowers with bearded petal lobes.

items.name: Andersonia caerulea
items.growersTips:
Grow in ericaceous compost mixed with grit to mimic Western Australian sand and prevent root rot.
Water with rainwater rather than tap water to maintain the essential highly acidic soil pH.
Position in a sheltered south-facing spot or cold greenhouse to protect from wet UK winters.
Prune lightly immediately after flowering in late spring to maintain a compact bushy shape.
Feed sparingly with low-phosphorus seaweed fertilizer as proteoid roots are sensitive to feed.
items.description: Andersonia caerulea, commonly known as foxtails, is a species of flowering plant in the family Ericaceae and is endemic to the southwest of Western Australia. It is an erect or spreading to low-lying shrub with variably-shaped leaves and pink and pale blue flowers, sometimes in spike-like groups.

items.name: Andersonia echinocephala
items.growersTips:
Grow in a highly acidic, peat-free ericaceous compost mixed with fifty percent grit for drainage.
Position in full sun but shelter from cold, drying winds using a cold frame or unheated greenhouse.
Water only with rainwater to keep the soil moist, never allowing the roots to dry out completely.
Avoid pruning this slow-growing shrub other than lightly removing dead tips in late spring.
Protect from winter wet by placing pot feet under containers to ensure excellent drainage.
items.description: Andersonia echinocephala is a species of flowering plant in the family Ericaceae and is endemic to the south of Western Australia. It is an erect, rigid shrub with lance-shaped leaves and heads of up to 15 or more, white or cream-soloured flowers.

items.name: Andersonia gracilis
items.growersTips:
Grow in a container using peat-free ericaceous compost mixed with plenty of perlite for drainage.
Protect from winter wet and hard frosts by moving the pot into an unheated greenhouse or porch.
Water exclusively with harvested rainwater to keep the soil acidic and prevent root damage from lime.
Place in a spot that receives full morning sun but is shielded from scorching midday summer heat.
Prune very lightly immediately after flowering by pinching out tips to maintain a bushy habit.
items.description: Andersonia gracilis is a species of flowering plant in the family Ericaceae and is endemic to the southwest of Western Australia. It is a slender erect or open straggly shrub with more or less lance-shaped leaves and groups of two to ten densely bearded, white or pinkish-purple, tube-shaped flowers.

items.name: Andersonia grandiflora
items.growersTips:
Grow in extremely acidic, sandy peat soil mimicking its native Western Australian heathland habitat.
Provide winter protection under glass or fleece to shield this tender shrub from hard UK frosts.
Water with rainwater only to keep the soil consistently damp without raising the pH level.
Position in full sun with excellent air circulation to prevent fungal rot in damp UK winters.
Avoid root disturbance entirely when potting on as this species has highly sensitive feeder roots.
items.description: Andersonia grandiflora, commonly known as red andersonia, is a species of flowering plant in the family Ericaceae and is endemic to the south-west of Western Australia. It is a prostrate cushion shrub with lance-shaped leaves and groups of two to four reddish orange, tube-shaped flowers.

items.name: Andersonia hammersleyana
items.growersTips:
Grow in extremely acidic, sandy peat soil mimicking its native Western Australian heathland habitat.
Provide shelter under glass or a cold frame to protect this tender shrub from wet UK winter frosts.
Water exclusively with soft rainwater to maintain the essential low soil pH and prevent chlorosis.
Avoid root disturbance entirely when potting on, as this species has highly sensitive micro-roots.
Prune very lightly immediately after flowering to maintain shape without cutting back into old wood.
items.description: Andersonia hammersleyana is a species of flowering plant in the family Ericaceae and is endemic to the southwest of Western Australia. It is an erect or low-lying, straggling shrub with twisted, linear to narrowly egg-shaped leaves and bright blue, tube-shaped flowers.

items.name: Andersonia heterophylla
items.growersTips:
Grow in extremely well-drained, acidic, sandy-peaty soil to prevent winter wet root rot in UK rain.
Water only with rainwater to maintain the low soil pH this ericaceous Australian shrub requires.
Provide a sheltered, frost-free microclimate or winter container protection against hard UK frosts.
Prune very lightly immediately after spring flowering to maintain shape without cutting woody stems.
