Plant alongside dwarf heathers or gaultheria which share its strict acidic, low-nutrient needs.
items.description: Andersonia heterophylla is a species of flowering plant in the family Ericaceae and is endemic to the south-west of Western Australia. It is an erect or ascending shrub with egg-shaped to more or less linear leaves and white or pink flowers.

items.name: Andersonia involucrata
items.growersTips:
Plant this acid-loving Australian shrub in a pot of ericaceous grit mix to survive wet UK winters.
Position in a sheltered, south-facing spot or cold greenhouse to protect from frosts below minus five.
Water only with rainwater to maintain the low soil pH and keep the compost damp but never waterlogged.
Avoid pruning the woody stems as this slow-growing shrub does not regenerate well from old wood.
Feed sparingly in spring with a highly diluted, phosphorus-free fertiliser suited for proteas.
items.description: Andersonia involucrata is a species of flowering plant in the family Ericaceae and is endemic to the south-west of Western Australia. It is a compact or straggling, spreading shrub with pointed egg-shaped to lance-shaped leaves and white or pink flowers.

items.name: Anemarrhena
items.growersTips:
Plant in spring in free-draining sandy loam with grit added to survive wet UK winters without rotting
Position in full sun to mimic its native dry Asian hillsides, ensuring maximum summer warmth
Water moderately during the spring growing season but keep almost dry throughout the damp winter
Sow seeds in cold frames during autumn so winter chill naturally breaks their physical dormancy
Protect the emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails which target the new growth in damp weather
items.description: Anemarrhena is a plant genus in family Asparagaceae, subfamily Agavoideae. It has only one species, Anemarrhena asphodeloides, native to China and Mongolia. Some authors have placed it in its own family, Anemarrhenaceae.

items.name: Narcissus-flowered anemone
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist well-drained humus-rich soil in partial shade to mimic UK woodland edge conditions
Sow fresh seed in cold frames in autumn as they require winter chilling to break dormancy in spring
Mulch annually in late winter with leaf mould to retain moisture and protect shallow fibrous roots
Divide congested clumps in early spring just as new growth emerges to maintain plant vigour
Watch for caterpillars and slugs in damp UK springs which rapidly damage the delicate new foliage
items.description: Anemonastrum is a genus of flowering plants in the family Ranunculaceae. Plants of the genus are native to the temperate and subarctic regions of North America, Greenland, Europe, Asia, South America, and New Zealand. The generic name Anemonastrum means "somewhat like anemone", a reference to the Anemone genus of closely related plants. It chiefly differs from Anemone in having a base chromosome number of x=7, as opposed to x=8.

items.name: Anemonastrum baicalense
items.growersTips:
Plant in partial shade using humus-rich, moist, well-drained soil to mimic Siberian woodland edges.
In dry UK summers, water weekly at the base to keep soil consistently damp but never waterlogged.
Mulch annually in autumn with leaf mould to protect rhizomes from severe British winter frosts.
Propagate by careful root division in early spring just as new growth begins to emerge.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.
items.description: Anemonastrum baicalense is a species of flowering plant in the genus Anemonastrum. It is native to forests, scrub, and grassy places at 500–3100 m. altitude in Siberia, Mongolia, northern China, and North Korea in Northeast Asia.

items.name: Anemonastrum canadense
items.growersTips:
Plant this vigorous spreader in moisture-retentive clay or loam in partial shade to mimic woodland.
Sow seeds in pots outdoors in autumn as they require winter cold stratification to germinate in UK.
Water weekly during dry UK summers to keep the soil consistently damp and prevent early dormancy.
Divide the dense rhizomatous root clumps in early spring just as new green growth begins to emerge.
Plant alongside aggressive companions like Matteuccia struthiopteris to contain its invasive habit.
items.description: Anemonastrum canadense, synonym Anemone canadensis, the Canada anemone, round-headed anemone, round-leaf thimbleweed, meadow anemone, windflower, or crowfoot, is a herbaceous perennial flowering plant in the family Ranunculaceae. It is native to moist meadows, thickets, streambanks, and lakeshores in North America, spreading rapidly by underground rhizomes. It is valued for its white flowers.

items.name: Flaccid anemone
items.growersTips:
Plant in autumn at a depth of five centimetres in moist, humus-rich soil under deciduous trees.
Water weekly during dry spring spells to mimic the damp woodland floor of its native habitat.
Mulch annually with leaf mould in November to protect rhizomes from severe UK winter frosts.
Propagate by dividing the delicate rhizomes in late summer once the foliage has died down.
Plant alongside Galanthus and Hepatica for a continuous early spring shade-garden display.
items.description: Anemonastrum flaccidum, commonly known as the flaccid anemone or soft windflower, is a species of flowering plant in the family Ranunculaceae. It is a low-growing perennial native to East Asia.

items.name: Narcissus-flowered anemone
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist but well-drained humus-rich soil in partial shade to mimic its alpine woodland home.
Sow fresh seed in autumn in cold frames as they require winter chilling to trigger UK spring growth.
Mulch annually in early spring with leafmould to retain moisture and keep roots cool in dry summers.
Divide established clumps in early spring just as new growth begins to maintain plant vigour.
Protect young spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers in damp UK weather.
items.description: Anemonastrum narcissiflorum, the narcissus anemone or narcissus-flowered anemone, is a herbaceous perennial in the genus Anemonastrum and the buttercup family. Basionym: Anemone narcissiflora Hook. & Arn.

items.name: Smell fox
items.growersTips:
Soak dry Anemone coronaria tubers in water for twenty hours before planting in autumn or spring.
Plant wood anemone rhizomes horizontally just two centimetres deep in moist, humus-rich shade.
Mulch autumn-flowering Japanese anemones in November to protect crowns from severe UK winter frosts.
Water newly planted anemones weekly during dry UK spring spells to establish deep, resilient roots.
Divide congested clumps of Japanese anemones in early spring to maintain vigour and control spread.
items.description: Anemone is a genus of flowering plants in the buttercup family Ranunculaceae. Plants of the genus are commonly called windflowers. They are native to the temperate and subtropical regions of all regions except Australia, New Zealand, and Antarctica. The genus is closely related to several other genera including Anemonoides, Anemonastrum, Hepatica, and Pulsatilla. Some botanists include these genera within Anemone.

items.name: Anemone narcissiflora
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist, free-draining, humus-rich soil, adding grit to heavy UK clay to prevent winter rot.
Sow fresh seed in cold frames during autumn, as they require winter chilling to germinate in spring.
Position in partial shade or dappled woodland light to mimic their natural alpine meadow habitat.
Water consistently during dry UK summer spells to keep the soil evenly moist but never waterlogged.
Divide established clumps in early spring just as new growth begins, replanting them immediately.
items.description: Anemonastrum narcissiflorum, the narcissus anemone or narcissus-flowered anemone, is a herbaceous perennial in the genus Anemonastrum and the buttercup family. Basionym: Anemone narcissiflora Hook. & Arn.

items.name: Smell fox
items.growersTips:
Plant rhizomes horizontally in autumn five centimetres deep in leaf-mould-rich soil under deciduous trees.
Water only during dry spring spells to keep soil damp, then leave completely dry during summer dormancy.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.
Propagate by dividing the brittle rhizomes in late summer once the foliage has completely died back.
Plant alongside wild garlic and primroses to mimic natural UK woodland communities and extend color.
items.description: Anemonoides nemorosa, the wood anemone, is an early-spring flowering plant in the buttercup family Ranunculaceae, native to Europe. Other common names include windflower, European thimbleweed, and smell fox, an allusion to the musky smell of the leaves. It is a perennial herbaceous plant growing 5–15 cm (2–6 in) tall.

items.name: Anemonoides nemorosa
items.growersTips:
Plant rhizomes 2-5cm deep in autumn, laying them horizontally in moisture-retentive, humus-rich soil.
Incorporate leafmould or well-rotted manure to mimic UK woodland soils before autumn planting.
Water during dry spring spells but leave soil dry during their summer dormancy to prevent rot.
Plant alongside early bulbs like Galanthus or under deciduous shrubs to match their light needs.
Leave dying foliage intact in late spring to naturally feed the rhizomes for next year's blooms.
items.description: Anemonoides nemorosa, the wood anemone, is an early-spring flowering plant in the buttercup family Ranunculaceae, native to Europe. Other common names include windflower, European thimbleweed, and smell fox, an allusion to the musky smell of the leaves. It is a perennial herbaceous plant growing 5–15 cm (2–6 in) tall.

items.name: Anemonoides quinquefolia
items.growersTips:
Plant rhizomes horizontally three centimetres deep in autumn, ensuring they do not dry out before.
Incorporate well-rotted leafmould to mimic UK deciduous woodland soil before planting in shade.
Water weekly during dry spring spells, but allow soil to dry slightly once summer dormancy begins.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.
Plant alongside native UK woodland companions like Primula vulgaris and Galanthus nivalis.
items.description: Anemonoides quinquefolia, a flowering plant in the buttercup family Ranunculaceae, is native to North America. It is commonly called wood anemone or windflower, not to be confused with Anemonoides nemorosa, a closely related European species also known by these common names. The specific epithet quinquefolia means "five-leaved", which is a misnomer since each leaf has just three leaflets. A plant typically has a single, small white flower with 5 sepals.

items.name: Anemonoides ranunculoides
items.growersTips:
Plant rhizomes shallowly at five centimetres deep in autumn using leaf mould to mimic UK woodlands.
Water weekly during dry spring active growth but keep soil relatively dry during summer dormancy.
Watch for slugs and snails in damp UK springs as they quickly destroy the emerging young foliage.
Do not prune or cut back dying summer foliage to allow the rhizomes to naturally store energy.
Plant under deciduous shrubs alongside Galanthus nivalis for a sequential spring woodland display.
items.description: Anemonoides ranunculoides, the yellow anemone, yellow wood anemone, or buttercup anemone, is a species of herbaceous and perennial plant that grows in forests across Europe to western Asia, and less frequently in the Mediterranean region. It is occasionally found as a garden escape.

items.name: Anemonoides trifolia
items.growersTips:
Plant rhizomes 2cm deep in autumn in moisture-retentive, humus-rich soil under deciduous trees.
Water weekly during dry spring spells but keep soil barely damp once foliage dies back in summer.
Mulch annually in January with leafmould to mimic British woodland soil and protect emerging buds.
Plant alongside Galanthus nivalis and Hepatica nobilis for a synchronized early spring display.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic iron phosphate pellets.
items.description: Anemonoides trifolia, the three-leaved anemone, is a perennial herbaceous plant in the buttercup family (Ranunculaceae).

items.name: Anemonopsis macrophylla
items.growersTips:
Plant in deep, moisture-retentive, acidic to neutral leafmould-rich soil in full or dappled shade.
Water weekly with rainwater during dry UK summers to keep the woodland soil consistently damp.
Shelter from strong winds to protect the delicate, nodding flower stems from snapping in summer.
Apply a thick mulch of decayed leafmould or composted bark every spring to mimic forest floor soils.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit or beer traps in April.
items.description:
Anemonopsis, the false anemone, is a monotypic genus in the family Ranunculaceae, containing only the species Anemonopsis macrophylla, endemic to Japan's main island of Honshu. 
The generic name Anemonopsis refers to it being Anemone-like, and its specific epithet macrophylla means "large-leaved".

items.name: Angelonia angustifolia
items.growersTips:
Grow in pots to easily move indoors before the first autumn frost as they cannot survive UK winters.
Plant out in late May only after all risk of frost has passed and soil has warmed to fifteen degrees.
Water deeply once a week rather than daily sprinkles to encourage deep roots in dry summer spells.
Pinch out the growing tips of young plants in June to promote a bushier habit and more flower spikes.
Mix grit into heavy UK clay soils to ensure the sharp drainage required to prevent root rot.
items.description: Angelonia angustifolia, the summer snapdragon, is a species of perennial plant in the family Plantaginaceae.

items.name: Angelonia biflora
items.growersTips:
Grow in free-draining gritty loam to prevent root rot during wet, cool UK summer spells.
Plant out only after late May frosts pass, spacing them thirty centimetres apart in full sun.
Water deeply once a week at the base rather than daily to encourage deep, drought-tolerant roots.
Deadhead spent flower spikes in midsummer to stimulate a second flush of blooms before autumn.
Overwinter potted plants indoors at minimum ten degrees Celsius as they cannot survive UK frosts.
items.description: Angelonia biflora is a species of flowering plant in the family Plantaginaceae. It is a subshrub native to Colombia, Guyana, and northeastern and west-central Brazil.

items.name: Angelonia salicariifolia
items.growersTips:
Overwinter in a heated greenhouse or indoors as this tender perennial cannot survive UK frosts.
Plant out in late May in free-draining gritty soil to prevent root rot during wet UK summers.
Water deeply only when the top two inches of soil are dry to mimic its drought-tolerant nature.
Pinch out the growing tips in June to encourage a bushier habit and more purple flower spikes.
Take softwood cuttings in late summer to guarantee new plants for the following spring season.
items.description: Angelonia salicariifolia is a species of flowering plant in the family Plantaginaceae. This species is native to Bolivia, Brazil, and northeast Argentina.

items.name: Angylocalyceae
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in April at a depth of two centimeters to protect young roots from late UK frosts.
Grow in well-drained, slightly acidic sandy loam to mimic native Fabaceae soils in wet UK climates.
Water deeply once a week at the base rather than daily misting to prevent damp-off in humid summers.
Position next to heavy-feeding brassicas as companion plants to utilize the natural nitrogen fixation.
Watch for black bean aphids in June and spray early with organic insecticidal soap to save foliage.
items.description:
The tribe Angylocalyceae is one of the subdivisions of the plant family Fabaceae. It has been circumscribed to include the following genera, which had been placed in tribe Sophoreae:Alexa Moq.
Angylocalyx Taub.
Castanospermum A.Cunn. ex Hook. 
Uleanthus Harms
Xanthocercis Baill.

items.name: Anisocarpus madioides
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in April under glass to protect from late UK frosts before outdoor transplanting.
Grow in sharply draining, gritty soil to prevent root rot during wet, unpredictable UK summers.
Water sparingly at the base once established, allowing the topsoil to dry out between waterings.
Position in your sunniest, south-facing border to maximise the limited British summer sunshine.
Deadhead spent yellow blooms weekly through August to prolong the flowering display until autumn.
items.description: Anisocarpus madioides is a North American species of flowering plant in the family Asteraceae known by the common name woodland madia.

items.name: Anisocarpus scabridus
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at a depth of two millimetres in April using a well-drained gritty compost mix.
Place pots in the sunniest south-facing spot to mimic its native dry, rocky Californian habitat.
Water only when the top two inches of soil are dry to prevent root rot in damp UK summers.
Protect young seedlings from slugs and snails using beer traps or copper tape during wet springs.
Plant alongside Mediterranean herbs like thyme to ensure shared needs for sharp drainage are met.
items.description: Anisocarpus scabridus, the leafy raillardiopsis, is a North American species of flowering plants in the family Asteraceae.

items.name: Anisochilus harmandii
items.growersTips:
Grow in free-draining gritty loam with a neutral to alkaline pH to prevent winter root rot in UK wet.
Overwinter containers in a frost-free greenhouse or conservatory as this plant cannot survive UK frost.
Water sparingly in winter, allowing the top five centimetres of soil to dry out completely between waterings.
Prune back by one third in early spring to promote bushy growth and prevent the stems from becoming leggy.
Position in full south-facing sun to maximise the aromatic oils in the foliage during the UK summer.
items.description:
Anisochilus is a genus in the family Lamiaceae, commonly called as Kapuri first described in 1830. It is native to China, the Indian subcontinent, and Indochina. Has healing properties that deal with treatment for ailments known as gastric ulcer and helps with dermis issues. Anisochilus also has active properties such as camphor, leutiolin, and apigenin. A new hygrine-like compound has been found within the DNA of this plant.SpeciesAnisochilus adenanthus Dalzell & A.Gibson - southern India
Anisochilus argenteus Gamble - southern India
Anisochilus cambodianus Murata - Thailand, Cambodia
Anisoch

items.name: Cicindela (Antennaria)
items.growersTips:
Plant in gritty well-drained soil in full sun to prevent winter wet rot in damp UK climates.
Water newly planted pussytoes weekly until established then leave to rely entirely on UK rainfall.
Divide congested clumps in early spring to maintain the dense silver carpet and promote fresh growth.
Position as a groundcover companion next to Campanula carpatica or dwarf spring bulbs in rockeries.
Watch for slugs on young spring shoots during wet British weather and protect with organic grit.
items.description: Antennaria is a genus of dioecious perennial herbs in the family Asteraceae, native to temperate regions of the Northern Hemisphere, with a few species in temperate southern South America; the highest species diversity is in North America. Common names include catsfoot or cat's-foot, pussytoes and everlasting.

items.name: Anthericum liliago
items.growersTips:
Plant in autumn at a depth of 10cm in free-draining, gritty soil to prevent winter root rot.
Position in full sun, ideally next to dark-leaved Heuchera to contrast the white star-like blooms.
Water weekly during the spring growing season, but keep dry once the summer flowering period ends.
Cut dead flower stems to the base in October and mulch with grit to protect crowns from wet frost.
Watch for slugs and snails on emerging spring shoots, using organic wool pellets around the clump.
items.description: Anthericum liliago, the St Bernard's lily, is a species of flowering plant in the family Asparagaceae. It is native to mainland Europe and Turkey, growing in dry pastures, stony places and open woods and flowering in early summer. In Sweden, the northernmost stable populations grows along the rocky shores of Lake Sommen, albeit on occasions it has been found as far north as Uppland.

items.name: Anthericum ramosum
items.growersTips:
Plant in free-draining chalky soil or add grit to heavy UK clay to prevent winter root rot.
Position in full sun to replicate its native European meadows for the best summer flowering.
Sow seeds in cold frames during autumn as they require winter chilling to trigger spring germination.
Cut the spent flower stems back to the base in autumn to keep the clump tidy and prevent self-seeding.
Divide established clumps in early spring just as new growth appears to propagate and maintain vigour.
items.description: Anthericum ramosum, known as branched St Bernard's-lily, is a herbaceous perennial plant with a rhizome. The genus Anthericum is currently placed in the family Asparagaceae, subfamily Agavoideae. It was formerly placed in its own family, Anthericaceae, and before that in the Liliaceae.

items.name: Anthonotha leptorrhachis
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in April at a depth of two centimetres to protect young roots from late UK frosts
Grow in acidic to neutral sandy loam to mimic native soils and prevent root rot in wet UK winters
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells rather than daily light sprinkles to boost roots
Position in a south-facing sheltered spot to maximise solar heat and shield from cold northern winds
Interplant with brassicas to benefit from the nitrogen-fixing nodules on these legume roots
items.description: Anthonotha is a genus within the subfamily Detarioideae of the plant family Fabaceae.

items.name: Anthopterus wardii
items.growersTips:
Grow in highly acidic peat-free ericaceous compost mixed with perlite to mimic its cloud forest home
Water exclusively with rainwater to keep the soil wet but free-draining and prevent root rot
Overwinter indoors or in a heated greenhouse as this tender shrub cannot survive UK frosts
Prune lightly immediately after flowering to shape the shrub and encourage new blooming wood
Position in bright indirect light or dappled shade to prevent the delicate foliage from scorching
items.description: Anthopterus wardii, also known as aengue mishito, is a species of neotropical blueberry in the family Ericaceae native to the tropical regions of Central and South America, such as Panama, Colombia, and Ecuador.

items.name: Antirrhinum barrelieri
items.growersTips:
Plant in free-draining gritty soil in full sun to prevent winter root rot in wet UK climates.
Sow seeds on the soil surface in early spring as they require light to germinate successfully.
Cut back the woody stems to ground level in late autumn to encourage fresh growth next spring.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells rather than daily shallow sprinkles.
Watch for snapdragon rust fungus in damp UK summers and space plants 30cm apart for air flow.
items.description: Antirrhinum barrelieri is a species of perennial flowering plant in the genus Antirrhinum in the family Plantaginaceae. Native to northeastern Spain, the species is a subshrub that favors subtropical conditions. A. barrelieri produce stems of between 30 cm (12 in) and 75 cm (30 in) tall, on which narrow leaves and 8 to 20 pink or purplish tubular flowers grow. Flowering and fruiting generally occurs between March and September within the species's native range.

items.name: Antirrhinum coulterianum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in early spring under glass as they need light and a propagator to germinate.
Grow in sharply draining gritty soil to survive wet UK winters and prevent root rot in containers.
Water sparingly at the base once established to avoid powdery mildew in humid British summers.
Pinch out the growing tips when plants reach ten centimetres high to encourage a bushier habit.
Protect young plants from slugs and snails during damp spring weather using beer traps or grit.
items.description: Sairocarpus coulterianus is a species of New World snapdragon known by the common name Coulter's snapdragon. Anterrhinum coulterianum is a host species for the Edith's checkerspot butterfly.

items.name: Antirrhinum hispanicum
items.growersTips:
Plant in gritty, sharply draining alkaline soil to prevent winter root rot in wet UK climates.
Position in full sun against a south-facing brick wall to mimic its native Spanish microclimate.
Water sparingly once established, allowing the soil to dry out completely between applications.
Cut back by half in late spring to encourage a bushy habit and prevent the stems from becoming leggy.
Protect from slugs and snails in damp UK springs using organic grit barriers around the base.
items.description: Antirrhinum hispanicum, the Spanish snapdragon, is a species of flowering plant belonging to the genus Antirrhinum that is native to southeastern Spain.

items.name: Antirrhinum majus
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in March on the surface of damp compost as they need light to germinate in the UK.
Pinch out the growing tips when plants are ten centimetres tall to encourage bushier multi-stem growth.
Water deeply at the base in the morning to prevent rust disease which thrives in damp UK summers.
Deadhead faded flower spikes weekly to stimulate a continuous display of blooms until the first frost.
Grow as a hardy annual in the UK by planting out in late spring after the last frost has passed.
items.description: Antirrhinum majus, the common snapdragon, is a species of flowering plant belonging to the genus Antirrhinum. The plant was placed in the family Plantaginaceae following a revision of its prior classical family, Scrophulariaceae.

items.name: Soft snapdragon
items.growersTips:
Plant in sharply draining gritty soil or a raised bed to survive wet UK winters without rotting.
Position in full sun against a south-facing stone wall to mimic its native warm Mediterranean cliffs.
Water sparingly once established, letting the soil dry out completely between watering sessions.
Prune back lightly in late spring to encourage bushy growth and prevent the stems from becoming woody.
Protect from slugs and snails in early spring when the tender new shoots first begin to emerge.
items.description: Antirrhinum molle, the dwarf snapdragon, is a species of flowering plant in the family Plantaginaceae. It is native to northeastern Portugal, the central and eastern Pyrenees, and adjacent areas of northern Spain. Available from commercial suppliers, it is a semi‑evergreen subshrub reaching 15 to 20 cm, with 3 cm (1.2 in) white to pale pink flowers.

items.name: Antirrhinum multiflorum
items.growersTips:
Plant this woody Californian native in sharply draining, gritty soil to survive wet UK winters.
Position in your garden's hottest, most sun-baked south-facing border or against a dry stone wall.
Water sparingly once established, allowing the soil to dry out completely between watering sessions.
Prune back lightly in late spring after the last frosts to encourage bushy growth and more blooms.
Protect young plants from slugs and snails in damp spring weather using beer traps or grit barriers.
items.description: Sairocarpus multiflorus is a species of New World snapdragon known by the common name Sierra snapdragon or multi-flowered snapdragon.

items.name: Antirrhinum orontium
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in spring by pressing them into well-drained soil without covering them.
Grow in full sun and poor, sandy soil to replicate its native UK shingle and arable habitats.
Water sparingly once established as this drought-tolerant annual dislikes wet winter-like soil.
Watch for snapdragon rust in damp UK summers and remove affected leaves immediately to stop spread.
Leave seed heads to self-sow naturally in gravel gardens for a display the following summer.
items.description: Misopates orontium, known as weasel's snout, is a herbaceous annual plant in the family Plantaginaceae. It is a native of disturbed ground in Europe. It is also naturalised as a weed in other parts of the world such as North America. The pink flowers resemble a miniature snapdragon and are followed by a hairy green fruit which is said to resemble a weasel's snout.

items.name: Antirrhinum siculum
items.growersTips:
Plant in free-draining, gritty soil in south-facing UK stone walls or gravel gardens to avoid rot.
Sow seeds on the soil surface in spring without covering them, as they require light to germinate.
Water sparingly once established, allowing the soil to dry out completely between watering sessions.
Cut back the faded flowering stems in late summer to encourage a second flush of autumn blooms.
Protect young plants from slugs and snails during wet UK springs using organic grit barriers.
items.description: Antirrhinum siculum is a species of herb in the family Plantaginaceae. They have simple, narrow leaves. Individuals can grow to 40 cm.

items.name: Antirrhinum tortuosum
items.growersTips:
Plant in gritty, free-draining soil in full sun to prevent winter wet from rotting the roots.
Sow seeds on the soil surface in spring as they need light to germinate, then mist gently.
Pinch out the growing tips when plants are ten centimetres tall to encourage bushy, floriferous growth.
Cut back the faded flower spikes in late summer to stimulate a second flush of autumn blooms.
Protect the crown with a dry mulch of gravel in autumn to shield it from severe UK winter frosts.
items.description: Antirrhinum tortuosum is a species of plant in the family Plantaginaceae. It is a herbaceous, perennial plant found naturally in the Western Mediterranean.

items.name: Antirrhinum virga
items.growersTips:
Plant in sharp-draining grit-amended soil to survive wet UK winters and prevent root rot.
Sow seeds on the soil surface in early spring as they require light to trigger germination.
Cut back the tall woody stems to the base in late autumn to encourage fresh spring growth.
Position in full sun against a south-facing wall to mimic its native dry Mediterranean climate.
Watch for rosemary beetle and capsid bug damage on the foliage during damp UK summer months.
items.description: Sairocarpus virga is a species of New World snapdragon known by the common name tall snapdragon.

items.name: Apatelantha albicans
items.growersTips:
Plant in spring at crown depth in well-drained chalky soil to prevent winter root rot in UK wet.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells, allowing the top two inches of soil to dry out.
Cut back the woody stems by half in late April to stimulate fresh, bushy growth and more flowers.
Protect young spring shoots from slugs and snails using beer traps or organic iron phosphate pellets.
Divide the root clumps every three years in autumn to maintain vigor and propagate new plants.
items.description:
Apatelantha is a genus of flowering plants in the mint family, Lamiaceae. It includes five species native to Western Australia.Apatelantha albicans (Hook.) T.C.Wilson & Henwood – Southwest Australia
Apatelantha chrysotricha (F.Muell.) T.C.Wilson & Henwood – central Western Australia
Apatelantha insignis (E.Pritz.) T.C.Wilson & Henwood – south-central Western Australia
Apatelantha lachnostachya (C.A.Gardner) T.C.Wilson & Henwood – southwest Australia
Apatelantha viscida (E.Pritz.) T.C.Wilson & Henwood – western Western Australia

items.name: Aphyllanthes monspeliensis
items.growersTips:
Plant in free-draining gravelly soil to prevent winter root rot in wet UK climates.
Position in full south-facing sun to mimic its native hot Mediterranean habitat.
Water sparingly only during prolonged dry summer spells once the deep roots establish.
Propagate by careful division in spring just as new growth begins rather than from seed.
Protect young plants from slugs and snails during damp UK spring weather.
items.description: Aphyllanthes is a genus of flowering plants with only one species, Aphyllanthes monspeliensis, endemic to the western Mediterranean region. It is the only genus in the Aphyllanthoideae, a subfamily of the family Asparagaceae. Aphyllanthoideae was formerly treated as a separate family, Aphyllanthaceae.

items.name: Yellow Grass Orchid
items.growersTips:
Grow this rare orchid in a heated greenhouse or conservatory to maintain a minimum of 18C year-round.
Pot in a free-draining mix of fine orchid bark, peat alternative, and perlite to mimic forest soil.
Water with tepid rainwater to keep the compost consistently damp but never waterlogged or soggy.
Position in dappled shade or indirect light, avoiding the harsh midday sun of UK south-facing glass.
Maintain high humidity above sixty percent by placing the pot on a tray of wet clay pebbles.
items.description:
Apostasia may refer to:Apostasia of 1965, a series of political events in Greece, which toppled the legally elected government of George Papandreou, senior
Apostasia (plant), a genus of primitive orchids, comprising 7 terrestrial species

items.name: Apostasia nuda
items.growersTips:
Grow this ultra-rare orchid in a heated glasshouse keeping temperatures strictly above fifteen Celsius
Plant in a free-draining acidic mix of fine orchid bark, peat alternative, and perlite, not soil
Water with tepid rainwater only to keep the compost consistently damp but never waterlogged or wet
Maintain seventy percent humidity around the foliage using a wet pebble tray to prevent leaf shrivel
Position in bright indirect light avoiding direct UK summer sun which scorches the delicate leaves
items.description: Apostasia nuda, or Grass Orchid, is a terrestrial orchid within the Orchidaceae family and the Apostasioideae subfamily. Most commonly found in the Mainland and Islands of Southeast Asia, this species remains native to Singapore. This perennial growing shrub is considered “critically endangered” in regions of Singapore due to deforestation and environmental pressures.

items.name: Yellow Grass Orchid
items.growersTips:
Grow this rare orchid in a heated greenhouse or conservatory to maintain a minimum of 18C year-round.
Use a highly free-draining mix of fine orchid bark, perlite, and peat to mimic its forest floor bed.
Water with tepid rainwater to keep the compost damp but never soggy, avoiding cold tap water shock.
Maintain humidity above sixty percent using gravel trays to prevent the delicate leaves from drying.
Position in bright, indirect light, shielding the foliage from direct mid-day UK summer sun.
items.description: Apostasia wallichii, commonly known as the yellow grass orchid, is a species of orchid that is native to India, Japan, China, Southeast Asia, New Guinea and northern Australia. It has many arching, dark green, grass-like leaves and up to forty small, star-like yellow flowers arranged on a branched flowering stem. It mainly grows in wet forest and rainforest.

items.name: Apostasioideae
items.growersTips:
Grow these primitive orchids in a heated greenhouse or conservatory to survive cold UK winters.
Use a highly free-draining, acidic mix of fine bark, peat alternative, and perlite for soil prep.
Keep the compost consistently moist but never waterlogged, using tepid rainwater, not tap water.
Position in bright, filtered light, avoiding direct midday summer sun to prevent leaf scorch.
Maintain high humidity above sixty percent year-round using wet gravel trays to mimic rainforests.
items.description: The subfamily Apostasioideae is one of five subfamilies recognised within the orchid family, Orchidaceae. Compared to the other orchid subfamilies, it is relatively species-poor, with only two genera and 15 species.

items.name: Appendicula reflexa
items.growersTips:
Grow this warm-loving epiphyte in a heated glasshouse or indoors at fifteen degrees Celsius minimum.
Plant in a highly aerated, free-draining medium of fine bark and perlite to prevent root rot.
Water with tepid rainwater weekly in summer, keeping the compost damp but never waterlogged.
Maintain high humidity above sixty percent using gravel trays to mimic its native tropical habitat.
Provide bright, filtered light but shade from direct summer sun to prevent leaf scorch.
items.description: Appendicula, commonly known as stream orchids, is a genus of flowering plants in the family Orchidaceae. Orchids in this genus are epiphytic, lithophytic or rarely terrestrial plants herbs with many flat, often twisted leaves and small resupinate, white or greenish flowers. The sepals are free from each other but the lateral sepals and labellum are fused to the base of the column.

items.name: Apuleia leiocarpa
items.growersTips:
Grow in a south-facing, sheltered spot against a warm wall to protect it from harsh UK winter winds.
Plant in exceptionally well-drained, sandy loam soil to prevent winter root rot in wet UK climates.
Water deeply once a week during summer dry spells, but keep the soil almost dry throughout winter.
Prune lightly in late spring after the frost risk passes, removing only dead wood to shape the shrub.
Grow in a container to easily move it into a frost-free greenhouse or conservatory for winter.
items.description: Apuleia is a genus of flowering plants in the family Fabaceae. It belongs to the subfamily Dialioideae. The only species in the genus is Apuleia leiocarpa. It is a tree native to northern South America, from Colombia and Venezuela to Ecuador, Peru, Bolivia, Brazil, Paraguay, Uruguay, and northeastern Argentina.

items.name: Apuleia leiocarpa
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender Brazilian native in a large pot to move indoors before the first autumn frost.
Use a gritty loam-based compost with added perlite to ensure the sharp drainage this shrub needs.
Water deeply only when the top five centimetres of soil are dry, reducing to monthly in winter.
Prune lightly in late spring after new growth starts to maintain shape and remove winter dieback.
Place in the sunniest, most sheltered south-facing spot in your garden to mimic its warm habitat.
items.description: Apuleia is a genus of flowering plants in the family Fabaceae. It belongs to the subfamily Dialioideae. The only species in the genus is Apuleia leiocarpa. It is a tree native to northern South America, from Colombia and Venezuela to Ecuador, Peru, Bolivia, Brazil, Paraguay, Uruguay, and northeastern Argentina.

items.name: Common columbine
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in late summer and barely cover with soil as they need light and UK winter cold to germinate
Plant in moist but well-drained soil in dappled shade to mimic their natural British woodland edge
Cut foliage to the ground in midsummer if powdery mildew or leaf miner damage spoils the leaves
Deadhead faded flowers in June to prevent prolific self-seeding and maintain cultivar purity
Interplant with hostas or ferns to hide the scruffy dying foliage after the spring flowering ends
items.description: Aquilegia, commonly known as columbines, is a genus of perennial flowering plants in the family Ranunculaceae (buttercups). The genus includes between 70 and 400 taxa with natural ranges across the Northern Hemisphere. Natural and introduced populations of Aquilegia exist on all continents but Antarctica. Known for their high physical variability and ease of hybridization, columbines are popular garden plants and have created many cultivated varieties.

items.name: Aquilegia × hybrida
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in spring on damp compost, barely covering them as they need light to germinate.
Plant in moist, well-drained soil in dappled shade to mimic their natural UK woodland edge habitat.
Cut foliage back to the ground after flowering to prevent powdery mildew and encourage fresh growth.
Watch for the devastating aquilegia downy mildew and destroy infected plants to stop it spreading.
Deadhead regularly to prevent prolific self-seeding if you want to keep cultivar colours true.
items.description: Aquilegia × hybrida is a hybrid species of columbine, the result of a cross between Aquilegia vulgaris and Aquilegia canadensis.

items.name: Aquilegia alpina
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist well-drained soil in dappled shade to mimic its native European alpine woodland home
Sow seeds shallowly in autumn as they require winter cold stratification in UK soil to germinate
Water weekly during dry spring spells but keep soil drier in winter to prevent crown rot in clay
Cut flower stems to the ground in July to prevent self-seeding and encourage fresh autumn foliage
Watch for aquilegia sawfly larvae in May and handpick them before they strip the leaves to stems
items.description: Aquilegia alpina, often called the alpine columbine or breath of God, is a perennial species of flowering plant in the family Ranunculaceae, native to the western and central Alps. Though rare in its Swiss, Austrian, and Italian range, it is commonly found in the French Maritime Alps. A. alpina is appreciated for its light blue to blue-purple flowers.

items.name: Aquilegia aragonensis
items.growersTips:
Plant this alpine dwarf in gritty, sharply draining neutral to alkaline soil to prevent winter rot.
Sow seeds in autumn in cold frames to allow natural UK winter chilling to trigger spring germination.
Water sparingly only during dry spells, targeting the base to keep the crown dry and prevent rot.
Watch for aquilegia sawfly larvae in May, handpicking them immediately to prevent total defoliation.
Position in full sun or rock crevices to mimic its native Spanish pyrenean limestone habitat.
items.description: Aquilegia aragonensis is a perennial flowering plant in the family Ranunculaceae, endemic to northern Spain.

items.name: Aquilegia barnebyi
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn in cold frames to mimic natural winter chilling needed for UK germination.
Plant in moist well-drained alkaline soil adding grit and leaf mould to mimic its Utah canyon home.
Position in partial shade to protect delicate pastel yellow and pink spurs from strong midday sun.
Cut back faded flower stems to the base in July to prevent invasive self-seeding in small gardens.
Watch for aquilegia sawfly larvae in May and handpick them to prevent total defoliation of leaves.
items.description: Aquilegia barnebyi, commonly known as the oil shale columbine or Barneby's columbine, is a perennial species of flowering plant in the buttercup family, with a native range comprising northeastern Utah and northwestern Colorado in the United States. It is named after Rupert Charles Barneby, who, with Harry Dwight Dillon Ripley, first discovered it in Colorado.

items.name: Aquilegia barykinae
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in late summer in cold frames to mimic the natural UK winter chill needed for germination.
Plant crowns shallowly in moist, well-drained humus-rich soil, keeping the bud just at the surface.
Water weekly during dry spring spells to establish roots before the typical UK summer dry periods.
Cut back faded foliage to ground level in July to prevent powdery mildew and encourage fresh growth.
Inspect leaf undersides in May for green sawfly larvae and handpick them to prevent defoliation.
items.description: Aquilegia barykinae is a perennial flowering plant in the family Ranunculaceae, endemic to the Russian Far East. The species was first described in 2014. Its flowers are lilac-blue.

items.name: Aquilegia bertolonii
items.growersTips:
Plant in gritty alkaline soil or scree in a raised bed to mimic its native European limestone habitat.
Sow seeds in cold frames during autumn to allow natural winter chilling for spring germination.
Protect the delicate blue spring flowers from slugs and snails using organic bait or grit barriers.
Water sparingly during wet UK winters to prevent the taproot from rotting in waterlogged soil.
Cut back faded flower stems to the base in July to encourage a fresh flush of blue-green foliage.
items.description: Aquilegia bertolonii, common name Bertoloni columbine or Bertoloni's columbine, is a perennial species of flowering plant in the family Ranunculaceae, native to Italy, southern France, and Slovenia.

items.name: Aquilegia brevistyla
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist, well-drained soil enriched with leaf mould to mimic its native woodland habitat.
Sow seeds in autumn in cold frames to allow natural winter chilling for successful germination.
Position in partial shade to protect the delicate blue and white blooms from strong afternoon sun.
Watch for the aquilegia sawfly in May, handpicking the green larvae before they strip the foliage.
Cut back faded flower stems to the ground in July to encourage a fresh flush of healthy leaves.
items.description: Aquilegia brevistyla is a species of flowering plant in the buttercup family known by the common name smallflower columbine. It is native to northern North America, where it has a disjunct distribution. Most of its range extends from Alaska through much of Canada, and it also occurs in a few areas in the contiguous United States, such as the Black Hills of South Dakota and central Montana. It is most common in eastern Alaska, Yukon, the southern Northwest Territories, and northern parts of Alberta, Manitoba, and Saskatchewan.

items.name: Aquilegia buergeriana
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist well-drained soil with crown at soil level to prevent rot in wet UK winters.
Sow seeds in autumn in cold frames to allow natural winter chilling for successful germination.
Cut back foliage to ground level in midsummer after flowering to encourage fresh mildew-free leaves.
Inspect regularly in spring for green aquilegia sawfly larvae to prevent complete defoliation.
Grow in dappled shade alongside hostas to protect the delicate yellow and purple blooms from sun.
items.description: Aquilegia buergeriana is a perennial species of flowering plant in the family Ranunculaceae, native to Japan.

items.name: Eastern red columbine
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn on the soil surface as they need winter cold and light to germinate in UK gardens
Plant in free-draining neutral soil to prevent winter crown rot during wet UK winters
Cut back foliage to the ground in July if columbine leaf miner leaves unsightly white trails
Water weekly during dry spring spells but leave established plants alone once summer rain returns
Sow away from Aquilegia vulgaris to prevent cross-hybridisation and keep the red species true
items.description: Aquilegia canadensis, the Canadian columbine, Canada columbine, eastern red columbine, or wild columbine, is a species of flowering plant in the buttercup family. It is a perennial plant that is native to the woodlands and rocky areas in eastern North America in both the United States and southern Canada. It readily hybridizes with other plants in the columbine genus and is a common garden plant.

items.name: Aquilegia chaplinei
items.growersTips:
Plant this rare yellow columbine in moist, well-drained alkaline soil, adding grit to prevent rot.
Sow seeds in cold frames during autumn to mimic natural winter chilling for spring germination.
Water consistently during dry UK summer spells to prevent powdery mildew on the delicate foliage.
Cut back faded flower stems to the base in July to encourage a fresh flush of healthy green leaves.
Isolate Chaplinei from other Aquilegias to prevent cross-hybridisation and preserve its yellow form.
items.description: Aquilegia chaplinei, also known as Chaplin's columbine, is a species of flowering plant in the family Ranunculaceae native to the arid Guadalupe and Sacramento Mountains of West Texas and southeastern New Mexico in the West South Central United States. A perennial plant with an average height of 40 centimeters (16 in), A. chaplinei is characterized as a dwarf version of its close relative Aquilegia chrysantha and is sometimes considered a variant of this species under the name Aquilegia chrysantha var. chaplinei.

items.name: Blue columbine
items.growersTips:
Plant in partial shade using moist well-drained soil to mimic cool UK woodland edge conditions.
Sow seeds shallowly in autumn as they require cold winter stratification to germinate in spring.
Cut back faded flower stems to the base in July to prevent messy self-seeding and encourage regrowth.
Watch for aquilegia sawfly larvae in May and handpick them before they strip the foliage to veins.
Grow alongside hostas or ferns to hide the dying aquilegia foliage as it goes dormant in summer.
items.description: Aquilegia coerulea, commonly called the Colorado columbine, Rocky Mountain columbine, or blue columbine, is a species of flowering plant in the buttercup family, native to the Rocky Mountains in the western United States. It is a moderate sized wildflower that grows in mountainous areas from the foothills to above timberline. The flowers are mainly pollinated by bumblebees and several species of hawkmoths. The species has been the state flower of Colorado since 1899 and with its large, showy flowers is a frequent garden plant and used in the breeding of columbine hybrids. The botanical name co

items.name: Aquilegia confusa
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in autumn in moist well-drained soil so winter cold triggers germination.
Water young plants weekly during dry spring spells but leave established clumps to rely on UK rain.
Cut faded flower stems to the ground in July to prevent self-seeding and encourage fresh foliage.
Check leaves weekly in May for green sawfly larvae and handpick them to prevent total defoliation.
Plant alongside hostas or ferns in partial shade to hide dying summer leaves as they go dormant.
items.description: Aquilegia confusa is a partially accepted species of flowering plant of the genus Aquilegia (columbines) in the family Ranunculaceae that is endemic to the eastern and southern European Alps in Switzerland and Italy.

items.name: Aquilegia desertorum
items.growersTips:
Plant in gritty, sharply drained alkaline soil to prevent winter crown rot in wet UK climates.
Sow seeds shallowly in autumn, barely covering them, to allow natural winter chilling for germination.
Water sparingly once established, allowing the soil to dry out completely between summer waterings.
Cut back faded flower stems to the base in July to prevent self-seeding and encourage fresh foliage.
Position in full sun to mimic its native desert habitat, avoiding damp, shaded woodland borders.
items.description: Aquilegia desertorum, the desert columbine, is a perennial species of flowering plant in the family Ranunculaceae, native to the Southwestern United States.

items.name: Aquilegia dichroa
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist well-drained neutral to acid soil to mimic its native damp Iberian woodland habitat
Sow seeds shallowly in autumn in cold frames to allow natural winter chilling for spring germination
Cut back faded flower stems to the base in July to prevent self-seeding and preserve species purity
Watch for aquilegia sawfly larvae in May and handpick them before they defoliate the delicate stems
Position in dappled shade under deciduous shrubs to protect the soft blue-and-white blooms from sun
items.description: Aquilegia dichroa is a perennial flowering plant in the family Ranunculaceae, native to Portugal and northwestern Spain.

items.name: Aquilegia dumeticola
items.growersTips:
Plant in partial shade using moist well-drained soil to mimic its native woodland edge habitat.
Sow seeds shallowly in cold frames during autumn to benefit from natural UK winter stratification.
Watch for aquilegia sawfly larvae in May and handpick them immediately to prevent defoliation.
Cut back faded flower stems to the ground in July to encourage a fresh flush of healthy foliage.
Isolate this species from other columbines to prevent hybridisation and preserve its true form.
items.description: Aquilegia dumeticola is a perennial flowering plant in the family Ranunculaceae, native to southeastern Europe.

items.name: Aquilegia ecalcarata
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn in cold frames to let winter chill naturally break dormancy for spring growth.
Plant in moisture-retentive, humus-rich soil in partial shade to mimic UK woodland edge conditions.
Water weekly during dry spring spells to keep soil damp but never waterlogged to prevent root rot.
Cut back faded flower stems to ground level in July to encourage a second flush of fresh foliage.
Watch for aquilegia sawfly larvae in May and handpick them immediately to prevent total defoliation.
items.description: Aquilegia ecalcarata, the spurless columbine or false columbine, is a perennial species of flowering plant in the family Ranunculaceae, native to central China.

items.name: Aquilegia flavescens
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn in cold frames to let winter chill break dormancy naturally in UK climates.
Plant in moisture-retentive, humus-rich soil in partial shade to mimic its native alpine woodland.
Water weekly during dry spring spells to keep soil damp but never waterlogged to prevent root rot.
Cut back faded flower stems to the ground in July to encourage a fresh flush of healthy foliage.
Watch for aquilegia sawfly larvae in May and handpick them immediately to prevent total defoliation.
items.description: Aquilegia flavescens, the yellow columbine, is a perennial species of flowering plant in the family Ranunculaceae, native to the Rocky Mountains of the United States and Canada.

items.name: Aquilegia gracillima
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in autumn using cold frames to mimic UK winter chill for natural germination.
Plant in moisture-retentive, humus-rich soil in dappled shade to replicate British woodland edges.
Cut back faded flower stems to the base in July to prevent self-seeding and encourage fresh leaves.
Watch for aquilegia sawfly larvae in May, hand-picking them before they strip the delicate foliage.
Divide established clumps in early spring, ensuring each division has a healthy bud and taproot.
items.description: Aquilegia gracillima is a species of flowering plant in the family Ranunculaceae native to the area near Ghazni in eastern Afghanistan. The plant is understood as related to Aquilegia moorcroftiana, which has a range spanning into Afghanistan.

items.name: Aquilegia hinckleyana
items.growersTips:
Plant in partial shade in moist, well-drained soil, adding grit to heavy UK clay to prevent rot.
Sow seeds shallowly in autumn, barely covering with compost, to let winter cold trigger germination.
Cut back faded flower stems to the base in July to prevent self-seeding and encourage fresh leaves.
Check leaves weekly in spring for the green sawfly larvae that can strip the foliage to veins.
Keep soil consistently damp during dry spring spells, watering at the base to avoid powdery mildew.
items.description: Aquilegia hinckleyana, or Hinckley's golden columbine, is a partially recognized species of flowering plant of the genus Aquilegia (columbines) in the family Ranunculaceae endemic to Capote Falls in northwestern Presidio County, Texas. The plant is found within a small region of the county and only grows in moister areas of its generally dry range. Considered a smaller version of Aquilegia chrysantha, A. hinckleyana has a height of around 60 centimetres (24 in) and possesses yellow flowers. It has seen modern cultivation, particularly in Texas. The species is named for L. C. Hinckley, who firs

items.name: Aquilegia longissima
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist well-drained soil enriched with leaf mould to mimic cool British woodland edges.
Sow seeds shallowly in autumn as they require cold winter stratification to germinate in UK climates.
Water deeply at the base during dry spring spells to support the development of the long flower spurs.
Cut back faded flower stems to the ground in July to prevent self-seeding and encourage fresh leaves.
Watch for aquilegia sawfly larvae in May and handpick them immediately to prevent total defoliation.
items.description: Aquilegia longissima, the long-spur columbine or long-spurred columbine, is a rare perennial flowering plant in the family Ranunculaceae that is native to northern Mexico, Texas, and Arizona.

items.name: Aquilegia lucensis
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade to mimic its native woodland habitat.
Sow seeds in autumn in cold frames to allow natural UK winter chilling for successful germination.
Watch for aquilegia sawfly larvae in May and handpick them immediately to prevent rapid defoliation.
Cut back flowering stems to the ground in summer after blooming to prevent unwanted self-seeding.
Plant alongside hostas and ferns in damp borders to provide shade and hide fading summer foliage.
items.description: Aquilegia lucensis is a perennial flowering plant in the family Ranunculaceae, endemic to Italy.

items.name: Aquilegia magellensis
items.growersTips:
Plant this alpine columbine in gritty, sharply draining neutral to alkaline soil to prevent winter rot.
Position in partial shade or a cool rock garden to mimic its native damp, scree-like mountain habitat.
Water moderately during dry spring spells but keep soil relatively dry during damp UK winter months.
Cut back faded flower stems to the base in July to encourage a second flush of healthy new foliage.
Watch for aquilegia sawfly larvae in May, handpicking them immediately to prevent total defoliation.
items.description: Aquilegia magellensis is a perennial species of plant in the family Ranunculaceae, native to Italy.

items.name: Aquilegia maimanica
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in autumn using cold frames to mimic UK winter chill for natural stratification.
Grow in moist but well-drained humus-rich soil, adding grit to heavy UK clay to prevent root rot.
Water consistently during dry spring spells to keep soil damp but never waterlogged or soggy.
Cut back faded flower stems to the base in July to prevent self-seeding and encourage fresh leaves.
Watch for aquilegia sawfly larvae in May, handpicking them immediately to prevent total defoliation.
items.description: Aquilegia maimanica is a species of flowering plant in the family Ranunculaceae native to the area of the former Meymaneh Province in northwestern Afghanistan. The plant is understood as related to Aquilegia moorcroftiana, which has a range spanning into Afghanistan. A. maimanica has pale-blue and white flowers. The species was first described by the Flora Iranica in 1992 from specimens collected by Karl Heinz Rechinger in 1959.

items.name: Aquilegia micrantha
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn in cold frames using gritty compost to mimic natural winter chilling cycles.
Plant in sharp-draining limestone rockeries or scree beds to prevent winter wet root rot in UK rain.
Water sparingly once established, allowing the gritty soil to dry out between waterings in summer.
Cut back faded flower stems to the base in July to prevent self-seeding and encourage fresh leaves.
Check regularly for aquilegia sawfly larvae in May, handpicking them to prevent rapid defoliation.
items.description: Aquilegia micrantha, the Mancos columbine or Bluff City columbine, is a perennial species of flowering plant in the family Ranunculaceae. It is native to Utah, Colorado, and Arizona. The species grows to between 30 cm (12 in) and 60 cm (24 in) tall and produces flowers that can be white, cream, blue, or pink. The species's flowers bloom during the spring and summer, from April to September. Also known as the alcove columbine, the species can be found on the on steep stone walls in the hanging gardens of the Colorado Plateau and Canyonlands.

items.name: Aquilegia micrantha var. grahamii
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn in cold frames to mimic the cold winter stratification required in UK climates.
Plant in gritty, free-draining alkaline soil to replicate its native Utah sandstone cliff habitat.
Water sparingly once established, allowing the soil to dry out between waterings to prevent rot.
Cut back faded flower stems to the base in July to prevent self-seeding and encourage fresh leaves.
Watch for aquilegia sawfly larvae in May, handpicking them immediately to prevent total defoliation.
items.description: Aquilegia micrantha var. grahamii, common name Graham's columbine, is a variety of perennial flowering plant in the family Ranunculaceae, endemic to Utah in the United States.

items.name: Aquilegia microcentra
items.growersTips:
Plant in sharp-draining, gritty soil to prevent winter wet rot in damp UK climates.
Sow seeds shallowly in autumn, barely covering them, to allow winter cold to trigger germination.
Position in partial shade to mimic its native canyon habitat and prevent summer leaf scorch.
Cut back faded flower stems to the base in July to encourage a second flush of fresh foliage.
Watch for aquilegia sawfly larvae in May, handpicking them immediately to prevent defoliation.
items.description: Aquilegia microcentra is a species of flowering plant in the family Ranunculaceae native to Uruzgan Province in central and southeastern Afghanistan. The plant is understood as related to Aquilegia moorcroftiana, which has a range spanning into Afghanistan. A. microcentra has small, white flowers. The species was first described by the Flora Iranica in 1992 from specimens collected by Karl Heinz Rechinger in 1967.

items.name: Aquilegia nuragica
items.growersTips:
Plant this rare dwarf columbine in sharply draining, gritty limestone soil to mimic its Sardinian home
Sow seeds in late summer in cold frames, barely covering them with grit to allow light germination
Water sparingly only during dry summer spells, as this alpine species is highly prone to root rot
Protect young spring shoots from slugs and snails using beer traps or copper tape in damp UK weather
Cut back faded flower stems to the base in July to prevent hybridisation with common garden Aquilegia
items.description: Aquilegia nuragica, commonly called Nuragica columbine, is a perennial flowering plant in the family Ranunculaceae. It is endemic to Italy, in a single canyon in the Supramonte mountain range on the island of Sardinia.

items.name: Aquilegia ottonis
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist well-drained alkaline soil adding grit and leaf mould to mimic its Greek mountain home
Sow seeds shallowly in cold frames during autumn to benefit from natural UK winter stratification
Water weekly during dry spring spells but keep crown dry in winter to prevent cold-weather rot
Cut back flower stems to the base in July to prevent self-seeding and encourage fresh autumn foliage
Check leaves weekly in May for green sawfly larvae and hand-pick them to prevent rapid defoliation
items.description: Aquilegia ottonis is a perennial flowering plant in the family Ranunculaceae, endemic to Greece.

items.name: Aquilegia paui
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn in cold frames to mimic UK winter chill for natural stratification and germination.
Plant in gritty, free-draining neutral soil to prevent crown rot during wet UK winters.
Position in partial shade to mimic its native Spanish mountain habitat and prevent leaf scorch.
Cut back faded flower stems to the base in July to encourage a second flush of fresh foliage.
Isolate from other Aquilegia species to prevent cross-hybridisation and preserve its rare form.
items.description: Aquilegia paui is a species of perennial flowering plant in the genus Aquilegia (columbines) in the family Ranunculaceae. The species has an extremely limited range, narrowly endemic only to the mountains of Ports de Tortosa-Beseit, a massif in the Province of Tarragona in Catalonia, northeastern Spain. Due to a herbarium filing error and the absence of observations of A. paui from 1920 until 1999, the species was long considered a subspecies or synonym of Aquilegia vulgaris.

items.name: Aquilegia pyrenaica
items.growersTips:
Plant in gritty alkaline soil in a raised bed or rockery to mimic its native Pyrenean limestone scree.
Sow seeds in autumn in a cold frame as they require winter cold stratification to germinate in UK.
Water sparingly in winter to prevent crown rot but keep moist during the active spring growing phase.
Protect young spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps in damp UK.
Cut back faded flower stems to the base in July to encourage a second flush of healthy blue foliage.
items.description: Aquilegia pyrenaica, common name Pyrenean columbine, is a species of flowering plant in the family Ranunculaceae. It is endemic to the Pyrenees where it grows on grassland and in rocky places. It was first described in 1805 by Augustin Pyramus de Candolle who gave it the name Aquilegia pyrenaica.

items.name: Aquilegia saximontana
items.growersTips:
Plant in gritty, sharply draining neutral to acid soil to mimic its native Rocky Mountain scree.
Sow seeds in pots outdoors in autumn as they require winter cold stratification to germinate in UK.
Position in partial shade or a cool rock crevice to protect delicate blue flowers from midday sun.
Water sparingly once established, allowing the gritty compost to dry out between watering sessions.
Watch for aquilegia sawfly larvae in May and handpick them immediately to prevent total defoliation.
items.description: Aquilegia saximontana, the alpine dwarf columbine, dwarf blue columbine, or alpine columbine, is a perennial plant that comes from the buttercup family.

items.name: Aquilegia scopulorum
items.growersTips:
Plant in gritty, sharply draining alkaline soil to mimic its native limestone scree habitat.
Position in full sun with protection from wet winter soil by using a deep mulch of gravel or grit.
Sow seeds in autumn in cold frames to allow natural UK winter chilling to trigger germination.
Watch for the aquilegia sawfly larvae in May and handpick them before they strip the foliage.
Grow in alpine troughs or raised beds to prevent slugs from damaging the delicate dwarf foliage.
items.description: Aquilegia scopulorum, also known as rock columbine or Utah columbine, is a species of plant in the buttercup family from Nevada and Utah in the western United States.

items.name: Aquilegia shockleyi
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist but well-drained neutral to alkaline soil, adding grit to heavy UK clay to avoid rot.
Sow seeds shallowly in cold frames during autumn to utilise natural UK winter chills for germination.
Water weekly during dry summer spells, targeting the base to keep soil damp but never waterlogged.
Cut back faded foliage to ground level in late autumn to prevent damp UK winters rotting the crown.
Watch for aquilegia sawfly larvae in May, handpicking them immediately to prevent total defoliation.
items.description: Aquilegia shockleyi, commonly known as Shockley's columbine, the Mojave columbine, and the desert columbine, is a species of perennial flowering plant of the genus Aquilegia (columbine) in the family Ranunculaceae. It is native to southern Nevada and southeastern California in the United States, where it congregates around wet areas.

items.name: Aquilegia transsilvanica
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist well-drained neutral to acid soil in partial shade to mimic its native woodland edge.
Sow seeds in autumn in cold frames to allow natural winter chilling for spring germination in the UK.
Mulch with leaf mould in spring to retain moisture and keep roots cool during dry summer spells.
Cut back faded foliage to ground level in late summer to prevent powdery mildew in damp UK weather.
Plant alongside hostas and ferns to hide dying leaves and provide essential shade for the roots.
items.description: Aquilegia transsilvanica is a species of flowering plant in the family Ranunculaceae. It is endemic to the southern Carpathian Mountains of Romania, where it occurs in temperate montane habitats.

items.name: Arbutus ×hybrida
items.growersTips:
Plant in free-draining acidic to neutral soil, adding grit to heavy UK clay to prevent root rot.
Position in full sun sheltered from cold, drying winds to protect the delicate peeling bark.
Water deeply during dry summer spells for the first two years until the root system is established.
Prune minimally in late spring only to remove misplaced branches and maintain a clear lower trunk.
Shelter young plants with fleece during severe UK winter frosts to prevent tip dieback.
items.description: Arbutus × andrachnoides, the hybrid strawberry-tree, is the result of a cross between Arbutus andrachne and Arbutus unedo. It is a naturally occurring hybrid, but hybrid cultivars have also been created. It has gained the RHS's Award of Garden Merit.

items.name: Arbutus andrachne
items.growersTips:
Plant in a sheltered south-facing spot to protect young stems from cold drying UK winter winds.
Provide sharply draining acidic to neutral soil as this species will rot in wet winter clay.
Water deeply during dry summer spells for the first two years until the root system is established.
Prune minimally in late spring only to remove frost-damaged wood and expose the peeling orange bark.
Protect young plants with fleece during severe UK frosts to prevent dieback of the tender branches.
items.description: Arbutus andrachne, commonly called the Greek strawberry tree, is an evergreen shrub or small tree in the family Ericaceae, native to the Mediterranean region and the Middle East.

items.name: Arbutus arizonica
items.growersTips:
Plant in a south-facing, sheltered spot to protect young stems from harsh, freezing UK winter winds.
Incorporate acidic peat-free compost into the planting hole to keep the soil pH below six point five.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells for the first two years to establish the roots.
Prine lightly in late spring after frost risk passes to maintain shape and remove winter dieback.
Mulch annually in spring with composted pine needles to maintain soil acidity and retain moisture.
items.description: Arbutus arizonica, commonly known as Arizona madrone, is a tree species in the heath family that is native to the southwestern United States and northwestern Mexico. Its range extends along the Sierra Madre Occidental cordillera from the Madrean Sky Islands of southeastern Arizona and southwestern New Mexico south as far as Jalisco. It has been found in Sonora, Chihuahua, Durango, and Sinaloa, with one isolated population in Tamaulipas.

items.name: Arbutus canariensis
items.growersTips:
Plant in acid to neutral soil as this species unlike unedo cannot tolerate chalky or alkaline soils
Grow in a sheltered south-facing spot or against a warm wall to protect it from harsh UK frosts
Water deeply but infrequently during dry summer spells to establish a deep drought-tolerant root system
Prine minimally in late spring only to remove winter-damaged wood and maintain a balanced shape
Protect young plants with horticultural fleece during severe winter snaps below minus five Celsius
items.description: Arbutus canariensis, known in Spanish as madroño canario; in English as Canary Islands strawberry tree, is a species of shrub or tree in the heath family. It is endemic to the Canary Islands of Spain, specifically Tenerife, La Gomera, Gran Canaria, El Hierro, and La Palma. It is threatened by habitat loss.

items.name: Arbutus glandulosa
items.growersTips:
Plant in well-drained acidic to neutral soil, adding sulfur if your UK garden soil is too alkaline.
Position in a sheltered, south-facing spot to protect young stems from harsh UK winter frosts.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells in the first two years to establish deep roots.
Prune minimally in late spring after frost risk passes, only removing dead wood or crossing limbs.
Mulch annually in spring with composted pine needles or ericaceous compost to maintain soil acidity.
items.description: Arbutus xalapensis, commonly known as the Texas madrone, Amazaquitl, or Texas madroño, is a species of flowering plant in the heather family. It is native to Central America, the southwestern United States, and throughout Mexico. It is found in canyons and mountains, on rocky plains, and in oak woodlands, at altitudes of up to 3,000 m (9,800 ft) in the south of the range, but lower, down to 600 m (2,000 ft) in the north of the range.

items.name: Arbutus menziesii
items.growersTips:
Plant in free-draining, acidic to neutral soil; add grit to the planting hole to prevent root rot.
Position in full sun against a south-facing wall to protect young stems from harsh UK winter winds.
Water deeply once a week during the first two dry summers, then leave to establish drought tolerance.
Prune minimally in late spring only to remove dead wood, as this species dislikes hard cutting back.
Protect young plants with horticultural fleece when UK temperatures are forecast to drop below -5C.
items.description: Arbutus menziesii, or Pacific madrone, is a species of broadleaf evergreen tree in the family Ericaceae. It has waxy foliage, a contorted growth habit, and flaky bark.

items.name: Arbutus unedo
items.growersTips:
Plant in free-draining acidic to neutral soil, adding grit to heavy UK clay to prevent root rot.
Position in full sun sheltered from cold, drying winds, especially in northern UK gardens.
Water deeply during dry spells in its first two summers to establish a deep, resilient root system.
Prunt lightly in late spring after frosts pass to shape the shrub and remove winter-damaged shoots.
Protect young plants with fleece during severe UK winter freezes to prevent bark splitting.
items.description: Arbutus unedo, commonly known as strawberry tree, also called madrone, is an evergreen shrub or small tree in the family Ericaceae, native to the Mediterranean Basin and Western Europe. The tree is well known for its fruits, the arbutus berry, which bear some resemblance to the strawberry, hence the common name strawberry tree. However, it is not closely related to true strawberries of the genus Fragaria.

items.name: Arbutus xalapensis
items.growersTips:
Plant in a south-facing, sheltered spot to protect young stems from harsh UK winter winds and frost.
Incorporate acidic peat-free compost and grit into the planting hole to ensure excellent drainage.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells for the first two years until fully established.
Prune lightly in late spring after frost risk passes to shape and remove any winter-damaged wood.
Apply a thick mulch of pine needles or composted bark annually in autumn to maintain soil acidity.
items.description: Arbutus xalapensis, commonly known as the Texas madrone, Amazaquitl, or Texas madroño, is a species of flowering plant in the heather family. It is native to Central America, the southwestern United States, and throughout Mexico. It is found in canyons and mountains, on rocky plains, and in oak woodlands, at altitudes of up to 3,000 m (9,800 ft) in the south of the range, but lower, down to 600 m (2,000 ft) in the north of the range.

items.name: Archeria eriocarpa
items.growersTips:
Grow in moist well-drained acidic soil with ericaceous compost to mimic its native Tasmanian habitat
Position in a sheltered spot with partial shade to protect delicate foliage from cold drying UK winds
Water regularly with rainwater rather than tap water to maintain the necessary low soil pH levels
Prune lightly immediately after flowering in late spring to maintain shape and remove dead wood
Protect roots in winter with a thick mulch of pine needles or composted bark to shield from hard frost
items.description: Archeria eriocarpa is a species of shrub in the family Ericaceae. It is endemic to Tasmania, Australia.

items.name: Archeria hirtella
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist but well-drained acidic soil using ericaceous compost to mimic its Tasmanian habitat.
Position in a sheltered spot with partial shade to protect delicate foliage from cold UK windburn.
Water consistently with rainwater rather than tap water to maintain the necessary low soil pH.
Prune lightly immediately after spring flowering to maintain shape without cutting into old wood.
Mulch annually with pine needles or composted bark to retain moisture and protect roots from frost.
items.description: Archeria hirtella is a species of shrub in the family Ericaceae. It is native to Tasmania, Australia.

items.name: Archeria serpyllifolia
items.growersTips:
Plant in acidic soil with a pH of 4.5 to 5.5 using ericaceous compost and pine needles for mulch.
Grow in a sheltered site with high humidity to mimic Tasmanian mountain mists in dry UK summers.
Water only with rainwater to prevent tapwater lime from raising soil pH and yellowing the leaves.
Prune lightly immediately after summer flowering to maintain its compact, thyme-like shrub habit.
Protect from harsh winter winds using fleece or plant in a container to move indoors during frosts.
items.description: Archeria serpyllifolia is a dense, compact, low growing shrub, that is endemic to Tasmania, Australia, inhabiting the undisturbed alpine areas of southern and south-west Tasmania. This plant is commonly referred to by Australasian naturalists as thyme archeria.

items.name: Arctomecon
items.growersTips:
Provide sharp drainage by mixing fifty percent grit into poor soil to prevent winter root rot.
Grow in a deep terracotta pot to shelter from persistent British rain and allow roots to spread.
Water only from the base during active growth and keep the crown completely dry to avoid fungal rot.
Position in the brightest south-facing spot to mimic its native hot Mojave desert light levels.
Protect the hairy foliage from winter wet using a rain shelter or cold frame from October to March.
items.description: Arctomecon is a genus of the poppy family Papaveraceae commonly called the bear poppies or bear-paw poppies, after the distinctive appearance of the leaves. The three species occur only in the northeastern part of the Mojave Desert of North America, and are all uncommon.

items.name: Arctomecon californica
items.growersTips:
Grow this desert poppy in a greenhouse or cold frame to protect it from wet UK winter rot.
Plant in a potting mix of eighty percent grit and twenty percent loam to mimic Mojave soils.
Water only from below during the summer active growth phase and keep completely dry in winter.
Sow seeds on the soil surface in autumn, exposing them to winter cold for natural stratification.
Position pots in the most sun-drenched, south-facing spot possible to maximise scarce UK light.
items.description: Arctomecon californica is a species of poppy known by several common names, including California bearpoppy, Las Vegas bearpoppy, golden bearpoppy, and yellow-flowered desert poppy. It is a perennial herb that is native to the eastern Mojave Desert.

items.name: Arctomecon humilis
items.growersTips:
Grow in a gritty, alkaline soil mix with fifty percent limestone chippings to mimic desert soils.
Keep completely dry in winter by sheltering under a cold frame or alpine house to prevent rot.
Water only from below during the summer active growth phase and never wet the hairy foliage.
Sow seeds shallowly in autumn and expose to winter cold for natural stratification and germination.
Protect the taproot by planting in deep clay pots and avoiding any root disturbance when potting.
items.description: Arctomecon humilis is an endangered flowering plant species in the family Papaveraceae. It is endemic to the Dixie Corridor in southwest Utah. A. humilis grows in a very harsh desert environment, requiring a specific soil type. The plant's common name is dwarf bear-poppy, which is indicative of the plant's jagged, three “clawed” leaves. The poppy is a perennial plant, meaning it blooms annually. The dwarf bear-poppy is protected under the Endangered Species Act as of 1979.
