The plant is threatened by urban development, off-road vehicle use, and mining. Although hard to estimate, its population

items.name: Arctomecon merriamii
items.growersTips:
Grow in a cold greenhouse or alpine house to protect the highly rot-prone foliage from winter wet.
Use a potting mix of three parts grit to one part loam to mimic its native Mojave desert scree.
Water only from below during the summer growing season and keep completely dry throughout winter.
Sow fresh seeds in autumn in a cold frame using a very thin covering of fine granite grit.
Place in the brightest south-facing position possible to maximise essential UK summer sunlight.
items.description: Arctomecon merriamii is a species of poppy known by several common names, including desert bearpoppy, white bearpoppy, and great bearclaw poppy. It is native to the Mojave Desert of California and Nevada, and parts of southwestern Utah.

items.name: Arctostaphylos alpina
items.growersTips:
Plant in highly acidic peat-free ericaceous compost mixed with plenty of grit to ensure sharp drainage
Grow in full sun in a cold rock garden or raised bed to mimic its native Scottish highland habitat
Water with rainwater rather than tap water to keep the soil pH low and prevent chlorosis of leaves
Prune only in late spring to remove dead wood as this slow-growing shrub dislikes hard cutting back
Watch for vine weevil grubs in container-grown plants which will rapidly destroy the root system
items.description: Arctous alpina, the alpine bearberry, mountain bearberry or black bearberry, is a dwarf shrub in the heather family Ericaceae. The basionym of this species is Arbutus alpina L..

items.name: Arctostaphylos andersonii
items.growersTips:
Plant in acidic, sandy soil mixed with grit to mimic its native chaparral and prevent root rot.
Position in full sun against a south-facing wall to shelter it from cold, wet UK winter winds.
Water deeply once a week during its first dry summer, then leave it entirely to natural rainfall.
Prune lightly in late spring after flowering, avoiding cutting back into old wood which will not regrow.
Grow in a large terracotta pot using ericaceous compost if your garden soil is heavy clay or alkaline.
items.description: Arctostaphylos andersonii, the Santa Cruz manzanita, is a species of Arctostaphylos.

items.name: Arctostaphylos auriculata
items.growersTips:
Plant in acidic sandy soil with grit to mimic its native chaparral and prevent UK winter wet rot.
Position in full sun against a south-facing wall to maximize summer heat and shelter from cold winds.
Water deeply once a week during its first UK summer, then leave dry to prevent root phytophthora.
Prune lightly in late spring after flowering, only cutting young wood as it will not regrow from old.
Grow in a raised bed or terracotta pot to ensure the rapid drainage this California native demands.
items.description: Arctostaphylos auriculata is an endangered species of Arctostaphylos endemic to California, and limited in geography to the area surrounding Mount Diablo, in Contra Costa County.

items.name: Arctostaphylos bakeri
items.growersTips:
Plant in acidic, free-draining sandy loam or add grit to soil to prevent winter root rot in UK rain.
Position in full sun against a south-facing wall to shelter from cold, drying easterly winter winds.
Water deeply once a week during the first summer, then leave to rely entirely on natural UK rainfall.
Prune lightly in late spring after flowering, cutting only soft new growth to maintain a neat shape.
Mulch with pine needles or composted bark to maintain the low soil pH this ericaceous shrub needs.
items.description: Arctostaphylos bakeri is a species of manzanita known by the common name Baker's manzanita. It is endemic to Sonoma County, California, where it grows in the chaparral and woodlands of the North Coast Ranges. It is sometimes a member of the serpentine soils flora.

items.name: Arctostaphylos canescens
items.growersTips:
Plant in extremely well-drained, acidic, sandy or gritty soil to prevent fatal winter root rot.
Position in full sun with shelter from cold, drying winds to protect the evergreen foliage.
Water sparingly only during the first summer, then leave to rely solely on natural UK rainfall.
Prune lightly in late spring after flowering, avoiding cutting back into old wood which will not regrow.
Grow in a raised bed or terracotta pot to ensure the sharp drainage this California native needs.
items.description: Arctostaphylos canescens, common name hoary manzanita, is a species of manzanita.

items.name: Arctostaphylos catalinae
items.growersTips:
Plant in extremely well-drained, acidic, sandy or gritty soil to prevent winter root rot in UK wet.
Position in full sun against a south-facing wall to mimic its native Californian warmth and light.
Water deeply once a week during its first UK summer, then leave completely dry once established.
Prune lightly in late spring after flowering, only cutting young wood to avoid dieback on old stems.
Grow in a raised bed or terracotta pot to ensure the sharp drainage this Ericaceae shrub demands.
items.description: Arctostaphylos catalinae, known by the common name Santa Catalina Island manzanita, is a species of manzanita native to Southern California. The evergreen shrub is found growing naturally only on Catalina and Santa Cruz Islands on the coast ridges. It thrives in maritime chaparral and can be used in coastal gardens.

items.name: Arctostaphylos columbiana
items.growersTips:
Plant in acidic, sandy soil with grit added to ensure the sharp drainage this shrub absolutely needs.
Position in full sun in a sheltered south-facing spot to mimic its native dry Californian climate.
Water sparingly only during its first UK summer, then leave to rely entirely on natural rainfall.
Prune lightly in late spring after flowering, cutting only new wood as it will not regrow from old.
Protect young plants from severe winter frosts with fleece, especially in wetter northern UK areas.
items.description: Arctostaphylos columbiana is a species of manzanita known by the common name hairy manzanita. It is native to the coast of western North America from northern California to southwestern British Columbia. This large manzanita is a shrub or small tree, usually 1–5 meters tall. It is erect with hairy branches. The leaves are oval-shaped and are usually 2-6 centimeters long and 2-3 wide, pale bluish green, fuzzy on both surfaces, occasionally glandular. The small, white, urn-shaped flowers are borne in bunched inflorescences. The fruit is a red drupe about a centimeter in diameter. The seed requir

items.name: Arctostaphylos confertiflora
items.growersTips:
Grow this rare tender shrub in a terracotta pot with acidic ericaceous grit mix to survive UK winters
Place in your garden's sunniest south-facing spot sheltered from cold winds by a brick wall
Water only with rainwater during dry summer spells and keep completely dry during damp UK winters
Prune lightly immediately after spring flowering to shape the shrub and prevent it from getting leggy
Watch out for phytophthora root rot in heavy clay by planting on a raised mound to ensure drainage
items.description: Arctostaphylos confertiflora is a rare species of manzanita known by the common name Santa Rosa Island manzanita. This shrub is endemic to California, where it grows on the sandstone bluffs of Santa Rosa Island in the Channel Islands. This manzanita is listed as an endangered species by the United States Government.

items.name: Arctostaphylos cruzensis
items.growersTips:
Plant in extremely well-drained, acidic, sandy or gritty soil to prevent fatal winter root rot.
Position in full sun and shelter from cold, drying winds to protect the delicate evergreen foliage.
Water sparingly only during dry summer spells once established, avoiding any winter waterlogging.
Prune very lightly in late spring after flowering, avoiding cutting back into old wood which dies.
Grow in a raised bed or container if your garden soil is heavy clay to ensure essential drainage.
items.description: Arctostaphylos cruzensis is a species of manzanita known by the common names La Cruz manzanita and Arroyo de la Cruz manzanita.

items.name: Arctostaphylos densiflora
items.growersTips:
Plant in acidic sandy soil with grit to mimic its native chaparral and prevent UK winter root rot.
Water deeply once a week during its first dry UK summer then leave to establish with zero irrigation.
Prune lightly immediately after spring flowering to shape the shrub and avoid cutting into old wood.
Grow in a raised bed or terracotta pot to ensure the rapid drainage this Californian native needs.
Shelter from cold drying winds in northern UK regions by planting against a south-facing brick wall.
items.description: Arctostaphylos densiflora, known by the common name Vine Hill manzanita, is a very rare species of manzanita. It is endemic to Sonoma County, California, where it is known from only one extant population of 20 to 30 individual plants. These last wild members of the species are on land near Sebastopol which is owned and protected by the California Native Plant Society. In addition, there are five to ten plants of this manzanita taxon growing on private property about a mile away. The local habitat is mostly chaparral on sandy shale soils.

items.name: Arctostaphylos edmundsii
items.growersTips:
Plant in acidic, sandy, free-draining soil or use ericaceous compost in pots to prevent root rot.
Position in full sun with shelter from cold, drying winds to mimic its native California coast.
Water sparingly once established, allowing the soil to dry out completely between applications.
Prune lightly in late spring after flowering to maintain its low, spreading groundcover shape.
Protect young plants from severe winter frosts using fleece or move containers to a cold greenhouse.
items.description: Arctostaphylos edmundsii, with the common name Little Sur manzanita, is a species of manzanita. This shrub is endemic to California where it grows on the coastal bluffs of Monterey County.

items.name: Arctostaphylos gabilanensis
items.growersTips:
Plant in free-draining acidic grit-heavy soil to mimic its native Californian chaparral habitat.
Position in full sun against a south-facing wall to protect from wet UK winters and cold winds.
Water deeply once a week during its first summer then leave to rely solely on natural UK rainfall.
Prune lightly in late spring after flowering only to shape and never cut back into old leafless wood.
Grow in a raised bed or terracotta pot to prevent the root rot caused by heavy clay UK soils.
items.description: Arctostaphylos gabilanensis is a rare species of manzanita known by the common name Gabilan manzanita.

items.name: Arctostaphylos glandulosa
items.growersTips:
Plant in extremely well-drained, acidic, sandy or gritty soil to prevent fatal winter root rot.
Position in full sun and shelter from cold, drying winds which damage the evergreen foliage in winter.
Water sparingly only during dry spells in the first summer, then leave completely dry once established.
Prune very lightly in late spring after flowering, only removing dead wood as they dislike hard cutting.
Grow in a raised bed or terracotta pot to mimic its native dry slopes in wet UK climates.
items.description: Arctostaphylos glandulosa, with the common name Eastwood's manzanita, is a species of manzanita.

items.name: Arctostaphylos glandulosa subsp. crassifolia
items.growersTips:
Plant in acidic, sandy, free-draining soil with grit to mimic its native dry chaparral habitat.
Water only during dry spells in its first summer, then leave completely dry to prevent root rot.
Grow in a terracotta pot to protect from winter wet, moving it under a cold frame or porch in rain.
Prune lightly in late spring after flowering, only cutting soft new wood to maintain its shape.
Position in the brightest, most sun-baked spot in your garden to encourage pink-white spring blooms.
items.description: Arctostaphylos glandulosa subsp. crassifolia is a rare perennial shrub, a subspecies of manzanita within the heather family commonly known as the Del Mar manzanita. It is narrowly endemic to the sandstone coastal terraces of San Diego County and northwestern Baja California. It is a burl-forming evergreen shrub typically found growing in a rambling habit on poor soils and hardpan. From December to February, white to pink urn-shaped flowers decorate its foliage, giving way to small fruits. It is listed as endangered and is threatened by land development, invasive species and modifications to th

items.name: Arctostaphylos glauca
items.growersTips:
Plant in extremely well-drained, acidic to neutral soil, adding grit to mimic its native chaparral.
Position in full sun against a south-facing wall to protect from cold, wet UK winter winds.
Water sparingly only during its first summer, then leave dry as wet soil causes root rot in the UK.
Prune lightly in late spring only to remove dead wood, as it does not regenerate from old wood.
Grow in a raised bed or terracotta pot to ensure the sharp drainage this drought-tolerant shrub needs.
items.description: Arctostaphylos glauca is a species of manzanita known by the common name bigberry manzanita. It is native to California and Baja California, where it grows in the chaparral and woodland of coastal and inland hills. In October 2025, Arctostaphylos glauca was established as the State Shrub of California.

items.name: Arctostaphylos glutinosa
items.growersTips:
Plant in acidic sandy loam with grit to mimic its native chaparral and prevent UK winter root rot.
Position in full sun against a south-facing wall to maximize summer heat and shield from cold winds.
Water deeply once a week during its first UK summer then leave dry to prevent fungal leaf spot.
Prune lightly in late spring after flowering only to remove dead wood as it dislikes hard cutting.
Grow in a raised bed or terracotta pot to ensure the rapid drainage this drought-lover requires.
items.description: Arctostaphylos glutinosa is a species of manzanita known by the common name Schreiber's manzanita. It is endemic to Santa Cruz County, California, where it is known from only a few occurrences on the western slopes of the Santa Cruz Mountains. It grows in the chaparral of the limestone and diatomaceous shale ridges on the coastline.

items.name: Arctostaphylos hispidula
items.growersTips:
Plant in extremely well-drained, acidic, sandy or gritty soil to prevent fatal winter root rot.
Position in full sun and shelter from cold, drying winds to protect the delicate pink spring blooms.
Water deeply but infrequently during the first summer, then leave dry once established in the UK.
Prune lightly only in late spring after flowering to shape the shrub and remove dead wood.
Grow in a raised bed or container with ericaceous compost if your garden has heavy clay or alkaline soil.
items.description: Arctostaphylos hispidula is a species of manzanita known by the common names Gasquet manzanita and Howell's manzanita. It is native to the coastal mountain ranges of southern Oregon and northern California, where it is an uncommon member of the serpentine soils flora and other mountain plant communities. This is a spreading or erect shrub reaching a maximum height between one and two meters. The twigs and foliage are bristly and glandular, the dark green leaves oval to broadly lance-shaped and up to 3 centimeters long. items.name: Arctostaphylos hookeri
items.growersTips:
Plant in extremely well-drained acidic soil or use ericaceous compost mixed with plenty of grit.
Position in full sun and shelter from cold drying winds to prevent winter leaf scorch in the UK.
Water sparingly once established, allowing the soil to dry out completely between summer waterings.
Prune lightly in late spring after flowering only to remove dead wood and maintain a compact shape.
Grow in raised beds or containers to ensure the sharp drainage this Californian native requires.
items.description: Arctostaphylos hookeri is a species of manzanita known by the common name Hooker's manzanita.

items.name: Arctostaphylos imbricata

Prune very lightly in late spring after flowering only to remove dead wood and maintain a neat shape
Protect from winter wet by planting on a slope or in a raised bed to prevent root rot in UK winters
items.description: Arctostaphylos imbricata is a species of manzanita known by the common name San Bruno Mountain manzanita.

items.name: Arctostaphylos insularis
items.growersTips:
Plant in acidic soil with excellent drainage, adding grit to mimic its native Californian slopes.
Water newly planted shrubs deeply once a week in dry UK summers, then leave to establish.
Position in full sun with shelter from cold, drying winds to prevent winter leaf scorch.
Prune lightly in late spring after flowering to maintain shape, avoiding cutting into old wood.
Grow in a raised bed or container to protect roots from waterlogging during wet British winters.
items.description: Arctostaphylos insularis is a species of manzanita known by the common name island manzanita. It is endemic to Santa Cruz Island, one of the Channel Islands of California.

items.name: Arctostaphylos klamathensis
items.growersTips:
Plant in acidic sandy loam with grit to mimic its native Klamath soil and prevent UK winter wet rot.
Position in full sun with maximum air circulation to prevent fungal leaf spot in humid UK summers.
Water deeply once a week during the first summer then leave to rely solely on natural UK rainfall.
Prune lightly in late spring after flowering only to remove dead wood as it dislikes hard cutting.
Grow in a raised bed or terracotta pot to guarantee the sharp drainage this alpine shrub demands.
items.description: Arctostaphylos klamathensis, with the common name Klamath manzanita, is a species of manzanita. It is endemic to the Klamath Mountains of far northern California, where it was first described during an ecological survey in Cedar Basin near the border between Siskiyou and Trinity Counties in 1982.

items.name: Arctostaphylos luciana
items.growersTips:

Position in full sun against a south-facing wall to mimic its native warm Californian climate.
Water sparingly once established only during prolonged dry summer spells to prevent fungal disease.
Prune lightly in late spring after flowering only to shape and remove dead wood from the shrub.
Grow in a container using ericaceous compost if your garden soil is naturally alkaline or clay.
items.description: Arctostaphylos luciana is a species of manzanita known by the common name Santa Lucia manzanita, is endemic to California.

items.name: Arctostaphylos manzanita
items.growersTips:
Plant in acidic, free-draining sandy loam or use ericaceous compost in pots to prevent root rot.
Position in full sun against a south-facing wall to shelter from cold, drying UK winter winds.
Water sparingly only during the first summer, then leave dry as damp UK soil causes fungal disease.
Prune lightly in late spring after flowering, avoiding cutting back into old wood which will not regrow.
Grow in raised beds or terracotta pots to ensure the sharp drainage this Mediterranean-style shrub needs.
items.description: One of many species of manzanita, Arctostaphylos manzanita has the common names common manzanita and whiteleaf manzanita.

items.name: Arctostaphylos manzanita subsp. elegans
items.growersTips:
Plant in acidic soil with a pH below 6.0, adding grit to ensure the sharp drainage this shrub needs.
Position in full sun against a south-facing wall to mimic its native warm Californian climate.
Water deeply once a week during the first summer, then leave to rely solely on natural UK rainfall.
Prune only in late spring after flowering, cutting back lightly to avoid dieback on old wood.
Protect young plants from severe winter frosts using fleece if temperatures drop below minus five.
items.description: Arctostaphylos manzanita subsp. elegans, also known as the Konocti manzanita, is a subspecies of the Common manzanita. It is endemic to California. It was originally described at the rank of species as Arctostaphylos elegans in 1893 by Willis Linn Jepson. It was reduced to a subspecies of Arctostaphylos manzanita by Philipp Vincent Wells in 1968.

items.name: Arctostaphylos mendocinoensis
items.growersTips:
Plant in acidic, sandy, free-draining soil to mimic its coastal California heathland habitat.
Position in full sun with shelter from harsh, cold drying winds to prevent winter leaf scorch.
Water sparingly once established, allowing the soil to dry out completely between waterings.
Prune lightly in late spring after flowering, avoiding cutting back into old wood which will not regrow.
Grow in a container using ericaceous compost if your garden soil is heavy clay or alkaline.
items.description: Arctostaphylos nummularia subsp. mendocinoensis, commonly known as pygmy manzanita, is a subspecies of manzanita. It is endemic to Mendocino County, California, where it is known from scattered occurrences in the pygmy forests near the coast.

items.name: Arctostaphylos mewukka
items.growersTips:
Plant in extremely well-drained, acidic, sandy or gritty soil to prevent winter wet root rot in the UK.
Position in full sun with shelter from cold, drying winds to protect the delicate evergreen foliage.
Water sparingly only during dry summer spells once established, allowing the soil to dry out fully.
Prune lightly in late spring after flowering, avoiding cutting back into old wood which does not regrow.
Grow in a raised bed or container if your garden soil is heavy clay to ensure the required drainage.
items.description: Arctostaphylos mewukka is a species of manzanita known by the common name Indian manzanita.

items.name: Arctostaphylos montaraensis

Position in full sun against a south-facing wall to maximize summer heat and protect from cold winds.
Water deeply once a week during its first UK summer then leave dry to prevent fungal pathogens.
Prune lightly in late spring after flowering only to shape and never cut back into old wood.
Grow in a raised bed or terracotta pot if your garden soil is heavy clay to ensure rapid drainage.
items.description: Arctostaphylos montaraensis, known by the common name Montara manzanita, is a species of manzanita in the family Ericaceae.

items.name: Arctostaphylos montereyensis
items.growersTips:
Plant in acidic, sandy soil with grit to mimic its native chaparral and prevent UK winter wet rot.
Water deeply once a fortnight in its first summer, then leave completely dry once established.
Do not prune into old wood; only tip-prune new spring growth lightly to maintain a bushy shape.
Grow in a raised bed or terracotta pot to ensure the rapid drainage this Californian shrub needs.
Shelter from cold, drying winds by planting against a south-facing wall to survive UK winters.
items.description: Arctostaphylos montereyensis is a species of manzanita known by the common names Monterey manzanita and Toro manzanita. It is endemic to Monterey County, California, where it is known from only a few occurrences around Fort Ord and Toro County Park near Salinas. It is a plant of maritime chaparral on sandy soils.

items.name: Arctostaphylos morroensis
items.growersTips:
Plant in highly acidic well-drained soil using sulfur to lower pH if your garden is alkaline
Water only during dry summer spells in the first year then leave to survive on UK rainfall alone
Grow in a raised bed or terracotta pot to prevent root rot during wet British winters
Prune lightly in late spring after flowering only to remove dead wood and maintain a compact shape
Position in full sun with shelter from cold drying winds to protect the delicate winter blooms
items.description: Arctostaphylos morroensis is a species of manzanita known by the common name Morro manzanita. This shrub is endemic to San Luis Obispo County, California, where it is known only from the vicinity of Morro Bay.

items.name: Arctostaphylos myrtifolia
items.growersTips:
Plant in extremely well-drained, acidic, sandy or gritty soil to prevent fatal winter root rot.
Position in full sun with shelter from cold, drying winds to mimic its native Californian climate.
Water sparingly only during dry summer spells once established, avoiding any winter waterlogging.
Avoid pruning this slow-growing shrub other than lightly removing dead wood in late spring.
Grow in a container with ericaceous compost and grit if your garden soil is heavy clay or alkaline.
items.description: Arctostaphylos myrtifolia is a rare species of manzanita known by the common name Ione manzanita. It is endemic to the Sierra Nevada foothills of California. It grows in the chaparral and woodland plant community on a distinctive acidic soil series, an oxisol of the Eocene-era Ione Formation, in western Amador and northern Calaveras counties. There are only eleven occurrences, of which three have not been recorded since 1976. This is a federally listed threatened species.

items.name: Arctostaphylos nevadensis
items.growersTips:
Plant in extremely well-drained, acidic, sandy or gritty soil to prevent winter root rot in UK wet.
Water deeply but infrequently during the first summer, then leave dry once established in the UK.
Prune lightly in late spring after flowering only to control spread, avoiding cutting into old wood.
Position in full sun on a sloped bed or rockery to mimic its native dry, alpine microclimate.
Protect young plants from winter waterlogging by mixing horticultural grit into the planting hole.
items.description: Arctostaphylos nevadensis, with the common name pinemat manzanita, is a species of manzanita native to western North America.

items.name: Arctostaphylos nissenana
items.growersTips:
Plant in acidic sandy loam with grit to mimic its native Sierra Nevada home and prevent root rot.
Position in full sun against a south-facing wall to protect from cold UK winds and winter wet.
Water deeply once a fortnight during its first UK summer then leave to rely solely on rainfall.
Prune lightly in late spring after flowering only to remove dead wood as it dislikes hard cutting.
Grow in a raised bed or terracotta pot to ensure the rapid drainage this rare shrub demands.
items.description: Arctostaphylos nissenana is a species of manzanita known by the common name Nissenana manzanita or El Dorado manzanita. It is endemic to California, where it grows in the woodlands and chaparral of the Sierra Nevada foothills, mostly in El Dorado County.

items.name: Arctostaphylos nummularia

Shelter from cold, drying easterly winds by planting against a south or west-facing garden wall.
Prune lightly in late spring after flowering only to remove dead wood and maintain a compact shape.
Grow alongside Calluna vulgaris or Erica carnea which share its love for acidic, low-nutrient soils.
items.description: Arctostaphylos nummularia is a species of manzanita known by the common names glossyleaf manzanita, dwarf manzanita and Fort Bragg manzanita. It is endemic to California, where it grows in the forests of the coastal and inland ranges north of the San Francisco Bay.

items.name: Arctostaphylos obispoensis
items.growersTips:
Plant in acidic sandy loam with grit to mimic its native chaparral and prevent UK root rot
Position in full sun against a south-facing wall to maximise summer heat and protect from frost
Water only during dry spells in its first summer then leave to rely entirely on UK rainfall
Prune lightly in late spring after flowering to shape the shrub but never cut back into old wood
Grow in a raised bed or terracotta pot to ensure the rapid drainage this California native needs
items.description: Arctostaphylos obispoensis is a species of manzanita, known by the common names bishop manzanita and serpentine manzanita, endemic to California.

items.name: Arctostaphylos ohloneana
items.growersTips:
Plant in acidic gritty soil or ericaceous compost with extra perlite to ensure perfect drainage.
Position in full sun and shelter from cold drying winds to mimic its native Californian climate.
Water sparingly only during dry summer spells once established to prevent root rot in wet UK winters.
Prune lightly in late spring after flowering only to shape and remove dead wood, avoiding hard cuts.
Grow in a raised bed or terracotta pot to protect roots from waterlogging during rainy UK winters.
items.description: Arctostaphylos ohloneana is a rare species of manzanita known by the common name Ohlone manzanita, in the Santa Cruz Mountains in California. It takes its name after the native American Ohlone people who settled along the California coast between San Francisco and Santa Cruz. It is endemic to northwest Santa Cruz County, where it is known only from four populations on Ben Lomond Mountain, just south of Big Basin Redwoods State Park.

items.name: Arctostaphylos osoensis
items.growersTips:
Plant in acidic well-drained soil using a grit-heavy ericaceous compost mix to prevent root rot.
Position in full sun with shelter from harsh drying winter winds to protect the evergreen foliage.
Water deeply during dry spells in its first summer then leave to rely on natural UK rainfall.
Prune lightly in late spring after flowering only to remove dead wood and maintain a compact shape.
Watch for leaf spot fungus during wet UK autumns and ensure excellent air circulation around stems.
items.description: Arctostaphylos osoensis is a species of manzanita known by the common name Oso manzanita. It is endemic to San Luis Obispo County, California, where it is known from only two occurrences on the northern edge of the Los Osos Valley. It grows exclusively on volcanic dacite from the Morro Rock-Islay Hill Complex associated with the Nine Sisters.

items.name: Arctostaphylos otayensis
items.growersTips:
Plant in extremely free-draining, acidic, gritty soil to prevent winter root rot in wet UK climates.
Position in full sun against a south-facing wall to mimic its native warm Californian chaparral.
Water young plants deeply once a fortnight in summer, then leave completely dry once established.
Prune lightly in late spring after flowering, avoiding cutting back into old wood which won't regrow.
Protect young plants from severe UK winter frosts using a temporary fleece jacket or cloche.
items.description: Arctostaphylos otayensis is a species of manzanita commonly known as the Otay manzanita. It is a rare perennial shrub native to the mountains of southwestern San Diego County, California and northwestern Baja California, where it grows in chaparral habitats on metavolcanic soils, mostly in the San Ysidro Mountains. The white urn-shaped flowers bloom from winter to spring. Because of the small range of this species and a number of threats, it is of conservation concern.

items.name: Arctostaphylos pajaroensis
items.growersTips:
Plant in acidic sandy soil with grit to mimic its native chaparral and prevent UK root rot.
Position in full sun against a south-facing wall to protect from cold wet winter winds.
Water deeply once a week during its first UK summer then leave completely dry once established.
Prune lightly in late spring after flowering only to shape and never cut back into old wood.
Grow in a raised bed or terracotta pot to ensure the rapid drainage this California native needs.
items.description: Arctostaphylos pajaroensis is a species of manzanita known by the common name Pajaro manzanita. It is endemic to California, where it is known mainly from Monterey County.

items.name: Arctostaphylos pallida
items.growersTips:
Plant in extremely well-drained, acidic, sandy or gritty soil to prevent fatal winter root rot.
Position in full sun and shelter from cold, drying winds to protect the delicate evergreen foliage.
Water sparingly only during dry summer spells once established, avoiding any waterlogged conditions.
Prune very lightly in late spring after flowering, only removing dead wood as it dislikes hard cutting.

items.description: Arctostaphylos pallida, commonly known as pallid manzanita, Oakland Hills manzanita, and Alameda manzanita, is an upright manzanita shrub from the Ericaceae, or heath family. It is endemic to the eastern San Francisco Bay Area of Northern California.

items.name: Arctostaphylos parryana

items.description: Arctostaphylos parryana, with the common name Parry manzanita, is a species of manzanita.
