Prune very lightly in late spring after flowering, avoiding cutting back into old wood which won't regrow.
Grow in a container using ericaceous compost if your garden soil is heavy clay or alkaline.
items.description: Arctostaphylos patula is a species of manzanita known by the common name greenleaf manzanita. This manzanita is native to western North America where it grows at moderate to high elevations.

items.name: Arctostaphylos pumila
items.growersTips:
Plant in acidic sandy loam with grit to mimic coastal dunes and prevent winter root rot in UK wet.
Water deeply once a week during the first dry summer then leave to rely on natural UK rainfall.
Protect from harsh freezing winds by planting against a south-facing wall to prevent leaf scorch.
Prune lightly in late spring after flowering only to remove dead wood and maintain a neat carpet.
Grow alongside Calluna vulgaris or Erica carnea which share the same acid soil and sun requirements.
items.description: Arctostaphylos pumila, with the common name sandmat manzanita, is a species of manzanita.

items.name: Arctostaphylos pungens
items.growersTips:
Plant in acidic, free-draining sandy loam or use ericaceous compost in a raised bed to avoid rot.
Position in full sun with shelter from cold, drying winds to mimic its native chaparral habitat.
Water sparingly once established, allowing the soil to dry out completely between summer waterings.
Prune lightly in late spring after flowering only to remove dead wood, as it does not regrow from old wood.
Grow in a terracotta pot to ensure excellent drainage and protect roots from winter waterlogging.
items.description: Arctostaphylos pungens, with the common name pointleaf manzanita, is a species of manzanita. It is native to the Southwestern United States and to northern and central Mexico, where it grows in chaparral and woodland habitats, and on desert ridges. Arctostaphylos pungens can be seen growing at Tent Rocks National Monument in New Mexico at an elevation of about 6000 feet.

items.name: Arctostaphylos purissima
items.growersTips:
Plant in acidic, sandy, free-draining soil to prevent winter root rot in wet UK climates.
Position in full sun against a south-facing wall to protect from cold, drying winter winds.
Water sparingly once established, only during prolonged dry summer spells to avoid root fungal rot.
Do not prune hard; only lightly trim wayward shoots in late spring after the flowering period.
Grow in a raised bed or large terracotta pot filled with ericaceous compost to ensure sharp drainage.
items.description: Arctostaphylos purissima is a rare species of manzanita known by the common name La Purisima manzanita.

items.name: Arctostaphylos rainbowensis
items.growersTips:
Plant in highly acidic, gritty, free-draining soil to mimic its native dry Californian chaparral.
Grow in a terracotta pot to protect from UK winter wet and move under a cold frame to prevent rot.
Water sparingly only during dry summer spells once established, using rainwater to keep soil acidic.
Do not prune beyond removing dead wood in late spring, as this shrub resents hard cutting back.
Position in the brightest, most sun-drenched spot in your garden to maximise warmth and flowering.
items.description: Arctostaphylos rainbowensis is a species of manzanita known by the common name Rainbow manzanita. It is endemic to California, where it is known only from northern San Diego and southern Riverside Counties in the Peninsular Ranges.

items.name: Arctostaphylos refugioensis
items.growersTips:
Plant in acidic, sandy, free-draining soil with no added fertilizer to mimic its native scrubland.
Position in full sun against a south-facing wall to protect it from cold, wet UK winter winds.
Water sparingly only during dry summer spells once established to prevent root rot in damp soil.
Prune lightly in late spring after flowering, avoiding cutting back into old wood which won't regrow.
Grow in a large terracotta pot with ericaceous grit mix if your garden has heavy clay or alkaline soil.
items.description: Arctostaphylos refugioensis is a species of manzanita, known by the common name Refugio manzanita. It is endemic to Santa Barbara County, California, where it can be found along the immediate coastline, including the vicinity of Refugio State Beach, and into the Santa Ynez Mountains of the northwestern Transverse Ranges.

items.name: Arctostaphylos regismontana
items.growersTips:
Plant in extremely free-draining, acidic, gritty soil to prevent winter root rot in wet UK climates
Position in full sun and shelter from cold drying winds, ideally against a south-facing brick wall
Water deeply once a week during the first summer, then leave completely dry once established in autumn
Prune lightly in late spring after flowering, only cutting young wood as it will not regrow from old
Grow in a raised bed or terracotta pot filled with ericaceous compost mixed with fifty percent grit
items.description: Arctostaphylos regismontana is a species of manzanita known by the common name Kings Mountain manzanita. It is endemic to California, where it is known from the northern slopes of the Santa Cruz Mountains in the southern San Francisco Bay Area.

items.name: Arctostaphylos rudis
items.growersTips:
Plant in extremely well-drained, acidic, sandy soil to prevent root rot in wet UK winters.
Position in full sun and shelter from cold, drying winds to protect the evergreen foliage.
Water sparingly once established, allowing the soil to dry out completely between waterings.
Prune lightly in late spring after flowering only to shape and remove dead wood, avoiding hard cuts.
Grow in a container using ericaceous compost if your garden soil is heavy clay or alkaline.
items.description: Arctostaphylos rudis, with the common names shagbark manzanita and sand mesa manzanita, is a species of manzanita.

items.name: Arctostaphylos silvicola
items.growersTips:
Plant in highly acidic sandy soil with grit to mimic its native Californian pine barrens habitat.
Grow in a raised bed or terracotta pot to ensure the sharp winter drainage required in wet UK climates.
Water deeply once a week during its first dry summer then leave completely dry once established.
Prune lightly in late spring after flowering only to remove dead wood as it dislikes hard cutting.
Position in full sun with shelter from cold drying winds to protect the delicate pink spring blooms.
items.description: Arctostaphylos silvicola is a species of manzanita known by the common names Bonny Doon or silverleaf manzanita. It is endemic to the sandhills of the southern Santa Cruz Mountains in California's Santa Cruz and Santa Clara counties.

items.name: Arctostaphylos stanfordiana
items.growersTips:
Plant in highly acidic, sandy soil with grit added to ensure the sharp drainage this shrub demands.
Position in full sun against a south-facing wall to mimic its native warm Californian climate.
Water sparingly only during the first summer, then leave to establish with zero summer irrigation.
Prune lightly immediately after spring flowering to maintain shape and avoid cutting into old wood.
Protect young plants from severe winter frosts using fleece or grow in a container to move indoors.
items.description: Arctostaphylos stanfordiana, with the common name Stanford's manzanita, is a species of manzanita that is endemic to northern California. It is known from the outer North Coast Ranges north of the San Francisco Bay Area.

items.name: Arctostaphylos tomentosa
items.growersTips:
Plant in extremely well-drained, acidic, sandy or gritty soil to prevent fatal winter root rot.
Position in full sun in a sheltered spot to mimic its native chaparral and protect from cold winds.
Water sparingly only during dry summer spells once established, as this shrub is highly drought-tolerant.
Prune lightly in late spring after flowering to shape the shrub, avoiding cutting back into old wood.
Grow in a container with ericaceous compost if your garden soil is heavy clay or alkaline.
items.description: Arctostaphylos tomentosa is a species of manzanita known by the common name woollyleaf manzanita or woolley manzanita. This shrub is endemic to California.

items.name: Red bearberry
items.growersTips:
Plant in acidic, sandy, free-draining soil; add sulphur chips if your UK garden loam is alkaline.
Water weekly during the first dry UK summer, then leave to rely entirely on natural rainfall.
Prune lightly in late spring after flowering to control spread and maintain a dense evergreen mat.
Grow alongside Calluna vulgaris or Erica carnea in a sunny rockery for compatible ericaceous care.
Watch for vine weevil larvae in autumn, which can chew through roots in damp UK container setups.
items.description: Arctostaphylos uva-ursi is a plant species of the genus Arctostaphylos widely distributed across circumboreal regions of the subarctic Northern Hemisphere. Kinnikinnick is a common name in Canada and the United States. Growing up to 30 centimetres in height, the leaves are evergreen. The flowers are white to pink and the fruit is a red berry.

items.name: Arctostaphylos virgata
items.growersTips:
Plant in acidic, sandy soil mixed with grit to mimic its native chaparral and prevent UK root rot.
Position in full sun against a south-facing wall to shelter it from cold, wet winter winds.
Water deeply once a week during its first UK summer, then leave dry once established.
Prune lightly in late spring after flowering, avoiding cutting back into old wood which won't regrow.
Grow alongside Calluna or Erica carnea which share its strict requirement for low-nutrient acid soil.
items.description: Arctostaphylos virgata is a species of manzanita known by the common names Bolinas manzanita and Marin manzanita.

items.name: Arctostaphylos viridissima
items.growersTips:
Grow in highly acidic, free-draining sandy loam or ericaceous grit mix to prevent fatal root rot.
Plant in full sun against a south-facing wall to shelter it from cold, wet winter winds in the UK.
Water sparingly only during dry summer spells once established, avoiding any waterlogged soil.
Prune lightly in late spring after flowering, cutting only new wood to maintain its bushy shape.
Protect young plants with horticultural fleece during severe, prolonged British winter frosts.
items.description: Arctostaphylos viridissima is a species of manzanita known by the common names whitehair manzanita and McMinn's manzanita. It is endemic to Santa Cruz Island, one of the Channel Islands of California.

items.name: Arctostaphylos viscida
items.growersTips:
Plant in extremely well-drained, acidic, sandy or gritty soil to prevent fatal winter root rot.
Position in full sun with shelter from cold, drying winds to mimic its native chaparral climate.
Water sparingly during the first summer, then leave dry as established plants hate summer moisture.
Prune lightly in late spring after flowering, avoiding cutting back into old wood which will not regrow.
Grow in a raised bed or terracotta pot if your garden soil is heavy clay to ensure perfect drainage.
items.description: Arctostaphylos viscida, with the common names whiteleaf manzanita and sticky manzanita, is a species of manzanita.

items.name: Arctous alpina
items.growersTips:
Grow in extremely acidic, nutrient-poor, sandy peat soil with a pH between 4.5 and 5.5.
Plant in a raised rockery or scree bed to mimic Scottish highland drainage and prevent root rot.
Water exclusively with soft rainwater to keep soil consistently damp without raising the pH level.
Position in full sun with maximum wind exposure to replicate alpine conditions and prevent mildew.
Propagate by taking semi-ripe cuttings in late summer and rooting them in a mist unit with bottom heat.
items.description: Arctous alpina, the alpine bearberry, mountain bearberry or black bearberry, is a dwarf shrub in the heather family Ericaceae. The basionym of this species is Arbutus alpina L..

items.name: Arctous rubra
items.growersTips:
Grow this acid-loving shrub in ericaceous compost with a pH between 4.5 and 5.5 to prevent chlorosis.
Water only with harvested rainwater to maintain soil acidity, keeping the root zone consistently damp.
Position in full sun or partial shade in northern UK gardens to mimic its native subarctic habitat.
Mulch annually in spring with pine needles or composted bark to retain moisture and cool the roots.
Propagate in late summer using semi-ripe heel cuttings rooted in a peat-free ericaceous sand mix.

items.name: Black Turnstone
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at a depth of two millimetres in early spring using a gritty free-draining loam.
Water sparingly once established, allowing the top five centimetres of soil to dry out completely.
Protect young seedlings from slugs and snails using organic bait during damp UK spring evenings.
Incorporate horticultural grit into heavy clay soils to prevent winter root rot in wet conditions.
Plant alongside slow-growing alpine sedums to prevent the vigorous annual from being overcrowded.
items.description: Arenaria, a Latin word meaning sand-loving, may refer to:

items.name: Arenaria balearica
items.growersTips:
Plant this perennial mossy sandwort in moist, shade-dappled acidic soil, not as a dry annual.
Press the tiny seeds lightly into damp compost in spring; do not bury them as they need light.
Water consistently during dry UK summers to keep the shallow root system from drying out and dying.
Grow it alongside ferns or hostas in damp rock crevices where it can creep over cool, wet stones.
Watch for slugs and snails in damp UK spring weather, as they will quickly eat the tender foliage.
items.description: Arenaria balearica, the mossy sandwort, is a species of flowering plant in the family Caryophyllaceae, native to the Balearic Islands, Corsica, Sardinia and mainland Italy. It was first described by Carl Linnaeus in 1768.

items.name: Arenaria grandiflora
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn in a cold frame using a gritty compost mix to mimic UK alpine conditions.
Water only when the top two inches of soil are dry to prevent root rot in damp UK winters.
Plant alongside Thymus serpyllum in a raised bed to ensure the sharp drainage this alpine needs.
Watch for slugs and snails during wet UK springs as they quickly destroy the soft young foliage.
Do not prune but gently clear away fallen autumn leaves to prevent the crown from rotting in winter.
items.description: Arenaria grandiflora is a species of plant in the family Caryophyllaceae. It is found in central and southern Europe, and north-western Africa. It has also been introduced to Germany.

items.name: Arenaria leptoclados
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn or early spring directly into gritty, well-drained soil at a depth of 2mm.
Water young seedlings sparingly once a week, allowing the topsoil to dry out fully between waterings.
Watch for slugs and snails during wet UK springs, protecting the delicate foliage with grit barriers.
Clear competing weeds by hand around these low-growing annuals to prevent them from being smothered.
Plant alongside Sedum album or Thymum serpyllum in sunny rock gardens to mimic natural gravel screes.
items.description: Arenaria leptoclados, the lesser thyme-leaved sandwort, is a species of flowering plant in the family Caryophyllaceae. It is an annual native to Europe, western and Central Asia, and northern and eastern Africa.

items.name: Thyme-leaved sandwort
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn on the surface of gritty, free-draining soil without burying them to aid light.
Water sparingly only during prolonged summer droughts as this plant thrives in dry, gravelly soils.
Position in full sun alongside companion plants like wild thyme or sedum in a rockery or wall crevice.
Allow the plant to self-seed naturally in late summer to ensure a continuous biennial cycle in UK gardens.
Hand-weed around the delicate shallow roots instead of hoeing to prevent accidental damage.
items.description: Arenaria serpyllifolia, commonly known as thyme-leaf sandwort or thyme-leaved sandwort, is an annual or biennial flowering plant in the pink and carnation family Caryophyllaceae that can be found from Nepal to Pakistan. It also has a wide distribution in the United Kingdom and southern Poland. It was introduced to Chile. The species is widespread in China.

items.name: Arethuseae
items.growersTips:
Plant hardy Bletilla striata pseudobulbs five centimetres deep in humus-rich, well-drained loam.
Water container-grown Calopogon heavily with rainwater in summer, keeping them damp but not soggy.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs using organic iron phosphate pellets or beer traps.
Mulch outdoor Bletilla with ten centimetres of dry bracken or straw in November to survive frosts.
Grow Pleione in shallow pans of bark and moss, keeping them completely dry and cold over winter.
items.description: Arethuseae is a mid-sized tribe of orchids in the subfamily Epidendroideae. This tribe was initially categorized by John Lindley in 1840. Its largest subtribes are Arethusinae and Coelogyninae.

items.name: Prickly poppy
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in April directly into poor, well-drained soil as taproots resent transplanting shock.
Position in the sunniest, most sheltered south-facing border to mimic their native dry habitat.
Water seedlings sparingly until established, then rely solely on natural UK rainfall to avoid rot.
Wear thick leather gloves when handling to protect your hands from the extremely sharp, toxic spines.
Leave seed heads over winter to self-seed naturally, as parent plants rarely survive wet UK winters.
items.description: Argemone is a genus of flowering plants in the family Papaveraceae commonly known as prickly poppies. There are about 32 species native to the Americas and Hawaii. The generic name originated as ἀργεμώνη in Greek and was applied by Dioscorides to a poppy-like plant used to treat cataracts.

items.name: Argemone albiflora
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in spring directly where they are to flower as taproots resent transplanting.
Grow in poor well-drained gravelly soil to mimic its native habitat and prevent winter root rot.
Water sparingly only during prolonged dry spells once established as this plant is highly drought-tolerant.
Protect young spring shoots from slugs and snails which target the tender growth in damp UK weather.
Deadhead spent blooms in late summer to prolong flowering and control its prolific self-seeding.
items.description: Argemone albiflora, the white prickly poppy, also known as the bluestem prickly poppy or the Texas prickly poppy, is a small erect plant with a decorative white flower with a yellow latex. It is deeply rooted with yellow or red stamens. The plant is known for the sharp prickles on its stem and leaves. The sepals fall off as the flower of this plant grows bigger. It grows in the arid regions of the southern Midwest along roadsides and disturbed pieces of land. Native Americans have long revered this plant for its medicinal and other uses.

items.name: Argemone corymbosa
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn in deep pots to avoid root disturbance as this poppy dislikes being transplanted
Grow in poor well-drained gravelly soil in full sun to mimic its native dry desert environment
Protect young plants from winter wet with a cloche or cold frame to prevent root rot in UK damp
Wear thick gloves when weeding around this plant to protect your hands from its sharp yellow spines
Plant alongside drought-tolerant Mediterranean herbs like rosemary and thyme in a raised gravel bed
items.description: Argemone corymbosa, the Mojave prickly poppy, is a flowering plant in the family Papaveraceae native to the eastern Mojave Desert of the southwestern United States. It especially common around Cima, California and the nearby community of Kelso, California. The plant grows in sandy places and on dry slopes, and is very similar to desert prickly poppy.

items.name: Argemone glauca
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in spring just below the surface in deep pots to avoid disturbing the sensitive taproot.
Grow in the poorest, fastest-draining sandy soil in full sun to mimic its native dry habitat.
Water sparingly only during prolonged summer droughts to prevent root rot in damp UK climates.
Protect young plants from slugs and snails in spring using physical barriers or organic bait.
Overwinter in a cold frame or unheated greenhouse to shield the crown from excessive winter wet.
items.description: Argemone glauca, the Hawaiian poppy or pua kala, is a species of flowering plant in the family Papaveraceae, native to Hawaii. A perennial, it is found in dry situations, including disturbed areas, from sea level up to 6,200 ft (1,900 m) on all of the main islands.

items.name: Prickly poppy
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at three millimetres deep in April directly where they are to grow in the garden
Grow in poor sandy soil with sharp sand added to the planting hole to prevent winter root rot
Water only during prolonged dry summer spells as this poppy is highly drought-tolerant once set
Wear thick heavy-duty gloves when weeding to protect your hands from the extremely sharp foliage spines
Position in your absolute sunniest south-facing border to maximise the short UK summer heat supply
items.description: Argemone mexicana, also known by the common names Mexican poppy, Mexican prickly poppy, flowering thistle, cardo, and cardosanto, is a species of poppy found in Mexico and now widely naturalized in many parts of the world. An extremely hardy pioneer plant, it is tolerant of drought and poor soil, often being the only cover on new road cuttings or verges. It has bright yellow latex. It is poisonous to grazing animals, and it is rarely eaten, but it has been used medicinally by many peoples, including those in its native area, as well as the indigenous peoples of the western United States, parts

items.name: Argemone munita
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn in deep pots of gritty soil to accommodate the long taproot without disturbance.
Position in the sunniest spot of the garden with sharp drainage to survive wet UK winter rot.
Water sparingly only during prolonged summer droughts once the deep taproot is fully established.
Wear thick leather gloves when handling to protect your hands from the extremely sharp yellow spines.
Do not prune the plant but leave the decorative seed pods intact for winter interest and self-seeding.
items.description: Argemone munita is a species of prickly poppy known by the common names flatbud prickly poppy and chicalote. "Munita" means "armed", in reference to the many long prickles. This flower is native to California, where it is widespread throughout the western part of the state and its eastern deserts, on slopes to 10,000 feet, and along roadsides. Its range also extends into Baja California, Arizona, and Nevada.

items.name: Argemone ochroleuca
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in spring directly into poor, well-drained soil as taproots resent transplanting.
Water sparingly only during prolonged summer droughts to prevent root rot in damp UK climates.
Position in the sunniest, most sheltered spot of your garden to mimic its native dry habitat.
Wear thick gloves when handling to protect against the sharp spines and toxic yellow sap.
Cut back dead stems in late autumn and apply a dry mulch like gravel to protect crowns from winter wet.
items.description: Argemone ochroleuca is a species of prickly poppy, a flowering plant commonly known as pale Mexican prickly poppy or Mexican poppy. It is native to Mexico and is also an introduced weed in many temperate and tropical regions of the world. It can grow up to 1 m in height and has a sticky yellow sap.

items.name: Argemone platyceras
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in spring directly where they are to flower as taproots resent transplanting shock.
Provide gritty sharply draining soil in full sun to prevent winter wet from rotting the crown.
Water sparingly only during prolonged dry spells once established to mimic its native dry habitat.
Wear thick gloves when handling to protect your hands from the extremely sharp spines on all parts.
Leave seed heads to dry on the plant for self-seeding but deadhead early to restrict invasive spread.
items.description: Argemone platyceras, the chicalote, is a species of flowering plant in the family Papaveraceae. It is native to seasonally dry areas of Mexico, and has been introduced to Uzbekistan. There appears to be a cultivar, 'Silver Charm'.

items.name: Argemone pleiacantha
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in spring 1mm deep directly into gritty, free-draining soil as taproots hate transplanting.
Grow in the sunniest, most sheltered south-facing border to mimic its native hot, dry US habitat.
Water only during prolonged dry spells in summer, keeping the crown completely dry during winter.
Cut back dead stems to the base in autumn using thick leather gloves to avoid the sharp spines.
Protect young spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.
items.description: Argemone pleiacantha is a species of flowering plant in the poppy family known by the common name southwestern prickly poppy. It is native to Arizona and New Mexico in the United States and Chihuahua, and Sonora in Mexico, where it occurs in dry woodlands and slopes of foothills and mountains. It is an annual or perennial herb with branching, erect stems up to 1.5 meters tall. The plant is covered in prickles, often densely. The blue-green leaves are divided into sharp, toothlike lobes. The flower buds are up to 2 centimeters long and covered in prickles. They bloom into showy white-petalled f

items.name: Prickly poppy
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds directly outdoors in late spring where they are to flower as taproots resent transplanting.
Plant in poor to moderately fertile well-drained soil as rich UK soils cause floppy weak growth.
Position in your garden's absolute full sun to prevent powdery mildew in damp British summers.
Water seedlings sparingly during dry spells and leave established plants to survive on UK rainfall.
Wear thick gloves when deadheading or clearing to protect your hands from the extremely sharp spines.
items.description: Argemone polyanthemos, the crested pricklypoppy, also known as bluestem prickly poppy, pricklypoppy, white prickly poppy, annual pricklypoppy, or as thistle poppy is an annual plant with yellow sap and showy white flowers in the poppy family (Papaveraceae).

items.name: Great Argus
items.growersTips:
Plant Argusia sibirica in sharply draining sandy soil to survive wet UK winters without root rot.
Water established plants only during prolonged dry spells to mimic their native arid coastlines.
Sow seeds in autumn in cold frames to allow natural winter chilling for successful germination.
Prune back dead stems in early spring just as new growth emerges to maintain a compact habit.
Protect young spring shoots from slugs and snails which target soft Boraginaceae foliage in wet UKs.
items.description: Tournefortia, often called soldierbushes, is a genus of flowering plants in the borage family, Boraginaceae.

items.name: Renga lily
items.growersTips:
Plant in spring at a depth where the crown sits just level with the soil surface to prevent rot.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells but keep it completely dry throughout the winter.
Protect the tender foliage from slugs and snails using organic wool pellets or beer traps in spring.
Cut back damaged outer leaves to the base in late spring once the risk of UK frosts has passed.
Grow in a sheltered south-facing border or container that can be moved into a greenhouse for winter.
items.description: Arthropodium cirratum commonly known as rengarenga, renga lily, New Zealand rock lily, or maikaika, is a species of herbaceous perennial plant, endemic to New Zealand, where it may once have been farmed. It is used for medicine as well as food, and has symbolic importance in traditional Māori culture.

items.name: Arthropodium milleflorum
items.growersTips:
Plant tubers 8cm deep in autumn using grit-heavy soil to survive wet UK winters without rotting.
Water weekly during dry spring spells to boost flowering, then reduce watering as it goes dormant.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic wool pellets or beer traps.
Cut back faded flower stems and yellowing foliage to the base in late autumn to keep plants tidy.
Divide congested clumps in early spring every three years to maintain vigor and propagate new plants.
items.description: Arthropodium milleflorum, the pale vanilla lily, is a species of herbaceous perennial plants native to Australia. It occurs in various habitats including alpine areas and grows to height of between 0.3 and 1.3 metres hand a width of and 0.3 metres. The fleshy tubers were eaten by Aboriginal Australians. The plant emits a strong vanilla fragrance, which becomes more noticeable on warm days.

items.name: Arthropodium minus
items.growersTips:
Plant in free-draining gritty loam to prevent winter root rot in wet UK soils.
Sow seeds shallowly in cold frames during autumn to allow natural winter stratification.
Provide cloche protection or deep dry mulch in winter to shield roots from frosts below minus five.
Water moderately during the spring growing season but keep almost dry during summer dormancy.
Position in partial shade under deciduous shrubs to mimic its natural open woodland habitat.
items.description:
Arthropodium minus, the small vanilla lily, is a species of herbaceous perennial plants native to the Southern Hemisphere. Valued as bush tucker as the roots are edible raw.
Found in a variety of habitats from the coast to alpine areas of eastern Australia. Eucalyptus forests, woodlands and sub-alpine meadows, favouring drier habitats than Arthropodium milleflorum.

items.name: Ascidieria cymbidifolia
items.growersTips:
Grow this tropical orchid in a warm conservatory or heated greenhouse to survive UK winter cold.
Pot in a free-draining medium of fine bark and sphagnum moss to prevent root rot in humid conditions.
Water with tepid rainwater only when the potting mix dries out, reducing frequency during winter.
Position in bright, filtered light but shield from direct mid-summer sun to avoid leaf scorch.
Maintain high humidity above fifty percent by placing the pot on a wet pebble tray year-round.
items.description: Cymboglossum, synonym Ascidieria, is a genus of flowering plants from the orchid family, Orchidaceae. It is native to Borneo, the Philippines, Sulawesi and Sumatra.

items.name: Purple Lip-Spur Orchid
items.growersTips:
Grow in slatted wooden baskets without compost to prevent root rot in damp UK winter humidity.
Provide bright indirect light in south-facing windows with supplementary LED grow lights in winter.
Water daily in summer using tepid rainwater then allow roots to dry completely by nightfall.
Maintain winter temperatures above twelve degrees Celsius to prevent leaf drop and bud blast.
Feed weekly with a weak high-nitrogen orchid fertilizer only during active spring and summer growth.
items.description: Vanda, abbreviated in the horticultural trade as V., is a genus in the orchid family, Orchidaceae. There are 90 species, and the genus is commonly cultivated for the marketplace. This genus and its allies are considered to be among the most specifically adapted of all orchids within the Orchidaceae. The genus is highly prized in horticulture for its showy, fragrant, long-lasting, and intensely colorful flowers. Vanda species are widespread across East Asia, Southeast Asia, and New Guinea, with a few species extending into Queensland and some of the islands of the western Pacific.

items.name: Ascocentrum miniatum
items.growersTips:
Grow in a slatted wooden basket with no compost to allow the roots to dry rapidly in UK humidity.
Hang in a south-facing window to provide the intense light needed to trigger spring orange blooms.
Water daily in summer but keep almost dry in winter, misting only on sunny mornings to avoid rot.
Maintain winter temperatures above fifteen Celsius using a heat mat to prevent sudden leaf drop.
Watch for mealybugs in the tight leaf axils and treat immediately with an organic insecticidal soap.
items.description: Vanda miniata, the rust-red ascocentrum, is a species of orchid found in Assam, Laos, Thailand, Vietnam, Java, Malaysia, Philippines, Sumatra. It was formerly known as Ascocentrum miniatum and was the type species of the genus Ascocentrum, now synonymous with Vanda.

items.name: Asparagoideae
items.growersTips:
Plant crowns in trench thirty centimetres wide and fifteen deep, spacing them forty centimetres apart.
Apply a thick mulch of well-rotted manure in autumn to protect crowns from wet UK winter freezes.
Stop harvesting spears by mid-June to allow ferns to grow and recharge the crown for next spring.
Cut yellowed autumn foliage down to ground level in November to prevent asparagus beetle overwintering.
Hand-weed beds carefully to avoid damaging the shallow, sensitive root systems with a hoe.
items.description: Asparagoideae is a subfamily of monocot flowering plants in the family Asparagaceae, order Asparagales, according to the APG III system of 2009. The subfamily name is derived from the generic name of the type genus, Asparagus. The group has previously been treated as a separate family Asparagaceae sensu stricto.

items.name: Asparagus acutifolius
items.growersTips:
Plant in autumn in free-draining sandy loam with grit added to prevent winter root rot in UK wet.
Bury crowns 15cm deep in trenches, covering with 5cm of soil, then backfill as shoots grow in spring.
Hand-weed beds carefully to avoid damaging the shallow, brittle root system of this wild species.
Mulch with well-rotted manure in late autumn to protect the crown from severe UK winter frosts.
Cut the yellowing, spiny fern-like foliage back to ground level in October to prevent rust disease.
items.description: Asparagus acutifolius, common name wild asparagus, is an evergreen perennial plant belonging to the genus Asparagus. The specific epithet, acutifolius is derived from Latin acutus, and -folius (-leaved), and refers to the characteristic shape of the leaves, a quite common feature in the typical plants of the Mediterranean.

items.name: Sprenger's asparagus
items.growersTips:
Bring indoors before first autumn frost as this South African native cannot survive UK winters outside.
Water thoroughly when the top two centimetres of compost feel dry but never let the pot sit in water.
Repot in spring using a loam-based John Innes No 2 compost mixed with one-third grit for drainage.
Prune yellowing or tangled stems at the base in spring to encourage fresh bright green fronds.
Watch closely for scale insects and mealybugs which hide in the dense thorny foliage indoors.
items.description: Asparagus aethiopicus, Sprenger's asparagus, is a plant native to the Cape Provinces and the Northern Provinces of South Africa. Often used as an ornamental plant, it is considered an invasive weed in many locations. Asparagus fern, asparagus grass and foxtail fern are common names; however, it is unrelated to true ferns. A. aethiopicus has been confused with A. densiflorus, now regarded as a separate species, so that information about A. aethiopicus will often be found under the name A. densiflorus.

items.name: Climbing asparagus fern
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender climber in a pot of loam-based compost so you can move it indoors before UK frosts.
Water sparingly in winter but keep soil consistently damp during the active spring and summer growth.
Provide a sturdy trellis or moss pole early in spring to support its vigorous, scrambling stems.
Prune yellowing or dead woody stems at the base in late autumn to encourage fresh spring shoots.
Check regularly for red spider mites and scale insects, which thrive in dry indoor winter air.
items.description: Asparagus africanus, also known as African asparagus, bush asparagus, wild asparagus, climbing asparagus fern, ornamental asparagus and sparrow grass, is an African species of plant that is found in a variety of habitats. It has multiple medicinal properties and is used to treat various ailments.

items.name: Asparagus albus
items.growersTips:
Plant in free-draining sandy soil with grit to prevent winter root rot in wet UK climates.
Sow seeds in spring at a depth of one centimetre in deep pots to protect the long taproots.
Grow in a south-facing sheltered spot or unheated greenhouse to shield from hard UK frosts.
Prune the spiny white stems back to the base in late autumn once they turn yellow and die back.
Water sparingly once established as this Mediterranean native prefers dry conditions over damp.
items.description: Asparagus albus is a widespread species of flowering plant in the family Asparagaceae, native to the western and central Mediterranean. It is found in the coastal maquis shrubland biome, and in ruderal situations.

items.name: Asparagus aphyllus
items.growersTips:
Plant in free-draining sandy loam with grit to prevent winter root rot in wet UK climates.
Sow seeds in spring at a depth of one centimetre using bottom heat of twenty degrees Celsius.
Protect young shoots from slugs and snails during damp UK springs using organic grit barriers.
Prune dead tangled stems back to the base in late autumn to prevent fungal diseases from overwintering.
Grow in full sun against a south-facing wall to mimic its native warm Mediterranean habitat.
items.description: Asparagus aphyllus is a species of plants in the family Asparagaceae. They are climbing plants. Flowers are visited by the Western honey bee, Syritta pipiens, Phthiria, and Halictus.

items.name: Asparagus asparagoides
items.growersTips:
Grow in containers to easily overwinter indoors as it is not frost-hardy in typical UK winters
Plant tubers 5cm deep in free-draining loam mixed with grit to prevent winter rot in wet UK soil
Water moderately in summer but keep compost barely moist during its semi-dormant winter phase
Provide a trellis or netting for the twining stems to climb up to three metres in a conservatory
Prune dead tangled scramblers to the base in late winter before new spring shoots emerge
items.description: Asparagus asparagoides, commonly known as bridal creeper, bridal-veil creeper, gnarboola, smilax or smilax asparagus, is a herbaceous climbing plant of the family Asparagaceae native to eastern and southern Africa. Sometimes grown as an ornamental plant, it has become a serious environmental weed in Australia and New Zealand.

items.name: Asparagus capensis
items.growersTips:
Grow in a gritty free-draining loam to prevent winter root rot in wet UK soils.
Overwinter in a frost-free greenhouse or conservatory as it cannot survive UK ground freezes.
Water sparingly in winter but keep soil damp during the active summer growing season.
Prune back dead woody stems in late autumn to encourage fresh thorny shoots next spring.
Propagate by dividing the tuberous root clump in early spring just as new growth begins.
items.description: Asparagus capensis, also called katdoring is a dense, thorny, shrub of the Asparagus genus, that is indigenous to South Africa and Namibia.

items.name: Asparagus cochinchinensis
items.growersTips:
Plant in free-draining sandy loam with grit to survive wet UK winters and prevent crown rot.
Sow seeds in spring at 1cm depth in a heated propagator at 20C before transplanting outdoors in May.
Protect young shoots from late spring frosts using horticultural fleece or cloches in northern UK.
Cut back the climbing, thorny stems to ground level in late autumn after foliage turns yellow.
Watch for asparagus beetle larvae in summer and hand-pick them to prevent severe defoliation.
items.description: Asparagus cochinchinensis is a species of flowering plant, sometimes called "Chinese asparagus", in the subfamily Asparagoideae of the family Asparagaceae. No subspecies are listed in the Catalogue of Life.

items.name: Asparagus dauricus
items.growersTips:
Plant in deep, well-drained sandy loam with a pH of 6.5 to 7.5, adding grit to prevent winter rot.
Sow seeds in spring at 1.5cm depth in pots before transplanting to permanent beds the next year.
Water young plants weekly in dry UK summers, but keep established crowns dry to avoid crown rot.
Cut the yellowing fern-like foliage back to 5cm above ground level in late autumn after first frost.
Hand-weed beds carefully to avoid damaging the shallow, spreading root system of the crowns.
items.description: Asparagus dauricus is a species of flowering plant in the family Asparagaceae. It is native to southeastern Siberia, Mongolia, Manchuria, northern and eastern China, and Korea. A perennial herb reaching 70 cm (28 in), it is typically found on arid slopes or sandy wastelands, at elevations from 0 to 2,200 m.

items.name: Asparagus declinatus
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender South African native in a pot with grit-heavy soil to move indoors before frost.
Water sparingly in winter but keep soil damp during its active autumn and winter growth phase.
Sow seeds 1cm deep in spring using a heated propagator kept at a constant 15 to 20 degrees Celsius.
Cut back yellowing scrambling stems to the base in late spring as the plant enters summer dormancy.
Watch closely for red spider mite when keeping this delicate climber in a dry UK greenhouse.
items.description: Asparagus declinatus, common name bridal veil, is a species of Asparagus plant. It is native to the Cape Provinces, Madagascar and Namibia and has been introduced into Central America, South Australia and Western Australia. It is a perennial vine. It is categorized as invasive in some areas.

items.name: Cwebe emerald fern
items.growersTips:
Bring indoors before first frost as this South African native cannot survive UK winter temperatures.
Water thoroughly once the top two centimetres of compost feels dry, reducing to monthly in winter.
Repot in spring only when the vigorous tuberous roots begin to push the plant up out of its pot.
Prune yellowing stems at the very base in spring using sharp shears to encourage fresh green growth.
Grow in a peat-free loam-based compost mixed with one-third grit to ensure essential fast drainage.
items.description: Asparagus densiflorus (among several species colloquially called asparagus ferns; no relation to actual ferns), or the foxtail fern (asparagus) or plume fern, is a variable, evergreen-perennial plant related to cultivated, edible asparagus.

items.name: Asparagus falcatus
items.growersTips:
Bring indoors before first autumn frost as this South African native cannot survive UK winters.
Water thoroughly when the top two inches of compost dry out, then let it drain completely.
Repot in spring using a loam-based John Innes No 2 compost mixed with one-third grit for drainage.
Prune old yellowing climbing stems at the base in spring to encourage vigorous new shoots.
Wear thick leather gloves when handling to protect your hands from its sharp, hooked thorns.
items.description: Asparagus falcatus is a large, thorny, climbing plant of the Asparagus genus, that is indigenous to South Africa and Mozambique. It is often grown as a security hedge in southern Africa.

items.name: Asparagus fallax
items.growersTips:
Plant this rare Canary native in free-draining gritty soil to survive wet UK winters without rot.
Grow in a container to easily move indoors to a greenhouse before the first autumn frosts hit.
Water sparingly in winter but keep soil consistently moist during the active spring growing season.
Propagate by carefully dividing the tuberous root clump in spring just as new shoots start to emerge.
Position in bright filtered light rather than direct UK sun to prevent the delicate foliage burning.
items.description: Asparagus fallax, the Monteverde asparagus, is a species of flowering plant in the family Asparagaceae.

items.name: Asparagus horridus
items.growersTips:
Grow in a terracotta pot with 50% grit to survive wet UK winters and prevent root rot.
Place in your garden's hottest south-facing spot or a cold greenhouse to mimic Mediterranean sun.
Water deeply only when the soil dries out completely, then keep dry throughout the winter months.
Prune back dead or crossing woody stems in late spring once the risk of hard UK frosts has passed.
Wear thick leather gauntlets when handling this shrub to protect your hands from its brutal thorns.
items.description: Asparagus horridus is a species of shrub in the family Asparagaceae. They are climbing plants. They have simple, broad leaves and fleshy fruit. Individuals can grow to 1 m (3.3 ft) tall.

items.name: Asparagus krebsianus
items.growersTips:
Grow in free-draining gritty loam with a pH of 6.5 to 7.5 to prevent winter root rot in wet UK soils.
Position in a sheltered south-facing spot or unheated greenhouse to protect from frost damage.
Water deeply once a week in summer but keep the compost barely damp during damp UK winter months.
Prune back dead woody stems to the base in late spring after the risk of hard frost has passed.
Mulch the root zone with well-rotted manure in April to boost leafy growth of this shrubby species.
items.description: Asparagus krebsianus is a shrub of the Asparagus genus that is native to rocky areas in southern Africa. It ranges from central Malawi through Mozambique to the Northern Provinces, KwaZulu-Natal, and Cape Provinces of South Africa.

items.name: Asparagus lignosus
items.growersTips:
Plant in free-draining sandy loam with grit to prevent winter root rot in wet UK climates.
Sow seeds in spring at a depth of two centimeters in deep pots to accommodate the taproot.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells, allowing the soil to dry out between waterings.
Cut back the woody stems to ground level in late autumn after they turn yellow to prevent pests.
Apply a thick layer of organic mulch in November to protect the crown from severe UK winter frosts.
items.description: Asparagus lignosus ("Katdoring") is a thorny, spindly creeper of the Asparagus genus, that is indigenous to the Western Cape Province of South Africa.

items.name: Asparagus maritimus
items.growersTips:
Grow in free-draining sandy soil with added grit to mimic its native UK coastal shingle habitat.
Plant crowns 15cm deep in trench systems during early spring to protect them from frost damage.
Water young plants weekly in dry summer spells but keep established beds dry to prevent root rot.
Cut yellowing autumn foliage back to 5cm above ground level to prevent overwintering of pests.
Hand-weed beds carefully to avoid damaging the shallow, spreading root systems of the crowns.
items.description: Asparagus maritimus is a dense, thorny, shrub of the genus Asparagus that is indigenous to southern Europe and the Mediterranean. It is dioecious, with male and female flowers borne on separate plants.

items.name: Asparagus mucronatus
items.growersTips:
Grow in free-draining sandy loam with grit to mimic Mediterranean soils and prevent winter root rot.
Plant container-grown shrubs in spring after frosts, keeping the root crown level with the soil.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells, but keep completely dry during wet UK winters.
Prune back dead woody stems in late winter to encourage fresh, ornamental needle-like growth.
Protect young plants from slugs in spring and shield from harsh, freezing winds using fleece.
items.description: Asparagus mucronatus ("Katdoring") is a thorny shrub or creeper of the Asparagus genus, that is indigenous to the southern Cape regions of South Africa.

items.name: Asparagus nesiotes
items.growersTips:
Plant in free-draining sandy loam with grit to survive wet UK winters and prevent crown rot.
Sow seeds in spring at a depth of one centimetre in deep pots to accommodate the taproot.
Water sparingly once established, allowing the soil to dry out completely between waterings.
Cut back dead foliage to ground level in late autumn to prevent overwintering pests.
Protect young shoots from slugs and snails in spring using grit barriers or beer traps.

items.name: Asparagus
items.growersTips:
Prepare a permanent bed by digging in well-rotted manure and grit to ensure excellent winter drainage
Plant bare-root crowns in April fifteen centimetres deep in trenches on a ridge of loose soil
Apply a thick mulch of garden compost in late autumn after the ferns have turned yellow and died back
Cut all yellowed foliage down to ground level in autumn using sharp shears to prevent asparagus beetle
Stop harvesting spears by the twenty-first of June to allow the plant to build energy for next year

items.name: Asparagus prostratus
items.growersTips:
Grow in free-draining sandy soil or shingle to mimic its wild UK maritime cliff habitat.
Water sparingly once established as this native coastal plant is highly drought-tolerant.
Protect young shoots from slugs and snails using grit barriers during damp UK spring weather.
Propagate by dividing the rhizomatous rootstock in early spring just as new growth begins.
Do not harvest spears for eating as this rare native species is grown purely for conservation.

items.name: Asparagus racemosus
items.growersTips:
Grow in pots using free-draining gritty compost so you can move them indoors before autumn frosts.
Water deeply once a week in summer but keep the soil almost dry during the cold winter dormancy.
Prune the thorny climbing stems back by half in late winter to encourage vigorous new spring shoots.
Repot every two years in spring using a mix of John Innes No 3, coarse grit, and well-rotted manure.
Watch for red spider mites under leaves in dry summer weather and mist regularly to boost humidity.

items.name: Asparagus retrofractus
items.growersTips:
Grow in a gritty, free-draining loam to prevent root rot during wet, cold UK winters.
Bring container-grown plants indoors to a bright, frost-free conservatory before November frosts.
Water thoroughly only when the top five centimetres of compost feels dry to the touch.
Prune out old, yellowing woody stems at the base in spring to encourage fresh, vibrant growth.
Inspect the dense, needle-like foliage regularly for spider mites in dry, heated indoor air.

items.name: Red-stemmed asparagus
items.growersTips:
Plant in free-draining sandy loam with grit to prevent winter root rot in wet UK climates.
Position in a sheltered south-facing spot to protect delicate shrubby stems from cold UK winds.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells, keeping the soil barely damp in winter.
Prune back dead woody stems to the base in late autumn to prevent fungal diseases like rust.
Apply a thick mulch of well-rotted manure in early spring to boost growth without touching stems.
items.description: Asparagus rubicundus, known as the red-stemmed asparagus, is a fluffy, thorny shrub of the Asparagus genus, that is endemic to the Cape Provinces of South Africa.

items.name: Asparagus scandens
items.growersTips:
Bring indoors or protect with fleece in winter as this South African native cannot survive UK frosts
Grow in pots of loam-based compost with added grit to ensure the sharp drainage this plant demands
Water moderately in summer but keep the soil barely moist during the cold dormant winter months
Position in bright indirect light or partial shade to prevent the delicate fern-like foliage scorching
Prune out yellowing or dead climbing stems at the base in early spring to encourage fresh green growth

items.name: Asparagus setaceus
items.growersTips:
Keep indoors year-round as a houseplant or move outside only during warm frost-free UK summer months
Water thoroughly once the top two centimetres of compost dry out then empty the drainage saucer
Position in bright indirect light near an east or west window to prevent the delicate fronds burning
Mist the foliage regularly or place on a wet pebble tray to combat dry centrally heated indoor air
Prune yellowing or bare stems right back to the soil level in spring to stimulate fresh green growth

items.name: Asparagus simulans
items.growersTips:
Grow in a warm greenhouse or conservatory as this tender South African native will not survive UK frost
Use a free-draining loam-based compost mixed with plenty of grit to prevent winter root rot indoors
Water moderately in summer but keep the soil almost dry during the cold dark UK winter months
Prune out old yellowing climbing stems in early spring to encourage vigorous new shoots from the base
Check regularly for red spider mite and mealybugs which thrive in dry indoor UK growing conditions

items.name: Asparagus sprengeri
items.growersTips:
Bring indoors before first autumn frost as it cannot survive UK winters below seven degrees Celsius
Water thoroughly once top inch of soil dries then let drain fully to prevent tuberous root rot
Prune yellowing or bare stems at the base in early spring to stimulate lush new feathery growth
Repot in spring only when the vigorous roots crack or push out of the pot using loam-based compost
Position in bright indirect light avoiding direct midday UK summer sun which scorches the fronds

items.name: Asparagus squarrosus
items.growersTips:
Plant in gritty, free-draining soil with added horticultural sand to survive wet UK winters.
Sow seeds in spring at a depth of five millimetres in a heated propagator at twenty degrees.
Water sparingly during summer, allowing the compost to dry out completely between soakings.
Overwinter pots in a frost-free greenhouse or cold frame to protect roots from freezing temperatures.
Prune yellowing stems back to the base in late autumn using sharp, sterilised secateurs.

items.name: Asparagus striatus
items.growersTips:
Grow in a gritty, free-draining loam to prevent root rot during wet, cold UK winters.
Position in a sheltered, south-facing spot or unheated greenhouse to protect from hard frosts.
Water thoroughly only when the top five centimetres of soil has dried out completely.
Prune back dead, yellowing stems in late autumn to maintain shape and prevent fungal disease.
Propagate by dividing the tuberous root clump in spring just as new growth begins to emerge.

items.name: Asparagus suaveolens
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender South African ornamental in pots to easily move indoors before autumn frosts hit UK
Plant in free-draining loam mixed with plenty of grit to prevent winter root rot in wet UK climates
Water thoroughly only when the top two inches of compost feel dry, reducing to monthly in winter
Prune yellowing woody stems at the base in early spring to encourage fresh bright green needle growth
Watch for red spider mite in dry indoor winter air and mist the fine foliage regularly to deter them

items.name: Asparagus virgatus
items.growersTips:
Overwinter in a cold frame or unheated greenhouse to protect young roots from wet UK winter rot.
Sow seeds in spring at a depth of five millimetres using a free-draining gritty loam compost mix.
Water sparingly once established allowing the top three centimetres of soil to dry out completely.
Prune the feathery stems back to the base in early spring before the new bright green shoots emerge.
Incorporate plenty of horticultural grit into heavy clay soils to prevent waterlogging in winter.

items.name: Asperugo
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn at five millimetres deep to mimic natural UK winter chilling for germination.
Water sparingly only during prolonged summer droughts as this plant thrives in dry, gravelly soils.
Grow in poor, well-drained alkaline soil to prevent the weak stems from becoming overly floppy.
Provide a low trellis or plant near sturdier shrubs to support its scrambling, hook-covered stems.
Monitor for powdery mildew in damp UK summers and space plants well to ensure good air circulation.

items.name: False spirea
items.growersTips:
Plant in moisture-retentive, humus-rich soil in partial shade, incorporating plenty of leaf mould.
Water deeply during dry UK summer spells to prevent the foliage from scorching and drying out.
Divide congested clumps every three to four years in early spring to maintain plant vigour.
Leave faded flower heads intact over winter to protect the crown from severe UK frosts.
Plant alongside Hostas and Ferns in damp, shady borders where they thrive in identical conditions.
items.description: Astilbe is a genus of 18 species of rhizomatous flowering plants within the family Saxifragaceae, native to mountain ravines and woodlands in Asia and North America. Some species are known by the common names false goat's beard and false spirea.

items.name: Astilbe × arendsii
items.growersTips:
Plant in moisture-retentive, humus-rich soil, incorporating well-rotted manure to prevent drying out.
Position in partial shade to protect the delicate feathery plumes from the drying UK midday sun.
Water deeply during dry summer spells to prevent the foliage from crisping and browning at the edges.
Divide congested clumps every three to four years in early spring to maintain plant vigour and bloom.
Leave the spent flower heads over winter to provide structural interest and protect the crown from frost.

items.name: Astilbe chinensis
items.growersTips:
Plant in moisture-retentive clay or loam enriched with leafmould to prevent the soil drying out.
Water deeply during dry UK summer spells to prevent leaf scorch, keeping the soil constantly damp.
Divide congested clumps every three to four years in early spring to maintain plant vigour and size.
Plant alongside Hostas or Rodgersia in partial shade to create a self-shading damp-loving canopy.
Leave faded bronze flower heads intact over winter to provide structural interest in frosty gardens.
items.description: Astilbe chinensis, commonly known as false goat's beard, tall false-buck's-beard or Chinese astilbe, is a species of flowering plant in the saxifrage family, Saxifragaceae. It is a perennial herb that grows near shaded streams and rivers. It is also commonly grown in shade gardens.

items.name: False spirea
items.growersTips:
Plant in moisture-retentive, acidic to neutral soil enriched with plenty of well-rotted manure.
Water deeply twice a week during dry UK summers to prevent the leaf margins from browning and curling.
Divide the root clumps every three to four years in early spring to maintain flowering vigour.
Mulch annually in March with leaf mould to protect shallow roots from drying out in spring sun.
Plant alongside Hostas or Rodgersias in dappled shade to shield the delicate fronds from midday sun.

items.name: Astilbe simplicifolia
items.growersTips:
Incorporate plenty of leaf mould or well-rotted manure to keep UK clay soils moisture-retentive.
Plant crowns shallowly with the buds just below the soil surface to prevent crown rot in wet winters.
Water deeply twice a week during dry UK summers to stop the delicate crinkled leaves from scorching.
Divide congested clumps every three years in early spring just as the bronze-tinted shoots emerge.
Plant alongside Hostas or ferns to provide the dappled shade needed to protect the pale pink blooms.

items.name: Astilbe thunbergii
items.growersTips:
Plant in moisture-retentive, acidic to neutral soil enriched with plenty of well-rotted manure.
Water deeply twice a week during dry UK summers to prevent the delicate leaf margins from scorching.
Divide congested clumps every three years in early spring to maintain vigor and flowering potential.
Mulch annually in autumn with leaf mould to protect shallow roots from hard winter frosts and drying.
Position in partial shade alongside Hostas and Ferns to shelter the tall arching stems from wind.

items.name: Astilboides tabularis
items.growersTips:
Plant in deep, rich, moisture-retentive soil in partial to full shade to prevent leaf scorch.
Water copiously during dry summer spells to keep the soil consistently damp but not waterlogged.
Shelter from strong winds to protect the massive, delicate umbrella-like leaves from tearing.
Apply a thick mulch of leaf mould or well-rotted manure every spring to retain vital soil moisture.
Protect emerging spring buds from late frosts using horticultural fleece or a layer of dry bracken.

items.name: Ateleia herbert-smithii
items.growersTips:
Sow Ateleia seeds indoors in April at 1cm depth in peat-free compost to bypass late UK spring frosts
Water young plants weekly at the base to keep soil moist but prevent waterlogging in damp UK summers
Incorporate grit into heavy UK clay soil before planting to ensure the sharp drainage this legume needs
Watch for slugs and snails on tender new shoots during wet May weather and protect with organic grit
Plant alongside nitrogen-loving leafy greens to benefit from this annual legume's soil-fixing traits

items.name: Silene armeria

Sow seeds shallowly in April at a depth of two millimetres into well-drained, gritty garden soil.
Position in full sun to prevent the weak stems of this annual from flopping in damp UK summers.
Water seedlings sparingly once established, allowing the top soil to dry out to prevent root rot.
Deadhead spent pink blooms weekly in July to prolong the flowering window before the plant dies.
Sow alongside companion plants like English lavender to support pollinators in dry gravel borders.

items.name: Babiana ambigua

Position pots in the brightest south-facing spot to mimic South African sun and trigger flowering.

items.name: Babiana angustifolia

Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.

items.name: Babiana bainesii

Water weekly during the spring growing season but keep completely dry during their summer dormancy.
Position in the sunniest south-facing spot available to mimic their hot South African habitat.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.

items.name: Babiana blanda
items.growersTips:
Plant Babiana blanda corms 8cm deep in autumn using pots you can move indoors to survive UK frosts.
Mix equal parts grit and peat-free compost to ensure the sharp drainage these South African bulbs need.
Water weekly during spring growth but keep the soil completely dry during their summer dormant phase.
Position pots in your garden's hottest, most south-facing sun trap to mimic their native climate.
Overwinter pots in a cold greenhouse or unheated conservatory to protect corms from wet winter rot.

items.name: Babiana brachystachys
items.growersTips:
Plant corms 8cm deep in autumn using a gritty, free-draining loam to prevent winter rot in wet soils.

Water sparingly from autumn to spring, then increase watering only when active leaf growth begins.
Position in the sunniest, most sheltered south-facing spot in your garden to mimic South Africa.
Allow the foliage to die back naturally in summer to feed the bulb for the next spring flowering.

items.name: Babiana cinnamomea

Plant corms in autumn 8cm deep in gritty, sharply draining soil to prevent winter rot in wet UK soil.

Sow seeds in autumn in a cold frame using a sandy compost mix and expect flowers in three years.

items.name: Babiana dregei
items.growersTips:
Plant Babiana dregei corms 8cm deep in autumn using a mix of loam, sharp sand, and grit for drainage.
Keep the soil moist from autumn to spring, then dry out completely in summer during dormancy.

Position in the sunniest, most sheltered south-facing spot to mimic their hot South African habitat.

items.name: Babiana ecklonii
items.growersTips:
Plant Babiana corms 8cm deep in autumn using a gritty compost mix to ensure sharp winter drainage.
Grow them in pots to easily move them into a frost-free greenhouse or conservatory over UK winters.
Water weekly during the spring growing season but keep the soil completely dry during summer dormancy.
Position pots in the sunniest south-facing spot of your garden to mimic their native South Africa.
Check foliage regularly for aphids and red spider mites when growing them under glass or in cold frames.

items.name: Babiana engysiphon
items.growersTips:
Plant corms in autumn 8cm deep in gritty, free-draining soil to prevent winter rot in wet UK climates.
