Cut faded flower spikes down to the base in late summer to redirect energy into new offset pups.
Watch for slugs and snails hiding in the dense lower foliage during damp UK spring weather.

items.name: Wood betony
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn outdoors as they require winter cold stratification to germinate in UK spring.
Plant in moisture-retentive, neutral to acidic clay or loam soil, avoiding dry chalky garden beds.
Grow alongside companion plants like Succisa pratensis or Origanum vulgare to attract UK pollinators.
Cut back the faded flower spikes to the ground in October to keep the basal foliage clump tidy.
Divide established clumps every three years in early spring to maintain plant vigour and health.

items.name: Bobgunnia madagascariensis
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in April at a depth of two centimeters using a heated propagator set to twenty degrees
Plant out in late May after frosts in a south-facing border with grit added for sharp drainage
Water deeply once a week at the base during dry summer spells to establish the deep taproot system
Watch for slugs and snails on young spring shoots by using beer traps or physical copper barriers
Grow alongside nitrogen-loving leafy greens to benefit from this legume's natural soil enrichment

items.name: Bocconia frutescens
items.growersTips:
Plant in deep fertile loam in spring, burying the crown just level with the soil surface.
Position in full sun sheltered from strong UK winds to prevent the tall hollow stems from snapping.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells to support the massive tropical foliage.
Cut the faded flower stems back to the base in late autumn and mulch heavily to protect from frost.
Watch for slugs and snails on young spring shoots and apply organic control early in the season.

items.name: Bocconia frutescens
items.growersTips:
Grow in a large pot to easily move it into a frost-free greenhouse or conservatory for UK winters.
Plant in free-draining loam enriched with grit to prevent winter root rot in wet UK soils.
Prune back hard in early spring to encourage fresh architectural foliage and manage its height.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells but keep the soil barely damp throughout winter.
Wear thick gloves when pruning to avoid skin irritation from its toxic orange-yellow sap.

items.name: Northern false coolwort
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist humus-rich soil in partial shade to mimic its native damp woodland canyon habitat
Water consistently during dry UK summers to keep the soil evenly moist but never waterlogged
Protect the delicate foliage from strong winds by planting near sheltered north-facing walls
Propagate by dividing the rhizomatous rootstock in early spring just as new growth begins
Watch for slugs and snails in damp spring weather as they target the tender emerging shoots

items.name: Northern false coolwort
items.growersTips:
Grow in a moist, shaded rock garden or crevice using gritty, humus-rich, neutral to acid soil.
Water regularly in summer to mimic its native damp cliffs, but ensure sharp drainage to prevent rot.
Sow seeds in cold frames during autumn to allow natural winter chilling for spring germination.
Protect the delicate foliage from slugs and snails during wet UK spring nights using organic grit.
Divide established clumps in early spring just as new growth begins to maintain plant vigour.

items.name: Borage
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds directly in spring at 1.5cm depth in free-draining soil to avoid taproot transplant shock.
Position in full sun to maximise nectar production for UK bumblebees and encourage self-seeding.
Cut back hard after the first summer flowering to stimulate a second flush of fresh edible leaves.
Plant alongside strawberries to improve fruit set and deter common UK pests like tomato hornworm.
Grow the white-flowered Alba cultivar in damp UK summers as it resists powdery mildew better.

items.name: Boykinia lycoctonifolia
items.growersTips:
Plant in moisture-retentive humus-rich soil in dappled shade to mimic native UK woodland edges.
Water consistently during dry summer spells to prevent the delicate foliage from crisping at the tips.
Divide congested clumps in early spring just as new growth begins to maintain plant vigour.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit or beer traps.
Combine with ferns and hostas in damp shady borders for contrasting foliage textures.

items.name: Boykinia aconitifolia
items.growersTips:
Plant in moisture-retentive, humus-rich acidic soil in partial shade to mimic UK woodland edges.
Water consistently during dry summer spells to keep the soil damp but avoid waterlogged conditions.
Divide congested clumps in early spring just as new growth begins to maintain plant vigour.
Position alongside Astilbes or Hostas in damp shade to create a contrasting foliage tapestry.
Protect emerging spring foliage from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.

items.name: Boykinia major
items.growersTips:
Plant in moisture-retentive, humus-rich acidic soil in a cool, dappled shade spot to mimic woodland.
Water deeply during dry UK summers to keep the soil consistently damp but never waterlogged.
Divide congested clumps in early spring just as new growth begins to maintain plant vigour.
Protect emerging spring foliage from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.
Partner with Astilbe or Hostas in bog gardens for contrasting foliage textures and shared care.

items.name: Boykinia occidentalis
items.growersTips:
Plant in moisture-retentive, humus-rich acid to neutral soil in a sheltered, fully shaded border.
Water weekly during dry UK summers to keep the soil consistently damp, mimicking its native creek beds.
Sow seeds in cold frames during autumn, as they require winter chill to germinate the following spring.
Cut back the faded flower stems and dead foliage to the ground in late autumn to prevent crown rot.
Watch for slugs and snails in damp spring weather, protecting the emerging tender bronze foliage.

items.name: Boykinia richardsonii
items.growersTips:
Plant in moisture-retentive, humus-rich acidic soil in partial shade to mimic its native stream banks.
Water consistently during dry UK summers to keep the soil constantly damp but never waterlogged.
Divide congested clumps in early spring just as new growth begins to maintain plant vigour.
Protect the emerging spring foliage from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.
Plant alongside Astilbe or hostas in a bog garden to complement its white summer flower spikes.

items.name: Boykinia rotundifolia
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist humus-rich soil in partial shade to mimic its native damp woodland ravine habitat.
Sow seeds in pots in a cold frame during autumn to allow natural winter chilling for germination.
Water consistently during dry UK summer spells to prevent the large rounded leaves from scorching.
Divide established clumps in early spring just as new growth begins to maintain plant vigour.
Plant alongside Astilbe or Hostas in bog gardens where soil never dries out completely.

items.name: Brachypeza semiteretifolia
items.growersTips:
Grow Brachypeza in a warm UK greenhouse or indoor terrarium to maintain the required high humidity.
Mount these epiphytic orchids on cork bark with sphagnum moss rather than planting them in soil.
Water with tepid rainwater daily in summer, allowing the roots to dry completely by nightfall.
Position in bright, indirect light, avoiding direct midday summer sun to prevent leaf scorching.
Maintain winter temperatures above fifteen degrees Celsius to prevent root rot and leaf drop.

items.name: Brachysola coerulea
items.growersTips:
Grow Brachysola in free-draining gravelly loam to prevent winter root rot in wet UK climates.
Position in a sheltered south-facing border to maximise summer sun and protect from cold winds.
Water sparingly once established, allowing the gritty soil to dry out fully between waterings.
Prune lightly in late spring after frosts pass to shape the shrub and encourage fresh new growth.
Overwinter young plants in a cold frame or unheated greenhouse to shield them from severe UK frosts.

items.name: Brachystegia nigerica
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in April at a depth of 1.5cm using a heated propagator to mimic tropical warmth.
Plant out in June after the last frost in a south-facing border with grit added for sharp drainage.
Water deeply once a week during dry UK summer spells, allowing the sandy soil to dry out between watering.
Protect young seedlings from slugs and snails using beer traps or copper tape during damp May nights.
Grow alongside nitrogen-loving ornamental grasses to complement this legume's natural soil chemistry.

items.name: Brachystegia bakeriana
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in early spring at a depth of two centimetres using a heated propagator at twenty degrees
Grow in free-draining sandy loam amended with grit to mimic dry African soils and prevent root rot
Water sparingly once a week during summer, allowing the compost to dry out completely between sessions
Position in the sunniest south-facing spot or a conservatory to maximise crucial UK summer heat
Protect young plants from slugs and snails using beer traps or copper tape during damp spring nights

items.name: Brachystegia boehmii
items.growersTips:
Grow in a heated greenhouse or conservatory as this tropical tree cannot survive UK winter frosts
Sow seeds in spring at a depth of two centimetres in a free-draining sandy loam potting compost
Water only when the top three centimetres of soil are dry to prevent root rot in damp UK weather
Position in the brightest south-facing spot possible to mimic its native African sunlight levels
Apply a low-nitrogen liquid fertiliser monthly during summer to support its nitrogen-fixing roots

items.name: Brachystegia glaucescens
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender African legume in containers of gritty loam to move indoors before autumn frosts.
Sow seeds in spring at a depth of two centimeters using a heated propagator set to twenty degrees.
Water only when the top three centimeters of soil dries out to prevent root rot in cool UK weather.
Position in the sunniest south facing spot available to mimic its native high light requirements.
Feed monthly with a low nitrogen fertilizer during summer to support foliage without scorching roots.

items.name: Brachystegia laurentii
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender African legume in a heated greenhouse or conservatory to survive UK winter frosts.
Use a highly acidic, free-draining sandy loam soil mix mimicking its native tropical riverine banks.
Water thoroughly with tepid rainwater only when the top three inches of potting compost dry out.
Prune lightly in late spring after new growth starts to maintain a manageable indoor shrub size.
Watch closely for glasshouse red spider mites and mealybugs under the leaves during dry summer heat.
items.description: Brachystegia laurentii, a plant in the family Fabaceae, is a species of large tree found in western Cameroon, Gabon, Equatorial Guinea, the Democratic Republic of the Congo and the Republic of the Congo. It has a dense, umbrella-shaped crown. The wood is known as bomanga and has many uses in building and construction.

items.name: Brachystegia spiciformis
items.growersTips:
Grow in a heated conservatory or greenhouse as this African native cannot survive UK winter frosts.
Use a very free-draining cactus compost mix with added grit to prevent root rot in damp UK winters.
Water only when the soil dries out completely, reducing to once a month during the winter dormancy.
Position in the brightest spot possible, ideally a south-facing glasshouse, to mimic savanna sun.
Prune lightly in late spring only to control size, avoiding hard cuts into old wood which stunts it.
items.description:
Brachystegia spiciformis, commonly known as zebrawood, or msasa, is a medium-sized African tree having compound leaves and racemes of small fragrant green flowers. The tree is broad and has a distinctive amber and wine red colour when the young leaves sprout during spring (August–September). It grows in savanna, both open woodland and closed woodland of Southern and Eastern Africa, mostly Tanzania, Zambia, Zimbabwe, Malawi and Mozambique.
The word msasa is commonly used as a proper name in African place names. The word also means 'rough plant' in Swahili.
Other common names: mundu, myombo, mto

items.name: Brickellia veronicaefolia
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in March at a depth of two millimetres to combat the cool wet British spring.
Plant out in late May in a south-facing border with grit-amended soil to ensure sharp drainage.
Water sparingly once established, allowing the top five centimetres of soil to dry out completely.
Pinch out the growing tips in June to encourage a bushier habit and increase the flower count.
Watch for slugs and snails on young spring shoots by using beer traps or physical barriers.
items.description: Brickellia is a North American genus of about 100 to 110 species of plants in the family Asteraceae, known commonly as brickellbushes. They are found in Canada, the United States, Mexico, and Central America. Many species are native to the American southwest, especially Texas. Brickellia is among the more basal lineages of the Eupatorieae and should not be assigned to a subtribe pending further research.

items.name: Broussaisia
items.growersTips:
Grow in a sheltered woodland border with acidic, humus-rich soil to prevent leaf yellowing.
Provide winter protection with a thick mulch layer to shield roots from severe UK frosts.
Water weekly with rainwater during dry summer spells to keep the moisture-loving roots damp.
Prune lightly in late spring after frost risk passes, removing only dead or damaged stems.
Plant alongside shade-loving ferns and hostas which thrive in the same damp, dappled light.
items.description: Broussaisia arguta, the kanawao, is a species of perennial flowering plant in the Hydrangea family, Hydrangeaceae, that is endemic to Hawaiʻi. It is the only species in the monotypic genus Broussaisia.

items.name: Brownea ariza
items.growersTips:
Grow Brownea grandiceps in a heated conservatory or greenhouse kept above fifteen degrees Celsius.
Sow seeds in spring at a depth of two centimeters in a heated propagator with bottom heat.
Water with tepid rainwater to keep the acidic, peat-free loam-based compost consistently moist.
Mist the foliage daily with soft water to maintain the high humidity this tropical plant requires.
Feed fortnightly in spring and summer using a high-potassium liquid fertiliser at half strength.
items.description: Brownea is a genus of flowering plants in the pea family (Fabaceae), subfamily Detarioideae. The genus includes about 22 species native to tropical regions of the Americas. The species are shrubs and trees growing to 20 m tall. Species range from Honduras through southern Central America and northern South America to Peru and northern Brazil, and to Trinidad and Tobago and the Windward Islands in the Caribbean. Species are typically understorey trees or shrubs in lowland tropical rain forest.Species

items.name: Brownea coccinea
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender tropical shrub in a heated conservatory or greenhouse kept above fifteen Celsius.
Water with tepid rainwater to keep the soil consistently moist but never waterlogged or soggy.
Plant in a large pot using a peat-free loam-based compost mixed with plenty of perlite for drainage.
Prune lightly immediately after flowering in late summer to maintain shape and remove dead wood.
Mist the foliage daily during dry summer months to simulate the high humidity of its native jungle.
items.description: Brownea coccinea is a species of small evergreen tree with compound leaves and clusters of bright scarlet flowers in the subfamily Detarioideae of the family Fabaceae. Common names include scarlet flame bean, mountain rose, rose of Venezuela and cooper hoop. The species is native to Colombia, Ecuador and Venezuela.

items.name: Brownea grandiceps
items.growersTips:
Grow this tropical shrub in a heated conservatory or greenhouse kept strictly above fifteen Celsius.
Plant in a large pot with acidic, loam-based compost mixed with plenty of perlite for fast drainage.
Water with tepid rainwater to keep soil consistently moist but never waterlogged to prevent rot.
Maintain high humidity above sixty percent by placing the pot on a tray of wet clay pebbles.
Prune lightly only in late spring after flowering to shape the shrub and remove dead wood.
items.description: Brownea grandiceps is a species of tree in the family Fabaceae. Its common names include the rose of Venezuela and the scarlet flame bean. It originated in South America but is now widely grown as a decorative tree in tropical gardens.

items.name: Brownea leucantha
items.growersTips:
Grow this tropical shrub in a heated conservatory or greenhouse kept strictly above fifteen Celsius.
Plant in a large pot with acidic, loam-based compost mixed with plenty of perlite for fast drainage.
Water with tepid rainwater to keep soil consistently damp but never waterlogged to prevent root rot.
Maintain high humidity above sixty percent by placing the pot on a tray of wet clay leca pebbles.
Prune lightly immediately after flowering in late summer to shape and remove dead wood safely.
items.description: Brownea leucantha, called roso blanco, is a species of flowering plant in the genus Brownea, native to Peru and Venezuela. It is the emblematic state tree of Miranda, Venezuela. It can be distinguished from other members of its genus by its white flowers.

items.name: Brownea macrophylla
items.growersTips:
Grow this tropical shrub in a heated conservatory or greenhouse with minimum winter temperatures of 15C.
Water with tepid rainwater to keep the soil consistently moist but never waterlogged or soggy.
Plant in a large pot using a peat-free loam-based compost mixed with plenty of grit for drainage.
Mist the foliage daily or use a humidifier to maintain the high humidity this rainforest plant needs.
Prune lightly immediately after flowering in late summer to control size and remove dead wood.
items.description: Brownea macrophylla is a tree in the legume family Fabaceae. The specific epithet macrophylla means 'large-leaved'.

items.name: Browneopsis ucayalina
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in early April at a depth of two centimetres using a heated propagator at twentyC
Grow in a peat-free loam compost mixed with thirty percent grit to ensure the sharp drainage needed
Water only when the top three centimetres of soil is dry to prevent root rot in cool UK summers
Position containers in a south-facing conservatory or greenhouse to maximise essential sun and heat
Check regularly for glasshouse red spider mite and mist the foliage weekly to maintain humidity
items.description: Browneopsis is a genus of flowering plants in the family Fabaceae. There are about 8 species of trees native to South America, ranging from Panama through Colombia and Ecuador to Peru and northern Brazil. Species typically grow in lowland tropical rain forests, including inundated and terra firme forests, and in sub-montane forests in the foothills of the Andes.

items.name: Brunnera macrophylla
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist but well-drained soil in full shade to prevent the delicate leaves from scorching.
Mulch annually in spring with leaf mould or well-rotted manure to retain crucial woodland moisture.
Cut back faded flower stems to the base in July to encourage a fresh flush of healthy new foliage.
Protect young spring shoots from slugs and snails using beer traps or organic wool pellets.
Divide congested clumps in early autumn or spring to propagate and maintain plant vigour.
items.description: Brunnera is a genus of flowering plants in the family Boraginaceae. They are rhizomatous perennials, native to the woodlands of Eastern Europe and North West Asia. They have hairy leaves and sprays of blue flowers in spring. Numerous cultivars are available, which are valued as groundcover in dappled shade. Some possess variegated foliage. The best known species is B. macrophylla, known as Siberian bugloss.

items.name: Brunnera macrophylla
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist well-drained soil in partial shade to prevent the delicate leaves from scorching.
Water young plants regularly in summer to establish a deep root system in damp UK woodland borders.
Cut back faded flower stems in summer to encourage a fresh flush of attractive heart-shaped foliage.
Protect young spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit or beer traps in damp weather.
Divide congested clumps in early autumn or spring to propagate and maintain vigorous growth.
items.description: Brunnera macrophylla, the Siberian bugloss, great forget-me-not, largeleaf brunnera or heartleaf, is a species of flowering plant in the family Boraginaceae, native to the Caucasus. It is a hardy, rhizomatous, herbaceous perennial, that can reach from 12 to 18 inches in height, and carries basal, simple cordate leaves on slender stems. Sprays of small blue flowers, similar to those seen in the related forget-me-nots, are borne from mid-Spring, and bloom for eight to ten weeks.

items.name: Bufonia tenuifolia
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn in well-drained gritty soil to mimic the cold winter stratification they need.
Grow in full sun in a raised bed or rockery to prevent winter wet from rotting the delicate roots.
Water sparingly once established, allowing the gritty substrate to dry out completely between feeds.
Protect young seedlings from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers in damp UK spring weather.
Sow alongside companion plants like wild thyme or sedums that share its love for poor, alkaline soil.
items.description: Bufonia is a genus of flowering plants belonging to the family Caryophyllaceae.

items.name: Bulbophyllinae
items.growersTips:
Grow in shallow pans of open bark and sphagnum moss to match their shallow-rooting creeping habit.
Keep winter temperatures above twelve Celsius and water weekly to prevent pseudobulbs from shrivelling.
Position under fleece or shade cloth in summer to protect delicate leaves from direct UK sunlight.
Water with rainwater only to prevent salt build-up on the sensitive, thread-like roots of species.
Watch for mealybugs in the tight crevices between pseudobulbs and treat with organic insecticidal soap.
items.description: Dendrobieae is a tribe in the subfamily Epidendroideae, in the family Orchidaceae. The Dendrobieae are mostly tropical, epiphytic orchids which contain pseudobulbs.

items.name: Burkea africana
items.growersTips:
Sow Burkea seeds indoors in April at a depth of 1cm using a heated propagator to mimic warm climates
Transplant seedlings outdoors in June into free-draining sandy loam after the last frost has passed
Water sparingly at the base only when the top 5cm of soil is dry to prevent root rot in damp UK summers
Position in the sunniest south-facing border or against a warm wall to maximise limited UK heat
Protect young plants from slugs using beer traps as damp UK spring weather makes them highly vulnerable
items.description:
Burkea may refer to:Burkea (plant), a genus of flowering plants in the family Fabaceae
Burkea (microsporidian), a fungus genus in the division Microsporidia

items.name: Peacock flower
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in March at a depth of two centimetres after soaking them in warm water for a day.
Plant out in late May in a south-facing border with grit added to the soil to ensure fast drainage.
Water young plants deeply once a week at the base during dry summer spells to establish deep roots.
Pinch out the growing tips when seedlings reach fifteen centimetres high to encourage bushy growth.
Watch for glasshouse red spider mite if growing under glass or in a very sheltered urban courtyard.
items.description: Caesalpinia is a genus of flowering plants in the family Fabaceae. It includes 10 species which range from southeastern Mexico through Central America to Colombia, Ecuador, and Peru, and to Cuba, Hispaniola, and the Bahamas.

items.name: Caesalpinia coriaria
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender Caribbean shrub in a pot of gritty loam to move indoors before autumn frosts hit.
Water sparingly in winter but drench thoroughly once soil dries completely during summer active growth.
Prune lightly in late spring only to shape the canopy and remove winter-damaged or crossing stems.
Blend thirty percent horticultural grit into peat-free compost to ensure the rapid drainage it needs.
Position in your hottest south-facing suntrap or unheated greenhouse to mimic its native warmth.
items.description: Libidibia coriaria, synonym Caesalpinia coriaria, is a leguminous tree or large shrub native to the Caribbean, Central America, Mexico, and northern and western South America. Common names include divi-divi, cascalote, guaracabuya, guatapana, nacascol, tan yong, and watapana (Aruba).

items.name: Caesalpinia mexicana
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in March at a depth of 1cm after soaking them in warm water for twenty-four hours
Grow in pots of free-draining loam-based compost with added grit to allow winter greenhouse shelter
Water deeply only when the top five centimetres of soil has dried out to prevent root rot in wet UKs
Position in the sunniest south-facing spot against a brick wall to maximise summer heat accumulation
Prune lightly in late spring to remove frost-damaged stems and maintain a compact container shape
items.description: Erythrostemon mexicanus, formerly Caesalpinia mexicana, is a species of plant in the genus Erythrostemon, within the pea family, Fabaceae. Common names include Mexican Bird of Paradise, Mexican holdback, Mexican caesalpinia, and tabachín del monte. It is native to the extreme lower Rio Grande Valley of Texas and to parts of Mexico: in the northeast and further south along the Gulf coast as well as the Pacific coast in Nayarit, Jalisco, Colima, and a small portion of Sinaloa.

items.name: Peacock flower
items.growersTips:
Grow in containers using free-draining loam-based compost with added grit to move indoors for winter
Sow seeds in spring at a depth of one centimetre after soaking them in warm water for twenty-four hours
Water thoroughly only when the top two inches of soil are dry to prevent root rot in cool UK summers
Place pots in the hottest south-facing spot or greenhouse to mimic the heat of its native climate
Prune back lightly in early spring to encourage bushy growth and more flowers on the new wood
items.description: Caesalpinia pulcherrima is a species of flowering plant in the pea family Fabaceae, native to the tropics and subtropics of the Americas. It could be native to the West Indies, but its exact origin is unknown due to widespread cultivation. Common names for this species include poinciana, peacock flower, red bird of paradise, Mexican bird of paradise, dwarf poinciana, pride of Barbados, flos pavonis, and flamboyant-de-jardin. The Hawaiian name for this plant is ʻohai aliʻi.

items.name: Caladeniinae
items.growersTips:
Plant tubers in late summer at a depth of twice their height in a highly gritty, free-draining mix.
Water sparingly in autumn to trigger growth, keeping the compost damp but never soggy over winter.
Keep pots in a cool, frost-free greenhouse or cold frame to protect from wet UK winter freezes.
Apply a very weak, low-nitrogen orchid fertilizer only during the active winter growing phase.
Repot annually during the summer dormant period when the compost is completely dry to prevent rot.
items.description: Caladeniinae is an orchid subtribe in the tribe Diurideae.

items.name: California macrophylla
items.growersTips:
Plant this native annual in autumn or early spring at a shallow depth of just two millimetres.
Sow in poor, sharply draining sandy soil to prevent winter root rot in wet UK climates.
Position in full south-facing sun to mimic its native dry grassland habitat and boost flowering.
Water sparingly only during prolonged dry summer spells, allowing the soil to dry out completely.
Collect the corkscrew-like seed pods in late summer before they self-disperse across your borders.
items.description: California macrophylla, commonly known as roundleaf stork's bill, is a species of flowering plant in the geranium family, Geraniaceae. It was formerly placed in the genus Erodium, but was later placed in a monotypic genus of its own named California.

items.name: Callicarpa acuminata
items.growersTips:
Plant in a warm sheltered south-facing spot to protect young spring growth from late UK frosts.
Incorporate well-rotted organic matter into clay soils to ensure excellent winter drainage.
Prune stems back to a low permanent framework in early spring to encourage vigorous berrying wood.
Water deeply during dry summer spells to prevent premature berry drop before autumn colour develops.
Grow alongside evergreen sarcococca to provide winter contrast and shelter from cold winds.
items.description: Callicarpa acuminata is a species of beautyberry native to Latin America from Mexico to Bolivia. Unlike the other species of this genus, C. acuminata produces small berry-like fruits which can be dark-purple or dark blue-purple. The fruit can sometimes be white. The flowers blooms are white. The fruit grow in tight clumps and sometimes resemble grapes. They are cultivated as garden trees.

items.name: Callicarpa americana
items.growersTips:
Plant in full sun against a south-facing wall to ensure enough summer heat for berry production.
Prune hard in early spring down to a low permanent framework to encourage vigorous berry-bearing wood.
Grow in acidic to neutral soil, adding compost to replicate their native woodland floor conditions.
Plant in groups of three to ensure cross-pollination, as single shrubs often berry poorly in the UK.
Water deeply during dry summer spells to prevent the developing autumn berries from dropping early.
items.description: Callicarpa americana, commonly called the American beautyberry, is an open-habitat, native shrub of the Southern United States which is often grown as an ornamental in gardens and yards. American beautyberries produce large clusters of purple berries, which birds and deer eat, thus distributing the seeds.

items.name: Callicarpa ampla
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender species in a large pot with loam-based compost to move indoors before autumn frosts.
Water deeply once a week in summer but keep the soil barely damp during its winter dormant period.
Prune stems back to a low permanent framework in early spring to stimulate new berry-bearing wood.
Blend grit and composted bark into heavy clay soils to ensure the sharp drainage this plant needs.
Position in a south-facing sheltered spot against a warm brick wall to maximise summer heat for fruit.
items.description: Callicarpa ampla, also called the capa rose, is a species of plant in the family Lamiaceae. It is found in Puerto Rico in the Caribbean region. It is threatened by habitat loss and is a critically endangered plant species.

items.name: Bodinier's beautyberry
items.growersTips:
Plant at least two Callicarpa bodinieri Profusion together to ensure successful cross-pollination.
Prune in early spring by cutting back one-third of old stems to the base to stimulate new wood.
Grow in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to maximise autumn berry production in UK weather.
Mulch annually in spring with well-rotted manure to retain moisture during dry UK summer spells.
Watch for capsid bugs in summer which damage young leaves and distort the autumn berry display.
items.description: Callicarpa bodinieri, or Bodinier's beautyberry, is a species of flowering plant in the genus Callicarpa of the family Lamiaceae, native to West and Central China. Growing to 3 m (10 ft) tall by 2.5 m (8 ft) wide, it is an upright deciduous shrub with dark green leaves turning red in autumn (fall). In midsummer, small lilac flowers are produced in the leaf axils. But it is grown in gardens primarily for its small, decorative purple berries in tight clusters in autumn.

items.name: Callicarpa cathayana
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist well-drained acidic to neutral soil enriched with leaf mould to prevent chlorosis.
Position in full sun sheltered from cold winds to ensure successful autumn berry production in the UK.
Plant at least two specimens close together to ensure cross-pollination and a heavy crop of berries.
Prune hard in early spring by cutting back to a low permanent framework to encourage vigorous growth.
Mulch annually in spring with composted bark to retain moisture and protect roots from winter frost.
items.description: Callicarpa cathayana is a species of beautyberry. It is grown in gardens and parks as an ornamental plant for its decorative pink flowers and berries. The purple berries are a drupe. They are not edible for humans. Birds eat the berries and disperse the seeds. The species are endangered in the wild. Callicarpa cathayana is native to China.

items.name: Callicarpa dichotoma
items.growersTips:
Plant in full sun and shelter from cold winds to ensure the best autumn berry display in UK climates
Prune stems back to a low permanent framework in early spring to stimulate vigorous berry-bearing wood
Grow in moist but well-drained acidic to neutral soil, adding leaf mould to mimic woodland conditions
Plant at least two shrubs close together to maximize cross-pollination and guarantee heavy fruiting
Water deeply during dry summer spells to prevent the developing autumn berries from dropping early
items.description: Callicarpa dichotoma is a species of flowering plant in the family Lamiaceae. It is sometimes referred to by the common names purple beautyberry or early amethyst. They are cultivated as garden shrubs. The flowers are pink to white. The berries which are small drupes are purple. The fruits grow closely together in large clusters. The fruit provides food for wild life. The berries are edible and have a mild taste. This species can be found in China, Vietnam, Korea and Japan.

items.name: Callicarpa formosana

items.description: Callicarpa pedunculata, commonly known as beautyberry or velvet-leaf, is a species of plant in the mint and sage family Lamiaceae. It is native to tropical areas from northeast India and southeast China, through the Philippines and New Guinea to eastern Australia. It was first described by Scottish botanist Robert Brown in 1810.

items.name: East Asian beautyberry

Prune hard in early spring back to a low permanent framework to stimulate vigorous berry-bearing wood.
Mulch annually in autumn with well-rotted manure to retain moisture in sandy or chalky UK soils.

Water deeply during dry summer spells in the first two years to establish a resilient root system.
items.description: Callicarpa japonica, commonly known as East Asian beautyberry or Japanese beautyberry, is a plant in the mint family.

items.name: Callicarpa kwangtungensis

Prune back hard in early spring to encourage vigorous new growth which bears the best autumn berries.

Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells to prevent premature berry drop in autumn.
Grow near evergreen shrubs like Sarcococca to provide a dark backdrop that highlights the purple berries.
items.description: Callicarpa kwangtungensis is a species of beautyberry. The tree is introduced in Europe as an ornamental plant. The fruit is light-pink and grows in small clusters. The flowers can range from pink to white. It is endemic to China. The berries are very bitter and inedible for human use. Birds and other wild life won't eat them unless all their food sources are depleted.

items.name: Callicarpa macrophylla
items.growersTips:
Plant in a sheltered south-facing spot to protect young spring growth from late UK frosts.
Prune stems back to a low permanent framework in March to promote vigorous berry-bearing new wood.

items.description: Callicarpa macrophylla is a species of beautyberry native to the Indian subcontinent. Its fruits are small white drupes.

Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells to prevent premature berry drop in September.

items.description: Callicarpa mollis is a species of beautyberry that is cultivated and grown in gardens and parks as ornamental plant. It has purple flowers. It is found in Korea and Japan.

Plant in moist but well-drained acidic to neutral soil enriched with plenty of composted bracken
Prune stems back to a low permanent framework in early spring to stimulate vigorous berry-bearing wood
Group three plants together to ensure successful cross-pollination for a heavy crop of purple berries
Protect young spring shoots from late frosts using horticultural fleece during cold UK nights
items.description: Callicarpa nudiflora is a species of beautyberry that is grown as an ornamental plant. It is native to Southeast Asia. It is a perennial evergreen shrub that grows most prevalently in the Guangdong, Guanxi, and Hainan Provinces. In China it is known as Luo-hua-zi-zhu and is a staple in Chinese folk medicine utilized for its anti-inflammatory, antibacterial, cytotoxic, and hemostatic abilities.

items.name: Velvet leaf
items.growersTips:
Plant in a sheltered south-facing spot to protect delicate autumn berries from cold UK winds.
Prune back hard in early spring to encourage vigorous new growth where the best berries form.
Grow in moist but well-drained acidic to neutral soil, adding compost to mimic forest floors.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells to prevent premature berry drop in autumn.
Plant near evergreen shrubs like Sarcococca to provide a dark backdrop that highlights the berries.

items.name: Callicarpa rubella

Plant in a sheltered south-facing spot to protect delicate pink summer blooms from cold UK winds.
Prune hard in early spring down to a low permanent framework to encourage vigorous berry-bearing wood.

items.description: Callicarpa rubella is a species of beautyberry native to Southeast Asia. It is a shrub that produces pink or purple flowers followed by dark-purple berries. The berries are actually drupes. It is grown in gardens as an ornamental plant. The fruit attracts wildlife such as birds.

items.name: Callicarpa shikokiana
items.growersTips:
Plant in a sheltered south-facing spot to protect late-autumn berries from harsh UK frosts and winds.
Incorporate well-rotted grit and compost into heavy UK clay to ensure the sharp drainage it requires.
Prune stems back to a low permanent framework in early spring to stimulate vigorous berry-bearing wood.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells to prevent premature autumn berry drop in UK heat.
Grow alongside evergreen Sarcococca to provide a dark winter backdrop that makes the berries pop.
items.description: Callicarpa shikokiana, commonly called Shikoku beautyberry or China beautyberry, is a plant species in the Lamiaceae family. It is native to Japan. It is a shrub with pink flowers in summer and purple fruit in the fall. The berry-like fruit is a drupe. It is cultivated in home gardens and national parks as an ornamental plant. The leaves turn yellow in the fall.

items.name: Callicarpa tikusikensis
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist well-drained acidic to neutral soil enriched with leaf mould to mimic woodland beds.
Position in full sun to partial shade sheltered from cold drying winds to protect delicate spring buds.
Water deeply weekly during dry summer spells to ensure the autumn berries develop to their full size.
Prune established stems back to a low framework in early spring to encourage vigorous berry-bearing wood.
Grow alongside evergreen sarcococca or skimmia to provide a dark backdrop that highlights the berries.
items.description: Callicarpa tikusikensis is a species of flowering plant in the mint family (Lamiaceae). It is a shrub endemic to northern Taiwan.

items.name: Callicarpa tomentosa
items.growersTips:
Plant in a sheltered, south-facing border to protect the delicate flower buds from late UK frosts.
Incorporate well-rotted manure into heavy UK clay soils to ensure the free-draining conditions it needs.

Grow alongside evergreen shrubs like Sarcococca to provide a dark backdrop that highlights the berries.
items.description: Callicarpa tomentosa is a species of beautyberry plant in the family Lamiaceae. It is found in Western Ghats of India and Sri Lanka. It is a small tree with about 5m tall. Leaves simple, opposite; elliptic to broadly elliptic; apex acute or acuminate. Purplish flowers show branched axillary cymes. Fruit is 3-4 seeded globose drupe. Fruits provide food for wildlife. They are sometimes used to make herbal medicine. The leaves are also food for wildlife.

items.name: Callitriche cophocarpa
items.growersTips:
Plant this native oxygenator in still or slow-flowing garden ponds at a depth of 10 to 30 centimetres.
Anchor bare roots in heavy clay loam using aquatic baskets to prevent them from floating to the top.
Grow alongside Caltha palustris to provide shade and reduce algae growth around the young shoots.
Thin out dense mats in late summer to maintain open water and prevent the pond from choking.
Monitor for water snails in spring as they can rapidly consume the delicate submerged foliage.
items.description: Callitriche cophocarpa is a species of flowering plant native to Europe, Russia, and Northern Africa.

items.name: Callitriche hamulata
items.growersTips:
Grow this native starwort in still or slow-moving water up to one meter deep to mimic UK streams.
Plant in a heavy clay and loam mix within aquatic baskets to prevent the fine roots from drifting.
Propagate in spring by taking stem cuttings and weighting them down into the pond substrate.
Clear fallen autumn leaves from the pond surface to maintain the high light levels this plant needs.
Introduce Ramshorn snails to your pond to naturally control algae growth on the delicate foliage.
items.description: Callitriche hamulata is a species of flowering plant belonging to the family Plantaginaceae.

items.name: Callitriche hermaphroditica
items.growersTips:
Plant this fully submerged aquatic perennial in still or slow-flowing neutral to alkaline garden ponds.
Anchor the delicate stems in heavy clay loam within shallow planting baskets to prevent them floating.
Position in partial shade to cool UK pond water and prevent filamentous algae from smothering stems.
Propagate in spring by taking stem cuttings and weighting them down in the muddy bottom of the pond.
Introduce Ramshorn snails to your pond to naturally control algae without damaging these fragile stems.
items.description: Callitriche hermaphroditica is a species of flowering plant belonging to the family Plantaginaceae.

items.name: Spring water-starwort
items.growersTips:
Plant this native oxygenator in still or slow-moving water up to thirty centimetres deep in spring.
Grow in full sun to partial shade in neutral to acidic pond soil or loam-filled planting baskets.
Thin out dense mats in late summer to prevent the plant from choking smaller garden ponds.
Watch for water snails which graze on the foliage but avoid chemical treatments in wildlife ponds.
Pair with native Caltha palustris in shallow margins to create structural contrast and shade.
items.description: Callitriche palustris, the vernal water-starwort, narrow-fruited water-starwort, or spiny water starwort, is a species of aquatic plants. It is the type species of its genus.

items.name: Calluna vulgaris
items.growersTips:
Plant in acidic, peat-free ericaceous compost mixed with grit to ensure the essential sharp drainage.
Water with stored rainwater rather than tap water to keep the soil pH below five point five.
Prune annually in early spring by cutting back dead flower spikes to just below the spent blooms.
Space plants thirty centimetres apart in full sun to prevent damp-induced powdery mildew and rot.
Grow alongside Erica carnea and dwarf conifers to provide year-round structure and acidic soil cover.
items.description: Calluna vulgaris, common heather, ling, or simply heather, is the sole species in the genus Calluna in the flowering plant family Ericaceae. It is a low-growing evergreen shrub growing to 20 to 50 centimetres tall, or rarely to 1 metre (40 in) and taller, and is found widely in Europe and Asia Minor on acidic soils in open sunny situations and in moderate shade.

items.name: Sego lily
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs in autumn at a depth of ten centimetres in sharply draining gritty soil to prevent rot
Grow them in terracotta pots kept in an unheated greenhouse or cold frame to shield from winter wet
Water weekly during active spring growth but keep completely dry during their summer dormant phase
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic pellets or copper barrier tape
Position pots in the sunniest spot possible to mimic their native hot dry Californian summers
items.description: Calochortus is a genus of flowering plants in the lily family. The group includes herbaceous, perennial and bulbous species, all native to North America.

items.name: Calochortus albus

Grow in pots kept in an unheated greenhouse or cold frame to shield them from excessive UK wet.
Withhold all water during their summer dormant phase after the foliage dies back in July.
Position in full sun or light dappled shade facing south to mimic their native Californian climate.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.
items.description: Calochortus albus is a North American species in the genus Calochortus in the family Liliaceae. It is also known by the common names fairy lantern, white fairy lantern, pink fairy lantern, lantern of the fairies, globe lily, white globe lily, white globe-tulip, alabaster tulip, Indian bells, satin bells, snowy lily-bell, and snow drops.

items.name: Calochortus amabilis
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs in autumn at a depth of eight centimetres in sharply draining gritty soil to prevent rot
Grow in pots under a cold glasshouse or cold frame to protect them from excessive winter wetness
Water moderately during spring growth but keep completely dry during their summer dormant period
Incorporate equal parts grit and leafmould into loam to mimic their native Californian woodland soil
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic bait or copper tape barriers
items.description: Calochortus amabilis is a species of the genus Calochortus in the family Liliaceae. It is also known by the common names Diogenes' lantern, yellow globe-tulip, golden globe-tulip, yellow globe lily, golden fairy lantern, golden lily-bell, Chinese lantern, and short lily.

items.name: Calochortus ambiguus
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs 10cm deep in autumn using a gritty compost mix to survive wet UK winters.
Grow in pots under a cold glasshouse or cold frame to protect from excessive winter rain.
Stop watering completely in summer once foliage dies back to mimic its dry native dormancy.
Use copper tape and grit barriers around pots to protect tender spring shoots from slugs.
Add sharp horticultural grit to the planting hole to ensure the rapid drainage this bulb demands.
items.description: Calochortus ambiguus, the Arizona mariposa lily or doubting mariposa lily, is a perennial plant in the lily family (liliaceae) that grows at higher elevations of the Sonoran Desert regions of Arizona, western New Mexico, southern Utah, and Sonora.

items.name: Calochortus amoenus

Grow in pots kept in an unheated greenhouse or cold frame to shield them from excessive UK wetness.
Withhold all water during their summer dormant phase from July to September to mimic Californian drys.
Position pots in full sun to light dappled shade to encourage the nodding pink lanterns to bloom.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.
items.description: Calochortus amoenus is a species of flowering plant in the lily family which is commonly known as purple fairy-lantern.

items.name: Calochortus apiculatus
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs in autumn at a depth of eight centimetres in sharply draining gritty soil to prevent rot
Grow in pots under a cold frame or unheated greenhouse to protect from wet UK winters and late frosts
Water moderately during spring growth but keep the soil completely dry during summer dormancy periods
Top dress pots with a two centimetre layer of horticultural grit to keep the bulb neck dry and rot-free
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic pellets or copper tape barriers
items.description: Calochortus apiculatus is a North American species of flowering plants in the lily family.

items.name: Calochortus argillosus

Plant bulbs in autumn 8cm deep in sharply draining gritty soil to prevent winter wet rot.

Keep soil completely dry during their summer dormant phase after the foliage dies back in July.

Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic bait or copper tape barriers.
items.description: Calochortus argillosus is a species of flowering plant in the lily family which is known by the common name clay mariposa lily.

items.name: Calochortus aureus

Plant this bulb 10cm deep in autumn using a gritty, sharply draining loam to prevent winter rot.
Grow in a cold greenhouse or alpine house to protect the bulb from persistent wet UK winter rain.
Withhold all water from July to September to mimic its native desert summer dormancy period.
Position in the brightest, most south-facing spot possible to maximise essential UK summer sun.
Use terracotta pots with extra grit and top-dress with gravel to keep the bulb neck dry and rot-free.
items.description: Calochortus aureus is a North American species of flowering plants in the lily family. It is native to the southwestern United States. Calochortus aureus is a bulb-forming perennial herb producing a single stalk up to 30 cm tall. Flowers are bright lemon-yellow with red or purple splotches on the petals.

items.name: Calochortus barbatus

Plant bulbs in autumn 8cm deep in gritty, sharply draining soil to prevent winter rot in wet UK clay.
Grow in pots kept in an unheated greenhouse or cold frame to shield them from excessive winter rain.
Water moderately during spring growth but keep completely dry in summer once the foliage dies back.
Position in the sunniest south-facing spot possible to mimic their hot Mexican mountain habitat.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.
items.description: Calochortus barbatus is a species of mariposa lilies in the lily family. It is endemic to Mexico.

items.name: Calochortus bruneaunis
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs 10cm deep in autumn using a gritty, sharply draining compost mix to prevent winter rot.
Grow this bulb in a terracotta pot kept in an unheated greenhouse to shield it from heavy UK rain.
Withhold all water from July to September to mimic its native dry summer dormant period.
Place the pot in the most sun-drenched, south-facing spot available to ripen the bulb for flowering.
Check regularly for slugs and snails in spring as they quickly destroy the emerging flower buds.
items.description: Calochortus bruneaunis is a species of flowering plant in the lily family, and is known by the common name Bruneau mariposa lily.

Position pots in the brightest south-facing spot possible to maximise essential summer baking.

items.description: Calochortus clavatus is a species of mariposa lily known by the common name clubhair mariposa lily. It is endemic to California where it is found in forests and on chaparral slopes.

items.name: Calochortus caeruleus

items.name: Cox's mariposa lily

items.description: Calochortus coxii is a rare species of flowering plant in the lily family known by the common names Cox's mariposa lily and crinite mariposa lily. It is endemic to Oregon in the United States, where it is known only from Douglas County.

items.name: Dunn's mariposa lily
items.growersTips:
Grow in a gritty loam-based compost with added sharp sand to ensure the sharpest possible drainage.
Keep completely dry during summer dormancy to mimic its native Californian Mediterranean climate.
Plant bulbs in autumn at a depth of eight centimetres in deep pots to accommodate long taproots.
Provide winter protection under glass or in a cold frame to shield from persistent wet UK rain.
Water sparingly from early spring only when active growth appears, then stop entirely after flowering.
items.description: Calochortus dunnii is a rare species of flowering plant in the lily family known by the common name Dunn's mariposa lily.

items.name: Calochortus elegans

Plant bulbs in autumn at a depth of eight centimetres in a sharply draining gritty soil mix.
Grow in pots kept in an unheated greenhouse or alpine house to protect from winter wet.
Water moderately during spring growth but keep the bulbs bone dry during their summer dormancy.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic pellets or copper tape.
Repot every two years in autumn using a mix of two parts grit to one part loam-based compost.
items.description: Calochortus elegans is a species of flowering plant in the lily family known by the common name elegant Mariposa lily, cat's ear, elegant cat's ears or star tulip. It is native to the western United States from northern California to Montana.

items.name: White mariposa lily

Stop watering completely in summer once foliage dies back to mimic their native dry dormant phase.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using beer traps or physical barriers.
Position pots in the sunniest spot possible to mimic the bright, open meadows of their origin.
items.description: Calochortus eurycarpus is a North American species of flowering plant in the lily family. It is native to the western United States: Montana, Idaho, eastern Oregon, western Wyoming, northeastern Nevada and southeastern Washington.

items.name: Calochortus excavatus
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs 10cm deep in autumn using a gritty, sharply draining soil mix to prevent winter rot.
Grow in pots kept in an unheated greenhouse to protect them from persistent wet UK winter weather.
Water weekly during spring growth, then stop watering completely once foliage dies back in summer.
Position in the sunniest spot possible to mimic their native hot, dry Californian summer dormant period.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic barriers or beer traps.
items.description: Calochortus excavatus is a species of flowering plant in the lily family known by the common name Inyo County star-tulip.

items.name: Calochortus fimbriatus
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs in autumn 8cm deep in a gritty, sharply draining mix to survive wet UK winters.
Grow this tender Californian native in pots kept in an unheated greenhouse to control moisture.
Withhold all water completely from July to September during the bulb's essential summer dormancy.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic bait or copper tape on pots.
Position pots in the sunniest spot possible to mimic its native hot, dry chaparral habitat.
items.description: Calochortus fimbriatus is a California species of flowering plant in the lily family known by the common name late-blooming mariposa lily. It is native to the coastal mountain ranges of southern Monterey, San Luis Obispo, Santa Barbara and northern Ventura counties, where it is a member of the chaparral flora.

items.name: Calochortus flexuosus
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs in autumn 8cm deep in extremely gritty, free-draining soil to prevent winter rot.
Grow in a cold greenhouse or alpine house to protect the fragile stems from heavy UK wind and rain.
Withhold all water during the summer dormant phase from July to September to mimic desert dry spells.
Water moderately only during active spring growth, allowing the gritty compost to dry out between times.
Position in the brightest south-facing spot possible to maximise essential UK spring sunshine.
items.description: Calochortus flexuosus is a species of lily known by the common names winding Mariposa lily and straggling Mariposa lily.

items.name: Greene's mariposa lily
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs in autumn 8cm deep in a gritty, free-draining mix using terracotta pots to prevent rot.
Keep pots in a cold frame or unheated greenhouse to shield them from excessive winter wet.
Water weekly from spring foliage emergence until flowering, then stop completely for summer dormancy.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic pellets or copper tape on pots.
Top-dress the soil with a 2cm layer of horticultural grit to keep the bulb neck dry and rot-free.
items.description: Calochortus greenei is a species of flowering plant in the lily family known by the common name Greene's mariposa lily. It is native to northern California and southern Oregon, where it grows in the forest and woodlands of the mountains. It is a perennial herb which produces a branching stem up to about 30 centimeters in maximum height. There is a basal leaf about 20 centimeters long which does not wither at flowering. The inflorescence bears 1 to 5 erect bell-shaped flowers. Each flower has three sepals and three light purple petals with darker areas at the bases. The petals are 3 to 4 centim

items.name: Calochortus gunnisonii
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs in autumn at a depth of 10cm in extremely sharp-draining, grit-heavy soil to prevent rot.
Grow in terracotta pots kept in an unheated greenhouse to shield them from excessive winter wet.
Stop watering completely in summer once foliage dies back to mimic their dry native dormant phase.
Protect early spring shoots from slugs and snails using beer traps or physical copper barriers.
Position in the sunniest south-facing spot possible to replicate the intense light of the Rockies.
items.description: Calochortus gunnisonii commonly known as Rocky Mountain mariposa or Gunnison mariposa lily is a North American species of flowering plant in the lily family. It is native to the western United States, primarily in the Rocky Mountains and Black Hills: Arizona, New Mexico, Utah, Colorado, Wyoming, Montana, South Dakota, Washington state (Grant County, northwestern Nebraska and eastern Idaho.

items.name: Howell's mariposa lily
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs in autumn at a depth of ten centimetres in sharply draining gritty soil to prevent rot.
Grow in a cold greenhouse or alpine house to protect the winter foliage from heavy UK winter rain.
Keep the compost damp during spring growth but completely dry during the summer dormant period.
Use a soil mix of equal parts John Innes number two, coarse grit, and perlite for perfect drainage.
Guard emerging spring shoots diligently against slugs and snails using organic copper tape or grit.
items.description: Calochortus howellii, or Howell's mariposa lily, is a rare North American species of flowering plants in the lily family, found only in Josephine and Curry Counties in south-western Oregon.

items.name: Calochortus invenustus
items.growersTips:

items.description: Calochortus obispoensis is a rare California species of flowering plants in the lily family known by the common name San Luis mariposa lily. items.description: Calochortus palmeri is a species of flowering plant in the lily family known by the common names Palmer's mariposa lily and strangling mariposa.

items.description: Calochortus persistens is a rare North American species of flowering plant in the lily family known by the common name Siskiyou mariposa lily. It is native to northern California and southern Oregon.

items.description: Calochortus pringlei is a bulbous plant of the lily family. It is sometimes known by the common name Pringle's cyclobothra and belongs to subsection Ghiesbreghtiani within section Cyclobothra in the genus Calochortus. It occurs in mountainous south-central Mexico.

items.description: Calochortus raichei is a rare species of flowering plant in the lily family known by the common name Cedars' fairy-lantern. items.description: Calochortus superbus is a North American species of flowering plants in the lily family known by the common name superb mariposa lily. items.description: Calochortus syntrophus is a rare species of flowering plant in the lily family known by the common names Callahan's mariposa lily and clustered mariposa lily. It is endemic to northern California, where it occurs in a remote area north of Montgomery Creek in Shasta County. It has also been spotted in adjacent Tehama County. Its habitat includes open, rocky areas with moist or wet soils in oak woodland territory. It was first discovered in 1993 and its description was published the following year.

items.description: Calochortus tiburonensis, the Tiburon Mariposa lily, is a rare member of the genus Calochortus in the family Liliaceae. There it occurs on a single serpentine outcrop in grasslands from 50–150 metres (160–490 ft) in elevation.

The flower has also been found at a single location in each of Josephine and Jackson Counties.

It is native to western Oregon and to California as far south as San Luis Obispo County. It grows in moist areas, such as meadows, in coastal hills and lower-elevation mountains. Most of the populations are found in the Coast Ranges, but some occur in the Cascades and in the foothills of the Sierra Nevada.

items.description: Calochortus vestae is a California species of flowering plants in the lily family known by the common name Coast Range mariposa lily. items.name: Caltha

Water container-grown marsh marigolds daily in summer to keep the compost constantly saturated.
Cut back faded foliage and spent flower stems in July to encourage a second flush of autumn blooms.
Watch for powdery mildew in dry UK summers and prune affected leaves to ground level immediately.
items.description: Caltha is a genus of rhizomatous perennial flowering plants in the family Ranunculaceae, to which ten species have been assigned. They occur in moist environments in temperate and cold regions of both the Northern and Southern Hemispheres. Their leaves are generally heart-shaped or kidney-shaped, or are characteristically diplophyllous. Flowers are star shaped and mostly yellow to white. True petals and nectaries are missing but the five or more sepals are distinctly colored. As usual in the buttercup family there is a circle of stamens around free carpels.

items.name: Caltha palustris
items.growersTips:
Plant this native marginal in heavy clay or wet soil at the pond edge up to ten centimetres deep.
Water container-grown specimens daily with rainwater during dry UK summers to prevent soil drying.
Cut back faded foliage to the base in July to encourage a fresh flush of leaves and autumn flowers.
Watch for powdery mildew in late summer and improve air circulation by thinning congested clumps.
Divide established clumps in early autumn or after flowering in May to maintain vigour and spread.
items.description: Caltha palustris, known as marsh-marigold and kingcup, is a small to medium sized perennial herbaceous plant of the buttercup family, native to marshes, fens, ditches and wet woodland in temperate regions of the Northern Hemisphere. It flowers between April and August, dependent on altitude and latitude, but occasional flowers may occur at other times.

items.name: Calylophus

items.description: Oenothera is a genus of about 145 species of herbaceous flowering plants native to the Americas. It is the type genus of the family Onagraceae. Common names include evening primrose, suncups, and sundrops. They are not closely related to the true primroses.

items.name: Calypsoeae

Keep potted Calypso in a cold frame over winter to mimic cool, damp UK woodland floor conditions.

items.description: Calypsoinae is an orchid subtribe in the tribe Epidendreae of subfamily Epidendroideae. It has previously been recognized as tribe Calypsoeae in the subfamily Epidendroideae.

items.name: Calypsoinae

items.description: Calypsoinae is an orchid subtribe in the tribe Epidendreae of subfamily Epidendroideae. It has previously been recognized as tribe Calypsoeae in the subfamily Epidendroideae.

Keep the soil consistently damp during spring growth but allow it to dry out after summer dieback.

Leave the faded flower spikes intact to self-seed and naturalise in damp UK wildflower orchards.
Watch for slugs and snails in damp spring weather as they quickly damage the emerging young shoots.
items.description: Camassia cusickii, common name Cusick's camas or Cusick's quamash, is a species of plant in the family Asparagaceae. It is native to parts of North America. C. cusickii originally appeared in horticultural journals in the late 1800s.

items.name: Camassia howellii
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs in autumn at a depth of 10cm to 15cm in moist, clay-heavy soil that mimics UK wet meadows.
Keep the soil consistently damp during spring growth but allow it to dry out slightly in summer.
Position in full sun to partial shade to prevent the tall, delicate flower spikes from flopping.
Leave the foliage to die back naturally in summer to feed the bulb for next year's spring blooms.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.
items.description: Camassia howellii, commonly known as Howell's camas, is a species of perennial flowering plant in the family Asparagaceae endemic to western Oregon.

items.name: Camassia leichtlinii
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs in autumn at a depth of fifteen centimetres in moisture-retentive, clay-friendly soil.
Water deeply during dry spring spells to prevent the flower spikes from aborting before they bloom.
Leave the foliage to die back naturally until July to feed the bulb for next year's spring display.
Plant alongside late-flowering perennials like hardy geraniums to hide the yellowing summer foliage.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.
items.description: Camassia leichtlinii, the great camas or large camas, is a species of flowering plant in the family Asparagaceae. This herbaceous perennial is native to western North America in British Columbia, Canada and California, Nevada, Oregon and Washington, in the United States.

items.name: Camassia quamash
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs in autumn at a depth of ten to fifteen centimetres in moisture-retentive clay soil.
Keep the soil consistently damp during spring growth but allow it to dry out after summer dieback.
Leave the foliage to die back naturally in July to allow the bulb to store energy for next spring.
Plant alongside late-flowering perennials like hardy geraniums to hide the yellowing summer foliage.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.
items.description: Camassia quamash, commonly known as camas, kwetlal, small camas, common camas, common camash or quamash, is a perennial herb. It is native to western North America in large areas of southern Canada and the northwestern United States.

items.name: Camassia scilloides
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs in autumn 8cm deep in moisture-retentive, clay-heavy soil that mimics UK damp meadows.
Water thoroughly during dry spring spells to support flowering, but keep soil drier during winter.
Watch for slugs and snails in damp UK springs as they quickly destroy emerging young foliage.
Leave the foliage to die back naturally in summer before cutting it down to feed next year's bulb.
Associate with late-flowering narcissi or damp-loving grasses in a naturalised UK wildflower lawn.
items.description: Camassia scilloides is a perennial herb known commonly as Atlantic camas, wild hyacinth, and eastern camas. It is native to the eastern half of North America, including Ontario and the eastern United States.

items.name: Camissonia
items.growersTips:
Plant in well-drained gritty soil in full sun to prevent winter wet from rotting the roots.
Sow seeds shallowly in spring after the last frost, barely covering them with a fine layer of grit.
Water sparingly once established, allowing the top few centimetres of soil to dry out completely.
Grow in raised beds or containers to ensure the sharp drainage this drought-tolerant plant needs.
Cut back faded flower stems in autumn to encourage a tidy habit and prevent excessive self-seeding.
items.description: Camissonia, sometimes commonly known as sun cup or sundrop, is a genus of annual and perennial plants in the evening primrose family Onagraceae. A total of 12 species are known, nearly all from western North America, especially in the California Floristic Province, but also one from South America. Previous circumscriptions of the genus had recognized up to 62 species before it was split among other closely related genera.

items.name: Camissonia benitensis
items.growersTips:
Grow in a container with gritty, free-draining soil to protect it from wet, cold UK winters.
Sow seeds in spring just below the soil surface, as they need light to trigger germination.
Water sparingly, letting the compost dry out completely between waterings to prevent root rot.
Position in your sunniest, south-facing spot to mimic its native hot, dry California habitat.
Overwinter pots in a cold frame or unheated greenhouse to shield them from heavy UK winter rain.
items.description: Camissonia benitensis is a species of evening primrose known by the common names San Benito suncup and San Benito evening primrose. It is endemic to the Diablo Range of the South Coast Ranges of California, where its range includes far southern San Benito County, far western Fresno County, and far eastern Monterey County.

items.name: Camissonia campestris
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in autumn using a gritty, free-draining compost mix to mimic desert soils.
Grow in containers to easily move plants under glass to protect from wet UK winter waterlogging.
Water sparingly only when the top two inches of soil dry out to prevent root rot in damp climates.
Position in the absolute sunniest south-facing spot of the garden to maximise the short blooms.
Plant alongside hardy succulents like Sedum to create a compatible low-water rockery display.
items.description: Camissonia campestris, is a flowering plant in the family Onagraceae, native to the Mojave Desert of the United States. It grows mostly on open, sandy flats, occurring from sea level to 2,000 m in the western and central part of the desert.

items.name: Camissonia contorta
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in spring just below the soil surface as they need light and a touch of warmth to sprout.
Grow in poor, sharply draining sandy soil to mimic its native dunes and prevent winter root rot.
Water sparingly only during prolonged dry spells, keeping the soil dry to touch between waterings.
Position in the sunniest south-facing spot of your garden to maximize the short-lived yellow blooms.
Let the plant self-seed naturally in gravel gardens to ensure a display for the following spring.
items.description: Camissonia contorta is a species of flowering plant, known by the common name plains evening primrose, in the family Onagraceae. It is an annual herb producing a slender, bending to curling red or green stem which is sometimes hairy. It is up to 30 centimeters long and erect or spreading out. The blue-green leaves are linear to very narrowly oval in shape and up to 3.5 centimeters long. The nodding inflorescence produces one or more small flowers. Each has bright yellow petals up to half a centimeter long, sometimes with small red dots near the bases. The fruit is a capsule about 3 centimeters

items.name: Camissonia parvula
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in spring just below the soil surface as they need light and a propagator to germinate.
Grow in poor, sharply drained sandy soil to mimic its native desert habitat and prevent root rot.
Water sparingly only during dry spells, allowing the gritty soil to dry out completely between times.
Position in the sunniest, most sheltered south-facing spot to maximise the cool UK summer warmth.
Plant alongside hardy sedums in gravel gardens to provide compatible dry-soil companion conditions.
items.description: Camissonia parvula is a species of evening primrose known by the common name Lewis River suncup. It is native to the Great Basin of the United States. It grows in sagebrush, woodland, and other Great Basin habitat. It is a slender annual herb producing a wiry erect stem 15 to 30 centimeters in maximum height. The leaves are linear in shape and 1 to 3 centimeters long. They are located along the stem as there is no basal rosette. The nodding inflorescence produces flowers with yellow petals only 2 or 3 millimeters long. The fruit is a capsule 2 to 3 centimeters long, swollen with seeds, and som

items.name: Camissonia pubens
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at a depth of two millimetres in early spring using a free-draining sandy loam.
Position in the sunniest spot of your garden to mimic its native dry habitat in the damp UK climate.
Water sparingly only when the top two inches of soil are dry to prevent root rot in wet UK summers.
Grow in terracotta pots to improve drainage and easily move the plant under cover during heavy rain.
Plant alongside drought-tolerant Sedums to create a compatible low-water container display.
items.description: Camissonia pubens is a species of evening primrose known by the common name hairy suncup. It is native to the desert and steppe of western Nevada and eastern California. It is an annual herb covered in glandular hairs generally made up of one or more erect, slender stems up to a third of a meter tall. The leaves are up to about 4 centimeters long and are lance-shaped with wavy, toothed edges. The nodding inflorescence produces flowers with yellow petals each a few millimeters long and sometimes dotted with red near the bases. The fruit is a straight or coiling capsule up to 5 centimeters long.

items.name: Camissonia pusilla
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at a depth of 2mm in early spring using a free-draining sandy loam soil mix.
Grow in the sunniest south-facing spot to mimic its native desert heat in the damp UK climate.
Water sparingly only when the top 5cm of soil is dry to prevent root rot in wet British summers.
Sow directly into final pots as this taprooted annual dislikes transplant shock and root damage.
Plant alongside gravel-loving Sedums or sempervivums to ensure similar low-moisture soil needs.
items.description: Camissonia pusilla is a species of evening primrose known by the common name little wiry suncup. It is native to the western United States from California to Idaho, where it grows in sagebrush and other habitat. It is a petite, hairy, glandular annual herb producing very slender erect stems up to about 22 centimeters in maximum height. The leaves linear with toothed edges and 1 to 3 centimeters long. The nodding inflorescence produces flowers with yellow petals 2 or 3 millimeters long and usually spotted with red near the bases. The fruit is a straight or coiling capsule up to 3 centimeters lo

items.name: Camissonia strigulosa
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn in a cold frame using a gritty, free-draining compost mix to mimic winter chill.
Plant in full sun in a raised bed or rockery to ensure the sharp drainage this dry-loving herb needs.
Water sparingly only during prolonged summer droughts, as wet winter soil will quickly rot the roots.
Protect young spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.
Position alongside thyme or sedums in a gravel garden to match its low-water, high-light demands.
items.description: Camissonia strigulosa is a species of flowering plant in the evening primrose family known by the common name sandysoil suncup.

items.name: Camissoniopsis
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in spring after the last frost, barely covering them with a light dusting of fine grit.
Position in the sunniest spot of your garden to mimic their native dry, open chaparral habitat.
Water sparingly once established, allowing the gritty, free-draining soil to dry out completely.
Grow in shallow terracotta pots to prevent waterlogging during wet, cool UK summer spells.
Collect the ripe seed pods in late summer to store indoors for sowing the following spring.
items.description: Camissoniopsis is a plant genus in the evening primrose family (Onagraceae).

items.name: Camissoniopsis cheiranthifolia
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in spring at a depth of 3mm in poor, sharply draining sandy soil to mimic coastal dunes.
Water sparingly only during prolonged dry spells as this plant is highly susceptible to root rot.
Position in your sunniest south-facing border or gravel garden to maximise crucial UK summer heat.
Protect young seedlings from slugs and snails which actively target the tender early spring growth.
Grow alongside companion plants like Armeria maritima that thrive in the same dry, low-nutrient soil.
items.description: Camissoniopsis cheiranthifolia, the beach suncup or beach evening primrose, is a species of the evening primrose family and is native to open dunes and sandy soils of coastal California, Baja California and Oregon.

items.name: Camissoniopsis hardhamiae
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds thinly in late spring directly into sandy, sharply drained soil in full UK sun.
Water seedlings sparingly once established, allowing the gritty topsoil to dry out completely.
Sow in shallow drills just two millimetres deep, pressing soil down lightly without burying.
Plant alongside low-growing sedums or thymes which share its need for dry, nutrient-poor soil.
Watch for slugs on young spring shoots, using beer traps or grit barriers to protect them.
items.description: Camissoniopsis hardhamiae is a species of evening primrose known by the common name Hardham's evening primrose. It is endemic to California, where it grows in the chaparral and woodland of San Luis Obispo and Monterey Counties. It is a robust annual herb producing a hairy stem up to about half a meter tall. The leaves are lance-shaped to narrowly oval and up to 12 centimeters long. The nodding inflorescence bears flowers with yellow petals each a few millimeters long. The fruit is a cylindrical capsule up to 2.5 centimeters long containing several dark-colored seeds.

items.name: Camissoniopsis hirtella
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds thinly in spring directly into poor, well-drained soil once the frost risk has passed.
Position in your garden's hottest, most sun-drenched spot to mimic its native dry habitat.
Water sparingly only during prolonged dry summer spells, as wet UK soil causes instant root rot.
Do not enrich the soil with compost or fertilisers, as high nutrients reduce its yellow blooms.
Allow the annual seed pods to dry on the plant in autumn to self-seed naturally for next year.
items.description: Camissoniopsis hirtella is a species of evening primrose known by the common name Santa Cruz Island suncup. It is native to California and Baja California, where it grows on the slopes of coastal and inland hills and mountains, especially in areas that have recently burned. It is an annual herb producing a hairy stem up to about half a meter in height. Most of the leaves are located in a basal rosette at ground level and are oval in shape and a few centimeters in length. The nodding inflorescence produces flowers with sepals coated in long, glandular hairs, and bright yellow petals under a cen

items.name: Camissoniopsis lewisii
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in spring at a depth of 3mm in sandy, sharply draining soil to prevent winter wet rot.
