Position in your sunniest south-facing border or gravel garden to mimic its native dry habitat.
Water sparingly only during dry spells, allowing the gritty compost to dry out completely between.
Watch for slugs and snails during wet UK springs when young seedlings are highly vulnerable.
Plant alongside Eschscholzia californica to create a drought-tolerant, low-maintenance display.
items.description: Camissoniopsis lewisii is a species of evening primrose known by the common name Lewis' evening primrose. It is native to southern California and Baja California, where it grows in coastal habitat and on the grasslands of the inland mountain ranges. as an example occurrence in Baja California, C. lewisii occurs in association with Mimulus aridus and Adiantum jordanii.

items.name: Camissoniopsis micrantha
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds thinly in spring directly into well-drained sandy soil at a shallow depth of two millimetres
Grow in the sunniest south-facing spot possible to mimic its native hot Californian coastal habitat
Water seedlings sparingly only during dry spells to prevent root rot in damp British summer weather
Position near low-growing California poppies to create a compatible drought-tolerant annual display
Leave faded summer flowers intact to allow self-seeding for a natural return the following spring
items.description: Camissoniopsis micrantha is a species of flowering plant in the evening primrose family known by the common names miniature suncup or small evening primrose. This is a small, hairy annual herb producing a basal rosette of leaves. It is characterized by small yellow flowers with petals less than 5 millimeters long. The flowers dry to a reddish color as they close. This species is found in Arizona and California in the United States, along with Baja California in Mexico. It grows in sandy areas in a number of habitats, from beaches to inland slopes. It is the smallest member of the genus Camisso

items.name: Camissoniopsis pallida
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in April under glass or outdoors in May once the late spring frosts have passed
Grow in poor sandy soil with sharp grit to mimic its native desert habitat and prevent root rot
Water sparingly only during prolonged dry spells as this annual thrives on neglect in UK summers
Position in the absolute brightest south-facing spot to maximise the short-lived yellow blooms
Deadhead spent flowers weekly in July to encourage continuous flushing until the autumn damp sets in
items.description: Camissoniopsis pallida is a low growing, yellow-flowered annual plant in the evening primrose family, Onagraceae. It is known by the common names pale primrose or pale yellow suncup. It is native to the desert and scrub habitat of the region where Arizona, California, and Nevada meet. It is a roughly hairy annual herb growing in a low patch on the ground, sometimes producing an erect stem from the basal rosette. The herbage is gray-green to reddish green. The leaves are lance-shaped and up to 3 centimeters long. The nodding inflorescence produces flowers with yellow petals 2 to 13 millimeters

items.name: Campanulorchis
items.growersTips:
Grow this rare orchid in a free-draining bark and perlite mix to prevent root rot in damp UK winters.
Position in bright indirect light, avoiding direct midday summer sun which scorches the foliage.
Water with harvested rainwater rather than tap water to prevent mineral buildup on the roots.
Maintain high humidity around the pot by using a gravel tray filled with water during dry spells.
Keep in a draft-free room or heated greenhouse as they cannot tolerate typical UK frost.
items.description: Campanulorchis is a genus of orchids. It was considered a synonym of the genus Eria, but eventually it has become an accepted name. It is native to Southeast Asia from Hainan to New Guinea.

items.name: Campsiandra
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in April at 2cm depth using bottom heat of 21C to counter cool UK spring soils.
Transplant to a south-facing wall in June to maximise solar heat required for Fabaceae flowering.
Water deeply twice a week at the base during July and August dry spells to prevent premature seed drop.
Pinch out the growing tips when seedlings reach 15cm to encourage bushy growth and more flower spikes.
Grow in pots of peat-free loam compost mixed with 30 percent grit to ensure excellent winter drainage.
items.description: Campsiandra is a genus of flowering plants in the family Fabaceae. It includes 22 species native to northern South America. The genus belongs to the subfamily Caesalpinioideae.

items.name: Canbya
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn in a gritty, well-drained soil mix to mimic their native dry habitat.
Keep seedlings in a cold frame over winter to protect them from excessive UK winter wetness.
Water sparingly from below only when the top two inches of gritty soil are completely dry.
Position pots in the brightest south-facing spot to maximise scarce UK summer sunshine.
Do not prune or pinch out stems as this delicate annual has a naturally compact tufted habit.
items.description: Canbya, also known as the pygmy poppies, is a genus of the poppy family Papaveraceae consisting of two species found in the dry parts of western North America. Both species are small, no more than a few centimeters tall, with flowers less than 10 mm across.

items.name: Canbya aurea
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn in a cold frame using a gritty, sharply draining compost to mimic alpine scree.
Place pots in the sunniest spot possible, protecting them from wet winter weather with a glass pane.
Water sparingly from below only when the soil is dry to prevent the delicate stems from rotting.
Watch for slugs and snails during wet spring spells as they can quickly consume the tiny seedlings.
Avoid transplanting by sowing directly into final terracotta pots to prevent root disturbance.
items.description: Canbya aurea, common name yellow pygmy-poppy, is a plant species endemic to the relatively cool northern deserts of the western United States. It is known only from central and southeastern Oregon and northwestern Nevada, as well as one collection reported from Mono County, California. It grows on dry, sandy soil, usually with sagebrush, at elevations of 900–1,700 metres (3,000–5,600 ft).

items.name: Canbya candida
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn on the surface of gritty, sharply draining soil as they need light to germinate.
Grow in a cold frame or alpine house to protect this desert annual from wet UK winter rot.
Water sparingly from below only when the soil is completely dry, keeping the foliage bone dry.
Position in the brightest, most sun-drenched spot available to mimic its native Mojave habitat.
Plant alongside hardy succulents like Sempervivum to ensure shared dry, low-nutrient soil needs.
items.description: Canbya candida is a tiny, white flowered annual plant in the genus Canbya of the poppy family. It is found in the western Mojave Desert of Southern California. It grows 1–3 cm tall. Its leaves are 5–9 mm long. The flowers are borne in leaf axils, and have 5–7 white petals that are each 3–4 mm long, and 6-9 stamens.

items.name: Capitanopsis
items.growersTips:
Grow in free-draining gritty soil to prevent root rot during wet United Kingdom winters.
Overwinter in a frost-free greenhouse or conservatory as this tender perennial cannot survive frost.
Water sparingly from autumn to spring, allowing the compost to dry out completely between waterings.
Prune back by one third in early spring to promote bushy growth and prevent the stems from going woody.
Propagate via softwood cuttings in late spring using a heated propagator to ensure reliable rooting.
items.description: Capitanopsis is a genus of plants in the family Lamiaceae, first described in 1916. It contains six known species, all endemic to Madagascar.

items.name: Capnoides
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in late summer on the soil surface of damp, shady borders as they need light to germinate.
Incorporate leaf mould to replicate UK woodland soils, keeping the pH neutral to slightly acidic.
Water consistently in dry summer spells to keep the soil moist but never waterlogged or boggy.
Leave faded flower stalks intact over winter to allow self-seeding before clearing dead foliage.
Protect young spring growth from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers in damp UK weather.
items.description: Capnoides sempervirens, the harlequin corydalis, rock harlequin, pale corydalis or pink corydalis, is an annual or biennial plant native to rocky woodland and burned or disturbed places in northern North America. Capnoides sempervirens is the only species in the genus Capnoides.Name(s) brought to synonymyCapnoides elegans Kuntze, a synonym for Corydalis elegans

items.name: Cardiocrinum
items.growersTips:
Plant the massive bulbs shallowly with the nose just showing at the soil surface to prevent rotting.
Incorporate leafmould and well-rotted manure deeply to mimic a damp, rich UK woodland floor.
Apply a thick mulch of organic matter in spring to keep the shallow root run cool and moist.
Protect the emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic pellets or beer traps.
Sow the fresh winged seeds in autumn in cold frames, as they require winter chilling to germinate.
items.description: Cardiocrinum is a genus of bulbous plants of the lily family first described in 1846. They are native to the Himalaya, China, the Russian Far East, and Japan. The bulbs are usually formed at the soil surface. The preferred habitat is woodland. The plants tend to be monocarpic, dying after flowering.

items.name: Cardiocrinum cordatum
items.growersTips:
Plant the bulb shallowly with its nose just showing at the soil surface in a humus-rich woodland bed
Water deeply and consistently throughout the dry summer months to prevent the large leaves crisping
Apply a thick mulch of leafmould annually in winter to mimic a damp UK deciduous forest floor
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic pellets or beer traps in April
Sow the fresh seed in autumn in cold frames as they require winter chilling to germinate in the UK
items.description: Cardiocrinum cordatum, known as turep in the Ainu languages, is a Northeast Asian species of plant in the lily family. It is native to Japan and to certain Russian islands in the Sea of Okhotsk.

items.name: Cardiocrinum giganteum
items.growersTips:
Plant the massive bulb shallowly with its nose just showing at the soil surface in autumn.
Provide deep rich humus soil in dappled woodland shade mimicking cool damp Scottish glens.
Water copiously during active spring growth to keep the soil constantly moist but never waterlogged.
Protect the emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic pellets or beer traps.
Sow the seeds immediately in cold frames as they require two winters of chilling to germinate.
items.description: Cardiocrinum giganteum, the giant Himalayan lily, is the largest species of any of the lily plants, growing up to 3.5 metres high. It is found in the Himalayas, China and Myanmar (Burma).

items.name: Cardionema andinum
items.growersTips:
Plant in sharply draining gritty soil or raised scree beds to prevent winter wet rot in UK rain.
Position in full south-facing sun to mimic its native dry habitat and ensure compact mat growth.
Water sparingly only during dry summer spells, keeping the crown completely dry during winter.
Protect from slugs and snails in spring as they target the dense, low-growing evergreen foliage.
Propagate by dividing the dense mats in spring just as new growth begins in the UK climate.
items.description: Cardionema is a genus of flowering plants belonging to the family Caryophyllaceae.

items.name: Cardionema ramosissimum
items.growersTips:
Grow in sharply drained, gritty soil to prevent winter root rot caused by wet UK winters.
Plant in full sun with the crown level with the soil surface to prevent stem rot in damp weather.
Water sparingly, only during prolonged summer droughts, allowing the gritty soil to dry completely.
Protect from heavy winter frosts using a dry mulch of grit or gravel around the base of the plant.
Grow alongside Sedums or Sempervivums in a rock garden or scree bed for compatible moisture needs.
items.description: Cardionema ramosissimum is a perennial plant in the family Caryophyllaceae, commonly known as sandcarpet, sandmat or tread lightly. It is a small, clumping, mat-forming plant found in a number of diverse habitats throughout its range, from sandy beaches and dunes to the high elevations of the Andes mountains. Cardionema ramosissimum has a disjunct distribution throughout the Americas, and is found on the Pacific coast of North America from Puget Sound to Baja California, in central Mexico, and widely across South America, from the Andes in Colombia to most of Argentina.

items.name: Carpenteria
items.growersTips:
Plant against a south-facing brick wall to shield it from cold, drying UK winter winds.
Grow in well-drained, neutral to acid soil, adding grit to the planting hole to prevent root rot.
Prune immediately after flowering in summer by cutting back flowered shoots to strong side buds.
Water deeply but infrequently during dry summer spells, allowing the soil to dry out between waterings.
Protect young plants with horticultural fleece when winter temperatures are forecast to drop below -5C.
items.description: Carpenteria, the tree anemone or bush anemone, is a genus of flowering plants in the hydrangea family Hydrangeaceae. It is closely related to the similar genus Philadelphus and is monotypic, being represented by the single species Carpenteria californica which is a flowering evergreen shrub native to the Sierra Nevada foothills in California.

items.name: Carpesium abrotanoides
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at two millimetres deep in April under glass to combat damp UK spring chills.
Plant in moisture-retentive clay loam enriched with leafmould to mimic woodland edge habitats.
Water weekly at the base during dry summer spells to prevent powdery mildew on the large leaves.
Position near ferns or hostas in partial shade to shield the delicate yellow disc florets from wind.
Watch for slugs and snails on young spring shoots by using beer traps or organic wool pellets.
items.description: Carpesium is a genus of flowering plants in the aster family, Asteraceae. They are distributed in Europe and Asia; most occur in China and several are endemic to the country.

items.name: Caryopteris clandonensis
items.growersTips:
Prune hard in late March to just above the woody base to encourage vigorous new flowering stems.
Plant in free-draining chalky or sandy soil to prevent winter root rot in wet UK climates.
Water newly planted shrubs weekly during their first summer then leave to be highly drought tolerant.
Position in full sun against a south-facing wall to maximise late-summer nectar for UK pollinators.
Protect young spring shoots from slug damage using organic grit barriers or beer traps.
items.description: Caryopteris is a genus of flowering plants in the family Lamiaceae. They are native to east Asia.

items.name: Golden rain
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in March at one centimetre deep using a heated propagator to beat the cool UK spring
Grow in a south-facing terracotta pot filled with gritty loam to ensure the sharp drainage they need
Water thoroughly only when the top two inches of compost feel dry to prevent root rot in damp weather
Check weekly for glasshouse red spider mite when growing under glass or in a warm conservatory
Feed fortnightly in summer with a high-potassium liquid tomato fertiliser to boost the yellow blooms
items.description: Cassia typically refers to cassia bark, the spice made from the bark of East Asian evergreen trees.

items.name: Cassiopea andromeda
items.growersTips:
Plant in acidic, moist, organic-rich soil, mixing plenty of composted pine needles or ericaceous grit.
Position in a cool, north-facing or partially shaded spot to mimic Scottish highland microclimates.
Water with rainwater only, keeping the soil consistently damp but never waterlogged during summer.
Prune very lightly after flowering in late spring, only removing dead tips to avoid ruining form.
Protect young spring shoots from late UK frosts using a temporary layer of horticultural fleece.
items.description: Cassiope is a genus of 18 small shrubby species in the family Ericaceae. It is the sole genus in the subfamily Cassiopoideae. They are native to the Arctic and north temperate montane regions. The genus is named after Cassiopeia of Greek mythology.

items.name: Clubmoss cassiope
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist, acidic, peat-free ericaceous compost mixed with plenty of grit for sharp drainage.
Position in a cool, north-facing rockery or alpine trough to mimic Scottish highland conditions.
Water only with soft rainwater to keep the soil consistently damp but never waterlogged or dry.
Provide light shade from midday summer sun to prevent the delicate scale-like leaves from scorching.
Propagate by taking semi-ripe heel cuttings in late summer rather than pruning the slow growth.
items.description: Cassiope lycopodioides is a plant species in the family Ericaceae, known by the common names clubmoss mountain-heather or Haida Gwaii mountain-heather. The species is native to northeast Asia and northwestern North America, where it grows on rocky slopes and crevices in arctic tundra and alpine tundra at elevations up to 2000 m.

items.name: Cassiope mertensiana
items.growersTips:
Grow in extremely acidic, moist, peat-free ericaceous compost mixed with plenty of grit for drainage.
Position in a cool, north-facing rockery or alpine sink to mimic Scottish highland conditions.
Water only with soft rainwater to maintain the low soil pH and prevent lime-induced chlorosis.
Avoid pruning this slow-growing shrub, only gently removing dead branch tips in early summer.
Shield from dry summer winds and midday sun using taller dwarf conifers as protective companions.
items.description: Cassiope mertensiana is a species of flowering plant known by the common names western moss heather and white mountain heather.

items.name: Cassiope tetragona
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist, acidic, humus-rich soil, mixing in plenty of composted pine needles or ericaceous peat.
Grow in a cool, partially shaded spot facing north or east to mimic its native Scottish highland home.
Water only with rainwater to keep the soil pH low and prevent lime-induced chlorosis in hard water areas.
Mulch annually with composted bark in autumn to protect shallow roots from winter frosts and drying out.
Prune very lightly after flowering in late spring, removing only dead stems to maintain its neat mound.
items.description: Cassiope tetragona is a plant native to the high Arctic and northern Norway, where it is found widely.

items.name: Catasetinae
items.growersTips:
Water heavily and fertilize weekly only after new roots reach ten centimeters long in late spring.
Stop watering completely in November when leaves yellow to trigger the essential winter dormancy.
Grow in Sphagnum moss in plastic pots to retain high moisture during the rapid summer growth phase.
Keep plants above fifteen Celsius on a bright south windowsill during the damp UK winter dormancy.
Check new spring growth weekly for spider mites which thrive in dry indoor UK winter heating.
items.description: Catasetinae is a subtribe within the Orchidaceae and contains 8 genera. Its members are widespread in lowland tropical Central and South America up to 1,500 meters. They are found on trees, stumps or old fence posts.

items.name: Cenostigma pluviosum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in April at a depth of two centimeters to protect young roots from late UK frosts
Water deeply once a week at the base rather than daily misting to prevent root rot in damp UK clay
Watch for pea aphids in June and spray them with garlic infusion to protect the delicate foliage
Prune back spent summer blooms in late August to encourage a second flush of flowers before autumn
Mix grit and well-rotted manure into heavy UK soil before planting to ensure the required drainage
items.description: Cenostigma is a genus of flowering plants in the family Fabaceae. It includes 15 species native to the tropical Americas, ranging from Mexico to northwestern Argentina and southern Brazil. It belongs to the subfamily Caesalpinioideae and tribe Caesalpinieae. Cenostigma pluviosa is being investigated as a possible antimalarial medication.

items.name: Centromadia fitchii
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at a depth of two millimetres in April to ensure light-induced germination.
Grow in poor, sharply drained sandy soil to mimic its native habitat and prevent winter root rot.
Water sparingly only during prolonged dry summer spells as this annual is highly drought-tolerant.
Position in the absolute brightest, south-facing spot to cope with cool, overcast UK summers.
Sow alongside low-growing thyme or sedum to provide ground cover that supports its upright stems.
items.description: Centromadia fitchii, common name Fitch's spikeweed or Fitch's tarweed, is a species of North American plants in the tribe Madieae within the family Asteraceae. It is native to California and southwestern Oregon.

items.name: Centromadia perennis
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in late spring after frosts, barely covering them with a light dusting of gritty compost.
Grow in a terracotta pot with free-draining sandy soil to mimic dry Californian coastal conditions.
Water sparingly only when the top three inches of soil are dry to prevent root rot in damp UK weather.
Position in your garden's brightest south-facing spot to maximize daily sunshine and flower opening.
Deadhead spent yellow blooms weekly in summer to prolong the flowering season before autumn frost.
items.description: Centromadia perennis is a species of Mexican plant in the tribe Madieae within the family Asteraceae. It is native to the State of Baja California Sur in western Mexico. The initial discovery of the species was near Boca del Salado in the East Cape Region near the south end of the peninsula.

items.name: Centromadia pungens
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in April at a depth of three millimetres into gritty, sharply draining alkaline soil.
Position in your sunniest south-facing border to mimic its native dry California habitat.
Water seedlings sparingly once established, allowing the gritty topsoil to dry out completely.
Wear thick gloves when weeding nearby to protect your hands from this plant's sharp, spiny bracts.
Leave the faded autumn flowerheads untouched to allow self-seeding for the following spring.
items.description: Centromadia pungens, the common spikeweed or common tarweed, is a species of North American plants in the tribe Madieae within the family Asteraceae. It is native to northern Baja California and the western United States. The plant is considered a noxious weed in parts of the Pacific Northwest.

items.name: Field chickweed
items.growersTips:
Plant in gritty, free-draining soil to prevent winter root rot during wet UK winters.
Cut back hard by half immediately after summer flowering to keep the silver foliage neat and compact.
Water newly planted divisions weekly until established, then rely solely on natural UK rainfall.
Divide congested clumps every three years in early spring to rejuvenate growth and maintain vigor.
Position in full sun next to dark-leaved Sedums or purple Heucheras for striking foliage contrast.
items.description: Cerastium is a genus of annual, winter annual, or perennial flowering plants belonging to the family Caryophyllaceae. They are commonly called mouse-ears or mouse-ear chickweeds. There are 214 accepted species, found nearly worldwide but with the greatest concentration in the northern temperate regions. A number of the species are common weeds in fields and on disturbed ground.

items.name: Cerastium aleuticum
items.growersTips:
Recreate its subarctic home by planting in gritty, sharply draining soil with zero organic mulch.
Water only during prolonged dry summer spells, as winter wet in UK climates will rot the roots.
Position in the brightest, most exposed spot in your rock garden to mimic wind-swept cliff tops.
Propagate by taking softwood cuttings in early summer or by carefully dividing clumps in spring.
Protect from winter waterlogging by placing a pane of glass or a cloche over the plant from November.
items.description: Cerastium aleuticum, common name Aleutian mouse-ear chickweed, is a plant species endemic to the US State of Alaska. It is found only on islands, not on the Alaskan mainland: Aleutian, St. Lawrence, St. Paul, Popof, and Kodiak Islands. It is found on rocky slopes and mountainsides up to an elevation of 700 m (2,300 ft).

items.name: Alpine chickweed
items.growersTips:
Plant in gritty, sharply drained soil to prevent winter rot caused by wet UK autumns and winters.
Position in full sun, ideally in a raised bed or rockery, to mimic its natural montane habitat.
Water sparingly once established, only during prolonged dry summer spells to avoid waterlogging.
Cut back the foliage hard after flowering in mid-summer to maintain a neat, compact cushion shape.
Propagate by dividing the clumps in early spring or taking softwood cuttings after summer flowering.
items.description: Cerastium alpinum, commonly called alpine mouse-ear or alpine chickweed, is a mat-forming perennial plant. The species was first described by Carl Linnaeus in 1753. It is native to Greenland, Canada and northern Europe. It is grown as a rock garden subject for its many small white flowers and silver haired stems and foliage. There are three subspecies.

items.name: Arctic mouse-ear
items.growersTips:
Plant in gritty, free-draining soil to prevent winter rot caused by wet UK winters.
Water sparingly, only during prolonged dry summer spells, to mimic its dry arctic habitat.
Position in full sun and a raised bed or rockery to ensure maximum light and sharp drainage.
Propagate by dividing the clump in early spring just as new growth begins to emerge.
Clear fallen autumn leaves quickly to prevent dampness from rotting the compact foliage cushion.
items.description: Cerastium arcticum, the Arctic mouse-ear chickweed or Arctic mouse-ear, is a flower found in parts of western and southern Greenland, Baffin Island, Labrador, Iceland, Faroe Islands, Scotland, Norway and Svalbard.

items.name: Field chickweed
items.growersTips:
Plant in gritty, free-draining soil to prevent winter root rot in wet UK clay.
Propagate by dividing established clumps in early spring or immediately after flowering in summer.
Shear the foliage back hard after summer flowering to maintain a neat, compact carpet.
Water newly planted divisions sparingly, only during prolonged dry spells in the UK summer.
Position in full sun alongside rockery companions like Thymus serpyllum or Sedum acre.
items.description: Cerastium arvense is a species of flowering plant in the pink family known by the common names field mouse-ear and field chickweed. It is a widespread species, occurring throughout Europe and North America, as well as parts of South America. It is a variable species. There are several subspecies, but the number and defining characteristics are disputed.

items.name: Cerastium biebersteinii
items.growersTips:
Plant in gritty, sharply draining soil to prevent winter root rot in wet UK climates.
Shear the foliage back by half immediately after summer flowering to keep the clump compact.
Water only during prolonged dry spells as this plant is highly drought-tolerant once established.
Divide congested clumps in early autumn to maintain vigor and propagate new plants easily.
Position in full sun alongside rock soapwort or sedums which share its love for dry conditions.
items.description: Cerastium biebersteinii, the boreal chickweed, is an ornamental plant in the genus Cerastium and the family Caryophyllaceae. It is an endemic of the Crimea. The species is named after a German botanist Friedrich August Marschall von Bieberstein.

items.name: Grey mouse ear
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn or early spring directly into poor, sharply draining soil with added grit.
Position in full sun to mimic its native dry UK banks, avoiding any waterlogged winter areas.
Water sparingly only during prolonged summer droughts, as this annual thrives on neglect.
Allow the plant to set seed naturally in late summer to ensure its return the following spring.
Weed hand-around the delicate shallow roots carefully to prevent disturbing the young seedlings.
items.description: Cerastium brachypetalum, commonly called gray chickweed, grey mouse-ear or gray mouse-ear chickweed, is a spring blooming annual plant species. It is native to Mediterranean and temperate Europe, northwestern Africa, the Caucasus, and Western Asia. It has been introduced and naturalized in North America.

items.name: Cerastium diffusum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn or early spring at a depth of two millimetres in poor, sharply draining soil.
Grow this annual in full sun alongside Sedum or Thymum species to mimic its native coastal habitat.
Water seedlings sparingly during damp UK springs to prevent dampening-off in heavy garden soils.
Avoid adding any compost or fertiliser to the soil as excess nutrients cause floppy, weak growth.
Collect the seed capsules in midsummer before they split to control self-seeding in gravel paths.
items.description: Cerastium diffusum, the fourstamen chickweed or sea mouse-ear, is a species of flowering plant in the pink and carnation family Caryophyllaceae. It is an annual herb, up to 30 cm.high, occurring in western Europe and northern Africa. It is mainly found in coastal areas of Algeria, the Baleares, Belgium, Corsica, Denmark, France, the Faroe Islands, Germany, Great Britain, Ireland, Italy, Libya, Morocco, Netherlands, Norway, Portugal, Sardinia, Sicily, Spain and Sweden. The flowers have 4 petals, 4 or 5 stamens appearing between March and May. The petals are much shorter than the sepals. The lea

items.name: Common mouse-ear
items.growersTips:
Control this invasive lawn weed by hand-pulling damp soil to extract the shallow, fibrous root system.
Mow your lawn at a high setting of seven centimeters to shade out and weaken these light-loving seeds.
Apply a nitrogen-rich lawn fertilizer in spring to help grass outcompete this low-growing weed.
Spot-treat dense patches in autumn using a selective lawn weedkiller containing fluroxypyr or MCPA.
Aerate compacted clay soils in autumn with a hollow-tine fork to reduce the damp conditions it loves.
items.description: Cerastium fontanum, also called mouse-ear chickweed, common mouse-ear, or starweed, is a species of mat-forming perennial or, rarely, annual plant. It is native to Europe but introduced elsewhere. Its identifying characteristics are tear-shaped leaves growing opposite one another in a star pattern, hairy leaves, and small white flowers. Mouse-ear chickweed typically grows to 4"-8" tall and spreads horizontally along the ground via the formation of roots wherever the stem falls over and contacts the ground.

items.name: Sticky Chickweed
items.growersTips:
Hand-weed young rosettes in early spring before they set seed in damp UK borders and gravel paths.
Sow seeds shallowly at two millimetres deep in autumn using gritty compost to ensure winter chill.
Avoid watering established plants in wet UK winters to prevent root rot in heavy clay soils.
Shear back the foliage by half immediately after flowering in June to stop aggressive self-seeding.
Grow alongside Thymus serpyllum in well-drained rockeries to create a competitive ground cover.
items.description: Cerastium glomeratum is a species of flowering plant in the family Caryophyllaceae known by the common names sticky mouse-ear chickweed and clammy chickweed. It is native to Europe, Macaronesia to Assam but is known on most continents as an introduced species. It grows in many types of habitat. The blooming period is February, March, April, and May.

items.name: Cerastium holosteoides
items.growersTips:
Keep this vigorous spreader in check by shearing it back hard immediately after flowering in July.
Grow in poor, sharply drained soil to prevent the plant from becoming excessively floppy and weak.
Water newly divided clumps weekly during dry UK spring spells until their shallow roots establish.
Divide congested mats every three years in autumn to maintain vigour and prevent center dieback.
Pair with robust rockery plants like Aubrieta to prevent this fast grower from smothering them.
items.description: Cerastium holosteoides, the common mouse-ear chickweed, is a species of flowering plant belonging to the family Caryophyllaceae.

items.name: Shetland mouse-ear
items.growersTips:
Plant in gritty scree or a raised alpine bed to ensure the sharp winter drainage this UK native needs
Water sparingly only during dry spring spells and keep completely dry during wet British winters
Cut back gently after summer flowering to maintain its tight cushion habit and prevent rotting off
Propagate by taking softwood cuttings in early summer to safeguard against winter wet losses
Position in full sun alongside non-vigorous alpine companions like Saxifraga to prevent smothering
items.description: Cerastium nigrescens var. nigrescens, commonly known as the Shetland mouse-ear, Shetland mouse-eared chickweed or Edmondston's chickweed, is an endemic variety of Arctic Chickweed, Cerastium nigrescens, found in Shetland, Scotland.

items.name: Cerastium pumilum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds thinly in autumn on the surface of gritty, well-drained soil to mimic UK wild habitats.
Position in full sun in a rock garden or gravel path where winter wet will not rot the roots.
Water sparingly only during dry spring spells, allowing the growing medium to dry out completely.
Leave faded flowers intact in midsummer to allow this annual to self-seed for the following year.
Clear surrounding aggressive weeds in early spring to prevent this small plant from being smothered.
items.description: Cerastium pumilum, the dwarf mouse-ear or European chickweed, is an annual or biannual herbaceous plant, between 2 and 20 cm high, native to Central and western Europe. The petals of the white flowers are shorter or equally long as the sepals, and split in the middle, up to a quarter of the length. The fruit petioles stand diagonal to the stems, often bent over at their top. Flowering occurs between March and May. Rarely occurs on the seacoast.

items.name: Cerastium regelii
items.growersTips:
Plant in gritty, sharply draining soil to prevent winter root rot in wet UK climates.
Water only during prolonged dry spells, letting the soil dry out completely between waterings.
Trim back the foliage by half in late summer after flowering to maintain a tight, compact cushion.
Position in full sun next to Campanula portenschlagiana to mimic natural alpine scree conditions.
Propagate by dividing the dense mats in early spring just as new growth begins to emerge.
items.description: Cerastium regelii, commonly known as Regel's chickweed, is a species of perennial flowering plant belonging to the family Caryophyllaceae.

items.name: Fivestamen chickweed
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in autumn on well-drained sandy soil to mimic UK coastal dunes for spring blooms.
Water sparingly only during dry spring spells as this annual thrives in dry, nutrient-poor soils.
Position in full sun alongside Sedum acre or Thymum to prevent more vigorous weeds from choking it.
Watch for slugs on young seedlings during damp British springs and protect with grit barriers.
Allow seed heads to dry and self-sow naturally in late summer to ensure its return next spring.
items.description: Cerastium semidecandrum, known as little mouse-ear in English, is an annual herbaceous plant in the flowering plant family Caryophyllaceae. It occurs in sandy, generally acid grassland and thin soils over bare rock. It is native to Europe, western Asia and north Africa and is widely established as an introduced species elsewhere.

items.name: Slovenian mouse-ear chickweed
items.growersTips:
Plant in gritty, free-draining soil to prevent winter root rot in wet UK climates.
Position in full sun to maintain the compact, low-growing habit and prevent leggy growth.
Cut back hard after flowering in midsummer to encourage fresh foliage and prevent self-seeding.
Water only during prolonged dry spells, as this alpine species is highly drought-tolerant.
Propagate by division in early spring or autumn to rejuvenate older, woody clumps.
items.description: Cerastium subtriflorum, the Slovenian mouse-ear chickweed, is a perennial plant species in the family Caryophyllaceae. It is mostly restricted to the Slovenian and Italian Alps.

items.name: Cerastium sylvaticum
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist but well-drained humus-rich soil in partial shade to mimic its native woodland edge.
Water weekly during dry UK summers to keep soil consistently damp but never waterlogged or boggy.
Divide congested clumps in autumn or early spring to maintain vigor and propagate new plants.
Shear back by half after summer flowering to promote fresh foliage growth and prevent self-seeding.
Plant alongside hostas or ferns in dappled shade to create a naturalistic woodland ground cover.
items.description: Cerastium sylvaticum is a species of flowering plant belonging to the family Caryophyllaceae.

items.name: Cerastium tomentosum
items.growersTips:
Plant in gritty, sharply draining soil to prevent winter root rot during wet UK winters.
Shear the foliage back by half immediately after flowering in July to keep the mat tight and neat.
Water only during prolonged summer droughts as this plant thrives on neglect and dry conditions.
Divide congested clumps every three years in early autumn to maintain vigour and prevent bald spots.
Plant alongside purple aubrieta or creeping phlox for a classic, contrasting dry stone wall display.
items.description: Cerastium tomentosum (snow-in-summer) is an herbaceous flowering plant and a member of the family Caryophyllaceae. It is generally distinguished from other species of its genus by "tomentose" or felty foliage. It is a low, spreading perennial native to the alpine regions of central and southern Italy. The stems and leaves are silvery-grey, whilst the flowers are star-like, white and about 15 mm (0.59 in) across.

items.name: Cerastium utriense
items.growersTips:
Plant in gritty, sharply draining soil to prevent winter root rot during wet UK winters.
Water sparingly only during prolonged summer droughts, as this alpine species hates soggy soil.
Trim back by half immediately after summer flowering to maintain a tight, cushion-like habit.
Position in full, unobstructed sun to mimic its native exposed limestone scree habitat.
Propagate by dividing the clump in early spring just as new growth begins to emerge.
items.description: Cerastium utriense is a species of perennial flowering plant in the genus Cerastium, belonging to the family Caryophyllaceae. It was first described in 1988. It is endemic to Italy.

items.name: Ceratiola
items.growersTips:
Grow in acidic, sandy, nutrient-poor soil with added grit to mimic its native scrub habitat.
Protect from winter wet by planting in a raised bed or container that drains rapidly.
Water sparingly only during prolonged summer droughts once the shrub is fully established.
Position in the absolute brightest, full-sun spot in your garden to prevent leggy growth.
Avoid pruning into old wood as this slow-growing shrub does not regenerate well from hard cuts.
items.description: Ceratiola is a genus of flowering plants with a single species, Ceratiola ericoides, a shrub endemic to the Southeastern United States.

items.name: Ceratocapnos claviculata
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn in a cold frame as they need winter cold to break dormancy before spring growth.
Grow in moist well-drained humus-rich soil in partial shade to mimic their native woodland habitat.
Provide a fine trellis or allow them to scramble naturally through sturdy shrubs like sarcococca.
Water consistently during dry UK summer spells to prevent the delicate foliage from dying back early.
Collect the explosive seed pods in summer just before they split to control self-seeding in borders.
items.description: Ceratocapnos is a genus of flowering plants belonging to the family Papaveraceae.

items.name: Ceratocapnos claviculata
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn in a shady woodland border with moist, acidic, humus-rich soil.
Provide a fine twiggy trellis or plant near shrubs to support its delicate climbing tendrils.
Water weekly during dry UK spring spells to keep the shallow root system consistently damp.
Check young shoots in spring for slug damage and protect them using organic beer traps.
Let the plant self-seed naturally in late summer to ensure its return the following year.
items.description: Ceratocapnos claviculata, the climbing corydalis, is a weak scrambling plant in the family Papaveraceae. It is endemic to Europe, growing mostly near the Atlantic fringe.

items.name: Ceratocephalus testiculatus
items.growersTips:
Grow this buttercup relative in sharply draining, gritty soil to prevent winter rot in wet UK rain.
Sow seeds in autumn at a depth of five millimetres to allow natural winter chilling for germination.
Water sparingly during the spring growing phase, allowing the soil to dry out completely between times.
Position in full sun to mimic its native dry habitat and prevent the plant from becoming leggy.
Plant alongside sedums or sempervivums in a rock garden to prevent vigorous plants from smothering it.

items.name: Carob
items.growersTips:
Plant this carob shrub in the sunniest south-facing spot against a warm wall to survive UK winters.
Grow in free-draining sandy soil mix with added grit to prevent root rot during wet UK winters.
Water young shrubs deeply once a week in summer, then reduce to zero watering during winter months.
Prune lightly in late spring after frost risk passes to shape the shrub and remove winter damage.
Keep in a large pot for its first three years so you can move it into a greenhouse during hard frosts.
items.description: The carob is a flowering evergreen tree or shrub in the Caesalpinioideae subfamily of the legume family, Fabaceae. The carob tree is native to the Mediterranean region and the Middle East. It is widely cultivated for its edible fruit, which takes the form of seed pods, and as an ornamental tree in gardens and landscapes. Spain is its largest producer, followed by Italy and Morocco.

items.name: Ceratostema alatum
items.growersTips:
Grow in a highly acidic, peat-free ericaceous compost mixed with plenty of perlite for drainage.
Position in a bright, humid conservatory or heated greenhouse to protect from frost below five degrees.
Water only with rainwater to keep the soil consistently damp but never waterlogged or soggy.
Apply a half-strength liquid ericaceous fertiliser monthly only during the active spring growth.
Prune lightly immediately after flowering in late summer to maintain its bushy, compact shape.
items.description: Ceratostema alatum is a species of Ceratostema found in Ecuador.

items.name: Ceratostema oellgaardii
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender Ecuadorian shrub in a heated greenhouse or conservatory to survive UK winters.
Use a highly acidic, peat-free ericaceous compost mixed with perlite for essential sharp drainage.
Water with harvested rainwater rather than tap water to keep the soil pH consistently below five.
Position in bright, filtered light away from direct midday sun to prevent leaf scorch in summer.
Propagate by taking semi-ripe stem cuttings in late summer using a heated propagator with misting.
items.description: Ceratostema oellgaardii is a shrub species of Ceratostema found in Loja, Ecuador at elevations from 2600 to 3300 meters.

items.name: Ceratostema rauhii
items.growersTips:
Grow in a highly acidic, peat-free ericaceous compost mixed with 50 percent perlite for sharp drainage.
Keep indoors in a heated greenhouse or conservatory as this tender shrub cannot survive UK frosts.
Water exclusively with rainwater to maintain the low soil pH required by this cloud forest native.
Feed monthly in spring and summer using a weak, diluted liquid ericaceous fertilizer.
Prune lightly immediately after flowering to shape the shrub and encourage fresh blooming wood.
items.description: Ceratostema rauhii, is a species of Ceratostema found in Peru south east of Chiclayo at elevations around 2200 meters.

items.name: Cercis siliquastrum
items.growersTips:
Plant in late spring after frosts in free-draining soil with grit to prevent winter root rot.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells rather than daily light sprinkling to establish.
Prune only in late summer to avoid bleeding sap and reduce the risk of coral spot fungus.
Protect young plants from strong winds by staking to prevent damage to the brittle branches.
Grow in full sun or dappled shade against a south-facing wall to maximise the spectacular blossom.
items.description: Cercis is a genus of about 10 species in the subfamily Cercidoideae of the pea family Fabaceae. It contains small deciduous trees or large shrubs commonly known as redbuds in the USA. They are characterised by simple, rounded to heart-shaped leaves and pinkish-red flowers borne in the early spring on bare leafless shoots, on both branches and trunk ("cauliflory"). The genus contains ten species, native to warm temperate regions of North America, southern Europe, western and central Asia, and China.

items.name: Chamaecrista greggii
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in April at a depth of 5mm using scarified seeds to improve UK germination rates.
Plant in poor, sandy, well-draining soil to prevent root rot in wet British summer weather.
Water sparingly only at the base once established, allowing the top 5cm of soil to dry out fully.
Position in the absolute brightest, south-facing spot to maximise limited UK summer sunshine.
Grow alongside native grasses to provide structural support for these delicate, sprawling annuals.
items.description: Chamaecrista is a genus of flowering plants in the pea family, Fabaceae, subfamily Caesalpinioideae. Members of the genus are commonly known as sensitive pea. Several species are capable of rapid plant movement. Unlike the related genera Cassia and Senna, members of Chamaecrista form root nodules.

items.name: Rosebay Willowherb
items.growersTips:
Plant Chamaenerion angustifolium Album in partial shade to control its vigorous UK woodland spread.
Cut stems to the ground in late autumn to prevent self-seeding across damp British clay soils.
Grow in deep pots to restrict invasive rhizomes from choking out delicate cottage garden plants.
Water newly divided spring offsets weekly until established in free-draining acidic UK soils.
Monitor young spring shoots for elephant hawk-moth caterpillars and hand-pick them off gently.
items.description: Chamaenerion is a genus of flowering plants in the family Onagraceae. It has sometimes been included in the genus Epilobium. Members of the genus may be called willowherbs, or fireweeds, based on a common name used for C. angustifolium. They are upright herbaceous perennials, growing from a woody base or from rhizomes, with racemes of usually purple to pink flowers. All species are found in the northern hemisphere. Most occur in moist habitats; C. angustifolium is the exception, favouring disturbed ground.

items.name: Rosebay Willowherb
items.growersTips:
Plant white cultivar Album to enjoy the showy flowers without the aggressive self-seeding of pinks.
Chop stems to the ground in late autumn to prevent wind-blown seeds from invading your UK lawn.
Grow in large sunken bottomless buckets to restrict the highly invasive underground running roots.
Water young plants weekly during dry UK springs but stop once established to prevent floppy growth.
Plant alongside robust native ferns and nettles in damp woodland edges to naturally curb its spread.
items.description: Chamaenerion angustifolium is a perennial herbaceous flowering plant in the willowherb family, Onagraceae. It is known in North America as fireweed and in the British Isles as both fireweed and rosebay willowherb. It is also known by the taxonomic synonyms Chamerion angustifolium and Epilobium angustifolium. It is native throughout the temperate Northern Hemisphere, including large parts of the boreal forests.

items.name: Chamaescilla corymbosa
items.growersTips:
Plant tubers five centimetres deep in autumn using gritty, free-draining soil to prevent winter rot.
Grow in pots to easily move undercover during wet UK winters, preventing waterlogged dormant roots.
Water moderately during active winter growth, then dry out completely after summer foliage dies back.
Position in full sun or a south-facing cold frame to mimic its native sunny Australian habitat.
Protect emerging winter shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.
items.description: Chamaescilla corymbosa, commonly known as blue stars, blue squill or mudrurt, is a tuberous perennial herb species in the genus Chamaescilla. It is endemic to southern Australia.

items.name: Chamaescilla spiralis
items.growersTips:
Plant these Australian native bulbs 5cm deep in gritty, sharply draining soil to survive UK winters.
Grow in pots of loam-based compost mixed with 50 percent grit to prevent winter wet root rot.
Water moderately during their autumn to spring active growth, then keep completely dry in summer.
Position pots in a cold frame or unheated greenhouse to shield them from heavy UK winter rainfall.
Watch for slugs and snails in early spring when the highly twisted, spiral leaves first emerge.
items.description: Chamaescilla spiralis is a plant species in family Asphodelaceae and genus Chamaescilla. It is located in Western Australia. The species name spiralis is derived from the curled shape of its leaves.

items.name: Dwarf fireweed
items.growersTips:
Plant in poor well-drained gravelly soil to mimic its native subarctic riverbed habitat in the UK
Sow seeds on the soil surface in autumn as they require cold stratification and light to germinate
Water sparingly once established only during prolonged dry summer spells to prevent root rot in clay
Cut stems back to ground level in late autumn after seed pods split to control self-seeding in borders
Grow alongside alpine plants like Saxifraga in a raised scree bed to prevent it being smothered
items.description: Chamaenerion latifolium is a species of flowering plant in the evening primrose family known by the English common names dwarf fireweed and river beauty willowherb. It has a circumboreal distribution, appearing throughout the northern regions of the Northern Hemisphere, including alpine, sub-Arctic, and Arctic areas such as snowmelt-flooded gravel bars and talus, in a wide range of elevations. This is a perennial herb growing in clumps of leaves variable in size, shape, and texture above a woody caudex. The leaves are 1 to 10 centimeters long, lance-shaped to oval, pointed or rounded at the ti

items.name: Chelidonium majus
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in autumn in damp, shady borders to mimic UK woodland edge conditions.
Wear thick gloves when weeding to avoid skin irritation from the toxic bright orange sap.
Cut back foliage to the ground in late summer to prevent aggressive self-seeding in damp soil.
Plant alongside shade-loving pulmonaria or hostas to mask the untidy post-flowering dieback.
Water young plants weekly in dry summer spells but leave established clumps to survive on rainfall.
items.description: Chelidonium majus, the greater celandine, is a perennial herbaceous flowering plant in the poppy family Papaveraceae. One of two species in the genus Chelidonium, it is native to Europe and western Asia and introduced widely in North America.

items.name: Cherleria laricifolia
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in early spring under a cold frame to protect from heavy UK spring downpours.
Grow in sharply draining gritty soil to prevent winter root rot in damp British climates.
Water sparingly once established, allowing the gritty compost to dry out fully between waterings.
Position in full sun to mimic their native alpine habitats and prevent leggy, weak growth.
Plant alongside sedums in rock gardens to provide compatible low-water companion conditions.
items.description: Cherleria is a genus of flowering plants in the family Caryophyllaceae, found in the Arctic and mountainous areas of the northern hemisphere. Its center of diversity is the Balkans. The species shows ecological differentiation and multiple colonisations of alpine habitats. In 2017, Cherleria was expanded to include species from other genera.

items.name: Cherleria biflora
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn in a cold frame using a gritty, free-draining compost to mimic alpine scree.
Water only when the top two inches of soil are dry to prevent root rot in damp UK winters.
Position in full sun and surround the base with a fine grit mulch to keep the foliage dry.
Grow alongside Saxifraga or Sempervivum in a raised alpine trough to ensure perfect drainage.
Check regularly for slugs and snails during wet spring nights as they love the soft foliage.
items.description: Cherleria biflora is a species of plant in the family Caryophyllaceae. It is known as mountain stitchwort.

items.name: Prince’s pine
items.growersTips:
Plant Chimaphila in acidic, humus-rich soil mixed with pine needles to mimic UK woodland floors.
Water with rainwater rather than tap water to keep the soil pH consistently below five point five.
Position in deep shade under conifers to protect the delicate evergreen foliage from UK winter sun.
Propagate by taking semi-ripe cuttings in late summer and rooting them in a shaded cold frame.
Mulch annually with leaf mould or composted bark to preserve moisture without waterlogging roots.
items.description:
Chimaphila is a genus of five species of small, evergreen, flowering plants native to temperate regions of the Northern Hemisphere. They are classified in the family Ericaceae, but were formerly placed in the segregate family Pyrolaceae.SpeciesChimaphila japonica
Chimaphila maculata 
Chimaphila menziesii 
Chimaphila monticola
Chimaphila umbellata

items.name: Chionophila tweedyi
items.growersTips:
Plant in a raised scree bed or alpine house using a gritty, sharply draining neutral to acid compost.
Water only from below or around the base in winter to prevent the crown from rotting in wet UK cold.
Position in a north-facing crevice or light afternoon shade to protect from hot midsummer UK sun.
Protect plants with a pane of glass or cloche from November to March to shield from persistent rain.
Watch closely for vine weevil larvae which target the roots of this alpine in container culture.
items.description: Chionophila tweedyi, or Tweedy's snowlover, is a perennial herb in the plantain family. It is native to Idaho and Montana in the western United States.

items.name: Chloraeinae
items.growersTips:
Plant these terrestrial orchids in a gritty, free-draining mix of loam, perlite, and fine bark.
Position pots in a cold greenhouse to protect tubers from excessive winter wet and hard UK frosts.
Water thoroughly during active spring growth but keep tubers almost dry during summer dormancy.
Watch for slugs and snails in spring as they quickly destroy the emerging flower spikes and buds.
Repot during late summer dormancy using deep pots to accommodate the long, fleshy root systems.
items.description: Chloraeinae is an orchid subtribe in the subfamily Orchidoideae.

items.name: Chlorogalum angustifolium
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs in autumn at a depth of eight centimetres in sharply draining, gritty soil to avoid rot.
Sow seeds in cold frames during October to allow natural winter chilling for spring germination.
Stop watering completely in July when the foliage dies back to mimic its dry summer dormancy.
Protect young spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.
Grow alongside hardy UK rockery plants like Sedum or Thymus that share its dry summer needs.
items.description: Chlorogalum angustifolium is a species of flowering plant, known by the common name narrowleaf soap plant.

items.name: Chlorogalum grandiflorum
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs in autumn at a depth of ten centimeters in sharply draining, gritty soil to prevent rot.
Sow seeds in cold frames during winter as they require UK winter chilling to break their dormancy.
Water moderately during spring growth but keep the soil completely dry during summer dormancy.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.
Grow in full sun in a south-facing gravel garden or raised bed to mimic its native dry habitat.
items.description: Chlorogalum grandiflorum is a species of flowering plant known by the common name Red Hills soap plant. It is endemic to the Sierra Nevada foothills, such as the Red Hills, of California, where it grows in chaparral, woodland, and forest.

items.name: Chlorogalum pomeridianum
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs 10cm deep in autumn using gritty, free-draining soil to prevent winter wet rot in UK rain.
Position in full south-facing sun to mimic its native California chaparral and trigger summer blooms.
Stop watering completely in July when foliage dies back to allow the bulb its essential dry dormancy.
Protect the emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails which love the tender new strap-like leaves.
Grow alongside low-growing Mediterranean herbs like thyme to cover the bare ground when it goes dormant.
items.description: Chlorogalum pomeridianum, the wavy-leafed soap plant, California soaproot, or Amole, is the most common and most widely distributed of the soap plants, soaproots or amoles, which make up the genus Chlorogalum of flowering plants. It is occasionally known as the "wild potato", but given the plant's lack of either resemblance or relationship to the potato, this name is not recommended.

items.name: Chlorophytum borivilianum
items.growersTips:
Grow in pots of gritty, peat-free compost to easily move indoors before the first autumn frosts.
Water sparingly in winter but keep soil consistently moist during the active spring growing season.
Plant tubers 5cm deep in late spring once soil temperatures consistently exceed 15 degrees Celsius.
Overwinter dormant tubers in dry sand inside a frost-free shed or greenhouse to prevent root rot.
Watch for slugs and snails attacking the tender new shoots during damp UK spring weather.
items.description: Chlorophytum borivilianum is a herb with lanceolate leaves, from tropical wet forests in the peninsular Indian region.

items.name: Chlorophytum comosum
items.growersTips:
Bring indoors before the first autumn frost as they cannot survive UK winter temperatures below 5C.
Water thoroughly only when the top two inches of compost feel dry to prevent root rot in UK damp.
Repot in spring using peat-free compost mixed with one-third grit to ensure fast drainage.
Snip off baby plantlets in summer and root them in small pots of moist compost to multiply stocks.
Watch for aphids on indoor plants in spring and wipe them off with a damp cloth immediately.
items.description: Chlorophytum comosum, usually called spider plant or common spider plant due to its spider-like look, also known as spider ivy, airplane plant, ribbon plant, and hen and chicks, is a species of evergreen perennial flowering plant of the family Asparagaceae. It is native to tropical and Southern Africa but has become naturalized in other parts of the world, including Western Australia and Bangladesh. Chlorophytum comosum is easy to grow as a houseplant because of its resilience, but it can be sensitive to the fluoride in tap water, which commonly gives it "burnt tips". Variegated forms are the

items.name: Chlorophytum debile
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender herb in pots to easily move it indoors before the first autumn frosts hit the UK
Plant tubers shallowly at a depth of three centimetres in free-draining peat-free potting compost
Water only when the top two centimetres of soil feel dry to prevent tuber rot in cool UK weather
Snip off faded outer leaves at the base in spring to encourage fresh new variegated growth clumps
Check the dense leaf bases weekly for mealybugs which thrive in warm indoor winter environments
items.description: Chlorophytum debile is a species of flowering plant in the family Asparagaceae, native to western and southern tropical Africa. It was first described by John Gilbert Baker in 1878.

items.name: Chlorophytum filipendulum
items.growersTips:
Grow indoors in a peat-free loam compost with added grit to ensure sharp drainage in damp UK winters.
Water only when the top three centimetres of soil dry out to prevent root rot in cool UK rooms.
Position in bright indirect light near an east window to avoid leaf scorch from direct summer sun.
Propagate in spring by dividing the fleshy rhizomes rather than waiting for runners which are rare.
Keep minimum winter temperatures above ten degrees Celsius to prevent the soft foliage from melting.
items.description: Chlorophytum filipendulum is a species of flowering plant in the Asparagaceae family. It is native to a variety of habitats across large areas of Equatorial Africa.

items.name: Chlorophytum holstii
items.growersTips:
Bring this tender African herb indoors before the first autumn frost to survive the cold UK winter.
Grow in a well-draining peat-free compost mixed with one-third grit to prevent winter root rot.
Water thoroughly only when the top two inches of soil feel dry, reducing this to monthly in winter.
Position in bright, indirect light near an east-facing window to avoid scorching the delicate leaves.
Repot in spring only when the thick, water-storing tuberous roots start pushing out of the pot base.
items.description: Chlorophytum holstii is a flowering plant species in the genus Chlorophytum, endemic to Tanzania and Kenya.

items.name: Chlorophytum inornatum
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender African native in pots to easily move it indoors before the first autumn frosts.
Water only when the top two centimetres of compost feel dry to prevent root rot in cool UK winters.
Repot in spring using a peat-free multi-purpose compost mixed with one-third grit for fast drainage.
Position in bright, indirect light near an east window to avoid leaf scorch from harsh summer sun.
Snip off faded lower leaves at the base in spring using sterilized shears to keep the clump tidy.
items.description:
Chlorophytum inornatum is a flowering plant species in the genus Chlorophytum. It is the type species of its genus.
It is related to the commonly known houseplant Chlorophytum comosum also referred to as a "spider plant".
3-(4'-Methoxybenzyl)-7,8-methylenedioxy-chroman-4-one, a homoisoflavanone with antimycobacterial activity, can be isolated from C. inornatum.

items.name: Chlorophytum laxum
items.growersTips:
Grow in a loam-based potting compost with added grit to ensure the sharp drainage this plant needs.
Water moderately from spring to autumn but allow the top two centimetres of soil to dry out first.
Overwinter indoors on a bright windowsill as this tender herb cannot survive UK frosts below eight degrees.
Snip off faded outer leaves at the very base in spring using sharp scissors to maintain neat growth.
Check the dense leaf clumps regularly for mealybugs which thrive in warm indoor UK microclimates.
items.description: Chlorophytum laxum is a flowering plant species in the genus Chlorophytum, widespread through tropical Africa, Asia, and Australia.

items.name: Chlorophytum tuberosum
items.growersTips:
Grow in free-draining sandy loam with grit to prevent winter tuber rot in wet UK soils.
Bring potted tubers indoors before the first autumn frost as they cannot survive UK winter freezes.
Water moderately during the active summer growth phase but keep compost nearly dry during dormancy.
Plant tubers 5cm deep in late spring once soil warms up, using terracotta pots for drainage.
Watch for slugs and snails attacking the tender emerging spring shoots in damp UK weather.
items.description: Chlorophytum tuberosum is a species of flowering plant in the Asparagaceae family. It is one of several species known by the common name musli. It is native to parts of Africa and India. It has historical uses in Ayurveda.

items.name: Chrysopsis delaneyi
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in spring under glass as this Florida native needs warmth to germinate in the UK.
Grow in sharply draining sandy soil or grit-amended compost to prevent winter wet rotting the roots.
Position in the absolute sunniest spot of your garden to mimic its native scrub habitat conditions.
Water sparingly only when the top two inches of soil are dry to avoid fatal root rot in wet summers.
Protect young spring shoots from slugs and snails which find the tender new foliage highly appealing.
items.description: Chrysopsis delaneyi, or DeLaney's goldenaster, is one of the endemic species to the U.S. state of Florida, recently discovered in the genus Chrysopsis, a small group of herbaceous plants of the family Asteraceae, known commonly as the "golden asters" and primarily native and restricted to Florida.

items.name: Chrysopsis floridana
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at two millimetres deep in spring using a free-draining sandy loam compost mix.
Water only when the top five centimetres of soil is dry to mimic its native drought-tolerant dunes.
Protect young plants from slugs and snails during wet UK springs using organic wool pellets.
Position in the sunniest south-facing spot to maximise summer heat and prevent waterlogged roots.
Grow in terracotta pots to ensure excellent drainage and easily move shelter during heavy autumn rain.
items.description: Chrysopsis floridana is a rare species of flowering plant in the family Asteraceae, known by its common name, Florida golden aster. It is endemic to Florida in the United States, where it is known from Hillsborough, Hardee, Manatee, and Pinellas Counties. It is considered an endemic of the west-central coast of the state in the general vicinity of Tampa Bay. There are 17 to 20 occurrences, many of which have few individuals, but one of which has over one million plants. In 1986 the plant was added to the US endangered species list because it was becoming increasingly rare, it was growing only

items.name: Chrysopsis gossypina
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly indoors in March at a depth of two millimetres to combat wet UK spring soil.
Grow in sharply draining sandy soil mixed with grit to prevent winter root rot in damp UK climates.
Water only when the top five centimetres of soil is bone dry to mimic its native dry habitat.
Position in the sunniest south-facing spot to maximise the limited summer heat of UK gardens.
Plant alongside lavender or thyme which share its strict requirement for low-nutrient dry soil.
items.description: Chrysopsis gossypina, the cottony goldenaster, is a North American species of flowering plant in the family Asteraceae. It is native to the Coastal Plain of the southeastern United States, from eastern Louisiana to southeastern Virginia.

items.name: Chrysopsis highlandsensis
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in spring under glass as this Florida native needs warmth to germinate in the UK.
Grow in sharply draining sandy soil or grit-amended compost to prevent winter wet from rotting roots.
Water sparingly once established, letting the soil dry out completely between watering sessions.
Position in your sunniest south-facing spot to mimic its native scrub habitat and trigger blooms.
Deadhead spent yellow flowers weekly in late summer to prolong the blooming display until autumn.
items.description: Chrysopsis highlandsensis, called the Highlands goldenaster, is a North American species of flowering plant in the aster family. It has been found only in three counties in central Florida: Highlands, Polk, and Glades.

items.name: Chrysopsis lanuginosa
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at two millimetres deep in spring using a free-draining sandy loam compost mix.
Position in the sunniest south-facing spot to mimic its native habitat and prevent damp-induced rot.
Water only when the top five centimetres of soil is bone dry to prevent waterlogging in wet summers.
Protect young spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.
Plant alongside drought-tolerant English lavender or thyme to ensure compatible low-moisture needs.
items.description: Chrysopsis lanuginosa, called the Lynn Haven goldenaster, is a North American species of flowering plant in the family Asteraceae. It has been found only in the Florida Panhandle.

items.name: Chrysopsis latisquamea
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly indoors in March, barely covering with grit, to combat damp UK spring weather.
Plant out in May in sharply draining, sandy soil to prevent root rot from heavy UK summer rainfall.
Water only at the base during dry spells, keeping foliage dry to prevent powdery mildew outbreaks.
Pinch out the growing tips in June to encourage a bushier habit and more late-summer yellow blooms.
Position next to lavender or thyme in full sun to mimic its native dry, open habitat requirements.
items.description: Chrysopsis latisquamea, the pineland goldenaster, is a North American species of flowering plant in the family Asteraceae. It has been found only in Florida.

items.name: Chrysopsis mariana
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in spring under glass as they need light and a UK temperature of 15C to germinate
Grow in poor sandy soil with sharp grit to mimic its native pine barren habitat and prevent rot
Water sparingly once established to survive dry UK summers but ensure excellent winter drainage
Deadhead faded yellow blooms in late summer to prolong the flowering display and prevent self-seeding
Plant alongside low-growing thyme or sedum to provide support and keep weeds from crowding it out
items.description: Chrysopsis mariana, known as the Maryland golden-aster, is a North American species of plants in the family Asteraceae. The Maryland golden-aster ranges from Rhode Island and New York, west to Kentucky and southern Ohio, and south as far as Florida and Texas.

items.name: Chrysopsis scabrella
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in March under glass at a depth of two millimetres using free-draining sandy compost.
Grow in terracotta pots of gritty loam to protect the roots from wet winter rot in UK climates.
Water only when the top five centimetres of soil is dry to mimic its native dry scrub habitat.
Pinch out the growing tips in late May to encourage a bushier habit and more yellow flower heads.
Position in your sunniest south-facing spot to ensure enough summer heat for successful blooming.

items.name: Alternate-leaved Golden-saxifrage
items.growersTips:
Plant golden saxifrage in permanently wet acidic soil alongside ferns in a deep shade bog garden.
Propagate by dividing the creeping stolons in spring to quickly carpet bare damp woodland soil.
Watch for slugs and snails in mild wet UK springs as they quickly devour the tender new foliage.
Grow Chrysosplenium oppositifolium in heavy clay shade where other groundcovers fail to establish.
Do not prune but clear fallen autumn leaves off the low mats to prevent the damp foliage rotting.

items.name: Alternate-leaved Golden-saxifrage
items.growersTips:
Plant in consistently damp acidic to neutral soil mimicking UK wet woodland stream banks.
Position in deep or partial shade as direct UK summer sun will quickly scorch the delicate foliage.
Propagate by dividing the creeping stolons in spring just after the yellow-green bracts fade.
Grow alongside Astilbe or hostas in bog gardens to provide contrasting leaf textures and heights.
Watch for slugs and snails in damp spring conditions which can rapidly consume the young shoots.

items.name: Chrysosplenium americanum
items.growersTips:
Plant in consistently boggy neutral to acid soil along shady pond edges or wet woodland hollows.
Propagate by dividing the creeping stolons in spring, planting them just below the soil surface.
Grow alongside native UK moisture-lovers like Caltha palustris or Primula vulgaris in deep shade.
Keep the soil constantly wet during dry summer spells to prevent the shallow roots from drying out.
Watch for slugs and snails in spring as they target the tender new succulent foliage in damp areas.

items.name: Chrysosplenium flagelliferum
items.growersTips:
Plant in moisture-retentive, humus-rich soil in deep shade to mimic UK woodland stream banks.
Water frequently in dry summer months to keep the soil constantly damp and prevent leaf scorch.
In autumn, clear fallen tree leaves off the low foliage to prevent crown rot in damp UK winters.
Propagate in spring by pinning down the running stolons into moist soil until they root.
Plant alongside Astilbe or Hostas which thrive in the same boggy, shaded British garden spots.

items.name: Chrysosplenium glechomifolium
items.growersTips:
Plant in consistently boggy neutral to acid soil in deep shade to mimic UK woodland stream banks.
Propagate by dividing the creeping stolons in early spring just as new green growth begins to emerge.
Water heavily during dry summer spells to prevent the shallow root system from drying out and dying.
Grow alongside Hostas and Astilbes which thrive in the same wet shade and mask summer dieback.
Watch for slugs and snails in spring as they target the tender young foliage in damp UK gardens.

items.name: Chrysosplenium iowense
items.growersTips:
Grow in constantly damp acidic to neutral boggy soil or wet woodland hollows to mimic its wild habitat
Plant bare roots shallowly in early spring just below the soil surface in deep shade under shrubs
Water daily during dry UK summers to keep the soil saturated as this species cannot tolerate drying out
Propagate by gently dividing the delicate creeping stolons in autumn after flowering has finished
Watch for slugs and snails in spring which quickly decimate the tender emerging golden-green bracts

items.name: Opposite-leaved golden-saxifrage
items.growersTips:
Plant this native in permanently damp acidic to neutral soil in deep shade near a pond or bog garden.
Propagate by dividing the creeping mats in spring or autumn and press shallowly into wet mud.
Keep the soil constantly wet during dry UK summers to prevent the shallow roots from drying out.
Watch for slugs and snails which target the tender succulent leaves in damp shady garden corners.
Grow alongside native ferns and primroses which thrive in the same cool wet woodland conditions.

items.name: Chrysosplenium pilosum
items.growersTips:
Plant in water-retentive, acidic to neutral boggy soil or wet woodland edges in partial to deep shade
Keep soil consistently wet or waterlogged, mimicking UK stream banks, never letting the roots dry out
Propagate by dividing the creeping stolons in spring just as new growth begins to establish easily
Watch for slugs and snails in damp UK spring weather, protecting the delicate emerging golden bracts
Grow alongside Astilbe or hostas in shady damp borders to create a naturalistic ground cover tapestry

items.name: Chrysosplenium sinicum
items.growersTips:
Plant in wet acidic soil near a pond edge or bog garden to mimic its native damp woodland habitat.
Water daily during dry UK summers to keep the soil constantly saturated and prevent foliage scorch.
Propagate by dividing the creeping stolons in early spring just as new growth begins to emerge.
Position in deep shade under ferns or hostas to protect the delicate leaves from strong UK sun.
Watch for slugs and snails during wet spring nights as they target the tender young spring shoots.

items.name: Chrysosplenium tosaense
items.growersTips:
Plant in wet acidic soil or boggy shade using leafmould to mimic UK woodland stream margins.
Water constantly to keep soil saturated as this plant cannot tolerate drying out in summer.
Position in deep or partial shade to prevent the delicate lime-green foliage from scorching.
Propagate by dividing the creeping stolons in spring once the yellow-green bracts fade.
Protect the tender evergreen leaves from slugs and snails during damp UK spring nights.

items.name: Chrysosplenium wrightii
items.growersTips:
Plant in wet acid peat or gritty loam in a cold frame to mimic its native subarctic conditions.
Keep the soil constantly saturated using rainwater as this species cannot tolerate drying out.
Provide deep shade and protection from hot summer sun which easily scorches this delicate alpine.
Propagate by carefully dividing the creeping stolons in early spring just as new growth begins.
Protect from slugs and snails in spring as they quickly consume the small fleshy green leaves.

items.name: Chuquiraga spinosa
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in spring at a depth of five millimetres using a gritty, free-draining cactus compost mix
Water only when the top five centimetres of soil is dry to prevent root rot in damp UK weather
Position pots in the sunniest south-facing spot to mimic the intense light of their native Andes
Protect young seedlings from slugs and snails using copper tape around the pots in wet UK springs
Plant alongside hardy sedums in containers to ensure similar low-water and high-drainage needs

items.name: Chylismia claviformis
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn in a cold frame using a gritty, free-draining compost mix to mimic desert soils.
Water sparingly from below only when the top two inches of soil are dry to prevent crown rot.
Overwinter container-grown plants in an unheated greenhouse to protect them from wet UK winters.
Position in the sunniest south-facing spot possible to encourage evening blooms in cool climates.
Mix horticultural grit and perlite into heavy UK garden clay to ensure rapid drainage for roots.

items.name: Chylismia brevipes
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in spring using a very free-draining sandy loam to mimic its desert habitat.
Grow in a terracotta pot to ensure excellent drainage and protect from wet winter root rot.
Water sparingly only when the soil is completely dry, keeping the foliage dry to prevent mildew.
Overwinter containers in a cold frame or unheated greenhouse to shield from heavy UK winter rain.
Position in the absolute brightest, south-facing spot in your garden to maximise summer blooms.

items.name: Chylismia cardiophylla
items.growersTips:
Grow in a heated greenhouse or conservatory as this desert native cannot survive wet UK winters.
Sow seeds on the surface of free-draining sandy loam mixed with grit and do not cover with soil.
Water sparingly from below during spring and summer, keeping the compost completely dry in winter.
Position in the brightest south-facing spot possible to mimic its native Mojave Desert sunlight.
Use terracotta pots rather than plastic to prevent root rot in the damp British atmosphere.

items.name: Chylismia claviformis
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in spring under glass using a gritty, free-draining cactus compost mix.
Overwinter this desert native in a frost-free greenhouse to protect it from wet UK winters.
Water sparingly only when the soil is dry, mimicking its natural arid Mojave desert habitat.
Position in the sunniest south-facing spot possible to maximise summer heat and encourage blooms.
Watch for slugs and snails which quickly destroy the soft rosette foliage in damp British spring weather.

items.name: Cimicifuga racemosa
items.growersTips:
