Plant in moisture-retentive, humus-rich soil in dappled shade to prevent the foliage from scorching.
In dry UK summers, water deeply once a week at the base to keep the soil consistently damp.
Mulch annually in spring with well-rotted manure to retain moisture and feed this hungry perennial.
Cut the spent flower spikes down to the base in late autumn or leave them for winter structure.
Watch for slugs and snails in damp spring weather as they quickly damage emerging young shoots.

items.name: Enchanter's nightshade
items.growersTips:
Plant Circaea lutetiana bare roots 5cm deep in moisture-retentive, humus-rich soil in autumn.
Water weekly during dry UK summer spells to keep the woodland soil consistently damp but not soggy.
Hand-pull invasive runners in spring to control spread in small shady borders or damp rock gardens.
Sow seeds in cold frames during autumn to allow natural UK winter stratification for spring growth.
Pair with native ferns and hostas in deep shade to create a natural damp woodland understory.

items.name: Circaea × intermedia
items.growersTips:
Plant this woodland native in damp shade using moisture-retentive, leaf-mould-enriched acidic soil.
Water weekly during dry UK summers to keep the soil consistently moist but never waterlogged.
Control its aggressive underground runners by planting in submerged pots to protect nearby plants.
Cut the stems to ground level in late autumn after the bur-like seed heads finish flowering.
Pair with shade-loving UK natives like Dryopteris filix-mas and Primula vulgaris for ground cover.

items.name: Enchanter's nightshade
items.growersTips:
Plant in damp acidic deciduous shade mimicking UK woodlands using leaf mould to enrich the soil
Water consistently to keep soil constantly moist but not waterlogged during dry summer spells
Sow seeds shallowly in autumn or divide the delicate creeping rhizomes in early spring to propagate
Watch for capsid bugs and vine weevil larvae which target the soft foliage in damp garden borders
Group with native ferns and wood anemones in a dedicated shade garden to control its spreading habit

items.name: Circaea canadensis

items.description: Clematis alpina, the Alpine clematis, is a flowering deciduous vine of the genus Clematis. Like many members of that genus, it is prized by gardeners for its showy flowers. It bears 1 to 3-inch spring flowers on long stalks in a wide variety of colors. C. alpina is native to Europe; in the United States it grows best in American Horticultural Society zones 9 to 6, which are generally found in the southern USA.

items.name: Forster's clematis

Plant in sharply draining gritty soil to prevent root rot during wet UK winters.
Grow in a sheltered south-facing spot or container to protect evergreen foliage from cold winds.
Prune immediately after spring flowering by lightly tidying stems to maintain its compact shape.
Water sparingly once established as this New Zealand native prefers dry conditions over damp soil.
Provide a low trellis or allow it to scramble naturally over sunny rockeries and gravel beds.

items.name: Clematis fremontii
items.growersTips:
Plant this non-climbing clematis in gritty, free-draining soil to prevent winter root rot in UK wet.
Cut the stems back to ground level in late autumn or early spring before new growth emerges.
Grow in full sun and shelter from strong winds, as its upright herbaceous stems can flop easily.
Top-dress the soil annually in spring with grit rather than organic mulch to keep the crown dry.
Propagate by taking softwood cuttings in spring, as this species does not transplant well once set.

items.name: Clematis glycinoides
items.growersTips:
Plant in free-draining UK soil with the crown exactly 5cm below the surface to prevent clematis wilt.
Water deeply once a week during dry British summers, keeping the roots cool with a layer of pebbles.
Prune this Group 1 clematis immediately after spring flowering, removing only dead or crowded stems.
Protect young spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers around the base.
Grow against a warm south-facing wall to protect the delicate white spring blooms from harsh frosts.

items.name: Clematis gouriana
items.growersTips:
Plant crown 8cm deep in moist, alkaline to neutral soil to protect against clematis wilt disease.
Prune hard in early March down to 30cm from the ground to manage its vigorous five-metre spread.
Position the roots in deep shade using flat stones while keeping the climbing foliage in full sun.
Water deeply once a week during dry UK summers to support the late August white flower explosion.
Provide a sturdy wooden trellis or archway to support the heavy weight of its woody winter stems.

items.name: Clematis hedysarifolia
items.growersTips:
Plant in a south-facing sheltered UK spot to protect this tender evergreen from cold winter winds.
Prune immediately after spring flowering by removing dead stems to keep the vigorous growth tidy.
Provide deep organic mulch in autumn to insulate the roots against wet and freezing UK winters.
Water deeply at the base twice a week during dry summer spells to keep the root run cool and moist.
Grow in a large terracotta pot using loam-based compost so you can move it into a greenhouse in frost.

items.name: Clematis heracleifolia
items.growersTips:
Plant in moisture-retentive, alkaline to neutral soil enriched with well-rotted garden compost.
Position in full sun or partial shade with the crown buried five centimetres deep to bud deeply.
Cut all stems back to ground level in early March just as new growth begins at the plant base.
Water deeply once a week during dry UK summer spells to prevent powdery mildew on the foliage.
Grow alongside sturdy shrub roses or hardy geraniums to support its floppy, non-climbing habit.
items.description: Clematis heracleifolia, the tube clematis, is a species of flowering plant in the buttercup family Ranunculaceae, native to central and northern China. Unlike most other members of the genus Clematis, it has a scrambling rather than a climbing habit.

items.name: Clematis hirsutissima
items.growersTips:
Plant in gritty, free-draining soil to mimic its native scree slopes and prevent winter wet rot.
Position in full UK sun with its roots shaded by flat stones to keep them cool and damp.
Cut back the dead herbaceous stems to ground level in late autumn after the foliage dies back.
Water deeply once a week during dry spring spells, but keep it dry during its winter dormancy.
Protect the emerging spring shoots from slugs using organic grit barriers or beer traps.

items.name: Clematis integrifolia
items.growersTips:
Plant this non-climbing clematis deeply with the crown five centimetres below the soil surface.
Provide a low metal hoop support in May to prevent the floppy herbaceous stems from splaying open.
Prune the entire plant down to ground level every March before the new spring growth emerges.
Water deeply at the base once a week during dry UK summer spells to prevent powdery mildew.
Grow alongside sturdy shrub roses or lavender which naturally prop up the weak herbaceous stems.

items.name: Clematis koreana
items.growersTips:
Plant Clematis koreana 5-8cm deeper than the pot level in autumn to encourage strong basal shoots.
Prune in group one style by only cutting back dead or weak stems immediately after spring flowering.
Water deeply once a week during dry UK summer spells rather than giving frequent shallow sprinkles.
Grow in free-draining neutral to alkaline soil, adding grit to heavy clay to prevent winter rot.
Plant low-growing hardy geraniums at the base to shade the roots while keeping the vines in sun.

items.name: Clematis lanuginosa
items.growersTips:
Plant the root ball five centimetres deeper than soil level to encourage shoots from below ground.
Prune in late February by cutting all stems back to thirty centimetres above strong buds.
Mulch the root zone with well-rotted manure in April to keep soil cool and damp in dry UK summers.
Apply a high-potassium tomato feed fortnightly from May until August to boost the large blooms.
Watch for earwigs chewing the petals in June by trapping them in upturned straw-filled pots.

items.name: Clematis lasiantha
items.growersTips:
Plant this Californian native in a south-facing, sheltered spot to mimic its warm chaparral home.
Plant the root ball 5cm deeper than soil level in extremely free-draining, gravel-amended soil.
Water deeply once a week during dry UK summers, keeping the base shaded with flat stones or mulch.
Prune lightly in late winter by removing dead stems to fit its Group 1 classification requirements.
Protect young spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.

items.name: Clematis ligusticifolia
items.growersTips:
Plant this vigorous climber in deep, moisture-retentive, alkaline to neutral soil to prevent wilt.
Prune in late winter by cutting all stems back to thirty centimetres above ground to group three rules.
Water deeply once a week during dry UK summers, targeting the roots while keeping the foliage dry.
Shade the root zone with flat stones or low-growing companion plants like hardy geraniums.
Monitor young spring shoots weekly for earwig and slug damage, using beer traps or organic pellets.

items.name: Clematis linearifolia
items.growersTips:
Plant in free-draining gritty soil to prevent winter root rot in wet UK climates.
Prune lightly in mid-spring after flowering by removing only dead or damaged stems.
Position in full sun against a south-facing wall to mimic its native warm habitat.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells rather than daily light sprinkling.
Protect young spring shoots from slugs using organic grit barriers around the base.

items.name: Clematis macropetala
items.growersTips:
Plant your Clematis macropetala 6cm deeper than its pot depth to protect against clematis wilt.
Prune in June immediately after flowering by removing dead stems and shaping to fit your space.
Water deeply once a week during dry UK spring spells to support the main April and May blooms.
Plant in free-draining alkaline to neutral soil as this species hates winter-wet clay roots.
Grow through a wall-trained shrub like Cotoneaster to support its delicate climbing leaf-petioles.

items.name: New Zealand dwarf clematis
items.growersTips:
Plant this dwarf evergreen in gritty, free-draining alkaline soil to prevent winter wet root rot.
Grow it in a container or alpine trough so you can move it under a cold glass frame during wet winters.
Position in full sun to partial shade, keeping the shallow roots cool with a layer of slate grit.
Do not prune this species hard; only tidy dead stems immediately after its spring flowering ends.
Watch out for slugs and snails in early spring as they highly prize the delicate emerging flower buds.

items.name: Clematis microphylla
items.growersTips:
Plant this Australian native in the UK's sharpest-draining soil to prevent winter root rot.
Position against a south-facing wall in full sun to mimic its warm, dry natural habitat.
Prune immediately after spring flowering by cutting back dead wood to keep the vine tidy.
Water deeply only during prolonged summer droughts, as this species is highly drought-tolerant.
Protect young shoots from slugs in early spring using organic grit barriers around the base.

items.name: Indian virgin's bower
items.growersTips:
Plant the root ball 8cm deep in moist, alkaline to neutral soil to prevent clematis wilt disease.
Prune immediately after flowering in June by cutting back overlong shoots to a strong side bud.
Shade the roots with flat stones or low-growing companion plants like hardy geraniums in summer.
Water deeply once a week during dry spring spells to support the rapid burst of early May blooms.
Watch for earwig damage on young petals and trap them overnight using upturned straw-filled pots.
items.description: Clematis montana, the mountain clematis, also Himalayan clematis or anemone clematis, is a flowering plant in the buttercup family Ranunculaceae. A vigorous deciduous climber, in late spring it is covered with a mass of small blooms for a period of about four weeks. The odorous flowers are white or pink, four-petalled, with prominent yellow anthers. It is native to mountain areas of Asia from Afghanistan to Taiwan.

items.name: Clematis morefieldii
items.growersTips:
Plant this rare US native in free-draining, gritty alkaline soil to mimic its limestone habitat.
Position the pot in a sheltered, south-facing UK sun trap to provide the high summer heat it needs.
Water deeply once a week in dry summer spells, keeping the crown dry to prevent rot in damp UK air.
Prune lightly in late winter by removing only dead stems, as it flowers on the previous year's wood.
Protect the emerging spring shoots from slugs using organic grit barriers in damp British springs.

items.name: Clematis napaulensis
items.growersTips:
Plant in autumn to match its unique summer-dormant growth cycle and active winter-spring flowering.
Provide deep, moist, alkaline to neutral soil in a sheltered south or west-facing UK garden spot.
Do not water or assume it is dead when it drops all its leaves and goes bare in July and August.
Prune immediately after spring flowering by cutting back dead wood to a pair of strong green buds.
Plant a low evergreen shrub nearby to shade its roots while letting its vines climb into the sun.

items.name: Clematis occidentalis
items.growersTips:
Plant this native climber in free-draining, alkaline to neutral soil to mimic its wild habitat.
Bury the root crown 8cm deep in a semi-shaded spot to prevent clematis wilt and keep roots cool.
Prune in early spring by cutting back dead stems to a pair of strong buds, as it is Group 1.
Water deeply once a week during dry UK summers, targeting the base while keeping foliage dry.
Protect young spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit or beer traps.

items.name: Clematis ochroleuca
items.growersTips:
Plant this non-climbing herbaceous species in free-draining, gritty soil to prevent winter root rot.
Position in full sun and shelter from strong winds to keep the upright, hairy stems from flopping.
Prune hard by cutting all stems back to ground level in early spring before new growth starts.
Protect the emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit or beer traps.
Incorporate plenty of leaf mould or composted bark to mimic its native open woodland habitat.

items.name: Clematis orientalis
items.growersTips:
Plant the root ball 8cm deep in well-drained soil to protect against clematis wilt in wet UK winters.
Prune hard to 30cm from the ground in late February to encourage vigorous new flowering growth.
Water deeply once a week during dry UK summer spells rather than giving frequent light sprinkles.
Position in full sun against a south or west wall to ensure the late summer yellow lanterns bloom.
Grow alongside climbing roses to provide support and mask the bare lower stems of the clematis.

items.name: Clematis paniculata
items.growersTips:
Plant Clematis paniculata with the root ball five centimetres deep in moist but well-drained soil.
Prune this Group three clematis hard in late February down to thirty centimetres above ground level.
Position in full sun against a warm south or west wall to ensure enough autumn heat for flowering.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells to prevent powdery mildew on the late foliage.
Mulch the root zone annually in March with well-rotted manure to keep the shallow roots cool.

items.name: Clematis patens
items.growersTips:
Plant Clematis patens with the crown 5cm deep in moist, alkaline soil to protect against clematis wilt
Prune Group 2 patens cultivars lightly in late February, removing dead stems to just above fat buds
Water deeply once a week at the base during dry UK summer spells, keeping the foliage entirely dry
Shade the roots with slate or low-growing campanula while keeping the top growth in full sun
Watch for earwigs and slugs in spring, which target the delicate early buds of patens varieties

items.name: Clematis pauciflora
items.growersTips:
Plant this tender evergreen in a warm south-facing UK microclimate against a sheltered sunny wall.
Grow in extremely free-draining gritty soil to prevent winter root rot during wet UK winters.
Prune immediately after spring flowering by cutting back dead or overgrown stems to healthy buds.
Water deeply but infrequently during dry summer spells, keeping the base shaded by companion plants.
Protect young spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.

items.name: Clematis pitcheri
items.growersTips:
Plant this deep-clematis 10cm below soil level in well-drained, humus-rich soil to prevent wilt.
Prune hard in late February to 30cm above ground, just above a strong bud, as it flowers on new wood.
Water deeply once a week during dry UK summers, keeping the roots cool with slate or low planting.
Protect young spring shoots from slugs using beer traps or grit, as they are highly vulnerable.
Grow through a silver-foliaged shrub like Lavender to support its scrambling stems and shade roots.

items.name: Clematis potaninii
items.growersTips:
Plant the root ball 8cm deep in fertile, moist soil to protect the crown from clematis wilt.
Prune in late February by cutting all stems back to 30cm above ground level to strong buds.
Position in full sun to partial shade with the roots shaded by low-growing companion plants.
Water deeply once a week during dry UK summer spells to keep the woodland-style soil moist.
Provide a sturdy trellis or allow it to scramble naturally through a large, established shrub.

items.name: Clematis pubescens
items.growersTips:
Plant this tender evergreen in a warm sheltered south-facing UK microclimate to prevent frost damage.
Plant the root ball 10cm deep in well-drained gritty soil to protect the crown from winter wet.
Prune lightly after spring flowering by removing dead stems to maintain its bushy climbing habit.
Water deeply once a week during dry UK summers but keep roots dry and free-draining in winter.
Grow in a large terracotta pot so you can move it into a frost-free greenhouse over cold winters.

items.name: Wild clematis
items.growersTips:
Plant this non-climbing herbaceous clematis deep with the crown five centimetres below soil level.
Insert a sturdy metal ring stake in April before the floppy stems collapse under their own weight.
Prune all stems down to ground level in late autumn or early spring before new growth starts.
Water deeply once a week during dry UK summers to prevent powdery mildew on the foliage.
Watch for earwigs and slugs in spring which quickly shred the tender emerging basal shoots.

items.name: Clematis rehderiana
items.growersTips:
Plant this vigorous climber in moist, well-drained soil with its root ball 5-8cm below the surface.
Prune hard in late February to 30cm above ground level, just above a strong pair of leaf buds.
Position in full sun to partial shade, ensuring the roots are kept cool and shaded by other plants.
Water deeply once a week during dry UK summer spells to support its late-season cowslip-scented blooms.
Grow up a sturdy pergola or through a large established shrub to support its vigorous 6-metre reach.
items.description: Clematis rehderiana is a species of Clematis native to Nepal and China. It has gained the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit.

items.name: Clematis reticulata
items.growersTips:
Plant this deep in moist well-drained soil with the crown five centimetres below the surface.
Shade the base with flat stones or low companion plants to keep the roots cool in UK summers.
Prune hard in late February by cutting all stems back to thirty centimetres above ground level.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells rather than giving frequent light sprinkles.
Protect young spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.

items.name: Hermitgold clematis
items.growersTips:
Plant this Clematis 6cm deeper than its pot level in autumn to encourage strong shoots from the base.
Prune hard in late February to 30cm above ground level to stimulate vigorous new flowering stems.
Water deeply once a week during dry UK summer spells, targeting the roots rather than the foliage.
Grow through a sturdy shrub like a yew or cotoneaster to support its vigorous scrambling habit.
Mulch the root zone with well-rotted manure in March to keep soil cool and retain essential moisture.

items.name: Clematis smilacifolia
items.growersTips:
Grow in a warm conservatory or south-facing sheltered wall as it is tender and dislikes UK frosts.
Plant in rich, free-draining loam with the root ball buried 5cm deep to encourage shoots from base.
Water weekly during the active summer growing season but keep soil barely damp throughout winter.
Prune immediately after late winter flowering by cutting back dead stems to a strong pair of buds.
Watch for slugs on new spring shoots and shield the delicate evergreen foliage from cold dry winds.

items.name: Clematis socialis
items.growersTips:
Plant this rare runner in a wide, shallow container to control its spreading underground stolons.
Provide sharp grit drainage in heavy UK clay to prevent winter wet from rotting the delicate crown.
Water deeply once a week during dry spring spells to mimic its native moist meadow habitat.
Cut all stems back to ground level in late winter before new growth emerges from the soil.
Protect the tender emerging spring shoots from slugs using organic grit barriers or beer traps.

items.name: Clematis tangutica
items.growersTips:
Plant the root ball 5cm deeper than the pot soil level to encourage strong shoots from the base.
Prune hard to 30cm from the ground in late February to promote vigorous new flowering stems.
Water deeply once a week during dry UK summer spells rather than giving daily light sprinkles.
Sow seeds in cold frames during autumn to easily propagate this specific species for free.
Grow through a sturdy dark evergreen shrub to showcase the bright yellow bell-shaped flowers.
items.description: Clematis tangutica, the golden clematis, is a species of flowering plant in the family Ranunculaceae. It is found from Central Asia through to most of China, and it has been introduced to western Canada, Czechia, Slovakia, Switzerland, and the South Island of New Zealand. Its cultivars 'Bill MacKenzie' and 'Lambton Park', both members of the Tangutica Group, have gained the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit.

items.name: Clematis terniflora
items.growersTips:
Plant this vigorous climber in full sun against a south-facing wall to ensure enough late-summer heat.
Prune hard to thirty centimetres in late February to control size and promote fresh flowering wood.
Plant the root ball five centimetres deeper than the pot level to protect against clematis wilt.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells rather than giving frequent shallow sprinkles.
Apply a thick mulch of well-rotted manure in March to keep the roots cool and feed spring growth.

items.name: Clematis ternifolia
items.growersTips:
Plant this vigorous climber against a warm south or west-facing wall to ensure enough late-summer sun.
Bury the root ball 8cm deeper than the pot soil level to encourage shoots and prevent clematis wilt.
Prune hard in late February by cutting all stems down to 30cm above ground level to strong buds.
Shade the roots with flat stones or low-growing companion plants while keeping the foliage in sun.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells rather than giving frequent light sprinkles.

items.name: Clematis texensis
items.growersTips:
Plant the crown 5 to 8cm deep in well-drained soil to protect it from clematis wilt and frost.
Prune hard to 30cm above ground level in late February to encourage vigorous new flowering stems.
Water deeply once a week during dry UK summer spells, keeping the base shaded and the foliage dry.
Grow through a sturdy shrub like a shrub rose to support its scrambling habit and shade its roots.
Watch out for slugs and snails on tender new spring shoots, using organic grit barriers to deter them.

items.name: Clematis urophylla
items.growersTips:
Plant this winter-flowering evergreen in a sheltered south or west facing spot to protect from frost.
Prune only after spring flowering by removing dead stems and tidying to fit your trellis space.
Plant the root ball 5cm deeper than the pot level in fertile, well-drained soil to deter wilt.
Mulch the base annually in autumn with well-rotted manure to keep roots cool and moist in summer.
Grow through a deciduous shrub like Forsythia to support its climbing habit and hide bare lower stems.

items.name: Clematis versicolor
items.growersTips:
Plant this native of warm US woods in a sheltered, south-facing UK border to maximize summer heat.
Bury the root crown five to eight centimetres deep in fertile, moist, well-drained alkaline soil.
Water deeply once a week during dry UK summers, keeping the roots shaded by low-growing companions.
Prune hard in late February by cutting all stems back to thirty centimetres above ground level.
Protect the tender emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic beer traps or grit.

items.name: Clematis viorna
items.growersTips:
Plant this deep-rooting species 8cm deeper than the pot level in autumn to prevent clematis wilt.
Mulch the root zone with well-rotted manure in March to keep soil cool and damp in dry UK summers.
Prune hard in late February to 30cm above ground level, just above a strong pair of leaf buds.
Provide a thin wire trellis or obelisk as the delicate leaf-stalk petioles need narrow supports.
Water weekly during dry English spells, targeting the base directly to avoid wetting the foliage.

items.name: Clematis virginiana
items.growersTips:
Plant this vigorous climber in moisture-retentive clay soil to mimic its native damp woodland edge.
Prune hard to thirty centimetres in late February to control its rapid, aggressive UK growth habit.
Provide a sturdy trellis away from walls so rain can naturally saturate its thirsty root system.
Mulch the root zone deeply with damp leaf mould in April to keep soil cool during dry summer spells.
Watch for earwigs chewing the delicate white flowers in August and trap them in straw-filled pots.

items.name: Clematis vitalba
items.growersTips:
Plant this vigorous native climber only in large gardens with strong support to avoid structural damage.
Prune hard to ground level in late winter to control its invasive spread across UK garden borders.
Grow in alkaline to neutral chalky soils, incorporating grit to ensure excellent winter drainage.
Position the roots in deep shade while training the active growing shoots into full UK sunshine.
Monitor for clematis wilt and shield young spring shoots from devastating slug and snail damage.

items.name: Grape clematis
items.growersTips:
Plant this rare native deep with its crown five centimetres below soil to prevent clematis wilt.
Water deeply once a week during dry UK summers to keep the woodland-style root run cool and damp.
Mulch the base annually in March with well-rotted manure to mimic its natural rich limestone soil.
Prune stems back to thirty centimetres above ground in February to promote vigorous new spring growth.
Position the roots in shade using low shrubs while allowing the vines to climb into south-facing sun.

items.name: Clematis viticella
items.growersTips:
Plant your viticella clematis deep with the root crown five to ten centimetres below the soil level.
Hard prune all stems down to thirty centimetres above ground level every year in late February.
Water deeply once a week during dry UK summer spells to keep the roots cool and damp.
Mulch the base in spring with compost and plant low shrubs to shade the roots from direct midday sun.
Watch for earwigs chewing the delicate flowers in July and trap them using upturned straw-filled pots.
items.description: Clematis viticella, the Italian leather flower, purple clematis, or virgin's bower, is a species of flowering plant in the buttercup family Ranunculaceae, native to Southern Europe and Western Asia, from the Italic Peninsula to Iran. This deciduous climber was the first clematis imported into English gardens, where it was already being grown in 1569 by Hugh Morgan, apothecary to Elizabeth I. By 1597, when it was already being called "virgin's bower", there were two varieties in English gardens, a blue and a red.

items.name: Peanut butter tree
items.growersTips:
Plant Clerodendrum trichotomum in moist, well-drained soil sheltered from cold UK easterly winds.
Prune established shrubs in late winter or early spring to control size and encourage new flowering wood.
Water container-grown bungei deeply once a week during dry summer spells to prevent leaf drop.
Protect young plants with a thick mulch of bark chips in late autumn to insulate roots from UK frosts.
Watch for glasshouse red spider mite on indoor or conservatory specimens during hot, dry summer weeks.

items.name: Clerodendrum bungei
items.growersTips:
Plant it in a sheltered south or west facing border to protect the late summer blooms from cold winds
Prun back hard to ground level in early spring to control its height and encourage vigorous new stems
Install deep root barriers during planting to contain its highly invasive underground suckering habit
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells to keep the large, soft leaves from wilting
Mulch the crown with ten centimetres of compost in late autumn to protect roots from severe UK frosts

items.name: Clerodendrum chinense
items.growersTips:
Grow in a large container so you can move it into a frost-free greenhouse or conservatory for winter.
Plant in a sheltered south-facing spot against a warm wall to protect it from cold UK winds.
Water generously during the summer active growth phase but keep the soil barely damp in winter.
Prune stems back hard to thirty centimeters in early spring to encourage vigorous new flowering wood.
Constantly monitor for glasshouse red spider mite and whitefly when overwintering indoors.

items.name: Lolly bush
items.growersTips:
Grow in a large pot with peat-free loam-based compost so you can move it indoors before first frost.
Water generously in summer but keep the soil barely damp during its winter dormant period indoors.
Position in the sunniest, most sheltered spot available, ideally against a south-facing brick wall.
Prune established stems by half in early spring to encourage bushy growth and more summer flowers.
Monitor closely for glasshouse whitefly and red spider mite when overwintering under glass.

items.name: Clerodendrum fortunatum
items.growersTips:
Grow in a large pot with peat-free loam-based compost so you can move it indoors before first frost.
Water generously in summer but let the top two inches of soil dry out completely before watering again.
Prune back hard in early spring just as new growth begins to maintain a compact shrubby habit.
Position in a conservatory or against a south-facing wall to maximise the sun needed for flowering.
Check regularly for glasshouse whitefly and red spider mite when keeping the plant overwintered indoors.

items.name: Clerodendrum glabrum
items.growersTips:
Grow in a large pot with loam-based compost so you can move it into a heated greenhouse for winter.
Water deeply once a week in summer but keep the soil almost completely dry during winter dormancy.
Prune hard in early spring just as new growth starts to maintain a compact shrub shape indoors.
Position in the sunniest south-facing spot available to mimic its native African heat and light.
Check regularly for glasshouse red spider mite and whitefly when keeping the plant under cover.

items.name: Clerodendrum glandulosum
items.growersTips:
Grow in a sheltered, south-facing border or large pot to protect against cold UK winter winds.
Water deeply once a week in summer, allowing the top two inches of soil to dry out between waterings.
Prune back hard in early spring after frosts pass to encourage vigorous new flowering wood.
Incorporate plenty of well-rotted manure into the planting hole to mimic its native rich woodland.
Overwinter container-grown plants in a frost-free greenhouse or conservatory as temperatures drop.

items.name: Clerodendrum heterophyllum
items.growersTips:
Grow in a large pot with peat-free loam-based compost so you can move it indoors before first frost.
Water weekly in summer but keep the soil barely moist during its winter dormancy in a conservatory.
Prune back hard in early spring to encourage vigorous new growth and maximize summer flowering.
Position in the sunniest south-facing spot possible to mimic its native tropical warmth in the UK.
Check regularly for glasshouse red spider mite and whitefly when overwintering the plant indoors.

items.name: Clerodendrum indicum
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender shrub in a large pot so you can move it into a heated greenhouse for UK winters.
Water generously in summer to keep soil moist but reduce watering to a bare minimum during winter.
Prune stems back by half in early spring to encourage bushy growth and more tubular white flowers.
Use a peat-free loam-based compost mixed with plenty of grit to ensure excellent winter drainage.
Check leaf undersides regularly for glasshouse whitefly and red spider mite when kept indoors.

items.name: Clerodendrum infortunatum
items.growersTips:
Grow in a large pot of loam-based compost so you can move it into a heated greenhouse for winter.
Water freely from spring to autumn but keep the soil barely moist during the cold winter dormancy.
Prune stems back to a strong bud in early spring to control size and encourage summer flowering.
Check leaves regularly for glasshouse whitefly and red spider mite when kept under cover in winter.
Feed weekly with a high-potassium liquid fertiliser from May to September to boost flower production.

items.name: Clerodendrum palmatolobatum
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender climber in a pot of peat-free loam compost so you can move it indoors for winter.
Water copiously in summer but keep the compost barely damp from November to March to prevent rot.
Provide a sturdy trellis in a warm conservatory or south-facing glasshouse to support its vines.
Prune back flowered stems by half in early spring to stimulate new blooming wood and maintain shape.
Watch closely for glasshouse red spider mite and whitefly under glass and use biological controls.

items.name: Pagoda flower
items.growersTips:
Grow in a large pot of loam-based compost so you can move it into a heated greenhouse for winter.
Water copiously in summer but keep the soil barely damp during its dormant winter period indoors.
Position in your warmest suncrest patio or conservatory to mimic its native tropical humidity.
Prune back hard in early spring to encourage the vigorous new growth that bears the orange flowers.
Watch closely for glasshouse whitefly and red spider mite when overwintering under cover in the UK.

items.name: Clerodendrum phlomidis
items.growersTips:
Grow in a large pot with peat-free loam-based compost so you can move it indoors before first frost.
Water deeply once a week in summer, then keep the soil barely damp during its winter dormancy.
Prune back hard by half in early spring to encourage bushy new growth and maximize summer flowers.
Position in the sunniest, most sheltered south-facing spot or against a warm wall to mimic heat.
Check weekly for glasshouse red spider mite and whitefly when overwintering under glass or indoors.

items.name: Fireworks plant
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender shrub in a large pot so you can move it into a heated greenhouse for UK winters.
Water heavily in summer but let the soil dry out completely between waterings during winter dormancy.
Prune stems hard in early spring just as new growth begins to maintain a compact indoor size.
Use a peat-free loam-based compost mixed with plenty of grit to ensure rapid winter drainage.
Position in your brightest south-facing conservatory to trigger the dramatic winter flower flush.

items.name: Clerodendrum schmidtii
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender shrub in a pot of peat-free loam-based compost so you can move it indoors for winter.
Keep the compost consistently moist but never waterlogged from April to September using rainwater.
Place in a bright conservatory or south-facing windowsill to provide the essential winter warmth.
Prune back the stems by half in early spring just as new growth starts to maintain a bushy habit.
Check the underside of leaves weekly for glasshouse whitefly and red spider mite in dry conditions.

items.name: Clerodendrum speciosissimum
items.growersTips:
Overwinter indoors in a heated conservatory or greenhouse as it cannot survive UK winter frosts.
Grow in pots using peat-free loam-based compost mixed with plenty of grit for essential drainage.
Water generously from spring to autumn but keep the soil barely damp during the winter dormancy.
Prune stems back to a low framework of buds in early spring to encourage vigorous new flowering growth.
Position in a south-facing spot under glass to provide the high light levels needed for red blooms.

items.name: Clerodendrum splendens
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender African vine in a pot so you can move it into a heated greenhouse for UK winters.
Water generously in summer but keep the soil barely damp from November to March to prevent root rot.
Prune stems back by half in late winter to encourage the new growth where summer flowers develop.
Feed fortnightly with high-potassium liquid tomato fertilizer from May to September for best blooms.
Inspect the dense leaf axils regularly for mealybugs and glasshouse whitefly in dry indoor air.

items.name: Clerodendrum thomsoniae
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender climber in a pot of peat-free loam compost to easily move it indoors for winter.
Water copiously with tepid rainwater in summer but keep the soil barely damp from November to March.
Prune stems back by half in late winter to encourage new flowering wood and maintain a bushy shape.
Position in a conservatory or near a south-facing window to provide the required bright indirect sun.
Watch for glasshouse red spider mite and whitefly under glass, using biological controls if needed.

items.name: Downy chance
items.growersTips:
Grow in a sheltered south-facing border or large pot to protect against cold drying UK winter winds
Prune hard in late winter or early spring to restrict its size and encourage vigorous new flowering wood
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells to mimic its native warm temperate moisture needs
Mulch the root zone thickly with organic matter in late autumn to insulate roots from hard UK frosts
Plant in well-drained loam enriched with grit to prevent winter waterlogging which causes root rot

items.name: Peanut butter tree
items.growersTips:
Plant in full sun sheltered from cold winds to ensure the late summer flowers and blue berries ripen.
Prune in late winter by removing suckers at the base to maintain a single-stemmed tree-like habit.
Grow in fertile well-drained soil enriched with garden compost to prevent winter waterlogging.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells until the root system is fully established.
Watch for glasshouse whitefly on leaves if growing against a warm south-facing wall in the south.

items.name: Clerodendrum umbellatum
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender climber in a pot of peat-free loam compost to easily move it indoors for winter.
Water copiously in active summer growth but keep the soil barely damp from November to March.
Prune stems back by half in early spring to stimulate new flowering wood and maintain shape.
Position in a conservatory or south-facing sheltered patio to meet its high light requirements.
Check leaf undersides weekly for glasshouse whitefly and red spider mite in dry indoor air.

items.name: Clintonia udensis
items.growersTips:
Plant in partial to full shade using acidic, humus-rich soil that mimics a damp UK woodland floor.
Set rhizomes shallowly at five centimetres deep in autumn, spacing them fifteen centimetres apart.
Water regularly with rainwater during dry UK summers to keep the soil consistently moist but damp.
Protect the emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using beer traps or organic pellets.
Propagate by dividing congested clumps in early spring just as the new growth begins to show.

items.name: Clintonia andrewsiana
items.growersTips:
Plant in deep shade under deciduous trees to mimic its native redwood forest canopy in UK gardens.
Incorporate leaf mould and pine needles into acidic soil to keep the pH low and mimic forest floor.
Sow fresh seed in autumn in cold frames as they require winter chilling to germinate the next spring.
Keep the soil consistently moist but never waterlogged during the dry UK summer months of July and August.
Protect the emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic pellets or beer traps.

items.name: Yellow clintonia
items.growersTips:
Plant in acidic soil enriched with pine needles or leaf mould to mimic native woodland conditions.
Sow fresh seed in autumn outdoors as they require a cold winter period of stratification to sprout.
Position in deep damp shade under deciduous trees to protect the delicate leaves from summer scorch.
Water with rainwater rather than tap water during dry spells to maintain the required low soil pH.
Protect the emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.

items.name: Clintonia udensis
items.growersTips:
Plant in partial to full shade in moisture-retentive, humus-rich, acidic soil mimicking UK woodlands.
Sow fresh seed in autumn in cold frames, as they require winter chilling to break dormancy.
Mulch annually with leaf mould in spring to retain soil moisture and mimic natural forest floors.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic pellets or beer traps.
Divide established clumps in early spring just as new growth begins, keeping the rhizomes moist.

items.name: White clintonia
items.growersTips:
Plant in acidic to neutral, humus-rich, moist but well-drained soil, mimicking a UK woodland floor.
Set the rhizomes 5cm deep in autumn, spacing them 20cm apart in dappled shade under deciduous trees.
Keep soil consistently moist during dry UK spring spells, but avoid waterlogging the winter roots.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.
Propagate by dividing the creeping rhizomes in early spring just as the new growth begins to show.

items.name: Bride's bonnet
items.growersTips:
Plant in partial to full shade in acidic, humus-rich soil that mimics a damp UK woodland floor.
Set the delicate rhizomes just two to three centimetres deep in autumn, spreading roots horizontally.
Water with rainwater to keep soil consistently moist but never waterlogged during dry summer spells.
Protect the emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic beer traps or copper tape.
Mulch annually in late autumn with leaf mould or pine needles to maintain the required soil acidity.

items.name: Codon royenii
items.growersTips:
Grow this South African desert native in a terracotta pot using a fifty-fifty grit and loam mix.
Keep the plant completely dry during its summer dormancy to prevent the fleshy roots from rotting.
Place the pot on a sunny, south-facing windowsill or in a heated greenhouse to mimic desert heat.
Water sparingly from below only when active growth appears in autumn, keeping foliage bone dry.
Protect the highly spiny leaves from slugs and snails which target the tender young growth.

items.name: Codonorchis
items.growersTips:
Plant tubers in autumn at a depth of five centimetres in a well-drained, humus-rich acidic soil mix.
Grow in partial shade to mimic beech woodland, using leaf mould to keep the soil moist but not wet.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.
Keep soil barely damp during summer dormancy to prevent the delicate tuberous roots from rotting.
Avoid any root disturbance or division, as this orchid relies on fragile mycorrhizal associations.

items.name: Coeliopsidinae
items.growersTips:
Grow this orchid in a warm greenhouse or indoors at fifteen degrees Celsius minimum in winter.
Plant in hanging baskets using coarse bark and charcoal to allow the pendant flower spikes to emerge.
Water heavily during summer growth but keep the compost barely damp during the winter rest period.
Maintain high humidity above sixty percent using gravel trays to prevent red spider mite attacks.
Feed fortnightly with a weak high-nitrogen orchid fertilizer only during active spring growth.

items.name: Coldenia procumbens
items.growersTips:
Grow this frost-tender tropical plant in containers to easily move indoors before autumn frosts.
Use a gritty, free-draining loam-based compost mix to prevent winter root rot in wet UK weather.
Water only when the top three centimeters of soil are dry, as this species hates waterlogged roots.
Position pots in your garden's hottest, most sun-drenched spot to mimic its native warm climate.
Sow seeds shallowly indoors in early spring using a heated propagator set to twenty-one Celsius.

items.name: Collabieae
items.growersTips:
Grow in a peat-free bark and perlite mix to mimic their native forest floor and prevent root rot.
Position in a cool greenhouse or shaded conservatory to protect from harsh UK frost and direct sun.
Water thoroughly with rainwater when the top centimetre of bark dries, keeping it drier in winter.
Watch for slugs and snails during damp UK spring nights as they quickly destroy the tender spikes.
Repot every two years in spring just as new growth begins to refresh the media and prevent souring.

items.name: Collinsia bartsiifolia
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds directly outdoors in April or May at a shallow depth of three millimetres in raked soil.
Grow in gritty, well-drained soil to prevent root rot during wet, cool British summer spells.
Water seedlings gently from the base to avoid flattening the delicate, slender stems of this annual.
Position in partial shade rather than full sun to mimic its native cool woodland edge habitat.
Sow alongside low-growing Nemophila to create a contrasting blue and white spring ground cover.

items.name: Collinsia callosa
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at two millimetres deep in autumn to mimic natural California winter cooling.
Grow in gritty, free-draining soil to prevent winter root rot during wet UK autumns and winters.
Water sparingly once established, letting the top five centimetres of soil dry out between feeds.
Position in partial shade rather than full sun to prevent the delicate foliage from scorching.
Sow alongside low-growing native UK annuals like poached egg plant to support early pollinators.

items.name: Collinsia childii
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at three millimetres deep in autumn for early spring UK blooms.
Grow in moist but well-drained sandy loam with leaf mould to mimic its native woodland floor.
Position in partial shade under deciduous shrubs to prevent strong midday UK summer sun scorch.
Water weekly to keep soil evenly damp but never waterlogged during dry British spring spells.
Watch for slugs and snails on young spring seedlings and protect them with organic pellets.
items.description: Collinsia childii is a species of flowering plant in the plantain family known by the common name Child's blue-eyed Mary.

items.name: Collinsia concolor
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn or early spring directly into well-drained, gritty soil to avoid root disturbance
Position in full sun but provide light dappled shade during hot, dry UK midsummer afternoons
Water sparingly once established, allowing the top two inches of soil to dry out to prevent rot
Watch for slugs and snails on young spring seedlings, using organic grit barriers to protect them
Sow alongside low-growing native annuals like poached egg plant to support local UK pollinators
items.description: Collinsia concolor is a species of flowering plant in the plantain family known by the common name Chinese houses.

items.name: Collinsia grandiflora
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn directly where they are to flower to benefit from winter cold stratification.
Thin seedlings to fifteen centimetres apart in spring to prevent mildew in damp UK weather.
Water the soil at the base weekly during dry spells to keep the shallow root system from drying out.
Sow alongside red campion in partial shade to mimic its natural woodland edge habitat in UK gardens.
Deadhead spent blooms in midsummer to encourage a second flush of blue flowers before autumn frosts.
items.description: Collinsia grandiflora is a species of flowering plant in the plantain family known by the common names giant blue eyed Mary and large-flowered collinsia. This wildflower is native to western North America from British Columbia to northern California where it grows in coniferous understory and woodland.

items.name: Collinsia heterophylla
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds outdoors in April at a depth of 3mm into moist, well-drained soil in partial shade.
Water seedlings weekly during dry UK spring spells to keep the soil consistently damp but not wet.
Protect young spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic wool pellets or beer traps.
Sow alongside native red campion or forget-me-nots to create a woodland-style pollinator border.
Deadhead spent Chinese houses blooms in midsummer to encourage a second flush of purple flowers.
items.description: Collinsia heterophylla, known as purple Chinese houses or innocence, is a flowering plant native to California and the Peninsular Ranges in northern Baja California.

items.name: Collinsia multicolor
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn directly where they are to flower to benefit from winter cold stratification.
Thin seedlings to fifteen centimetres apart in spring to prevent dampening off in damp UK weather.
Plant in partial shade under deciduous shrubs to mimic their native woodland edge habitat.
Water the soil at the base weekly during dry spring spells to keep the woodland soil evenly moist.
Watch for slugs and snails on young spring shoots by using beer traps or organic wool pellets.
items.description: Collinsia multicolor is a species of flowering plant in the plantain family, known by the common names San Francisco blue eyed Mary and San Francisco collinsia. It is endemic to the San Francisco Bay Area, where it is known from San Francisco to Santa Cruz. As of 2008 there are 22 known occurrences. Populations south of Santa Cruz have been extirpated.

items.name: Collinsia parryi
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn or early spring directly into well-drained, gritty soil to mimic alpine scree.
Keep soil consistently moist but never waterlogged during the spring active growing period.
Position in partial shade or dappled light to prevent the delicate blue flowers from bleaching.
Protect young spring seedlings from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.
Sow alongside low-growing spring bulbs like dwarf daffodils to provide natural support for stems.
items.description: Collinsia parryi is a species of flowering plant in the plantain family known by the common name Parry's blue eyed Mary. It is endemic to central and southern California, where it is found in the southern Coast Ranges and in the Transverse Ranges north and east of Los Angeles.

items.name: Collinsia parviflora
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at two millimetres deep in autumn to mimic natural UK winter cold stratification.
Grow in moist well-drained acidic soil in partial shade to replicate its native damp woodland edge.
Water gently at the base weekly during dry spring spells to keep the shallow fibrous roots damp.
Watch for slugs and snails during wet UK springs as they quickly consume the delicate young stems.
Plant alongside native red campion or wild primroses which share its preference for dappled shade.
items.description: Collinsia parviflora is a species of flowering plant in the family Plantaginaceae known by the common names maiden blue eyed Mary and small-flowered collinsia.

items.name: Collinsia sparsiflora
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn directly into well-drained grit-amended soil to mimic natural UK winter chilling.
Plant seeds shallowly at a depth of two millimetres and keep the soil damp until spring germination.
Position in partial shade under deciduous shrubs to replicate its native woodland edge habitat.
Water sparingly once established, allowing the top three centimetres of soil to dry out completely.
Grow alongside native spring bulbs like wild daffodils to support early emerging UK bumblebees.
items.description: Collinsia sparsiflora is a flowering plant in the family Plantaginaceae known by the common names spinster's blue-eyed Mary and few-flowered collinsia. One variety of the species is native to the West Coast of the United States as far north as Washington, while the other three varieties are limited to California alone.

items.name: Collinsia tinctoria
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at two millimetres deep in autumn for early spring blooms in mild UK regions.
Water sparingly once established as this California native dislikes wet winter soil and root rot.
Sow directly into gritty, free-draining soil in full sun to mimic its natural scree habitat.
Watch for slugs and snails on young spring seedlings during damp UK April weather and protect them.
Grow alongside low-water annuals like Eschscholzia californica to match its dry soil needs.
items.description: Collinsia tinctoria is a species of flowering plant in the family Plantaginaceae known by the common names sticky Chinese houses and tincture plant.

items.name: Collinsia torreyi
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at two millimetres deep in autumn to mimic natural cold stratification outdoors.
Grow in moist, well-draining acidic soil enriched with leaf mould to replicate redwood forest floors.
Position in dappled shade under deciduous shrubs to protect delicate blooms from strong UK summer sun.
Water consistently to keep soil damp but never waterlogged, especially during dry post-spring spells.
Protect young spring seedlings from slugs and snails using organic wool pellets or beer traps.
items.description: Collinsia torreyi is a species of flowering plant in the plantain family known by the common name Torrey's blue-eyed Mary. It is native to California and adjacent sections of Oregon and Nevada, where it grows in the coniferous forests of several mountain ranges, including the Sierra Nevada.

items.name: Collinsia verna
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds outdoors in autumn as they require winter cold stratification to germinate the next spring
Plant seeds shallowly at a depth of two millimetres in moist, well-drained soil in partial shade
Water consistently to keep the soil damp but not waterlogged, mimicking damp UK woodland floors
Grow alongside native primroses or wood anemones which share the same spring shade requirements
Leave faded flowers to self-seed naturally in late summer to ensure a display the following year
items.description: Collinsia verna, or blue-eyed Mary, is a winter annual that is native to the eastern and central parts of North America but has become endangered in the states of New York and Tennessee. The flowers are bicolored white and blue. It is a plant of valley bottoms and moist bottom slopes, in areas with moderate lighting and requires some shade.

items.name: Colophospermum mopane
items.growersTips:
Grow in a free-draining mix of two parts grit to one part loam to prevent winter root rot in UK wet.
Overwinter indoors under grow lights keeping temperatures above ten degrees Celsius to avoid frost.
Water deeply only when the soil dries out completely in summer then keep almost dry through winter.
Prune in late spring after new growth starts to shape the canopy and remove any frost-damaged stems.
Sow seeds in spring after soaking in warm water for twenty-four hours and burying one centimetre deep.
items.description: Colophospermum mopane, commonly called mopane, mopani, butterfly tree, turpentine tree, or balsam tree, is a tree in the legume family (Fabaceae), that grows in hot, dry, low-lying areas, 200 to 1,200 metres in elevation, in parts of Southern Africa. The tree only occurs in Africa and is the only species in genus Colophospermum. Its distinctive butterfly-shaped (bifoliate) leaf and thin kidney-shaped/nearly semi-circular seed pod make it easy to identify.

items.name: Colquhounia coccinea
items.growersTips:
Plant against a south-facing wall in free-draining soil to protect from wet UK winter root rot.
Prune hard in mid-spring by cutting back to a low framework of buds to promote vigorous red flowers.
Propagate via semi-ripe cuttings in late summer using a heated propagator to ensure winter survival.
Apply a thick dry mulch of bark over the root zone in November to insulate against severe UK frosts.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells only, as this Himalayan shrub dislikes wet feet.
items.description: Colquhounia coccinea is a species of flowering plant in the mint family Lamiaceae. It is commonly known as scarlet-flowered colquhounia or Himalayan mint shrub. It is native to China, Bhutan, Nepal, Myanmar, India and Thailand. It is an evergreen or semi-evergreen shrub growing to 2.5 m (8.2 ft) tall and broad, with aromatic leaves which are felted underneath (tomentose). Spikes of red or deep orange flowers, with yellow interiors, appear in late summer. Its native habitats include slopes, stony grassy hillsides, thickets, and river valleys.

items.name: Colvillea
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in early spring at a depth of two centimetres using a heated propagator at 22C.
Grow in pots of gritty, free-draining loam-based compost to easily move indoors before autumn frosts.
Water thoroughly only when the top three centimetres of soil have dried out to prevent root rot.
Position in the sunniest, most sheltered south-facing spot to mimic its native tropical warmth.
Monitor weekly for glasshouse red spider mite and treat early with biological control predators.
items.description: Colvillea is a monotypic genus of legume in the family Fabaceae. Its only species is Colvillea racemosa. The genus is named for Sir Charles Colville, an ex Governor of Mauritius.

items.name: Comarostaphylis arbutoides
items.growersTips:
Plant in acidic well-drained soil using ericaceous compost to prevent chlorosis in UK gardens.
Position in a sheltered south-facing spot or against a warm wall to protect from harsh UK frosts.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells until the root system is fully established.
Prune lightly in late spring after flowering to shape the shrub and remove any winter-damaged wood.
Protect young plants with horticultural fleece when winter temperatures are forecast to drop below -5C.
items.description: Comarostaphylis arbutoides is a species of shrub in the heath family. Its range extends from central Mexico south to Guatemala, Honduras, Nicaragua, Costa Rica, and western Panama. It is found in oak and pine forests in mountainous locations, and on the summits of Central American volcanoes, at elevations from 1,350 to 3,800 m. There are two subspecies: arbutoides, distinguished by the presence of a rust-colored tomentum on the leaf underside, and costaricensis which lacks the tomentum.

items.name: Comarostaphylis diversifolia
items.growersTips:
Plant in acidic to neutral well-drained soil, incorporating pine needles to mimic its native habitat.
Position in full sun against a south-facing wall to protect it from harsh UK winter winds and frost.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells, using rainwater rather than alkaline tap water.
Prune lightly in late spring after flowering to shape the shrub and remove any frost-damaged stems.
Mulch annually in autumn with composted bark to protect the shallow root system from winter freezes.
items.description: Comarostaphylis diversifolia, known by the common names summer holly and California comarostaphylos, is a species of shrub in the heath family.

items.name: Congea tomentosa
items.growersTips:
Grow in a heated conservatory or greenhouse as this tropical climber cannot survive UK winter frost
Plant in free-draining loam-based compost mixed with plenty of grit to prevent winter root rot
Water generously during active summer growth but keep the soil barely damp throughout the winter
Prune hard immediately after the spring flowering finishes to control its vigorous climbing habit
Position in the brightest spot possible under glass to trigger the showy pink bracts to develop
items.description: Congea tomentosa is a large tropical evergreen vine, commonly referred to as wooly congea, shower orchid, or shower of orchid.. It is called lluvia de orquideas or terciopelo in Spanish, krua on in Thai, and rong bao teng in Chinese. Native to Myanmar and Thailand, it can be found elsewhere in South Asia, including Laos, Vietnam, Malaysia (Kedah), China (Yunnan), Bangladesh, and India. Its native habitat is mixed forests 600–1200 meters above sea level.

items.name: Conoclinium
items.growersTips:
Plant in moisture-retentive, humus-rich soil in full sun to partial shade to mimic its boggy habitat.
Water deeply during dry UK summer spells to keep the soil consistently damp but never waterlogged.
Cut the dead stems back to ground level in early spring just as new basal growth begins to emerge.
Divide overgrown clumps in March or April to maintain vigor and propagate new plants easily.
Protect young spring shoots from slug damage using organic pellets or beer traps in damp weather.
items.description: Conoclinium, the mistflowers, is a genus of four species of herbaceous perennial flowering plants, native to North America. They are 0.5 to 2 metres tall, and have blue to purple or violet flowers.

items.name: Conostephium
items.growersTips:
Grow in extremely well-drained, acidic, sandy soil to mimic its native Australian heathland habitat.
Protect from hard UK frosts by planting in a sheltered, south-facing spot or using winter fleece.
Water sparingly with rainwater rather than tap water to maintain the necessary low soil pH levels.
Prine lightly immediately after spring flowering to maintain a compact, bushy shrub shape.
Grow in pots using peat-free ericaceous compost mixed with plenty of grit for excellent drainage.
items.description: Conostephium is a genus of flowering plants in the family Ericaceae and is endemic to the south-west of Western Australia. The name of the genus comes from Greek words, conos, "cone" and stephanos, "that which encircles, a crown or wreath", referring to the petal tube that encloses the stamens.

items.name: Consolida
items.growersTips:
Direct sow seeds in autumn for stronger plants that survive UK winters and flower earlier in summer
Sow seeds shallowly at five millimetres deep as they require a period of cold to trigger germination
Support the tall flower spikes early in spring using hazel twigs before heavy UK summer rain winds
Water deeply at the base once a week during dry spells to prevent powdery mildew on the foliage
Deadhead spent blooms regularly to encourage a second flush of flowers before the autumn frosts occur
items.description: Consolida is a genus of about 40 species of annual flowering plants in the family Ranunculaceae, native to western Europe, the Mediterranean and Asia. Phylogenetic studies show that Consolida is actually an annual clade nested within the genus Delphinium and it has been treated as a synonym of Delphinium in Kew's Plants of the World Online. The name of the genus comes from an archaic use of consolidation, meaning "healing", in reference to the plant's medieval use for healing wounds.

items.name: Consolida regalis
items.growersTips:
Direct sow seeds in autumn for early spring blooms, as they dislike root disturbance from transplanting.
Sow seeds shallowly at five millimetres deep in well-drained, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun.
Water young plants weekly during dry UK spring spells, but keep mature plants dry to avoid crown rot.
Support the slender stems with brushwood stakes in late spring to prevent damage from UK summer winds.
Watch for slugs and snails on young spring shoots, using organic grit barriers to protect them.
items.description: Consolida regalis, known as forking larkspur, rocket-larkspur, and field larkspur, is an annual herbaceous plant belonging to the genus Consolida of the buttercup family (Ranunculaceae).

items.name: Convallaria majalis
items.growersTips:
Plant bare-root pips in autumn five centimetres deep in moisture-retentive, humus-rich acidic soil.
Water weekly during dry spring spells to ensure robust flowering before the summer dormancy phase.
Apply a leaf mould mulch in November to mimic their native UK woodland floor and boost spring growth.
Watch for the scarlet lily beetle in May, hand-picking them to prevent severe foliage damage.
Divide congested clumps in September after foliage yellows to maintain vigorous flowering displays.
items.description: Lily-of-the-valley, also written as lily of the valley, is a woodland flowering plant with sweetly scented, pendent, bell-shaped white flowers borne in sprays in spring. It is native to Europe, Western Asia and Northern Asia.

items.name: Conzattia
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in April at a depth of 1cm using peat-free compost to beat the cool UK spring.
Plant out in late May after the last frost in a south-facing spot with sharp-draining sandy soil.
Water deeply once a week at the base during dry summer spells to establish the taproot system.
Protect young seedlings from slugs and snails using beer traps or copper tape in damp UK weather.
Clear the entire plant in autumn to compost, as this annual will not survive the British winter.
items.description: Conzattia is a genus of flowering plants in the legume family, Fabaceae. It belongs to the subfamily Caesalpinioideae.

items.name: Copaifera langsdorffii
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender tropical shrub in a container of acidic, sandy loam to move indoors before winter.
Keep soil consistently moist but never waterlogged, reducing watering significantly during winter.
Position in the sunniest spot of a heated greenhouse or south-facing conservatory to mimic heat.
Prune lightly in late spring after new growth starts to maintain shape and remove frost damage.
Watch closely for glasshouse red spider mite and mealybugs under the leaves in dry indoor air.
items.description: Copaifera langsdorffii, also known as the diesel tree, is a tropical rainforest tree. It has many names in local languages, including kupa'y, cabismo, and copaúva.

items.name: Coptis
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist acidic humus-rich soil under deciduous trees to mimic native UK woodland conditions.
Water with rainwater weekly during dry UK summers to keep the shallow fibrous root system damp.
Sow fresh seed in cold frames in autumn as they require winter chilling to germinate the next spring.
Protect the delicate evergreen foliage from dry winter winds using a mulch of leaf mould or bracken.
Divide established clumps in early spring just as new growth begins to propagate healthy plants.
items.description: Coptis is a genus of between 10 and 15 species of flowering plants in the family Ranunculaceae, native to Asia and North America.

items.name: Coptis aspleniifolia
items.growersTips:
Recreate a Scottish highland forest floor by mixing acidic peat-free compost with pine needle leafmould
Plant the delicate rhizomes shallowly just two centimetres below the soil surface in early autumn
Water weekly with harvested rainwater to keep the soil constantly damp but never waterlogged or muddy
Position in deep damp shade under deciduous ferns or dwarf rhododendrons to mimic UK woodland canopies
Protect the evergreen fern-like foliage from drying winter winds using a mulch of composted bark
items.description: Coptis aspleniifolia, commonly known as fernleaf goldthread or spleenwort-leaf goldthread, is found in the northern two-thirds of British Columbia, in Alaska, and along the Cascades into Washington and is a native plant of the temperate rain forests of the region. It is often found in the understory of the herb layer of coniferous forests as part of a multilayered canopy system on gleysolic or organic soils. Also found in wet woods and bogs, the fernleaf goldthread is not invasive or poisonous. The plant is considered common and widespread in its native range.

items.name: Coptis japonica
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist acidic humus-rich soil under deciduous shade to mimic native cool woodland conditions.
In the UK dry summers water weekly to keep the shallow fibrous root system from drying out completely.
Sow fresh seed in autumn in cold frames as they require winter chilling to germinate the next spring.
Protect the evergreen foliage from harsh drying winter winds using fleece or planting in sheltered spots.
Plant alongside shade-loving Hepatica or dwarf ferns which share its preference for damp acidic soil.
items.description: Coptis japonica, the Japanese goldthread, is a species of flowering plant in the family Ranunculaceae, native to central and southern Japan, and introduced to Korea. In Asia it is grown for medicinal purposes, with the main alkaloid being berberine.

items.name: Coptis laciniata
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist, acidic woodland soil enriched with leafmould to mimic UK ancient forest floors.
Position in deep or partial shade, ensuring the soil never dries out during dry British summers.
Plant rhizomes shallowly, just below the soil surface, in autumn while the ground is still warm.
Protect the delicate evergreen foliage from harsh, drying winter winds using a cold frame or cloche.
Sow fresh seed in pots outdoors in autumn, as they require winter cold stratification to germinate.
items.description: Coptis laciniata is a species of flowering plant in the buttercup family known by the common name Oregon goldthread. It is native to Washington, Oregon, and northern California on the west coast of the United States, where it grows in wet habitat in the understory of mountain and coastal coniferous forests. It is a small perennial herb creeping on a yellow stolon through other vegetation and leaf litter. There are a few leaves on its short stem which are divided into leaflets subdivided into several toothed lobes. The stemlike inflorescence arises up to 19 centimeters tall from the stem at gro

items.name: Coptis occidentalis
items.growersTips:
Recreate its native woodland home by mixing leaf mould and pine needles deep into acidic UK soils.
Plant the shallow rhizomes just two centimetres deep in moist, shaded borders during early spring.
Water weekly with harvested rainwater to keep the soil damp but never waterlogged during dry summers.
Protect the delicate evergreen foliage from harsh drying winter winds using a temporary fleece wrap.
Grow alongside shade-loving companions like dwarf ferns and Hepaticas that share its soil needs.
items.description: Coptis occidentalis, the Idaho goldthread, is a species of flowering plant native to western North America. It is a member of the buttercup family. This plant has also been known under the binomial Chrysocoptis occidentalis and the common name western goldthread.

items.name: Coptis trifolia
items.growersTips:
Plant in moisture-retentive, acidic humus-rich soil, mimicking a cool UK woodland floor.
Position in deep or partial shade, ensuring the soil never dries out during dry UK summers.
Apply a leaf mould mulch annually in autumn to protect the shallow, delicate gold thread roots.
Plant companion shade-lovers like dwarf ferns and Gaultheria procumbens to maintain soil humidity.
Propagate by dividing the creeping rhizomes in early spring just as new growth begins to emerge.
items.description: Coptis trifolia, commonly known as the threeleaf goldthread or savoyane, is a perennial plant in the family Ranunculaceae native to North America.

items.name: Cordia africana
items.growersTips:
Grow in a large pot with loam-based compost so you can move it into a heated greenhouse for winter.
Water sparingly in winter but keep soil consistently moist during the active summer growing season.
Prune lightly in late spring after frost risk passes to maintain shape and remove dead wood.
Position in the sunniest, most sheltered south-facing spot possible to mimic its native warmth.
Check regularly for glasshouse red spider mite and mealybugs when overwintering the plant indoors.
items.description: Cordia africana or Sudan teak is a mid-sized, white-flowered, evergreen tree in the family Cordiaceae, native to Africa. It produces edible fruit, and its wood is used for drums or other carpentry.

items.name: Cordia alliodora
items.growersTips:
Grow in a large pot with loam-based compost so you can move it into a heated greenhouse for winter.
Water sparingly in winter to prevent root rot but keep soil moist during the active summer growth.
Prune lightly in late spring after the last frost to shape the shrub and remove winter dieback.
Position in the sunniest, most sheltered south-facing spot to mimic its native tropical warmth.
Watch out for glasshouse red spider mite and whitefly when overwintering the shrub indoors.
items.description: Cordia alliodora is a species of flowering tree in the family Cordiaceae, that is native to the American tropics. It is commonly known as Spanish elm, Ecuador laurel, cypre or salmwood. It can reach 35 m in height.

items.name: Cordia boissieri
items.growersTips:
Grow in a pot with grit-heavy loam so you can move it into a heated greenhouse before autumn frosts.
Water deeply once a week in summer, but keep the compost almost completely dry throughout winter.
Position in the hottest, brightest spot against a south-facing brick wall to mimic Mexican heat.
Prune lightly in late spring only to remove winter dieback and shape the shrub after new growth starts.
Feed with a low-nitrogen, high-potassium fertilizer in June to encourage the white trumpet flowers.
items.description: Cordia boissieri is a white-flowered, evergreen shrub or small tree in the family Cordiaceae. Its native range extends from southern Texas in the United States south to central Mexico. Common names include anacahuita, Mexican olive, white cordia, and Texas wild olive.

items.name: Cordia decandra
items.growersTips:
Grow in a pot with grit-heavy loam to move indoors before the first autumn frosts hit your area
Water only when the top five centimetres of compost are dry to prevent root rot in cool weather
Prune lightly in late spring after new growth starts to maintain a compact shrub shape in pots
Position in your warmest south-facing suntrap or unheated greenhouse to maximise summer heat
Check weekly for glasshouse red spider mite and whitefly when overwintering the shrub indoors
items.description: Cordia decandra, commonly known in Spanish as carbón and carbonillo, is a species of woody plant in the family Cordiaceae. It is a native shrub in the southern reaches of the Atacama Desert in Chile. More specifically, it grows mainly in the dry hills of the Atacama and Coquimbo Regions, and is not known to grow south of latitude 30 S. It grows from sea-level up to 1,500 m AMSL. It produces a small edible fruit that can be eaten dry or toasted.

items.name: Cordia dentata
items.growersTips:
Grow in a large pot with loam-based compost so you can move it into a heated greenhouse for winter.
Water sparingly in winter but keep soil consistently moist during the active summer growing season.
Prune in late spring after the frost risk passes to maintain shape and encourage new flowering wood.
Position in the sunniest south-facing spot available to mimic its native tropical warmth and light.
Feed fortnightly with a high-potassium liquid fertilizer from May to September to boost blooming.
items.description:
Cordia dentata, commonly known as white manjack, is a species of flowering plant in the family Cordiaceae. 
It is native to the southern United States, Mexico, Central America, Colombia and Venezuela. In the Caribbean, it is found in Jamaica, Cuba, Virgin Islands and Puerto Rico. It is also found in Madagascar.

items.name: Cordia dichotoma
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender shrub in a large pot of loam-based compost to easily move it indoors for winter.
Water deeply once a week in summer but keep the soil barely damp during the cold UK winter months.
Prune in late spring after the last frost to remove dead wood and maintain a compact shrub shape.
Position your pot against a south-facing brick wall to maximise heat absorption in the UK climate.
Feed monthly from May to August with a high-potassium liquid fertiliser to encourage summer flowering.
items.description: Cordia dichotoma is a species of flowering tree in the family Cordiaceae, that is native to the Indomalayan realm, northern Australia, and western Melanesia.

items.name: Cordia dodecandra
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender Mexican shrub in a large pot to overwinter indoors before the first autumn frost.
Plant in a loam-based compost mixed with one-third grit to ensure the sharp drainage it requires.
Water deeply only when the top five centimetres of soil is dry, reducing to monthly in winter.
Prune lightly in late spring after new growth starts to maintain shape and remove frost damage.
Position in your warmest south-facing spot or conservatory to maximise the sun needed for orange blooms.
items.description: Cordia dodecandra is a small tree in the family Cordiaceae native to southern Mexico, Central America, and the Caribbean.

items.name: Cordia gerascanthus
items.growersTips:
Grow this tropical shrub in a heated conservatory or greenhouse to survive cold UK winters.
Use a free-draining loam-based compost mixed with one-third grit to prevent winter root rot.
Water thoroughly only when the top five centimetres of soil feels dry, reducing to monthly in winter.
Prune lightly in late spring after flowering to maintain shape and fit inside your indoor space.
Check leaf undersides weekly for glasshouse red spider mite and scale insects in dry indoor air.
items.description: Cordia gerascanthus, sharing the names Spanish elm and princewood with other species, is a tree occurring in Mexico, Central America and the Caribbean. It belongs to the mostly tropical and subtropical family Cordiaceae'.

items.name: Cordia myxa
items.growersTips:
Grow in a large pot with loam-based compost so you can move it into a heated greenhouse for winter.
Water deeply once a week in summer, then keep the soil almost completely dry throughout winter.
Prune in late spring after frost risk passes, cutting back leggy stems to encourage a bushy habit.
Position in the hottest, most sheltered south-facing spot possible to mimic its native warmth.
Scout weekly for glasshouse red spider mite and mealybugs when overwintering the plant indoors.
items.description:
Cordia myxa, also called Sebesten plum, Assyrian plum, Indian cherry, Glue berry, Lasura, or Bambar
is a mid-sized, deciduous tree in the family Cordiaceae, native to Asia. It produces small, edible fruit and is found in warmer areas across Africa and Asia.

items.name: Cordia obliqua
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender shrub in a large pot of loam-based compost so you can move it indoors for winter.
Water deeply once a week in summer, then keep the soil barely damp from November through to March.
Prune in late spring after frost risk passes to shape the canopy and remove any cold-damaged stems.
