Position in your warmest, brightest spot, such as against a south-facing wall, to encourage blooms.
Check regularly for glasshouse red spider mite when keeping this plant under cover during winter.
items.description: Cordia obliqua, the clammy cherry, is a flowering plant species in the genus Cordia.

items.name: Cordia sebestena
items.growersTips:
Grow in a large pot of gritty loam so you can move it into a heated conservatory for winter warmth.
Water only when the top five centimetres of soil dries out completely to prevent root rot in winter.
Prune lightly in late spring after frost risk passes to maintain a compact shrub shape in glasshouses.
Feed fortnightly from May to September with a high-potassium liquid fertiliser to boost orange blooms.
Inspect leaf undersides weekly in winter for glasshouse red spider mite and spray with horticultural oil.
items.description: Cordia sebestena is a shrubby tree in the family Cordiaceae, native to the American tropics. It ranges from southern Florida in the United States and the Bahamas, southwards throughout Central America and the Greater Antilles. Common names have included siricote or kopté (Mayan) in 19th Century northern Yucatán, scarlet cordia in Jamaica, and Geiger tree in Florida.

items.name: Cordia sinensis
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender shrub in a large pot with grit-heavy loam to easily move it indoors for UK winters.
Water sparingly in winter but keep soil damp during summer to mimic its native dry-season cycle.
Prune lightly in late spring after frost risk passes to shape the shrub and remove dead wood.
Position in your hottest south-facing suntrap or a conservatory to compensate for cool UK summers.
Watch for glasshouse red spider mite when overwintering this plant in a heated greenhouse or indoors.
items.description: Cordia sinensis  is a species of flowering tree in the family Cordiaceae. Common names include grey-leaved saucer berry, grey-leaved cordia, marer, mnya mate, mkamasi and tadana. It is found in Africa and Asia.

items.name: Sea trumpet
items.growersTips:
Overwinter indoors in a heated conservatory as this tropical shrub cannot survive UK frost.
Grow in a large pot with a loam-based compost mixed with plenty of grit to ensure sharp drainage.
Water deeply only when the top five centimetres of soil dries out to prevent root rot in winter.
Prune lightly in late spring after new growth starts to maintain a compact shape for indoor spaces.
Position in your brightest south-facing window or heated greenhouse to maximise essential sunlight.
items.description: Cordia subcordata is a species of flowering tree in the family Cordiaceae. It can be found growing in eastern Africa, South Asia, Southeast Asia, northern Australia and the Pacific Islands. The plant is known by a variety of names, including kou, beach cordia, sea trumpet, and kerosene wood.

items.name: Cordia sulcata
items.growersTips:
Grow in a large pot with loam-based compost so you can move it into a heated greenhouse for winter.
Water sparingly in winter but keep soil consistently moist during the active summer growing season.
Position in the sunniest, most sheltered south-facing spot possible to mimic its tropical habitat.
Prune lightly in late spring after the frost risk passes to maintain shape and remove dead wood.
Check regularly for glasshouse red spider mite and mealybugs when overwintering the plant indoors.
items.description: Cordia sulcata is known commonly as moral, white manjack, or mucilage manjack. It is a tree that can be found throughout the Caribbean islands from Cuba to Trinidad.

items.name: Cordia trichotoma
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender tropical in a large pot with loam-based compost to move indoors before autumn frosts.
Water sparingly in winter but keep soil consistently moist during the active summer growing season.
Position in the sunniest, most sheltered south-facing spot possible to mimic its native warmth.
Prune lightly in late spring after frost risk passes to maintain shape and remove dead wood.
Monitor closely for glasshouse red spider mite and mealybugs when overwintering indoors.
items.description: Cordia trichotoma, or louro pardo, is a species of a medium-sized deciduous tree that belongs to the family Cordiaceae. It is a perennial species native to humid tropical and subtropical forests in Brazil, Bolivia, Argentina and others.

items.name: Cordylanthus kingii
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in April at a depth of two centimeters to protect young roots from late UK frosts
Grow in a free-draining sandy loam enriched with grit to prevent winter root rot in wet UK soils
Water deeply once a week at the base during dry summer spells to establish the deep taproot system
Position in your warmest south-facing border against a brick wall to maximize essential summer heat
Interplant with low-growing annual grasses to provide physical support for the weak climbing stems
items.description: Cordyla is a genus of flowering plants in the family Fabaceae. It includes seven species native to sub-Saharan Africa, ranging across northern Africa from Senegal to Somalia, and through eastern Africa from Sudan to KwaZulu-Natal, including Madagascar.

items.name: Cabbage Tree
items.growersTips:
Wrap the crown with fleece in late autumn to protect the growing point from severe UK winter frosts.
Plant in free-draining soil with added grit to prevent root rot during wet British winters.
Cut back winter-damaged stems in mid-spring to encourage fresh new shoots from the base.
Water container-grown plants weekly in summer but keep them almost dry from November to March.
Watch for cordyline slime flux in wet springs and prune affected stems back to healthy wood.
items.description: Cordyline australis, commonly known as the cabbage tree, or by its Māori name of tī or tī kōuka, is a widely branched monocot tree endemic to New Zealand.

items.name: Cordyline cannifolia
items.growersTips:
Plant in a sheltered south-facing spot using grit to ensure rapid winter drainage in wet UK soil.
Wrap the crown with fleece or bring container-grown plants into a greenhouse before first UK frost.
Water deeply once a week in summer but keep the soil almost dry during the cold winter months.
Prune away frost-damaged lower leaves in late spring only after the threat of hard frost has passed.
Grow alongside Phormium or Heuchera in neutral to slightly acidic soil to complement leaf textures.
items.description: Cordyline cannifolia, one of several plants known as palm lily, is a species of evergreen shrub in the family Asparagaceae. It is known to occur in the Australian states of Queensland and the Northern Territory and may possibly occur in New Guinea. It was first described by botanist Robert Brown in 1810.

items.name: Narrow-leaved palm lily
items.growersTips:
Grow in a pot with grit to move this tender shrub into a frost-free greenhouse before winter frosts.
Water only when the top five centimetres of soil dries out to prevent root rot in damp UK winters.
Prune leggy stems back to fifteen centimetres from the base in late spring to stimulate bushy growth.
Blend one part grit with two parts peat-free compost to ensure the sharp drainage this plant needs.
Check the tight leaf axils weekly for mealybugs which thrive in sheltered UK conservatory spots.
items.description: Cordyline congesta, often referred to as narrow-leaved palm lily, is an evergreen Australian plant. It is a rare shrub that grows up to 3 meters tall and was discovered on the margins of a rainforest, and in riverine scrub and moist gullies in eucalyptus forest. Growing north from the Clarence River, New South Wales.

items.name: Ti Tree
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender shrub in a pot to easily move it indoors before the first autumn frost hits.
Water only when the top five centimetres of soil dries out to prevent root rot in damp UK winters.
Plant in a loam-based compost mixed with one-third grit to ensure the rapid drainage it requires.
Wipe the broad leaves with a damp cloth monthly to deter spider mites in dry indoor winter air.
Prune leggy stems in spring by cutting back to a node to stimulate fresh, bushy lower growth.
items.description: Cordyline fruticosa is an evergreen flowering plant in the family Asparagaceae. It is known by a wide variety of common names, including ti plant, palm lily, and cabbage palm.

items.name: Cordyline indivisa
items.growersTips:
Plant in deep, well-drained loam with grit to prevent winter root rot in wet UK soils.
Wrap the crown with fleece from November to March to protect the growing point from severe frost.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells, but keep the soil dry throughout the winter.
Position in partial shade rather than full sun to mimic its cool, damp New Zealand forest habitat.
Prune dead lower leaves in late spring by cutting them close to the trunk with sterilized shears.
items.description: Cordyline indivisa is a monocot tree endemic to New Zealand. It is commonly known as mountain cabbage tree or bush flax. It is also known as the broad-leaved cabbage tree, and in the Māori language as tōī.

items.name: Giant palm-lily
items.growersTips:
Plant this Australian native in a warm south-facing sheltered spot to protect from harsh UK frosts.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells but keep the soil almost dry throughout winter.
Apply a thick organic mulch around the base in late autumn to insulate roots from freezing ground.
Prune damaged leaves in late spring only after the risk of severe winter frost has fully passed.
Grow in extremely well-draining loam amended with grit to prevent root rot during wet UK winters.
items.description: Cordyline manners-suttoniae, commonly known as the giant palm lily, is an evergreen plant found only in rainforest of northeastern Queensland, Australia.

items.name: Cordyline murchisoniae
items.growersTips:
Grow in a container of peat-free loam-based compost so you can move it indoors before winter frosts.
Water only when the top five centimetres of soil is dry to prevent root rot in damp UK winters.
Position in a sheltered spot facing south or west to maximise sunlight and block cold easterly winds.
Prune dead lower leaves in late spring by pulling them downwards sharply to keep the stem clean.
Check leaf axils weekly for mealybugs which thrive in the dense foliage of this compact shrub.
items.description: Cordyline murchisoniae, known as the dwarf palm lily is an evergreen Australian plant. A shrub to 6 metres tall. The range of distribution is coastal Queensland rainforests.

items.name: Cordyline obtecta
items.growersTips:
Plant in free-draining loam with grit added to the planting hole to prevent winter root rot in wet UK soil.
Protect the crown with fleece or straw during prolonged UK winter temperatures below minus five.
Water deeply once a week in dry summer months, allowing the top five centimetres of soil to dry out.
Prunings should be limited to removing dead lower leaves in late spring to prevent rot at the trunk.
Grow alongside purple Heucheras or Phormiums to create a striking foliage contrast in UK borders.
items.description: Cordyline obtecta is a widely branching monocot tree native to Norfolk Island, and to northern New Zealand. The species name obtecta derives from the Latin obtegere, alluding to the way the inflorescence barely protruded beyond the leaves in the plant first described.

items.name: Cordyline petiolaris
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender shrub in a large pot so you can move it into a frost-free greenhouse for UK winters.
Plant in extremely free-draining loam mixed with plenty of grit to prevent winter root rot.
Water thoroughly once a week in summer but keep the compost almost entirely dry from November to March.
Prune dead lower leaves in late spring by pulling them sharply downwards to keep the stem clean.
Watch for mealybugs in the leaf axils when overwintering indoors and treat with organic insecticidal soap.
items.description: Cordyline petiolaris, known as the broad leaved palm lily is an evergreen Australian plant. A shrub to around 5 metres tall. Found in warm rainforest and moist eucalyptus forest. The range of natural distribution is from the Nambucca River to near Gladstone, Queensland.

items.name: Cordyline pumilio
items.growersTips:
Plant this dwarf species in a sheltered, south-facing border with gritty, free-draining soil.
Protect the crown from winter wet using a cloche or fleece jacket from November to March.
Water moderately in summer but allow the top five centimetres of compost to dry out between feeds.
Grow in pots using a mix of peat-free loam and grit so you can move it indoors during hard frosts.
Prune out dead lower leaves in late spring by pulling them gently downwards to keep the stem clean.
items.description: Cordyline pumilio, commonly known as the dwarf cabbage tree, pygmy cabbage tree or by its Māori names tī koraha or tī rauriki, is a narrow-leaved monocot shrub endemic to the North Island of New Zealand. It usually grows up to 1 metre tall, although rare examples of 2 metres tall have been reported. It has long leaves and can easily be mistaken for a grass or a sedge. C. pumilio grows in the north of the North Island from North Cape at 34°S to Kawhia and Ōpōtiki at about 38°S, generally under light forest and scrub. It was cultivated by Māori as a source of carbohydrate and used as a relish to

items.name: Cordyline rubra
items.growersTips:
Grow in a pot to easily move it indoors or to a heated greenhouse before the first UK winter frost.
Water only when the top five centimetres of soil dries out to prevent root rot in damp UK winters.
Plant in a mix of two parts peat-free compost to one part grit for essential sharp drainage.
Prune damaged lower leaves in late spring by pulling them downwards sharply to keep the stem clean.
Position in a sheltered spot facing south or west to maximise sunlight and block cold UK winds.
items.description: Cordyline rubra, known as the palm lily, is an evergreen Australian plant. Growing as a shrub to around 4 metres (13 ft) tall, it is found in warm rainforest and moist eucalyptus forest. The range of natural distribution is from Lismore to near Bundaberg, Queensland.

items.name: Cordyline stricta
items.growersTips:
Plant in a sheltered south-facing spot using grit to ensure the sharp winter drainage they require.
Water deeply once a week in summer but keep the root zone almost dry from November through March.
Wrap the main stem in fleece during wet UK freezes below minus five to protect the growing tip.
Prune leggy stems back to twelve inches in mid-spring to force fresh leafy shoots from the base.
Grow in pots alongside Heuchera to easily move this tender shrub into a frost-free greenhouse.
items.description: Cordyline stricta, known as the slender palm lily or narrow-leaved palm lily, is an evergreen Australian plant. A shrub to 5 metres tall found in wet sclerophyll forest and rainforest, usually on the coastal lowlands. From near Bilpin, New South Wales further north to Queensland. C. stricta has become naturalised in Victoria.

items.name: Cornutia obovata
items.growersTips:
Grow this rare tropical shrub in a large pot so you can move it into a heated greenhouse for winter.
Water generously in summer but keep the soil barely moist during winter to prevent root rot indoors.
Prune lightly in early spring after frost risk passes to maintain shape and encourage fresh growth.
Use a peat-free loam-based compost mixed with plenty of grit to ensure the sharp drainage it needs.
Position in your sunniest sheltered spot or conservatory to mimic its native Caribbean warmth.
items.description: Cornutia obovata is a rare species of tree in the mint family, and formerly considered a member of the verbena family. It is endemic to forested slopes in Puerto Rico, where its common names are capá jigüerilla, nigua, and palo de nigua. When it was added to the endangered species list of the United States in 1988 there were only seven individuals known to remain in the wild. By 1998 there were eight plants known. This is considered one population divided amongst a few locations in the mountain forests of the island.

items.name: Corunastylis laminata
items.growersTips:
Grow this rare native Australian orchid in a cold glasshouse to protect it from wet UK winters.
Use a very free-draining compost of one part peat-free loam, one part perlite, and one part grit.
Water only when the slender autumn-flowering spike emerges, keeping the pot dry during summer.
Place pots in full sun on a gravel tray to mimic dry, open eucalyptus woodland conditions.
Repot dormant tubers in late summer at a depth of three centimetres, handling brittle roots gently.
items.description: Corunastylis is a historically recognized genus of about 50 species of orchids, native to Australia and New Zealand, now included in the genera Genoplesium and Prasophyllum.

items.name: Corydalis cava
items.growersTips:
Plant blue Corydalis flexuosa in moist acidic soil to prevent summer dormancy in dry UK summers.
Sow fresh Corydalis solida seeds immediately in autumn as they lose viability rapidly if dried.
Plant tuberous Corydalis solida five centimetres deep in well-drained soil under deciduous trees.
Watch for slugs and snails on fresh spring shoots of Corydalis during damp UK April mornings.
Divide fibrous-rooted Corydalis ochroleuca in early spring just as new green growth appears.
items.description: Corydalis is a genus of about 540 species of annual and perennial herbaceous plants in the family Papaveraceae, native to the temperate Northern Hemisphere and the high mountains of tropical eastern Africa. They are most diverse in China and the Himalayas, with at least 357 species in China. Corydalis species are the only dicots having only a single cotyledon.

items.name: Corydalis ambigua
items.growersTips:
Plant tubers five centimetres deep in autumn in moist well-drained soil rich in leaf mould.
Keep soil consistently damp during spring growth but dry out slightly once summer dormancy begins.
Plant alongside snowdrops and wood anemones to fill the bare gaps left when it dies back in June.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.
Avoid disturbing the soil in summer when the plant has vanished to prevent damaging dormant tubers.
items.description: Corydalis ambigua is a tuberous early flowering east Asian flowering plant species in the poppy family Papaveraceae. Its exact native range is obscure due to taxonomic confusion. It is one of the sources of the drug tetrahydropalmatine.

items.name: Corydalis aurea
items.growersTips:
Sow fresh seed in late summer in a cold frame as they need winter chilling to germinate in spring.
Plant in moisture-retentive but sharply draining grit-amended soil to prevent winter crown rot.
Water weekly during dry spring spells but keep relatively dry during their summer dormant phase.
Position in dappled shade under deciduous shrubs to mimic their natural woodland edge habitat.
Watch for slugs and snails in damp UK springs as they quickly destroy the delicate young foliage.
items.description: Corydalis aurea, also known as scrambled eggs, golden smoke, or golden corydalis, is a flowering plant in the poppy family (Papaveraceae). The plant has a broad range stretching across North America and is able to thrive within a variety of ecosystems. The plant possesses numerous distinct characteristics. Its fruit most closely resembles that of a pea pod and is typically around 3/4 of an inch in length. The plant has numerous medicinal uses, as well as uses for gardens.

items.name: Corydalis caseana
items.growersTips:
Plant in deep, humus-rich soil that mimics a damp UK woodland floor, keeping pH neutral to acidic.
Position in partial to full shade, ensuring the soil remains consistently moist even during summer.
Incorporate leaf mould and grit into the planting hole to provide moisture retention with drainage.
Watch for slugs and snails in early spring as the delicate new shoots emerge from the ground.
Propagate by dividing the fibrous rootstock in early spring just as the plant begins active growth.
items.description: Corydalis caseana, also known as Sierra corydalis, Sierra fumewort, or fitweed, is a species of plant in the poppy family from the western United States.

items.name: Corydalis caucasica
items.growersTips:
Plant tubers five centimetres deep in autumn in moist well-drained soil rich in leaf mould.
Siting is key so plant under deciduous shrubs to mimic UK woodland shade and prevent summer baking.
Keep soil consistently moist during active spring growth but allow to dry out during summer dormancy.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.
Do not disturb the soil or replant companions in summer when the delicate foliage has died back.
items.description: Corydalis caucasica is a species of flowering plant in the poppy family Papaveraceae, native to the Caucasus and northern Turkey.

items.name: Corydalis cava
items.growersTips:
Plant tubers five to eight centimetres deep in autumn to prevent them drying out in UK winters.
Incorporate leaf mould into heavy clay soil to mimic the damp deciduous woodland floor they love.
Water only during spring growth and keep the soil relatively dry during summer dormant periods.
Plant under deciduous shrubs so they get spring sun before being shaded by summer leaf canopies.
Watch for slugs and snails in damp UK springs as they quickly destroy the tender emerging shoots.
items.description:
Corydalis cava is a species of flowering plant in the family Papaveraceae, native to moist, shady, woodland habitats throughout most of mainland Europe, although commonest in central and southeast Europe.
Its range extends from Spain in the west to Ukraine, Belarus and the Caucasus in the east and as far north as Sweden. It is absent from Iceland, the UK, the Netherlands, Norway, Finland, Russia and Greece.

items.name: Corydalis cheilanthifolia
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist but well-drained humus-rich soil in partial to full shade to mimic UK woodland edges.
Sow fresh seed in autumn directly into cold frames as they require winter chilling to germinate.
Water consistently during dry UK summers to prevent the fern-like foliage from dying back early.
Position away from aggressive spreading plants to protect its delicate, slow-growing crown.
Watch for slugs and snails in damp spring weather which quickly devour the emerging yellow flowers.
items.description: Corydalis cheilanthifolia, the fern-leaved corydalis or fern-leaf corydalis, is a flowering plant in the family Papaveraceae. It is a perennial growing from rhizomes, native to western and central China. It is a source of the benzylisoquinoline alkaloid, cheilanthifoline.

items.name: Corydalis chelidoniifolia
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist but well-drained humus-rich soil in dappled shade to mimic its woodland habitat.
Sow seeds in autumn in cold frames as they require winter chilling to germinate the following spring.
Water regularly during dry UK summers to prevent the delicate fern-like foliage from dying back early.
Position away from aggressive ground cover to protect its brittle stems and delicate root system.
Divide established clumps in early spring just as new growth appears to propagate successfully.
items.description: Corydalis chelidoniifolia is a flowering plant in the poppy family Papaveraceae.

items.name: Corydalis flavula
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn outdoors as they require winter cold stratification to germinate in UK spring.
Plant in moist well-drained soil enriched with leafmould to mimic their native woodland floor.
Position in dappled shade under deciduous shrubs to protect delicate foliage from hot summer sun.
Water consistently during dry spring spells but allow soil to dry slightly when dormant in summer.
Watch for slugs and snails in damp UK springs as they quickly consume the tender young shoots.
items.description: Corydalis flavula is an herbaceous perennial plant native to the eastern United States. Its natural habitat is open woods and slopes.

items.name: Corydalis flexuosa
items.growersTips:
Plant in partial shade using humus-rich, moist but well-drained soil that mimics woodland conditions.
Water regularly during dry spring spells to prevent the plant from entering premature summer dormancy.
Watch for slugs and snails in early spring when the delicate blue-flowered shoots first emerge.
Let the foliage die back naturally in summer, then top-dress with leaf mould to nourish the tubers.
Divide congested clumps in autumn or early spring to propagate and maintain vigorous blue blooms.
items.description: Corydalis flexuosa is a species of flowering plant in the genus Corydalis, of the family Papaveraceae. It is a shade-loving perennial originating in woodland and mountainous areas of China. Growing to 30 cm (12 in), in spring it produces masses of bright blue tubular flowers with a white throat. It is summer dormant, meaning that the foliage dies down in summer.

items.name: Corydalis incisa
items.growersTips:
Plant this biennial in moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade to mimic its native woodland edge.
Deadhead flowers before they set seed to prevent this highly invasive species from choking borders.
Sow fresh seeds in late summer in cold frames as they require winter chilling to germinate.
Watch for slugs and snails on young spring growth, especially during wet UK April weather.
Grow alongside robust ferns or hostas that can withstand this plant's aggressive self-seeding.
items.description: Corydalis incisa, incised fumewort, is an annual or biennial herbaceous species of plant in the poppy family. It is also known as purple keman or murasa-kike-man. Some authorities report it in the family Fumariaceae. The wildflower is native to Japan, Korea, Taiwan, and China, found in forests, clearings, and irrigation channels.

items.name: Corydalis intermedia
items.growersTips:
Plant tubers five centimetres deep in autumn in moist but well-drained soil under deciduous trees.
Keep soil consistently moist during spring growth but allow it to dry out when dormant in summer.
Plant alongside early snowdrops and wood anemones to mimic their natural UK woodland habitat.
Leave dying foliage intact after flowering in May to allow the tuber to store energy for next year.
Watch for slugs and snails in damp UK springs as they quickly consume the tender emerging shoots.
items.description: Corydalis intermedia is a species of flowering plant belonging to the family Papaveraceae.

items.name: Yellow corydalis
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist well-drained soil in partial to full shade, mimicking UK woodland edge conditions.
Sow seeds immediately when ripe in summer, as they require winter cold to germinate next spring.
Do not overwater in winter; damp UK soils can cause the delicate tuberous roots to rot.
Grow in stone wall crevices or gravel paths where it self-seeds freely without overtaking beds.
Combine with shade-loving ferns and hostas to hide the foliage when it dies back in late summer.
items.description: Pseudofumaria lutea, the yellow corydalis or rock fumewort, is a short-lived perennial plant in the poppy family Papaveraceae. It is native to the southern foothills of the south-western and central Alps of Italy and Switzerland, but widely introduced elsewhere.

items.name: Corydalis malkensis
items.growersTips:
Plant tubers 8cm deep in late summer in moist, well-drained soil under deciduous trees or shrubs.
Keep soil consistently moist during spring growth but allow it to dry out during summer dormancy.
Sow fresh seed immediately in summer as dry stored seeds of this species quickly lose viability.
Protect emerging spring foliage from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.
Associate with early snowdrops and winter aconites which share its woodland soil requirements.
items.description: Corydalis caucasica is a species of flowering plant in the poppy family Papaveraceae, native to the Caucasus and northern Turkey.

items.name: Corydalis mucronifera
items.growersTips:
Plant this alpine in gritty, sharply draining soil to prevent winter wet rot in damp UK climates.
Position in a cool, partially shaded rock garden or alpine house to shield it from hot summer sun.
Water moderately during the spring growing season but keep almost dry during its summer dormancy.
Protect the delicate, blue-green foliage from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers.
Propagate by carefully dividing the fragile tuberous roots immediately after flowering in summer.
items.description: Corydalis mucronifera is a species of flowering plant. It does not have a common name as it is quite rare in nature. This plant has also previously been recorded as Corydalis boweri. Being as rare as it is, it has only been found in two regions: China and Tibet. The range where the plant can be found is small as it is only found near rocky beaches or high mountain ranges at altitudes between 4200 and 5300 meters. Corydalis mucronifera is small in size and displays a variety of colors: purple, yellow, white, and cream. The plant has similar structures to other plants found in Europe and North A

items.name: Corydalis nobilis
items.growersTips:
Plant in moisture-retentive, humus-rich soil in partial shade to mimic its native woodland edge.
Sow fresh seed immediately in summer as they lose viability quickly and need winter cold to sprout.
Mark its location in summer because the foliage dies back completely after flowering in May.
Water during dry spring spells but keep soil relatively dry during its summer dormant period.
Watch for slugs and snails in early spring as they target the emerging tender shoots and buds.
items.description: Corydalis nobilis, the Siberian corydalis, is a perennial plant native to Siberia, Xinjiang and Kazakhstan. It was introduced to Europe by Linnaeus, who had asked his friend Erich Laxmann for seeds of Lamprocapnos spectabilis, but was sent seeds of C. nobilis instead. Both Lamprocampnos and Corydalis are members of the family Papaveraceae, with seeds having an attached elaiosome that makes them attractive to ants, which disperse the seeds.

items.name: Corydalis pumila
items.growersTips:
Plant tubers in autumn at a depth of eight centimetres in moist but well-drained deciduous shade.
Incorporate leaf mould into heavy UK clay soils to mimic their natural woodland floor habitat.
Allow the plant to die back naturally in summer and keep the soil relatively dry during dormancy.
Watch for slugs and snails in damp UK springs as they eagerly devour the emerging young foliage.
Associate them with snowdrops and wood anemones for a synchronized early spring woodland display.
items.description: Corydalis pumila is a species of plant in the family Papaveraceae. It is found in Central Europe and has a small, fragmented distribution. In Poland, it is a rare species found only in the western part of the country. It grows mainly in fertile deciduous forests, rarely in cemeteries and parks. The aboveground shoot develops only for two months in early spring. As a very rare species losing its habitats, it is subject to legal protection in Poland.

items.name: Corydalis rutifolia
items.growersTips:
Plant tubers 8cm deep in autumn using gritty loam to mimic their native dry Mediterranean winters.
Water sparingly during summer dormancy to prevent the tuberous roots from rotting in wet UK soil.
Protect emerging spring foliage from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.
Sow fresh seed in pots outdoors during summer so winter cold naturally triggers spring germination.
Grow in a raised bed or alpine house to shield the delicate pink flowers from heavy UK winter rain.
items.description: Corydalis rutifolia is a species of flowering plant in the family Papaveraceae, endemic to the Troodos Mountains in Cyprus. It was first described by James Edward Smith in 1821 as Fumaria rutifolia.

items.name: Spring Fumewort
items.growersTips:
Plant tubers 8cm deep in autumn in humus-rich, well-drained soil that mimics woodland conditions.
Keep soil moist during spring growth but allow tubers to dry out during their summer dormant phase.
Watch for slugs and snails in early spring as they quickly devour the emerging tender flower shoots.
Plant alongside late-emerging hostas or ferns to cover the bare patches left when foliage dies back.
Avoid disturbing the soil from June onwards when the plant has completely disappeared underground.
items.description: Corydalis solida, fumewort or bird-in-a-bush, is a species of flowering plant in the family Papaveraceae, native to moist, shady habitats in northern Europe and Asia. Growing to 25 cm (10 in), it is a spring ephemeral, with foliage that appears in spring and dies down to its tuberous rootstock in summer. It is cultivated for its deeply divided, ferny leaves and narrow, long-spurred flowers which appear in spring. The flowers show color variation, and may be mauve, purple, red, or white.

items.name: Cotoneaster ×watereri
items.growersTips:
Plant in autumn using a wide hole twice the rootball width to establish roots before winter rains.
Water deeply once a week during the first dry summer to prevent leaf drop in sandy UK soils.
Prune in late spring after flowering to shape the shrub without sacrificing the winter berry display.
Watch for fireblight in warm damp UK summers by immediately cutting back blackened wilted branches.
Grow in well-drained loam enriched with garden compost to prevent waterlogging in wet British winters.
items.description: Cotoneaster × watereri, or Waterer's cotoneaster, is a large evergreen shrub belonging to the genus Cotoneaster.

items.name: Cotoneaster acuminatus
items.growersTips:
Plant in autumn using well-drained soil enriched with grit to prevent winter root rot in UK clay.
Prune in late winter by removing one-fifth of old stems at the base to boost autumn berry display.
Water deeply once a week during the first dry summer, then leave to rely on natural UK rainfall.
Watch for cotoneaster webworm in late spring and prune out infested silk-webbed shoots immediately.
Grow alongside Viburnum opulus to create a wind-resistant screen that thrives in UK partial shade.
items.description: Cotoneaster acuminatus, commonly known as acuminate cotoneaster, is a species of flowering plant in the family Rosaceae that is native to the Himalayas. In forests it can be found at elevations of 1,300–3,000 metres (4,300–9,800 ft), while on hillsides it is found at 2,500–3,500 metres (8,200–11,500 ft). The species has also been introduced to Oregon.

items.name: Cotoneaster acutifolius
items.growersTips:
Plant in autumn in well-drained UK clay or loam at the same depth as the original nursery pot.
Water weekly during the first dry British summer, then leave to rely solely on natural rainfall.
Prune in late winter to remove dead wood and maintain shape before spring sap starts to flow.
Check leaves in June for cotoneaster webworm caterpillars and remove webbing nests immediately.
Grow alongside Viburnum opulus in sun or partial shade to boost local UK pollinator biodiversity.
items.description: Cotoneaster acutifolius, the Peking cotoneaster, is a species of flowering plant in the family Rosaceae. It is native to southern Siberia, Mongolia, and most of China, and it has been introduced to Canada, the northern United States, and northern Europe. It is a shrub typically 2–4 m (7–13 ft) tall, found in a wide variety of habitats. Some authorities consider Cotoneaster lucidus, the shiny cotoneaster, to be a synonym of Cotoneaster acutifolius.

items.name: Cotoneaster adpressus
items.growersTips:
Plant in autumn using well-drained grit-amended soil to prevent root rot during wet UK winters.
Water weekly during the first dry summer then leave to rely solely on natural UK rainfall.
Prune wayward upright shoots in late spring to maintain the signature flat prostrate ground cover.
Watch for fireblight disease in warm wet springs by pruning out and burning any blackened stems.
Grow alongside Thymus serpyllum on sunny banks to match its dry soil needs and suppress weeds.
items.description: Cotoneaster adpressus, commonly known as creeping cotoneaster, is a species of flowering plant in the genus Cotoneaster of the family Rosaceae, native to western China. A prostrate, dense, deciduous shrub growing to 2 metres wide, it has masses of tiny rounded leaves, with white flowers followed by bright scarlet berries. Furthermore, it is cultivated as groundcover in gardens in temperate regions.

items.name: Cranberry cotoneaster
items.growersTips:
Plant in autumn in well-drained UK soil, keeping the root flare exactly level with the ground.
Water deeply once a week during the first dry summer, then leave to survive on natural UK rainfall.
Prune wayward stems in late winter to maintain the low, herringbone shape and maximise spring bloom.
Watch for cotoneaster webworm caterpillars in June, hand-picking them to protect the dense foliage.
Grow alongside spring bulbs like daffodils to bring colour before the red berries and autumn leaves.
items.description: Cotoneaster apiculatus, the cranberry cotoneaster, is a species of flowering plant in the family Rosaceae. It is native to central China, and it has been introduced to various locales in Europe and the United States. A rabbit-tolerant shrub reaching 3 ft (1 m) tall but spreading to 6 ft (2 m), and hardy in USDA zones 4 through 7, it is recommended for covering large areas. It is good on streambanks and slopes where erosion control is desired, as its branches will grow roots where they touch soil.

items.name: Purple-flowered cotoneaster
items.growersTips:
Plant this low-growing shrub in well-drained soil to prevent root rot in wet UK winter conditions.
Prune immediately after flowering in late spring to shape the plant without losing autumn berries.
Water newly planted shrubs weekly during dry summer spells until their root system is established.
Watch for cotoneaster webworm caterpillars in summer and prune out infested branches immediately.
Grow alongside spring bulbs like daffodils to provide color before the shrub leaf out in early May.
items.description: Cotoneaster atropurpureus, the purple-flowered cotoneaster, is a species of flowering plant in the genus Cotoneaster of the family Rosaceae, native to the Hubei province of China. It is a prostrate, deciduous shrub growing to 2.5 metres wide. It can be used as groundcover or trained to ascend up a wall or other support. Its fan-shaped, arching branches bear small, rounded, glossy green leaves turning purple in autumn. Red/black flowers are followed by small, globose, scarlet fruits (pomes).

items.name: Cotoneaster bullatus
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist well-drained loamy soil at the same depth as the nursery pot during autumn leaf fall.
Water deeply once a week during the first dry UK summer to establish its deep foraging root system.
Prune in late winter by removing one-fifth of old stems at the base to boost autumn berry production.
Watch for fireblight disease in warm wet springs and immediately prune out infected black branches.
Underplant with spring-flowering bulbs like Narcissus to draw early pollinators to your shrub.
items.description: Cotoneaster bullatus, the hollyberry cotoneaster, is a species of shrub in the genus Cotoneaster within the rose family. Its natural range is in Western China, where it is found in a range of woodland and shrub biotopes from 900 to 3200 m above sea level.

items.name: Cotoneaster cambricus
items.growersTips:
Plant in free-draining limestone soil or add grit to mimic its native Great Orme cliff habitat.
Water newly planted shrubs weekly during dry UK spring spells but keep established plants dry.
Prune lightly in late winter to remove dead wood without ruining its natural prostrate shape.
Watch for cotoneaster webworm caterpillars in summer and handpick them to protect the foliage.
Propagate by taking semi-ripe cuttings in late summer to help conserve this critically rare species.
items.description: Cotoneaster cambricus is a species of Cotoneaster endemic to the Great Orme peninsula in north Wales. It is the only species of Cotoneaster native to the British Isles. It has never been found naturally at any other location. In the past, it was included within the widespread eastern European Cotoneaster integerrimus, but differs from that in genetic profile.

items.name: Cotoneaster cashmiriensis
items.growersTips:
Plant in well-drained UK soil with the root flare exactly level with the surrounding ground.
Water deeply once a week during dry British summers until the root system is fully established.
Prune lightly in late spring after flowering to maintain its low-growing, spreading carpet habit.
Watch for cotoneaster webworm caterpillars in summer and remove their silk nests immediately by hand.
Grow in full sun to maximise the production of its signature white spring flowers and red autumn berries.
items.description: Cotoneaster microphyllus, the small-leaved cotoneaster or rockspray cotoneaster, is a species of flowering plant in the family Rosaceae. It is native to the Indian Subcontinent, Tibet, Sichuan, and Yunnan in China, and Myanmar, and it has been introduced to various locales in Europe, Australia, and the United States. A rabbit-tolerant shrub reaching 1 m (3 ft) tall but spreading to 2.5 m (8 ft), and hardy in USDA zones 5 through 7, it is recommended for rockeries and hedges. Care should be taken not to plant it where it can become invasive.

items.name: Cotoneaster cochleatus
items.growersTips:
Plant in autumn in well-drained UK soil to establish roots before winter waterlogging occurs.
Prune lightly in late spring after flowering to maintain its low-growing, ground-hugging habit.
Water newly planted shrubs weekly during dry UK summer spells until their deep root system adapts.
Watch for cotoneaster web moth caterpillars in June and remove infested silk webs immediately.
Grow on a sunny, sloping bank to prevent waterlogging and showcase the bright red autumn berries.
items.description: Cotoneaster cochleatus, the Yunnan cotoneaster, is a species of flowering plant in the family Rosaceae. It is native to rocky slopes in Tibet, Sichuan, and Yunnan in China, and it has been introduced to the United Kingdom, Belgium and New York State. Its specific epithet cochleatus refers to its twisting stem.

items.name: Cotoneaster conspicuus
items.growersTips:
Plant this shrub in well-drained soil at the same depth as its nursery pot to prevent stem rot.
Water deeply once a week during the first dry UK summer to establish a resilient, deep root system.
Prune lightly in late spring after flowering to shape the shrub without sacrificing winter berries.
Watch for fireblight in warm UK springs, pruning out infected blackened branches immediately.
Grow alongside spring-flowering bulbs like daffodils to provide colour before the shrub blooms.
items.description: Cotoneaster conspicuus is a slow-growing, densely-branched, evergreen shrub native to southeast Tibet. It grows to 1 to 1.5 meters in height, with white five-stellate flowers followed by scarlet fruit, 8–10 mm in diameter.

items.name: Late cotoneaster
items.growersTips:
Plant in autumn using well-drained loam enriched with grit to prevent winter root rot in UK clay.
Prune in late winter by removing one-fifth of old stems to the base to boost autumn berry display.
Water deeply once a week during the first dry summer, then leave to rely solely on UK rainfall.
Inspect leaves in May for cotoneaster webmoth caterpillars and physically remove the silk nests.
Grow alongside Pyracantha to create a dense, burglar-proof wildlife hedge that deters intruders.
items.description: Cotoneaster coriaceus, the late cotoneaster or milkflower cotoneaster, is a species of flowering plant in the family Rosaceae, native to Tibet and south-central China. It is a large evergreen shrub growing to 4 m (13 ft) tall and wide. Clusters of white flowers are followed by masses of small, globose, red fruits (pomes) in autumn. Unusually for this genus, the fruits are avoided by birds, hence garden escapes are rare, and the fruit persists on the plant throughout the winter.

items.name: Bearberry cotoneaster
items.growersTips:
Plant in autumn to allow roots to establish in moist UK soil before the spring growing season.
Water deeply once a week during the first summer dry spells to establish a deep, drought-proof root system.
Prune in late spring after flowering to control spread and shape without sacrificing the red autumn berries.
Incorporate grit into heavy UK clay soils before planting to prevent root rot in wet winter conditions.
Watch for woolly aphid infestations in summer and treat immediately with organic insecticidal soap.
items.description: Cotoneaster dammeri, the bearberry cotoneaster, is a species of flowering plant in the genus Cotoneaster, belonging to the family Rosaceae, native to central and southern China and naturalized in Europe.

items.name: Cotoneaster divaricatus
items.growersTips:
Plant in autumn in well-drained UK clay or loam, keeping the root flare level with the soil surface.
Water deeply once a week during the first dry summer, then leave to rely on natural UK rainfall.
Prune in late winter to remove rubbing branches and maintain the characteristic arching habit.
Watch for fireblight in warm, wet UK springs, cutting back infected wood well into healthy growth.
Underplant with spring-flowering bulbs like crocus to add colour before the shrub leafs out.
items.description: Cotoneaster divaricatus, the spreading cotoneaster, is a species of flowering plant in the family Rosaceae. It is native to China, and has been introduced to Ontario in Canada, the Midwest United States, northern and central Europe, Kenya, and the South Island of New Zealand. A shrub reaching 1.8 m (6 ft) tall but spreading to 2.4 m (8 ft), and hardy in USDA zones 4 through 7, it is considered a valuable landscaping plant by the Missouri Botanical Garden. The Centre for Agriculture and Bioscience International lists it in its Invasive Species Compendium.

items.name: Cotoneaster franchetii
items.growersTips:
Prune in late winter to shape the shrub and encourage berries without disrupting nesting birds.
Plant in well-drained soil with the root flare level with the ground to prevent collar rot.
Water deeply once a week during the first dry UK summer to establish a deep, resilient root system.
Inspect leaves in spring for cotoneaster webworm caterpillars and prune out infested silk webs.
Grow alongside Pyracantha or Holly to create a dense, wildlife-friendly hedge for UK songbirds.
items.description: Cotoneaster franchetii is a species of Cotoneaster native to southwestern China, in the provinces of Guizhou, Sichuan, Tibet, and Yunnan, and also in adjacent northern Myanmar and northern Thailand.

items.name: Tree Cotoneaster
items.growersTips:
Plant in autumn to allow winter rains to establish the deep root system in well-drained UK soils.
Prune in late winter by removing one-fifth of old stems to the base to boost autumn berry display.
Watch for fireblight in warm wet UK springs by pruning infected blackened shoots well back into healthy wood.
Grow the cultivar Cornubia for its exceptionally heavy berry yield and semi-evergreen winter foliage.
Underplant with Galanthus nivalis to utilise the light shade of its deciduous canopy in early spring.
items.description: Cotoneaster frigidus, the tree cotoneaster, is a species of flowering plant in the genus Cotoneaster of the family Rosaceae, native to the Himalayas.

items.name: Cotoneaster glaucophyllus
items.growersTips:
Plant in autumn in well-drained UK soil to let winter rain establish roots before summer dry spells.
Prune lightly in late spring after flowering to shape the shrub without sacrificing winter berries.
Watch for fireblight in warm UK summers, cutting infected branches back 30cm into healthy wood.
Grow in full sun to maximize the distinctive blue-green leaf hue and heavy autumn berry display.
Propagate in late summer using semi-ripe cuttings rooted in a cold frame under typical UK weather.
items.description: Cotoneaster glaucophyllus, commonly known as glaucous cotoneaster' or bright bead cotoneaster, is a native plant of China and the Himalayas.

items.name: Cotoneaster horizontalis
items.growersTips:
Plant against a south or west wall using rawlplugs and wire to train the herringbone branches flat.
Prune in late winter to remove dead wood and keep the flat shape before new spring growth starts.
Watch for cotoneaster webworm caterpillars in summer and cut out silk-webbed branches immediately.
Grow in well-drained UK soil as wet winter clay causes root rot; add grit to the planting hole.
Do not plant near pear orchards due to fireblight risk, a serious bacterial disease in the UK.
items.description: Cotoneaster horizontalis is a species of flowering plant in the genus Cotoneaster of the family Rosaceae.

items.name: Cotoneaster integerrimus
items.growersTips:
Plant in free-draining limestone or chalky soil to mimic its native UK limestone cliff habitat.
Water deeply once a week during the first summer, then leave to rely solely on UK rainfall.
Prune lightly in late winter to remove dead wood and maintain its naturally compact, rounded shape.
Watch for cotoneaster web moth caterpillars in spring and remove their silken webs immediately.
Plant alongside wild thyme or marjoram in sunny rock gardens to support native UK pollinators.
items.description: Cotoneaster integerrimus, the common cotoneaster, is a species of Cotoneaster native to central and eastern Europe and southwest Asia, from southern Belgium and eastern France south to Italy, and east through Germany to the Balkans, northern Turkey, the Crimea, the Caucasus and northern Iran; plants in Spain may also belong in this species. In the past, it was treated in a wider sense, including plants from Wales now split off as Cotoneaster cambricus and plants from Scandinavia now treated as Cotoneaster scandinavicus, but differs from these in genetic profile and detail of foliage and fruit.

items.name: Cotoneaster integrifolius
items.growersTips:
Plant in free-draining chalky or sandy soil to prevent root rot during wet UK winters.
Prune lightly in late spring after flowering to shape and control its low, spreading habit.
Water newly planted shrubs weekly during dry summer spells until their root system is established.
Watch for fireblight disease in warm, wet springs, pruning out infected wood immediately.
Grow alongside companion plants like hardy geraniums or thymes that thrive in dry, sunny borders.
items.description: Cotoneaster integrifolius, the entire-leaved cotoneaster, is a species of Cotoneaster that is a low growing shrub. It has been grown as an ornamental plant in gardens and public rock gardens. It has been introduced to Ireland, but has become naturalised. It produces a red berry-like pome fruit that are an important food source for birds that disperse the seeds in their droppings. They are sometimes grown as a hedge for home security.

items.name: Cotoneaster kweitschoviensis
items.growersTips:
Plant in autumn using a double-width hole backfilled with grit to prevent winter root rot in clay.
Water deeply once a week during the first dry UK summer then leave to rely on natural rainfall.
Prune lightly in late spring after flowering to shape the shrub without sacrificing autumn berries.
Check leaves in damp spring weather for fireblight and prune out infected branches immediately.
Grow alongside spring bulbs like daffodils to provide color before the shrub leafes out in May.
items.description: Cotoneaster kweitschoviensis is a species of flowering plant in the family Rosaceae.

items.name: Cotoneaster lucidus
items.growersTips:
Plant in autumn at the same depth as the pot to let winter rain settle roots in UK clay soils.
Prune immediately after flowering in June to preserve the autumn crop of black berries.
Water deeply once a week during dry UK summers for the first two years until fully established.
Watch for fireblight in warm wet springs, pruning out infected blackened shoots into healthy wood.
Grow alongside Viburnum opulus to create a wildlife hedge that thrives in damp British climates.
items.description:
Cotoneaster lucidus, the shiny cotoneaster, or hedge cotoneaster, is a deciduous, medium-sized shrub with long, spreading branches reaching heights of 6' to 10'. It is native to parts of northern Asia, and adapted to tolerate colder weather
(to zone 4). C. lucidus was described in 1856 by Diederich Franz Leonhard von Schlechtendal. Some authorities consider it to be a synonym of Cotoneaster acutifolius, the Peking cotoneaster.

items.name: Cotoneaster microphyllus
items.growersTips:
Plant in free-draining UK soil at the same depth as the nursery pot to prevent crown rot in wet winters
Water weekly during the first dry UK summer then leave to rely solely on natural rainfall once settled
Prune back unruly shoots in late spring after flowering to maintain its low-growing groundcover shape
Watch for fireblight in warm damp UK springs by pruning out and burning any blackened dying branches
Grow on a sunny south-facing bank to maximise the autumn berry display and attract local UK pollinators
items.description: Cotoneaster microphyllus, the small-leaved cotoneaster or rockspray cotoneaster, is a species of flowering plant in the family Rosaceae. It is native to the Indian Subcontinent, Tibet, Sichuan, and Yunnan in China, and Myanmar, and it has been introduced to various locales in Europe, Australia, and the United States. A rabbit-tolerant shrub reaching 1 m (3 ft) tall but spreading to 2.5 m (8 ft), and hardy in USDA zones 5 through 7, it is recommended for rockeries and hedges. Care should be taken not to plant it where it can become invasive.

items.name: Cotoneaster nitidus
items.growersTips:
Plant in autumn in well-drained UK soil to establish roots before winter waterlogging occurs.
Prune lightly in late spring after flowering to shape the shrub without losing winter berries.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells in the first year to establish deep roots.
Watch for cotoneaster webworm caterpillars in June and remove their silk nests immediately by hand.
Grow in full sun to maximise the autumn crop of bright red berries that feed local UK songbirds.
items.description: Cotoneaster nitidus (两列栒子) is a species of deciduous or semi-evergreen shrub in the family Rosaceae endemic to altitudes of 1600–4000 meters in northeastern India, Bhutan, Nepal, Sikkim, and northern Myanmar, as well as the Sichuan, Xizang, and Yunnan provinces in China. It grows to 2.5 m in height, with leaves broadly ovate or broadly obovate, and typically 0.8–1.5 × 0.7–1.3 cm in size.

items.name: Nummular or coinwort cotoneaster
items.growersTips:
Plant in free-draining chalky soil on a sunny south-facing bank to mimic its native limestone habitat.
Water deeply once a week during the first dry UK summer, then leave fully drought-tolerant.
Prune lightly in late winter to remove congested stems and maintain its naturally arching habit.
Watch for cotoneaster webworm caterpillars in May and hand-pick them to protect the foliage.
Propagate by taking semi-ripe cuttings in late summer and rooting them in a cold frame.
items.description: Cotoneaster nummularius, the nummular or coinwort cotoneaster, is a deciduous shrub in the rose family. It is native to a wide geographical range spanning from Morocco and Greece eastward through the Middle East, Central Asia, and into parts of China and India. It typically grows at altitudes between 800 and 2,400 meters in semi-arid montane climates, forming dense, rounded thickets. Characterized by its small, alternate leaves with dark green upper surfaces and densely grey undersides, C. nummularius produces white to pinkish-white hermaphroditic flowers from April to June. These are followed

items.name: Cotoneaster pannosus
items.growersTips:
Prune in late winter to shape the arching branches and avoid cutting off spring flowers.
Plant in well-drained soil with the root flare exactly level with the surrounding ground.
Water deeply once a week during the first dry UK summer to establish the deep root system.
Inspect leaves in summer for cotoneaster webworm and prune out any webbed branch tips immediately.
Grow alongside Pyracantha or Holly to create a dense wildlife hedge that feeds UK birds in winter.
items.description: Cotoneaster pannosus is a species of Cotoneaster known by the common name silverleaf cotoneaster. This woody shrub is native to south central China but it has been introduced to other areas of the world, including southern Africa and Australia as an ornamental. It has become naturalized in some areas but it is a troublesome noxious weed in others, for example, in Hawaii. This is a sprawling shrub easily reaching over 3 meters in height. It is covered in dull green oval-shaped leaves with fuzzy white undersides and blooms in white flowers. The fruits are red-orange pomes containing two seeds ea

items.name: Cotoneaster roseus
items.growersTips:
Plant in autumn in well-drained chalky or loamy soil to establish roots before wet UK winters.
Prune lightly in late winter to remove dead wood without ruining the natural arching habit.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells in the first year to prevent leaf drop.
Watch for fireblight in warm damp UK springs by checking for blackened, scorched-looking shoots.
Grow alongside hardy geraniums or salvias to cover the bare lower stems of this upright shrub.
items.description: Cotoneaster roseus is native to portions of the Himalayas, Iran, northern and western Pakistan, northwest India and Kashmir. The Latin name roseus means rosy or pink, and refers to its flower petals. It was first described by the Irish botanist Michael Pakenham Edgeworth as Cotoneaster rosea in 1846.

items.name: Cotoneaster salicifolius
items.growersTips:
Plant in autumn in well-drained UK soil to establish roots before the wet winter waterlogging sets in
Prune lightly in late spring after flowering to shape the shrub without sacrificing winter berries
Watch for fireblight in warm wet UK summers and prune out infected blackened branches immediately
Grow alongside companion plants like hardy geraniums to cover the bare lower stems of older shrubs
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells in the first two years to establish deep roots
items.description: Cotoneaster salicifolius, the willow-leaved cotoneaster, is a drought-tolerant, evergreen to semi-evergreen, low-lying, small to medium-sized shrub with an arched branching habit. Specimens growing in the wild, however, are generally larger, averaging five meters in height. Although native to the mountains, mixed forests, and open places in western China, it is commonly cultivated in temperate climates worldwide. Cultivars have been bred in a variety of forms, as ornamental groundcovers or shrubs.

items.name: Cotoneaster scandinavicus
items.growersTips:
Plant in free-draining UK chalk or limestone soils to mimic its native Scandinavian cliff habitat.
Water deeply once a week during its first dry British summer, then leave to rely on natural rain.
Prune lightly in late winter to shape, avoiding heavy cuts that ruin its arching natural form.
Watch for fireblight in warm UK springs, pruning out infected blackened shoots immediately.
Underplant with wild thyme or sedums to complement its low-growing, rock-loving coastal habit.
items.description: Cotoneaster scandinavicus, commonly known as Scandinavian cotoneaster, is a species of Cotoneaster native to Scandinavia, in Norway, Sweden and Finland south of the Arctic Circle, the Danish island of Bornholm, and also the Baltic States of Estonia and Latvia.

items.name: Cotoneaster simonsii
items.growersTips:
Plant in autumn using a double-depth hole enriched with grit to prevent winter root rot in wet clay.
Water deeply once a week during the first UK summer dry spells to establish its deep taproot system.
Prune in late winter by removing one-fifth of old stems at the base to boost autumn berry production.
Watch for fireblight disease in warm wet UK springs, cutting infected blackened branches back by 30cm.
Grow alongside Viburnum opulus to create a dense windbreak that attracts diverse UK garden wildlife.
items.description: Cotoneaster simonsii, the Himalayan cotoneaster, is a species of flowering plant in the family Rosaceae. It is native to Nepal, the eastern Himalayas, Assam, and Myanmar, and has been introduced to a number of locales in Europe, the west coast of North America, and Australia as a garden escapee. The Royal Horticultural Society considers it to be an undesirable invasive non-native species.

items.name: Cotoneaster tauricus
items.growersTips:
Plant in autumn in well-drained chalky soil to mimic its native Crimean limestone habitat.
Water deeply once a week during the first UK summer, then leave to rely solely on natural rainfall.
Prune lightly in late winter to remove dead wood and maintain its compact, arching shrub shape.
Check regularly for fireblight in warm, wet UK springs, cutting back infected wood to healthy tissue.
Grow alongside Origanum vulgare or Thymus to complement its drought tolerance and attract pollinators.
items.description: Cotoneaster tauricus is a species of flowering plant in the family Rosaceae, native to Ukraine and Crimea. A shrub, it is often found in association with relict populations of Pistacia atlantica trees.

items.name: Cranichideae
items.growersTips:
Grow UK native Goodyera repens in damp, acidic pine leaf mould rather than standard potting compost.
Water terrestrial Spiranthes with rainwater to keep soil constantly moist but never waterlogged.
Protect winter-green leaves of autumn lady's-tresses from slugs using copper tape around pots.
Overwinter tender tropical Cranichis indoors at fifteen degrees Celsius under bright indirect light.
Propagate Ludisia discolor by taking stem cuttings in spring and rooting them in damp sphagnum moss.
items.description: Cranichideae is an orchid tribe in the subfamily Orchidoideae.

items.name: Crassula alata
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in spring on free-draining gritty compost as they need light to germinate.
Water sparingly only when the top two inches of soil dry out to prevent root rot in damp UK weather.
Grow in pots to easily move plants indoors before autumn frosts as this annual cannot survive frost.
Mix horticultural grit into standard compost to mimic their native dry soils in wet UK climates.
Position in the sunniest south-facing spot possible to prevent leggy growth in weak British sunlight.
items.description: Crassula alata is a herb in the family Crassulaceae. It is native to the Mediterranean basin and is now also found in southern Australia and New Zealand. The succulent annual herb typically grows to a height of 5 centimetres (2.0 in). It produces white flowers in the spring time between August and October in the Southern Hemisphere.

items.name: Crassula alba
items.growersTips:
Grow in a gritty free-draining loam-based compost with fifty percent horticultural sand or perlite.
Sow seeds shallowly on the soil surface in early spring using a heated propagator at fifteen degrees.
Water only when the top three centimetres of soil are dry and keep completely dry during winter damp.
Position in a south-facing unheated greenhouse or porch to maximize light and protect from UK frost.
Inspect leaf axils weekly for mealybugs and treat infestations immediately with organic neem oil.
items.description: Crassula alba is a species of flowering plant in the genus Crassula found in western Africa ranging from South Africa to Sudan.

items.name: Crassula alpestris
items.growersTips:
Grow this winter-active annual in a gritty, free-draining loam-based compost with 50 percent grit.
Water only when the soil is bone dry, keeping it completely dry during its summer dormant phase.
Sow seeds shallowly on the soil surface in late summer to match its natural autumn growth cycle.
Keep containers in a frost-free greenhouse or south-facing windowsill to survive wet UK winters.
Watch for mealybugs in the tight leaf crevices and treat immediately with organic insecticidal soap.
items.description: Crassula alpestris, also known as the sand-coated crassula, is a species of flowering plant in the genus Crassula endemic to the Cape Provinces of South Africa. Crassula alpestris subsp. massonii is a variety of the species, also found in South Africa.

items.name: Crassula alstonii
items.growersTips:
Grow this succulent in a gritty, free-draining loam-based compost with fifty percent horticultural grit.
Keep completely dry in winter indoors to prevent rot, watering only when the leaves begin to wrinkle.
Position on a south-facing windowsill or heated greenhouse to maximise essential UK winter sunlight.
Propagate by gently detaching leaf cuttings in late spring and laying them on dry gritty compost.
Watch for mealybugs in the tight leaf crevices and treat immediately with an alcohol-soaked swab.
items.description: Crassula alstonii is a species of succulent plant in the family 'Crassulaceae. It is endemic to the Cape Provinces of South Africa. The species is in USDA hardiness zone 10a-11.

items.name: Crassula aquatica
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in late spring on wet, acidic mud at pond edges, leaving them uncovered to receive light.
Keep the soil constantly saturated or submerged in shallow water, mimicking UK wetland habitats.
Grow in full sun in a garden pond margin to prevent this tiny annual from being shaded out by algae.
Protect from aggressive pond snails and smothering blanket weed which easily overwhelm this species.
Sow alongside slow-growing native oxygenators like Hottonia palustris to avoid being outcompeted.
items.description: Crassula aquatica is a succulent plant known by the common names water pygmyweed, common pygmyweed and just pigmyweed. It is an annual plant of salt marshes, vernal pools, wetlands, and other fresh to brackish water bodies. It is at least partially aquatic, living in areas which are submersed much of the time. It also lives along muddy banks and in tidally-active areas of estuaries.

items.name: Crassula arborescens
items.growersTips:
Bring indoors before October frosts and keep in a bright unheated room until spring to prevent rot.
Water only when the top five centimetres of gritty compost is dry, reducing to monthly in winter.
Repot in spring using a mix of two parts John Innes Number 2 to one part horticultural grit or sand.
Prune leggy stems in late spring to encourage a bushy habit and use the cuttings for propagation.
Check leaf crevices weekly for woolly aphids or mealybugs, treating with organic insecticidal soap.
items.description: Crassula arborescens—the silver jade plant, silver dollar (jade) plant, beestebul, Chinese jade, cookie plant, money plant, or money tree, that is endemic to Western Cape, South Africa, is a species of succulent plant in the family Crassulaceae.

items.name: Crassula atropurpurea
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in early spring at a shallow depth of two millimetres using a heated propagator
Grow in a free-draining gritty compost mix with fifty percent perlite to prevent winter root rot
Water only when the top three centimetres of soil are bone dry then drench and let drain fully
Position in a south-facing unheated greenhouse or porch to maximise crucial UK autumn sunlight
Watch for vine weevil grubs in autumn which chew the roots of these succulents in container pots
items.description: Crassula atropurpurea is a succulent plant, very common and widespread in the southern Karoo regions of South Africa and Namibia.

items.name: Crassula ausensis
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in spring on the surface of gritty, free-draining compost without burying them deep.
Water only when the top two inches of gritty soil are dry, reducing to a trickle in damp autumns.
Grow in pots to easily move them indoors before the first wet frost of a typical UK autumn.
Check the tight leaf rosettes weekly for mealybugs, which thrive in humid British glasshouses.
Mix fifty percent horticultural grit into peat-free compost to prevent winter root rot in the UK.
items.description: Crassula ausensis is a species of succulent in the genus Crassula found in Namibia. Crassula ausensis subsp. giessii and Crassula ausensis subsp. titanopsis are varieties of the species.

items.name: Crassula barbata
items.growersTips:
Grow in a gritty, free-draining loam-based compost with fifty percent horticultural grit or perlite.
Water only when the soil is bone dry, keeping the rosette completely dry to prevent winter rot.
Overwinter indoors on a south-facing windowsill or in a heated greenhouse kept above five degrees.
Sow the dust-like seeds on the soil surface in spring without burying them, keeping them humid.
Watch for mealybugs in the tight leaf hairs and treat immediately with an organic neem oil spray.
items.description: Crassula barbata, also known as the bearded-leaved crassula, is a species of flowering plant in the genus Crassula endemic to the Cape Provinces of South Africa. Crassula barbata subsp. broomii is a subspecies, also found in South Africa.

items.name: Crassula barklyi
items.growersTips:
Grow in a gritty, free-draining cactus compost with fifty percent perlite or horticultural grit.
Water only when the soil is bone dry from spring to autumn, and keep completely dry during winter.
Overwinter indoors on a south-facing windowsill to protect from frost and damp UK winter weather.
Watch closely for mealybugs hiding between the tightly overlapping, scale-like leaves of the stem.
Propagate in late spring by taking stem cuttings and letting them callous for a week before potting.
items.description: Rattlesnake tail is a perennial succulent plant native to Lesotho, Namibia, South Africa, and Eswatini.

items.name: Crassula biplanata
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in spring using a gritty, free-draining compost mix to prevent winter rot.
Water only when the top two inches of soil are dry, reducing to a minimum during damp autumn days.
Position in a south-facing window or greenhouse to maximise scarce UK winter and spring sunlight.
Watch for vine weevil larvae in the compost and treat with nematodes in late summer or autumn.
Sow alongside hardy Sedums in pots to create a dry-tolerant display that copes with UK wet spells.
items.description: Crassula biplanata is a succulent plant native to rocky ledges and mountainous areas in the southern parts of South Africa.

items.name: Crassula brevifolia
items.growersTips:
Grow in a free-draining mix of two parts grit to one part loam to prevent winter root rot in UK damp.
Water only when the top three centimetres of soil are bone dry, reducing to once a month in winter.
Keep on a south-facing windowsill or in a heated greenhouse to meet its high winter light needs.
Propagate in late spring by taking stem cuttings and letting them callus for three days before potting.
Inspect leaf joints weekly for mealybugs, treating infestations immediately with rubbing alcohol.
items.description: Crassula brevifolia is a succulent plant in the family Crassulaceae. It is native to the arid western edge of South Africa as well as southern Namibia.

items.name: Crassula capitella
items.growersTips:
Bring indoors before first frost as it cannot survive UK winters below five degrees Celsius.
Water only when the gritty compost is bone dry, reducing to once a month during winter.
Grow in a mix of two parts peat-free compost to one part horticultural grit for sharp drainage.
Place on a south-facing windowsill to trigger the vibrant red foliage of the Campfire cultivar.
Take stem cuttings in late spring by letting them callus for three days before potting in grit.
items.description: Crassula capitella, is a perennial succulent plant native to southern Africa.

items.name: Crassula clavata
items.growersTips:
Bring indoors before first autumn frost as this tender succulent cannot survive wet UK winters.
Water only when soil is bone dry, reducing to once a month from November to March to prevent rot.
Plant in a mix of fifty percent grit and fifty percent peat-free compost to ensure rapid drainage.
Position on a south-facing windowsill to maximize light and bring out the deep red leaf coloration.
Watch for mealybugs in leaf joints and treat immediately with an organic insecticidal soap spray.
items.description: Crassula clavata, is a species of succulent plant in the genus Crassula endemic to the Cape Provinces of South Africa.

items.name: Crassula closiana
items.growersTips:
Grow in a gritty, free-draining loam-based compost with fifty percent horticultural grit or perlite.
Water only when the soil is bone dry from spring to autumn, and keep completely dry during winter.
Overwinter indoors on a south-facing windowsill to protect from frost and damp UK winter rot.
Propagate in late spring by taking stem cuttings, letting them callus for three days before potting.
Watch for mealybugs in leaf axils and treat immediately with an organic insecticidal soap spray.
items.description: Crassula closiana is a herb in the family Crassulaceae that is native to Mexico, Peru, Bolivia, Chile and Western Australia.

items.name: Crassula colligata
items.growersTips:
Grow in gritty, free-draining soil with fifty percent perlite or horticultural sand to prevent rot.
Keep outdoors in summer but move indoors before the first autumn frost to protect from UK damp cold.
Water only when the soil is bone dry, reducing to once a month or less during dark winter months.
Propagate in spring by taking stem cuttings, letting them callus for three days before potting up.
Watch for mealybugs in leaf joints and treat immediately with an organic insecticidal soap spray.
items.description: Crassula colligata is a herb in the family Crassulaceae that is native to southern Australia and New Zealand.

items.name: Crassula colorata
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in spring using a free-draining mix of half grit and half peat-free compost.
Water only when the top two inches of gritty soil are dry, keeping it barely damp during winter.
Grow in pots to easily move indoors to a sunny windowsill before the first autumn frost arrives.
Position in a south-facing conservatory or greenhouse to maximise intense light and prevent leggy growth.
Watch for mealybugs in leaf crevices and treat immediately with an organic insecticidal soap spray.
items.description: Crassula colorata, the dense pigmyweed or dense stonecrop, is an annual plant in the family Crassulaceae. The species is endemic to Australia, occurring in Western Australia, South Australia, New South Wales and Victoria.

items.name: Crassula columella
items.growersTips:
Grow in a gritty loam-free compost with fifty percent perlite or horticultural sand for drainage.
Water only when the soil is completely dry from spring to autumn, keeping it dry throughout winter.
Keep on a south-facing windowsill indoors as the damp UK winter cold will rot this tender succulent.
Propagate in late spring by taking stem cuttings and letting them callus for three days before potting.
Inspect the tight column of velvety leaves regularly for mealybugs hiding in the dense crevices.
items.description: Crassula columella is a species of succulent plant in the family Crassulaceae. It is native to the west coast of South Africa and Namibia. It grows slowly in spring and autumn, and is dormant in summer.

items.name: Crassula columnaris
items.growersTips:
Grow in a gritty, free-draining cactus compost with fifty percent perlite or horticultural grit.
Water only when the soil is bone dry from spring to autumn, keeping it completely dry in winter.
Keep indoors on a south-facing windowsill or in a heated greenhouse to protect from UK winter frost.
Do not prune this monocarpic succulent, as it dies naturally after its single, terminal summer bloom.
Sow seeds shallowly in spring on the soil surface under glass, maintaining a temperature of 18C.
items.description: Crassula columnaris is a succulent plant native to South Africa and Namibia.

items.name: Crassula connata
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in spring on the surface of gritty, free-draining soil without burying them to aid light.
Water sparingly only when the top two inches of soil are dry to prevent root rot in damp UK weather.
Grow in shallow pots outdoors in full sun to mimic their natural dry, gravelly habitat conditions.
Position near Sedum album in rock gardens to create a compatible, drought-tolerant succulent display.
Protect from heavy autumn rains by moving pots under a cold frame or greenhouse to prevent decay.
items.description: Crassula connata is a succulent plant in the family Crassulaceae. It is known by the common names sand pygmyweed and pygmy stonecrop. It is a very small plant which grows in patches on the ground, especially in rocky areas. It is also sometimes associated with vernal pool plant communities. The stems are a few centimeters in length and are covered with tiny fleshy pointed leaves. Each leaf is only millimeters long. The plant is green when new and it matures to shades of pink and red. It is found in western North America and in parts of Central and South America.

items.name: Crassula corallina
items.growersTips:
Grow in a gritty, free-draining loam-based compost with fifty percent horticultural sand or grit.
Water only when the soil is bone dry, keeping the foliage completely dry to prevent winter rot.
Sow seeds shallowly in early spring under glass with bottom heat to combat cool UK spring soil.
Position in a south-facing cold frame or unheated greenhouse to maximise crucial UK sunlight hours.
Watch closely for mealybugs in the tight leaf crevices, treating immediately with rubbing alcohol.
items.description: Crassula corallina is a species of succulent plant in the genus Crassula from Central South Africa and Southeastern Namibia. It grows as mats in dry habitats and is typically short-lived.

items.name: Crassula cotyledonis
items.growersTips:
Bring potted plants indoors to a bright windowsill before the first autumn frost to prevent rot.
Sow seeds in spring on the surface of free-draining gritty compost without burying them deep.
Water only when the top two inches of soil are dry, reducing to once a month in damp winter.
Watch for mealybugs in leaf joints and dab them with a cotton bud dipped in rubbing alcohol.
Mix equal parts peat-free compost and horticultural grit to ensure the rapid drainage they need.
items.description: Crassula cotyledonis is a succulent plant endemic to the arid Namaqualand and Karoo regions of South Africa.

items.name: Crassula cultrata
items.growersTips:
Bring indoors before October frosts as this succulent cannot survive wet UK winter freezes.
Sow seeds shallowly in spring on a gritty, free-draining compost mix without burying them deeply.
Water only when the top two inches of soil dry out completely to prevent root rot in damp climates.
Grow in a south-facing conservatory or windowsill to maximise the limited UK summer sunlight.
Pruning stem tips in early summer encourages a bushier habit and prevents leggy growth.
items.description: Crassula cultrata is a succulent plant native to the southern parts of South Africa.

items.name: Crassula deceptor
items.growersTips:
Grow in a gritty mix of seventy percent pumice and thirty percent loam to prevent winter root rot.
Water only from April to September when the soil is dry and keep completely bone dry all winter.
Position on a south-facing windowsill or in a heated greenhouse to maximise scarce UK winter sun.
