Check the tight leaf crevices weekly for mealybugs using a cotton bud dipped in rubbing alcohol.
Propagate in late spring by gently detaching side offsets and letting them calloused before potting.
items.description: Crassula deceptor is a succulent plant native to South Africa and Namibia. This species occurs from southern Namibia, to as far south as the town of Vanrhynsdorp in South Africa.

items.name: Crassula decumbens
items.growersTips:
Grow in free-draining gritty loam with 50% grit or perlite to prevent winter root rot in UK wet.
Water only when the soil is bone dry from spring to autumn, and keep almost dry throughout winter.
Overwinter indoors on a south-facing windowsill or in a heated greenhouse to protect from UK frost.
Propagate in late spring by pressing stem cuttings lightly into damp, sandy compost to root.
Watch for mealybugs in leaf axils during humid UK summers and treat with organic insecticidal soap.
items.description: Crassula decumbens, commonly known as rufous stonecrop, cape crassula or spreading crassula, is a herb in the family Crassulaceae that is native to southern parts of Australia, South Africa, and Chile. There are generally two accepted varieties: Crassula decumbens var. decumbens and C. decumbens var. brachyphylla.

items.name: Crassula dichotoma
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly on free-draining gritty compost in spring, barely covering them with fine sand.
Water sparingly from below only when the soil dries completely to prevent stem rot in damp UK air.
Grow in pots on a south-facing windowsill or greenhouse to ensure maximum light and warmth in summer.
Watch for aphids and mealybugs in the leaf joints, treating them with a cotton swab dipped in alcohol.
Sow fresh seeds annually in March as this species is a true annual and will die after flowering.
items.description: Crassula dichotoma, known as the gold stonecrop, is a species of succulent plant in the genus Crassula. It is endemic to the Fynbos region from Namaqualand to Agulhas in South Africa.

items.name: Crassula elegans
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in spring on gritty compost and cover with a very fine layer of vermiculite.
Water only when the top two inches of soil are dry to prevent root rot in damp UK autumns.
Grow in a terracotta pot to ensure rapid drainage and move indoors before the first winter frosts.
Mix equal parts peat-free compost and horticultural grit to recreate its native free-draining soil.
Inspect stem bases regularly for mealybugs which thrive in cool British greenhouse conditions.
items.description: Crassula elegans, the elegant crassula, is a flowering plant species in the genus Crassula.

items.name: Crassula ericoides
items.growersTips:
Bring indoors to a frost-free greenhouse or windowsill from October to April to survive UK winters.
Grow in a mix of two parts grit to one part peat-free compost to ensure rapid drainage in wet weather.
Water only when the soil is bone dry in summer, and keep completely dry from November to March.
Prune leggy stems by one third in late spring after flowering to maintain a compact, bushy shrub habit.
Check the dense, scale-like foliage weekly for mealybugs, which hide easily in the tight leaf joints.
items.description: Crassula ericoides is a species of succulent plant in the genus Crassula native to South Africa. Growing in the fynbos ecosystem of South Africa, C. ericoides somewhat resembles a heather, growing into an upright shrub with bare lower stems and yellow flowers at the tips.

items.name: Crassula exserta
items.growersTips:
Grow this tiny annual in a gritty, free-draining soil mix of equal parts John Innes No 1 and grit.
Sow seeds in spring by pressing them lightly onto the soil surface without covering them with compost.
Water sparingly from below during the spring growing season, keeping the soil dry throughout winter.
Bring pots indoors to a south-facing windowsill by October to protect them from wet UK winter frosts.
Position containers alongside hardy Sedums or Sempervivums to create a compatible low-water display.
items.description: Crassula exserta is a herb in the family Crassulaceae that is native to Western Australia.

items.name: Crassula glomerata
items.growersTips:
Grow this tiny annual in a gritty, free-draining soil mix of equal parts loam and horticultural grit.
Sow seeds shallowly on the soil surface in spring, keeping them indoors at fifteen degrees Celsius.
Water only when the top two centimetres of soil are dry, reducing to almost nothing in damp autumns.
Grow in pots to easily move them under glass or a porch to protect from persistent UK winter wet.
Watch for vine weevil grubs in container compost and pick off aphids by hand during humid summers.
items.description: Crassula glomerata, the orange stonecrop, is a herb in the family Crassulaceae.

items.name: Crassula helmsii
items.growersTips:
Keep this highly invasive weed strictly in sealed garden ponds and never let it escape to waterways.
Grow it in a submerged container to restrict its rapid spread and prevent it choking other plants.
Rake out excess growth in autumn and compost it securely in a closed bin to avoid wild spread.
Check your pond weekly for tiny pink-white flowers in summer to monitor its rapid growth rate.
Do not introduce this plant to any natural UK water body as it is legally banned from the wild.
items.description: Crassula helmsii, known as swamp stonecrop or New Zealand pigmyweed, is an aquatic or semiterrestrial species of succulent plant in the family Crassulaceae. Originally found in Australia and New Zealand, it has been introduced around the world. In the United Kingdom, this plant is one of five introduced invasive aquatic plants that were banned from sale from April 2014, the first ban of its kind in the country. It is on the Global Biodiversity Information Facility's Global Register of Introduced and Invasive Species of eleven countries.

items.name: Crassula lactea
items.growersTips:
Bring indoors before October frosts or grow year-round in a bright conservatory to prevent freeze damage.
Water only when the top three centimetres of gritty, peat-free compost is completely dry to the touch.
Prune leggy stems in late spring after winter flowering to encourage a bushier, more compact habit.
Watch for mealybugs in leaf axils during winter when indoor heating makes air dry and stagnant.
Mix fifty percent horticultural grit into standard compost to ensure the rapid drainage it requires.
items.description: Crassula lactea is a perennial flowering plant native to southern Africa. It blooms in the winter with white flowers.

items.name: Crassula marnieriana
items.growersTips:
Bring indoors before October frosts as this succulent cannot survive wet UK winters outdoors.
Water only when the gritty compost is bone dry, reducing to once a month from November to March.
Propagate in spring by snipping stems, drying for two days, then inserting 2cm deep in sharp sand.
Grow in a south-facing window or greenhouse to prevent the trailing stems from stretching out.
Watch for mealybugs in the tight leaf crevices, treating immediately with an alcohol-soaked swab.
items.description: Crassula marnierana, common name Jade Necklace or Chinese Pagoda, is a species of succulent flowering plant in the family Crassulaceae.

items.name: Crassula moschata
items.growersTips:
Plant in gritty free-draining soil or rockeries to survive wet UK winters and prevent root rot.
Position in full coastal sun or bright light to maintain its compact creeping mat-forming habit.
Water sparingly in summer only when soil is dry and keep almost completely dry during winter.
Propagate easily in spring by snipping stem cuttings and inserting them directly into sandy grit.
Protect from severe frosts below minus five Celsius using horticultural fleece or move containers.
items.description: Crassula moschata, commonly known as the Shore Stonecrop, Musky Stonecrop, or Musky Crassula, is a hairless, mat-forming, succulent, perennial herb. It is widespread on the subantarctic and cool temperate shores of the Southern Ocean.

items.name: Crassula multicava
items.growersTips:
Bring indoors or move to a frost-free greenhouse from October to April to survive UK winter wet.
Water only when the top three centimetres of gritty, free-draining soil mix has dried out completely.
Propagate easily by pinning the small plantlets that form on spent flower stems directly into compost.
Grow in partial shade rather than full sun to prevent the succulent green leaves from turning red.
Watch for vine weevil grubs in pots during autumn and drench with parasitic nematodes if found.
items.description: Crassula multicava is a perennial succulent plant from the family Crassulaceae. It is also known under various English common names including the fairy crassula, pitted crassula and London pride. In Zulu, it is known as umadinsane, one of several plants known by this name.

items.name: Crassula muscosa
items.growersTips:
Bring indoors by late September to protect this frost-tender succulent from cold UK winter wet.
Water only when the top two inches of gritty compost are bone dry, reducing to monthly in winter.
Grow in a mix of two parts peat-free compost to one part horticultural grit for rapid drainage.
Propagate in spring by snipping three-inch stem cuttings and inserting them directly into dry grit.
Watch for mealybugs in the dense, scale-like foliage during dry summer spells under glass.
items.description: Crassula muscosa, synonyms Crassula lycopodioides and Crassula pseudolycopodioides, is a succulent plant native to South Africa and Namibia, belonging to the family Crassulaceae and to the genus Crassula. It is a houseplant grown worldwide and commonly known as rattail crassula, watch chain, lizard's tail, zipper plant and princess pines.

items.name: Crassula namaquensis
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in spring using a free-draining loam and grit mix to prevent winter wet rot.
Water only when the soil is completely dry, keeping it entirely water-free during damp winter days.
Grow in pots to easily move indoors to a frost-free greenhouse or windowsill before autumn frosts.
Position in the brightest south-facing spot possible to maintain its compact shape and leaf colour.
Watch for mealybugs in leaf joints and treat immediately with an organic insecticidal soap spray.
items.description: Crassula namaquensis is a species of succulent plant in the genus Crassula native to South Africa. Easily confused with some forms of Crassula tecta and Crassula sericea, this species has rounded to elongated leaves that are usually blue, covered in fine hairs, and form clumps.

items.name: Crassula nudicaulis
items.growersTips:
Bring indoors before the first autumn frost as this succulent cannot survive wet UK winters outside.
Water only when the potting mix is bone dry, reducing to once a month during dull winter months.
Plant in a gritty, free-draining mix of two parts horticultural sand to one part peat-free compost.
Grow on a south-facing windowsill or in a heated greenhouse to maximise essential daily sunlight.
Propagate in spring by taking leaf cuttings and letting them callus for three days before potting.
items.description: Crassula nudicaulis is a succulent plant native to South Africa, and Lesotho.

items.name: Crassula ovata
items.growersTips:
Bring indoors before the first autumn frost as they cannot survive UK winter temperatures below 5C.
Water only when the compost is bone dry, then drench fully and let it drain completely.
Repot in a fifty-fifty mix of peat-free multi-purpose compost and horticultural grit for drainage.
Prune in spring by cutting back to a leaf joint to encourage a bushy, tree-like structure.
Place on a south-facing windowsill to prevent leggy growth and encourage red-edged leaves.
items.description: Crassula ovata, commonly known as jade plant, lucky plant, money plant or money tree, is a succulent plant with small pink or white flowers that is native to the KwaZulu-Natal and Eastern Cape provinces of South Africa, and Mozambique; it is common as a houseplant worldwide. Much of its popularity stems from the low levels of care needed; the jade plant requires little water and can survive in most indoor conditions. It is sometimes referred to as the money tree; however, Pachira aquatica also has this nickname.

items.name: Crassula peduncularis
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in spring on the surface of free-draining gritty compost without burying them.
Water only when the top two centimetres of soil are dry, keeping it barely damp during winter.
Grow in shallow terracotta pots to prevent waterlogging during wet UK autumns and winters.
Position in full sun on a south-facing windowsill or in an unheated greenhouse to prevent legginess.
Watch for vine weevil grubs in the compost and pick off any visible mealybugs with a cotton bud.
items.description: Crassula peduncularis, commonly known as purple stonecrop, is a herb in the family Crassulaceae. It is native to southern South America, Australia and New Zealand. It is an introduced species in Portugal, Germany and Japan.

items.name: Crassula pellucida
items.growersTips:
Bring indoors before the first autumn frost as this succulent cannot survive wet UK winter freezes.
Grow in a mix of two parts peat-free compost to one part horticultural grit for essential drainage.
Water only when the soil dries out completely, reducing to once a month during dark winter months.
Take stem cuttings in late spring by letting them callus for two days before potting in sandy soil.
Position in a south-facing window or greenhouse to maintain the vibrant purple leaf margins.
items.description: Crassula pellucida is a creeping, succulent ground-cover, or low-growing, spreading succulent shrub. It is native to eastern and southern Africa, ranging from Kenya and Angola to South Africa.

items.name: Crassula perfoliata
items.growersTips:
Bring indoors by October to protect this tender South African succulent from wet UK winter frosts.
Grow in a mix of two parts grit to one part peat-free compost to ensure rapid drainage in damp air.
Water only when the soil is bone dry, reducing to once a month from November through to March.
Position on a south-facing windowsill or in a heated greenhouse to maximize scarce UK winter sun.
Watch for mealybugs in the leaf joints and treat immediately with an organic insecticidal soap.
items.description: Crassula perfoliata is the type species of the genus Crassula, in the succulent/flowering plant family Crassulaceae, where it is placed in the subfamily Crassuloideae. Formally described by Linnaeus in 1753 as one of 10 species of Crassula, the plant is endemic to Southern Africa, where it may be found in Eswatini, Mozambique, South Africa and Zimbabwe.

items.name: Crassula perforata
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender South African succulent in pots of 50% grit and 50% peat-free compost to ensure drainage
Bring pots indoors to a south-facing windowsill by October to protect from wet UK winter frosts
Water only when the soil is dry to the touch in summer, and keep almost completely dry in winter
Take stem cuttings in late spring by letting the cut ends dry for three days before potting up
Watch for mealybugs in the leaf joints and dab them with a cotton bud dipped in rubbing alcohol
items.description: Crassula perforata is a succulent plant native to the Cape Provinces and KwaZulu-Natal in South Africa.

items.name: Crassula picturata
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly on the surface of free-draining gritty compost in spring under a heated propagator
Water only when the top two inches of gritty soil are dry to prevent root rot in damp UK winters
Move pots indoors to a south-facing windowsill by October to protect this tender succulent from frost
Snip off faded summer flower stalks at the base in autumn to keep the compact rosette foliage tidy
Mix fifty percent horticultural grit into standard peat-free compost to ensure rapid winter drainage
items.description: Crassula picturata is a species of plant in the family Crassulaceae, native to Cape Province in South Africa. It is a stemless plant with triangular, dark green leaves measuring approximately 10–12 cm long by 1 cm wide.

items.name: Crassula pubescens
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds on the soil surface in spring without burying them as they need light to germinate.
Water only when the top two inches of compost are dry to prevent root rot in damp UK weather.
Grow in a gritty mix of two parts peat-free compost to one part horticultural sand for drainage.
Bring pots indoors to a sunny windowsill by October to protect this tender annual from UK frosts.
Pinch out the growing tips in late spring to encourage a bushier habit and more star-shaped flowers.
items.description: Crassula pubescens is a succulent plant, common and widespread in the southern Karoo regions of South Africa.

items.name: Crassula rubricaulis
items.growersTips:
Overwinter indoors in a frost-free greenhouse or windowsill as this succulent cannot survive UK frost
Plant in a gritty cactus compost mix with fifty percent perlite to prevent root rot in wet autumns
Water only when the soil is bone dry then soak thoroughly and let drain completely to mimic drought
Take stem cuttings in June to propagate new plants easily before the cold autumn damp sets in
Position in full south-facing sun to bring out the vibrant red coloration on the leaf margins
items.description: Crassula rubricaulis is a succulent plant native to the coastal mountains of the Eastern Cape and Western Cape of South Africa.

items.name: Crassula rupestris
items.growersTips:
Grow in a gritty loam-based compost with fifty percent perlite or horticultural sand for drainage.
Water only when the soil is bone dry, reducing to once a month during the cold UK winter months.
Keep on a south-facing windowsill indoors or move to a sunny patio only when night temperatures exceed ten degrees.
Prune leggy stems in spring just above a leaf node to encourage bushier growth and propagate cuttings.
Check leaf crevices regularly for mealybugs, treating infestations with an organic neem oil spray.
items.description: Crassula rupestris, called buttons on a string, is a species of Crassula native to Namibia and to the Cape Provinces of South Africa. It has gained the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit. It is also called bead vine, necklace vine, and rosary vine.

items.name: Crassula sarcocaulis
items.growersTips:
Plant in sharply draining gritty soil or a rockery to prevent winter root rot in wet UK climates.
Position in full south-facing sun against a warm house wall to mimic its native Drakensberg habitat.
Water only when the soil is bone dry from spring to autumn, then withhold water entirely in winter.
Prune lightly in late spring after frosts pass to shape the bonsai-like stems and remove dieback.
Provide fleece protection or move potted specimens under a cold glasshouse if temperatures drop below -5C.
items.description: Crassula sarcocaulis is a small shrubby succulent plant known by the common name bonsai crassula, due to its bonsai-like appearance. It is a perennial plant native to the southern and southeastern Africa, ranging from Malawi and Mozambique through Zimbabwe, Swaziland, Lesotho, and South Africa. It grows on mountain slopes in rocky terrain.

items.name: Crassula sarmentosa
items.growersTips:
Bring indoors before first autumn frost as it cannot survive UK winters below freezing temperatures.
Grow in a gritty loam-based potting compost with fifty percent perlite or horticultural sand.
Water thoroughly only when the soil dries out completely, then keep dry throughout winter.
Take stem cuttings in late spring to easily propagate new plants and maintain a compact habit.
Place on a south-facing windowsill or in a greenhouse to get the best red-edged leaf variegation.
items.description: Crassula sarmentosa, commonly known as trailing jade plant and showy trailing jade, is a perennial succulent plant in the family Crassulaceae. It is native to southern Africa.

items.name: Crassula setulosa
items.growersTips:
Grow in gritty loam-based compost with fifty percent horticultural grit to prevent winter wet rot.
Water only when the soil is bone dry, reducing to once a month from October to March in UK wet cold.
Sow seeds on the soil surface in spring without burying them as they require light to germinate.
Protect from slugs and snails in damp UK springs using organic wool pellets or beer traps.
Position in a south-facing unheated greenhouse or cold frame to shield from persistent autumn rain.
items.description: Crassula setulosa is a species of stonecrop in the family Crassulaceae. It is found mostly in eastern South Africa and Lesotho.

items.name: Crassula sieberiana
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in spring on the surface of free-draining gritty compost without covering them with soil
Grow in unheated greenhouses or alpine sinks to protect the shallow roots from winter wet rot
Water only when the top two inches of soil are dry and stop watering completely during winter dormancy
Position in full south-facing sun to prevent the delicate stems from stretching and losing color
Plant alongside sedums in shallow gravel scree beds to ensure rapid drainage during heavy UK rains
items.description: Crassula sieberiana, the Australian stonecrop, is a succulent plant found in a variety of habitats in Australia, New Zealand and Lord Howe Island. It has been introduced to Hawaii. Usually seen in rock crevices. It may be found in desert areas such as Sturt National Park, or high rainfall areas near the coast including rainforest. Sub species are not recognized on New South Wales Plantnet, however some authors recognize several subspecies. It is listed as endangered in South Australia.

items.name: Crassula spathulata
items.growersTips:
Bring indoors before the first autumn frost as this tender South African succulent cannot survive UK winters.
Grow in a gritty loam-based potting mix with fifty percent perlite to prevent root rot in damp UK air.
Water only when the soil is bone dry, reducing to once a month during the dark, cold winter months.
Take stem cuttings in late spring to easily propagate new plants before the active summer growth.
Place on a south-facing windowsill to maximize light levels during the overcast British winter.
items.description: Crassula spathulata is a creeping, succulent ground-cover, indigenous to the Eastern Cape Province of South Africa, where it is found in leaf-litter on rocky ridges, often around the edges of forests.

items.name: Crassula subaphylla
items.growersTips:
Grow in a free-draining gritty loam with fifty percent horticultural sand to prevent winter root rot
Water only when the top three centimetres of soil are bone dry and keep completely dry in winter
Position in a south-facing unheated greenhouse or cold frame to maximise scarce UK winter sunlight
Protect from frost by moving pots indoors to a cool windowsill when temperatures drop below five C
Propagate from stem cuttings in late spring by letting them callus for three days before potting up
items.description: Crassula subaphylla is a succulent plant belonging to the family Crassulaceae. It is widespread in the Karoo regions of South Africa and Namibia.

items.name: Crassula tecta
items.growersTips:
Grow in a gritty, free-draining cactus compost with fifty percent perlite or horticultural grit.
Water only when the soil is completely dry, keeping it bone dry throughout the damp UK winter.
Position on a south-facing windowsill to maximise light and prevent the compact rosettes stretching.
Overwinter indoors or in a heated greenhouse as this succulent cannot survive wet UK frosts.
Watch for mealybugs in the tight leaf crevices, treating infestations with an alcohol-soaked swab.
items.description: Crassula tecta is a species of succulent plant in the genus Crassula native to South Africa. Easily confused with Crassula namaquensis, this species has a compact growth habit forming clusters of round, blue-white leaves. Kept in cultivation since the 18th century, Crassula tecta is known for the beautiful patterning on its leaves and white flowers.

items.name: Crassula tetragona
items.growersTips:
Bring indoors before October frosts or grow year-round in a bright south-facing UK windowsill.
Water only when the gritty compost is dry to the touch, reducing to once a month during winter.
Mix two parts horticultural grit with one part peat-free compost to ensure rapid winter drainage.
Prune leggy stems in spring just above a leaf node to encourage a bushy, bonsai-like shrub habit.
Propagate easily in summer by drying stem cuttings for three days before inserting into dry grit.
items.description: Crassula tetragona is a succulent plant native to Southern Africa. It is widely distributed from the Orange River boundary of Namaqualand to beyond the Kei River in the Eastern Cape. "Tetragona" comes from the phyllotaxy of the leaves. It is popularly named the "miniature pine tree" among ornamental plant enthusiasts, for its popular use as a "pine tree" in Bonsai.

items.name: Crassula tillaea
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn on the soil surface of sharply draining gravelly paths to mimic UK wild habitats.
Water only during extreme summer droughts to prevent this damp-sensitive annual from rotting away.
Weed hand-pull competitors in spring to prevent vigorous garden plants from smothering this tiny succulent.
Plant alongside slow-growing stonecrops in gritty scree beds to prevent soil erosion on dry banks.
Allow the plant to turn red in full summer sun and self-seed naturally before it dies back in autumn.
items.description: Crassula tillaea is a succulent plant known by its common names mossy stonecrop and moss pygmyweed. It is a small fleshy plant growing only a few centimeters in height. It is green when new and gradually turns orange and then deep red when mature. It has tiny triangular pointed leaves only a few millimeters long. A tiny flower or pair of flowers grows between each oppositely-arranged pair of leaves; the flowers are about two millimeters in length and width. The fruit is a minute follicle containing one or two seeds. This plant is native to Eurasia, particularly the Mediterranean Basin, but is

items.name: Crassula umbella
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds on the soil surface in autumn as they need winter light and cool UK temperatures to sprout.
Water only from below when the soil dries completely to prevent the delicate cup-shaped leaves from rotting.
Grow in a gritty, free-draining loam-based compost with fifty percent perlite or horticultural grit.
Keep in a frost-free greenhouse or bright UK windowsill as this winter-grower damages below five degrees.
Watch for vine weevil grubs in winter which target the shallow root system of this delicate succulent.
items.description: Crassula umbella is a succulent plant species in the genus Crassula. It is endemic to the Cape Provinces of South Africa.

items.name: Crassula vaillantii
items.growersTips:
Grow in gritty, free-draining soil with 50 percent horticultural grit to survive wet UK winters.
Water only when the top two inches of soil are dry, reducing to once a month in damp UK winters.
Sow seeds in spring by pressing them lightly onto the soil surface without burying them.
Grow in shallow pots that can be moved indoors to a frost-free greenhouse or windowsill by October.
Position in full south-facing sun to bring out the vibrant red stress coloration on the foliage.
items.description: Crassula vaillantii is a species of herb in the family Crassulaceae. They are succulents plants.

items.name: Crataegus fluviatilis
items.growersTips:
Plant in autumn in well-drained clay loam at the same depth as the nursery pot to avoid stem rot.
Water deeply once a week during the first dry UK summer to establish a deep, resilient root system.
Prune in late winter to remove crossing branches and maintain a compact, open-centred shrub shape.
Monitor in spring for hawthorn leaf blight and clear fallen leaves to prevent fungal spore survival.
Underplant with Geranium rozanne to suppress weeds and thrive in the light shade of the canopy.
items.description: Crataegus fluviatilis is a species of hawthorn similar to C. flabellata and to C. macrosperma. The name C. apiomorpha has been applied to a form of the species that is most similar to C. macrosperma.

items.name: Crocus abantensis
items.growersTips:
Plant these Turkish native bulbs in autumn at a depth of eight to ten centimetres in gritty soil.
Grow them in raised beds or rock gardens to ensure the sharp winter drainage they need in UK wet.
Position in full sun where they can bake dry during their dormant summer phase without watering.
Protect the early spring blooms from slugs and mice which frequently target this specific species.
Pair with dwarf conifers or early sedums to support the weak stems of this delicate blue flower.
items.description: Crocus abantensis is a species of flowering plant in the genus Crocus of the family Iridaceae. It is a cormous perennial native to northwestern Turkey.

items.name: Crocus adanensis
items.growersTips:
Plant corms in autumn at a depth of 8cm to 10cm in gritty, sharply draining soil to prevent winter rot.
Position in full sun or light dappled shade under deciduous shrubs to mimic their native woodland edge.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic wool pellets or beer traps.
Allow the foliage to die back naturally for six weeks after flowering before mowing or tidying up.
Grow in raised beds or alpine troughs to ensure the dry summer dormancy this Turkish native requires.
items.description: Crocus adanensis is a species of flowering plant in the genus Crocus of the family Iridaceae. It is a cormous perennial native to southern Turkey.

items.name: Crocus alatavicus
items.growersTips:
Plant in autumn at a depth of 8cm to 10cm in gritty, sharply draining soil to prevent winter rot.
Grow in a raised bed or alpine house to protect the early spring blooms from heavy UK winter rain.
Water sparingly during summer dormancy as this Central Asian native requires a dry summer baking.
Guard emerging shoots in January against slugs and mice which target the early succulent growth.
Position in full south-facing sun to ensure the flowers open fully during weak UK spring light.
items.description: Crocus alatavicus is a species of flowering plant in the genus Crocus of the family Iridaceae. It is a cormous perennial native to Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Uzbekistan, and Xinjiang.

items.name: Crocus aleppicus
items.growersTips:
Plant this autumn-flowering bulb in July at a depth of 8cm to ensure roots establish before winter.
Grow in a gritty, free-draining loam to prevent winter rot during wet UK winters under cold glass.
Provide a dry summer dormancy period from June to August by withholding all water from the pots.
Protect the delicate white autumn blooms from heavy rain by growing them in an unheated greenhouse.
Guard emerging autumn shoots from slugs and snails using organic pellets or copper barriers.
items.description: Crocus aleppicus is a species of flowering plant in the genus Crocus of the family Iridaceae, that is found from West Syria to the Palestine region.

items.name: Crocus ancyrensis
items.growersTips:
Plant these bulbs in September or October at a depth of 8cm to 10cm to protect them from UK frosts.
Grow them in gritty, free-draining soil to prevent winter rot during wet UK autumn and winter months.
Position in full sun to ensure the golden flowers open fully during chilly February and March days.
Protect emerging shoots from slugs and mice in early spring using physical barriers or grit collars.
Leave the foliage to die back naturally for six weeks after flowering to feed the bulb for next year.
items.description: Crocus ancyrensis, sometimes known as the Ankara crocus, is a species of flowering plant in the family Iridaceae. It is endemic to North and Central Turkey. It was named ancyrensis as it was first discovered in Ankara.

items.name: Crocus angustifolius
items.growersTips:
Plant these bulbs in September or October at a depth of eight to ten centimetres in gritty soil.
Grow them in full sun and sharply draining soil to mimic their native dry Ukrainian hillsides.
Avoid watering during their summer dormant phase to prevent the corms from rotting in wet UK soil.
Let the foliage die back naturally until June before clearing it to feed next year's gold flowers.
Protect the early spring blooms from mice and squirrels using wire mesh laid just beneath the soil.
items.description: Crocus angustifolius, the cloth-of-gold crocus, is a species of flowering plant in the genus Crocus of the family Iridaceae, native to southern Ukraine and Armenia. It is a cormous perennial growing to 5 cm (2.0 in) tall and wide. The narrow grass-like leaves with silver central stripe appear in late winter or early spring. They are followed by bright yellow fragrant flowers with maroon blotches on the outer petals.

items.name: Crocus autranii
items.growersTips:
Plant corms 8 to 10cm deep in late summer using gritty, free-draining soil to prevent winter rot.
Grow in a cold frame or alpine house to protect the delicate autumn blooms from heavy UK rain.
Water moderately during active autumn growth but keep the corms almost dry during summer dormancy.
Top-dress pots with sharp grit to keep the collar dry and deter slugs from eating emerging shoots.
Repot every two years in July using a mix of equal parts loam, leafmould, and coarse grit.
items.description: Crocus autranii is a species of flowering plant in the genus Crocus of the family Iridaceae. It is a cormous perennial native to the western Transcaucasus (Abkhazia).

items.name: Crocus banaticus
items.growersTips:
Plant corms in late summer at a depth of 8 to 10cm in humus-rich soil that mimics woodland conditions.
Grow in partial shade rather than full sun to prevent the delicate autumn petals from bleaching.
Keep the soil consistently moist during summer dormancy as this species dislikes baking dry.
Protect the autumn-emerging flowers from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.
Propagate by lifting and dividing established clumps in July before the new autumn roots activate.
items.description: Crocus banaticus, is a species of flowering plant in the family Iridaceae. It is native to the Balkans, particularly in Serbia, Romania and south western Ukraine. It creates its own subgenus in the Crocus subfamily known as Crociris. It is a cormous perennial growing to 10 cm (4 in).

items.name: Crocus baytopiorum
items.growersTips:
Plant these bulbs in autumn at a depth of 8 to 10cm in gritty, sharply draining soil to prevent rot.
Grow them in a cold greenhouse or alpine house to protect the delicate pale blue flowers from UK rain.
Water moderately during their winter-to-spring growing phase but keep them dry during summer dormancy.
Apply a top layer of fine horticultural grit around the shoots to deter slugs and snails in spring.
Feed with a low-nitrogen, high-potash liquid fertiliser just as the foliage begins to die back.
items.description: Crocus baytopiorum is a species of flowering plant in the genus Crocus of the family Iridaceae. It is a cormous perennial native to Turkey.

items.name: Crocus biflorus
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs 8cm deep in autumn in gritty, free-draining soil to prevent winter rot in wet UK clay.
Siting them in a south-facing rockery or gravel garden ensures the maximum winter sun they require.
Protect emerging spring buds from slugs and birds using fine twigs or physical barriers in February.

Plant bulbs 10 to 15cm deep in late summer to protect them from squirrels and summer soil heat.
Grow in gritty, free-draining soil in full sun to prevent the autumn-flowering bulbs from rotting.
Plant under deciduous shrubs or active summer perennials to absorb excess moisture during dormancy.
Avoid mowing lawns or cutting back companion grass until the foliage dies down fully in late spring.
Watch for mice and voles in autumn, protecting newly planted areas with buried wire mesh.

items.name: Early crocus
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs in September or October at a depth of 8cm to 10cm to protect them from winter frosts.
Plant in gritty, free-draining soil to prevent the bulbs from rotting during wet UK winters.
Protect newly planted bulbs from squirrels by laying wire mesh just under the soil surface.
Mow lawns only after the foliage has naturally died back in late spring to ensure blooms next year.
Plant under deciduous trees or shrubs to ensure they get full sun before the canopy leaves emerge.
items.description: Crocus tommasinianus, the woodland crocus, early crocus, or Tommasini's crocus, is a species of flowering plant in the family Iridaceae. It is named after the botanist Muzio G. Spirito de Tommasini (1794–1879). It is native to Bulgaria, Hungary, Albania, and the former Yugoslavia. It is often referred to as the early or snow crocus, but these terms are shared with several other species, although C. tommasinianus is amongst the first to bloom. Multiple plants are often called tommies in the horticultural trade.

items.name: Crocus tournefortii
items.growersTips:
Plant corms in late summer at a depth of 8cm in sharply draining, gritty soil to prevent winter rot.
Grow them in a cold frame or alpine house to protect the delicate autumn blooms from heavy UK rain.
Position in full south-facing sun to ensure the flowers open fully, as they do not close at night.
Water moderately during their autumn growth but keep the soil almost dry during summer dormancy.
Protect the emerging autumn shoots from slugs and snails using grit barriers or organic pellets.

items.name: Crocus vallicola
items.growersTips:
Plant corms in late summer at a depth of 8cm in gritty, free-draining soil to prevent winter rot.
Grow in a cool, partially shaded rock garden or alpine house to mimic their native damp meadows.
Keep the soil consistently moist during their active late summer flowering and autumn growth phase.
Protect the delicate autumn blooms from slugs and snails using organic barriers or beer traps.
Avoid dry summer baking by top-dressing the soil with leaf mould to retain cool moisture.

items.name: Crocus veluchensis

Plant corms 8cm deep in autumn in gritty, free-draining soil to prevent winter rot in wet UK climates.
Position in full sun or dappled shade under deciduous shrubs to mimic their native Balkan woodland.
Avoid watering during their dormant summer phase from July to September to prevent the corms rotting.
Leave foliage to die back naturally for six weeks after spring flowering to feed next year's bloom.
Protect emerging spring buds from slugs and house sparrows using copper tape or physical barriers.

items.name: Giant crocus
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs in autumn at a depth of 10cm to protect them from winter frosts and foraging squirrels.
Plant in well-drained soil as wet UK winter clay will rot the bulbs; add grit to the planting hole.
Protect emerging spring buds from birds by placing physical barriers or black cotton thread nearby.
Let the foliage die back naturally for six weeks after flowering before mowing lawns with crocuses.
Divide congested clumps in late spring after flowering to maintain vigorous blooms in future years.
items.description: Crocus vernus is a species of flowering plant in the family Iridaceae, native to the Alps, the Pyrenees, and the Balkans. Its cultivars and those of Crocus flavus are used as ornamental plants. The Dutch crocuses are larger than the other cultivated crocus species. Depending on the year, Crocus vernus starts flowering about the same time or up to 2 weeks after Crocus chrysanthus starts flowering. Height: 4–6 inches (10–15 cm).

items.name: Crocus versicolor

Grow in full sun to ensure the delicate striped petals fully open during cool UK spring days.
Protect emerging buds from mice and birds by covering the planting area with fine wire mesh.
Allow the foliage to die back naturally for six weeks after flowering before mowing your lawn.
Divide congested clumps in late summer while the bulbs are dormant to maintain vigorous flowering.

items.description: Dianthus barbatus, the sweet William, is a species of flowering plant in the family Caryophyllaceae, native to southern Europe and parts of Asia. It has become a popular ornamental garden plant. It is a herbaceous biennial or short-lived perennial plant growing to 13–92 cm tall, with flowers in a dense cluster of up to 30 at the top of the stems. Each flower is 2–3 cm diameter with five petals displaying serrated edges. items.description: Dianthus caryophyllus, commonly known as carnation or clove pink, is a species of Dianthus native to the Mediterranean region. Propagate by taking non-flowering heel cuttings in July to maintain vigor as plants age.
Protect from winter wet with a pane of glass or open cloche from November through to March.

items.name: Cheddar pink
items.growersTips:
Plant in gritty, free-draining soil with a handful of horticultural grit to prevent winter wet rot.
Position in full sun and water only during prolonged dry spells once established to avoid root rot.
Shear off faded flower stems in July to encourage a second flush of blooms and keep the cushion tidy.
Protect young spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.
Propagate by taking semi-ripe cuttings in midsummer to replace woody, short-lived parent plants.

items.name: Dianthus japonicus
items.growersTips:
Plant in sharply draining gritty soil to prevent winter root rot in wet UK climates.
Sow seeds shallowly at two millimetres deep in spring using a cold frame to protect young seedlings.
Water only when the top five centimetres of soil is dry to avoid waterlogging this coastal species.
Cut back faded flower stems to the base in late autumn to keep the evergreen foliage clump tidy.
Watch for slugs and snails on young spring shoots during damp British weather and apply grit barriers.

items.name: Dianthus micropetalus
items.growersTips:
Plant in gritty, free-draining alkaline soil to prevent winter root rot in wet UK climates.
Position in full south-facing sun to mimic its native dry, rocky South African habitat.
Water sparingly only during dry summer spells, allowing the soil to dry out completely between waterings.
Trim back faded flower stems in late summer to maintain a tight, cushion-like evergreen habit.
Protect the low foliage cushion from winter slugs and snails using organic grit barriers.

items.name: Dianthus monspessulanus
items.growersTips:
Plant in gritty, free-draining alkaline soil to prevent winter root rot in wet UK climates.
Position in full south-facing sun to mimic its native alpine slopes and prevent leggy growth.
Cut back by half after the midsummer flush to promote a second wave of fragrant autumn blooms.
Water only during prolonged dry summer spells once established, as this plant hates damp soil.
Propagate by taking softwood cuttings in July to maintain plant vigour as older clumps woody up.

items.name: Dianthus nardiformis
items.growersTips:
Plant in sharply draining grit-heavy soil to prevent winter wet root rot in damp UK climates.
Position in full south-facing sun to mimic its native dry Balkan cliffs and encourage tight growth.
Water sparingly only during prolonged summer droughts once established to avoid crown rot.
Trim back flower stems to the cushion base in late summer to maintain a compact mound.
Protect from slugs and snails in early spring when the new needle-like foliage emerges.

items.name: Dianthus pavonius
items.growersTips:
Plant in sharply draining gritty soil or a raised scree bed to survive wet UK winter root rot.
Position in full south-facing sun to mimic its native alpine slopes and prevent leggy growth.
Water sparingly only during dry summer spells once established to keep the gritty compost dryish.
Cut back spent flower stems to the cushion base in late July to encourage a neat hummock habit.
Topdress the surrounding soil with limestone chippings to keep wet foliage off damp winter ground.

items.name: Wild pink
items.growersTips:
Incorporate plenty of grit into heavy UK clay soil to ensure the sharp drainage these pinks require.
Plant with the crown exactly level with the soil surface to prevent rot in damp British winters.
Deadhead spent blooms in July by cutting stems back to the cushion base to trigger a second flush.
Water only during prolonged dry spells as established plants are highly drought-tolerant in the UK.
Take semi-ripe cuttings in summer to propagate and replace woody, short-lived parent plants.

items.name: Dianthus rigidus
items.growersTips:
Plant in sharply draining gritty soil or raised beds to survive wet UK winters and prevent root rot.
Position in full south-facing sun to mimic its native dry steppes and encourage summer flowering.
Water sparingly only during dry spells once established, as this species is highly drought-tolerant.
Cut back spent flower stems to the base in late summer to maintain a tight, cushion-like habit.
Protect young spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers in damp UK weather.

items.name: Sequier's pink
items.growersTips:
Plant in gritty, free-draining soil with a handful of horticultural grit to prevent winter wet rot.
Position in full south-facing sun and water only during prolonged dry spells once established.
Cut back the spent flowering stems by half in late summer to encourage a second flush of blooms.
Protect young spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic wool pellets or beer traps.
Divide the clumps every three years in early spring to maintain vigor and prevent center dieback.

items.name: Large pink
items.growersTips:
Plant in free-draining gritty neutral to alkaline soil to prevent winter root rot in wet UK climates
Sow seeds shallowly at two millimetres deep in spring using a cold frame to protect from heavy rain
Water only when the top two inches of soil are dry as this species hates waterlogged summer soil
Cut back flower stems to the base in late autumn to encourage a compact habit and fresh spring growth
Protect young spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps

items.name: Dianthus sylvestris
items.growersTips:
Plant in sharply draining gritty soil or raised beds to survive wet UK winters without root rot.
Position in full south-facing sun to mimic its native alpine slopes and prevent leggy growth.
Water sparingly only during dry summer spells once established, avoiding any winter irrigation.
Cut back spent flowering stems to the base in late summer to encourage a neat cushion habit.
Incorporate limestone chippings into the planting hole to raise soil pH and improve drainage.

items.name: European seabass
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist well-drained soil enriched with leaf mould to mimic their native woodland habitat
Position in partial shade to prevent the delicate foliage from scorching in midday summer sun
Water deeply during dry spring spells to extend the flowering period of Dicentra spectabilis
Cut back yellowing stems to ground level in midsummer once the plant naturally goes dormant
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit or beer traps in damp weather

items.name: Squirrel corn
items.growersTips:
Plant its fragile tubers five centimetres deep in late autumn before the ground freezes.
Incorporate leaf mould to mimic UK woodland soils and keep the pH slightly acidic to neutral.
Water weekly during dry spring spells but keep soil dryish in summer when tubers go dormant.
Protect the delicate emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic beer traps.
Partner with dry-shade tolerant ferns to cover the bare patches left when foliage dies in July.

items.name: Dicentra cucullaria
items.growersTips:
Plant pink-tinged white tubers 5cm deep in autumn in moist, humus-rich soil under deciduous trees.
Water weekly during spring growth but keep soil drier in summer when the plant goes fully dormant.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.
Mark the planting spot in May as foliage dies back completely to avoid digging it up in summer.
Plant alongside early-flowering primroses and wood anemones for a classic UK woodland display.

items.name: Bleeding heart
items.growersTips:
Plant in moisture-retentive, humus-rich soil, adding leaf mould to mimic UK woodland conditions.
Position in partial shade to prevent the delicate fern-like foliage from scorching in midday sun.
Water weekly during dry UK summer spells to keep the soil consistently moist but never waterlogged.
Divide congested clumps in early spring just as new growth appears to maintain plant vigour.
Watch for slugs and snails in damp spring weather, protecting the tender emerging shoots.

items.name: Wild bleeding heart
items.growersTips:
Plant in moisture-retentive, humus-rich soil in partial shade, mimicking UK woodland conditions.
Incorporate leaf mould or well-rotted manure into the planting hole to mimic damp forest floor soil.
Water weekly during dry UK spring spells, keeping soil consistently moist but never waterlogged.
Divide congested clumps in early spring just as new growth appears to maintain plant vigour.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit or beer traps.
items.description: Dicentra formosa is a species of flowering plant in the poppy family, Papaveraceae. With its fern-like foliage and inflorescence of drooping pink, purple, yellow or cream "hearts", this species is native to the Pacific Northwest of North America.

items.name: Dicentra nevadensis
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist well-drained humus-rich acidic soil in partial shade to mimic its native woodland.
Water weekly during dry UK summers to keep the soil consistently damp but never waterlogged.
Apply a thick mulch of leaf mould or composted bark in autumn to protect roots from winter wet.
Watch for slugs and snails in early spring as new delicate fern-like foliage begins to emerge.
Propagate by dividing the fragile rhizomes in early spring just as new growth starts to show.
items.description: Dicentra nevadensis, the Sierra bleeding heart or Tulare County bleeding heart, is a perennial plant endemic to gravelly outcroppings in the Sierra Nevada peaks of Tulare and Fresno Counties in California.

items.name: Dicentra pauciflora
items.growersTips:
Plant in gritty, humus-rich soil in a cool, partially shaded rock garden to mimic alpine scree.
Provide sharp drainage using a mix of leafmould and grit to prevent winter wet from rotting tubers.
Water moderately during the spring growing season but keep the soil barely damp during summer dormancy.
Protect the delicate emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic bait or grit barriers.
Avoid disturbing the fragile brittle roots once planted in their permanent UK garden position.
items.description: Dicentra pauciflora is a species of flowering plant in Dicentra, the genus containing the bleeding-hearts. Its common names include shorthorn steer's head and few-flowered bleeding-heart. This perennial wildflower is native to the US states of Oregon and California, where it grows high in the mountains in gravelly soils. This is a short bleeding-heart, approaching 10 centimeters (3.9 in) in maximum height. From a rhizome beneath the soil it extends several erect petioles, each holding a leaf divided into leaflets which are each divided into smooth, fingerlike lobes. It also erects a thin stem

items.name: Dicentra peregrina
items.growersTips:
Grow in a scree bed or alpine house using a gritty, sharply draining, alkaline to neutral compost
Water sparingly in summer but ensure the roots never dry out completely during the growing season
Protect from winter wet by covering with a glass cloche or keeping in a cold frame from November
Plant the delicate rhizomes shallowly with the growing tips just below the grit mulch surface
Position in a cool north-facing spot to mimic alpine conditions and prevent summer heat stress
items.description: Dicentra peregrina is a herbaceous perennial growing from a rhizome, native to mountains in Japan and nearby areas of East Asia.

items.name: Dicentra uniflora
items.growersTips:
Plant this tiny tuber just three centimetres deep in gritty, sharply draining soil to prevent rot.
Replicate its native alpine habitat by keeping the soil damp in spring but completely dry in summer.
Grow this miniature species in a cold frame or alpine house to protect it from excessive UK winter wet.
Surround the planting area with fine grit to deter slugs from eating the highly vulnerable new shoots.
Position in a north-facing rockery or trough where it receives cool morning sun but no midday heat.
items.description: Dicentra uniflora, the longhorn steer's head, is a herbaceous perennial flowering plant growing from a tuber, native to gravelly soils in mountains of the western United States.

items.name: Dicheranthus plocamoides
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in March at a depth of two millimetres using free-draining peat-free compost.
Grow in a south-facing gravel garden or containers to mimic its native dry Canary Island habitat.
Water sparingly only when the top two inches of soil are dry to prevent root rot in damp UK summers.
Protect young plants from slugs and snails using beer traps during wet British spring nights.
Plant alongside Mediterranean herbs like thyme to provide the sharp drainage and full sun it needs.
items.description: Dicheranthus is a monotypic genus of flowering plants belonging to the family Caryophyllaceae. The only species is Dicheranthus plocamoides.

items.name: Dicheranthus plocamoides
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at two millimetres deep in April using a heated propagator to mimic Canary heat.
Grow in a sharply draining gritty compost mix to prevent root rot during wet UK summer spells.
Water only when the top two inches of soil are dry, keeping the foliage dry to avoid mildew.
Position in the brightest south-facing spot or greenhouse to maximise scarce UK summer sunshine.
Protect young plants from slugs and snails which target the tender stems during damp May nights.
items.description: Dicheranthus is a monotypic genus of flowering plants belonging to the family Caryophyllaceae. The only species is Dicheranthus plocamoides.

items.name: Dichodon cerastoides
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at a depth of two millimetres in early spring using a gritty, free-draining soil
Water sparingly only when the top two centimetres of soil are dry to prevent alpine root rot
Position in full sun in a raised bed or rockery to mimic its native gravelly scree habitat
Protect young spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps
Plant alongside low-growing Sedum or Saxifraga to provide natural support and complementary blooms
items.description: Dichodon cerastoides, commonly known as the mountain chickweed or starwort mouse-ear, is a species of flowering plant in the pink family Caryophyllaceae. It is found in the mountains of Europe.

items.name: Dichopogon strictus
items.growersTips:
Plant tubers five centimetres deep in autumn using gritty, free-draining soil to prevent winter rot.
Grow in a terracotta pot to easily move this tender Australian native into a frost-free greenhouse.
Water weekly during the active spring growing season but keep the soil almost bone dry in winter.
Cut back the chocolate-scented flower stems to the base in autumn once the seed pods turn brown.
Position in your warmest, south-facing border alongside hardy succulents like Sempervivum.
items.description: Dichopogon strictus, commonly known as chocolate lily, is a herbaceous perennial plant species native to Australia.

items.name: Chinese Quinine
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist well-drained acidic soil to ensure the berries develop their signature metallic blue.
Grow in a sheltered woodland border or against a south-facing wall to protect buds from UK frosts.
Water deeply and consistently during dry summer spells to mimic its native damp forest habitat.
Prune lightly in mid-spring by removing dead wood and spent flower heads down to a strong pair of buds.
Overwinter young plants in a cold greenhouse or wrap established shrubs in fleece during hard freezes.
items.description: Dichroa was a genus of 12 species of flowering plants in the family Hydrangeaceae, native to eastern and southeastern Asia. It is now included in genus Hydrangea. These are deciduous shrubs growing to 1–3 m tall, with their leaves arranged in opposite pairs. The flowers are produced in a broad inflorescence similar to that of the related genus Hydrangea. The fruit is a glossy metallic purple-blue berry.

items.name: Chinese Quinine
items.growersTips:
Plant in partial shade sheltered from cold winds in moist well-drained acidic soil to boost blue fruit
Protect roots with a thick winter mulch of bark to survive hard frosts in colder UK regions
Water weekly with rainwater during dry summer spells to keep the soil consistently damp but not wet
Prune lightly in mid-spring after frosts pass by removing dead wood and spent flower heads only
Grow in a large patio pot using ericaceous compost so you can move it into a greenhouse for winter
items.description: Hydrangea febrifuga is a flowering plant in the family Hydrangeaceae. It is a subshrub or shrub native to central and southern China, Indochina, Malesia, and New Guinea.

items.name: Dicorynia guianensis
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in April at a depth of 2cm using bottom heat of 21C to counter cool UK springs.
Plant out in June after all frost risk passes, choosing the sunniest, most sheltered south wall.
Water deeply once a week at the base rather than daily sprinkles to encourage deep taproot growth.
Grow in poor, sharply drained sandy soil to prevent root rot in wet British summer conditions.
Pinch out the growing tips when seedlings reach 15cm high to promote a bushier flowering habit.
items.description:
Dicorynia is a genus of flowering plants in the legume family, Fabaceae. It belongs to the subfamily Dialioideae. It includes two species of trees native to northern South America, ranging through Peru, Colombia, Venezuela, the Guianas, and northern Brazil.Dicorynia guianensis Amshoff – the Guianas
Dicorynia paraensis Benth. – Peru, Colombia, Venezuela, and northern Brazil

items.name: Dicranostigma lactucoides
items.growersTips:
Grow in gritty, sharply draining neutral to alkaline soil to prevent winter root rot in wet UK clay.
Sow seeds shallowly in spring directly where they are to flower as taproots resent transplanting.
Position in full sun or light woodland shade to mimic its native East Asian mountain habitat.
Deadhead spent blooms weekly in summer to prolong flowering and control its prolific self-seeding.
Protect the crown with a dry mulch of gravel in autumn to shield it from persistent UK winter damp.
items.description: Dicranostigma, also known as the eastern horned poppies, is a genus in the poppy family Papaveraceae, the species of which are native to the Himalaya and western China. Although resembling the true horned poppies of Glaucium, they have stigmas with two lobes and fruit with only traces of the "horns".

items.name: Dicrastylis exsuccosa
items.growersTips:
Grow in a gritty, free-draining loam with added horticultural sand to prevent winter root rot.
Overwinter in a heated greenhouse or conservatory to protect from frost below five degrees Celsius.
Water sparingly from below only when the top five centimetres of soil is completely dry to the touch.
Prune lightly in late spring after frost risk passes to maintain a compact, bushy growth habit.
Position in the sunniest, south-facing spot available to mimic its native arid Australian climate.
items.description: Dicrastylis is a genus of plants in the Lamiaceae, first described in 1855. The entire genus is endemic to Australia. The type species is Dicrastylis fulva.

items.name: Dicymbe altsonii
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in early April at a depth of two centimetres using a heated propagator at twenty degrees
Plant out in late May after the last frost into a sheltered south-facing border with grit-heavy soil
Water deeply once a week at the base during dry summer spells to mimic tropical wet-dry cycles
Watch for red spider mites in dry July weather and mist the foliage early in the morning to deter them
Grow alongside climbing French beans to help support nitrogen fixation in the surrounding soil structure
items.description: Dicymbe is a genus of 20 species of canopy trees in the family Fabaceae, within subfamily Detarioideae. It is found throughout the Guyana Shield region and parts of W Amazonia. Certain species within the genus are strongly associated with ectomycorrhizal fungi.

items.name: Didelotia brevipaniculata
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in April at a depth of 2cm using peat-free compost to protect from late UK frosts
Transplant outdoors in late May into well-drained, neutral soil in a sheltered, south-facing spot
Water deeply at the base once a week during dry summer spells to support the shallow root system
Protect young spring shoots from slugs and snails using beer traps or physical copper barriers
In autumn clear the dead annual foliage and compost it to return nitrogen to your vegetable beds
items.description: Didelotia is a genus of flowering plants in the family Fabaceae. It includes 13 species native to western and west-central tropical Africa, ranging from Sierra Leone to the Democratic Republic of the Congo.

items.name: Dierama argyreum
items.growersTips:
Plant in a sheltered south-facing spot in moist, well-drained soil that never dries out in summer.
Sow fresh seed in autumn in cold frames as division of established clumps often leads to failure.
Apply a thick dry mulch of bracken or bark in November to protect the crown from wet UK winter rot.
Cut back dead foliage and old flower stems in spring rather than autumn to protect the crown.
Plant alongside low-growing ornamental grasses to support the heavy, arching flower stems in wind.
items.description: Dierama argyreum is a perennial geophyte that is part of the Iridaceae family. The species is endemic to South Africa and occurs in KwaZulu-Natal and the Eastern Cape.

items.name: Dierama cupuliflorum
items.growersTips:
Plant in spring at a depth of 10cm in deep, fertile, moist but free-draining soil in full sun.
Water weekly during dry summer spells to keep soil moist, but keep dry in winter to prevent rot.
Sow fresh seed in autumn in a cold frame, as this species dislikes root disturbance from division.
Cut back dead foliage and collapsed flower stems in early spring before the new growth emerges.
Protect the crown with a thick dry mulch of bark in autumn to survive wet UK winter frosts.
items.description: Dierama cupuliflorum is a perennial geophyte that is part of the Iridaceae family. The species is native to Ethiopia, Kenya, Malawi, Tanzania, and Uganda.

items.name: Drakensberg Hairbell
items.growersTips:
Plant corms 8 to 10cm deep in autumn using a handful of grit at the base to prevent winter wet rot.
Position in full sun and shelter from cold drying winds to protect the delicate arching stems.
Water deeply during dry spring spells to encourage flowering but keep soil dry during winter dormancy.
Leave faded foliage intact over winter to protect the crown then tidy dead leaves in early spring.
Grow in fertile well-drained soil that does not bake dry in summer or waterlog in wet UK winters.
items.description: Dierama dracomontanum, the Drakensberg hairbell, is a perennial geophyte that is part of the Iridaceae family. The species is native to Lesotho and South Africa and occurs in KwaZulu-Natal, Eastern Cape and the Free State.

items.name: Fairy Bell
items.growersTips:
Plant corms 8 to 10cm deep in autumn using grit at the base of the hole to prevent winter rot.
Grow in moist, humus-rich soil that drains freely, avoiding heavy clay that bakes dry in summer.
Position in full sun sheltered from cold easterly winds to protect the delicate arching stems.
Leave faded foliage intact over winter to protect the crown, then tidy up dead leaves in spring.
Propagate by dividing congested clumps in spring, though they may take a year to flower again.
items.description: Dierama igneum, the fiery wandflower, is a species of flowering plant in the iris family Iridaceae, native to the southeastern Cape Provinces and southern KwaZulu-Natal in South Africa. It is a slow-growing, bulbous perennial growing to 1 m (3.3 ft) tall from clumps of grass-like leaves. Evergreen in its native Africa, it may become herbaceous in colder regions. The trumpet shaped flowers are borne on long, arching stems, and are normally salmon pink in colour. The specific epithet igneum, meaning "glowing" or "fiery", may refer to these arching sprays of blooms.

items.name: Dierama latifolium
items.growersTips:
Plant in spring at a depth of 10cm in deep, fertile, moist but free-draining soil in full sun.
Water consistently during the active summer growing season to prevent the soil from drying out.
Leave faded foliage over winter to protect the crown from wet UK frosts, then tidy in spring.
Sow fresh seed in autumn in a cold frame, as this species dislikes being divided or moved.
Position on a slope or raised bed to ensure essential winter drainage in wet UK climates.
items.description: Dierama latifolium is a perennial geophyte that is part of the Iridaceae family. The species is endemic to South Africa and occurs in KwaZulu-Natal and the Eastern Cape.

items.name: Dierama luteoalbidum
items.growersTips:
Plant corms 10cm deep in autumn using gritty, well-drained soil to prevent winter rot in wet UK clay.
Position in full sun sheltered from cold winds to protect the delicate cream-white summer bells.
Water deeply during dry spring spells to establish roots but keep dry in dormant winter months.
Leave faded foliage intact until spring to insulate the crown from severe UK frosts and freezes.
Grow alongside low-growing ornamental grasses to support the tall, arching stems without staking.
items.description: Dierama luteoalbidum is a perennial geophyte that is part of the Iridaceae family. The species is endemic to South Africa and occurs in the KwaZulu-Natal Midlands. It has a range of 1 200 - 5 500 km2 and there are eight to ten subpopulations. The species has lost habitat to plantations and overgrazing is also a threat.

items.name: Dierama nixonianum
items.growersTips:
Plant in free-draining gravelly loam to prevent winter root rot in wet UK climates.
Position the corms exactly 8cm deep in full sun to encourage summer flowering.
Water deeply during dry spring spells but keep soil dry during dormant winter months.
Leave the semi-evergreen foliage intact over winter and only tidy dead leaves in April.
Grow alongside low-growing thyme or sedum to protect the corm base from cold winds.
items.description: Dierama nixonianum is a perennial geophyte that is part of the Iridaceae family. The species is endemic to South Africa and occurs in KwaZulu-Natal. The species has a distribution area of less than 1000 km2 and occurs from the KwaZulu-Natal Midlands to Wakkerstroom.

items.name: Dierama pauciflorum
items.growersTips:
Plant in moisture-retentive, acidic to neutral soil that never dries out, unlike other dieramas.
Position in full sun but shelter from cold, drying winds that scorch the delicate evergreen foliage.
Plant corms 5-8cm deep in spring, spacing them 10cm apart in a bog garden or beside a garden pond.
Apply a thick mulch of leafmould in autumn to protect the shallow corms from severe UK winter frosts.
Divide congested clumps in spring just as new growth starts, keeping the roots constantly damp.
items.description:
Dierama pauciflorum, the few-flowered wandflower, is a species of flowering plant in the iris family Iridaceae, native to south and east Africa. This bulbous perennial forms short, evergreen, grass-like clumps to 
30–40 cm (12–16 in) high. The sparse trumpet-shaped flowers are borne on arching stems which are only slightly longer than the foliage. They are rich pink, and fuller in shape than its close relative Dierama igneum.

items.name: Common Harebell
items.growersTips:
Plant corms 8 to 10cm deep in spring using fertile well-drained soil to prevent winter waterlogging.
Position in full sun sheltered from cold drying winds which can damage the delicate arching stems.
Water newly planted corms regularly in summer but keep them relatively dry during wet UK winters.
Do not cut back old foliage in autumn; instead tidy by pulling away dead leaves gently in spring.
Plant near paving or gravel paths so the heavy bell-shaped pink flowers can drape without obstruction.
items.description: Dierama pendulum, commonly known as fairy bell, hair bell and wedding bell, is a species of Iridaceae endemic to the Eastern Cape in South Africa and first collected in 1772 by the Swedish naturalist Carl Peter Thunberg near Essenbos on the Kromme River or Kromrivier which flows down the Langkloof. In 1845 the genus Dierama was established by Karl Koch (1809-1879) based on this specimen. Before that the plant had been placed in various genera including Ixia, Sparaxis and Watsonia. The species name has been misapplied to D. inyangense, D. densiflorum and to D. plowesii.

items.name: Dierama pulcherrimum
items.growersTips:
Plant corms 8 to 10cm deep in autumn using fertile, sharply draining soil to prevent winter rot.
Siting is crucial; choose a sheltered, south-facing border to protect arching stems from UK winds.
Water newly planted corms regularly in summer, but keep them completely dry during winter dormancy.
Leave old foliage intact over winter to protect the crown, then tidy brown leaves in spring by hand.
Avoid dividing established clumps as they hate root disturbance; propagate instead by sowing seed.
items.description: Dierama pulcherrimum, angel's fishing rod, is a species of flowering plant in the iris family Iridaceae, native to the southeastern Cape Provinces of South Africa. Growing to 1.5 m (4.9 ft) tall by 0.5 m (1.6 ft) broad, it is an arching evergreen perennial with drooping rosy pink bell-shaped flowers in summer.

items.name: Dierama reynoldsii
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist but well-drained humus-rich soil in full sun, avoiding heavy clay that waterlogs.
Sow seeds in pots in a cold frame during autumn, barely covering them with a fine layer of grit.
Water deeply during dry summer spells to mimic its native South African mountain stream habitat.
Leave old foliage over winter to protect the crown from frost, then tidy up dead leaves in spring.
Plant alongside low-growing ornamental grasses to support its tall, arching stems in windy sites.
items.description: Dierama reynoldsii is a perennial geophyte that is part of the Iridaceae family. The species is endemic to South Africa and occurs in KwaZulu-Natal and the Eastern Cape.

items.name: Digitalis ×fulva
items.growersTips:
Plant this hybrid foxglove in partial shade with moist, humus-rich soil to mimic UK woodland edges.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells to keep the soil consistently damp but not soggy.
Cut back faded flower spikes in late summer to encourage a second flush of blooms before autumn.
Apply a thick mulch of leaf mould or compost in autumn to protect roots from wet winter rot.
Watch for foxglove aphids in spring and spray them off with a sharp blast of water from the hose.
items.description: Digitalis × fulva, the strawberry foxglove, is a hybrid species of flowering plant within the family Plantaginaceae. It is a naturally occurring fertile hybrid between the species Digitalis grandiflora and Digitalis purpurea. The species is widely marketed in the UK under the common name of strawberry foxglove or its taxonomic synonym Digitalis × mertonensis. The species has been used to produce various cultivars and has gained the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit.

items.name: Digitalis canariensis
items.growersTips:
Grow in a sheltered, south-facing spot in well-drained, gritty soil to prevent winter root rot.
Overwinter in a cold greenhouse or wrap in fleece to protect from UK frosts below minus five.
Water deeply but infrequently during dry summer spells, allowing the soil to dry out between waterings.
Prune back faded flower spikes in late summer to encourage a second flush of autumn blooms.
Plant alongside Mediterranean herbs like rosemary and lavender that share its love for dry sun.
items.description: Digitalis canariensis is a member of the genus Digitalis.

items.name: Digitalis chalcantha
items.growersTips:
Plant this tender evergreen shrub in well-drained, gritty loam to prevent winter root rot in UK wet.
Position in a sheltered, south-facing border or container to protect it from harsh UK winter frosts.
Water moderately during the summer growing season, allowing the soil to dry out between waterings.
Prune lightly in late spring after flowering to maintain its compact, bushy shrub habit and shape.
Propagate by taking semi-ripe cuttings in late summer to overwinter young plants safely indoors.
items.description: Digitalis chalcantha is a flowering evergreen shrub in the family Plantaginaceae. It is native to the Canary Islands, specifically Gran Canaria.

items.name: Digitalis ciliata
items.growersTips:
Plant in autumn at a depth of five centimetres in well-drained, gritty loam to prevent winter rot.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells, keeping the crown dry to avoid fungal decay.
Cut spent flower spikes back to the base in late August to encourage a second flush of blooms.
Sow seeds in late spring on the soil surface as they require light and UK spring warmth to germinate.
Position near dark-leaved Heuchera in partial shade to highlight the pale yellow, hairy bell flowers.
items.description: Digitalis ciliata, commonly called hairy foxglove is a member of the genus Digitalis. It has thimble-shaped, yellow to cream-colored flowers produced on perennial plants with evergreen foliage. It is native to the Caucasus and is grown as an ornamental plant in other parts of the world. The species name is derived from the fine hairs that cover the plant's stems and flowers.

items.name: Digitalis davisiana
items.growersTips:
Plant in well-drained alkaline loam with added grit to prevent winter wet rot in damp UK climates.
Position in partial shade or dappled woodland edge to mimic its native Turkish mountain habitat.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells but keep completely dry during dormant winter.
Cut back faded flower spikes in late August to encourage a second flush of yellow-bronze blooms.
Watch for slugs and snails on young spring shoots by using organic wool pellets around the base.
items.description: Digitalis davisiana is a species of foxglove, a herbaceous plant in the genus Digitalis in the family Plantaginaceae, formerly in the Scrophulariaceae and briefly the Veronicaceae. It is native to Turkey.

items.name: Rusty foxglove
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds on the soil surface in late spring as they need light to germinate in UK conditions.
Grow in well-drained soil to prevent crown rot during wet, cold British winters.
Leave the architectural copper flower spikes through winter to feed goldfinches and self-seed.
Plant alongside Astrantia or ornamental grasses like Stipa tenuissima for a classic gravel garden.
Wear gloves when handling any part of this highly toxic plant during division or cutting.
items.description: Digitalis ferruginea, the rusty foxglove, is a species of flowering plant in the family Plantaginaceae, native to Hungary, Romania, Turkey and the Caucasus. It is a biennial or short-lived perennial plant growing to 1.2 metres in height, which forms a rosette of oblong dark green leaves and carries spikes of russet, tubular flowers in summer.

items.name: Yellow foxglove
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds on the soil surface in late spring as they need light to germinate in UK conditions.
Grow in moist but well-drained humus-rich soil in partial shade to mimic their native woodland edge.
Cut back the faded flower spikes in August to encourage a second flush of blooms and prevent self-seeding.
Watch for foxglove aphids in May and squash them by hand to protect the emerging flower buds.
Plant alongside ferns and hostas which thrive in the same damp shade and mask the fading lower leaves.
items.description: Digitalis grandiflora, the yellow foxglove, big-flowered foxglove, or large yellow foxglove, is a species of flowering plant in the genus Digitalis, family Plantaginaceae. It is native to southern Europe and Asia. In mountains it grows on warm, bushy slopes or areas left after logging. The Latin specific epithet grandiflora means "large flowered".

items.name: Digitalis isabelliana
items.growersTips:
Grow in a sheltered, south-facing spot to protect its tender shrubby stems from cold UK winter winds
Plant in extremely free-draining, gritty soil to prevent root rot during wet British winters
Water moderately during the summer growing season but keep the compost nearly dry throughout winter
Prune back lightly in late spring after frosts pass to maintain a bushy shape and remove dead wood
Overwinter in a cold greenhouse or wrap in fleece if temperatures in your UK region drop below -5C
items.description: Digitalis isabelliana, known commonly as Canary Island foxglove, Isabel's foxglove, or Gran Canaria Pineforest foxglove, is a type of flowering shrub, one of three species of foxglove native to the Canary Islands.

items.name: Digitalis laevigata
items.growersTips:
Plant in free-draining gravelly loam to prevent winter root rot in wet UK clay soils.
Sow seeds shallowly in spring on the soil surface as they require light to germinate.
Cut back faded flower spikes in late summer to encourage a second flush of blooms.
Water deeply once a week during dry UK summer spells rather than daily light sprinkling.
Position in partial shade alongside ferns and hostas to mimic its natural woodland habitat.
items.description: Digitalis laevigata, common names Grecian foxglove or giraffe foxglove, is a species of flowering plant in the genus Digitalis, in the family Plantaginaceae.

items.name: Digitalis lamarckii
items.growersTips:
Plant in free-draining chalky or sandy soil to prevent winter root rot in wet UK climates.
Sow seeds shallowly on the soil surface in spring as they require light to germinate.
Cut back faded flower spikes in late summer to encourage a second flush of blooms.
Position in full sun to partial shade, mimicking its native dry, stony Mediterranean habitat.
Grow alongside drought-tolerant partners like lavender or salvia in gravel beds.
items.description: Digitalis lamarckii is a species of flowering plant in family Plantaginaceae that is native to Turkey.

items.name: Woolly foxglove
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds on the soil surface in late spring as they need light to germinate in the UK climate.
Grow in well-drained chalky or sandy loam to prevent winter crown rot during wet British winters.
Wear thick gloves when handling this highly toxic plant and keep it away from pets and children.
Cut back faded flower spikes in August to encourage a second flush of smaller woolly blooms.
Plant alongside Salvia nemorosa or Stachys byzantina to complement the unusual coppery-bronze flowers.
items.description: Digitalis lanata, vernacularly often called woolly foxglove or Grecian foxglove, is a species of foxglove, a flowering plant in the plantain family Plantaginaceae.
