It gets its name due to the woolly indumentum of the leaves. D. lanata, like other foxglove species, is toxic in all parts of the plant. Symptoms of digitalis poisoning include nausea, vomiting, severe headache, dilated pupils, problems with eyesight, and convulsions and cardiac arrhythmias at the worst level of toxicity. The plant is also harmful to other animals.

items.name: Digitalis lutea
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in spring on compost surface as they need UK spring light to germinate.
Grow in moist well-drained soil enriched with leafmould to mimic British woodland edge conditions.
Water consistently during dry summer spells to keep the soil damp but never waterlogged.
Cut back faded flower spikes in August to encourage a second flush of pale yellow blooms.
Watch for leaf spots and aphids in damp UK weather, treating early with organic sprays.
items.description: Digitalis lutea, the straw foxglove or small yellow foxglove, is a species of flowering plant in the plantain family Plantaginaceae, that is native to western and southern Europe and North West Africa.

items.name: Digitalis mariana
items.growersTips:
Plant in gritty, sharply drained soil to prevent winter crown rot in wet UK climates.
Position in full sun to mimic its native Spanish cliffs, unlike native UK woodland foxgloves.
Sow seeds on the soil surface in spring as they require light to germinate, do not cover them.
Cut back faded flower spikes in late summer to encourage a second flush of blooms and neat habit.
Grow alongside Mediterranean herbs like rosemary and thyme which share its dry, low-nutrient needs.
items.description: Digitalis mariana is a flowering plant species in the family Plantaginaceae. It is a perennial foxglove with evergreen foliage and rose-red flowers, which are produced in summer. It is native to Portugal and Spain.

items.name: Digitalis minor
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds on the soil surface in spring as they need light to germinate in the UK climate.
Grow in gritty, sharply draining neutral to alkaline soil to prevent winter root rot in wet weather.
Water sparingly once established, allowing the gritty compost to dry out between watering sessions.
Position in full sun or very light dappled shade to mimic its native Balearic cliffside habitat.
Protect young spring growth from slugs and snails using beer traps or physical barriers in damp areas.
items.description: Digitalis minor is a species of flowering plant in family Plantaginaceae, which has been called dwarf Spanish foxglove. It is a biennial or short-lived perennial species of foxglove which is endemic to the Balearic islands with large, pendulous, pink or purple flowers. Closely related to the common purple foxglove, it is best distinguished by its small fruits. It is one of the only foxgloves to grow in calciferous, alkaline soils.

items.name: Digitalis nervosa
items.growersTips:
Plant this perennial foxglove in moisture-retentive, humus-rich soil in partial shade or woodland edge.
Sow seeds on the soil surface in late spring as they require light and UK warmth to germinate.
Water consistently during dry summer spells to keep the soil damp but avoid waterlogged winter pots.
Cut back the faded yellow flower spikes in August to encourage a second flush of late-season blooms.
Watch for slugs and snails on young spring shoots and protect them with organic beer traps or grit.
items.description: Digitalis nervosa is a species of flowering plant in family Plantaginaceae. It is native to the Caucasus down to north western and northern Iran.

items.name: Digitalis obscura
items.growersTips:
Plant this Spanish willow-leaved foxglove in sharply draining, gritty soil to survive wet UK winters.
Position in full sun, unlike native woodland foxgloves, to mimic its dry Mediterranean habitat.
Water sparingly once established, allowing the soil to dry out completely between summer waterings.
Cut back faded flower spikes in late summer to encourage a second flush of blooms and tidy the shrub.
Protect young plants from slugs and snails in damp British springs using beer traps or copper tape.
items.description: Digitalis obscura, commonly called willow-leaved foxglove or dusty foxglove or Spanish rusty foxglove, is a flowering plant native to regions in Spain and Morocco. It is also grown as an ornamental flower. This foxglove is a woody perennial plant belonging to the family Plantaginaceae. Along with the other foxgloves it used to be placed in the figwort family, Scrophulariaceae; however, recent genetic research has moved the genus Digitalis to a larger family. It is similar to many of the foxglove species in its high toxicity and medicinal use as a source for the heart-regulating drug digoxin. I

items.name: Smallflowered foxglove
items.growersTips:
Plant in well-drained, gritty soil to prevent winter root rot in wet UK clay.
Sow seeds on the soil surface in spring, as they need light to germinate in UK conditions.
Cut faded flower spikes to the base in late summer to encourage a second flush of blooms.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells, allowing the soil to dry out between waterings.
Position in full sun or very light dappled shade to mimic its native dry Mediterranean habitat.
items.description: Digitalis parviflora, the small-flowered foxglove, is a species of flowering plant in the plantain family Plantaginaceae. It is endemic to northern and central Spain. It grows at 500–2000 metres in altitude.

items.name: Digitalis purpurea
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds thinly on the surface of damp peat-free compost in June, as they need light to germinate.
Plant out young rosettes by autumn in moist, humus-rich soil, spaced thirty centimetres apart.
Water young plants weekly during dry summer spells to establish strong roots before winter wet.
Cut spent flower spikes to the ground in July to encourage a second flush of late-summer blooms.
Leave some seed heads intact in autumn to self-seed naturally in shady borders or woodland edges.
items.description: Digitalis purpurea, the foxglove or common foxglove, is a toxic species of flowering plant in the plantain family Plantaginaceae, native to and widespread throughout most of temperate Europe. It has also naturalized in parts of North America, as well as some other temperate regions. The plant is a popular garden subject, with many cultivars available. It is the original source of the heart medicine digoxin. This biennial plant grows as a rosette of leaves in the first year after sowing, before flowering and then dying in the second year. It generally produces enough seeds so that new plants wi

items.name: Digitalis sceptrum
items.growersTips:
Overwinter this tender Madeiran shrub in a frost-free greenhouse or conservatory during UK winters.
Grow in a large pot using well-drained loam-based compost mixed with plenty of grit to prevent rot.
Water moderately in summer but keep the compost barely moist during the dark, cold winter months.
Prune lightly in late spring after frost risk passes to maintain a compact, bushy shrub shape.
Position in a sheltered spot that receives full sun to partial shade to mimic its cliff habitat.
items.description: Digitalis sceptrum is a species of Digitalis from Madeira.

items.name: Digitalis sect. Isoplexis
items.growersTips:
Grow in free-draining gravelly soil to prevent winter root rot in wet UK climates.
Overwinter in a cold greenhouse or wrap in fleece to protect from frosts below minus five.
Prune lightly in late spring after the last frost to shape the shrub and encourage new flowering wood.
Water deeply but infrequently during dry summer spells once established to mimic its native habitat.
Position in full sun against a south-facing wall to maximise summer heat and boost flower production.
items.description: Digitalis sect. Isoplexis is a section of four species of flowering plants within the genus Digitalis in the plantain family Plantaginaceae. The species of section Isoplexis differ from other plants in the genus Digitalis in that their monosymmetric flowers have a distinctive large upper lip rather than large lower lip and the species are endemic to the Canary Islands and Madeira.

items.name: Digitalis thapsi
items.growersTips:
Plant in gritty, sharply drained soil to prevent root rot during wet UK winters.
Water sparingly once established, allowing the top five centimetres of soil to dry out completely.
Cut back faded flower spikes in late summer to encourage a second flush of blooms.
Protect young spring growth from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.
Sow seeds shallowly in spring, barely covering them with compost as they need light to germinate.
items.description: Digitalis thapsi, which has been called mullein foxglove in the US, is a flowering plant in the genus Digitalis that is endemic to the Iberian Peninsula, where it occurs in eastern Portugal and central and western Spain. It is of commercial importance as an ornamental plant. Hybrids with D. purpurea have proved successful and are fertile.

items.name: Digitalis viridiflora
items.growersTips:
Plant in autumn in moisture-retentive, humus-rich soil, keeping the crown level with the soil surface.
Water deeply once a week during dry UK summer spells to keep the soil consistently damp but not wet.
Inspect the base weekly in damp spring weather for slugs and snails to protect the young emerging shoots.
Cut spent flower spikes down to the base in late August to encourage a second flush of green blooms.
Sow seeds in trays in late spring, leaving them uncovered on the surface as they need light to sprout.
items.description: Digitalis viridiflora is a species of flowering plant commonly called green foxglove in family Plantaginaceae. It is a perennial species with greenish-yellow flowers produced on stems that grow 60 cm (23.6 in) to 80 cm (31.5 in) tall. It is native to the Balkans. It is found growing in woodlands and on heaths.

items.name: Dimorphandra mollis
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in early spring at a depth of two centimetres using a heated propagator at twenty degrees.
Grow in free-draining sandy loam enriched with grit to prevent root rot during wet British summers.
Water deeply once a week only when the top five centimetres of soil has dried out completely.
Position in the sunniest, most sheltered south-facing spot to maximise limited UK summer heat.
Protect young outdoor plants from slugs and snails using organic wool pellets around the stems.
items.description: Dimorphandra is a genus of legume in the family Fabaceae, subfamily Caesalpinioideae. It includes 26 species native to northern South America, ranging from Colombia and Venezuela to Bolivia, Paraguay, and southeastern Brazil.

items.name: Dimorphandra mollis
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender Brazilian shrub in a pot of loamy, acidic soil to move indoors before UK frosts.
Water deeply only when the top five centimetres of soil dries out to prevent root rot in winter.
Place in the sunniest south-facing spot or conservatory to mimic its native savannah heat.
Prune lightly in late spring after frost risk passes to maintain shape and remove dead wood.
Watch for glasshouse red spider mite and mealybugs when overwintering this plant indoors.
items.description: Dimorphandra mollis, the Fava d'anta, is a tree species in the genus of Dimorphandra. It is a plant of the Cerrado vegetation of Brazil. The seeds are known to be toxic to cattle.

items.name: Dinizia excelsa
items.growersTips:
Start seeds indoors in March using deep root trainers to protect the sensitive Fabaceae taproot.
Plant out in late May after all frost risk, spacing thirty centimetres apart in full southern sun.
Water deeply at the base once a week during dry summer spells to establish the deep root system.
Incorporate grit and well-rotted manure into heavy UK clay soils to ensure excellent drainage.
Protect young spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic wool pellets or beer traps.
items.description: Dinizia is a genus of flowering plants in the legume family, Fabaceae. It was believed to be monotypic until 2017, when Dinizia jueirana-facao was described. Dinizia is native to Brazil, Guyana and Suriname. Both species are colossal forest trees.

items.name: Diplocaulobium gracilicolle
items.growersTips:
Grow this orchid in a heated greenhouse or warm conservatory with minimum winter temperatures of 12C.
Mount on cork bark or tree fern slabs with a little sphagnum moss to ensure rapid drainage of roots.
Water daily in summer using rainwater, but let the roots dry out completely before nightfall.
Reduce watering to a light misting once a week during the dark, cool UK winter dormant period.
Provide bright, filtered light but shade from direct midday summer sun to prevent leaf scorch.
items.description: Dendrobium is a genus of mostly epiphytic and lithophytic orchids in the family Orchidaceae. It is a very large genus, containing more than 1,800 species that are found in diverse habitats throughout much of south, east and southeast Asia, including China, Japan, India, the Philippines, Indonesia, Australia, New Guinea, Vietnam and many of the islands of the Pacific. Orchids in this genus have roots that creep over the surface of trees or rocks, rarely having their roots in soil. Up to six leaves develop in a tuft at the tip of a shoot and from one to a large number of flowers are arranged alo

items.name: Dipterygeae
items.growersTips:
Sow these tropical annual seeds indoors in April at a depth of two centimeters using a heated mat
Grow in free-draining acidic loam enriched with compost to mimic rainforest floor conditions
Water deeply once a week at the base to keep soil moist but prevent root rot in cool UK summers
Position in your warmest south-facing suntrap or an unheated greenhouse to maximize summer heat
Watch for glasshouse red spider mite under cover and mist leaves regularly to keep humidity high
items.description:
The tribe Dipterygeae is one of the subdivisions of the plant family Fabaceae. It was recently recircumscribed to include the following genera:Dipteryx Schreb.
Monopteryx Spruce ex Benth.
Pterodon Vogel
Taralea Aubl.

items.name: Diseae
items.growersTips:
Plant Disa tubers in a mix of pure peat and perlite, keeping the soil constantly wet with rainwater.
Grow Disa orchids in unheated UK greenhouses to protect them from winter frost while keeping them cool.
Water Disa only with soft rainwater or deionised water to prevent fatal mineral buildup in the soil.
Repot Disa annually in late autumn using plastic pots to maintain the required high root moisture.
Watch for aphids on emerging Disa flower spikes in spring and treat immediately with organic sprays.
items.description: Diseae is an orchid tribe in the subfamily Orchidoideae. It was recognized in Genera Orchidacearum volume 2, which was published in 2001. It consisted of 12 genera in five subtribes. In molecular phylogenetic studies that were published after 1999, it was shown that Diseae is paraphyletic over the tribe Orchideae. In a classification of orchids that was published in 2015, Diseae was not recognized, but was instead placed in synonymy under Orchideae.

items.name: Distemonanthus benthamianus
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender African native in a large pot of acidic loam to move indoors before autumn frosts.
Water deeply only when the top five centimetres of soil dries out to prevent root rot in UK winters.
Prune lightly in late spring after new growth starts to maintain a compact shrub shape in patios.
Position in the sunniest south-facing spot available to mimic its tropical light requirements.
Feed monthly from May to August with a low-nitrogen fertiliser to support its Fabaceae root nodules.
items.description: Distemonanthus is a genus of flowering plants in the family Fabaceae. It belongs to the subfamily Dialioideae. It contains a single species, Distemonanthus benthamianus, a deciduous tree, which occurs widely but sparsely in the forest regions of Tropical West and Central Africa; it is sometimes confused with Pericopsis laxiflora due to similar morphological features.

items.name: Diurideae
items.growersTips:
Grow in a gritty compost of equal parts loam, perlite, and coarse sand to ensure sharp winter drainage.
Keep tubers completely dry during their summer dormancy, restarting watering only in early autumn.
Protect these terrestrial orchids from frost by overwintering pots in a cold greenhouse or frame.
Plant tubers shallowly at a depth of two to three centimetres with the growing tip pointing upwards.
Water thoroughly from autumn to spring, allowing the gritty potting mix to dry out between waterings.
items.description: Diurideae is a tribe of orchid in the subfamily Orchidoideae. The tribe has a centre of diversity in Australia, with occasional dispersals to New Zealand, New Calendonia, Papua New Guinea, and Malesia.

items.name: Diuridinae
items.growersTips:
Grow in a mix of 70% coarse grit and 30% loam to mimic Australian soils in wet UK winters.
Keep tuberoids completely dry from June to August during their mandatory summer dormant phase.
Plant tuberoids 5cm deep in late August to protect them from early autumn frosts in the UK.
Water thoroughly once in autumn to trigger growth, then only when the grit mix is completely dry.
Overwinter pots in a cold greenhouse kept above 2C to prevent freezing while maintaining air flow.
items.description: Diuridinae is an orchid subtribe in the tribe Diurideae.

items.name: Dockrillia wassellii
items.growersTips:
Grow in free-draining bark and perlite in hanging baskets to mimic their natural epiphytic habit.
Water weekly in summer but keep almost dry from November to March to match the dry UK winter light.
Position in a south-facing conservatory or greenhouse to provide the high light they need to flower.
Bring indoors by October as these Australian orchids cannot survive UK frosts below five degrees.
Check the pencil-like leaves regularly for mealybugs hiding in the tight crevices between stems.
items.description: Dendrobium section Rhizobium is a section of the genus Dendrobium.

items.name: × Doritaenopsis
items.growersTips:
Position your orchid on a bright east or west windowsill to avoid the harsh UK summer midday sun.
Water only when the roots turn silvery-grey, using tepid rainwater to avoid tap water limescale.
Repot every two years in coarse pine bark to prevent root rot in damp, cool British winters.
Maintain a minimum room temperature of fifteen degrees Celsius and avoid cold draughty windows.
Feed weekly with a weak orchid fertiliser during summer, then flush with pure rainwater monthly.
items.description: × Doritaenopsis was a genus of artificial hybrids first formally described in 1935 by André Guillaumin in the Archives du Muséum national d'histoire naturelle. The name was intended for hybrids involving Doritis and Phalaenopsis. As of May 2026, Doritis was considered to be a synonym of Phalaenopsis, so plants placed in × Doritaenopsis belong in Phalaenopsis.

items.name: Austrian leopard's bane
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist but well-drained soil in partial shade to mimic UK woodland edge conditions.
Sow seeds shallowly at a depth of two millimetres in early spring under glass or cold frames.
Water regularly during dry spring spells to prevent the shallow root system from drying out.
Watch for slugs and snails in damp UK springs as they quickly destroy the emerging young foliage.
Deadhead faded yellow daisy flowers weekly in late spring to encourage a second flush of blooms.
items.description: Doronicum is a genus of flowering plants in the sunflower family, known as leopard's bane. They are all herbaceous perennials native to Europe, southwest Asia and Siberia. They produce yellow, daisy-like flowerheads in spring and summer. The plants typically thrive in cool, mountainous regions and prefer well-drained soil with partial to full sunlight exposure. Due to their bright and vibrant flowers, Doronicum species are often cultivated as ornamental plants in gardens, particularly for early-season color.

items.name: Drakaeinae
items.growersTips:
Grow hammer orchids in a cold greenhouse with free-draining, gritty, low-nutrient terrestrial mix.
Water pots from below only during autumn and winter growth, keeping the soil dry during summer dormancy.
Do not fertilise these orchids as their sensitive mycorrhizal fungi partners will be destroyed.
Hand-pollinate the flowers yourself because their specific Australian wasp pollinator is absent in the UK.
Protect emerging autumn shoots from slugs and snails using copper tape around the greenhouse staging.
items.description: Drakaneinae is an orchid subtribe in the tribe Diurideae.

items.name: Drymaria cordata
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at two millimetres deep in early spring once UK frosts have fully passed
Water the soil only when the top two centimetres are dry to prevent root rot in damp UK weather
Hand-pull plants before summer flowering to stop aggressive self-seeding in your garden borders
Grow in gritty loam with added horticultural sand to mimic their native well-drained conditions
Position in full sun to maximise the short summer blooming period typical of this annual herb
items.description:
Drymaria is a genus of plants in the family Caryophyllaceae. It contains many species including these from northeastern Mexico:Drymaria arenarioides
Drymaria coahuilana
Drymaria cordata
Drymaria lyropetala
Drymaria monticola
Drymaria pattersonii
Drymaria pratheri

items.name: Drymaria cordata
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at two millimetres deep in spring once UK frosts pass to ensure germination.
Water the soil only when the top two centimetres are dry to prevent root rot in damp UK climates.
Hand-pull plants before summer flowering to stop aggressive self-seeding in your garden beds.
Grow in well-drained sandy loam with a neutral pH to mimic its preferred natural habitat.
Check regularly for slugs and snails which target the tender young foliage during wet UK springs.
items.description: Drymaria cordata, the tropical chickweed, stangries, West Indian chickweed, or golondrina, is a species of flowering plant in the family Caryophyllaceae. It is native to moist habitats in Latin America and sub-Saharan Africa, and has been introduced to many places in the tropics and subtropics, including the southeast US, the Caribbean, the Indian Subcontinent, southern China, Japan, and a number of islands. It is known as one of the most aggressive weeds of the tropical and subtropical parts of the world.

items.name: Santa Cruz Island liveforever
items.growersTips:
Plant Dudleyas at an angle in gritty soil so winter rain drains out of the delicate rosette center.
Water Dudleyas only from the base during winter to prevent deadly rot in damp UK conditions.
Grow Dudleyas in terracotta pots with fifty percent grit to survive wet UK autumns and winters.
Position Dudleyas in full sun on a south-facing windowsill or unheated greenhouse during winter.
Watch for vine weevil grubs in autumn which destroy the roots of container-grown Dudleyas.
items.description: Dudleya, commonly known as liveforevers, is a genus of rosette-forming succulent plants in the stonecrop family, Crassulaceae, consisting of about ~70 taxa found in southwestern North America and Guadalupe Island. The genus is very morphologically diverse, with species ranging from large evergreen plants to tiny deciduous geophytic plants. The flowers of Dudleya have parts numbered in fives, with the petals arranged in tubular, star-shaped, or bell-shaped forms and, when fruiting, are filled with tiny, crescent-shaped seeds.

items.name: Dudleya abramsii
items.growersTips:
Grow in a gritty, free-draining soil mix of seventy percent grit or perlite to prevent root rot.
Keep in an unheated greenhouse or sunny windowsill to shield from persistent winter wet and frost.
Water only from the base or at the soil level to avoid trapped water rotting the rosette center.
Position in maximum sunlight to maintain the compact rosette form and prevent weak, leggy growth.
Watch for mealybugs in the tight leaf crevices during the dry dormant summer resting period.
items.description: Dudleya abramsii is a species complex of succulent plants native to California and parts of Baja California. There are numerous subspecies, some critically endangered, with varying habits and lifestyles, but most often characterized by a smaller size, yellow flowers, and an affinity for rocky habitats. The subspecies may be polyphyletic.

items.name: Dudleya acuminata
items.growersTips:
Plant in extremely gritty, free-draining soil with fifty percent horticultural grit to prevent rot.
Position in a cold greenhouse or south-facing windowsill to protect from wet UK winters and frosts.
Water only from the base or edge of the pot to keep the delicate white powdery leaf coating intact.
Water sparingly from autumn to spring and keep almost completely dry during summer dormant periods.
Check regularly for vine weevil larvae in the compost and treat with nematodes in late summer.
items.description: Dudleya acuminata is a species of succulent perennial plant in the family Crassulaceae known by common name as the Vizcaino liveforever. A rosette-forming leaf succulent, it has reddish yellow flowers that emerge from April to May. It is native to the Pacific coast of the Vizcaino Desert on the Baja California Peninsula, and on neighboring islands.

items.name: Dudleya anomala
items.growersTips:
Grow in a gritty, free-draining soil mix of equal parts John Innes No. 2, coarse grit, and perlite.
Water only from autumn to spring, keeping the soil completely dry during its summer dormant phase.
Overwinter indoors on a south-facing windowsill or in a heated greenhouse to protect from UK frosts.
Position the plant at a slight angle when potting to prevent water from pooling in the rosette.
Watch for mealybugs in the tight leaf axils during winter and treat immediately with rubbing alcohol.
items.description: Dudleya anomala is a rare species of succulent plant in the family Crassulaceae commonly known as the Todos Santos liveforever. With a dense, cushion-forming habit, this leaf succulent is characterized by elongated stems, slightly sticky leaves, and bell-shaped flowers with white, spreading petals. This species is native to Baja California, Mexico, and is found primarily on islands and one coastal locality.

items.name: Dudleya anthonyi
items.growersTips:
Plant in a terracotta pot using a fifty-fifty mix of loam-free compost and horticultural grit.
Water only from autumn to spring, keeping the rosette completely dry to prevent crown rot.
Overwinter indoors on a south-facing windowsill or in a heated greenhouse to protect from frost.
Watch for vine weevil grubs in winter and treat with systemic nematodes in late summer.
Position in full sun but provide light midday shade during rare hot UK summer heatwaves.
items.description: Dudleya anthonyi is a species of perennial succulent plant known commonly as the San Quintín liveforever. It is endemic to the San Quintín volcanic field, which encompasses the Bahia San Quintín and the adjacent Isla San Martín in Baja California. Dudleya anthonyi is a relatively large rosette-forming succulent and is characterized by its leaves and inflorescences that are coated in a white, chalky powder. It is quite similar to its close relative, the widespread Dudleya pulverulenta, but Dudleya anthonyi is distinguished by its narrower and acute basal leaves and bracts, along with narrower a

items.name: Dudleya arizonica
items.growersTips:
Grow in a gritty loam-free compost with fifty percent horticultural grit to prevent winter wet rot.
Keep in unheated glasshouses or cold frames over winter to protect the powdery leaves from rain damage.
Water only from the base or around the pot edge to avoid washing away the protective white epicuticular wax.
Position in the brightest south-facing spot possible to maintain the compact rosette and red leaf tips.
Propagate by sowing seeds in spring on a sandy surface without covering them as they need light to sprout.
items.description: Dudleya arizonica is a species of perennial succulent plant commonly known as the Arizona chalk dudleya and the Arizona liveforever. A member of the genus Dudleya, this species is characterized by long, red flowers that adorn a waxy rosette of succulent leaves. It resembles a reduced desert form of the more coastal chalk dudleya, Dudleya pulverulenta, but differs in its smaller stature, lower number of leaves, and orientation of the flowers. Native to the southwestern United States and northwestern Mexico, it is widespread in range, but is primarily found in scattered, widely separated localit

items.name: Blochman's dudleya
items.growersTips:
Grow in a gritty alpine mix of two parts horticultural sand to one part loam for winter drainage.
Keep completely dry during summer dormancy from June to September to prevent tuberous root rot.
Position in a cold greenhouse or unheated porch to protect from persistent UK winter wet.
Water sparingly from autumn to spring only when the tiny rosette leaves show signs of wrinkling.
Watch for vine weevil grubs in winter which target the delicate underground tuberous stems.
items.description: Dudleya blochmaniae is a summer-deciduous succulent plant known by the common names Blochman's liveforever or Blochman's dudleya. This species of Dudleya survives part of the year with no aboveground presence, surviving as underground corm-like roots in deciduous months. It is characterized by white, star-shaped and spreading flowers that emerge after sufficient rainfall. It is found along the Pacific coast of the California Floristic Province, from the vicinity of San Luis Obispo in California to Punta Colonet in Baja California.

items.name: Dudleya brevifolia
items.growersTips:
Grow in a gritty, soil-free mix of pumice and perlite to prevent winter wet rot in damp UK climates.
Keep completely dry during summer dormancy from June to August to mimic its native dry season.
Water only from below in autumn and winter, keeping moisture off the delicate, chalky leaves.
Overwinter in a cold greenhouse or bright windowsill to protect from frost and persistent rain.
Plant shallowly with the crown slightly elevated on a bed of pure grit to ensure rapid drainage.
items.description: Dudleya brevifolia, is a rare succulent plant known by the common name short-leaved liveforever, short-leaved dudleya or rarely the Del Mar Hasseanthus. It is an edaphic endemic that only grows on Lindavista formation marine terraces, on surfaces with ironstone nodules. The leaves are deciduous, and disappear after the inflorescence develops. The small white flowers are star-shaped with a yellow center. After flowering, any above ground trace of the plant will disappear, and it survives under the earth with a starch-rich subterranean caudex. Dudleya brevifolia is only found on coastal mesas al

items.name: Britton's dudleya
items.growersTips:
Protect the chalky white powder on leaves by watering only the soil and never touching the foliage
Plant in a gritty soil mix of seventy percent grit or perlite to survive damp UK winters
Keep in a pot to move indoors to a greenhouse or bright windowsill from October to April
Water only when the soil is bone dry from spring to autumn and keep completely dry in winter
Watch for vine weevil grubs in the compost and treat with nematodes in late summer
items.description: Dudleya brittonii, with the common names Britton's dudleya, Britton's liveforever and giant chalk dudleya, is a large succulent plant in the family Crassulaceae, the same genus as jade plants. It is native to the coast of northern Baja California, Mexico. Uniquely, Britton's Dudleya has a green form, or variant of the white form. Both forms of the plant have yellow leaves on a clustered rosette atop a large reddish-purple peduncle. The white form of the plant has a chalky epicuticular wax that reflects light and reacts with water. The green form of the plant is more common and found throughout

items.name: Dudleya candelabrum
items.growersTips:
Grow in a gritty alpine mix with fifty percent pumice or perlite to survive wet UK winters.
Position in a south-facing unheated greenhouse or cold frame to shield from winter rain.
Water only from the base or edge of the pot to keep the powdery white leaf rosette dry.
Keep completely dry during summer dormancy from July to August to prevent root rot.
Inspect leaf crevices regularly for mealybugs which thrive in the dense rosette structure.
items.description: Dudleya candelabrum is a species of succulent plant known by the common names candleholder liveforever or candleholder dudleya. Endemic to California, this species grows wild only on the northern Channel Islands, where it is found in open rocky places and north-facing slopes. It is characterized by thin, spade-shaped green leaves and an inflorescence covered in long, reflexed bracts, with pale yellow flowers. It has been threatened by poachers shipping plants to South Korea.

items.name: Dudleya candida
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender Mexican succulent in a gritty, free-draining loam-based compost with 50% perlite.
Keep the plant completely dry during its summer dormant phase to prevent the roots from rotting.
Water only from the base or side to avoid wetting the powdery white farina on the rosette leaves.
Overwinter indoors on a south-facing windowsill or in a heated greenhouse kept above five degrees.
Plant at an angle in containers so winter rainwater drains away from the crown to prevent rot.
items.description: Dudleya candida is a species of perennial succulent plant in the family Crassulaceae known by the common names Coronados liveforever or chalk rose. It is a rosette-forming, green to white-colored leaf succulent, and in bloom yellow flowers atop red stalks stand above the foliage. It has some visual similarities to the mainland Dudleya brittonii, and has found uses in horticulture as an ornamental plant. It is restricted to the Coronado Islands, an island group off of the extreme northern Baja California coast, visible from the United States.

items.name: Sea lettuce
items.growersTips:
Plant in a gritty soil mix of two parts horticultural sand to one part peat-free compost for drainage.
Position in a terracotta pot on a south-facing windowsill to protect from winter wet and frost.
Water only when the soil is bone dry from spring to autumn, keeping the central rosette completely dry.
Check the tight lower leaves weekly for mealybugs and remove them using a cotton bud dipped in alcohol.
Avoid outdoor winter planting in the UK as cold rain causes fatal root rot in this coastal succulent.
items.description: Dudleya caespitosa is a succulent plant known by several common names, including sea lettuce, sand lettuce, and coast dudleya. It is endemic to California, where it grows along the coastline in the southern half of the state. Taxonomically, this species is a highly variable complex of polymorphic and polyploid plants, closely related to numerous neighboring species such as Dudleya farinosa, Dudleya greenei and Dudleya palmeri. It is delimited from neighboring species on an arbitrary basis of distribution and chromosome number, and may not be immediately separable from the other species it appr

items.name: Dudleya chasmophyta
items.growersTips:
Grow in a gritty, free-draining alpine compost mix with fifty percent horticultural grit or perlite.
Keep completely dry in winter by overwintering in an unheated greenhouse or cold frame to avoid rot.
Water only from autumn to spring during its active growth, avoiding the central rosette to prevent rot.
Plant at an angle in a rock crevice or terracotta pot to mimic its natural vertical cliff habitat.
Watch for mealybugs in the tight leaf rosettes during dry spring spells and treat with alcohol.
items.description: Dudleya chasmophyta, commonly known as the Santiago Canyon liveforever or the crevice live-forever, is a rare succulent endemic to Orange County, California. It is known from a single population occupying a steep cliff band. When first classified this population was originally lumped with Dudleya cymosa ssp. ovatifolia, but genomic testing led to Dudleya chasmophyta's confirmation as a separate species in 2024. It has yellow flowers and blooms late spring - early summer.

items.name: Dudleya cymosa
items.growersTips:
Plant it sideways in a rock crevice or wall to prevent water collecting in the rosette and rotting.
Grow in a container with fifty percent grit to survive wet UK winters and move under glass by November.
Water only when the soil is bone dry from spring to autumn and keep completely dry during winter.
Watch for vine weevil grubs in autumn and treat with nematodes to protect the delicate root system.
Position in full south-facing sun to mimic its native California cliffs and maintain leaf colour.
items.description: Dudleya cymosa is a species complex of evergreen and deciduous succulent plants in the family Crassulaceae known by the common name: canyon liveforever. It is a loosely defined polyphyletic species with a diverse number of subspecies, varying highly in morphology, distribution, and habitat.

items.name: Dudleya densiflora
items.growersTips:
Grow in a gritty, free-draining cactus compost mix with fifty percent perlite or horticultural grit.
Water only from the base or soil level in summer to prevent water collecting in the leaf rosette.
Keep completely dry in winter by overwintering indoors or in a greenhouse to prevent frost rot.
Position in full sun on a south-facing windowsill or unheated glasshouse to maintain white farina.
Watch for mealybugs in the tight leaf crevices and treat immediately with an isopropyl alcohol swab.
items.description: Dudleya densiflora is a species of succulent plant in the family Crassulaceae known commonly as the San Gabriel Mountains liveforever or San Gabriel Mountains dudleya. A very rare plant confined to the San Gabriel Mountains of Los Angeles County, California, it is known only from three to five spots in the mountain range, with an estimated 1,700 individual plants remaining. Growing in the cracks of the granite slopes of three canyons in this single mountain range, it is threatened by human activity such as rock quarrying and off-trail recreation.

items.name: Ladies' fingers
items.growersTips:
Grow in a free-draining mix of two parts grit to one part loam to prevent winter wet root rot.
Keep in a cold greenhouse or sunny windowsill over winter as this species cannot tolerate UK frosts.
Water only when the potting mix is bone dry from autumn to spring, keeping the foliage dry.
Position in a south-facing unshaded spot to mimic its native Californian sun exposure.
Watch for mealybugs in the tight leaf axils and treat immediately with organic insecticidal soap.
items.description: Dudleya edulis is a species of perennial, succulent flowering plant of the Crassulaceae, known by the common names fingertips, lady-fingers, mission lettuce, or simply the San Diego dudleya. The common name "fingertips" denotes the finger-like shape of the leaves; the specific epithet edulis refers to the Kumeyaay people's traditional foraging and consumption of the plant's young scapes. Dudleya edulis is native to the dry, coastal cliffs and chaparral hills of Southern California and northern Baja California, where it has adapted to absorb as much moisture as possible from the nightly fog and

items.name: Bluff lettuce
items.growersTips:
Plant in a gritty, free-draining mix of equal parts John Innes No. 2, coarse grit, and perlite.
Tilt the pot slightly when planting to prevent winter rain from pooling in the central rosette.
Keep the plant completely dry in winter by overwintering it in an unheated, frost-free greenhouse.
Water only from the base or edge of the pot to avoid washing away the delicate white powdery wax.
Watch for vine weevil grubs in autumn and treat with nematodes to protect the shallow root system.
items.description: Dudleya farinosa is a species of succulent plant in the family Crassulaceae known by several common names, including bluff lettuce, powdery liveforever, and powdery dudleya. A coastal plant of northern California and southern Oregon, it is typically found on ocean bluffs just directly above the reach of the waves, and sometimes inland. Its appearance is characterized by lotus-like rosettes of beveled leaves, and in summer the plant erects a tall pink to red peduncle densely covered in bracts, topped with branches of pale yellow flowers. The green or white rosettes of this plant can be seen cov

items.name: Dudleya gnoma
items.growersTips:
Grow in a gritty, free-draining loam-based compost with fifty percent horticultural grit or pumice.
Keep completely dry in winter by overwintering under glass in a cold greenhouse or bright windowsill.
Water only from the base or edge of the pot to avoid wetting the powdery white farina on the leaves.
Position in full sun on a south-facing patio during summer to maintain its compact rosette form.
Watch for mealybugs hiding in the tight lower leaves and treat immediately with organic insect spray.
items.description: Dudleya gnoma is a rare species of succulent plant in the stonecrop family known by the common names munchkin liveforever and munchkin dudleya. It is characterized by its diminutive stature, small yellow flowers, and distinctive white rosettes. It is endemic to the eastern portion of Santa Rosa Island, one of the Channel Islands of California, where it is known from one population at the type locality, containing three colonies of plants.

items.name: Greene's liveforever
items.growersTips:
Grow in a gritty loam-based compost with fifty percent horticultural grit to prevent winter rot.
Keep in unheated glasshouses or cold frames over winter to shield from persistent UK rain.
Water only from the base or edge of the pot to avoid washing away the delicate white leaf powder.
Check weekly in spring for aphids and mealybugs hiding deep within the tight, powdery rosettes.
Position in the brightest south-facing spot possible to maintain the compact, chalky growth habit.
items.description: Dudleya greenei is a perennial species of succulent plant known by the common names Greene's liveforever, or Greene's dudleya. It is endemic to the Channel Islands of California, where it grows along the cliffs of four of the eight islands. It is a highly variable plant, presenting with multiple forms and varying levels of ploidy. Taxonomically, this species is an insular segregate of Dudleya caespitosa, and was placed as a stopgap taxon by Reid Moran in his 1951 thesis on the genus. It is characterized by white or green leaf rosettes, loomed over by inflorescences bearing pale yellow to white

items.name: Dudleya hendrixii
items.growersTips:
Grow this winter-active succulent in a gritty, free-draining mix of 70% pumice to prevent root rot.
Keep dry in summer dormancy and water sparingly from October to April when the plant actively grows.
Overwinter indoors on a south-facing windowsill or in a heated greenhouse to protect from UK frost.
Avoid wetting the chalky, powdery leaves when watering to prevent fungal rot in damp UK winters.
Plant in a terracotta pot tilted slightly to the side to help rain drain quickly from the rosette.
items.description: Dudleya hendrixii is a species of succulent plant known by the common name Hendrix's liveforever. It is a rare endemic restricted to undisturbed habitat near in the vicinity of Punta Colonet, Baja California, Mexico. The species is a small succulent that grows from an underground stem, producing small flowers in late spring to early summer before becoming summer deciduous and dormant. It was discovered in late 2016 by researchers from San Diego State University and the University of California, Santa Cruz, and is named in honor of the late musician Jimi Hendrix.

items.name: Dudleya ingens
items.growersTips:
Bring indoors to a frost-free greenhouse or windowsill from October to April to prevent winter rot.
Plant in a gritty, free-draining mix of two parts horticultural sand to one part peat-free compost.
Water only from the base or tilt the pot to avoid getting water trapped in the powdery rosette.
Position in a south-facing spot to maximize summer sun and maintain the white powdery farina coat.
Check weekly for mealybugs nestled deep within the tightly packed lower leaves during warm weather.
items.description: Dudleya ingens is a species of perennial succulent plant in the family Crassulaceae commonly known as the rock liveforever or Baja liveforever. A relatively large member of the genus Dudleya, this species has long green succulent leaves, and in April to June is characterized by pale yellow to white pink-tinged flowers topping tall, reddish inflorescences. It has a stem clothed densely with old, leathery leaves, and the inflorescence may be nodding, with the floral branches bearing the flowers tending to unfurl like the fronds of a fern. It is similar in appearance to Dudleya brittonii, but dif

items.name: Dudleya lanceolata
items.growersTips:
Grow in a gritty loam-based compost with fifty percent horticultural grit to prevent winter wet rot.
Keep in unheated glasshouses or cold frames from October to April to shield from heavy UK rainfall.
Water only when the soil is bone dry from spring to autumn, keeping the central rosette completely dry.
Position in the sunniest south-facing spot possible to mimic its native hot Californian hillsides.
Watch for vine weevil grubs in autumn and treat with nematodes to protect the delicate root system.
items.description: Dudleya lanceolata is a succulent plant known by the common name lanceleaf liveforever or lance-leaved dudleya. It is an extremely variable and widely ranging species that occurs from Monterey County and Kern County in California south through Ensenada in Baja California. It is characterized by green to purple lanceolate leaves, red, orange, or less commonly yellow petals, and is typically tetraploid. Despite its diversity, it is quite stable as a species, but hybrids may be discovered with other species of Dudleya, which can make it difficult to discern in areas where numerous species converg

items.name: Dudleya multicaulis
items.growersTips:
Plant in a gritty cactus compost with fifty percent perlite or horticultural sand to prevent rot.
Keep dry in winter by overwintering under glass or on a bright indoor windowsill to avoid UK damp.
Water sparingly from autumn to spring during its active growth but keep almost dry in summer dormancy.
Watch for vine weevil larvae in the roots and mealybugs nestled in the dense, narrow leaf rosettes.
Position in full south-facing sun to mimic its native Californian chaparral heat and light levels.
items.description: Dudleya multicaulis is a succulent plant known by the common name manystem liveforever or many-stemmed dudleya. This Dudleya is endemic to southern California, where it is rare and seriously threatened as its habitat is altered by humans. Many occurrences of this species have been extirpated. This species is characterized by a few short, fingerlike cylindrical leaves with pointed tips, and its erect peduncle, which is topped with a branching inflorescence bearing up to 15 flowers on each long, thin branch. The flowers, which appear in late spring, have pointed yellow petals and long stamens. I

items.name: Dudleya nesiotica
items.growersTips:
Grow in a gritty, free-draining loam-based compost with fifty percent horticultural grit or perlite.
Water only from autumn to spring, keeping the plant completely dry during its summer dormancy phase.
Overwinter indoors on a sunny windowsill or in a heated greenhouse to protect from freezing wet.
Position in a terracotta pot to help moisture evaporate quickly and prevent fatal root rot.
Watch for mealybugs in the tight leaf rosettes during the damp UK winter and treat with alcohol.
items.description: Dudleya nesiotica is a very rare succulent plant known by the common name Santa Cruz Island liveforever. This Dudleya is endemic to Santa Cruz Island, one of the Channel Islands of California. This is a squat plant growing in mats on the rocky, exposed ground of the windswept island. It is a federally listed threatened species.

items.name: Dudleya nubigena
items.growersTips:
Grow in a gritty, free-draining cactus compost mix with fifty percent perlite or horticultural grit.
Keep completely dry in winter and water only from below in spring and summer to avoid crown rot.
Overwinter indoors on a south-facing windowsill or in a heated greenhouse to protect from UK frost.
Watch for mealybugs in the tight leaf rosettes and treat immediately with an isopropyl alcohol spray.
Position in maximum UK sunlight to maintain the protective white powdery farina coating on leaves.
items.description: Dudleya nubigena is a species of succulent plants in the family Crassulaceae. It is a rosette forming perennial with flattish leaves. Endemic to southern Baja California Sur, the species is found in the Sierra de la Laguna and the surrounding lowlands, a small southern portion of the Sierra de la Giganta, and on Isla Espíritu Santo, with a subspecies endemic to Cerralvo Island.

items.name: Dudleya pachyphytum
items.growersTips:
Keep this Mexican succulent in a gritty, free-draining soil mix of seventy percent pumice or grit.
Water only from the base or edge of the pot to keep the powdery white farina on the leaves dry.
Overwinter indoors on a south-facing windowsill or heated greenhouse to protect from UK frosts.
Position in a terracotta pot to help moisture evaporate quickly and prevent deadly root rot.
Watch for mealybugs hiding in the tight leaf rosettes during the damp UK autumn and winter months.
items.description: Dudleya pachyphytum is an insular succulent plant known by the common name Cedros Island liveforever. It is a member of the genus Dudleya, in the family Crassulaceae. Characterized by thick, blunt leaves covered in a white, powdery wax and adorned by white flowers in bloom, it is regarded as one of the most attractive and charismatic members of its genus. It is endemic to the foggy northern end of Mexico's Cedros Island, occupying an ecological niche shared with the Cedros Island Pine.

items.name: Dudleya palmeri
items.growersTips:
Grow in a gritty loam-based compost with fifty percent horticultural grit to prevent winter wet rot.
Position in a terracotta pot on a south-facing patio to maximise summer sun and allow fast drying.
Water only from the base or edge of the pot to keep the powdery rosette leaves dry and rot-free.
Bring indoors to a frost-free greenhouse or unheated windowsill from November to March in the UK.
Watch for mealybugs nestled deep within the tight leaf rosettes during the dry winter dormancy.
items.description: Dudleya palmeri is a species of succulent plant in the family Crassulaceae known by the common name Palmer's liveforever. This Dudleya is endemic to California where it grows along the coast. It is characterized by orange to red over yellow or pink flowers. It is a polyploid species that closely resembles Dudleya lanceolata but has a coastal habit, and hybridizes with Dudleya caespitosa and Dudleya cymosa.

items.name: Dudleya parva
items.growersTips:
Grow in a gritty loam-based compost with fifty percent horticultural grit to prevent winter rot.
Keep in unheated glasshouses or cold frames over winter to shield from persistent UK rain.
Water sparingly from autumn to spring during its active winter growth and keep dry in summer.
Position in full south-facing sun to maintain its compact rosette shape and pale green colour.
Watch for vine weevil grubs in the roots and treat with nematodes in late summer or spring.
items.description: Dudleya parva, known by the common name Conejo dudleya, is a species of deciduous succulent plant native to the Conejo Valley and surrounding regions. It blooms from May to June, and has vernal leaves. It is only found from the western end of Simi Hills along the Montclef Ridge to the Conejo Grade in Newbury Park.

items.name: Dudleya pulverulenta
items.growersTips:
Keep this chalky succulent in a pot so you can move it under glass to protect from wet UK winters.
Water only from the base or around the pot rim to avoid washing off the delicate white leaf powder.
Plant in a gritty, free-draining mix of equal parts John Innes number two, horticultural sand and grit.
Tilt the rosette slightly at an angle when planting to prevent winter rainwater pooling in the crown.
Position on a south-facing windowsill or unheated greenhouse to maximise essential UK sunlight hours.
items.description: Dudleya pulverulenta is a species of perennial succulent plant known by the common names chalk lettuce, chalk dudleya, and chalk liveforever. It is one of the largest Dudleya, with a silvery, waxy rosette that may greatly contrast with its habitat. It is also regarded as one of the most distinctive members of the Dudleya, with one of the most specialized inflorescences in the genus, adapted to hummingbird pollination through its red pendent flowers, the longest corolla, and the highest nectar output. Dudleya pulverulenta has the largest range of all Dudleya, over 1,000 kilometres (620 mi), bei

items.name: Dudleya rigida
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender succulent in a gritty, free-draining loam-based compost with fifty percent grit.
Keep plants completely dry in winter by overwintering them in a frost-free greenhouse or indoors.
Water only from the base or edge of the pot to avoid rotting the delicate, powdery leaf rosettes.
Position in the brightest possible spot, such as a south-facing windowsill or a sunny glasshouse.
Watch closely for mealybugs hiding deep within the tightly packed lower leaves during dry spells.
items.description: Dudleya rigida is a species of succulent perennial plant in the family Crassulaceae known commonly as the La Laguna liveforever. Characterized by a tall inflorescence with pendant yellowish-red flowers, it is a very rare plant whose existence was doubtful until botanist Reid Moran accidentally re-discovered it. It is endemic to the highest peaks of the Sierra de la Laguna in Baja California Sur, Mexico.

items.name: Dudleya rubens
items.growersTips:
Plant in a gritty, free-draining loam-free compost mix with fifty percent horticultural grit.
Position in a cold greenhouse or unheated porch to protect the powdery farina from winter rain.
Water only from the base or side during spring and autumn to prevent crown rot in wet UK weather.
Keep completely dry throughout the dormant summer months and the freezing depths of winter.
Watch for vine weevil grubs in autumn by checking roots if the rosette becomes loose in its pot.
items.description: Dudleya rubens is a species of succulent perennial plant in the family Crassulaceae known by the common name as the San Francisco liveforever, native to the mountains of Baja California Sur, Mexico. It is a rosette-forming plant with waxy leaves, characterized by branching stems and dull red to apricot flowers. It is only found above 500 metres (1,600 ft) in the Sierra de San Francisco and the Sierra de la Giganta ranges in Baja California Sur, primarily on north-facing volcanic slopes.

items.name: Dudleya saxosa
items.growersTips:
Grow in a gritty, free-draining loam-less compost mix with fifty percent horticultural grit or pumice.
Keep completely dry in winter by overwintering under glass in a cold greenhouse or bright windowsill.
Water only from autumn to spring during its active winter growth, avoiding the central rosette.
Plant at a tilted angle in rock crevices or containers to prevent water collecting in the crown.
Position in the sunniest south-facing spot possible to maintain the protective white powdery wax.
items.description: Dudleya saxosa is a perennial succulent plant species in the family Crassulaceae, within the genus Dudleya, which are commonly known as liveforevers. This species is a complex of 3 subspecies of plants, isolated and disjunct in distribution from one another, each with varying levels of ploidy and morphology. One plant is native throughout the deserts and mountains of Southern California, another is found in the Panamint Mountains, and one is found throughout central Arizona.

items.name: Dudleya setchellii
items.growersTips:
Grow in a gritty loam-based compost with fifty percent horticultural grit to prevent winter wet rot
Position in a terracotta pot on a south-facing windowsill or unheated greenhouse to avoid UK frost
Water only when the soil is bone dry from spring to autumn and keep completely dry during winter
Keep water off the powdery rosette leaves to prevent fungal decay in the damp British climate
Watch for vine weevil grubs in the compost and treat with nematodes in late summer or early autumn
items.description: Dudleya abramsii subsp. setchellii, known by common name as the Santa Clara Valley dudleya or Santa Clara Valley liveforever, is a member of the Dudleya genus of succulent perennials, members of the family Crassulaceae. The Santa Clara Valley dudleya, endemic to the Santa Clara Valley region in the southern San Francisco Bay Area, was listed on 3 February 1995, as an endangered species. It is considered to be a subspecies of Dudleya abramsii, but its taxonomic status is still unclear. Its closest relative is Dudleya cymosa subsp. paniculata, which is a morphologically similar sister taxon.

items.name: Dudleya stolonifera
items.growersTips:
Grow in a gritty, free-draining soil mix of two parts pumice or grit to one part peat-free compost.
Position in a cold greenhouse or south-facing porch to protect from persistent winter wet and frost.
Water only from the base or pot edge during autumn and spring, keeping the rosette completely dry.
Keep the plant bone dry throughout its summer dormant phase to prevent stem rot and root loss.
Inspect the tight leaf crevices regularly for mealybugs, treating immediately with rubbing alcohol.
items.description: Dudleya stolonifera is a succulent plant known by the common name Laguna Beach liveforever or Laguna Beach dudleya. This is a rare plant which is endemic to the coastline of Orange County, California. It is known from only about six populations in the vicinity of Laguna Beach, totaling about 30,000 individuals. It is federally listed as a threatened species of the United States.

items.name: Dudleya traskiae
items.growersTips:
Bring indoors to a frost-free greenhouse or windowsill from October to April to prevent winter rot.
Plant in a gritty, free-draining mix of two parts horticultural sand to one part peat-free compost.
Water only from below or around the base to keep the powdery white rosette leaves completely dry.
Position in your brightest south-facing spot to mimic its native Californian island sun exposure.
Watch for mealybugs hiding deep within the tight leaf rosettes during the warm summer months.
items.description: Dudleya traskiae is a rare succulent plant known by the common name Santa Barbara Island liveforever. Dudleya is endemic to Santa Barbara Island, one of the Channel Islands of California, where it grows on rocky bluffs. The plant has a basal rosette of flat, spade-shaped fleshy leaves up to 15 centimeters long, which are pale green to yellowish. It erects tall stems bearing dense, rounded inflorescences of many bright yellow flowers.

items.name: Dudleya variegata
items.growersTips:
Grow in a gritty loam-based compost with fifty percent horticultural grit to prevent winter wet rot.
Water only from the base or edge of the pot to avoid trapping moisture in the delicate leaf rosette.
Overwinter indoors on a south-facing windowsill or in a heated greenhouse to protect from UK frost.
Watch for vine weevil grubs in autumn which target the roots of these small succulent rosettes.
Position in a terracotta pot to help the soil dry out quickly during damp British summer spells.
items.description: Dudleya variegata is a deciduous succulent plant in the family Crassulaceae known by the common names variegated liveforever, variegated dudleya or rarely San Diego Hasseanthus. A cryptic plant that survives part of the year dormant underground from starch reserves in a corm, after sufficient rainfall, leaves will emerge, soon giving way to small inflorescences with yellow star-shaped flowers. It is native to Baja California and adjacent San Diego County in California, where it grows in several habitat types, including chaparral and vernal pools.

items.name: Dudleya verityi
items.growersTips:
Grow in a gritty, free-draining soil mix of two parts pumice or grit to one part peat-free compost.
Keep completely dry during summer dormancy from June to August to prevent root rot in UK humidity.
Overwinter indoors on a south-facing windowsill or in a heated greenhouse to protect from wet frost.
Water only from autumn to spring when the soil dries out completely, avoiding the central rosette.
Watch for mealybugs in the tight leaf clusters and treat immediately with an organic neem spray.
items.description: Dudleya verityi is a rare species of succulent plant known by the common name Verity's liveforever. It is endemic to Ventura County, California, where it is known from only three occurrences in the vicinity of Conejo Mountain between Camarillo and Thousand Oaks. It probably occurs in a few additional locations nearby which have not yet been officially vouchered.

items.name: Dudleya virens
items.growersTips:
Plant in a 50% grit and loam mix to survive wet UK winters, keeping the crown above the soil level.
Water only from the bottom or at the base during winter to prevent fatal rot in the central rosette.
Overwinter indoors or under a rain shelter as this succulent cannot tolerate wet UK winter freezes.
Position in full south-facing sun to maintain the bright white powdery farina coating on leaves.
Watch for mealybugs in the tight leaf crevices during spring and treat with organic insecticidal soap.
items.description: Dudleya virens, the green liveforever or bright green dudleya, is an uncommon species of perennial, succulent plant in the family Crassulaceae, native to several coastal southern California and Baja California locations.

items.name: Dudleya viscida
items.growersTips:
Grow in a gritty, free-draining loam-based mix with fifty percent horticultural grit or perlite.
Keep completely dry in winter by sheltering under glass to prevent fatal rot from cold UK rain.
Water lightly from autumn to spring during its active winter growth, avoiding the central rosette.
Position in a terracotta pot on a south-facing patio for maximum summer sun and essential drainage.
Watch for mealybugs in the tight, sticky leaves and treat immediately with organic insecticidal soap.
items.description: Dudleya viscida is a rare succulent plant known by common name as the sticky liveforever, sticky dudleya or the San Juan stylophyllum. It is endemic to California, where it is found on rocky slopes. It is unique among the genus Dudleya in that it has sticky, fragrant leaves, a trait only shared with Dudleya anomala.

items.name: Dupuya
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in April at 2cm depth, then transplant outside in late May after the last frost.
Grow in a south-facing border with free-draining sandy soil to mimic its native dry habitat.
Water deeply once a week at the base during dry summer spells, avoiding any waterlogged soil.
Protect young spring shoots from slugs and snails using beer traps or physical copper barriers.
Support the climbing stems with a sturdy hazel wigwam or trellis as soon as tendrils appear.
items.description: Cordyla is a genus of flowering plants in the family Fabaceae. It includes seven species native to sub-Saharan Africa, ranging across northern Africa from Senegal to Somalia, and through eastern Africa from Sudan to KwaZulu-Natal, including Madagascar.

items.name: Echeandia reflexa
items.growersTips:
Plant tubers five centimeters deep in autumn using extremely free-draining gritty soil to avoid rot
Provide a dry winter mulch or move potted plants into a cold greenhouse to survive wet UK frosts
Water moderately during the active summer growing season but keep completely dry throughout winter
Position in your warmest south-facing border to maximise the sun needed for late summer flowering
Grow alongside hardy succulents or sedums which share its requirement for low-nutrient sharp drainage
items.description: Echeandia reflexa is a species of flowering plant in the family Asparagaceae from south Texas through Mexico to Honduras. It was first described by Antonio José Cavanilles in 1795 as Anthericum reflexum and moved to Echeandia by Joseph Nelson Rose in 1906. It is placed in the subfamily Agavoideae.

items.name: Echium
items.growersTips:
Plant in gritty, free-draining soil in full sun to prevent winter root rot in wet UK climates.
Sow seeds shallowly in summer and overwinter young rosettes in a cold frame to protect from frost.
Wrap the central crown of Echium pininana with fleece in late autumn to survive British winters.
Leave faded flower spikes intact over winter to allow self-seeding for a continuous biennial cycle.
Watch for slugs and snails on young spring rosettes and clear damp debris from around the base.
items.description: Echium is a genus of flowering plants in the family Boraginaceae that contains about 70 species and several subspecies.

items.name: Echium wildpretii subsp. trichosiphon
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in late spring on the surface of gritty, free-draining compost as they need light to sprout.
Grow in terracotta pots of peat-free compost mixed with one-third grit to ensure winter drainage.
Move pots into a dry, frost-free greenhouse or conservatory from November to March to prevent rot.
Water only when the top two inches of soil are dry, reducing to once a month during winter dormancy.
Position in the absolute sunniest spot of the garden against a south-facing wall to mimic Tenerife.
items.description: Echium wildpretii subsp. trichosiphon is a species of Echium that is found high up in the area of La Caldera de Taburiente on the Canary Island of La Palma. Like its sister plant on Tenerife, this plant forms a large rosette of silvery leaves which eventually give rise to tall spikes of bright pink flowers. The plant is biennial and dies after flowering. This plant can be grown in gardens, but requires good drainage and fairly mild conditions. The plant hates water falling in the centre of the rosette and will often rot in such conditions.

items.name: Ecuadendron
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in April at a depth of two centimeters using a heated propagator set to twenty-oneC
Plant out in June after the last frost in a south-facing border with grit added for sharp drainage
Water deeply once a week at the base rather than daily sprinkles to encourage deep taproot growth
Protect young stems from slugs in wet UK summers using copper tape or beer traps around the base
Sow alongside nasturtiums to deter aphids and mask the foliage from common Fabaceae pests
items.description: Ecuadendron is a monotypic genus of flowering plants in the legume family, Fabaceae, containing the single species Ecuadendron acosta-solisianum. It is endemic to Ecuador, where it is known from three populations on the coast. It is threatened because the wood is valuable and it is vulnerable to logging.

items.name: Ehrendorferia
items.growersTips:
Plant Ehrendorferia chrysantha in sharply draining, gritty soil to prevent winter root rot in UK wet.
Sow seeds in autumn outdoors as they require winter cold stratification to germinate in spring.
Water sparingly only during dry summer spells, allowing the soil to dry out completely between waterings.
Position in full sun against a south-facing wall to mimic its native hot, dry Californian chaparral.
Protect young spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.
items.description: Ehrendorferia (eardrops) is a genus of two species of biennial or perennial herbaceous plants native to wildfire-prone areas of California and the Baja California peninsula. It was named after the Austrian botanist Friedrich Ehrendorfer on the occasion of his 70th birthday.

items.name: Ehrendorferia chrysantha
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn using a cold frame to provide the winter chill required for UK germination.
Plant in sharply draining gravelly soil to prevent winter wet from rotting the delicate crown.
Water sparingly only during active spring growth and keep the soil almost dry throughout winter.
Position in full sun against a south-facing wall to mimic its native hot dry chaparral habitat.
Protect young spring shoots from slugs and snails using beer traps or physical copper barriers.
items.description: Ehrendorferia chrysantha, with the common name golden eardrops, is a biennial to perennial plant in the family Papaveraceae.

items.name: Ehrendorferia ochroleuca
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn in a cold frame as they require winter chilling to break dormancy in UK climates
Plant in extremely well-drained gritty soil to prevent root rot during wet British winters
Position in partial shade mimicking its native woodland edge habitat to avoid scorching summer sun
Water sparingly once established allowing the gritty growing medium to dry out completely between wets
Protect young spring shoots from slugs and snails which find the tender poppy foliage highly appealing
items.description: Ehrendorferia ochroleuca, commonly known as white eardrops or yellow bleeding-heart, is a biennial or perennial, native to gravelly areas in the chaparral and woodlands of California and in Baja California.

items.name: Ehretia acuminata
items.growersTips:
Plant in a south-facing, sheltered spot to protect young wood from late UK spring frosts.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells, allowing the soil to dry out between waterings.
Prune in late winter by removing dead wood to maintain a compact shrub habit in small UK gardens.
Incorporate grit and well-rotted manure into heavy clay soils to ensure the free drainage it needs.
Mulch the root zone with bracken or straw in November to insulate roots against wet UK winter cold.
items.description: Ehretia acuminata is a deciduous tree native to regions from India to Japan and south to eastern Australia. It was first described in 1810 and has the conservation status of least concern. In Australia it is commonly known as koda.

items.name: Ehretia alba
items.growersTips:
Plant this tender shrub in a south-facing, sheltered microclimate to protect it from cold UK winds.
Grow in free-draining, gritty loam to prevent root rot during wet, waterlogged British winters.
Prune lightly in late spring after frost risk passes to shape the shrub and remove winter dieback.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells, allowing the soil to dry out between waterings.
Overwinter young specimens in a container kept in a frost-free greenhouse or conservatory.
items.description: Ehretia alba is a semi-deciduous shrub or small tree up to 4m high, growing in Namibia, Botswana and the western, drier regions of South Africa, and was first collected by Hermann Merxmüller at Breitenberg in the Gobabis district of Namibia. As with other species of Ehretia it is twiggy with rigid branches, its fascicled leaves showing a large variation in size, with acute or obtuse apices, and appressed setae along margins. Midribs and secondary veins are prominent on the lower surfaces, while the petioles are only 3 mm long. Leaves are generally clustered or fascicled on abbreviated twigs. F

items.name: Ehretia anacua
items.growersTips:
Plant in a sheltered south-facing spot to protect it from cold UK winds and frost damage.
Use well-drained, gritty soil with added organic matter to prevent winter root rot in wet clay.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells, but keep it dry during damp winter months.
Prune in late spring after the last frost to shape the shrub and remove any winter-damaged wood.
Apply a thick layer of bark mulch around the base in late autumn to insulate roots from hard frost.
items.description: Ehretia anacua is medium-sized tree found in eastern Mexico and southern Texas in the United States. It is a member of the family Ehretiaceae. One of its common names, anacua, is derived from the Mexican Spanish word anacahuite, as is that of the related Cordia boissieri, the anacahuita. That word in turn is derived from the Nahuatl words āmatl, meaning "paper," and cuahuitl, meaning "tree," possibly referring to the bark. It is also known as knockaway, a corruption of anacua, and sandpaper tree. Alternate spellings are anaqua and anachua.

items.name: Ehretia cymosa
items.growersTips:
Plant in a sheltered south-facing spot to protect it from harsh UK winter frosts and cold winds.
Prune in late spring after frost risk passes to remove winter dieback and shape the shrub.
Grow in well-drained loamy soil amended with grit to prevent winter root rot in wet UK climates.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells to establish the root system in its early years.
Watch for aphids on new spring shoots and blast them off with a hose to prevent leaf curl.
items.description: Ehretia cymosa is a small tree belonging to the family Ehretiaceae. It occurs over a wide range of habitat throughout of western, central and eastern Africa, including Benin, Côte d'Ivoire, Cameroon, Ethiopia, Kenya, Comoros, Madagascar, Mascarenes, Zimbabwe and Mozambique.

items.name: Ehretia dicksonii
items.growersTips:
Plant in deep well-drained loamy soil with added grit to protect roots from wet UK winter rot.
Position in a sheltered south-facing spot to shield early summer blooms from cold drying winds.
Prune immediately after flowering in late summer to shape the canopy and remove dead wood.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells until the root system is fully established.
Apply a thick organic mulch in late autumn to insulate the root zone against severe UK frosts.
items.description: Ehretia dicksonii is a tree that is native to Asia and cultivated as an ornamental plant.

items.name: Ehretia laevis
items.growersTips:
Grow in a terracotta pot with grit-heavy loam to easily move it indoors before first autumn frosts.
Water deeply once a week in summer but keep the compost barely damp during its winter indoor rest.
Prune lightly in late spring after flowering to shape the shrub and encourage fresh blooming wood.
Position in the sunniest south-facing spot or against a warm brick wall to mimic its native heat.
Watch for glasshouse red spider mite when overwintering the shrub in a heated conservatory.
items.description: Ehretia aspera is a species of flowering plant belonging to the family Ehretiaceae. It is a small tree native to the Indian subcontinent, Indochina, Peninsular Malaysia, and Hainan. It grows in dry deciduous forests. It flowers and fruits in January and February.

items.name: Ehretia microphylla
items.growersTips:
Grow in a pot with loam-based compost so you can move it indoors before the first autumn frosts.
Water sparingly in winter but keep soil consistently moist during the active spring growing phase.
Prune new shoots back to two leaves in late spring to maintain its compact bonsai-like shape.
Position in your brightest south-facing spot or under glass to meet its high summer light needs.
Check weekly for spider mites and scale insects which thrive in dry indoor winter environments.
items.description: Ehretia microphylla is commonly known as the Fukien tea tree or Philippine tea tree, is a species of flowering plant. The genus Ehretia is placed in the family Ehretiaceae.

items.name: Ehretia rigida
items.growersTips:
Grow in a terracotta pot with grit-heavy loam to easily move it indoors before first autumn frosts.
Water deeply once a week in summer but keep the compost almost completely dry throughout winter.
Prune lightly in late spring after new growth starts to shape the canopy and remove winter dieback.
Position in the hottest, most sheltered south-facing spot or against a brick wall for maximum sun.
Blend equal parts John Innes No 3, coarse grit, and perlite to mimic its native free-draining soil.
items.description: Ehretia rigida, is a small, multi-stemmed tree with a tangled growth habit belonging to the family Ehretiaceae. It occurs over a wide range of habitat throughout the eastern part of South Africa, and in Namibia, Botswana, Zimbabwe and Mozambique.

items.name: Ehretia saligna
items.growersTips:
Grow in a south-facing sheltered spot using well-drained loamy soil with added grit to prevent rot.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells but keep the soil almost dry throughout winter.
Prune lightly in late spring after frosts pass to shape the shrub and remove any winter dieback.
Protect the root zone in winter with a thick dry mulch of bark chips to shield it from UK frosts.
Watch for aphids and spider mites in dry summer weather, washing them off with a sharp water spray.
items.description: Ehretia saligna, commonly known as peach bush, native willow and peachwood is a species of shrubs or small trees, endemic to Northern Australia. The natural range extends from the Gascoyne, across the Northern Territory throughout northern Queensland and coastal; regions of Southern Queensland and New South Wales.

items.name: Ehretia tinifolia
items.growersTips:
Grow in a large pot with grit-heavy loam so you can move it into a heated greenhouse for UK winters.
Water sparingly in winter but keep soil consistently moist during the active spring growing season.
Prune lightly in late spring after frost risk passes to shape the canopy and remove dead wood.
Position in the sunniest, most sheltered south-facing spot possible to mimic its native warmth.
Watch for glasshouse red spider mite and whitefly when overwintering this tender shrub indoors.
items.description: Ehretia tinifolia is a woody, perennial tree, usually 0.5 to 3 m in height, branched from the base, from reddish-brown to red-purple bark, exfoliating ; The leaves are coriaceous, elliptic, from 1 to 3.3 cm long. The flower is urceolate, white to Mexican pink and grouped in clusters of five to eight flowers. The plant can reproduce vegetatively from branches that are buried, but this type of reproduction is rare.

items.name: Eleutherine
items.growersTips:
Plant Eleutherine bulbs 8cm deep in autumn using pots you can move indoors before the first UK frost.
Grow in a gritty loam-based compost mixed with one-third horticultural grit to prevent winter rot.
Water freely during the summer active growth phase but keep the soil almost dry throughout winter.
Position pots against a south-facing brick wall to maximize summer heat and mimic tropical warmth.
Dig up and divide congested clumps every three years in spring just as new green shoots emerge.
items.description: Eleutherine is a genus of herbaceous, perennial and bulbous plants in the family Iridaceae, first described as a genus in 1843. It is native to Latin America and the West Indies.

items.name: Eligmocarpus
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender Madagascan shrub in a large pot of gritty loam to move indoors before autumn frosts.
Water sparingly in winter, allowing the compost to dry out completely between light waterings.
Position in the brightest spot of a heated greenhouse or south-facing conservatory during winter.
Prune lightly in late spring after new growth starts to maintain a compact shape for indoor storage.
Feed monthly from May to August with a low-nitrogen liquid fertiliser to support healthy foliage.
