items.description: Eligmocarpus is a genus of flowering plants in the family Fabaceae. It belongs to subfamily Dialioideae. It contains a single species, Eligmocarpus cynometroides. It is a tree endemic to southeastern Madagascar. Currently, it occurs only on the edge of a relatively humid spiny forest in Petriky. The species is critically endangered, with only 21 adult trees remaining as of 2012, down from 23 in 2004 and 27 in 2001. The surviving trees do have high genetic diversity. The trees' wood is used as timber by local communities, which has contributed heavily to the species' decline. Prior to human col

items.name: Ellisiophyllum pinnatum
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade to mimic its native forest floor habitat.
Water consistently during dry UK summers to keep the soil evenly moist but never waterlogged.
Protect the delicate, creeping stems from slugs and snails during wet spring and autumn weather.
Propagate in spring by dividing the rooted runners and replanting them just below the soil surface.
Grow alongside hostas and ferns in a shady rockery or woodland border as a ground-covering partner.
items.description: Ellisiophyllum is a monotypic genus of flowering plants belonging to the family Plantaginaceae. It contains a single species, Ellisiophyllum pinnatum (Wall. ex Benth.) Makino

items.name: Empetrum nigrum subsp. asiaticum
items.growersTips:
Incorporate plenty of acidic peat-free ericaceous compost and grit to ensure a soil pH below 5.0.
Water only with stored rainwater to prevent tapwater lime from raising soil pH and yellowing leaves.
Plant in full sun to mimic UK moorlands, keeping the root crown exactly level with the soil surface.
Prune lightly in late spring after flowering only to restrict spread and maintain a neat carpet.
Position alongside Calluna vulgaris or Erica carnea which share its need for wet, acidic conditions.
items.description: Empetrum nigrum subsp. asiaticum, the Korean crowberry, is a subspecies of the flowering plant species Empetrum nigrum in the heather family, Ericaceae. The plant is called siromi (시로미) in Korean and gankōran (岩高蘭) in Japanese.

items.name: Engelmannia peristenia
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in March under glass at a depth of three millimetres to protect from early spring frosts
Plant out in May in a south-facing spot with gritty, free-draining soil to prevent winter root rot
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells rather than daily light sprinkles to encourage roots
Deadhead spent yellow blooms weekly from July to October to prolong the flowering season in UK rain
Watch for slugs and snails on young spring shoots by using organic wool pellets around the stems
items.description: Engelmannia peristenia, called Engelmann daisy or cutleaf daisy, is a North American species of flowering plants in the family Asteraceae. It is native to the south-central United States, primarily from Texas, New Mexico, Oklahoma, and southeastern Colorado, but with more isolated populations in Arizona, Louisiana, Arkansas, Missouri, Nebraska, and South Dakota.

items.name: Ennealophus foliosus
items.growersTips:
Grow in pots of loam-based grit mix to easily move them indoors before the first autumn frosts hit.
Plant the small bulbs five centimetres deep in spring once the risk of frost has entirely passed.
Water freely during the summer active growth phase but keep the soil completely dry during winter.
Watch for red spider mites when keeping them in a greenhouse or conservatory over the winter months.
Position in the sunniest south-facing spot of your garden to mimic their native South American heat.
items.description: Ennealophus is a genus of perennial, herbaceous and bulbous plants in the family Iridaceae. It consists in five species distributed from Ecuador to Northern Brazil and Northwest Argentina. The genus name is derived from the Greek words ennea, meaning "nine", and lophus, meaning "crest".

items.name: Eomecon chionantha
items.growersTips:
Plant this invasive poppy in a submerged container to restrict its rapidly spreading underground runners.
Grow in moist organic soil under dappled shade to mimic its native woodland edge habitat in the UK.
Water weekly during dry UK summers to keep the soil consistently damp and prevent the leaves browning.
Protect the tender emerging spring shoots from slug damage using beer traps or organic pellets.
Propagate in autumn by lifting the shallow rhizomes and cutting them into five centimetre sections.
items.description: Eomecon is a monotypic genus of flowering plants in the poppy family containing the single species Eomecon chionantha. Its common names include snow-poppy and dawn-poppy. It is native to China.

items.name: Epacris impressa
items.growersTips:
Plant in ericaceous compost mixed with grit to mimic the acidic sandstone soils of their native home
Water only with rainwater as tap water contains calcium which will quickly kill these acid lovers
Grow in pots to easily move them into a frost-free greenhouse or conservatory for winter protection
Prune stems back by half immediately after spring flowering to prevent the shrub from becoming leggy
Position in full sun but shelter from cold drying winds which scorch the delicate heath-like foliage
items.description: Epacris is a genus of about forty species of flowering plants in the family Ericaceae. It was formerly treated in a closely related but separate family Epacridaceae, but the various genera within Epacridaceae including Epacris have been revised in their relationships to each other and brought under the common umbrella of the Ericaceae. The genus Epacris is native to eastern and southeastern Australia, and New Zealand. The species are known as heaths or Australian heaths.

items.name: Eperua bijuga
items.growersTips:
Grow Eperua in a heated conservatory or greenhouse as it cannot survive UK winter frosts outdoors
Use a highly acidic sandy loam soil mix with added perlite to mimic its native tropical riverbanks
Water with tepid rainwater only keeping the soil consistently damp but never waterlogged or soggy
Prune lightly in late spring after new growth begins to maintain shape and remove dead wood
Monitor closely for glasshouse red spider mites and mealybugs under warm indoor UK conditions
items.description:
Eperua is a genus of flowering plants in the legume family, Fabaceae. It belongs to subfamily Detarioideae. It includes 16 species native to northern South America, in Colombia, Venezuela, the Guianas, and northern Brazil. They live in the jungles, often along rivers or streams. The leaves are compound pinnate, with smooth margins, and the fruits are long pods. The wood of E. falcata is called wallaba and is often used in construction.Eperua banaensis G.A.Romero & Aymard
Eperua bijuga Mart. ex Benth.
Eperua duckeana R.S.Cowan

items.name: Epidendreae
items.growersTips:
Grow cool-growing Masdevallia in moisture-retentive sphagnum moss, never letting the medium dry out.
Position Epidendrum radicans in south-facing UK conservatories to ensure the high light they need.
Overwinter potted Pleione pseudobulbs completely dry in a frost-free shed at five degrees Celsius.
Repot Coelogyne cristata in coarse bark only when the pseudobulbs spill over the container edge.
Water Restrepia with harvested rainwater to prevent mineral salt buildup on their sensitive roots.
items.description: The tribe Epidendreae of the Orchidaceae, within the subfamily Epidendroideae, includes six subtribes, approximately 120 genera, and over 6,000 species. Popular among orchid collectors, it features well-known genera such as Laelia, Cattleya, and Encyclia, as well as smaller species like Dracula, Dryadella, Masdevallia, and Restrepia.

items.name: Epidendroideae
items.growersTips:
Grow UK-hardy Bletilla striata in free-draining loam-grit mix with pseudobulbs just 5cm deep.
Water potted Pleione weekly in active spring growth but keep totally dry and frost-free in winter.
Check indoor Phalaenopsis weekly for mealybugs in leaf axils and treat with organic neem oil spray.
Prune spent Dendrobium nobile flowering canes only when they shrivel to preserve stored nutrients.
Repot Cymbidiums after spring flowering using coarse bark mix to prevent waterlogged winter roots.
items.description: Epidendroideae is a subfamily of plants in the orchid family, Orchidaceae. Epidendroideae is larger than all the other orchid subfamilies together, comprising more than 15,000 species in 576 genera. Most epidendroid orchids are tropical epiphytes, typically with pseudobulbs. There are, however, some terrestrials such as Epipactis and even a few myco-heterotrophs, which are parasitic upon mycorrhizal fungi.

items.name: Epigaea asiatica
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist, acidic, humus-rich soil, mixing in plenty of composted pine needles or leaf mould.
Position in deep or partial shade, mimicking woodland canopies to prevent UK summer leaf scorch.
Water with rainwater rather than tap water to maintain the low soil pH this ericaceous shrub needs.
Apply an annual autumn mulch of leaf mould to protect the shallow root system from hard winter frosts.
Propagate by carefully pegging down low-growing stems in spring to encourage natural layering.
items.description: Epigaea asiatica is a species of flowering plant in the family Ericaceae. It is endemic to Japan. It has pale pink flowers, and seeds that are dispersed by ants.

items.name: Epigaea gaultherioides
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in deep shade, mimicking a cool Scottish woodland floor.
Incorporate composted pine needles and leaf mould into the planting hole to lower soil pH below 5.5.
Water exclusively with soft rainwater to prevent lime-induced chlorosis in hard-water UK areas.
Protect the delicate evergreen foliage from drying winter winds using a physical fleece barrier.
Apply a loose mulch of composted bark annually in spring, keeping it clear of the main stem.
items.description: Epigaea gaultherioides is a species of flowering plant in the Ericaceae family. It is native to Transcaucasia and Turkey.

items.name: May flower(trailing arbutus)
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist acidic soil enriched with pine needles or leaf mould to mimic UK woodland floors.
Position in deep shade under conifers or ericaceous shrubs to prevent strong UK summer sun scorch.
Water with harvested rainwater rather than tap water to maintain the essential low soil pH level.
Avoid digging near the base as this shallow-rooting shrub hates root disturbance once planted.
Protect young spring growth from slugs and snails which thrive in the damp shade this plant loves.
items.description: Epigaea repens, the mayflower, trailing arbutus, or ground laurel, is a low, and spreading shrub in the family Ericaceae. It is found from Newfoundland to Florida, west to Kentucky and into the Northwest Territories. It is the provincial flower of Nova Scotia.

items.name: Epigeneium triflorum
items.growersTips:
Grow this orchid in a slatted basket with coarse bark to prevent root rot in damp UK winters.
Provide bright filtered light but shade from direct summer sun to prevent leaf scorch on windowsills.
Water copiously in summer but reduce watering drastically in winter to match UK seasonal light levels.
Maintain high humidity above fifty percent using gravel trays to counter dry indoor central heating.
Grow in a cool greenhouse or cool room keeping winter night temperatures between ten and twelve Celsius.
items.description: Dendrobium is a genus of mostly epiphytic and lithophytic orchids in the family Orchidaceae. It is a very large genus, containing more than 1,800 species that are found in diverse habitats throughout much of south, east and southeast Asia, including China, Japan, India, the Philippines, Indonesia, Australia, New Guinea, Vietnam and many of the islands of the Pacific. Orchids in this genus have roots that creep over the surface of trees or rocks, rarely having their roots in soil. Up to six leaves develop in a tuft at the tip of a shoot and from one to a large number of flowers are arranged alo

items.name: Great willowherb
items.growersTips:
Deadhead Epilobium angustifolium in August to stop aggressive self-seeding across damp UK borders.
Grow Epilobium canum in gritty, south-facing raised beds to survive wet British winter root rot.
Propagate garden-worthy cultivars by taking soft basal cuttings in spring as new shoots emerge.
Water Epilobium hirsutum deeply once a week in summer to mimic its natural UK riverbank habitat.
Check young spring shoots weekly for flea beetles which skeletonise the foliage in humid weather.
items.description: Epilobium is a genus of flowering plants in the family Onagraceae, containing about 197 species. The genus has a worldwide distribution. It is most prevalent in the subarctic, temperate and subantarctic regions, whereas in the subtropics and tropics Epilobium species are restricted to the cool montane biomes, such as the New Guinea Highlands.

items.name: Epilobium alpestre
items.growersTips:
Grow in moist, humus-rich, acidic to neutral soil to mimic its native UK montane stream habitats.
Position in partial shade or cool sun, avoiding hot south-facing borders that dry out the roots.
Water consistently during dry summer spells to keep the soil constantly damp but never waterlogged.
Cut the faded flowering stems back to the basal rosette in late autumn to keep the plant tidy.
Propagate by dividing the fibrous root clumps in early spring just as new green growth appears.
items.description: Epilobium alpestre is a species of willowherb in the family Onagraceae. It is native to Europe and Asia.

items.name: Chickweed willowherb
items.growersTips:
Plant this alpine native in a permanently wet, acidic scree garden or beside a cold garden stream.
Keep soil constantly saturated using rainwater to mimic its natural wet UK upland spring habitats.
Position in full sun to partial shade but ensure the roots remain chilled during warm summer days.
Propagate by dividing the creeping mats in early spring just as new green shoots begin to emerge.
Control surrounding vigorous weeds manually to prevent this delicate low-growing plant from being smothered.
items.description: Epilobium alsinifolium is a species of willowherb known by the common name chickweed willowherb. This small flowering plant can be found in European arctic regions and further south in mountainous regions with an Arctic climate, as well as in Greenland. It is a perennial found in low clumps approximately 10 to 25 centimeters in height. It has wide, rounded basal leaves and narrower leaves further up the stem. It bears purple or pinkish trumpet-shaped flowers, 7 to 12 millimeters in diameter, and the fruit is a capsule two or three centimeters long.

items.name: Epilobium anagallidifolium
items.growersTips:
Grow in a gritty, acidic peat-free compost mix to mimic wet Scottish mountain scree habitats.
Water constantly from below using rainwater to keep the soil soggy but never stagnant or warm.
Position in a cold, north-facing rockery or alpine trough to protect it from hot UK summer sun.
Propagate by carefully dividing the delicate creeping mats of runners in early spring as growth starts.
Watch for vine weevil grubs in containers which will rapidly destroy the shallow, fragile root system.
items.description: Epilobium anagallidifolium is a species of willowherb known by the common names pimpernel willowherb and alpine willowherb. This small flowering plant has a near-circumboreal distribution and can be found in mountain ranges further south, where grows in alpine climates. It is a perennial found in low clumps rarely exceeding 20 centimeters in height.

items.name: Epilobium brachycarpum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds thinly on the soil surface in spring as they need light to germinate in UK conditions.
Grow in poor, well-drained gravelly soil to prevent this vigorous annual from overwatering.
Deadhead flowers by late summer to stop aggressive self-seeding across your borders and gravel paths.
Position in full sun to mimic its native dry habitat and prevent leggy, weak stem growth.
Pull up excess shallow-rooted seedlings in spring to control spread and leave space for companions.
items.description: Epilobium brachycarpum is a species of willowherb known by the common names tall willowherb, tall annual willowherb, panicled willowherb and tall fireweed. It is native to North America, including Canada from Quebec to British Columbia, the western United States and the Dakotas, and southwestern and Central Mexico. It is a resident of varied open and woodland habitats. It has also been introduced to some areas in South America. This is a tall glandular, hairy annual herb occasionally reaching 2 metres in height. It is somewhat gangly and thin like an erect weed, with narrow, curving, pointed l

items.name: Epilobium canum
items.growersTips:
Plant in sharply draining gritty soil to prevent winter root rot in wet UK climates.
Position in your garden's hottest south-facing border to mimic its native chaparral habitat.
Cut the woody stems back to ground level in early spring just as new green shoots appear.
Water deeply once a week during its first UK summer then leave fully established plants dry.
Protect young spring shoots from slug damage using organic pellets or beer traps.
items.description: Epilobium canum, also known as California fuchsia or Zauschneria, is a species of willowherb in the evening primrose family (Onagraceae). It is native to dry slopes and in chaparral of western North America, especially California. It is a perennial plant, notable for the profusion of bright scarlet flowers in late summer and autumn.

items.name: Purple-leaved willowherb
items.growersTips:
Hand-pull young plants in damp spring soil before the taproot anchors deeply in heavy UK clay.
Sever flower heads by mid-June to stop the explosive wind-dispersed seed pods from colonising lawns.
Smother infested borders with a ten-centimetre layer of bark mulch to block light from seed beds.
Spot-treat stubborn rosettes in gravel paths with a systemic glyphosate spray during dry active growth.
Grow aggressive ground cover like Geranium macrorrhizum to outcompete this weed in damp shady spots.
items.description: Epilobium ciliatum, known by the common names fringed willowherb, American willowherb, slender willow herb, and northern willow herb is a species of flowering plant in the willowherb family Onagraceae. This species is native to much of North America, southern South America, and East Asia. It is an introduced species in much of Eurasia and Australia.

items.name: Epilobium clavatum
items.growersTips:
Plant in sharply draining grit-rich soil to prevent winter crown rot during wet UK winters.
Position in full sun in a rock garden or raised bed to mimic its native alpine scree habitat.
Water sparingly once established, allowing the gritty growing medium to dry out between waterings.
Propagate by taking softwood cuttings in early summer or by dividing the clumps in spring.
Protect young spring shoots from slugs and snails which thrive in damp British garden climates.
items.description: Epilobium clavatum is a species of flowering plant in the evening primrose family known by the common names talus willowherb and clavatefruit willowherb. It is native to western North America from Alaska to northern California to Colorado, where it grows in rocky high mountain habitat such as talus. It is a clumping perennial herb forming bristly mounds up to about 20 centimeters high and spreading outward via tough stolons. The oval-shaped leaves are 1 to 3 centimeters long. The inflorescence is an erect raceme of flowers, each with four small pink petals. The fruit is a capsule up to 4 centi

items.name: Epilobium collinum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn on the surface of gritty, well-drained soil as they require light to germinate.
Water sparingly once established, allowing the top five centimetres of soil to dry out completely.
Cut stems back to ground level in late autumn to prevent self-seeding and maintain a neat habit.
Grow in full sun alongside Campanula rotundifolia to mimic natural UK rocky scree environments.
Hand-pull unwanted seedlings in spring before their deep taproots establish in paving crevices.
items.description: Epilobium collinum is a species of flowering plant belonging to the family Onagraceae.

items.name: Epilobium coloratum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in autumn on damp soil surface as they need winter cold and light to germinate.
Grow in boggy clay or near pond edges to mimic its natural UK wetland habitat and keep soil wet.
Cut back the faded flower spikes in late summer before they release wind-blown seeds across lawns.
Watch for elephant hawk-moth caterpillars in summer which feed heavily on this specific foliage.
Plant alongside native UK moisture-lovers like Caltha palustris to balance its vigorous spread.
items.description: Epilobium coloratum, known by the common names purpleleaf willowherb and cinnamon willow-herb, is a species of flowering plant in the genus Epilobium of the willowherb family Onagraceae. This species is native to the Midwest and Eastern United States, as well as the Canadian provinces of Ontario, Québec, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, and Newfoundland. It is also native to the Dominican Republic and Haiti.

items.name: Epilobium densiflorum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in spring directly onto weed-free, finely raked soil as they need light to germinate.
Water young plants weekly during dry UK summers until established, then leave to tolerate drought.
Grow in poor, well-drained sandy soil to prevent floppy growth and encourage maximum flowering.
Sow alongside native annuals like Clarkia or Gilia to create a cohesive wildflower border display.
Deadhead spent blooms in late summer to prevent aggressive self-seeding across your garden beds.
items.description: Epilobium densiflorum is a species of willowherb known by the common names denseflower willowherb, dense spike-primrose or dense boisduvalia. It is native to western North America from British Columbia to Baja California, where it is found in a variety of habitats. This is an erect annual often exceeding a meter in height with fuzzy green foliage. The pointed leaves are up to 8 centimeters long near the base of the plant, and the upper leaves are generally more hairy than the lower. The stem may branch or not. The top of the stem is occupied by a hairy, leafy, densely flowered inflorescence. E

items.name: Epilobium dodonaei
items.growersTips:
Plant in sharply drained, gritty soil in full sun to mimic its native alpine gravel riverbeds.
Propagate by taking softwood cuttings in spring or dividing established clumps from March to May.
Cut the woody stems back to ground level in late autumn to maintain a tidy shape for next spring.
Water sparingly once established, only during prolonged UK summer droughts to prevent root rot.
Position alongside Mediterranean herbs like thyme or lavender which share its dry, sunny preferences.
items.description: Chamaenerion dodonaei is a perennial herbaceous flowering plant in the willowherb family, Onagraceae.

items.name: Epilobium glaberrimum
items.growersTips:
Plant in moisture-retentive, acidic to neutral soil in a partially shaded, cool spot of your garden.
Sow seeds on the soil surface in autumn as they require cold stratification to germinate in spring.
Water consistently during dry UK summer spells to mimic its native damp, subalpine creek habitat.
Cut back the faded flowering stems to ground level in late autumn to keep the clump neat and tidy.
Divide established clumps in early spring to propagate and maintain the vigor of the parent plant.
items.description: Epilobium glaberrimum is a species of willowherb known by the common name glaucous willowherb. This clumping perennial wildflower is native to western North America from central Canada to northern Mexico. It generally grows at some elevation in moist places. This plant is somewhat variable in appearance. It may exceed half a meter in height and has hairless foliage with leaves between one and 8 centimeters long. The flower has four notched petals in purple, pink, or white which may be only a couple of millimeters long to over a centimeter long each. The fruit is a narrow, sticklike capsule 2 t

items.name: Great willowherb
items.growersTips:
Grow in moist, clay-heavy soil near ponds or bog gardens to mimic its natural UK wetland habitat.
Cut stems to the ground in late autumn to prevent aggressive self-seeding across your garden.
Watch for the elephant hawk-moth caterpillar in summer, as this plant is its crucial UK food source.
Propagate by dividing the tough, creeping rhizomes in early spring before active growth begins.
Plant alongside Lythrum salicaria to create a balanced, wildlife-friendly UK wetland border.
items.description: Epilobium hirsutum is a flowering plant belonging to the willowherb genus Epilobium in the family Onagraceae. It is commonly known as the great willowherb, great hairy willowherb or hairy willowherb. Local dialectal names include codlins and cream, apple pie and cherry pie.

items.name: Epilobium howellii
items.growersTips:
Grow in boggy soils or pond edges to mimic its wet habitat, keeping the crown just above water level
Provide partial shade to replicate UK woodland seeps, avoiding dry, full-sun border positions
Sow seeds in autumn on the soil surface, as they require winter cold stratification to germinate
Propagate by dividing the creeping stolons in early spring just as new green growth begins to emerge
Watch for water snails and slugs in spring, which target the tender emerging shoots in damp areas
items.description: Epilobium howellii is an uncommon species of flowering plant in the evening primrose family known by the common names Yuba Pass willowherb and subalpine fireweed. It is endemic to the High Sierra Nevada of California, where it is known from only about 65 occurrences.

items.name: Epilobium lactiflorum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn on the surface of acidic, gritty compost as they require light to germinate.
Grow in a damp, rock-garden pocket or scree bed that mimics cool, moist Scottish mountain rills.
Water daily during dry UK summer spells to keep the soil constantly moist but free-draining.
Divide congested clumps in early spring just as new growth emerges to maintain plant vigour.
Plant alongside native Saxifraga stellaris or mossy saxifrages in a partially shaded rockery.
items.description: Epilobium lactiflorum is a species of willowherb known by the common name milkflower willowherb or whiteflower willowherb. This plant is found throughout northern North America and northern Eurasia, where it most often grows in moist, rocky areas at some elevation. It is a hairy, clumping perennial with thin stems reaching 10 to 50 centimeters in height, and leafy stolons. The leaves are 2 to 5 centimeters long and have hairs along the edges and winged petioles. The tiny flowers are usually white, sometimes pink, and have notched petals 3 to 6 millimeters long. The fruit is a hairy capsule up

items.name: Epilobium leptophyllum
items.growersTips:
Grow this UK-hardy bog plant in permanently wet, acidic to neutral soil or at a pond edge.
Sow seeds shallowly in spring on a damp compost surface as they require light to germinate.
Propagate by dividing the creeping rhizomes in early spring just as new green shoots emerge.
Cut back the dead stems to ground level in late autumn to keep the water margin tidy.
Watch for elephant hawk-moth caterpillars in summer which feed heavily on the foliage.
items.description: Epilobium leptophyllum is a species of flowering plant in the evening primrose family known by the common names bog willowherb and linear-leaved willowherb. It is native to much of eastern and northern North America, where it grows in moist areas, such as bogs. It is a perennial herb growing up to a meter tall and spreading with tiny stolons. The leaves are generally linear in shape but may be wider to nearly oval, and reach up to about 7.5 centimeters. The inflorescence is a raceme of small flowers with white to pink petals a few millimeters long. The fruit is a hairy, elongated capsule up to

items.name: Epilobium minutum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn on the surface of gritty, well-drained soil as they need light to germinate.
Water sparingly once established, allowing the gritty soil to dry out completely between waterings.
Grow in full sun in a rock garden or scree bed to mimic its natural dry, gravelly habitat.
Cut back the faded flowering stems in late autumn to prevent excessive self-seeding in gravel paths.
Plant alongside low-growing UK alpines like Sedum acre to provide compatible dry soil companions.
items.description: Epilobium minutum is a species of flowering plant, known by the common names little willowherb, chaparral willowherb and desert willowherb, in the family Onagraceae. It is also called "smallflower willowherb" in reference to its relatively small size. However that name, in particular the British English variant "small-flowered willowherb", typically refers to Epilobium parviflorum.

items.name: Broad-leaved Willowherb
items.growersTips:
Pull it up by the roots before seed pods burst in late summer to stop aggressive garden takeover.
Sow seeds shallowly in autumn on moist, weed-free clay loam to mimic natural UK woodland edges.
Water young plants weekly during dry UK spring spells, then leave established clumps to self-sustain.
Grow alongside robust native ferns or red campion to naturally contain its rapid lateral spread.
Cut stems back to ground level in October to prevent winter rot and keep the rosette tidy.
items.description: Epilobium montanum or Broad-leaved Willowherb is a species of flowering plant in the willowherb family Onagraceae.

items.name: Epilobium obcordatum
items.growersTips:
Plant in gritty, sharply drained soil to prevent winter wet rot in damp UK climates.
Position in full sun within a raised bed or rock garden to mimic its native scree habitat.
Water sparingly only during dry summer spells once established to avoid root decay.
Propagate by taking softwood cuttings in late spring before the rose-pink flowers appear.
Protect young spring shoots from slug damage using grit barriers or organic beer traps.
items.description: Epilobium obcordatum is a species of perennial plant in the evening-primrose family (Onagraceae), known by the common name rockfringe willowherb and rock fringe. It is native to the western United States from California to Idaho, where it is found in rocky mountainous areas, at altitudes of 7,000 ft (2,100 m) to 13,000 ft (4,000 m). This small perennial is clumpy to mat-forming and spreads from a woody caudex, especially in nooks between rocks. It has stems lined with oval or rounded leaves which spread parallel to the ground or ascend somewhat. At the tips of the thin stems are flowers each w

items.name: Epilobium obscurum
items.growersTips:
Pull up the creeping stolons in autumn to stop this invasive UK native from choking your borders.
Sow seeds in spring just below the soil surface in damp, clay-heavy areas where other plants fail.
Water heavily during dry summer spells to mimic its natural British wetland and ditch habitats.
Cut flower spikes in July before they release wind-blown seeds to prevent garden-wide infestation.
Grow alongside moisture-loving native ferns or yellow flag iris to create a balanced bog garden.
items.description: Epilobium obscurum is a species of flowering plant belonging to the family Onagraceae.

items.name: Epilobium oreganum
items.growersTips:
Plant this Oregon native in a consistently damp, boggy border or beside a UK garden pond in full sun.
Incorporate plenty of leaf mould or well-rotted compost to mimic wet, acidic mountain meadow soils.
Propagate by taking softwood cuttings in spring or dividing the root clump in early autumn.
Cut the faded flower stems back to the ground in late autumn to keep the clump tidy and vigorous.
Watch for slugs and snails on the fresh emerging spring shoots and protect them with organic grit.
items.description: Epilobium oreganum is an uncommon species of flowering plant in the evening primrose family known by the common names Grants Pass willowherb and Oregon fireweed. It is native to southern Oregon and northern California, where it is historically known mostly from the Klamath Mountains. It is currently confirmed to exist only in Josephine County, Oregon, and Trinity County, California, where it grows in boggy areas on serpentine soils. It is a perennial herb growing up to a meter in height with thin, hairless stems. The red-veined leaves are oval to lance-shaped and up to 9 centimeters long. The

items.name: Epilobium oregonense
items.growersTips:
Grow in consistently wet, acidic to neutral soil, mimicking UK bog gardens or damp stream edges.
Propagate by dividing the delicate rootstocks in early spring just as new green shoots emerge.
Position in full sun to partial shade to prevent the foliage from scorching in dry summer spells.
Control surrounding vigorous weeds manually to prevent this small alpine willowherb from being choked.
Plant in containers of peat-free ericaceous compost if your garden soil is naturally chalky or dry.
items.description: Epilobium oregonense is a species of flowering plant in the evening primrose family known by the common name Oregon willowherb. It is native to western North America from British Columbia to Arizona, where it generally grows in moist places in several types of habitat. It is a perennial herb growing spindly upright stems approaching 40 centimeters high or sometimes forming mats spreading via stolons. The small leaves are rounded near the base of the plant and linear in shape higher up the stem. The inflorescence bears flowers with four white to pink petals each a few millimeters long. The frui

items.name: Epilobium palustre
items.growersTips:
Grow in boggy, acidic soil or pond edges to mimic its natural UK wet fen and marshland habitats.
Propagate by dividing the creeping stolons in early spring just as new green shoots begin to emerge.
Position in full sun to partial shade, keeping the soil constantly saturated or submerged in water.
Cut back the faded flower stems in autumn to control self-seeding in small UK garden ponds.
Plant alongside Caltha palustris or Myosotis scorpioides for compatible damp-loving companions.
items.description: Epilobium palustre is a species of willowherb known by the common name marsh willowherb. This plant has a circumboreal distribution, and can be found further south in mountainous areas.

items.name: Epilobium parviflorum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in spring on the surface of moist compost as they need light and UK spring rain to germinate.
Grow in damp, poorly drained clay soils or bog gardens where other perennials struggle to survive.
Cut stems back to ground level in late autumn to prevent aggressive self-seeding across your lawn.
Water deeply during dry UK summer spells to mimic their natural damp ditch and riverbank habitats.
Position next to moisture-loving native ferns or marsh marigolds to create a balanced bog display.
items.description: Epilobium parviflorum, commonly known as the hoary willowherb or smallflower hairy willowherb, is a herbaceous perennial plant of the family Onagraceae.

items.name: Epilobium septentrionale
items.growersTips:
Plant in gritty, sharply draining soil in full sun to mimic its native dry Californian habitat.
Water sparingly once established, allowing the soil to dry out completely between summer waterings.
Protect the crown from winter wet using a gravel mulch to prevent rot in damp UK winters.
Cut back the woody stems close to the base in early spring to encourage fresh, compact new growth.
Grow in a raised bed or alpine trough to ensure the essential sharp drainage this plant requires.
items.description: Epilobium septentrionale, with the common names Humboldt County fuchsia and northern willowherb, is a species of willowherb. Like the wildflower zauschneria, this plant was once treated as a member of genus Zauschneria but has more recently been placed with the willowherbs.

items.name: Epilobium siskiyouense
items.growersTips:
Plant this Siskiyou willowherb in sharply draining gravelly soil to survive wet UK winter rot.
Position in full sun and shelter from cold winds to mimic its native dry alpine scree habitat.
Water sparingly only during dry summer spells once established to prevent root decline in clay.
Protect the crown with a dry grit mulch in autumn to guard against persistent UK winter dampness.
Propagate by taking softwood cuttings in spring or sowing seed in cold frames during early spring.
items.description: Epilobium siskiyouense is a rare species of flowering plant in the evening primrose family known by the common names Siskiyou willowherb and Siskiyou fireweed.

items.name: Square stalked willow herb
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in autumn on the surface of moist, weed-free clay loam to mimic UK wild habitats.
Water young plants weekly during dry spring spells, then leave to rely on natural UK rainfall.
Cut stems back to ground level in late autumn to prevent aggressive self-seeding across your lawn.
Hand-pull unwanted seedlings in early spring before their deep, fibrous root systems anchor in clay.
Grow alongside native Lythrum salicaria in damp, sunny borders to create a resilient wetland patch.
items.description: Epilobium tetragonum, commonly known as the square stalked willow herb, is a species of flowering plant in the willowherb family Onagraceae.

items.name: Helleborus hyemalis L.
items.growersTips:
Plant Eranthis hyemalis tubers 5cm deep in autumn, soaking them in water overnight before planting.
Grow them in moist, well-drained soil rich in leafmould under deciduous trees to mimic woodland.
Divide congested clumps green immediately after flowering in spring rather than when they are dry.
Protect emerging yellow flowers from slugs and snails during wet UK winters using organic grit.
Sow fresh seed in summer as it loses viability quickly and needs winter cold to germinate.
items.description: Eranthis is a genus of eight species of flowering plants in the buttercup family Ranunculaceae, native to southern Europe and east across Asia to Japan. The common name winter aconite comes from the early flowering time and the resemblance of the leaves to those of the related genus Aconitum, the true aconite. Like the notoriously toxic Aconitum Eranthis is poisonous, although the toxins are different, being mainly cardiac glycosides similar to those found in various other plant species such as Adonis vernalis or Asclepias incarnata, rather than the neurotoxic alkaloids of Aconitum.

items.name: Helleborus hyemalis L.
items.growersTips:
Plant tubers in late summer at a depth of five centimetres and space them ten centimetres apart.
Soak the shrivelled tubers in water for twenty-four hours before planting to trigger active growth.
Grow in moist well-drained alkaline soil enriched with leafmould under deciduous trees or shrubs.
Associate with Galanthus nivalis and Cyclamen coum for a synchronized late winter colour display.
Propagate by lifting and dividing the congested clumps in green immediately after flowering in spring.
items.description: Eranthis hyemalis, the winter aconite, is a species of flowering plant in the buttercup family Ranunculaceae, native to calcareous woodland habitats in France, Italy and the Balkans, and widely naturalized elsewhere in Europe.

items.name: Eremogone kansuensis
items.growersTips:
Incorporate sharp grit into UK clay soils to prevent winter wet root rot in these alpine perennials.
Sow Eremogone seeds in autumn in cold frames to allow natural UK winter stratification for spring.
Water sparingly only during prolonged summer droughts once established to mimic dry scree conditions.
Trim back faded flower stems in late summer to maintain a tight cushion habit and prevent self-seeding.
Plant alongside Thymus serpyllum in raised beds for compatible low-nutrient and sharp-drainage needs.
items.description: Eremogone is a genus of flowering plants in the family Caryophyllaceae, native to western North America, northern Asia, eastern Europe and northeastern Africa. Attempts to resolve taxonomic relationships within the Caryophyllaceae have resulted in the enlargement of Eremogone with species from other genera.

items.name: Eremogone aculeata
items.growersTips:
Plant in gritty, sharply draining alkaline soil to survive wet UK winters and prevent root rot.
Position in full, unobstructed sun to mimic its native high-elevation dry scree habitat.
Water sparingly only during prolonged summer droughts, keeping the crown dry to avoid decay.
Propagate by taking softwood cuttings in early summer or by dividing established clumps in spring.
Protect from winter wet using a rain shelter or by top-dressing the soil with a thick layer of grit.
items.description: Eremogone aculeata is a species of flowering plant in the family Caryophyllaceae known by the common name prickly sandwort. It is native to the western United States, where it grows in the southern sagebrush steppe, mountainous areas, and volcanic soils, as well as on rocky slopes.

items.name: Eremogone cliftonii
items.growersTips:
Plant in gritty, sharply draining alkaline soil to prevent winter wet rot in damp UK climates.
Position in full sun, ideally in a raised bed or rockery to mimic its native rocky habitat.
Water sparingly only during dry summer spells, allowing the soil to dry out completely between waterings.
Propagate by taking softwood cuttings in early summer or by carefully dividing clumps in spring.
Protect young spring growth from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.
items.description: Eremogone cliftoniii is a species of flowering plant in the family Caryophyllaceae known by the common name Clifton's eremogone. It is endemic to California, where it is known from 27 to 33 occurrences in Butte and Plumas Counties. It occurs in forests and chaparral habitat on weathered granite soils. Although limited in distribution it may be relatively abundant where it does occur. The plant was only described to science in 2007.

items.name: Porter's sandwort
items.growersTips:
Plant in gritty, free-draining soil with added horticultural grit to survive wet UK winters.
Position in full sun and shelter from cold winds, ideally in a raised bed or alpine rockery.
Water sparingly only during dry summer spells, as this plant is highly susceptible to root rot.
Protect the crown from winter wet by top-dressing the surrounding soil with a layer of gravel.
Propagate by taking softwood cuttings in early summer or by dividing the clumps in spring.
items.description: Eremogone fendleri, or Fendler's sandwort, is a perennial plant in the family Caryophyllaceae found in the Colorado Plateau and Canyonlands region of the southwestern United States.

items.name: Eremothera boothii
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in April 1cm deep in free-draining sandy soil to prevent rot in wet UK spring weather.
Water only during prolonged dry spells as these drought-tolerant annuals dislike soggy British soil.
Watch for flea beetles in June, using fine insect mesh to protect young leaves from damage.
Deadhead faded blooms weekly in July to prolong the flowering season before autumn frosts arrive.
Sow alongside poached egg plants to attract hoverflies that naturally control aphids on the stems.
items.description:
Eremothera is the scientific name of two genera of organisms and may refer to:Eremothera (arachnid), a genus of wind scorpions in the family Eremobatidae
Eremothera (plant), a genus of plants in the family Onagraceae

items.name: Eremothera boothii
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in early spring under glass at a depth of three millimetres to combat wet UK winters.
Grow in poor, sharply draining sandy soil to mimic its native desert habitat and prevent root rot.
Water sparingly only during prolonged dry summer spells, allowing the soil to dry out completely.
Position in the absolute sunniest spot of your garden to maximise the short UK summer heat.
Watch for slugs and snails on young spring shoots, using beer traps or grit barriers to protect them.
items.description: Eremothera boothii is a species of wildflower known as Booth's evening primrose or Booth's sun-cup. This plant is native to the western United States and northwestern Mexico where it is most abundant in arid areas such as deserts. This is an annual plant with hairy reddish-green stems and mottled foliage. The stem ends in a nodding inflorescence of many small flowers which may be white to red or yellowish, often with darker shades on the external surfaces of the four spoon-shaped petals. They have long stamens with clublike yellowish anthers. Flowers of this species tend to open at dusk rather

items.name: Eremothera chamaenerioides
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in spring directly into poor well-drained soil as they dislike root disturbance of potting
Position in the sunniest spot of your garden to mimic their native hot dry desert environment
Water sparingly only during prolonged dry spells to prevent root rot in damp British summers
Avoid adding compost or fertilizer to the soil as high nutrients cause floppy weak growth
Allow the plant to self-seed naturally in autumn to ensure a display the following year
items.description: Eremothera chamaenerioides is a species of evening primrose known by the common name long-capsule suncup. It is native to the southwestern United States and northern Mexico, where it grows especially in desert regions. It is an annual herb producing an erect, hairy, glandular stem which is reddish in color and up to half a meter tall. The leaves are lance-shaped or oval and up to 7 or 8 centimeters long. The nodding inflorescence produces several flowers, each with white petals a few millimeters long and drying to dull red. The fruit is a capsule 3 to 5 centimeters long.

items.name: Eremothera refracta
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at a depth of two millimetres in early spring using a cold frame to protect them
Grow in sharply draining sandy soil mix with added grit to mimic its native dry desert habitat
Water sparingly only when the top two inches of soil are dry to prevent root rot in damp UK weather
Position in the sunniest south-facing spot of your garden to maximise essential summer heat levels
Protect young plants from slugs and snails which eagerly target the tender spring foliage in the UK
items.description: Eremothera refracta is a species of evening primrose known by the common name narrowleaf suncup. It is native to the southwestern United States, especially desert areas. It is an annual herb producing a hairy red or reddish green leafy stem up to about 45 centimeters in maximum height. The nodding inflorescence produces flowers with white petals a few millimeters long which turn reddish as they wither. The fruit is a straight or coiling capsule up to 5 centimeters long.

items.name: Eria parviflora
items.growersTips:
Grow Eria in a free-draining bark and perlite mix rather than soil to prevent winter root rot.
Position in a bright, unheated conservatory or east-facing windowsill to mimic cool UK spring light.
Water thoroughly with rainwater once a week in summer but keep almost dry from November to March.
Maintain a minimum winter temperature of ten degrees Celsius to protect these tender orchids from frost.
Feed with a weak high-nitrogen orchid fertilizer only during the active growing season of May to August.
items.description: Eria is a genus of orchids with more than 50 species distributed in China, the Himalayas, the Indian subcontinent, Southeast Asia, New Guinea, Polynesia, Melanesia and Micronesia.

items.name: Tree heath
items.growersTips:
Plant in acidic, free-draining soil, adding composted pine needles to lower pH if your soil is neutral.
Shed heavy snow from branches in winter to prevent the brittle, woody stems from splitting apart.
Prune lightly immediately after spring flowering, cutting back spent shoots but avoiding old wood.
Water with stored rainwater rather than tap water to prevent lime-induced chlorosis in summer.
Position in full sun in a sheltered south-facing spot to protect buds from harsh UK winter winds.
items.description: Erica arborea, the tree heath or tree heather, is a species of flowering plant (angiosperms) in the heather family Ericaceae, native to the Mediterranean Basin and Ethiopia, Kenya and Tanzania in East Africa. It is also cultivated as an ornamental.

items.name: Spring heath
items.growersTips:
Plant in acidic to neutral soil, adding composted pine needles to lower pH if your soil is alkaline.
Prune immediately after flowering in late spring by shearing faded spikes to keep the shrub bushy.
Water with stored rainwater rather than tap water during dry summer spells to prevent chlorosis.
Space plants thirty centimetres apart in full sun to prevent damp-induced fungal root rot in winter.
Plant alongside dwarf conifers or pieris which share the same acidic soil and moisture needs.
items.description: Erica carnea, the winter heath, winter-flowering heather, spring heath or alpine heath, is a species of flowering plant in the family Ericaceae, native to mountainous areas of central, eastern and southern Europe, where it grows in coniferous woodlands or stony slopes.

items.name: Erica ciliaris
items.growersTips:
Plant in acidic soil with a pH below 5.5, incorporating peat-free ericaceous compost before planting.
Water with collected rainwater rather than tap water to maintain the necessary low soil pH.
Prune lightly in mid-spring by cutting back faded flower stems to encourage bushy new growth.
Plant in full sun and shelter from cold, drying winds, especially in northern UK gardens.
Mulch annually with composted pine needles or leaf mould to retain moisture and mimic heathland.
items.description: Erica ciliaris, the dorset heath, is a species of flowering plant in the genus Erica.

items.name: Erica cinerea
items.growersTips:
Plant in extremely acidic, free-draining sandy or peaty soil with a pH between 4.5 and 5.5.
Water only with stored rainwater as UK tap water is too alkaline and will cause yellowing leaves.
Prune immediately after flowering in late summer by cutting back faded spikes to keep it bushy.
Position in full, unobstructed sun to prevent leggy growth and ensure vibrant summer blooms.
Avoid adding any manure or rich fertilizers, as this species thrives in nutrient-poor soils.
items.description: Erica cinerea, the bell heather, is a species of flowering plant in the heath family Ericaceae, native to western and central Europe.

items.name: Erica erigena
items.growersTips:
Plant in acidic to neutral soil amended with pine needles to prevent chlorosis in hard water areas.
Prune immediately after flowering in late spring by cutting back faded spikes to keep growth bushy.
Water with stored rainwater rather than tap water during dry summer spells to avoid lime buildup.
Position in full sun to partial shade with shelter from freezing north-easterly winter winds.
Grow alongside Calluna vulgaris or dwarf conifers to provide the required acidic soil companions.
items.description: Erica erigena, the Irish heath, is a European species of flowering plant in the family Ericaceae.

items.name: Erica multiflora
items.growersTips:
Plant in a sunny, sheltered south-facing spot to protect it from harsh UK winter winds and frosts.
Incorporate grit and peat-free ericaceous compost to ensure the essential sharp drainage it needs.
Water with harvested rainwater rather than tap water to maintain the required acidic soil pH.
Prune lightly in spring immediately after flowering to keep the shrub compact and prevent legginess.
Grow in a container if your garden has heavy clay soil to easily control the drainage and acidity.
items.description: Erica multiflora is a species of flowering plant in the family Ericaceae. It is native to the Mediterranean Basin. It is a shrub which can grow up to 2.5 m (8 ft) tall.

items.name: Erica patersonia
items.growersTips:
Grow in a container using acidic peat-free ericaceous compost to easily manage the strict low pH.
Water only with stored rainwater as UK tap water contains too much calcium for this Cape heath.
Place in the most sun-drenched, south-facing spot possible to mimic its native South African climate.
Protect from frost below minus two Celsius by moving the pot into a cold greenhouse for winter.
Prune lightly immediately after spring flowering by cutting back spent spikes to maintain bushiness.
items.description: Erica patersonia is a species of Erica heath native to the fynbos region of South Africa.

items.name: Cross-leaved heath
items.growersTips:
Plant in wet, acidic soil with a pH below 5.5, mixing in peat-free ericaceous compost before planting
Water only with stored rainwater, keeping the soil constantly damp to mimic native UK bog habitats
Prune lightly in September after flowering by trimming faded spikes to keep the shrub compact
Grow alongside Calluna vulgaris or Vaccinium oxycoccos which share the same wet, acid soil needs
Watch for Phytophthora root rot in winter by ensuring the wet soil does not become completely stagnant
items.description: Erica tetralix, the cross-leaved heath, is a species of flowering plant in the family Ericaceae, native to western Europe.

items.name: Wandering heath
items.growersTips:
Plant in acidic to neutral soil, adding composted pine needles or sulfur if your soil is alkaline.
Prune in spring by cutting back spent flower stems to the base of the current year's growth.
Water with stored rainwater rather than tap water to maintain the low soil pH this heather needs.
Space plants forty centimeters apart in full sun to prevent damp rot in wet UK winters.
Grow alongside Calluna vulgaris or dwarf conifers which share its love for acidic, well-drained soil.
items.description: Erica vagans, the Cornish heath or wandering heath, is a species of flowering plant in the family Ericaceae, native to Ireland, Cornwall, western France and Spain. It is a vigorous, spreading, evergreen heather reaching 75 cm (30 in) tall and wide, with pink flowers borne in racemes 14 cm (6 in) long in summer and autumn. The Latin specific epithet vagans literally means "wandering"; in this context it means "widely distributed".

items.name: Ericeae
items.growersTips:
Incorporate pine needles or composted bark into UK clay soils to lower the pH to a necessary 4.5 to 5.5.
Water only with stored rainwater as UK tap water contains too much calcium for acid-loving roots.
Prune spring-flowering heaths immediately after blooming in June to prevent woody, leggy growth.
Plant with the top of the root ball level with the soil surface to prevent stem rot in wet winters.
Grow alongside dwarf conifers or Gaultheria mucronata which thrive in the same acidic soil conditions.
items.description: Ericeae is a tribe of flowering plants in the family Ericaceae. The members of this tribe are known as the heaths. It contains three genera, with the largest being Erica.

items.name: Erinus alpinus
items.growersTips:
Plant in gritty, free-draining soil in wall crevices or rockeries to prevent winter wet root rot.
Sow seeds in spring by pressing them lightly into the soil surface without covering them with compost.
Water sparingly only during dry spells, allowing the gritty soil to dry out completely between waterings.
Cut back faded flower stems in late summer to encourage a neat cushion habit and prevent self-seeding.
Grow alongside Sempervivum or Saxifraga in alpine troughs to create a complementary dry-loving display.
items.description: Erinus alpinus, the fairy foxglove, alpine balsam, starflower, or liver balsam, is a species of flowering plant in the family Plantaginaceae, native to Central and Southern Europe and also to Morocco and Algeria.

items.name: Eritrichium nanum
items.growersTips:
Grow in a gritty, alkaline scree mix with fifty percent grit to survive wet UK winters.
Water only from below or use a collar of pure granite grit to prevent the woolly foliage from rotting.
Protect with an open-ended glass cloche from October to March to shield from persistent UK rain.
Position in an unheated alpine house or cold frame with maximum ventilation and bright, cool light.
Propagate by carefully taking tiny rosette cuttings in early summer using a very sharp, sterile blade.
items.description: Eritrichium nanum, the arctic alpine forget-me-not or king-of-the-Alps, is a circumpolar alpine cushion plant which occurs in the European Alps and the North American Rocky Mountains.

items.name: Common Stork's-bill
items.growersTips:
Plant Erodium in gritty, free-draining soil to prevent winter root rot in wet UK climates.
Water sparingly once established, letting the soil dry out completely between watering sessions.
Cut back faded flowers and stems in late summer to encourage a second flush of autumn blooms.
Protect alpine Erodium varieties from winter wet using a rain shelter or cloche from November.
Divide congested clumps in early spring to maintain vigor and propagate new plants easily.
items.description: Erodium is a genus of flowering plants in the botanical family Geraniaceae. The genus includes about 120 species with a subcosmopolitan distribution, native to Europe, North Africa, Asia, Australia, and more locally in North and South America. They are perennials, annuals, or subshrubs, with five-petalled flowers in shades of white, pink, and purple, that strongly resemble the better-known Geranium (crane's-bills). In English-speaking areas of Europe, the species are known as stork's-bills. In North America they are known as filarees or heron's bill.

items.name: Erodium acaule
items.growersTips:
Plant in gritty, sharply draining alkaline soil to prevent winter root rot in wet UK climates.
Position in full sun, ideally in a raised bed or rockery to mimic its native scree habitat.
Water sparingly once established, allowing the soil to dry out completely between waterings.
Propagate by taking basal cuttings in late spring to ensure new plants establish before winter.
Protect the crown from excessive winter wet using a cloche or by mulching with horticultural grit.
items.description: Erodium acaule is a species of plant in the family Geraniaceae.

items.name: Erodium botrys
items.growersTips:
Plant in gritty, free-draining soil to prevent winter root rot in wet UK climates.
Sow seeds shallowly in spring, barely covering them with a fine layer of grit or compost.
Water sparingly once established, allowing the soil to dry out completely between waterings.
Position in full sun, such as a south-facing rockery or gravel garden, to mimic Mediterranean heat.
Deadhead spent flowers regularly in summer to encourage continuous blooms and prevent self-seeding.
items.description: Erodium botrys is a species of flowering plant in the geranium family known by the common names longbeak stork's bill, Mediterranean stork's-bill and broadleaf filaree.

items.name: Erodium chium
items.growersTips:
Plant in gritty, sharply draining soil to prevent winter root rot in wet UK climates.
Water only during prolonged summer droughts, allowing the soil to dry out completely between waterings.
Sow seeds in cold frames during autumn, barely covering them with a thin layer of sharp grit.
Position in full south-facing sun to mimic its native Mediterranean coastal habitat.
Cut back faded flowering stems in late summer to encourage a second flush of blooms.
items.description: Erodium chium is a species of flowering plant in the family Geraniaceae.

items.name: Erodium chrysanthum
items.growersTips:
Plant in sharply draining gritty soil or rock gardens to prevent winter wet root rot in UK rain.
Position in full south-facing sun to mimic its native Greek cliffs and keep the silver foliage dry.
Water sparingly only during dry summer spells once established, as this plant is highly drought-tolerant.
Propagate by taking basal cuttings in early summer rather than trying to divide the woody taproot.
Protect the crown with a layer of gravel mulch to shed water away from the fuzzy leaves in winter.
items.description: Erodium chrysanthum, the yellow heron's bill, is a species of flowering plant in the family Geraniaceae, native to central and southern Greece. The flowers are a pale yellow, or rarely a pale pink. A dioecious perennial, it is hardy in USDA zones 6 through 8, and is recommended for rock gardens, trough gardens, and borders.

items.name: Erodium ciconium
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn or early spring at a depth of three millimetres in free-draining sandy soil.
Grow in full sun and shelter from heavy UK winter wet by using a cold frame or gritty raised bed.
Water sparingly once established, allowing the gritty compost to dry out completely between drinks.
Sow alongside companion plants like Thymus or Sedum that thrive in the same dry, nutrient-poor soil.
Watch for slugs and snails on young spring seedlings, protecting them with grit barriers or beer traps.
items.description: Erodium ciconium, the common stork's bill, is a species of annual herb in the family Geraniaceae. They have a self-supporting growth form and simple, broad leaves. Individuals can grow to 21 cm tall.

items.name: Common Stork's-bill
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn in free-draining sandy loam to mimic UK coastal dunes and ensure overwintering.
Water sparingly only during prolonged summer droughts as this plant thrives in dry, nutrient-poor soil.
Hand-weed taproots before spring flowering to prevent aggressive self-seeding across gravel gardens.
Position in full south-facing sun to prevent winter rot in damp British clay soils.
Grow alongside Thymus serpyllum in rockeries to provide essential drainage and matching low vigor.
items.description: Erodium cicutarium, also known as common stork's-bill, redstem filaree, redstem stork's bill or pinweed, is a herbaceous annual – or in warm climates, biennial – member of the family Geraniaceae of flowering plants. It is native to Macaronesia, temperate Eurasia and north and northeast Africa, and was introduced to North America in the eighteenth century, where it has since become naturalized, particularly in the deserts and arid grasslands of the southwestern United States. It is also naturalized elsewhere, including South America and southern Africa.

items.name: Erodium cygnorum
items.growersTips:
Plant this Australian native in sharply draining sandy loam to survive wet UK winters without rotting
Sow seeds shallowly in spring under glass at fifteen degrees Celsius before transplanting outdoors
Water only during prolonged dry spells as this hardy herb is highly drought-tolerant once established
Position in your sunniest south-facing border or gravel garden to mimic its hot natural habitat
Grow alongside Mediterranean herbs like thyme and oregano which share its need for dry nutrient-poor soil
items.description: Erodium cygnorum is a species of herb native to Australia.

items.name: Erodium glandulosum
items.growersTips:
Plant in sharply draining gritty soil or a raised rockery to prevent winter wet rot in UK rain.
Position in full south-facing sun to mimic its native Pyrenean cliffs and maximize summer blooms.
Water sparingly only during dry spells once established, allowing the gritty soil to dry out fully.
Propagate by taking basal cuttings in early summer or by carefully dividing the clump in spring.
Protect the crown from heavy winter wet using a pane of glass or by planting on a sloped crevice.
items.description: Erodium glandulosum, called the black-eyed heron's bill, is a species of flowering plant in the genus Erodium, native to the Pyrenees. It has gained the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit.

items.name: Erodium laciniatum
items.growersTips:
Plant in sharply draining gritty soil to prevent winter root rot in wet UK climates.
Sow seeds shallowly at a depth of two millimetres in early spring using a cold frame.
Water only during prolonged dry spells once established to mimic its native Mediterranean habitat.
Position in a south-facing rockery or gravel garden to maximise essential daily sunlight.
Protect the crown with a dry mulch of grit or gravel before the onset of winter wet.
items.description: Erodium laciniatum is a species of flowering plant in the family Geraniaceae.

items.name: Erodium lebelii
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn in a cold frame using a gritty compost mix to mimic UK shingle beach conditions.
Water sparingly only during prolonged dry spells as this coastal native easily rots in damp soil.
Position in full sun in a raised bed or rockery to ensure the sharpest drainage during wet winters.
Watch for slugs and snails during damp UK springs as they target the delicate feathery foliage.
Plant alongside Thymus serpyllum to create a drought-tolerant gravel garden display.
items.description: Erodium lebelii, sticky stork's-bill, is an annual plant in the family Geraniaceae. It occurs on sand dunes and heaths on the Atlantic and Mediterranean coasts of western Europe. Its taxonomic status is uncertain: some authorities consider it merely a variety or subspecies of common stork's-bill while others consider it to be the same as the north African species Erodium aethiopicum.

items.name: Erodium malacoides
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in late summer in free-draining sandy soil to mimic UK gravel garden conditions.
Water sparingly once established, allowing the soil to dry out completely between watering sessions.
Protect young autumn rosettes from winter waterlogging by planting on a slope or in raised beds.
Cut back faded flower stems in midsummer to prevent aggressive self-seeding across your borders.
Grow alongside Thymus serpyllum in full sun to provide excellent drainage and complementary blooms.
items.description: Erodium malacoides is a species of flowering plant in the geranium family known by the common names mallow-leaved stork's bill, Mediterranean stork's bill, and soft stork's-bill. It is an annual or biennial herb which is native to the Mediterranean region in southern Europe, northern Africa, and southwest Asia. It can be found locally elsewhere is an introduced species.

items.name: Erodium manescavi
items.growersTips:
Plant in grit-amended, free-draining soil to prevent winter root rot in wet UK clay.
Position in full sun to mimic its native Pyrenean habitat and ensure continuous summer blooms.
Cut back faded flower stems and tatty foliage in autumn to keep the rosette tidy for winter.
Water sparingly once established, only during prolonged dry spells in the height of UK summer.
Sow seeds in cold frames during autumn, as they require winter chilling to germinate by spring.
items.description: Erodium manescavi, called the garden stork's-bill, large purple storksbill, Manescau storksbill, Manescau heronsbill and showy heron's bill, is a species of flowering plant in the family Geraniaceae. Endemic to the western Pyrenees mountains, this plant occurs in France and Spain.

items.name: Erodium maritimum
items.growersTips:
Plant in sharply draining gritty soil or rock crevices to survive wet UK winters without rotting.
Position in full sun to mimic its native UK coastal cliffs and encourage compact, healthy growth.
Water sparingly once established, allowing the soil to dry out completely between waterings.
Sow seeds shallowly in spring using a gritty compost mix and keep them in a cold frame.
Protect from slugs and snails during damp UK springs when young foliage is most vulnerable.
items.description: Erodium maritimum, the sea stork's-bill, is a herbaceous perennial plant in the family Geraniaceae. It occurs on free-draining stony soils close to the sea and, very occasionally, in similar situations inland. Most of the world's population occurs in southern Britain and Brittany, but it is found in scattered locations around the coast of Europe as far as Corsica and Italy, and south to the Canary Isles.

items.name: Erodium moschatum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in late summer in free-draining sandy soil to mimic UK coastal habitats.
Water sparingly once established, letting the gritty soil dry out fully between winter rains.
Watch for slugs and snails on young rosettes during damp UK autumns and protect with grit barriers.
Cut back the spent flowering stems in late summer to control its prolific self-seeding habit.
Grow alongside Thymus serpyllum in sunny rock gardens to provide essential winter drainage.
items.description: Erodium moschatum is a species of flowering plant in the geranium family known by the common names musk stork's-bill and whitestem filaree. This is a weedy annual or biennial herb which is native to much of Eurasia and North Africa but can be found on most continents where it is an introduced species. In North America, it is found in most of the northeast United States and in Washington, Oregon, California, and Arizona, as well as the Canadian provices of Québec and Ontario.

items.name: Erodium texanum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn in a cold frame using grit-heavy compost to mimic its native dry habitat.
Position in the sunniest spot of your garden with sharp drainage to survive wet UK winters.
Water only when the top five centimetres of soil is bone dry to prevent crown rot in damp weather.
Protect young plants from slugs and snails during wet UK springs using copper tape or beer traps.
Plant alongside hardy sedums and thymes which share its strict requirement for low-nutrient soil.
items.description: Erodium texanum, also known as Texas filaree, Texas stork's bill, or heronbill, is a flowering plant which is native to the southwestern United States and northern Mexico. It is an annual or biennial herb.

items.name: Erythronium grandiflorum
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs in autumn at a depth of 10cm in moist, humus-rich soil that mimics woodland conditions.
Position in dappled shade under deciduous shrubs to prevent the delicate foliage from scorching.
Mulch annually with leafmould in winter to retain moisture and replicate natural forest floors.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.
Divide congested clumps immediately after flowering while the foliage is still green and active.
items.description: Erythronium, the fawn lily, trout lily, dog's-tooth-violet or adder's tongue, is a genus of Eurasian and North American plants in the lily family, most closely related to tulips. The name Erythronium derives from Ancient Greek ἐρυθρός (eruthrós) "red" in Greek, referring to the red flowers of E. dens-canis. Of all the established species, most live in North America; only seven species are found in Europe and Asia.

items.name: Erythronium japonicum
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs 10cm deep in autumn in moisture-retentive, humus-rich soil that mimics woodland floors.
Position in partial to full shade under deciduous shrubs to prevent summer sun from baking the soil.
Water during dry spring spells but keep soil barely damp, not soggy, during summer dormancy.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.
Leave foliage to die back naturally to feed the bulb and avoid disturbing the soil in summer.

items.name: Erythronium multiscapideum
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs in autumn at a depth of 10cm in humus-rich, moisture-retentive but well-draining soil.
Grow in dappled shade under deciduous shrubs to mimic their native woodland canopy conditions.
Keep soil consistently moist during spring growth but allow to dry out slightly during summer dormancy.
Protect emerging spring foliage from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.
Propagate by lifting and dividing congested clumps in late summer just as the foliage dies back.

items.name: Erythronium purpurascens
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs in autumn 10cm deep in moist, humus-rich, acidic to neutral soil under deciduous trees.
Incorporate leafmould or composted bark to mimic UK woodland soil and prevent summer drying out.
Position in dappled shade as strong afternoon UK sun scorches the delicate purplish-green foliage.
Keep soil consistently moist during spring growth but avoid waterlogging to prevent bulb rot.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.

items.name: Erythronium sajanense
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs in autumn at a depth of 10cm in moisture-retentive, humus-rich, acidic to neutral soil.
Position in dappled shade under deciduous trees to mimic its native Siberian woodland habitat.
Keep soil consistently moist during spring growth but allow it to dry out slightly during summer.
Mulch annually in autumn with leaf mould to protect bulbs from severe UK winter wet and frosts.
Watch for lily beetle larvae in spring and handpick them immediately to prevent foliage damage.

items.name: Erythronium sulevii
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs in autumn at a depth of ten centimetres in humus-rich, moisture-retentive, acidic soil.
Position in dappled shade under deciduous shrubs to mimic their natural woodland floor habitat.
Keep soil consistently moist during spring growth but avoid waterlogging during summer dormancy.
Apply a thick leaf mould mulch annually in autumn to replicate woodland leaf litter and feed bulbs.
Protect emerging spring foliage from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.

items.name: Erythronium tuolumnense

Artificial strawberry flavourings and aromas are widely used in commercial products. Botanically, the strawberry is not a berry, but an aggregate accessory fruit. Position in dappled shade under deciduous shrubs to match its natural UK woodland edge habitat.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.
Propagate by lifting the clump after foliage dies back in June to separate and replant bulbils.

items.name: Gagea lacaitae
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs in autumn at a depth of five centimetres in sharply draining gritty soil to prevent rot.
Position in full sun or dappled shade under deciduous shrubs to mimic its native open woodland edge.
Water moderately during spring growth but keep the soil almost entirely dry during summer dormancy.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.
Grow in containers using a loam-based John Innes number two mix with fifty percent added grit.

items.name: Gagea liotardii
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs in autumn at a depth of 8cm in well-drained, gritty soil to mimic alpine scree conditions.
Position in full sun or light dappled shade under deciduous shrubs to match UK woodland edge habitats.
Keep soil moist during winter and spring growth, but allow a dry summer dormancy once foliage dies.
Grow in shallow terracotta alpine pans using a loam, grit, and leafmould mix to prevent winter rot.
Avoid disturbing the soil around established clumps as they propagate slowly via delicate offsets.

items.name: Yellow star-of-Bethlehem
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs in autumn at a depth of eight centimetres in moist, well-drained soil under deciduous trees.
Replicate woodland conditions by incorporating leaf mould into the soil before planting the bulbs.
Keep the soil consistently moist during winter and spring but allow it to dry out during summer dormancy.
Associate with early wild garlic or wood anemones to mimic natural UK deciduous woodland communities.
Avoid weeding or disturbing the soil in late spring to protect the delicate, dying foliage of bulbs.

items.name: Gagea peduncularis
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs in autumn at a depth of eight centimetres in sharply draining, gritty neutral to alkaline soil
Position in a rock garden or raised bed facing south or west to maximise crucial winter and spring sun
Keep soil moist during spring growth but allow the bulb to dry out completely during summer dormancy
Protect the delicate early spring flowers from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps
Associate with low-growing thymes or sedums to provide summer ground cover without smothering the bulbs

items.name: Gagea spathacea
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs in autumn at a depth of eight centimetres in moist, deciduous woodland-style leafmould.
Position in dappled spring shade under hazel or birch to mimic its native UK woodland habitat.
Keep the soil consistently damp during winter and spring but allow it to dry slightly in summer.
Avoid disturbing the soil in summer as this species relies on delicate bulbils for propagation.
Protect the emerging spring foliage from slugs and snails using beer traps or organic pellets.

items.name: Gagea tenera
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs in autumn at a depth of 5cm to 8cm in well-drained, gritty soil to prevent winter rot.
Position in a rock garden or raised bed facing south or west to maximise crucial early spring sun.
Keep the soil moist during active spring growth but allow it to dry out completely during summer.
Avoid disturbing the soil in summer when the tiny bulbs are dormant and easily damaged by digging.
Grow alongside low-growing sedums or thymes which will not overcrowd this delicate, small species.

items.name: Galeola faberi
items.growersTips:
Do not try to grow Galeola in UK gardens as it is a parasitic orchid requiring specific host fungi.
If attempting conservation, plant seeds directly next to decaying oak wood to provide host fungi.
Maintain constant dampness in acidic, leaf-mold rich soil to mimic native woodland conditions.
Provide deep shade and winter mulch to protect the delicate underground rhizomes from UK frosts.
Never apply standard garden fertilizers as chemical nutrients will kill the essential mycorrhizae.

items.name: Hairy hempnettle
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn at 5mm depth in moist, well-drained soil to allow natural winter cold stratifying.
Grow in partial shade to mimic UK woodland edges, watering weekly to keep the soil consistently damp.
Prune back the stems by half in midsummer after the first flush of pink flowers to encourage regrowth.
Watch for mint rust fungus on leaves in damp UK summers, removing affected foliage immediately to stop spread.
Plant alongside native wood anemone or wild garlic in neutral to acidic clay soils for best growth.

items.name: Galtonia gibbidens
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs 15cm deep in autumn or spring in fertile, well-drained soil to protect from winter frost.
Water generously during the summer growing season but keep bulbs dry in winter to prevent rotting.
Apply a thick mulch of bark chips in November to protect the dormant bulbs from severe UK frosts.
Watch for slugs and snails in spring as they eagerly target the emerging fleshy Galtonia shoots.
Lift and store bulbs in a cool greenhouse over winter if gardening in cold, wet northern UK regions.

items.name: Gastrodieae
items.growersTips:
Grow native Gastrodia in deep shade beneath beech trees to mimic their natural woodland habitat.
Inoculate your leaf mould soil mix with Armillaria mellea fungi as these orchids cannot feed themselves.
Keep the planting site constantly damp but never waterlogged using collected rainwater, not tap water.
Protect emerging flower spikes from slugs in spring using organic wool pellets or copper barriers.
Do not disturb the soil or dig near established patches to avoid breaking delicate fungal networks.

items.name: Gaultheria shallon
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist acidic soil with ericaceous compost and pine needles to maintain the low pH they need.
