Water with stored rainwater rather than tap water to prevent lime-induced chlorosis in hard water areas.
Position in partial shade under taller shrubs like rhododendrons to mimic their woodland habitat.
Prune lightly in spring only to remove dead stems and maintain a compact berry-bearing shape.
Mulch annually with leaf mould in autumn to protect shallow roots from dry summers and hard frosts.

items.name: Gaultheria adenothrix
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist acidic soil enriched with pine needles or composted bark to mimic UK woodland floors.
Position in partial shade to protect the delicate white bell-shaped flowers from harsh midday sun.
Water with rainwater rather than tap water to maintain the low soil pH this ericaceous shrub needs.
Mulch annually in spring with leaf mould to retain moisture and protect the shallow root system.
Prune lightly after fruiting in late winter only to remove dead wood and maintain its neat habit.

items.name: Gaultheria antipoda
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist well-drained acidic soil enriched with composted pine needles or ericaceous compost.
Position in partial shade to mimic its native forest edge protecting it from harsh afternoon sun.
Water consistently with rainwater rather than tap water to maintain the necessary low soil pH.
Prune lightly in late spring after flowering only to restrict spread or remove dead wood.
Shelter from cold drying winds using fleece during severe UK winter frosts to prevent leaf scorch.

items.name: Gaultheria cuneata
items.growersTips:
Incorporate plenty of composted pine needles or composted bark to lower soil pH below six before planting
Plant so the root flare sits exactly level with the soil surface to prevent stem rot in wet winters
Water with collected rainwater rather than tap water to maintain the acidic soil conditions it needs
Prune lightly in mid spring after frosts pass to shape the shrub and remove winter damaged shoots
Grow alongside dwarf rhododendrons or heathers which share its need for moist acidic partial shade

items.name: Gaultheria depressa
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist acidic soil enriched with pine needles or composted bark to mimic UK woodland floors.
Water with rainwater rather than tap water to keep the soil pH low and prevent leaf yellowing.
Position in partial shade to protect the delicate white berries from scorching in midday summer sun.
Do not prune this slow-growing shrub other than removing dead stems in late spring after frosts pass.
Watch for vine weevil grubs in UK container plants as they rapidly destroy the shallow root system.

items.name: Gaultheria hispida
items.growersTips:
Incorporate plenty of composted pine needles or composted bark to lower soil pH below five point five.
Water with stored rainwater rather than tap water to prevent lime-induced chlorosis in dry summers.
Plant the root ball level with the soil surface in a sheltered spot with dappled shade from trees.
Prune lightly in mid-spring after frosts to remove dead wood and maintain a compact rounded shape.
Mulch annually with leaf mould or ericaceous compost in autumn to protect shallow roots from frost.

items.name: Gaultheria hispidula
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist, acidic peat-free ericaceous compost mixed with pine needles to mimic forest soil.
Position in deep or partial shade, ensuring the soil never dries out during dry UK summer spells.
Grow in a shallow container or raised bed to easily manage its low, creeping, mat-forming habit.
Propagate by layering the trailing stems in autumn or taking semi-ripe cuttings in late summer.
Avoid pruning this slow grower, only removing dead stems in spring to protect the delicate habit.

items.name: Alpine wintergreen
items.growersTips:
Incorporate plenty of composted pine needles or composted bark to lower soil pH below five point five.
Water with stored rainwater rather than tap water to prevent lime-induced chlorosis in hard areas.
Plant the root ball level with the soil surface in a damp, mossy rock garden or peat-free bog edge.
Protect the shallow roots from drying out in dry UK summers by applying a thick leaf mould mulch.
Grow alongside dwarf rhododendrons or vacciniums which thrive in the same cool, acidic conditions.

items.name: Gaultheria lanigera
items.growersTips:
Plant in highly acidic peat-free ericaceous compost mixed with pine needles to mimic moorland soil.
Water only with stored rainwater to keep the soil pH low and prevent yellowing from tap water lime.
Position in partial shade to mimic UK woodland edges and prevent summer leaf scorch from strong sun.
Mulch annually in autumn with leaf mould or composted bark to protect shallow roots from UK frosts.
Prune lightly in late spring after flowering to maintain its compact dwarf shrub habit and shape.

items.name: Gaultheria mucronata
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist, acidic soil with plenty of ericaceous compost to prevent leaf yellowing in UK gardens.
Grow one male plant like Thatcher's Gold alongside female cultivars to guarantee winter berries.
Water with rainwater rather than tap water to keep the soil pH low and prevent lime-induced chlorosis.
Prune lightly in mid-spring after winter berries fade to maintain a compact, bushy shrub shape.
Mulch annually with pine needles or composted bark in autumn to protect shallow roots from UK frosts.

items.name: Gaultheria nummularioides
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist acidic soil enriched with pine needles or composted bark to mimic UK woodland floors.
Water weekly with rainwater rather than tap water to maintain the low soil pH this ericaceous shrub needs.
Position in partial to full shade to prevent the delicate trailing evergreen foliage from scorching.
Prune lightly in mid-spring by removing dead tips to maintain its neat prostrate carpeting habit.
Grow alongside dwarf rhododendrons or vacciniums which share its love for damp acidic UK conditions.

items.name: Gaultheria ovatifolia
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist acidic soil enriched with pine needles or ericaceous compost to mimic UK woodland.
Water weekly with rainwater rather than tap water to maintain the low soil pH this shrub requires.
Position in dappled shade under deciduous trees to prevent summer leaf scorch in southern UK gardens.
Prune lightly in late spring after flowering only to remove dead wood and restrict its spreading habit.
Mulch annually in autumn with composted bark to protect the shallow root system from winter frosts.

items.name: Eastern teaberry
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist well-drained acidic soil with a pH of 4.5 to 5.5 using ericaceous compost in spring
Water weekly with harvested rainwater rather than tap water to maintain the required soil acidity
Plant at the same depth as the nursery pot to prevent stem rot and encourage spreading runners
Prune lightly in early spring by removing dead stems to maintain a compact berry-bearing carpet
Grow alongside companion plants like dwarf rhododendrons or heathers in partial shade spots

items.name: Gaultheria rupestris
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist but well-drained acidic soil enriched with composted pine needles or ericaceous compost.
Water with rainwater rather than tap water to maintain the low soil pH this ericaceous shrub needs.
Position in partial shade to mimic its native subalpine habitat and prevent UK summer leaf scorch.
Prune lightly in late spring after flowering to maintain its compact shrubby shape and remove dead wood.
Mulch annually with composted bark in autumn to protect shallow roots from hard UK winter frosts.

items.name: Gaultheria shallon
items.growersTips:
Plant in acidic soil with plenty of composted pine needles or leaf mould to mimic UK woodland floors.
Water deeply during dry UK summers to keep the shallow roots moist but never waterlogged.
Prune hard in early spring to control its vigorous spreading habit and encourage fresh new growth.
Watch for vine weevil larvae in container-grown plants and treat with nematodes in late summer.
Grow alongside acid-loving companions like Pieris or Vaccinium which thrive in the same damp shade.

items.name: Gaura
items.growersTips:
Plant in free-draining grit-amended soil to prevent winter root rot in wet UK clay.
Cut back hard to ground level in early spring rather than autumn to protect the crown from frost.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells only until established, then leave to tolerate drought.
Position in full sun to prevent the long, delicate flowering stems from flopping and seeking light.
Divide congested clumps in spring every three years to maintain vigor and prevent center die-out.

items.name: Gaura sinuata
items.growersTips:
Plant in gritty, free-draining soil to prevent winter root rot in wet UK clay.
Cut stems back to ground level in early spring to encourage fresh, bushy new growth.
Water sparingly once established, only during prolonged dry spells in the UK summer.
Position in full sun to prevent the delicate flower stems from flopping and seeking light.
Propagate by taking softwood cuttings in spring to replace short-lived parent plants.

items.name: Gaylussacia baccata
items.growersTips:
Prepare acidic soil with a pH of 4.5 to 5.5 using plenty of composted pine needles and peat-free ericaceous compost.
Water with harvested rainwater rather than tap water to keep the soil consistently damp but not waterlogged.
Plant in full sun to partial shade to mimic its native woodland edge habitat and maximize berry yield.
Prune in late winter by removing only the oldest stems to ground level to stimulate productive new wood.
Mulch annually with composted pine bark to conserve moisture and protect the shallow root system in winter.

items.name: Gaylussacia brachycera
items.growersTips:
Grow in highly acidic, peaty, well-draining soil with a pH of 4.5 to 5.2 to prevent leaf chlorosis.
Water exclusively with stored rainwater rather than tap water to maintain the required soil acidity.
Plant in partial shade to mimic its native woodland canopy and protect it from harsh UK afternoon sun.
Apply a thick annual mulch of pine needles or composted bark in spring to retain shallow root moisture.
Propagate by taking semi-ripe cuttings in late summer, as UK seed germination is extremely slow.

items.name: Gaylussacia dumosa
items.growersTips:
Grow in highly acidic peat-free ericaceous compost mixed with pine needles to mimic bog conditions.
Water only with rainwater to maintain the low soil pH required by this native North American shrub.
Plant in full sun to partial shade in a damp, sheltered spot to protect from drying UK winds.
Prune lightly in late winter only to remove dead wood and maintain its compact, suckering habit.
Mulch annually with composted pine bark or sulfur to keep roots cool and maintain soil acidity.

items.name: Gaylussacia frondosa
items.growersTips:
Plant in highly acidic, peaty soil with a pH of 4.5 to 5.2, incorporating composted pine needles.
Water exclusively with stored rainwater to prevent tapwater lime from raising the soil pH.
Grow in a sheltered, semi-shaded spot to mimic its native woodland edge and protect from dry winds.
Prune in late winter by removing a third of the oldest stems to the ground to boost berry yield.
Mulch annually with composted bracken or pine bark to conserve moisture and maintain soil acidity.

items.name: Gayophytum diffusum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds thinly in late spring directly onto well-drained, gritty soil as they need light to sprout.
Water sparingly only during prolonged dry spells to mimic their arid native North American habitat.
Position in the sunniest, most sheltered spot of your gravel garden to maximize UK summer warmth.
Grow alongside low-nutrient companions like Sedum or Thymus to prevent soil from becoming too rich.
Allow the delicate seed pods to dry on the plant in autumn to encourage self-seeding for next year.
items.description: Gayophytum diffusum is a species of flowering plant in the evening primrose family known by the common name spreading groundsmoke. It is native to western North America where it is a common member of many different habitats. This is a spindly, branching annual herb reaching a maximum height of about half a meter. Its thin stems have sparse narrow leaves a few centimeters long. The occasional flowers are petite and usually white in color. The fruit is a cylindrical, knobby capsule up to 1.5 centimeters long.

items.name: Gayophytum heterozygum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in late spring at a depth of two millimetres once the UK frost risk has fully passed
Grow in sharply draining sandy loam with no added fertiliser to mimic its native scree habitat
Water sparingly only during prolonged dry spells as this annual is highly prone to root rot
Position in full south-facing sun to ensure the delicate flowers open and set seed successfully
Allow the plant to self-seed naturally in autumn to guarantee a display the following spring
items.description: Gayophytum heterozygum is a species of flowering plant in the evening primrose family known by the common name zigzag groundsmoke. It is native to the western United States where it grows mainly in forested mountain habitat. This is a spindly annual herb with a few forking branches which approaches 80 centimeters in maximum height. It has a sparse foliage of small, narrow leaves, most of which are on the lower half of the plant. It produces tiny white flowers toward the tops of the thin stems. The fruit is a lumpy-looking capsule.

items.name: Gayophytum humile
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds thinly in spring at a depth of 2mm into poor, sharply draining sandy soil to limit rot.
Grow in full sun in a gravel garden or scree bed to mimic its native dry, rocky habitat in the UK.
Water sparingly only during prolonged dry spells, allowing the gritty growing medium to dry fully.
Do not enrich the soil with compost or fertilizer, as high nutrients cause weak, floppy growth.
Let the plants naturally self-seed in autumn to ensure a display the following spring.
items.description: Gayophytum humile is a species of flowering plant in the evening primrose family known by the common name dwarf groundsmoke. It is native to western North America from Alberta to California, and can also be found in parts of South America. It lives in many types of mountain habitats, especially moist areas. It is a small, thin annual herb not exceeding 30 centimeters in height. Its erect stem has few branches and sparse narrow leaves. The stem and leaves are green to bright red, or green with reddish edges and tips. The plant produces tiny white flowers each about half a centimeter across. The

items.name: Gelasine
items.growersTips:
Plant Gelasine bulbs in autumn at a depth of eight centimetres in sharply draining, gritty soil.
Grow Gelasine in pots to easily move them into a frost-free greenhouse or cold frame for UK winters.
Water weekly during the active spring growing season but keep the bulbs completely dry during winter.
Position pots in full sun against a south-facing brick wall to maximise essential summer warmth.
Protect the emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using beer traps or physical barriers.
items.description: Gelasine is a genus of flowering plants in the family Iridaceae, first described in 1840. The entire group is endemic to South America.

items.name: Genistoids
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds directly outdoors in May at a depth of one centimetre to avoid damaging the taproot.
Water young seedlings weekly during dry summer spells but keep soil dry once they are established.
Incorporate grit into heavy UK clay soils to ensure the sharp drainage these dry-loving plants need.
Watch for slugs and snails on tender spring shoots and protect them with organic wool pellets.
Position in full south-facing sun next to lavender to mimic their native dry Mediterranean habitat.
items.description: The Genistoids are one of the major radiations in the plant family Fabaceae. Members of this phylogenetic clade are primarily found in the Southern Hemisphere. Some genera are pollinated by birds. The genistoid clade is consistently resolved as monophyletic in molecular phylogenetic analyses. It is estimated to have arisen 56.4 ± 0.2 million years ago. A node-based definition for the genistoids is: "the MRCA of Poecilanthe parviflora and Lupinus argenteus." One morphological synapomorphy has been tentatively identified: production of quinolizidine alkaloids. Some genera also accumulate pyrroli

items.name: Genyorchis
items.growersTips:
Grow this miniature epiphyte in a warm UK greenhouse on tree fern bark rather than in standard soil
Mist the exposed pseudobulbs daily in summer to mimic tropical humidity while keeping winter dry
Maintain a minimum winter temperature of fifteen degrees Celsius to prevent pseudobulb rot in UK
Position in bright filtered light avoiding direct midsummer sun to prevent leaf scorch on bulbs
Treat with systemic insecticide at the first sign of mealybugs hiding in the tight bulb crevices
items.description: Bulbophyllum is a genus of mostly epiphytic and lithophytic orchids in the family Orchidaceae. It is the largest genus in the orchid family and one of the largest genera of flowering plants with more than 2,000 species, exceeded in number only by Astragalus. These orchids are found in diverse habitats throughout most of the warmer parts of the world including Africa, southern Asia, Latin America, the West Indies, and various islands in the Indian and Pacific Oceans. Orchids in this genus have thread-like or fibrous roots that creep over the surface of trees or rocks or hang from branches. The

items.name: Geocarpon
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn on the soil surface of wet, acidic, sandy clay to mimic natural vernal pools.
Keep the growing medium constantly saturated during winter and spring, then let it dry out in summer.
Grow this tiny annual in a dedicated alpine trough to prevent larger garden weeds from smothering it.
Protect the delicate seedlings from slugs and snails using organic bait or copper tape in spring.
Position the container in full sun to provide the high light levels required for seed germination.
items.description: Geocarpon is a genus of flowering plants in the carnation family, Caryophyllaceae. It includes seven species native to North America, from the eastern subarctic through the eastern, southeastern, and central United States.

items.name: Geocarpon minimum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn on the surface of sandy, acidic, nutrient-poor soil to mimic its native glades.
Grow in a cold frame to protect this tiny annual from heavy UK winter rain while keeping it cold.
Keep the soil damp but never waterlogged in spring, then allow it to dry out completely in summer.
Position in full sun to maximize light during the short spring growing and flowering season.
Weed the container by hand constantly as this tiny species is easily smothered by vigorous mosses.
items.description: Geocarpon minimum is a species of flowering plant in the carnation family (Caryophyllaceae) which is known by the common names tinytim and earth-fruit. It is a rare plant known from about 34 populations in the US states of Arkansas, Louisiana, Missouri, Texas, and Oklahoma. There are a number of threats to its survival and it was listed as a threatened species of the United States in 1987.

items.name: Geranium
items.growersTips:
Cut back Geranium pratense to ground level after the first summer flush to stimulate fresh new leaves.
Divide large congested clumps of Geranium Rozanne in early spring to maintain vigor and plant health.
Plant bare-root hardy cranesbills with the crown sitting exactly level with the UK damp soil surface.
Watch for vine weevil grubs eating roots in container-grown cultivars during wet autumn months.
Grow Geranium macrorrhizum in dry shade beneath birch trees where other ground cover plants struggle.
items.description: Geranium is a genus of 422 species of annual, biennial, and perennial plants that are commonly known as geraniums, hardy geraniums, or cranesbills. They are found throughout the temperate regions of the world and the mountains of the tropics, with the greatest diversity in the eastern part of the Mediterranean region.

items.name: Geranium ×cantabrigiense
items.growersTips:
Plant in autumn or spring at crown depth in well-drained soil to prevent winter rot in wet UK clay.
Water weekly during the first dry summer after planting, then leave to rely on natural UK rainfall.
Shear foliage to the ground after the main June flush to trigger fresh leaves and late summer blooms.
Divide congested clumps every three years in early spring to maintain vigorous ground cover density.
Grow alongside spring bulbs like Narcissus to naturally hide their dying foliage as the cranesbill expands.
items.description: Geranium × cantabrigiense is a hybrid flowering plant in the cranesbill family Geraniaceae. It is an hybrid between Geranium dalmaticum and G. macrorrhizum.

items.name: Geranium ×magnificum
items.growersTips:
Cut back hard to ground level right after the July flowering to trigger fresh lush foliage growth.
Plant in fertile moist but well-drained soil in full sun to prevent floppy stems in wet UK summers.
Divide congested clumps every three years in early spring to maintain vigor and flower abundance.
Underplant with early spring bulbs like narcissus to cover the bare ground before geranium leaves emerge.
Watch for sawfly larvae in May and handpick them immediately to prevent rapid defoliation of leaves.
items.description: Geranium × magnificum, the purple cranesbill, is a species of hardy flowering herbaceous perennial plant in the genus Geranium, family Geraniaceae. The multiplication symbol × indicates that it is the result of hybridisation, in this case between Geranium platypetalum and Geranium ibericum. Growing into a clump 70 cm (28 in) high and broad, it has the decorative, deeply-lobed leaves typical of the genus Geranium. Violet-blue flowers with darker veins are borne relatively briefly in early summer. Extremely hardy, to below −20 °C (−4 °F), it is suitable for cultivation throughout all temperate r

items.name: Geranium albanum
items.growersTips:
Plant in well-drained gritty soil to survive wet UK winters and prevent root rot in clay.
Position in partial shade as hot UK summer sun can scorch its delicate deeply-lobed leaves.
Water weekly during dry spring spells but let the soil dry out completely between waterings.
Cut back faded flower stems to ground level in July to encourage a second flush of autumn blooms.
Propagate by division in early spring just as new growth emerges to maintain plant vigour.
items.description: Geranium albanum, the crested cranesbill or Albanian cranesbill, is a species of flowering plant in the family Geraniaceae, native to the Caucasus and northern Iran. A clumping perennial reaching 50 cm (20 in), the Royal Horticultural Society considers it a good plant to attract pollinators. There is a cultivar, 'Pink and Stripes'.

items.name: Geranium arboreum
items.growersTips:
Grow in a sheltered south-facing spot with gritty, sharply draining soil to prevent winter root rot.
Bring container-grown plants into a frost-free greenhouse or conservatory from November to March.
Water deeply only when the top five centimetres of soil are dry, reducing to once a month in winter.
Prune back leggy stems by one-third in early spring to encourage bushy growth and more red flowers.
Propagate in midsummer using semi-ripe cuttings rooted in a fifty-fifty mix of peat-free compost and grit.
items.description: Geranium arboreum is a rare species of geranium known by the common names Hawaiian red-flowered geranium and Hawaii red cranesbill. It is endemic to Hawaii, where it is known only from the island of Maui. It was federally listed as an endangered species in 1992. Like other Hawaiian geraniums, this plant is known as hinahina and nohoanu.

items.name: Geranium argenteum
items.growersTips:
Plant this alpine in sharp-draining scree or grit-enriched soil to survive wet UK winters.
Position in full sun and shelter from winter wet using a cloche or pane of glass over the crown.
Water sparingly only during dry summer spells, keeping the foliage dry to prevent crown rot.
Propagate by taking basal cuttings in early spring just as new growth begins to emerge.
Grow alongside Sempervivum or Saxifraga in a raised bed or alpine trough for compatible drainage.
items.description: Geranium argenteum, the silvery crane's bill, is an ornamental plant in the family Geraniaceae, which is native to Europe.

items.name: Geranium asphodeloides
items.growersTips:
Plant in well-drained loamy soil at a depth where the crown sits level with the UK soil surface.
Water weekly during dry English summers until established, then only during prolonged droughts.
Cut back faded flower stems to ground level in July to encourage a second flush of autumn blooms.
Divide congested clumps in early spring or autumn to maintain vigor and propagate new plants.
Position in dappled shade under deciduous shrubs to mimic its natural woodland edge habitat.
items.description: Geranium asphodeloides, the asphodel cranesbill, is a species of flowering plant in the family Geraniaceae. It is native to southeastern Europe, Crimea, the Transcaucasus, Turkey, and Lebanon/Syria. A spreading perennial, it is recommended as a pollinator-attracting ground cover, for rock and gravel gardens, and for planting beneath roses.

items.name: Geranium bicknellii
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in late summer to mimic natural UK self-seeding before winter cold stratifies them.
Grow in gritty, free-draining soil to prevent winter root rot during wet British winters.
Allow the first-year rosettes to overwinter undisturbed, protecting them from heavy waterlogging.
Position near native UK wildflowers like red campion to attract local pollinators to the blooms.
Let seed pods turn brown and fling seeds naturally to maintain this biennial in your garden borders.
items.description: Geranium bicknellii is a species of geranium known by the common names Bicknell's cranesbill and northern cranesbill. It is native to much of the northern half of North America, where it can be found in a number of forest and woodland habitats. This is an annual or biennial herb which grows hairy stems up to about half a meter long. It may be erect or lie near the ground. Each leaf is several centimeters long and wide and is divided into several lobes, each of which may have smaller lobes or teeth. Flowers grow singly or in pairs and have pointed sepals and small lavender petals, each with a n

items.name: Geranium bohemicum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn and expose them to winter cold as they require stratification to germinate.
Plant in poor to moderately fertile well-drained soil to prevent excessive leafy growth over flowers.
Water young plants weekly during dry UK summers but keep established clumps dry to avoid root rot.
Cut back faded flower stems to ground level in late summer to encourage a second flush of blooms.
Sow in pots of gritty compost and leave outdoors in a cold frame to mimic natural UK winter chill.
items.description: Geranium bohemicum is a species of flowering plant belonging to the family Geraniaceae. It was first described in 1756 by Carl Linnaeus.

items.name: Geranium brevicaule
items.growersTips:
Plant this alpine in gritty, sharply draining soil to prevent winter wet rot in damp UK climates.
Position in full sun or very light shade, keeping the shallow, creeping rhizomes just below soil level.
Water moderately during dry spring spells but allow the gritty compost to dry out between waterings.
Protect the delicate foliage from slugs and snails during wet UK springs using organic grit barriers.
Propagate in spring by carefully dividing the compact clumps or taking semi-ripe cuttings in summer.
items.description: Geranium brevicaule is a species of flowering plant, indigenous to New Zealand and Australia.

items.name: Geranium caespitosum
items.growersTips:
Plant in free-draining gritty soil to prevent winter root rot in wet UK climates.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells, allowing the soil to dry out between waterings.
Cut back faded flower stems to ground level in late summer to encourage a second flush of foliage.
Position in full sun to light shade, ideally on a raised bed or rockery to mimic its native habitat.
Divide established clumps in early spring every three years to maintain vigor and propagate new plants.
items.description: Geranium caespitosum, the purple cluster geranium or pineywoods geranium, is a perennial herb native to the western United States and northern Mexico. Its US distribution includes Arizona, Colorado, Nevada, New Mexico, Texas, Utah, and Wyoming.

items.name: Geranium californicum
items.growersTips:
Plant in free-draining neutral soil with the crown level with the surface to prevent winter rot.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells, allowing the topsoil to dry out between waterings.
Cut back faded flower stems to ground level in July to encourage a second flush of autumn foliage.
Protect young spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.
Divide established clumps in early spring every three years to maintain vigour and propagate.
items.description: Geranium californicum is a species of Geranium known by the common name California cranesbill. It is endemic to California, where it grows in the Sierra Nevada and coastal ranges in the southern part of the state.

items.name: Geranium carolinianum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at a depth of three millimetres in autumn to mimic natural UK self-seeding.
Grow in poor, sharply draining sandy soil to prevent excessive leafy growth and encourage blooms.
Water only during prolonged summer droughts as this hardy annual easily rots in damp UK winters.
Pull up the shallow roots in late summer before seed pods explode to control its aggressive spread.
Plant alongside spring bulbs to provide attractive ground cover as the bulb foliage dies back.
items.description: Geranium carolinianum is a species of geranium known by the common name Carolina crane's-bill, or Carolina geranium. It is an annual herb native to North America, where it is widespread and grows in many types of habitat. There are two varieties; G. carolinianum var. carolinianum and G. carolinianum var. sphaerospermum. It may be considered an invasive species outside the southeastern United States.

items.name: Geranium cinereum
items.growersTips:
Plant in gritty, sharply draining soil to prevent winter root rot in wet UK climates.
Position in full sun to keep the compact, low-growing foliage tight and prevent leggy growth.
Water sparingly once established, only during prolonged dry summer spells to avoid waterlogging.
Shear back faded flowers and stems in midsummer to stimulate a fresh flush of foliage and blooms.
Divide congested clumps in early spring to maintain vigor and propagate new plants easily.
items.description:
Geranium cinereum, the ashy cranesbill, is a species of flowering plant in the family Geraniaceae, native to the Pyrenees. Growing to 50 cm (20 in) tall and wide, it is a small, deciduous or semi-evergreen perennial usually grown for low ground cover, rockeries or underplanting larger subjects like roses. Leaves are deeply divided and grey-green – whence the Latin specific epithet cinereum "ash-grey". It flowers in summer, with striking black-eyed flowers with black stamens. 
The plant grows in full sunlight, and is hardy down to −15 °C (5 °F).

items.name: Geranium clarkei
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist well-drained soil in partial shade to stop the running rhizomes from drying out.
Propagate by lifting and dividing the vigorous underground runners in early spring or autumn.
Shear the foliage to ground level after the first flush of flowers in July to trigger fresh leaves.
Space plants forty centimetres apart to allow the spreading groundcover habit to fill in quickly.
Watch for vine weevil grubs eating the roots in container-grown plants during wet UK autumns.
items.description: Geranium clarkei, called Clarke's geranium, is a species of perennial flowering plant in the family Geraniaceae, native to India and cultivated for use in gardens.

items.name: Geranium columbinum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn or early spring just 2mm deep in free-draining, gritty soil to mimic UK wilding.
Grow in poor, alkaline soil with crushed chalk to prevent lush leaf growth and encourage flowering.
Water seedlings sparingly during dry UK springs, as established plants thrive on drought-like neglect.
Hand-weed surrounding soil in late summer to expose bare patches for self-seeding the next generation.
Pair with native dry-meadow plants like wild thyme and marjoram to support local UK pollinators.
items.description: Geranium columbinum, common name long-stalked crane's-bill or longstalk cranesbill, is a herbaceous annual plant in the family Geraniaceae.

items.name: Geranium cuneatum
items.growersTips:
Grow this Hawaiian native in a container of gritty, acidic soil to move indoors before winter frost.
Water only when the top two inches of soil dry out completely to prevent root rot in damp UK winters.
Prune lightly in late spring after new growth starts to maintain its compact, rounded shrub shape.
Position in your sunniest south-facing spot or unheated greenhouse to mimic its high-altitude habitat.
Check regularly for glasshouse red spider mite and whitefly when overwintering the plant indoors.
items.description: Geranium cuneatum, or silver geranium, is a medium alpine shrub endemic to the islands of Hawai'i and Maui, where it grows in high elevation shrubland near or above the treeline. Like other geraniums native to Hawai'i, it is known as hinahina in Hawaiian.

items.name: Geranium dalmaticum
items.growersTips:
Plant in gritty, free-draining soil in full sun to prevent winter wet rot in damp UK climates.
Water sparingly once established, letting the soil dry out completely between waterings.
Divide congested clumps in early spring to maintain vigor and propagate new plants easily.
Shear back flowered stems and old foliage in late summer to encourage a fresh flush of leaves.
Position on a raised bed or rockery edge so the trailing stems can cascade over stone.
items.description: Geranium dalmaticum, commonly called Dalmatian cranesbill, is a species of hardy flowering herbaceous perennial plant in the genus Geranium of the family Geraniaceae. It is native to the Pelješac peninsula of Dalmatia on the west coast of Croatia. Growing to only 10 cm (3.9 in) tall by up to 50 cm (20 in) broad, it is cultivated as a garden subject in temperate regions for its low mound of aromatic leaves and soft mauve colored flowers. The palmately lobed glossy green leaves are tinted red in the Autumn. It has gained the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit.

items.name: Geranium dissectum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn in cold frames to mimic UK winter chill for successful spring germination.
Grow in moderately fertile, well-drained soil to prevent winter root rot in wet UK clay.
Water young plants weekly during dry spring spells, then leave established plants to rain.
Shear back hard in midsummer after flowering to stimulate fresh foliage and a second bloom.
Watch for slugs on young spring shoots and handpick them during damp British evenings.
items.description: Geranium dissectum or cut-leaved crane's-bill is a plant species of the genus Geranium. It is native to Europe.

items.name: Geranium endressii
items.growersTips:
Cut back hard to ground level in July after the first flush to get fresh leaves and autumn flowers.
Divide congested clumps in early spring or autumn to maintain vigor and control its invasive spread.
Plant in moisture-retentive clay or loam, but avoid waterlogged winter soil to prevent root rot.
Position in partial shade to stop the pale pink flowers from bleaching white in strong UK summer sun.
Shear back spreading runners in autumn to prevent it smothering smaller alpine or border companions.
items.description: Geranium endressii, commonly called Endres cranesbill or French crane's-bill, is a species of hardy flowering herbaceous or semi-evergreen perennial plant in the genus Geranium, family Geraniaceae.

items.name: Geranium erianthum
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist but well-drained humus-rich soil, mimicking its native cool subalpine woodland home.
Position in partial shade to protect the delicate violet-blue flowers from bleaching in midday sun.
Water weekly during dry UK spring spells to establish strong roots before the summer flowering peak.
Cut back faded flower stems to ground level in July to encourage a fresh flush of healthy foliage.
Divide congested clumps in early autumn every three years to maintain vigour and propagate new plants.
items.description: Geranium erianthum, the woolly geranium, is a flowering plant found in China, Japan, Russia, North America and England. Within its range, it is often known as "wild geranium" or "cranesbill", but note that these common names are also used for several other species within the genus Geranium.

items.name: Geranium himalayense
items.growersTips:
Plant bare roots in autumn at a depth where the crown sits just below the soil surface to avoid rot.
Shear the foliage to ground level in July after the first flush to trigger fresh leaves and blooms.
Water deeply once a week during dry UK summers to prevent powdery mildew on the dense lower leaves.
Divide congested clumps every three years in early spring to maintain vigorous flowering and habit.
Grow alongside Alchemilla mollis in partial shade to suppress weeds and create a classic cottage look.
items.description: Geranium himalayense is a species of hardy flowering herbaceous perennial plant in the genus Geranium, family Geraniaceae. It is native to West Himalaya, Afghanistan, Kyrgyzstan, Nepal, Pakistan, Tajikistan, Tibet, and Uzbekistan.

items.name: Geranium ibericum
items.growersTips:
Plant in well-drained soil at crown depth to prevent winter rot in wet UK clay.
Shear foliage to the ground in July after the first flush to trigger fresh leaves and autumn blooms.
Water deeply once a week during dry UK spring spells, but leave established clumps to survive drought.
Divide congested clumps every three years in early spring to maintain vigor and prevent center dieback.
Position in full sun or partial shade alongside Alchemilla mollis to suppress weeds in cottage borders.
items.description: Geranium ibericum, commonly called Caucasian crane's-bill or Iberian geranium or Caucasus geranium, is a herbaceous plant species in the family Geraniaceae. It is native to Western Asia, including Turkey and the Caucasus, and is cultivated as a garden subject. It has a dense mounding habit, and violet colored flowers.

items.name: Geranium lucidum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn or early spring by pressing them lightly into moist, well-drained soil.
Grow in partial to deep shade under deciduous trees to mimic its natural UK woodland habitat.
Hand-pull plants in May before seed pods explode to control its highly invasive self-seeding habit.
Water young plants weekly during dry UK spring spells, then leave established plants to rain alone.
Plant alongside native Primroses or Wood Anemones to create a cohesive shade-tolerant ground cover.
items.description: Geranium lucidum, commonly known as shining cranesbill or shining geranium or shiny geranium, is a herbaceous annual plant of the genus Geranium. It is native to Europe, western Asia and North Africa. It has been introduced to North America as a garden plant and in places, particularly the Pacific Northwest, has become naturalised and is viewed as an invasive species and noxious weed.

items.name: Hardy geranium
items.growersTips:
Plant in dry shade under mature birch trees where other ground cover struggles to survive.
Divide congested clumps in autumn or early spring by slicing the woody rhizomes with a sharp spade.
Shear the foliage back to ground level in July after flowering to trigger a flush of fresh leaves.
Plant rhizomes horizontally just below the soil surface leaving the growing tips slightly exposed.
Grow alongside spring bulbs like Galanthus nivalis to naturally mask their dying foliage in May.
items.description: Geranium macrorrhizum is a species of hardy flowering herbaceous perennial plant in the genus Geranium, family Geraniaceae. It is native to the South east Alps and the Balkans. Its common names include bigroot geranium, Bulgarian geranium, and rock crane's-bill.

items.name: Wild geranium
items.growersTips:
Plant bare roots in autumn at a depth of five centimetres with the crown just below the soil surface
Water weekly during dry UK spring spells until established then leave to rely on natural rainfall
Cut foliage back to the ground after the first summer flowering to encourage fresh autumn growth
Improve heavy UK clay with leaf mould and grit to prevent winter root rot in waterlogged soil
Plant alongside native wood anemones or hostas in partial shade for a classic woodland combination
items.description: Geranium maculatum, the wild geranium, spotted geranium, or wood geranium, is a perennial plant native to woodlands in eastern North America, from southern Manitoba and southwestern Quebec south to Alabama and Georgia and west to Oklahoma and South Dakota.

items.name: Geranium maderense
items.growersTips:
Plant in gritty, free-draining soil against a south-facing wall to survive wet UK winters.
Water only when the top two inches of soil are dry, as this plant is highly prone to root rot.
Prop up the heavy lower leaf stalks with stones to support the plant and prevent stem collapse.
Move container-grown plants into a frost-free greenhouse or conservatory from November to April.
Collect the seeds immediately after flowering as the parent plant will die after its main bloom.
items.description: Geranium maderense, known as giant herb-Robert or the Madeira cranesbill, is a species of flowering plant in the family Geraniaceae, native to the island of Madeira. It is sometimes confused with another Madeira endemic, Geranium palmatum.

items.name: Dove's-foot Crane's-bill
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at a depth of two millimetres in autumn to match natural UK germination cycles.
Grow in poor, sharply drained sandy soil to prevent lush leaf growth at the expense of pink flowers.
Water only during prolonged summer droughts as this taprooted annual easily rots in wet UK winters.
Shear back by half in midsummer to stimulate a second flush of blooms and prevent excessive seeding.
Sow alongside wild thyme in sunny rockeries where its low-scrambling habit fills bare gaps easily.
items.description: Geranium molle, the dove's-foot crane's-bill or dovesfoot geranium, is an annual herbaceous plant of the family Geraniaceae.

items.name: Geranium multiflorum
items.growersTips:
Plant in well-drained gritty soil to survive wet UK winters, adding grit to the planting hole.
Position in full sun to light dappled shade to mimic its native Hawaiian volcanic scrub habitat.
Water moderately during dry summer spells but allow the soil to dry out completely between waterings.
Propagate by taking basal cuttings in spring or dividing the root clump every three to four years.
Protect the crown with a dry mulch of bracken or fleece during severe, wet UK winter frosts.
items.description: Geranium multiflorum is a rare species of geranium known by the common names manyflower geranium, or manyflowered cranesbill. It is endemic to Hawaii, where it is known only from Haleakalā, the main volcano on the island of Maui. It was federally listed as an endangered species in 1992. Like other Hawaiian geraniums, this plant is known as hinahina and nohoanu.

items.name: Geranium nodosum
items.growersTips:
Plant this cranesbill in dry shade under deciduous trees where other UK shade lovers struggle.
Divide congested clumps in early spring or autumn to propagate and maintain vigorous flowering.
Cut back to ground level after the first flush in July to encourage fresh foliage and late blooms.
Mulch with leaf mould in autumn to mimic its native woodland soil and retain light moisture.
Plant alongside dry-shade companions like Galium odoratum and Dryopteris filix-mas for contrast.
items.description: Geranium nodosum, the knotted crane's-bill, is a perennial herbaceous plant in the family Geraniaceae.

items.name: Geranium oreganum
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist well-drained soil enriched with leaf mould to mimic its native woodland edge habitat.
Position in partial shade to protect the delicate violet-blue flowers from bleaching in hot UK sun.
Cut the foliage back to ground level after the first summer flush to encourage fresh autumn growth.
Divide mature clumps in early spring just as new growth appears to maintain plant health and vigour.
Water deeply during dry UK summer spells to prevent the woodland-loving root system from drying out.
items.description: Geranium oreganum is a species of geranium known by the common name Oregon cranesbill, or Oregon geranium. It is native to western North America from California to Alberta, where it grows in mountain forests and meadows. This is a perennial herb growing generally erect to heights of 40 to 80 centimeters. The slender stems have a foliage of large palmate leaves up to 15 centimeters wide and divided into several segments, each of which is subdivided into rounded or pointed lobes. The flower has pointed sepals beneath rounded lavender to purple petals. The fruit has a small body with a pointed st

items.name: Geranium oxonianum
items.growersTips:
Cut back hard to ground level after the first flush in July to trigger fresh leaves and new blooms.
Plant bare roots in autumn or spring with the crown sitting exactly level with the soil surface.
Divide congested clumps every three years in early spring to maintain vigour and control spreading.
Grow in well-drained soil as wet UK winter clay causes root rot; dig in grit to improve drainage.
Plant alongside Alchemilla mollis or Nepeta in partial shade for a classic cottage garden scheme.
items.description: Geranium × oxonianum, the Oxford geranium, is a hybrid variety of flowering plant in the family Geraniaceae, which is a 1932 cross of garden origin between Geranium endressii and Geranium versicolor. Growing to 0.5 m (1.6 ft) tall by 1 m (3.3 ft), it is a highly variable plant with round palmate leaves and often veined flowers in various shades of pink. It can be invasive.

items.name: Geranium palmatum
items.growersTips:
Plant in a sheltered south-facing spot with sharp-draining soil to prevent winter root rot.
Protect the central crown with dry bracken or fleece during wet UK frosts below minus five.
Water deeply but infrequently during dry summer spells, allowing the top soil to dry out.
Cut back faded flower stems to the base in late summer to encourage fresh foliage growth.
Sow fresh seeds in autumn in cold frames to ensure replacement plants if winter wet kills the parent.
items.description: Geranium palmatum, falsely called Canary Island geranium, is a species of flowering plant in the family Geraniaceae, native to the island of Madeira. Growing in a rosette 1.5 m (4.9 ft) tall by 1 m (3.3 ft) broad, it is an evergreen perennial with divided palmate leaves and pink flowers 4 cm (1.6 in) in diameter on long red stems.

items.name: Geranium palustre
items.growersTips:
Plant in moisture-retentive, humus-rich soil in partial shade to mimic its native European wetland.
Water weekly during dry UK summers to keep the soil consistently damp but never waterlogged.
Cut back flowered stems to ground level in August to encourage a fresh flush of healthy foliage.
Space plants 50cm apart in autumn to allow their sprawling, scrambling stems room to scramble.
Divide congested clumps in early spring just as new growth appears to maintain plant vigour.
items.description: Geranium palustre is a perennial species of flowering plant belonging to the family Geraniaceae.

items.name: Black widow
items.growersTips:
Plant in damp shade under deciduous trees to mimic its natural woodland edge habitat in UK gardens.
Cut back to ground level immediately after the first flowering in July to trigger fresh new foliage.
Divide congested clumps in early autumn or spring to maintain plant vigour and propagate for free.
Sow fresh seeds in cold frames during autumn to allow winter chill to naturally break dormancy.
Position near pale yellow hostas or ferns to create a striking contrast with the dark plum blooms.
items.description: Geranium phaeum, commonly called dusky crane's-bill, mourning widow or black widow, is a herbaceous plant species in the family Geraniaceae. It is native to southern, central, and western Europe, and is cultivated as a garden subject. It has dark violet colored flowers. It is unmistakable with dark purple petals turned backwards and with conspicuous projecting stamens and style. Petals crinkly-edged and pointed. Leaves often blotched brown.

items.name: Geranium platypetalum
items.growersTips:
Plant in autumn or spring at the same depth as the pot in moist, well-drained soil in partial shade.
Shear foliage and faded flowers to ground level in July to encourage a fresh flush of healthy leaves.
Water weekly during dry UK summer spells until established, then only during prolonged droughts.
Divide congested clumps every three years in early spring to maintain vigor and propagate new plants.
Watch for vine weevil larvae in container-grown plants and treat with nematodes in late summer.
items.description: Geranium platypetalum, commonly called glandular crane's-bill or broad-petaled geranium, is a herbaceous plant species in the family Geraniaceae. It is native to Iran, Turkey, Armenia, Azerbaijan, Georgia, and the Russian Federation, and is cultivated as a garden subject, under a number of different cultivar names. It has blue-colored flowers.

items.name: Geranium potentilloides
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist but well-drained acidic to neutral soil in a partially shaded, cool woodland border.
Water weekly during dry UK summers to keep the soil consistently damp but never waterlogged.
Propagate by dividing the root clump in early spring just as new green shoots begin to emerge.
Shear back the sprawling stems after flowering in late summer to encourage fresh compact foliage.
Watch for vine weevil larvae in container-grown plants and apply biological nematodes in autumn.
items.description: Geranium potentilloides, belongs to the family Geraniaceae, and is a small prostrate perennial herb that can grow up to 60cm high. The species is commonly referred to as Soft Cranesbill or Cinquefoil geranium.

items.name: Meadow Geranium
items.growersTips:
Cut back faded stems to ground level in July to stimulate a fresh flush of foliage and autumn flowers.
Plant bare roots in autumn at a depth where the crown sits just two centimetres below the soil surface.
Grow in moist but well-drained neutral to alkaline soil to prevent winter crown rot in wet UK climates.
Check leaves in damp British summers for powdery mildew and prune affected foliage immediately to ground.
Divide congested clumps every three years in early spring to maintain vigour and propagate new plants.
items.description: Geranium pratense, the meadow crane's-bill or meadow geranium, is a species of flowering plant in the family Geraniaceae, native to Europe and Asia. Forming a clump up to 1 m (3.3 ft) broad, it is a herbaceous perennial with hairy stems and lax saucer-shaped blooms of pale violet. It is extremely hardy to at least −20 °C (−4 °F), reflecting its origins in the Altai Mountains of central Asia.

items.name: Geranium psilostemon
items.growersTips:
Stake the tall floppy stems in early spring using birch brushwood before the heavy flowers collapse.
Cut the foliage and spent blooms back to ground level in July to trigger a fresh flush of leaves.
Plant bare roots in autumn with the crown resting just below the soil surface in moist clay-loam.
Divide congested clumps every three years in March to maintain vigor and propagate new plants.
Position in full sun or partial shade next to silvery Artemisia to contrast the magenta petals.
items.description: Geranium psilostemon, commonly called Armenian cranesbill, is a species of hardy flowering herbaceous perennial plant in the genus Geranium, family Geraniaceae. It is native to Turkey, Armenia, Azerbaijan, and the Russian Federation. Forming a large clump to 120 cm (47 in) tall, it has glowing reddish purple colored flowers with prominent dark centres, and divided leaves tinted red in Autumn. It is cultivated as a garden subject, and a number of different cultivars exist. G. psilostemon has the UK’s hardiest rating, surviving temperatures as low as −20 °C (−4 °F).

items.name: Geranium purpureum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in autumn in free-draining grit to mimic UK shingle beaches where they thrive.
Water sparingly only during prolonged summer droughts as this plant is highly adapted to dry soils.
Hand-weed surrounding soil early in spring to prevent vigorous grasses from smothering young rosettes.
Shear back the faded flowering stems in late summer to restrict its prolific self-seeding habit.
Plant alongside Thymus serpyllum in sunny rock gardens to recreate natural British coastal habitats.
items.description: Geranium purpureum, the little-robin, is a species of flowering plant in the geranium family Geraniaceae. It is native to Europe, Africa, and western Asia, and introduced on all continents except Antarctica. It is similar in appearance to Geranium robertianum, a close relative.

items.name: Small-flowered Crane's-bill
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn or early spring just below the soil surface in free-draining sandy garden loam.
Water seedlings sparingly once established as this UK native annual thrives in dry, gravelly soils.
Hand-pull plants in midsummer before seed pods explode to prevent aggressive self-seeding in lawns.
Interplant with taller perennials like lavender to provide the light shade this low creeper prefers.
Watch for slugs on young spring shoots during wet UK weather and protect with organic grit barriers.
items.description: Geranium pusillum, commonly known as small-flowered crane's-bill or small geranium, is a herbaceous annual plant of the genus Geranium.

items.name: Hedgerow Crane's-bill
items.growersTips:
Plant Bill of Warminster in moist well-drained soil at a depth matching its original nursery pot
Cut back to ground level in July after the first flush to encourage fresh foliage and autumn blooms
Water young plants weekly during dry UK spring spells until their deep taproot system establishes
Sow seeds in cold frames during autumn to mimic natural UK winter chilling for spring germination
Position near Nepeta or Alchemilla mollis in partial shade to naturally suppress invasive self-seeding
items.description:
Geranium pyrenaicum, otherwise known as hedgerow cranesbill or mountain cranesbill is a perennial species of plant in the family Geraniaceae. 
It can be found on roadside verges and along hedgerows.

items.name: Hardy geranium
items.growersTips:
Plant in sharply draining soil with grit to survive wet UK winters and prevent root rot in clay.
Position in full sun to maximize the short June flowering window and keep the textured foliage tight.
Cut back faded flower stems to the base in July to encourage a neat mound of velvety grey leaves.
Divide established clumps in early spring just as new growth starts to maintain plant vigour.
Grow alongside silver-leaved stachys or dark-leafed heucheras to contrast the pale violet veining.
items.description:
Geranium renardii is a species of hardy flowering herbaceous perennial plant in the genus Geranium, family Geraniaceae. It is native to the Caucasus region. Growing to 30 cm (12 in) tall and broad, it has palmate leaves and pale pink flowers striped violet. This plant has gained the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit. 
It grows well in sunny positions or shade both and well drained soils.

items.name: Geranium retrorsum
items.growersTips:
Plant in well-drained gritty soil to prevent winter root rot in wet UK winters.
Position in full sun to partial shade to mimic its native southern hemisphere grassland habitat.
Water deeply but infrequently during dry summer spells, allowing the soil to dry out between watering.
Cut back the sprawling foliage after the first flush of flowers to encourage fresh compact growth.
Protect the fleshy taproot with a thick dry mulch of bark or grit before the first winter frosts.
items.description: Geranium retrorsum is a species of Geranium known by the common name New Zealand geranium in the United States and common cranesbill in Australia. It is native to Australia and New Zealand but can be found on other continents as an introduced species which is often a noxious weed as well. This is a perennial herb growing generally erect to a maximum height approaching half a meter. The stems are green to reddish and have stiff hairs. The leaves are a few centimeters wide and divided into several segments which are further divided into small lobes. The small flowers are fuchsia to purple in col

items.name: Geranium reuteri
items.growersTips:
Plant in free-draining gritty loam to prevent winter root rot in wet UK winters.
Position in partial shade under deciduous trees to mimic its native woodland habitat.
Water moderately during dry spring spells but allow the soil to dry out between waterings.
Propagate by taking softwood cuttings in early summer or by dividing clumps in spring.
Protect the crown with a dry bracken mulch in cold regions to shield it from hard frosts.
items.description: Geranium reuteri, the giant geranium, is a species of flowering plant in the family Geraniaceae, endemic to the Canary Islands. It was known for many years under the name Geranium canariense. In Spanish, it is called pata de gallo.

items.name: Geranium richardsonii
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist well-drained soil enriched with leaf mould to mimic its native woodland edge habitat.
Position in partial shade to protect the delicate white flowers from scorching in hot UK summers.
Water weekly during dry summer spells keeping the soil consistently damp but never waterlogged.
Cut back faded flower stems to ground level in late summer to encourage a fresh flush of foliage.
Divide established clumps in early spring just as new growth appears to maintain plant vigour.
items.description: Geranium richardsonii is a species of geranium known by the common name Richardson's geranium. It is native to western North America from Alaska to New Mexico, where it can be found in a number of habitats, especially mountains and forests. This is a perennial herb varying in maximum height from 20 to 80 centimeters. The plant grows from a tough, woody taproot and older plants develop rhizomes. The leaves are up to 15 centimeters wide and are divided into generally five segments, each segment subdivided into small rounded or pointed lobes. The flower has five pointed sepals beneath five rounde

items.name: Red robin
items.growersTips:
Pull up shallow roots by hand in late summer before seed pods explosively eject to control spreading.
Sow seeds in autumn just under the soil surface in damp, shaded woodland borders or clay-heavy soil.
Plant alongside native ferns and hostas to provide attractive ground cover in dry shade garden spots.
Water young plants weekly during dry UK spring spells, but leave established clumps to survive drought.
Check leaves in damp British summers for powdery mildew and remove affected foliage to stop spread.
items.description: Geranium robertianum, commonly known as herb-robert or, in North America, as Robert's geranium, is a species of cranesbill that is widespread throughout the northern hemisphere and introduced to some countries in the southern. It is common in woods, hedges, gardens, and on waste ground, and can also be found on shingle beaches and limestone pavements. It is not rare or threatened and in some places it is considered to be invasive.

items.name: Geranium rotundifolium
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn or spring just below the soil surface in free-draining, gritty UK garden loam.
Water sparingly once established, allowing the gritty soil to dry out fully between waterings.
Hand-pull plants in late summer before seed pods explode to prevent aggressive self-seeding.
Grow alongside native wild marjoram or thyme to attract UK pollinators to dry, sunny borders.
Watch for slugs on young spring seedlings, using organic beer traps in damp UK weather.
items.description: Geranium rotundifolium, is a species of annual herb in the family Geraniaceae. It is native in temperate climates across much of Europe, northern Africa, and southwestern Asia; its distribution is spreading north, in response to global warming. The species favours dry, sandy or stony habitat, including old walls, rail ballast, and building rubble, including in urban areas.

items.name: Geranium rubricum
items.growersTips:
Plant in well-drained grit-amended soil to prevent winter root rot in wet UK clay.
Position in full sun to light dappled shade to maximise the deep pink summer blooms.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells rather than daily light sprinkles.
Cut back faded flower stems to ground level in August to encourage a fresh flush of leaves.
Divide established clumps in early spring every three years to maintain plant vigour.
items.description: Geranium rubricum is a species of perennial herb in the family Geraniaceae, native to the South Island of New Zealand, where it is found on ultramafic rock outcrops.

items.name: Geranium sanguineum
items.growersTips:
Plant in free-draining chalky or sandy soil to prevent winter root rot in wet UK climates.
Shear foliage to the ground after the first summer flush to trigger fresh leaves and autumn blooms.
Propagate by taking root cuttings in late autumn or dividing the woody crown in early spring.
Position in full sun to maximise the vibrant magenta flower density and tight hummock growth habit.
Space plants forty centimetres apart to allow the sprawling rhizomatous stems to form weed cover.
items.description: Geranium sanguineum, common name bloody crane's-bill or bloody geranium, is a species of hardy flowering herbaceous perennial plant in the cranesbill family Geraniaceae. It is the county flower of Northumberland.

items.name: Geranium sibiricum
items.growersTips:
Plant in free-draining chalky soil 10cm deep in spring to prevent winter root rot in wet UK clay.
Water weekly during dry summer spells but keep soil dry in winter to survive British frosts.
Cut back to ground level in late autumn after the first frost to encourage fresh spring growth.
Divide congested clumps every three years in March to maintain vigor and control its invasive spread.
Position near robust cranesbills like Johnson's Blue to mask its sparse, sprawling summer habit.
items.description: Geranium sibiricum is a species of perennial flowering plant belonging to the family Geraniaceae.

items.name: Geranium solanderi
items.growersTips:
Plant in well-drained gritty soil to prevent root rot during wet UK winters.
Position in full sun to partial shade to mimic its native Australian open woodland habitat.
Water moderately during dry summer spells but allow the soil to dry out completely between waterings.
Cut back hard after the first flush of flowers in midsummer to encourage fresh foliage and new blooms.
Protect the crown with a dry mulch of bracken or straw in autumn to survive severe UK frosts.
items.description: Geranium solanderi is a species of plant in the family Geraniaceae. It is native to Australia, and to New Zealand.

items.name: Geranium subcaulescens
items.growersTips:
Plant in sharply draining gritty soil to prevent winter root rot in wet UK climates.
Position in full sun to mimic its native Balkan mountain habitat for maximum flowering.
Cut back faded stems and leaves to ground level in midsummer to trigger a fresh flush of foliage.
Propagate by division in early spring just as new growth begins to emerge from the crown.
Plant alongside silver-foliaged alpines or dwarf conifers that thrive in the same dry conditions.
items.description: Geranium subcaulescens is a species of flowering plant in the geranium family Geraniaceae, that is native to Italy, Turkey and the Balkans. A low, mounded evergreen perennial, it typically grows to 8 in (20 cm) tall by more than 11 in (28 cm) broad, with grey-green orbicular and lobed leaves, and masses of bright magenta pink flowers with black centres in summer.

items.name: Wood Crane's-bill
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist, well-drained soil in dappled shade to mimic its native UK woodland edge habitat.
Cut back to ground level after the June bloom to encourage fresh foliage and a late summer flush.
Divide congested clumps in early spring or autumn to maintain vigor and propagate new plants.
Watch for vine weevil grubs in container-grown plants and treat with nematodes in late summer.
Plant alongside native UK woodlanders like dryopteris ferns and wild primroses for spring color.
items.description: Geranium sylvaticum, the wood cranesbill or woodland geranium, is a species of hardy flowering plant in the family Geraniaceae, native to Europe and northern Turkey.

items.name: Geranium thunbergii
items.growersTips:
Plant in moisture-retentive, humus-rich soil in partial shade to mimic its native woodland edge.
Water weekly during dry UK summers to keep the soil consistently damp but never waterlogged.
Divide congested clumps in early spring just as new growth begins to maintain plant vigour.
Cut back faded flowering stems to ground level in late summer to encourage a fresh flush of foliage.
Watch for vine weevil larvae in autumn which can chew through the roots of this fibrous-rooted crane.
items.description: Geranium thunbergii is a cranesbill species that is commonly known as Japanese geranium or Japanese cranesbill. It is one of the most popular folk medicines and also an official antidiarrheic drug in Japan. It is called ゲンノショウコ.

items.name: Chatham Island geranium
items.growersTips:
Plant this Chatham Island native in sharply draining gritty soil to survive wet UK winters.
Position in full sun and shelter from cold drying winds to mimic its coastal cliff habitat.
Propagate by taking semi-ripe cuttings in late summer to guarantee survival of winter losses.
Trim back faded flowering stems in autumn to maintain its compact silvery carpet growth habit.
Protect the crown from winter wet using a cloche or deep grit mulch in high-rainfall UK areas.
items.description: Geranium traversii, the Chatham Island geranium, is a species of flowering plant in the family Geraniaceae. It is native to the Chatham Islands of New Zealand. A perennial, it is found in a wide variety of habitats on its home islands, and is cultivated elsewhere.

items.name: Geranium tuberosum
items.growersTips:
Plant tubers 8cm deep in autumn in well-drained soil to survive wet UK winters without rotting.
Grow in dappled shade under deciduous shrubs to mimic their native woodland edge habitat.
Stop watering completely in midsummer when the plant goes dormant and the foliage dies back.
Propagate by lifting and dividing the tuberous roots in late summer while the plant is dormant.
Plant alongside early spring bulbs like snowdrops to cover their fading foliage in May.
items.description: Geranium tuberosum, the tuberous-rooted cranesbill, is a species of flowering plant in the family Geraniaceae. It is native to the Mediterranean region, the Caucasus, and western Asia. The Royal Horticultural Society considers it a good plant to attract pollinators, and it is widely available from commercial suppliers. There are a number of cultivars available, including 'Rosie's Mauve' and 'Richard Hobbs'.

items.name: Veiny geranium
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist well-drained soil at a depth where the crown sits level with the soil surface.
Cut back faded flower stems and old leaves to ground level in July to encourage fresh new foliage.
Water deeply once a week during dry UK summers until the root system is fully established.
Divide congested clumps in early spring or autumn to maintain vigour and propagate new plants.
Plant under deciduous shrubs where they tolerate dry summer shade once they are established.
items.description: Geranium versicolor, the pencilled geranium, pencilled cranesbill, veined cranesbill, or veiny geranium, is a species of flowering plant in the family Geraniaceae. It is native to southeastern Europe, and has been introduced as a garden escapee to Ireland, Great Britain, France, the former Czechoslovakia, and the US state of Pennsylvania. A semi‑evergreen perennial reaching 45 cm (18 in), it is widely available from commercial suppliers, with the Royal Horticultural Society considering it to be a good plant to attract pollinators. With Geranium endressii it is a parent of the artificial garden

items.name: Geranium viscosissimum
items.growersTips:
Plant in well-drained gritty soil to prevent winter root rot in wet UK climates.
Water deeply only during prolonged dry summer spells once the plant is established.
Cut back faded flower stems to ground level in July to encourage a second flush of autumn blooms.
Divide congested clumps in early spring to maintain vigor and propagate new plants.
Watch for vine weevil larvae in container-grown plants during damp autumn months.
items.description: Geranium viscosissimum, commonly known as the sticky purple geranium, is a perennial in the flowering plant family Geraniaceae. It is thought to be a protocarnivorous plant.

items.name: Wallich Geranium
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist, well-drained soil enriched with leaf mould to mimic their native woodland edge.
Position in partial shade to prevent the blue flowers of cultivars like Buxton's Variety from fading.
Water deeply during dry UK summer spells to prevent the sprawling stems from crisping at the tips.
Cut back hard to ground level in early spring to clear old foliage and encourage fresh new growth.
Propagate by taking semi-ripe heel cuttings in midsummer rather than trying to divide the taproot.
items.description: Geranium wallichianum is a species of hardy flowering herbaceous perennial plant in the genus Geranium, family Geraniaceae. It is native to the Himalayas. It grows to 60 cm (24 in) tall and broad, with hairy toothed leaves and masses of bright blue flowers in summer. It is suitable for cultivation in temperate climates, in the front of the border.

items.name: Gibbaria scabra
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at three millimetres deep in April using free-draining peat-free compost.
Grow in full sun and sheltered south-facing borders to mimic its native warm Mediterranean climate.
Water sparingly at the base only when the top two centimetres of soil have dried out completely.
Protect young spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic wool pellets or beer traps.
Deadhead faded daisy-like flowers weekly in summer to prolong the blooming season until autumn.
items.description: Gibbaria scabra is a species of flowering plant in the family Asteraceae, endemic to the Cape Provinces of South Africa. It was first described in 1943 as Osteospermum scabrum.

items.name: Glaucidium palmatum
items.growersTips:
Plant in moisture-retentive, humus-rich, acidic to neutral soil in a sheltered, fully shaded spot.
Sow fresh seed in autumn in cold frames, as they require winter chill to germinate the next spring.
Apply a thick leaf-mould mulch annually in March to mimic woodland soil and retain vital moisture.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.
Divide established clumps carefully in early spring just as new growth begins to show.
items.description: Glaucidium is a genus of plants in family Ranunculaceae, comprising a single species Glaucidium palmatum. It is endemic to northern and eastern Japan on Hokkaidō and northeastern Honshū on mountains close to the Sea of Japan.

items.name: Yellow horned poppy
items.growersTips:
Plant in sharply draining, gritty soil to prevent winter root rot in wet UK climates.
Sow seeds directly outdoors in spring at a depth of five millimetres in a sunny, gravelly border.
Cut back faded flower stems to the base in late summer to encourage a second flush of blooms.
Protect young spring foliage from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.
Position next to Mediterranean companions like lavender and rosemary that share its dry soil needs.
items.description: Glaucium is a genus of about 25 species of annual, biennial or perennial herbaceous flowering plants in the family Papaveraceae, native to Europe, north Africa, and southwest and central Asia. The species commonly occur in saline habitats, including coasts and salt pans.

items.name: Glaucium corniculatum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in autumn directly where they are to flower to mimic natural UK winter chilling.
Grow in poor, sharply drained chalky or sandy soil to prevent winter wet from rotting the roots.
Water sparingly only during prolonged dry spells as this coastal poppy is highly drought-tolerant.
Position in the absolute brightest, south-facing spot of your garden to maximise the daily blooms.
Leave the decorative, horn-like seed pods intact over winter to encourage self-seeding for next year.
items.description: Glaucium corniculatum, the blackspot hornpoppy or red horned-poppy, is a species of the genus Glaucium in the poppy family (Papaveraceae). It is an annual flowering plant, occurring in southern Europe, and grows up to 1 foot (30 cm) high. The stem and leaves are hairy, the capsule fruit is covered with stiff hair, the flower is red, with a black spot on the base of the tepal bract, which has a yellow margin around it. The flower appears from June until August.

items.name: Yellow horned poppy
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn in deep pots to avoid disturbing the long taproot when planting out in spring.
Incorporate plenty of horticultural grit into heavy UK clay soils to prevent winter root rot.
Position in full sun and do not water once established, as this seaside native thrives on neglect.
Cut back faded flower stems in late summer to encourage a second flush of blooms and fresh foliage.
Leave some seed pods intact over winter to allow self-seeding in gravel paths and sunny borders.
items.description: Glaucium flavum, the yellow horned poppy, yellow hornpoppy or sea poppy, is a summer flowering plant in the family Papaveraceae. It is native to Europe, Northern Africa, Macaronesia and temperate zones in Western Asia. The plant grows on the seashore and is never found inland. All parts of the plant, including the seeds, are toxic. It is classed as a noxious weed in some areas of North America, where it is an introduced species. It is grown in gardens as a short-lived perennial but usually grown as a biennial.

items.name: Glaucium grandiflorum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn in deep pots to avoid disturbing the long taproot when planting out in spring.
Plant in poor, sharply drained soil or gravel in full sun to prevent winter wet from rotting roots.
Water sparingly only during prolonged dry spells in summer as this plant is highly drought-tolerant.
Cut back faded flowering stems to the base in late summer to encourage a neat rosette for winter.
Protect young foliage from slugs and snails in damp UK springs using grit barriers or beer traps.
items.description: Glaucium grandiflorum, the great-flowered horned poppy, is a species of flowering plant in the horned poppy genus which is native to the Middle East.

items.name: Glaucium oxylobum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn or early spring at a shallow depth of five millimetres in free-draining grit.
Plant in poor, sharply drained alkaline soil to prevent winter root rot in wet UK climates.
Water newly planted seedlings sparingly, then leave established plants to rely solely on rainfall.
Cut back faded flower stems in late autumn to encourage a tidy basal rosette of foliage for winter.
Grow alongside Mediterranean herbs like rosemary and thyme which share its need for dry, sunny spots.
items.description: Glaucium oxylobum, called Lotus sweetjuice, is a species of flowering plant in the horned poppy genus which is native to Afghanistan, Iran, Turkmenistan, and Uzbekistan. It was originally described by Pierre Edmond Boissier and Friedrich Alexander Buhse in 1860 in the 12th volume of the Nouveaux mémoires de la Société impériale des naturalistes de Moscou.

items.name: Glaucium secmenii
items.growersTips:
Plant in gritty sharply draining soil or gravel beds to prevent winter wet root rot in UK climates
Sow seeds shallowly in autumn or spring directly where they are to flower as they resent transplanting
Position in full sun against a south-facing wall to mimic its native dry Mediterranean habitat
Water sparingly only during prolonged dry spells once established to avoid crown rot in damp summers
Cut back faded flowering stems to the base in late autumn to encourage fresh basal foliage growth
items.description: Glaucium secmenii is a species of flowering plant in the horned poppy genus which is endemic to Turkey.

items.name: Glossocarya scandens
items.growersTips:
Grow in a heated greenhouse or conservatory as this tropical Lamiaceae cannot survive UK frosts.
Use a very free-draining loam-based compost mixed with plenty of perlite to prevent winter root rot.
Water sparingly in winter, only when the top five centimetres of soil has dried out completely.
Prune back leggy stems by one third in early spring to encourage a bushier, more compact habit.
Position in the brightest spot possible, such as a south-facing windowsill, to mimic tropical sun.
items.description:
Glossocarya is a genus of flowering plants in the mint family, Lamiaceae, first described in 1843. It is native to Indochina, Sri Lanka, New Guinea, and Queensland.SpeciesGlossocarya calcicola Domin - Queensland
Glossocarya coriacea Munir - Queensland
Glossocarya crenata H.R.Fletcher - Thailand
Glossocarya hemiderma (F.Muell. ex Benth.) Benth. ex B.D.Jacks. - Queensland, New Guinea
Glossocarya longiflora H.R.Fletcher - Thailand
Glossocarya mollis Wall. ex Griff - Myanmar, Thailand, Vietnam, Paluan Rabana in Malaysia
Glossocarya premnoides Ridl. - Thailand, Perlis in Malaysia
Glossocarya puberu

items.name: Glossocarya hemiderma
items.growersTips:
Grow in a large pot with peat-free loam-based compost to easily move indoors before autumn frosts.
Water sparingly in winter but keep soil consistently moist during the active spring growing season.
Prune lightly in late spring after frost risk passes to maintain a compact shrubby shape in pots.
Position in the warmest south-facing sheltered spot or greenhouse to maximise UK summer heat.
Check regularly for glasshouse red spider mite and whitefly when overwintering the plant indoors.
items.description: Glossocarya hemiderma is a species of plants in the mint and sage family Lamiaceae. It is native to Papua New Guinea and eastern parts of Queensland, Australia. It is a scrambling shrub or vine with a stem diameter up to 9 cm (3.5 in), and it inhabits rainforest and monsoon forest.

items.name: Gmelina arborea
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender tropical shrub in a container of loam-based compost to move indoors before frosts.
Water copiously in summer but keep the soil barely moist during its winter dormant period indoors.
Position in your sunniest south-facing spot or a heated conservatory to meet its high heat needs.
