Prune back leggy stems in early spring to encourage a bushier habit and manage its indoor size.
Watch closely for glasshouse red spider mite and whitefly when overwintering the plant indoors.
items.description: Gmelina arborea,, locally known as gamhar, is a fast-growing deciduous tree in the family Lamiaceae.

items.name: Gmelina asiatica
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender shrub in a pot of loam-based compost so you can move it indoors before first frost.
Water sparingly in winter but keep soil consistently moist during the active spring and summer growth.
Prune hard in late winter to manage its vigorous, thorny scrambling habit and encourage fresh shoots.
Position the pot in your sunniest south-facing spot or a heated greenhouse to mimic its native heat.
Feed fortnightly with a high-potassium liquid fertilizer from May to September to promote flowering.
items.description: Gmelina asiatica is a plant species, described by Linnaeus, in the family Lamiaceae. No subspecies are listed in the Catalogue of Life.

items.name: Grey Teak
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender tropical shrub in a large pot with loam-based compost to move indoors for winter.
Water sparingly in winter but keep soil consistently moist during the active summer growing season.
Position the pot in a south-facing conservatory or heated greenhouse to maximize essential light.
Prune lightly in late spring after the last frost to maintain shape and encourage bushier growth.
Feed fortnightly in spring and summer with a high-potassium liquid fertilizer to promote blooms.
items.description: Gmelina dalrympleana is a species of plant in the family Lamiaceae. A tree of moist and swampy areas, sometimes on the margins of rainforests. It is found growing in Papua New Guinea and tropical Queensland, in Australia.

items.name: Grey teak
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender Australian native in a large pot to move indoors before the first autumn frosts.
Use a free-draining loam and grit mix to prevent root rot during wet, cold UK winter months.
Water deeply once a week in summer, but keep the soil barely damp during its winter dormancy.
Prune lightly in late spring after new growth starts to maintain a compact shape for patio life.
Check indoor-overwintered plants weekly for spider mites and mealybugs in dry conservatory air.
items.description: Gmelina fasciculiflora, known as the northern white beech, is a species of trees endemic to the Queensland tropical rain forests, Australia, of the mint (Lamiaceae) plant family. It is one of four recognised species of the genus Gmelina found in Australia.

items.name: Gmelina leichhardtii
items.growersTips:
Grow in a large pot of loam-based compost so you can move it into a heated greenhouse for winter.
Water sparingly in winter but keep soil consistently moist during the warm active summer growth.
Prune lightly in late spring after frost risk passes to maintain shape and encourage bushier growth.
Check regularly for glasshouse red spider mite and whitefly when keeping the plant under glass.
Mix plenty of grit into the soil to ensure excellent drainage and prevent root rot in wet winters.
items.description: Gmelina leichhardtii, the white beech, is a tree of eastern Australia. Scattered individuals or small groups of trees naturally occur from the Illawarra district of New South Wales to near Proserpine in tropical Queensland. The white beech or grey teak is a fast-growing tree, growing on volcanic and alluvial soils in areas of moderate to high rainfall. It also grows on poorer sedimentary soils in fire free areas. White beech may occasionally be seen in Australian rainforests, though their status is considered "uncommon". Unlike the Australian red cedar, the white beech has not recovered partic

items.name: Gmelina philippensis
items.growersTips:
Grow this tropical shrub in a container so you can move it indoors before autumn temperatures hit 10C
Plant in free-draining loam mixed with one-third grit to prevent winter root rot in damp UK air
Water deeply only when the top three inches of soil dry out, reducing to once a month in winter
Prune back leggy stems by half in late spring to encourage the pendulous, yellow-flowered bracts
Inspect the unusual tube-like flowers weekly for glasshouse mealybugs and treat with organic oil
items.description: Gmelina philippensis is a plant species in the family Lamiaceae. No subspecies are listed in the Catalogue of Life.

items.name: Low cudweed
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds on the soil surface in spring without covering them as they need UK light to germinate
Water only when the top two inches of soil are dry to prevent root rot in damp UK autumn weather
Grow in poor sandy soil with grit added to the planting hole to ensure the sharp drainage they need
Position in full south-facing sun to prevent the woolly foliage from rotting in humid UK summers
Sow alongside gravel garden plants like Sedum to prevent taller neighbours from blocking their light
items.description: Gnaphalium is a genus of flowering plants in the family Asteraceae, commonly called cudweeds or (formerly) chafeweeds. They are widespread and common in temperate regions, although some are found on tropical mountains or in the subtropical regions of the world.

items.name: Goniorrhachis marginata
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in April at a depth of two centimeters using a heated propagator to beat UK cold.
Plant out in late May in a south-facing border with grit added to the soil to ensure sharp drainage.
Water deeply once a week at the base during dry summer spells to establish the deep taproot system.
Pinch out the growing tips in June to encourage a bushier habit and increase the summer blooms.
Grow alongside nasturtiums to act as a sacrificial trap crop for black bean aphids in midsummer.
items.description: Goniorrhachis is a genus of flowering plants in the legume family, Fabaceae. It belongs to the subfamily Detarioideae. It contains a single species, Goniorrhachis marginata, native to eastern Brazil.

items.name: Beetle Daisy
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in early spring using a gritty, free-draining compost to combat UK dampness.
Place pots on a south-facing windowsill to mimic the intense South African sun these annuals need.
Water only when the top two inches of soil are dry to prevent root rot in cool British summers.
Plant out in late May after frosts pass, spacing ten centimetres apart in rockeries or gravel.
Watch for slugs and snails on young seedlings during wet spring nights and use organic barriers.
items.description: Gorteria diffusa is a highly variable, small annual herbaceous plant or rarely a shrublet that is assigned to the daisy family. Like in almost all Asteraceae, the individual flowers are 5-merous, small and clustered in typical heads, and are surrounded by an involucre, consisting of in this case several whorls of bracts, which are merged at their base. In G. diffusa, the centre of the head is taken by relatively few male and bisexual yellow to orange disc florets, and is surrounded by one complete whorl of 5–14 infertile cream to dark orange ray florets, sometimes with a few ray florets nearer

items.name: Gorteria personata
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in early spring using a gritty, free-draining compost to combat wet UK weather.
Plant out in late May in your sunniest south-facing spot to mimic its native South African heat.
Water sparingly only when the top two inches of soil are dry to prevent root rot in damp climates.
Watch for slugs on young seedlings as damp UK spring nights can quickly destroy this tender annual.
Deadhead spent blooms weekly in summer to encourage continuous flowering until the first autumn frost.
items.description: Gorteria personata, the mini beetledaisy, is a small annual herbaceous plant in the daisy family. It is endemic to the Cape Provinces of South Africa. It is called bosduifdoring in Afrikaans.

items.name: Little amphianthus
items.growersTips:
Grow this rare aquatic annual in shallow acidic pond margins or mud flats under full UK summer sun.
Sow seeds in late spring by pressing them gently onto wet, peat-free ericaceous compost without burying.
Maintain constant water levels just covering the soil surface to mimic natural vernal pool habitats.
Protect young plants from slugs and snails which quickly consume the delicate submerged foliage.
Overwinter collected seeds in damp sand in a cold frame to undergo essential winter stratification.
items.description: Gratiola amphiantha is a rare species of flowering plant known by the common names little amphianthus, pool sprite and snorkelwort. It was previously the only species in the monotypic genus Amphianthus, but it was moved to genus Gratiola after genetic analysis in 2008. It is native to the Piedmont region of the southeastern United States, with a center of distribution in Georgia. It occurs in Alabama and South Carolina as well. It is limited to granite outcrops, a high-biodiversity habitat type that is threatened by activities such as quarrying, off-road vehicles, and trash and debris dumping.

items.name: Boggs Lake hedgehyssop
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in late spring on wet, muddy soil surfaces without covering them, as they need light.
Grow this obligate wetland annual in a bog garden or pond margin with water up to five cm deep.
Maintain a constant acidic to neutral pH by using rainwater rather than chlorinated UK tap water.
Position in full sun to mimic its vernal pool habitat and ensure successful summer flowering.
Collect seed capsules in late summer to resow next spring, as this annual will not survive winter.
items.description: Gratiola heterosepala is a species of flowering plant known by the common name Boggs Lake hedgehyssop.

items.name: Clammy hedgehyssop
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds on the surface of wet, acidic compost in spring as they need light to germinate in the UK.
Grow this mud-loving annual in bog gardens or pond margins with water levels up to five centimetres.
Keep the soil constantly saturated using rainwater rather than tap water to maintain low pH levels.
Position in full sun to partial shade to mimic its natural North American wetland habitat in the UK.
Sow indoors in March to protect young seedlings from late UK frosts before planting out in May.
items.description: Gratiola neglecta is a species of flowering plant known by the common name clammy hedgehyssop. It is native to much of North America, including most all of the United States and the southern half of Canada. It is generally found in moist to wet habitat. This is an unobtrusive annual herb producing a glandular stem up to about 30 centimeters tall. The lance-shaped to oval leaves are arranged oppositely about the stem. They are up to 5 centimeters long and sometimes toothed along the edges. The inflorescence is a raceme of nearly cylindrical tubular whitish flowers each about a centimeter long.

items.name: Gratiola officinalis
items.growersTips:
Plant in heavy clay or boggy soil at the pond edge with the crown submerged no deeper than five cm.
Keep the soil permanently wet or waterlogged, never allowing this marsh plant to dry out in summer.
Cut back the sprawling stems to ground level in late autumn to keep the clump tidy for spring growth.
Propagate by dividing the fibrous root rhizomes in early spring just as new green shoots appear.
Position in full sun to partial shade to ensure the small white flowers bloom reliably in July.
items.description: Gratiola officinalis, the gratiole, common hedgehyssop, grace of God, Gratia Dei, hedge hyssop, hedge-hyssop, or herb of grace, is an ornamental plant in the family Plantaginaceae. It is a rhizomatous perennial herb native to Europe.

items.name: Gratiola peruviana
items.growersTips:
Grow this native bog plant in a permanently wet, acidic to neutral soil or shallow pond margin.
Plant crowns just below the soil surface in spring to allow roots to establish in warm mud.
Position in full sun to partial shade to mimic its natural damp UK meadow and creek habitats.
Propagate in spring by dividing the creeping rhizomes or taking softwood cuttings in early summer.
Cut back the dieback in late autumn to prevent decaying foliage from fouling small garden ponds.
items.description: Gratiola peruviana, commonly known as austral brooklime, is a small perennial herb in the family Plantaginaceae. The species is native to South America and Australasia. It grows to between 10 and 30 centimetres high and has pink or white tubular flowers with red-purple stripes inside. These are followed by ovoid capsules that are up to 7mm long. The stem-clasping ovate leaves are arranged in opposite pairs and have shallowly toothed edges.

items.name: Greeneocharis circumscissa
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn on the surface of gritty, free-draining soil to allow winter cold to break dormancy
Grow in a raised scree bed or alpine trough to protect the roots from wet winter rot in UK climates
Water only during dry spring spells, allowing the gritty substrate to dry out completely between feeds
Position in full south-facing sun to mimic its native dry habitat and prevent leggy, weak growth
Surround the collar with fine granite grit to prevent damp soil from rotting the lower foliage
items.description: Greeneocharis circumscissa is a species of flowering plant in the borage family, known by the common name cushion cryptantha. It is native to western North America from Washington to Baja California to Colorado and it is also found in Argentina. It grows in sandy or gravelly types of habitat, from mountains to desert, below 9,500 m (31,200 ft) above sea level.

items.name: Guibourtia coleosperma
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in April at a depth of two centimeters to protect them from late UK spring frosts.
Plant in well-drained, sandy loam soil mixed with grit to prevent waterlogging during wet summers.
Water deeply once a week at the base during dry spells, allowing the topsoil to dry out between.
Position in the sunniest, south-facing spot of your garden to maximize limited UK summer heat.
Protect young shoots from slugs and snails using organic beer traps or physical copper barriers.
items.description: Guibourtia is a flowering plant genus in the family Fabaceae, also known by the common names as Rhodesian copalwood, African Rosewood, amazique, bubinga, kevazingo, and ovangkol.

items.name: Guibourtia coleosperma
items.growersTips:
Grow this frost-tender African shrub in a container of free-draining loam to move indoors by October.
Water only when the top five centimeters of soil dries out to prevent root rot in cool UK summers.
Prune lightly in late spring after new growth starts to maintain shape and remove winter dieback.
Position in your sunniest south-facing spot or unheated greenhouse to maximize essential summer heat.
Feed monthly from May to August with a low-nitrogen fertilizer to support its legume root nodules.
items.description: Guibourtia coleosperma, the African rosewood (ambiguous), large false mopane, Rhodesian copalwood or machibi, is a species of plant in the family Fabaceae. It is a large evergreen tree found in open woodland and dry forest, almost exclusively on Kalahari Sand in Angola, southern Democratic Republic of Congo, Namibia, Botswana, Zambia, and Zimbabwe.

items.name: Guibourtia sousae
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in April at a depth of 2cm using free-draining peat-free grit-amended compost.
Plant out in late May after frosts in a south-facing spot with maximum sun to mimic warm climates.
Water deeply once a week at the base only when the top 5cm of soil feels dry to prevent root rot.
Pinch out the growing tips in June to encourage a bushier habit and increase the flower yield.
Protect young plants from slugs using beer traps or copper tape during damp UK spring nights.
items.description: Guibourtia sousae is a species of plant in the family Fabaceae. It is found only in Mozambique.

items.name: Guilandina bonduc
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in April at a depth of two centimetres using bottom heat to ensure germination.
Scarify the hard seed coat with sandpaper before soaking in warm water for twenty-four hours.
Plant out in late May in a south-facing border with free-draining sandy soil to prevent root rot.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells rather than giving frequent light sprinkles.
Protect young plants from slugs using beer traps or copper tape during damp British spring nights.
items.description: Guilandina is a genus of flowering plants in the legume family, Fabaceae. It belongs to the subfamily Caesalpinioideae and tribe Caesalpinieae.

items.name: Guilandina bonduc
items.growersTips:
Grow in a large pot of gritty, free-draining soil to move indoors before the first autumn frost.
Scarify the hard seed coat with sandpaper and soak in warm water for 24 hours before sowing.
Position the container in your warmest, brightest south-facing spot to mimic its tropical habitat.
Water deeply only when the top five centimetres of compost is dry, keeping it barely damp in winter.
Prune back leggy stems in late spring after new growth starts to maintain a compact container shape.
items.description: Guilandina bonduc, commonly known as nicker nut amongst other names, is a species of flowering plant in the bean family Fabaceae that has a mostly pantropical distribution. It is a scrambling, thorny shrub or vine that is mostly found close to coastlines, and was first described in 1753 by Carl Linnaeus.

items.name: Giant mother-in-law vine
items.growersTips:
Start seeds indoors in April using deep root trainers to protect the sensitive taproot before May frost
Sow seeds exactly two centimeters deep in a free-draining peat-free loam mixed with sharp grit
Water only when the top three centimeters of soil are dry to prevent root rot in damp UK summers
Protect young stems from slugs using beer traps or copper tape during wet British spring nights
Position in the sunniest south-facing border sheltered from cold winds to encourage summer blooms
items.description: Guilandina robusta, commonly known as giant mother-in-law vine, is a species of climbing plant in the pea family Fabaceae. It is found only in the Wet Tropics bioregion of Queensland, Australia.

items.name: Gymnocarpos decandrus
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in April under glass in a gritty, free-draining compost mix to prevent dampening off.
Plant out in May in a south-facing rockery or gravel garden to maximise scarce UK summer sun.
Water sparingly only during prolonged dry spells, allowing the gritty soil to dry out completely.
Protect young plants from slugs and snails using beer traps during wet British spring nights.
Grow alongside Sedums or Sempervivums in containers to ensure the sharp drainage this annual needs.
items.description: Gymnocarpos is a genus of plants in the family Caryophyllaceae.

items.name: Gymnocarpos bracteatus
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at two millimetres deep in early spring under glass to protect from UK frosts.
Grow in sharply draining gritty soil mix to prevent root rot during wet British summer spells.
Water sparingly only when the top two inches of soil are dry to mimic its native arid habitat.
Position in the brightest south-facing spot or greenhouse to maximise limited UK summer sunlight.
Pinch out the growing tips of young plants in May to encourage a bushier habit and more bracts.
items.description: Gymnocarpos bracteatus is a species of plant in the family Caryophyllaceae. It is endemic to the Hajhir Mountains of Socotra in Yemen. Its natural habitat is subtropical or tropical dry shrubland.

items.name: Gymnocladus dioicus
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in March at a depth of two centimeters using bottom heat to ensure germination.
Water young plants weekly during dry UK summers to establish their deep taproot system.
Grow in deep fertile loam enriched with well-rotted manure to mimic their native river valley soil.
Protect young spring shoots from late UK frosts using fleece or a cold frame to prevent dieback.
Position in full sun next to early-flowering bulbs to mask the late leaf-out of this species.
items.description: Gymnocladus is a small genus of leguminous trees. The common name coffeetree is used for this genus. It includes six species native to eastern North America and southeastern Asia.

items.name: Gymnocoronis spilanthoides
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender plant in a submerged pot at a depth of 5 to 10cm in a sunny, sheltered garden pond.
Bring containerized plants indoors to a frost-free greenhouse or conservatory before October frosts.
Prune aggressive stems weekly in summer to prevent this vigorous spreader from choking pond life.
Plant in heavy, nutrient-rich clay loam to anchor the roots and prevent the plant from floating.
Propagate in spring by taking 10cm stem cuttings and rooting them directly in wet, muddy compost.
items.description: Gymnocoronis spilanthoides, also known by its common name Senegal tea or Senegal tea plant  is a species from the genus Gymnocoronis. The species was first described by Augustin Pyramus de Candolle.

items.name: Baby's breath
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds directly outdoors in late spring after frosts, barely covering them with 3mm of soil.
Water seedlings sparingly only during dry spells, as wet UK soil causes root rot in annual types.
Pinch out the growing tips when plants are 10cm tall to encourage a bushier, flower-filled habit.
Support the floppy stems early using brushwood or twiggy pea sticks before the heavy blooms open.
Sow a second batch in July for a continuous supply of fresh cut flowers into the British autumn.
items.description: Gypsophila is a genus of flowering plants in the carnation family, Caryophyllaceae. They are native to Eurasia, Africa, Australia, and the Pacific Islands. Turkey has a particularly high diversity of Gypsophila taxa, with about 35 endemic species. Some Gypsophila are introduced species in other regions.

items.name: Gypsophila oldhamiana
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in April under cover or outdoors in May once the late spring frosts have passed
Grow in sharply draining gritty alkaline soil to prevent winter root rot in wet UK climates
Water sparingly only during dry spells as this species thrives on neglect and dislikes soggy roots
Support the tall wiry stems with brushwood twigs in windy UK gardens before flowers open in July
Cut back faded flower stems to ground level in late summer to encourage a potential second flush
items.description: Gypsophila oldhamiana, the Manchurian baby's-breath or Oldham's baby's-breath, is a flowering plant of the family Caryophyllaceae.

items.name: Gyrocaryum oppositifolium
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn in cold frames to mimic UK winter chill for natural stratification.
Grow in gritty, alkaline soil with sharp drainage to prevent winter wet rot in damp UK climates.
Water sparingly from below during summer to keep the foliage dry and prevent powdery mildew.
Plant alongside small sedums or thymes in gravel gardens to provide support and prevent soil splash.
Protect the delicate crown with a glass cloche during wet winter months to prevent rot.
items.description: Gyrocaryum is a genus of plant in family Boraginaceae. It contains a single species, Gyrocaryum oppositifolium, which is endemic to Spain. The genus and species were described by Spanish botanist Benito Valdés in 1983. It was considered to be extinct in Andalucía until a population was found in 2025.

items.name: Haastia pulvinaris
items.growersTips:
Grow in a raised scree bed or alpine house using a mix of fifty percent grit to survive UK winter wet.
Protect the woolly foliage from autumn and winter rain using a pane of glass or a cold frame cover.
Water only from the base or plunge the pot to keep the felted cushion dry and prevent rot.
Plant in full sun with maximum air circulation to mimic its native high-altitude alpine habitat.
Topdress the surrounding soil with a thick layer of granite chippings to keep the collar dry.
items.description: Haastia pulvinaris, or vegetable sheep, is a species of perennial alpine plant that grows in a bizarre, sheep-like formation on scree slopes in the South Island of New Zealand.

items.name: Haastia sinclairii
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds on the surface of gritty, free-draining compost in early spring as they need light to sprout
Water only from below to keep the woolly foliage dry and prevent rot in damp UK winter conditions
Mix fifty percent horticultural grit into your soil to mimic its native alpine scree habitat
Protect the woolly leaves from slugs and snails using copper tape around your alpine containers
Position pots in the sunniest south-facing spot to maximize light during overcast British summers
items.description: Haastia sinclairii is a species of small flowering plant in the South Island of New Zealand.

items.name: Logwood tree
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in April at a depth of two centimetres using a heated propagator set to twenty-oneC
Grow in pots of loam-based compost mixed with plenty of grit to ensure the sharp drainage it needs
Water only when the top five centimetres of soil is dry to prevent root rot in damp UK summers
Bring pots inside to a heated greenhouse or conservatory by October before the first autumn frosts
Position in the sunniest south-facing spot available to mimic its native tropical light levels
items.description: Haematoxylum is a genus of flowering plants in the legume family, Fabaceae, subfamily Caesalpinioideae and the tribe Caesalpinieae. It includes five species, four of which are native to the tropical Americas from Mexico to Colombia, and one to Namibia.

items.name: Haematoxylum brasiletto
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender Mexican shrub in a pot of gritty loam to move indoors before autumn frosts arrive.
Water sparingly in winter, allowing the compost to dry out completely between light waterings.
Prune lightly in late spring after new growth starts to maintain a compact shape for overwintering.
Keep in a south-facing conservatory or heated greenhouse to meet its high light and warmth needs.
Watch for glasshouse red spider mite and scale insects when keeping this plant indoors over winter.
items.description: Haematoxylum brasiletto, or Mexican logwood, is a species of tropical hardwood tree in the legume family, Fabaceae. It is known in its native Mexico and Guatemala as "palo de brasil" or "palo de tinto". The timber is used to make bows for stringed instruments, the manufacture of dyes and in ethnobotany.

items.name: Logwood tree
items.growersTips:
Grow in a pot with peat-free loam compost so you can move it indoors before the first autumn frost.
Water only when the top three centimetres of soil are dry to prevent root rot in cool UK weather.
Place on a south-facing windowsill or in a heated conservatory to maximise essential light levels.
Prune lightly in late spring after new growth starts to maintain its compact container size.
Check weekly for glasshouse red spider mite and scale insects which thrive on indoor woody plants.
items.description: Haematoxylum campechianum is a species of flowering tree in the legume family, Fabaceae, that is native to southern Mexico, and introduced to the Caribbean, northern Central America, and other localities around the world.

items.name: Hardwickia binata
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender Fabaceae shrub in a large pot of gritty loam to move indoors before autumn frosts.
Water deeply once a week in summer, then keep the soil almost completely dry throughout UK winters.
Prune lightly in late spring after frost risk passes to shape the shrub and remove dead wood.
Blend thirty percent horticultural grit into peat-free compost to ensure the sharp winter drainage.
Position the pot against a south-facing brick wall to maximise summer heat and light in UK gardens.
items.description: Hardwickia is a monotypic genus of flowering plant in the subfamily Detarioideae of the legume family, Fabaceae. The only species is the anjan, Hardwickia binata, a tree which is native to India and Bangladesh, and which grows to height of 25-30 meters. This plant genus was named after Thomas Hardwicke by William Roxburgh.

items.name: False Indian plantain
items.growersTips:
Plant this deep-rooted perennial in moisture-retentive, humus-rich soil that never dries out fully.
Position in partial shade to mimic its native woodland edge, protecting leaves from hot UK sun.
Water deeply during dry summer spells to prevent the large, architectural foliage from wilting.
Propagate by division in early spring just as new growth emerges to maintain plant vigour.
Cut the tall flower stems back to the ground in late autumn after the white blooms fade.
items.description: Hasteola suaveolens, known by the common names false Indian plantain and sweet scented Indian plantain, is a perennial forb native to the northeastern and north-central United States. It is found from Massachusetts south to Virginia and North Carolina, and west as far as Minnesota and Minnesota and Missouri.

items.name: Hastingsia alba
items.growersTips:
Plant in moisture-retentive, acidic to neutral boggy soil or wet pond margins in full UK sun.
Sow seeds in autumn in cold frames, as they require winter chilling to germinate the next spring.
Water consistently during dry summer spells to mimic their native wet meadow and seepage habitats.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.
Divide congested clumps in early spring just as new growth begins to maintain plant vigour.
items.description: Hastingsia alba is a species of flowering plant known by the common names white rushlily and white schoenolirion.

items.name: Hastingsia serpentinicola
items.growersTips:
Plant in a sharp-draining, gritty loam with a pH of 7.5 to 8.5 to mimic its native serpentine soils.
Keep soil consistently moist during spring growth but reduce watering in winter to prevent root rot.
Sow fresh seeds in cold frames during autumn, allowing natural UK winter chills to break dormancy.
Position in full sun to light dappled shade to ensure strong flower spikes and prevent leggy growth.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.
items.description: Hastingsia serpentinicola is a species of flowering plant known by the common name Klamath rushlily. It is native to the mountains of northwestern California and southwestern Oregon, where it grows in serpentine soils.

items.name: Hauya elegans
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender Mexican shrub in a large pot of gritty loam to move indoors before autumn frosts.
Water moderately in summer but keep the compost barely moist during its winter dormant period.
Position in the sunniest, most sheltered south-facing spot or against a warm wall to mimic Mexico.
Prune lightly in early spring to shape the plant and encourage new flowering wood for late summer.
Check regularly for glasshouse red spider mite and whitefly when overwintering under glass.
items.description: Hauya elegans is a species of flowering plant in the Onagraceae family. It is native to Oaxaca and Chiapas, Mexico to Honduras, Costa Rica, and Guatemala.

items.name: Hauya heydeana
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender Mexican shrub in a large pot with grit-heavy loam to move indoors before UK frosts.
Water moderately in summer but keep the compost barely damp during its dormant winter greenhouse stay.
Position in your sunniest south-facing sheltered spot to mimic its native warm montane habitat.
Prune lightly in early spring to shape the woody stems and encourage fresh flowering wood.
Watch closely for glasshouse red spider mite and whitefly when overwintering under glass in the UK.
items.description: Hauya heydeana is a species of Hauya that is native to Chiapas, Mexico and Guatemala.

items.name: Hazardia berberidis
items.growersTips:
Plant in free-draining gravelly soil against a south-facing wall to survive wet UK winters.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells, but keep completely dry throughout the winter.
Prune lightly in late spring after frost risks pass to maintain a compact, bushy shrub shape.
Protect from severe winter frosts below minus five Celsius using a temporary fleece wrap.
Grow in a terracotta pot filled with a gritty alpine compost mix to ensure excellent drainage.
items.description: Hazardia berberidis is a species of flowering plant in the family Asteraceae commonly known as the barberry-leaf goldenbush. A woody shrub, it is characterized by sawtooth leaves and yellow ray flowers that bloom from March to August. It is endemic to the coastal sage scrub and coastal succulent scrub habitats of Baja California, Mexico, but with populations of uncertain origin in San Diego County, California.

items.name: Hazardia brickellioides
items.growersTips:
Grow in a terracotta pot with fifty percent grit to survive wet UK winters and prevent root rot.
Position against a south-facing brick wall to maximize summer heat and shield from freezing winds.
Water only when the top five centimeters of soil is bone dry, reducing to zero during winter.
Prune lightly in late spring after frosts pass to shape the shrub and remove winter-damaged stems.
Protect with fleece or move to a cold greenhouse when UK temperatures are forecast to drop below -5C.
items.description: Adiaphila brickellioides is a species of shrub in the family Asteraceae known by the common name brickellbush goldenweed. It is native to the Mojave Desert of California and Nevada, where it grows in rocky limestone habitat.

items.name: Hazardia cana
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in spring at a depth of 3mm in free-draining sandy loam to prevent waterlogging in wet UK weather.
Water sparingly only when the top 5cm of soil is dry, as this island native is highly rot-prone.
Position in the sunniest south-facing border or a gravel garden to maximise scarce UK summer heat.
Protect young seedlings from slugs and snails using organic bait or copper tape during damp springs.
Grow in terracotta pots that can be moved under a cold frame to shield them from excessive autumn rain.
items.description: Hazardia cana is a rare North American species of shrubs in the family Asteraceae known by the common names Guadalupe hazardia, San Clemente Island hazardia, or simply island hazardia. It is native to San Clemente Island, one of the Channel Islands of California, and to Guadalupe Island.

items.name: Hazardia detonsa
items.growersTips:
Grow in sharply drained gritty soil or a raised bed to survive wet UK winters and prevent root rot.
Position in the warmest south-facing sun trap or against a brick wall to mimic its native climate.
Water sparingly only during dry summer spells and keep completely dry during cold winter months.
Prunt lightly in late spring after frost passes to maintain a compact shape and remove dead wood.
Protect with fleece or move container-grown plants into a cold greenhouse during severe UK frosts.
items.description: Hazardia detonsa is a rare species of shrub in the family Asteraceae known by the common name island bristleweed. It is endemic to the Channel Islands of California, having been found on 4 islands.

items.name: Hazardia orcuttii
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at three millimetres deep in early spring under glass to combat wet UK soils.
Water sparingly only when the top five centimetres of soil dries out to prevent root rot in damp UKs.
Grow in a gritty loam mix with fifty percent perlite to mimic its arid native Mexican habitat.
Position pots in the sunniest south-facing spot to maximise heat during cool British summers.
Monitor closely for slugs and snails which aggressively target young seedlings in damp spring weather.
items.description: Hazardia orcuttii is a rare North American species of flowering plant in the family Asteraceae known by the common names Orcutt's bristleweed and Orcutt's goldenbush. It is native to California in the United States and Baja California in Mexico. It can be found in one location in California, in the city of Encinitas. There, it is located in and near a protected zone known as the Manchester Conservation Area. In Baja California it can be found at 11 to 17 locations.

items.name: Hazardia squarrosa
items.growersTips:
Plant in free-draining gravelly soil against a south-facing wall to survive wet UK winters.
Water sparingly only during prolonged summer droughts once established to prevent root rot.
Prune lightly in late spring after frosts pass to shape the shrub and remove winter dieback.
Protect with horticultural fleece during severe UK winter frosts below minus five Celsius.
Grow in a terracotta pot using a gritty loam-based compost to easily move indoors for winter.
items.description: Hazardia squarrosa is a North American species of shrub in the family Asteraceae known by the common name sawtooth goldenbush. It is native to California in the United States and Baja California in Mexico.

items.name: Hazardia stenolepis
items.growersTips:
Plant in free-draining gravelly loam to prevent winter root rot in wet UK climates.
Position against a south-facing brick wall to maximise sun exposure and trap essential summer heat.
Water sparingly only during dry summer spells, keeping the soil completely dry throughout winter.
Prune lightly in late spring after frosts pass to shape the shrub and remove winter-damaged stems.
Grow in a terracotta pot with grit-heavy compost to easily move indoors before heavy winter frosts.
items.description: Hazardia stenolepis, the serpentine bristleweed, is a North American species of shrub in the daisy family. It has been found only in California in the western United States, and in Baja California in northwestern Mexico.

items.name: Hazardia whitneyi
items.growersTips:
Plant in sharply draining gritty soil or a raised bed to survive wet UK winters without root rot.
Position in full sun against a south-facing wall to maximize summer heat and protect from frost.
Water sparingly only during dry summer spells once established, keeping the crown dry in winter.
Prune lightly in late spring after frost risk passes to maintain a compact, bushy shrub shape.
Protect with fleece or move container-grown plants into a cold greenhouse during severe UK freezes.
items.description: Adeia whitneyi, common name Whitney's bristleweed, is a North American species of shrub in the daisy family. It has been found only in the state of California in the western United States.

items.name: Curry plant
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in March at a depth of two millimetres and transplant out after the May frosts.
Grow in poor to moderately fertile gritty soil as rich soils cause floppy stems and fewer flowers.
Water young plants weekly until established then only during prolonged dry spells to avoid root rot.
Pinch out the growing tips when plants reach fifteen centimetres to encourage bushy lateral growth.
Harvest strawflowers for drying just as the outer petals open before the yellow centre is visible.
items.description: The genus Helichrysum consists of an estimated 600 species of flowering plants in the sunflower family (Asteraceae). The type species is Helichrysum orientale. They often go by the names everlasting, immortelle, and strawflower. The name is derived from the Ancient Greek words ἥλιος and χρῡσός.

items.name: Heliomeris longifolia
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at two millimetres deep in April under glass to protect from late UK frosts.
Grow in free-draining sandy loam with added grit to prevent root rot during wet British summers.
Water only when the top two inches of soil are dry to mimic its native arid North American habitat.
Deadhead spent yellow blooms weekly from July to October to prolong the late-season flowering display.
Position near purple Salvia nemorosa to provide a structural and colour contrast in sunny borders.
items.description: Heliomeris longifolia is a North American species of flowering plants in the family Asteraceae called the longleaf false goldeneye. It is widespread across much of Mexico from Chihuahua and Sonora south to Chiapas, and found also in the southwestern United States from Nevada to western Texas.

items.name: Heliomeris multiflora
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at two millimetres deep in April under glass to protect from late UK frosts.
Plant in free-draining sandy soil to prevent root rot during wet British summer spells.
Water deeply once a week at the base rather than daily to encourage deep, drought-tolerant roots.
Pinch out the growing tips in May to promote a bushier habit and increase the number of yellow blooms.
Position near dark-foliaged Physocarpus to create a striking colour contrast in UK borders.
items.description: Heliomeris multiflora is a North American species of flowering plants in the family Asteraceae called the showy goldeneye. It grows in Mexico and the western United States from Montana to Jalisco.

items.name: Heliosperma pusillum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at two millimetres deep in early spring under glass to beat late UK frosts.
Water sparingly at the base only when the top two centimetres of gritty, alkaline soil feel dry.
Watch for slugs on young spring shoots by using beer traps or organic wool pellets around plants.
Deadhead spent blooms weekly in July and August to prolong the short annual flowering window.
Plant alongside Dianthus or Sedum in raised beds to ensure the sharp winter drainage they require.
items.description: Heliosperma is a genus of flowering plants in the family Caryophyllaceae. As such, it is closely related to the large genus Silene, but its members can be told apart from Silene by the crest of long papillae on the seeds. The majority of the species are narrow endemics from the Balkan Peninsula, but H. alpestre is endemic to the Eastern Alps, and H. pusillum is found from the Cordillera Cantábrica in northern Spain to the Carpathians. Like members of the genus Silene and other related genera, Heliosperma is attacked by species of the anther smut fungus Microbotryum. Cases of parallel divergenc

items.name: Heliosperma pusillum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn in a cold frame using a gritty compost mix to mimic UK alpine scree conditions.
Water sparingly from below to keep the foliage dry and prevent rot in damp British winters.
Position in a raised bed or rockery facing south to maximise scarce UK winter sunshine.
Protect young plants from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers during wet spring weather.
Grow alongside Saxifraga or Sempervivum in shallow troughs to ensure perfect sharp drainage.
items.description: Heliosperma pusillum is a species of flowering plants in the family Caryophyllaceae. It is native to mountain ranges of Western Europe. It's a species of plants with a complex evolutionary history characterized by repeated ecological divergence.

items.name: Heliotropium
items.growersTips:
Overwinter potted heliotropes indoors at ten degrees Celsius to survive wet UK winter frosts.
Plant out in late May after the last frost in a south-facing border to maximise essential sunlight.
Water the base deeply twice a week in dry summer spells to prevent leaf drop and powdery mildew.
Pinch out the growing tips of young plants in spring to encourage a bushier habit and more blooms.
Grow in peat-free compost mixed with one-third grit to ensure the fast drainage they require.
items.description: Heliotropium is a genus of flowering plants with around 325 species commonly known as heliotropes. They are highly toxic to dogs and cats, as well as to humans.

items.name: Heliotropium amplexicaule
items.growersTips:
Plant in free-draining gritty soil in full sun to prevent winter root rot in wet UK climates.
Overwinter container plants in a frost-free greenhouse or conservatory to survive UK frosts.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells, allowing the top soil to dry out completely.
Prune back hard in early spring to encourage bushy growth and maximize summer flowering stems.
Watch for aphids and glasshouse whitefly when keeping plants indoors or under glass in spring.
items.description: Heliotropium amplexicaule is a species of heliotrope known by several common names, including clasping heliotrope, blue heliotrope, and summer heliotrope. It is native to South America, especially Argentina, but it is known on several other continents where it is an introduced species, and in some areas such as eastern Australia, a noxious weed.

items.name: Heliotropium angiospermum
items.growersTips:
Overwinter in a heated greenhouse or indoors as this tender perennial cannot survive UK frosts.
Grow in pots of free-draining loam-based compost with added grit to prevent winter root rot.
Water only when the top two inches of soil are dry to mimic its native dry-scrub habitat.
Prune back by half in early spring to encourage bushy growth and prevent the stems from flopping.
Watch for glasshouse whitefly and spider mites when keeping the plant indoors over the winter.
items.description: Heliotropium angiospermum, common name scorpion's tail or scorpion-tail, is a flowering plant in the Heliotropium genus and family Heliotropiaceae. An annual or short-lived perennial it grows in Florida and Texas into Mexico as well as on various islands in arid lowlands. Its nectar is sought-out by butterflies and also provides food for bees and birds. The stems terminate in scorpioid inflorescences.

items.name: Heliotropium anomalum
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender coastal shrub in a gritty loam-based compost with fifty percent horticultural grit
Overwinter containers in a heated greenhouse or conservatory kept strictly above five degrees Celsius
Water only when the top three inches of soil are dry to prevent root rot in damp UK winters
Take semi-ripe cuttings in late summer to ensure replacement plants survive the cold British winter
Position in your sunniest south-facing spot or against a warm brick wall to mimic its native habitat
items.description: Heliotropium anomalum is a species of flowering shrub in the family Heliotropiaceae. Its common names include Polynesian heliotrope, Pacific heliotrope, Scrub heliotrope and hinahina kū kahakai (Hawaiian).

items.name: Heliotropium arborescens
items.growersTips:
Overwinter plants indoors at 10C from October to May as they cannot survive UK frosts.
Water thoroughly only when the top 2cm of soil dries to prevent root rot in damp UK summers.
Pinch out the growing tips in spring to encourage bushy growth and more cherry-pie scented blooms.
Grow in pots using peat-free compost mixed with 20 percent grit for essential wet-weather drainage.
Position in full south-facing sun to maximise the intense vanilla fragrance on warm summer evenings.
items.description: Heliotropium arborescens, the garden heliotrope or just heliotrope, is a species of flowering plant in the family Heliotropiaceae, native to Bolivia, Colombia, and Peru. Common names also include cherry pie and common heliotrope.

items.name: Heliotropium arboreum
items.growersTips:
Grow in a free-draining sandy loam with neutral pH to prevent winter root rot in wet UK soils.
Position in a terracotta pot in full sun so you can move it indoors before the first autumn frost.
Water deeply only when the top two inches of soil dry out, as this shrub hates waterlogged roots.
Prune back lightly in early spring after overwintering to encourage bushy new flowering growth.
Monitor closely for glasshouse whitefly and red spider mite when sheltering indoors over winter.
items.description: Heliotropium arboreum is a species of flowering plant in the family Heliotropiaceae. It is native to tropical Asia including southern China, Madagascar, northern Australia, and most of the atolls and high islands of Micronesia and Polynesia. Common names include velvetleaf soldierbush, tree heliotrope, veloutier, and octopus bush. It is a shrub or small tree typical of littoral zones reaching a height of 3.6 m (12 ft), with a spread of about 5 m (16 ft).

items.name: Heliotropium crispum
items.growersTips:
Plant this tender perennial in free-draining sandy loam enriched with grit to prevent winter rot.
Position in your warmest south-facing border or container to maximise essential UK summer sun.
Water deeply only when the top two inches of soil dry out to avoid fatal root rot in damp climates.
Bring containers into a frost-free greenhouse by October before the first autumn frosts hit.
Take softwood cuttings in late summer to guarantee new plants survive the damp British winter.
items.description: Heliotropium crispum is a species of flowering plant in the family Heliotropiaceae. It is native to western Africa, Egypt, Sudan, south-western Asia, and Pakistan. It was first described by René Louiche Desfontaines.

items.name: Heliotropium curassavicum
items.growersTips:
Grow in free-draining sandy soil or gravel to prevent winter root rot in wet UK climates.
Position in full sun against a south-facing wall to mimic its native warm coastal habitat.
Water sparingly once established, allowing the soil to dry out completely between waterings.
Overwinter in a frost-free greenhouse or bring indoors as this plant is tender in UK winters.
Propagate by taking softwood cuttings in late summer to ensure survival of the plant for next year.
items.description: Heliotropium curassavicum, commonly called salt heliotrope, is a species of flowering plant in the family Heliotropiaceae. It is native to the Americas and has been introduced elsewhere.

items.name: Heliotropium dentatum
items.growersTips:
Grow in free-draining gritty loam with a neutral pH to prevent winter root rot in wet UK climates.
Sow seeds shallowly at two millimetres deep under glass in March keeping temperatures at twenty degrees.
Water moderately allowing the top two centimetres of soil to dry out fully between watering sessions.
Overwinter containers indoors in a frost-free greenhouse or conservatory before late autumn frosts.
Prune back leggy stems by one third in early spring to encourage bushy growth and more flower spikes.
items.description: Heliotropium dentatum is a species of plant in the family Heliotropiaceae. It is endemic to northern Socotra island in Yemen. Its natural habitats are subtropical or tropical dry forests and subtropical or tropical dry shrubland.

items.name: Heliotropium europaeum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly indoors in March and transplant out only after the last late-May frosts.
Water sparingly once established as this Mediterranean native thrives in dry, well-drained soil.
Watch for slugs and snails on young spring shoots, especially during damp UK spring weather.
Grow in pots to easily move indoors to a frost-free greenhouse or conservatory before October.
Pinch out the growing tips of young plants in June to encourage a bushier habit and more blooms.
items.description: Heliotropium europaeum is a species of heliotrope known by the common names European heliotrope and European turn-sole.

items.name: Heliotropium hirsutissimum
items.growersTips:
Grow in a terracotta pot with grit-heavy compost to protect roots from wet UK winters and rot.
Position in the sunniest south-facing spot or unheated greenhouse to mimic its native Aegean heat.
Water only when the top three inches of soil are dry to prevent fatal root rot in damp UK air.
Overwinter indoors on a bright windowsill keeping the compost barely damp to survive frosts.
Propagate by taking softwood cuttings in late spring to ensure backup plants for the next year.
items.description: Heliotropium hirsutissimum, the hairy heliotrope, is a species of flowering plant in the family Heliotropiaceae. It is native to the eastern Mediterranean.

items.name: Heliotropium indicum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in March at three millimetres deep using bottom heat of twenty degrees Celsius.
Plant out in late May after all frost risk has passed into a sheltered spot with full southern sun.
Water the soil deeply once a week at the base to prevent powdery mildew on the hairy foliage.
Watch for glasshouse whitefly and red spider mite when growing in UK conservatories or cold frames.
Grow in free-draining sandy loam mixed with grit to prevent root rot during wet British summers.
items.description: Heliotropium indicum, commonly known as Indian heliotrope or Indian turnsole, is an annual, hirsute plant. It has a curved arrangement of small flowers and velvety broad green leaves.

items.name: Heliotropium stenophyllum
items.growersTips:
Grow in a terracotta pot with grit-heavy loam to survive wet UK winters and move indoors by October
Water only when the top three inches of soil are dry to prevent root rot in cool British summers
Prune back by one third in early spring to encourage bushy growth and prevent leggy stems
Position in the sunniest south-facing spot against a brick wall to maximize essential heat retention
Watch for glasshouse whitefly and spider mites when overwintering this tender shrub indoors
items.description: Heliotropium stenophyllum is a species of plant in the family Heliotropiaceae. It is endemic to Chile. Its natural habitats are semi-desert coastal areas of Northern Chile, in the 3 and 4 Region.

items.name: Helminthotheca echioides
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in autumn onto bare clay soil to mimic natural UK wayside germination patterns.
Hand-pull rosettes before the deep taproot matures in spring to prevent aggressive self-seeding.
Grow alongside red clover to improve heavy soil structure while managing this wildflower's spread.
Sever the taproot three inches below the surface in winter to kill the plant without chemicals.
Mow infested lawns on a low setting in late summer to decapitate yellow flowerheads before seeding.
items.description: Helminthotheca echioides, known as bristly oxtongue, is a sprawling annual or biennial herb native to Europe and North Africa. It was originally placed within the genus Picris but is often separated within the small genus Helminthotheca alongside a few other plants which also have the distinctive outer row of bracts around the flowerheads. It is a ruderal plant, found on waste ground and agricultural soils around the world, and in some places it is considered a troublesome weed.

items.name: Hemiandra
items.growersTips:
Grow Hemiandra pungens in a terracotta pot with fifty percent grit to survive wet UK winters.
Move this tender Australian shrub into a frost-free greenhouse or conservatory from October to April.
Water only when the top five centimetres of soil is bone dry to prevent root rot in damp climates.
Prune lightly in late spring after frost risk passes to maintain a compact, non-straggly shape.
Position in your sunniest south-facing spot next to heat-retaining brickwork to mimic its homeland.
items.description: Hemiandra is a genus of nine species of flowering plants of the family Lamiaceae and is endemic to Western Australia. Plants in the genus Hemiandra are shrubs with sessile leaves arranged in opposite pairs, petals with five lobes arranged in two "lips" and the fruit a capsule usually containing four nuts.

items.name: Hemigenia
items.growersTips:
Plant in free-draining gritty loam with added horticultural sand to survive wet UK winters.
Position in a sheltered south-facing border or container to maximize summer sun and warmth.
Water sparingly once established, allowing the top five centimetres of soil to dry out completely.
Prune lightly immediately after summer flowering to maintain a compact shape and prevent legginess.
Overwinter in a cold greenhouse or conservatory to protect the roots from freezing UK ground frost.
items.description: Hemigenia is a genus of flowering plants in the mint family, Lamiaceae and is endemic to Australia where most species occur in Western Australia, although some are also found in New South Wales and Queensland. Plants in this genus are shrubs or bushes with simple leaves and tube-shaped flowers with the petals forming two "lips" - the upper one with two lobes and the lower one with three.

items.name: Hemiphora
items.growersTips:
Plant in gritty, free-draining soil with added horticultural grit to survive wet UK winters.
Position in full south-facing sun against a warm wall to mimic its native Australian climate.
Water sparingly only during dry summer spells, allowing the soil to dry out completely between waterings.
Protect from frost by moving container-grown plants into a cold greenhouse from November to March.
Prune lightly in late spring after the last frost to maintain shape and encourage fresh flowering stems.
items.description: Hemiphora is a genus of five species of flowering plants in the mint family, Lamiaceae and is endemic to Western Australia. Plants in this genus are woolly shrubs with warty, hairy leaves and with five petals joined to form a tube-shaped flower with four stamens. These species are similar to those in the genus Chloanthes in that the base of the leaves extends down the stem. They differ from Chloanthes, in that the leaves only extend a short distance down the stem.

items.name: Hemiphragma heterophyllum
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich acidic soil in a sheltered, partially shaded rock garden.
Water consistently in dry UK summers to keep the soil damp, mimicking its native Himalayan habitat.
Protect the delicate prostrate stems from winter wet using a cloche or grit mulch to prevent rot.
Propagate in spring by carefully dividing the rooted creeping stems or sowing seed in a cold frame.
Watch for slugs and snails in spring as they easily damage the soft, mat-forming evergreen foliage.
items.description: Hemiphragma heterophyllum is a genus of flowering plants belonging to the family Plantaginaceae. It is a perennial native to the central and eastern Himalaya, Myanmar, central and southern China, Taiwan, the Philippines, and Sulawesi.

items.name: Hemitomes congestum
items.growersTips:
Plant this parasitic wildflower near its host fungus, specifically under mature UK beech or oak trees.
Do not water or fertilise this mycoheterotroph as it relies entirely on underground fungal networks.
Maintain a thick undisturbed layer of damp leaf mould to protect the host mycelium in dry summers.
Never prune or cut back the fleshy pinkish stems as they must naturally wither to disperse seeds.
Avoid digging or soil compaction in the root zone to prevent destroying the delicate host hyphae.
items.description: Hemitomes is a monotypic genus of plants containing the single species Hemitomes congestum, which is known as gnome plant and cone plant. This rare and unusual plant is native to the west coast of North America from British Columbia to California, where it grows in dense, dark forests such as the redwood and Douglas-fir forests of the region. This is a small, fleshy, stemless perennial plant forming lumps in the leaf litter. It is white, yellowish, or reddish-pink in color, like Monotropa and other close relatives, little is known about the life cycle of the plant due to its rarity, but it pro

items.name: Hemizonella minima
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in spring at a depth of two millimetres in free-draining sandy loam to prevent waterlogging.
Position in full sun to mimic its native dry habitat and prevent damp-related rot in UK weather.
Water sparingly only during prolonged summer dry spells, allowing the soil to dry out completely.
Grow alongside low-growing alpines or sedums in a scree garden to prevent taller plants smothering it.
Collect seed heads in late summer to resow next spring as this annual will not survive UK winters.
items.description: Hemizonella is a genus of North American plants in the tribe Madieae belonging to the family Asteraceae.

items.name: Hemizonia congesta
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at a depth of two millimetres in April using a gritty, free-draining compost mix.
Position in your garden's brightest south-facing spot to mimic its native hot Californian sun.
Water sparingly only when the top five centimetres of soil is dry to prevent root rot in UK damp.
Sow directly into final pots to avoid transplant shock as this annual dislikes root disturbance.
Deadhead spent yellow blooms weekly through August to prolong flowering before autumn frosts arrive.
items.description: Hemizonia congesta, known by the common name hayfield tarweed, is a species of flowering plant in the family Asteraceae, native to western North America.

items.name: Hepatica
items.growersTips:
Plant in free-draining, humus-rich alkaline soil under deciduous trees to mimic UK woodland floors.
Mulch annually in autumn with leaf mould to protect shallow roots and maintain consistent moisture.
Water during dry spring spells but keep relatively dry in summer when the plants go semi-dormant.
Watch for vine weevil grubs in container-grown plants and hand-pick slugs from emerging spring buds.
Plant alongside early bulbs like snowdrops and winter aconites which share their growth cycle.
items.description: Hepatica is a genus of herbaceous perennials in the buttercup family, native to central and northern Europe, Asia and eastern North America. Some botanists include Hepatica within a wider interpretation of Anemone.

items.name: Herbertia
items.growersTips:
Plant Herbertia bulbs 8cm deep in autumn using gritty, free-draining soil to prevent winter rot.
Grow Herbertia in pots to easily move them into a frost-free greenhouse or cold frame over winter.
Water moderately during spring growth but keep the bulbs completely dry during their summer dormancy.
Position pots in full sun facing south or west to mimic their warm South American native habitat.
Watch for slugs and snails in spring as they quickly destroy the delicate emerging flower spikes.
items.description:
Herbertia may refer to:Herbertia (plant), a plant genus in the family Iridaceae
Herbertia (wasp), a wasp genus in the family Herbertiidae
Herbertia (journal), an international journal published by the International Bulb Society devoted to the botany and horticulture of geophytic plants with a special emphasis on the Amaryllidaceae and other petaloid monocot families rich in bulbous or cormous plants

items.name: Herniaria
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in April by pressing them lightly into gritty soil without covering them.
Water seedlings sparingly once a week to prevent dampening off in damp UK spring weather.
Mix sharp sand into heavy clay beds to ensure the rapid drainage this alpine-like annual requires.
Grow alongside Thymus serpyllum in sunny rockeries to create a resilient low-water groundcover.
Watch for slugs and snails during wet British summers as they will quickly devour young foliage.
items.description: Herniaria is a genus of flowering plants in the family Caryophyllaceae known generally as ruptureworts. They are native to Eurasia and Africa but several species have been widely introduced to other continents. These are flat, mat-forming annual herbs. The genus gets its scientific and common names from the once-held belief that species could be used as an herbal remedy for hernias.

items.name: Herniaria cinerea
items.growersTips:
Plant in sharply draining gritty soil or gravel to prevent winter wet rot in damp UK climates.
Position in full south-facing sun to maintain its tight, prostrate, carpet-like evergreen habit.
Water sparingly only during prolonged summer droughts once the deep taproot is fully established.
Propagate by taking semi-ripe cuttings in late summer rather than dividing the delicate taproot.
Sow seeds in cold frames during autumn to allow natural winter stratifying under UK temperatures.
items.description: Herniaria cinerea is a species of herb in the family Caryophyllaceae (carpetweeds).

items.name: Herniaria glabra
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in autumn or spring by pressing them lightly into gritty, free-draining soil.
Water sparingly only during prolonged summer droughts to prevent root rot in damp UK winters.
Grow alongside thyme or sedum in rockeries or between paving stones to suppress weeds naturally.
Trim the edges in late summer with shears to keep the carpet-like spread neat and prevent patchiness.
Watch for slugs and snails during wet UK springs as they can quickly decimate the tender foliage.
items.description: Herniaria glabra, the smooth rupturewort, is a plant of the family Caryophyllaceae, and grows in North America and Europe. It contains herniarin, a methoxy analog of umbelliferone.

items.name: Herniaria hirsuta
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in spring at a depth of two millimetres into free-draining sandy loam to prevent rot.
Water sparingly only during dry spells to mimic its native gravelly Mediterranean habitat.
Watch for slugs and snails during wet UK springs as they target the tender young foliage.
Plant alongside Sedum album or Thymum serpyllum which share its love for dry, sunny rockeries.
Clear dead patches in autumn to allow the plant to self-seed naturally for the next spring.
items.description: Herniaria hirsuta is a species of flowering plant in the family Caryophyllaceae known by the common name hairy rupturewort. It is native to Eurasia and North Africa, and it is known on other continents, including North America, as an introduced species. This is an annual herb with stems up to 20 cm (8 in) long usually growing prostrate along the ground. The small, fuzzy, pale green leaves are up to about a centimeter long and coat the stems. The inflorescences appear in the leaf axils. Each contains three to eight hairy green sepals and no petals. The fruit is a tiny bumpy utricle containing o

items.name: Herrickia glauca
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in spring at a depth of 3mm in free-draining sandy loam to prevent winter wet root rot.
Water young plants weekly during dry UK summers, letting the top 2cm of soil dry out between waterings.
Position in full sun next to lavender or thyme to help attract pollinators and improve air flow.
Monitor young shoots in May for slug damage, using beer traps or organic wool pellets to protect them.
Deadhead spent flowers in late August to prolong the blooming display and prevent excessive self-seeding.
items.description: Eurybia glauca is a North American species of flowering plants in the family Asteraceae, called the gray aster. It is native to the western United States, primarily in Arizona, New Mexico, Utah, Colorado, and Wyoming, with a few populations in Idaho and Montana.

items.name: Herrickia kingii
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at two millimetres deep in April using a cold frame to protect from UK frosts.
Water the base weekly during dry summer spells to keep soil moist but prevent waterlogged roots.
Incorporate grit into heavy UK clay soils to ensure the sharp drainage this alpine native needs.
Watch for slugs and snails on young spring shoots by using beer traps or organic wool pellets.
Position in full south-facing sun next to low-growing sedums to mimic its natural scree habitat.
items.description: Eurybia kingii is a North American species of flowering plants in the family Asteraceae, called the King's serpentweed or King's aster. It has been found only in the State of Utah in the western United States.

items.name: Hesperaloe funifera
items.growersTips:
Plant in a terracotta pot using fifty percent horticultural grit and fifty percent peat-free compost.
Move the pot into an unheated greenhouse or porch from October to March to prevent winter wet rot.
Water only when the soil is bone dry during summer and stop watering completely throughout winter.
Position in the absolute sunniest spot of the garden against a south-facing brick wall for heat.
Do not cut back the tough leaves but do prune the spent flower spikes at the base in late autumn.
items.description: Hesperaloe funifera is a species of flowering plant in the family Asparagaceae. It is native to Texas and northern Mexico, but sometimes cultivated as an ornamental elsewhere.

items.name: Hesperaloe parviflora
items.growersTips:
Plant in a raised bed of 50 percent grit and sharp sand to survive wet UK winters without root rot.
Position in your garden's hottest south-facing spot against a brick wall to maximize summer heat.
Water only during prolonged dry summer spells and keep completely dry from October through March.
Protect the crown with a temporary rain shelter or cloche during persistent winter downpours.
Cut faded flower spikes right back to the base in late autumn using sharp, sterilized loppers.
items.description: Hesperaloe parviflora, also known as red yucca, hummingbird yucca, redflower false yucca and samandoque, is a succulent plant in the Asparagaceae family that is native to the Chihuahuan and Coahuilan deserts of Northern Mexico, as well as Central, Southern and Western Texas; today, it is often seen in roadside planting swathes and public areas, or used for corporate or office exterior landscaping. It is also quite popular in collector gardens and among private gardeners who are striving for a more water-wise approach.

items.name: Hesperantha coccinea
items.growersTips:
Plant in spring at a depth of 5cm in moisture-retentive soil that does not dry out during summer.
Position in full sun near a south-facing wall to trap autumn heat and prolong the late bloom.
Divide congested clumps every three years in early spring to maintain vigorous flowering.
Cut back dead flower stems and untidy foliage to the ground in late winter before new growth starts.
Mulch the crown with bark in cold UK regions in November to protect shallow roots from hard frosts.
items.description: Hesperantha coccinea, the river lily, or crimson flag lily, synonym Schizostylis coccinea, is a species of flowering plant in the iris family Iridaceae, native to Southern Africa and Zimbabwe. It is a semievergreen perennial growing to 60 cm (24 in) tall, with slender lanceolate leaves up to 40 cm (16 in) long and 1 cm (0.4 in) broad. The flowers are red, occasionally pink or white, 30–35 mm long, with six petals; they are produced four to ten alternately on a spike in late summer to autumn.

items.name: Hesperevax acaulis
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in early spring under glass to protect from damp UK winters before planting out
Grow in sharply draining gritty soil or a scree bed to prevent winter wet from rotting the roots
Water sparingly only during dry summer spells allowing the gritty growing medium to dry out fully
Position in your sunniest south-facing rockery or alpine trough to mimic its native dry habitat
Plant alongside low-growing sedums or sempervivums which share its need for dry nutrient-poor soil
items.description: Hesperevax acaulis is a species of flowering plant in the family Asteraceae known by the common name stemless dwarf cudweed. It is native to California and Oregon where it grows in many types of mountain, valley, and coastal habitats, including areas recently affected by wildfire. This petite woolly annual forms a small bunch on the ground. Despite its common name it sometimes has a stem a few centimeters long. The wool-coated leaves appear in pairs or clusters, each leaf measuring a few millimeters to three centimeters long. In the center of the leaf array is the inflorescence, which is a sin

items.name: Hesperevax caulescens
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in early spring under glass to protect seedlings from late UK frosts and slugs.
Grow in sharply draining gritty soil or rock scree to prevent winter rot in wet British climates.
Water sparingly only when the top two inches of soil are dry to mimic its native arid habitat.
Position in full south-facing sun to maximise warmth and light during the short UK summer.
Plant alongside low-growing alpine sedums to provide structural support and prevent soil erosion.
items.description: Hesperevax caulescens is a small flowering plant in the family Asteraceae. One common name for the plant is hogwallow starfish, as it is a somewhat flat, star-shaped plant which grows in mud. Another common name is dwarf dwarf-cudweed, as the three members of genus Hesperevax are known as dwarf-cudweeds and this species is smaller than the others. It may also be called involucrate evax, since its former Latin name was Evax involucrata. This annual plant is a member of the vernal pool plant community in California, where it is possibly an endemic species, although its range might extend into Ba

items.name: Hesperevax sparsiflora
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in spring at a depth of two millimetres in free-draining sandy loam to prevent rot.
Place pots in the sunniest south-facing spot to mimic its native warm, dry Californian climate.
Water sparingly only when the top two centimetres of soil are dry to avoid waterlogging the roots.
Grow alongside low-growing sedums or thymes which share its need for dry, nutrient-poor UK soil.
Protect young seedlings from slugs using copper tape around pots during damp British spring nights.
items.description: Hesperevax sparsiflora is a species of flowering plant in the family Asteraceae known by the common name erect dwarf cudweed. It is native to California and Oregon, where it grows in several habitat types including sandy coastal areas and the serpentine soils of inland hills. This is a small woolly annual herb reaching maximum heights under 18 centimeters. It has oval to rounded or scoop-shaped leaves on short petioles which vary in morphology across varieties. Small flower heads appear between the leaves. They contain greenish or whitish disc florets.These florets are remarkably small, each b

items.name: Hesperostellaria
items.growersTips:
Plant in autumn at a depth of five centimetres in gritty, free-draining soil to prevent winter rot.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells, allowing the top soil to dry out completely first.
Cut back dead stems to ground level in late February before the new spring growth begins to emerge.
Protect young spring shoots from slugs using organic grit barriers or beer traps in damp UK weather.
Divide congested clumps every three years in early spring to maintain vigour and propagate new plants.
items.description: Hesperostellaria is a genus of flowering plants in the family Caryophyllaceae. It contains a single species, Hesperostellaria americana, a perennial native to subalpine areas of Alberta and Montana.

items.name: Hesperoxiphion
items.growersTips:
Plant Hesperoxiphion bulbs in autumn at a depth of ten centimetres in sharply draining sandy loam.
Grow them in terracotta pots to easily move them into a frost-free greenhouse during wet UK winters.
Water weekly during active spring growth but keep bulbs completely dry during their summer dormancy.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using beer traps or organic wool pellets.
Position containers against a south-facing brick wall to maximise heat and mimic Andean sun levels.
items.description:
Hesperoxiphion is a genus of flowering plants in the family Iridaceae, first described as a genus in 1877. It is native to northwestern South America. The genus name is derived from the Greek words hesperos, meaning "western", and xiphos, meaning "sword".SpeciesHesperoxiphion herrerae (Diels ex R.C.Foster) Ravenna - Cajamarca region in Peru
Hesperoxiphion huilense Ravenna - Colombia
Hesperoxiphion niveum (Ravenna) Ravenna - Cajamarca region in Peru
Hesperoxiphion pardalis (Ravenna) Ravenna - Apurímac region in Peru
Hesperoxiphion peruvianum (Baker) Baker - Bolivia, Peru

items.name: Hesperoyucca newberryi
items.growersTips:
Plant in a raised bed or gravel garden with fifty percent grit to survive wet UK winters.
Position in your garden's hottest south-facing spot to mimic its native arid desert habitat.
Protect the crown with a temporary glass cloche from November to March to prevent winter rot.
Water only during prolonged summer droughts and keep completely dry throughout the winter months.
Grow in a terracotta pot using alpine compost so you can move it under fleece during hard frosts.
items.description: Hesperoyucca newberryi, commonly known as the Grand Canyon Quixote plant or Newberry's yucca, is a plant species endemic to Arizona. It is found only in Mohave and Coconino Counties, on the walls of canyons near the Colorado River.

items.name: Hesperoyucca whipplei
items.growersTips:
Plant in a raised bed or gravel mound with fifty percent grit to survive wet UK winters.
Position in your garden's hottest south-facing spot against a brick wall to maximize summer heat.
Water only during active summer growth and keep completely dry from October through to March.
Protect the crown from winter rot by covering it with a temporary rain shelter or glass cloche.
Grow in a heavy terracotta pot that resists tipping over and can be moved under cover for winter.
items.description: Hesperoyucca whipplei, the chaparral yucca, our Lord's candle, Spanish bayonet, Quixote yucca or foothill yucca, is a species of flowering plant closely related to, and formerly usually included in, the genus Yucca. It is native to southwest communities of North America.

items.name: Heterochroa
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at three millimetres deep in April once the late spring frosts have passed.
Grow in free-draining sandy loam with a neutral pH to prevent winter wet from rotting the roots.
Water sparingly at the base only when the top two centimetres of soil feel completely dry.
Position in full south-facing sun to maximise the short flowering window of this annual.
Deadhead spent blooms weekly in July to encourage a second flush of flowers before autumn.
items.description: Heterochroa is a genus of flowering plants in the carnation family, Caryophyllaceae. It includes six species native to temperate Eurasia, ranging from Iran to Central Asia, Mongolia, Siberia, and the Russian Far East.

items.name: Heuchera
items.growersTips:
Plant the crown slightly proud of the soil level to prevent rot in wet UK winter conditions.
Divide congested clumps every three years in spring to prevent woody stems lifting out of the soil.
Drench soil with beneficial nematodes in autumn to target devastating vine weevil larvae.
Cut back tattered winter foliage in early spring to encourage fresh, vibrant new leaf growth.
Grow dark-leaved varieties in sun and lime-green types in dappled shade to avoid leaf scorch.
items.description: Heuchera is a genus of largely evergreen perennial plants in the family Saxifragaceae. All species are native to North America except for Heuchera sichotensis, native to the Russian Far East. Common names include alumroot and coral bells.

items.name: Heuchera abramsii
items.growersTips:
Plant in sharply draining grit-rich soil to mimic its native scree and prevent winter crown rot.
Position in full sun to very light shade to replicate its high-altitude alpine habitat in the UK.
Water sparingly only during dry summer spells once established as this species is highly drought-tolerant.
Protect from vine weevil grubs by applying biological nematodes to the soil in spring and autumn.
Grow in a raised bed or alpine trough to ensure the perfect drainage this compact perennial demands.
items.description: Heuchera abramsii is a rare species of flowering plant in the saxifrage family known by the common names San Gabriel alumroot and Abrams' alumroot.

items.name: Heuchera americana
items.growersTips:
Plant crowns slightly above soil level to prevent rot in wet UK winters and improve drainage.
Water deeply once a week in dry summer spells rather than daily light sprinkling to avoid root rot.
Watch for vine weevil grubs in autumn by checking container roots if leaves suddenly wilt and detach.
Cut back tattered winter foliage in early spring just as new green growth begins to emerge.
Incorporate grit and leaf mould into heavy UK clay soils to ensure the free drainage they require.
