items.description: Heuchera americana, or American alumroot, is a small evergreen perennial native to eastern and central North America while also ranging into Ontario, Canada. It is a part of the Saxifrage family.

items.name: Heuchera brevistaminea
items.growersTips:
Plant in free-draining neutral soil on a slight mound to prevent winter crown rot in wet UK climates.
Position in partial shade to protect the delicate pale pink flowers and green leaves from leaf scorch.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells, allowing the top two inches of soil to dry out.
Handpick vine weevil grubs from roots in autumn and apply biological nematodes in August or September.
Divide the woody crown every three years in early spring to prevent the plant from lifting out of soil.
items.description: Heuchera brevistaminea is a rare species of flowering plant in the saxifrage family known by the common name Laguna Mountains alumroot. It is endemic to the Laguna Mountains of San Diego County, California. It grows in rock crevices and steep cliffsides in chaparral and yellow pine forest habitats. This is a rhizomatous perennial herb producing an inflorescence up to 25 centimeters tall. The flowers are bright pink or magenta.

items.name: Heuchera cylindrica
items.growersTips:
Plant in free-draining neutral to slightly acidic soil to prevent winter root rot in wet UK clay.
Position in partial shade or dappled woodland edge to prevent the pale green foliage from scorching.
Mulch crowns annually in spring with leaf mould but keep it clear of the central growing point.
Divide the woody rootstock every three years in early autumn to prevent the plant lifting out of soil.
Snip faded flower spikes at the base in late summer to encourage fresh foliage growth before winter.
items.description: Heuchera cylindrica is a species of perennial flowering plant in the saxifrage family known by the common names poker alumroot, roundleaf alumroot, and coral bells. It is native to western North America, where it is found from British Columbia to California, and east to Wyoming and Montana.

items.name: Heuchera elegans
items.growersTips:
Plant in well-drained loam with the crown level with the soil to prevent crown rot in wet UK winters.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells, allowing the top two inches of soil to dry out.
Hand-pick vine weevil grubs from roots in autumn, as they are the main pest in UK container plants.
Cut back tattered winter foliage in early spring to encourage fresh, vibrant new leaf growth.
Divide the woody crowns every three years in autumn to maintain plant vigour and prevent dieback.
items.description: Heuchera elegans is a species of flowering plant in the saxifrage family known by the common name urn-flowered alumroot.

items.name: Heuchera maxima
items.growersTips:
Plant in free-draining neutral soil on a slight slope to prevent winter crown rot in wet UK clay.
Position in partial shade under deciduous trees to mimic its native woodland edge habitat in the UK.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells but keep the crown dry to avoid fungal diseases.
Cut back woody stems to ground level in early spring to encourage fresh new foliage from the base.
Divide the fibrous root clumps every three years in autumn to maintain plant vigour and shape.
items.description: Heuchera maxima is a species of flowering plant in the saxifrage family, known by the common names island alum root, Channel Islands coral bells, and Jill of the rocks.

items.name: Heuchera merriamii
items.growersTips:
Plant in gritty, sharply draining soil to prevent winter crown rot in wet UK climates.
Position in a sheltered rock garden or container with morning sun and afternoon shade.
Water sparingly once established, letting the top few centimetres of soil dry out completely.
Watch for vine weevil grubs in autumn and drench pots with biological nematodes if found.
Divide the woody crown every three years in early spring to rejuvenate growth and prevent dieback.
items.description: Heuchera merriamii is a species of flowering plant in the saxifrage family known by the common name Merriam's alumroot. It is native to the Klamath Mountains of southern Oregon and northern California, where it grows on the rocky slopes. This is a rhizomatous perennial herb producing a patch of leaves which are rounded and have five to seven lobes along the edges. It produces an erect inflorescence up to about 23 centimeters tall with sparse clusters of pinkish, yellow, or cream flowers. The inflorescence is covered in glandular hairs. Each flower has small spoon-shaped petals and protruding s

items.name: Heuchera micrantha
items.growersTips:
Plant in partial shade using well-drained soil enriched with grit to prevent winter root rot.
Gently firm soil around the crown but keep it just above the surface to avoid rot in wet winters.
Divide the woody crown every three years in early autumn to prevent the plant from lifting out.
Watch for vine weevil grubs in autumn and drench the soil with nematodes to protect the roots.
Cut back tattered winter foliage in early spring to encourage fresh, colorful new leaf growth.
items.description: Heuchera micrantha is a species of flowering plant in the saxifrage family known by the common name crevice alumroot, or small-flowered alumroot.

items.name: Heuchera parviflora
items.growersTips:
Plant in partial to full shade in moist well-drained soil to prevent leaf scorch in UK summers
Set the crown level with the soil surface to avoid rot in wet British autumns and winters
Divide the woody crown every three years in early spring to rejuvenate growth and prevent dieback
Watch for vine weevil grubs in autumn which chew the roots and cause the plant to collapse
Pair with ferns and hostas in woodland borders to complement its delicate autumn-blooming white flowers
items.description: Heuchera parviflora is a species of flowering plant in the saxifrage family known by the common names cave alumroot and littleflower alumroot. It is native to the eastern United States, where it is found primarily in the Ozark Mountains, Appalachian Mountains, and Cumberland Plateau. It is found in deeply shaded areas such as under rock overhangs and cliffs, almost always where no direct sunlight falls. In this habitat, it is often the only vascular plant found. H. parviflora is an uncommon species throughout its range. It flowers in late summer through fall.

items.name: Common alumroot
items.growersTips:
Plant in free-draining neutral soil with the crown sitting just above ground level to prevent rot.
Water deeply once a week during dry UK summers, allowing the top two inches of soil to dry out first.
Handpick vine weevil grubs from roots in autumn, as they are the main pest of UK Heuchera species.
Divide the woody crown every three years in early spring to rejuvenate growth and prevent dieback.
Position in partial shade alongside ferns and hostas to protect the pale foliage from scorching.
items.description: Heuchera parvifolia is a species of flowering plant in the saxifrage family known by the common names littleleaf alumroot and common alumroot. It is native to California and the Interior West of the United States, where it grows primarily on rocky ledges on slopes and canyon walls.

items.name: Seaside alumroot
items.growersTips:
Plant this California native in free-draining, gritty soil to survive wet UK winters without rotting.
Position in partial shade to protect the hairy, pale green foliage from scorching in midday sun.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells, allowing the top soil to dry out between watering.
Cut back the woody, leggy stems in early spring to encourage fresh, compact growth from the base.
Watch for vine weevil grubs in autumn, which target the roots of these shallow-rooting perennials.
items.description: Heuchera pilosissima is a species of flowering plant in the saxifrage family known by the common name seaside alumroot and Parish's alumroot. It is endemic to the northern two thirds of the California coastline, where it grows on coastal bluffs and in nearby forests. This is a rhizomatous perennial herb producing lobed oval-shaped leaves 4 to 9 centimeters wide, each on a long petiole. The erect inflorescence reaches over half a meter in maximum height and is covered in glandular hairs. It bears dense clusters of rounded, hairy flowers. Each flower has pink or yellowish lobes tipped with small

items.name: Heuchera rubescens
items.growersTips:
Plant in free-draining gritty soil to prevent winter root rot in wet UK clay.
Bury the woody crown slightly deeper when planting to stop the typical stem lifting.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells rather than daily light sprinkling.
Cut back tattered winter foliage in March just as new spring growth begins to emerge.
Watch for vine weevil grubs in autumn by checking under the pot rim for C-shaped larvae.
items.description: Heuchera rubescens, with the common name pink alumroot, is a species of Heuchera.

items.name: Heuchera sanguinea
items.growersTips:
Plant in free-draining neutral soil with compost to prevent winter root rot in wet UK climates.
Keep the crown exactly level with the soil surface to prevent stem rot in damp British weather.
Divide every three years in autumn to prevent the woody central stem from lifting out of the ground.
Drench the soil with parasitic nematodes in August to kill devastating vine weevil larvae.
Cut back tattered winter foliage in March to encourage fresh new leaves and summer flower spikes.
items.description: Heuchera sanguinea, called coral bells, is a species of flowering plant in the genus Heuchera, native to the US states of Arizona and New Mexico, and to northern Mexico. A number of cultivars are commercially available. The Latin specific epithet sanguinea means blood-red, in reference to the color of the flowers. Flowers are deep pink to red, sweetly fragrant, and bell-shaped. Heuchera sanguinea is a perennial herb. The plant attracts bees and hummingbirds.

items.name: Heuchera villosa
items.growersTips:
Plant in partial shade to prevent leaf scorch from strong afternoon sun in southern UK gardens.
Incorporate grit into heavy UK clay soils to prevent winter root rot, keeping the crown above soil.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells rather than daily shallow sprinkles to build roots.
Cut back tattered winter-damaged foliage in early spring just as new growth begins to emerge.
Watch for vine weevil grubs in autumn and drench the soil with beneficial nematodes to kill them.
items.description: Heuchera villosa, the hairy alumroot, is a small evergreen perennial native to the Eastern United States. It is found only on rock outcrops, growing on cliffs and boulders. Considered locally endangered in the state of Ohio.

items.name: Hidalgoa ternata
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in early spring at a depth of five millimetres using a heated propagator at twentyC
Plant out in late May after the last frost in a sheltered south-facing spot with moist fertile soil
Provide a sturdy trellis or obelisk immediately to support its rapid climbing leaf-stalk tendrils
Water deeply twice a week during dry summer spells to keep the soil consistently moist but not wet
Monitor foliage closely in damp UK summers for slugs and snails which devour the tender young shoots
items.description: Hidalgoa ternata is a flowering plant in the tribe Coreopsideae of the family Asteraceae. It is found in areas of the tropics in the Americas.

items.name: Hippuris vulgaris
items.growersTips:
Plant bare-root runners in heavy clay loam in aquatic baskets at a depth of 10 to 30cm below water level.
Submerge pots in a sunny garden pond to restrict the highly invasive running rhizomes from spreading.
Prune brown stems back to the pond basket base in late autumn to prevent rotting debris in the water.
Grow alongside Caltha palustris to provide structural contrast and absorb excess pond nutrients.
Monitor submerged foliage in spring for water snails and manually clear duckweed to maintain light.
items.description: Hippuris vulgaris, known as mare's-tail or common mare's-tail, is a common aquatic flowering plant in the family Plantaginaceae. Its distribution ranges from Eurasia and North America to Greenland, the Tibetan Plateau and Arizona. It prefers non-acidic waters.

items.name: Hoffmannseggia falcaria
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in early April at a depth of 1cm using free-draining sandy loam to prevent rot.
Place containers in the sunniest south-facing spot to mimic their native warm desert habitat.
Water sparingly only when the top 5cm of soil is dry to avoid waterlogging in damp UK summers.
Protect young seedlings from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers during wet May nights.
Grow alongside drought-tolerant companion plants like sedums to match their low-moisture needs.
items.description:
Hoffmannseggia is a genus of flowering plants in the pea family, Fabaceae, known generally as rushpeas. These are pod-bearing herbs and subshrubs native to the Americas. In North America they range from California and Nebraska to southern Mexico, and from Colombia, Ecuador, and Peru to southern Argentina and Chile in South America.
The generic name honors Johann Centurius, Count of Hoffmannsegg, a nineteenth-century German nobleman and botanist.

items.name: Hoffmannseggia glauca
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in March at a depth of five millimetres using a heated propagator to ensure heat
Plant out in late May after frosts in a south facing border with sharply draining gritty soil
Water sparingly once established allowing the compost to dry out fully between light waterings
Grow alongside drought tolerant companions like lavender or thyme to match its dry soil needs
Protect young plants from slugs and snails using organic bait during damp spring nights
items.description: Hoffmannseggia glauca is a dicot found in the legume family, Fabaceae. Its common names include Indian rushpea, hog potato, and pig nut.

items.name: Hoffmannseggia microphylla
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in early spring at a depth of five millimetres using a heated propagator at twentyC
Grow in free-draining sandy loam mixed with grit to mimic its native desert-like soil conditions
Position in the hottest south-facing spot of your garden to maximise limited UK summer sunshine
Water sparingly only when the top five centimetres of soil is bone dry to prevent root rot
Protect young plants from slugs and snails using copper tape or beer traps during damp UK springs
items.description: Hoffmannseggia microphylla is a species of flowering plant in the legume family known by the common name wand holdback. It is native to the southwestern United States and Baja California and grows in gullies, canyons, slopes and primarily creosote bush scrub.

items.name: Hoffmannseggia tenella
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in spring at a depth of five millimetres using a free-draining sandy loam potting mix.
Keep soil consistently moist but never waterlogged to prevent root rot in cool UK spring weather.
Place pots in the sunniest south-facing spot or greenhouse to mimic its native warm environment.
Protect young seedlings from slugs and snails using beer traps or physical barriers in damp weather.
Grow in containers so you can move them under glass to protect the delicate roots from heavy rain.
items.description: Hoffmannseggia tenella is a rare species of flowering plant in the legume family known by the common name slender rushpea. It is endemic to Texas, where it is known from only two counties. It persists in small remnants of its gulf coastal prairie habitat. It is a federally listed endangered species of the United States.

items.name: Holocalyx balansae
items.growersTips:
Grow in a large pot with loam-based grit mix to move indoors before the first autumn frost hits.
Water deeply once a week in summer, then keep the soil almost dry throughout the damp UK winter.
Prune lightly in late spring after new growth starts to maintain a compact shrub shape in pots.
Feed with a low-nitrogen, high-potassium fertilizer in June to encourage root and stem strength.
Position in the brightest south-facing spot or conservatory to maximise scarce UK summer sun.
items.description: Holocalyx balansae is a species of flowering plant in the legume family, Fabaceae. It belongs to the subfamily Faboideae. It is the only member of the genus Holocalyx. It is a tree native to South America, where it ranges from eastern, southern, and west-central Brazil to Bolivia, Paraguay, and northeastern Argentina.

items.name: Jagged chickweed
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn or early spring at a depth of two millimetres in free-draining sandy soil
Grow in full sun in gritty containers to protect delicate stems from persistent UK winter wet
Water sparingly only during dry spring spells to mimic dry gravel habitats and prevent root rot
Deadhead immediately after spring flowering to control its rapid self-seeding in gravel gardens
Position alongside slow-growing alpines like Sedum to prevent this delicate annual being smothered
items.description: Holosteum is a genus of plants in the family Caryophyllaceae with 3 or 4 species native from southern Europe through central and south western Asia and in Africa. They are herbs with an annual life span, some growing as winter annuals. They have slender roots and thin stems that are upright or ascending. The genus name was given by Linnaeus, and named because of the sprawling nature of the plants: Greek holos, meaning whole or all, and osteon, meaning bone, because of the frailty of the plant.

items.name: Jagged chickweed
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at a depth of two millimetres in autumn to match natural UK winter stratification.
Grow in sharply draining sandy soil or gravel scree to prevent winter wet from rotting the roots.
Water sparingly only during dry spring spells as this annual adapted to dry stone walls hates damp.
Position in full south-facing sun to mimic its native UK Breckland habitat and trigger flowering.
Allow the plant to self-seed naturally in late spring before clearing away the dead annual stems.
items.description: Holosteum umbellatum, the jagged chickweed, is a species of flowering plant in the family Caryophyllaceae. It is native to Europe but has also been introduced to North America.

items.name: Honckenya peploides
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn in a cold frame using a gritty, free-draining mix to mimic UK coastal shingle.
Water sparingly only during prolonged dry spells to prevent root rot in damp UK winter conditions.
Plant alongside sea kale or thrift in a dedicated gravel bed to recreate their natural beach habitat.
Keep soil pH alkaline to neutral by mixing crushed oyster shells or lime into your sandy garden soil.
Protect young spring shoots from slugs and snails which thrive in damp British garden borders.
items.description: Honckenya peploides, the sea sandwort (UK) or seaside sandplant (Canada), is the only species in the genus Honckenya of the plant family Caryophyllaceae. Other common names include sea chickweed, sea pimpernal, sea-beach sandwort, and sea purslane. The scientific name is often spelled "Honkenya", and is named after the German botanist Gerhard August Honckeny. This plant has a circumboreal distribution.

items.name: Honckenya peploides
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn in a mix of three parts sharp sand to one part compost to mimic UK shingle beaches
Water only during prolonged dry summer spells as this coastal succulent easily rots in wet soil
Position in your sunniest south-facing spot to replicate the bright open dunes of the British coast
Protect young spring shoots from slugs and snails which target the fleshy leaves in damp UK weather
Grow in deep terracotta pots to allow the extensive creeping rhizomatous root system room to spread
items.description: Honckenya peploides, the sea sandwort (UK) or seaside sandplant (Canada), is the only species in the genus Honckenya of the plant family Caryophyllaceae. Other common names include sea chickweed, sea pimpernal, sea-beach sandwort, and sea purslane. The scientific name is often spelled "Honkenya", and is named after the German botanist Gerhard August Honckeny. This plant has a circumboreal distribution.

items.name: Small-flower soaproot
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs in autumn at a depth of eight centimetres in sharply draining gritty soil to prevent rot.
Water sparingly during the summer dormant phase to mimic its native dry Mediterranean-style climate.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using beer traps or copper tape in damp weather.
Grow in a south-facing gravel garden or container to maximise essential UK summer sun exposure.
Divide congested clumps immediately after summer flowering finishes to maintain plant vigour.
items.description: Hooveria parviflora is a species of perennial herb in the subfamily Agavoideae known by the common name smallflower soap plant. It is a monocot, native to coastal southern California and Baja California, where it is a member of the coastal sage scrub flora. It resembles a smaller version of Chlorogalum pomeridianum, with wavy leaves and white flowers that open during the day.

items.name: Hoplestigma pierreanum
items.growersTips:
Grow in a warm, sheltered south-facing border with grit-amended, free-draining soil to prevent rot.
Water deeply once a week in dry summer spells, but keep the crown completely dry throughout winter.
Apply a thick layer of dry bracken mulch in late autumn to protect the crown from severe UK frosts.
Propagate by taking root cuttings in late winter while the plant is dormant to increase your stock.
Watch for slugs and snails on new spring shoots and protect them with organic beer traps.
items.description: Hoplestigma pierreanum is a species of plant in the family Hoplestigmataceae. It has also been placed in the family Boraginaceae s.l. It is endemic to Cameroon. Its natural habitat is subtropical or tropical dry forests. It is threatened by habitat loss.

items.name: Hosta × tardiva
items.growersTips:
Plant in moisture-retentive, neutral to acidic soil enriched with well-rotted leafmould or manure.
Water deeply at the base twice a week during dry UK summers to keep the soil consistently damp.
Apply organic slug pellets or garlic drench in early spring as new purple shoots begin to emerge.
Divide congested clumps in early spring or autumn using a sharp spade to maintain plant vigour.
Plant alongside Astilbe or ferns in partial shade to shield the delicate leaves from midday sun.

items.name: Hosta capitata
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist, well-drained acidic to neutral soil enriched with leaf mould to mimic woodland beds.
Water deeply at the base weekly during dry UK summers to keep the shallow, fibrous roots hydrated.
Apply organic slug pellets or copper tape in early spring as the delicate purple-tinged shoots emerge.
Divide overgrown clumps in early spring just as growth starts, keeping the crown level with the soil.
Grow in partial shade alongside ferns and astilbes to protect the small, wavy leaves from scorch.
items.description: Hosta capitata is a perennial species of flowering plant in the genus Hosta, native to central and southern Japan as well as South Korea.

items.name: Plantain lily
items.growersTips:
Plant this running hosta in moisture-retentive, humus-rich clay soil to control its spreading stolons.
Water deeply weekly in dry UK summers to keep the soil consistently damp but never waterlogged.
Surround emerging spring shoots with organic grit or wool pellets to deter slugs in damp UK climates.
Mow or shear the foliage to the ground in late autumn after the first frost to prevent crown rot.
Divide the spreading underground stolons in early spring to control its invasive growth habit.
items.description: Hosta clausa is a medium-sized flowering plant in the genus Hosta, native to Korea, Manchuria and Primorye in the Russian Far East. It was first identified in 1930.

items.name: Hosta fluctuans
items.growersTips:
Plant this giant in moist humus-rich soil sheltered from strong winds to prevent leaf tearing.
Surround emerging spring shoots with organic slug wool to protect the large blue-green leaves.
Water deeply at the base twice a week during dry UK summers to maintain the massive foliage.
Divide congested clumps in early spring just as the pointed noses begin to push through the soil.
Underplant with early snowdrops that bloom and fade before the massive hosta leaves unfurl in May.
items.description: Hosta sieboldiana, Siebold's plantain lily, is a species of hosta native to Japan. A putative variety, Hosta sieboldiana var. elegans, has gained the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit, as has a putative variety of its synonym; Hosta fortunei var. aureomarginata, the gold-edged plantain lily. The cultivars 'Blue Angel', 'Blue Mammoth', and 'Olive Bailey Langdon' have also gained the RHS Award of Garden Merit.

items.name: Hosta kiyosumiensis
items.growersTips:
Plant in dappled shade using moisture-retentive, acidic to neutral soil rich in well-rotted manure.
Water deeply at the base twice a week during dry UK summers to keep the delicate leaves from burning.
Apply organic copper slug pellets or beer traps early in March as the purple-tinged shoots emerge.
Divide the clump in early spring just as the eyes break the soil to propagate this rare species.
Mulch annually in November with leaf mould to protect the shallow rhizomes from severe UK frosts.
items.description: Hosta kiyosumiensis is a species of Hosta, found in Japan from Kanto south to Chubu and Kansai, and encompassing the entire central part of Honshu. Plants range from 30 to 45 cm in diameter, and up to 25 cm high. Petiole is 7.5–10 by 0.7 cm, erect, broadly grooved, keeled, triangular in cross section, green in color and at the base barely purple dotted. Leaves are 10–15 by 5–7.5 cm. Specimens exhibit many different leaf shapes from narrow-lanceolate to widely-ovate, with straight or wavy margins.

items.name: Hosta laevigata
items.growersTips:
Plant in moisture-retentive acidic to neutral clay loam enriched with well-rotted leafmould.
Position in partial to full shade to protect the delicate wavy leaf margins from UK summer scorch.
Water deeply at the base weekly during dry spring spells to support its vigorous early growth.
Apply organic slug pellets or copper tape around the crown in March before the new shoots emerge.
Divide the dense root clumps in late autumn or early spring using a sharp spade to propagate.
items.description: Hosta is a genus of plants commonly known as hostas, plantain lilies and occasionally by the Japanese name gibōshi. Hostas are widely cultivated as shade-tolerant foliage plants. The genus is placed in the family Asparagaceae, subfamily Agavoideae, and is native to northeast Asia. Like many "lilioid monocots", the genus was once classified in the Liliaceae. The genus was named by Austrian botanist Leopold Trattinnick in 1812, in honor of the Austrian botanist Nicholas Thomas Host. In 1817, the generic name Funkia was used by German botanist Kurt Sprengel in honor of Heinrich Christian Funck, a

items.name: Narrow-leaved hosta
items.growersTips:
Plant in moisture-retentive, humus-rich soil at a depth where the crown sits just level with the surface
Water deeply at the base twice a week in dry UK summers, keeping the narrow, lance-shaped leaves dry
Apply organic slug pellets or beer traps in early spring as the delicate pointed shoots emerge
Divide congested clumps in late autumn or early spring to maintain the neat, mounding growth habit
Cut back the yellowing foliage to the ground in November to prevent overwintering pests in the crown
items.description: Hosta lancifolia, the narrow-leaved plantain lily or narrow-leaved hosta, is a species of flowering plant in the family Asparagaceae. It is native to the southern Russian Far East and Japan, and it has been introduced to the northeastern United States and Bulgaria. A perennial cultigen reaching 0.5 m (20 in), it is available from commercial nurseries. Hardy in USDA zones 3 through 8, it is recommended for shady situations.

items.name: Hosta minor
items.growersTips:
Plant in moisture-retentive, acidic to neutral soil enriched with well-rotted leaf mould or compost.
Position in partial shade, keeping them sheltered from harsh midday sun and drying easterly winds.
Water deeply at the base twice a week in dry summer spells to keep the shallow root system moist.

items.description: Hosta minor is a species of flowering plant in the Asparagaceae family. It is one of the smallest hostas. It is also known as Hosta sieboldii 'Alba'.

items.name: Hosta nigrescens

items.description: Hosta is a genus of plants commonly known as hostas, plantain lilies and occasionally by the Japanese name gibōshi. Hostas are widely cultivated as shade-tolerant foliage plants. The genus is placed in the family Asparagaceae, subfamily Agavoideae, and is native to northeast Asia. Like many "lilioid monocots", the genus was once classified in the Liliaceae. The genus was named by Austrian botanist Leopold Trattinnick in 1812, in honor of the Austrian botanist Nicholas Thomas Host. In 1817, the generic name Funkia was used by German botanist Kurt Sprengel in honor of Heinrich Christian Funck, a

items.name: Hosta plantaginea
items.growersTips:

Water deeply at the base weekly during dry summer spells to keep the large thin leaves from scorching
Apply a thick layer of organic mulch in spring to retain moisture in free-draining UK garden soils
Surround the plant with copper tape or beer traps in spring to protect emerging shoots from slugs
Cut back dead foliage to the ground in late autumn after the first frost to prevent overwintering pests
items.description: Hosta plantaginea, the fragrant plantain lily or August lily, is a species of flowering plant in the family Asparagaceae, native to southeast and south-central China, and a garden escapee in scattered locations worldwide. This species and cultivars and hybrids derived from it are the only fragrant hostas. As a wild plant, it is typically found growing in the herb layer of mountain forests, below 2000 m.

items.name: Hosta sieboldiana

items.description: Hosta sieboldiana, Siebold's plantain lily, is a species of hosta native to Japan. A putative variety, Hosta sieboldiana var. elegans, has gained the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit, as has a putative variety of its synonym; Hosta fortunei var. aureomarginata, the gold-edged plantain lily. The cultivars 'Blue Angel', 'Blue Mammoth', and 'Olive Bailey Langdon' have also gained the RHS Award of Garden Merit.

items.name: Hosta sieboldii

items.name: Hosta undulata and its varieties

items.name: Plantain lily

items.description: Hyacinthoides non-scripta is a bulbous perennial plant found in Atlantic areas from the north-western part of the Iberian Peninsula to the British Isles, and also frequently used as a garden plant. It is known in English as the common bluebell, English bluebell or simply bluebell, a name which is used in Scotland to refer to the harebell, Campanula rotundifolia. In spring, H. non-scripta produces a nodding, one-sided inflorescence of 5–12 tubular, sweet-scented violet–blue flowers, with strongly recurved tepals, and 3–6 long, linear, basal leaves.

items.description: Hydrangea is a genus of more than 70 species of flowering plants native to Asia and the Americas. Hydrangea is also used as the common name for the genus; some are also often called hortensia. The genus was first described from Virginia in North America, but by far the greatest species diversity is in eastern Asia, notably China, Korea, and Japan. Most are shrubs 1–3 m tall, but some are small trees, and others lianas reaching up to 30 m (100 ft) by climbing up trees. They can be either deciduous or evergreen, though the widely cultivated temperate species are all deciduous.

items.name: Japanese climbing-hydrangea

Plant this self-clinging climber against a damp, north or east-facing wall to prevent leaf scorch.

items.description: Hydrangea arborescens, commonly known as smooth hydrangea or sevenbark, is a species of flowering plant in the family Hydrangeaceae. It is a small- to medium-sized, multi-stemmed, deciduous shrub up to 2 m (7 ft) tall that is native to the eastern United States.

items.description: Hydrangea macrophylla is a species of flowering plant in the family Hydrangeaceae, native and endemic to Japan. It is a deciduous shrub growing to 3 m (10 ft) tall by 2.5 m (8 ft) or more broad with large heads of pink or blue flowers in summer and autumn. It is currently treated as monotypic, with no subspecies or varieties. Common names include bigleaf hydrangea, and, for particular cultivar groups, the names lacecap hydrangea, mophead hydrangea, and hortensia. It is widely cultivated in many parts of the world in many climates. It is not to be confused with H. aspera 'Macrophylla'.

items.description: Hydrangea paniculata, or panicled hydrangea, is a species of flowering plant in the family Hydrangeaceae native to southern and eastern China, Korea, Japan and Russia (Sakhalin). It was first formally described by Philipp Franz von Siebold in 1829.

Protect young spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.
Avoid transplanting established plants by sowing seeds directly into their final flowering positions.

items.name: Hypecoum imberbe

items.name: Hypecoum pendulum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn directly into well-drained gritty soil as they dislike root disturbance.

Avoid overwatering by letting the soil dry out completely between waterings to prevent root rot.
Protect young spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.
Allow the plant to self-seed naturally in gravel gardens to ensure a display the following year.

items.name: Hypecoum procumbens
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn in gritty, free-draining soil to allow winter cold to naturally break dormancy.

Protect young spring shoots from slugs and snails using beer traps or grit barriers in wet weather.
Avoid transplanting established plants by sowing directly where they are to flower in the garden.

items.name: Hypseocharis pimpinellifolia
items.growersTips:
Grow in sharply draining gritty soil to prevent root rot during wet UK winters.
Plant tubers five centimetres deep in a sheltered south-facing rockery or alpine house.
Water sparingly from May to September and keep completely dry during winter dormancy.
Protect from slugs and snails in early spring when the delicate new foliage emerges.
Overwinter in a cold frame or unheated greenhouse to shield from heavy UK frosts.

items.name: Ichtyoselmis
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist well-drained humus-rich soil in deep or partial shade to mimic its woodland habitat
In dry UK summers water deeply at the base weekly to keep the soil consistently damp but not soggy
Protect the delicate emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit or beer traps
Mulch annually in autumn with leaf mould or well-rotted compost to protect roots from winter frost
Propagate by careful division in early spring just as new growth begins to show above the ground

items.name: Illecebrum verticillatum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in spring by pressing them lightly into damp, acidic, sandy soil without burying them.
Grow this damp-loving annual in bog gardens or pond edges to mimic its native UK heathland habitat.
Water frequently with rainwater to keep the soil consistently wet, as tap water is too alkaline.
Position in full sun to ensure the tiny white axillary flowers bloom fully from July to September.
Clear competing weeds by hand regularly because this prostrate plant is easily smothered by turf.

items.name: Ingeae
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in April at 2cm depth using peat-free compost to beat the cool UK spring soil.
Water deeply once a week at the base rather than daily sprinkles to encourage deep taproot growth.
Watch for black bean aphid attacks on young shoots in June and wash them off with a sharp water spray.
Incorporate grit into heavy clay soils before planting to prevent root rot during wet UK summers.
Plant alongside brassicas as companions to benefit from the nitrogen-fixing nodules on the roots.

items.name: Johnstone River teak
items.growersTips:
Sow Intsia seeds indoors in April at 2cm depth using bottom heat of 21C to counter cool UK springs.
Grow Intsia in terracotta pots with free-draining sandy loam to prevent root rot in wet UK summers.
Water only when the top 5cm of soil is dry, mimicking dry spells, to avoid waterlogging the roots.
Place pots against a south-facing brick wall to maximize sun exposure and trap essential heat.
Check weekly for glasshouse red spider mite under leaves when growing Intsia in UK conservatories.

items.name: Johnstone River teak
items.growersTips:
Grow this tropical legume in a heated conservatory or greenhouse to survive cool UK temperatures.
Sow seeds in spring at a depth of two centimeters after scarifying and soaking them in warm water.
Water deeply once the top three centimeters of free-draining, sandy loam soil has dried out completely.
Apply a low-nitrogen, high-potassium liquid fertilizer monthly during the active summer growth.
Inspect regularly for glasshouse red spider mites and maintain high humidity to deter infestations.

items.name: Intsia palembanica
items.growersTips:
Grow this tropical tree indoors in a heated conservatory to mimic its native warm rainforest habitat
Sow seeds in spring after scarifying and soaking them in warm water for twenty-four hours to sprout
Water consistently to keep the acidic loamy soil moist but never waterlogged during summer months
Provide a minimum winter temperature of fifteen degrees Celsius using grow lights to prevent leaf drop
Watch for glasshouse red spider mites and mist the foliage daily to maintain high humidity levels

items.name: Iostephane heterophylla
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in early spring at a depth of three millimetres to protect them from late frosts
Plant out in late May in a south-facing border with free-draining soil to maximise summer warmth
Water deeply once a week at the base rather than daily to prevent root rot in damp UK summers
Deadhead faded blooms weekly through August to prolong the flowering display until the first frost
Protect young spring shoots from slugs and snails using beer traps or physical copper barriers

items.name: Iris
items.growersTips:
Plant dwarf bulbs like Iris reticulata in autumn at a depth of three times the bulb height in pots.
Ensure sharp drainage by mixing grit into heavy clay soils to prevent winter bulb rot in wet weather.
Force potted bulbs indoors in December for early winter blooms then transplant outside in spring.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic pellets or beer traps in March.
Allow the foliage to die back naturally and turn yellow before removing it to feed next years bulb.

items.name: Iris laevigata
items.growersTips:
Grow in heavy clay or boggy soil at a planting depth of up to fifteen centimetres of standing water.
Position in full sun to ensure reliable flowering during the typical British midsummer wet season.
Propagate by dividing the rhizomes, not bulbs, in late summer after the flowering period has ended.
Cut back dead foliage to the ground in autumn to prevent rot in damp UK winter conditions.
Plant alongside Caltha palustris to create a vibrant colour contrast in pond margins.
items.description: Iris laevigata, known as Japanese iris, rabbit-ear iris, or shallow-flowered iris, is a species of flowering plant in the family Iridaceae, native to Japan. It is related to other members of Iris subgenus Limniris, including other species of Japanese irises.

items.name: Water flag
items.growersTips:
Plant rhizomes shallowly with the tops exposed to the sun in heavy, moisture-retentive clay soil.
Position at the margins of a garden pond up to twenty centimeters deep to control its vigorous spread.
Cut the foliage back to the ground in autumn to prevent rotting leaves from polluting pond water.
Divide congested clumps in late summer using a sharp spade to maintain vigor and control size.
Wear thick gloves when handling to avoid skin irritation from the toxic sap of this native plant.
items.description: Iris pseudacorus, the yellow flag, yellow iris, or water flag, is a species of flowering plant in the family Iridaceae. It is native to Europe, western Asia and northwest Africa. Its specific epithet pseudacorus means "false acorus", referring to the similarity of its leaves to those of Acorus calamus, as they have a prominently veined mid-rib and sword-like shape. However, the two plants are not closely related.

items.name: Category:Isoberlinia tomentosa
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in April at 2cm depth in peat-free compost to protect from late UK spring frosts.
Plant out in June in a south-facing border with grit added to clay soil to ensure sharp drainage.
Water deeply once a week at the base during dry July spells rather than daily light sprinklings.
Protect young shoots from slugs using beer traps or copper tape during damp British spring nights.
Grow alongside nitrogen-loving leafy greens like spinach to benefit from this legume's root nodules.

items.name: Isopyrum thalictroides
items.growersTips:
Plant in partial shade under deciduous shrubs to mimic their native UK woodland edge habitat.
Incorporate leaf mould into moisture-retentive, acidic to neutral soil before planting in autumn.
Keep soil consistently moist but never waterlogged during their active spring growing period.
Propagate by dividing the delicate rhizomes in late summer once the foliage has died back.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.

items.name: Ixia curta
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs 8cm deep in autumn using pots of gritty compost to easily move them indoors for winter.

Water weekly during spring growth but keep bulbs bone dry from July to October during dormancy.
Protect from hard UK frosts by overwintering pots in a cold greenhouse or bright conservatory.
Mix plenty of horticultural grit into heavy UK soils to prevent bulb rot in wet winter weather.

items.name: Ixia dubia

Overwinter containers in a frost-free greenhouse or cold frame once autumn temperatures drop below 5C.

items.name: Ixia latifolia

Water weekly during spring growth but stop completely once foliage dies back for a dry summer rest.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.

items.name: Ixia odorata

items.name: Ixia paniculata

items.name: Ixia polystachya

items.name: Ixia scillaris

items.name: Ixia viridiflora

Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.

items.name: Jefea brevifolia
items.growersTips:

Plant out in late May after frosts in a south-facing border with added grit for sharp drainage.
Water only when the top 5cm of soil is dry to prevent root rot in damp British summer weather.
Protect young seedlings from slugs and snails using beer traps or physical barriers in wet weather.
Deadhead faded yellow blooms weekly from July to October to prolong the flowering season in the UK.

items.name: Jepsonia

Plant dormant tubers in late summer at a depth of three centimetres in gritty, sharply draining soil.
Keep the soil completely dry during summer dormancy, then water weekly once autumn flowers emerge.

Keep compost moist during winter growth but completely dry during summer dormancy to prevent rot.

items.name: Kalaharia uncinata
items.growersTips:
Grow in free-draining sandy loam with added grit to survive wet UK winters and prevent root rot.
Position in the sunniest, south-facing spot or a container you can move indoors before first frost.

Overwinter in a heated greenhouse or bright windowsill kept above five degrees Celsius.

items.name: Kalanchoe arborescens
items.growersTips:
Grow in a gritty loam-based potting mix with fifty percent perlite to prevent winter root rot.
Water only when the top five centimetres of soil is bone dry, then drench and drain fully.
Position on a south-facing indoor windowsill to maximise crucial winter light levels in the UK.
Move outdoors only from June to August when night temperatures consistently stay above ten degrees.
Prune leggy stems in early spring just above a leaf node to encourage a bushier growth habit.

items.name: Kalanchoe beauverdii

Grow in a gritty loam-based compost with fifty percent perlite or horticultural sand for drainage.
Provide a sturdy trellis or bamboo cane support for its scrambling, vining stems to climb up.
Water only when the soil is completely dry, then reduce to once a month during damp UK winters.
Overwinter indoors on a south-facing windowsill as this succulent cannot tolerate UK frosts.
Take stem cuttings in late spring to propagate new plants before the autumn temperature drop.

items.name: Kalanchoe beharensis
items.growersTips:
Bring indoors by October as this Madagascar native cannot survive wet UK winters below five degrees.
Water only when the top five centimetres of gritty, free-draining cactus compost is completely dry.
Propagate in spring by pinning a single mature leaf flat onto damp sand to trigger new plantlets.
Prune leggy stems in April just above a leaf node to encourage a bushier, more compact habit.
Wipe the felted leaves with a dry brush rather than water to prevent rot and powdery mildew.

items.name: Kalanchoe bentii
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds on the surface of free-draining gritty compost in early spring under heated glass at 18C.
Keep pots on a south-facing windowsill to maximise the intense sunlight this desert species craves.

Overwinter indoors in a heated room or greenhouse as this tender succulent cannot survive UK frosts.
Watch for mealybugs in leaf axils and treat immediately with an organic insecticidal soap spray.

items.name: Kalanchoe blossfeldiana

Bring indoors by September before UK frosts hit as they cannot survive temperatures below ten degrees
Water only when the top two inches of gritty peat-free compost have dried out completely to avoid rot
Deadhead spent flower stems at the base in spring to encourage a second flush of colourful blooms
Place on a south-facing windowsill to get the daily four hours of direct sun needed for bud growth
To trigger winter flowering cover the plant for fourteen hours daily in autumn to mimic short days

items.name: Kalanchoe bouvetii
items.growersTips:
Bring pots indoors by October to protect this tender succulent from wet and freezing UK winters.
Water only when the top two inches of gritty, free-draining cactus compost have dried out completely.

Pinch out the growing tips in May to encourage a bushier habit and prevent leggy stem growth.

items.name: Kalanchoe daigremontiana

Grow indoors in a gritty, free-draining cactus compost to prevent root rot in damp UK winters.
Water only when the top two inches of soil are dry, reducing to once a month from November to March.
Keep pots on a south-facing windowsill to maximise light levels during overcast British winters.
Pick off the plantlets from leaf margins before they drop and weed them out of adjacent housepots.
Maintain indoor temperatures above ten degrees Celsius to protect this succulent from frost damage.

items.name: Kalanchoe delagoensis
items.growersTips:
Bring pots indoors before first autumn frost as this succulent cannot survive wet UK winters.
Water only when the top two inches of compost are dry then drain fully to prevent root rot.
Grow in a gritty mix of fifty percent peat-free compost and fifty percent horticultural sand.
Remove the tiny plantlets from leaf tips regularly to stop them invading neighbouring pots.
Place on a south-facing windowsill to maximise winter light and prevent leggy growth.

items.name: Kalanchoe farinacea
items.growersTips:
Bring indoors before October frosts as this tender succulent cannot survive wet UK winter freezes.
Water only when the top three centimeters of gritty, free-draining soil mix has dried out completely.
Grow in a south-facing conservatory or windowsill to provide the maximum daily sunlight UK offers.
Propagate in late spring by taking stem cuttings and letting them callous for three days before potting.
Watch for mealybugs in leaf axils and treat immediately with organic insecticidal soap or alcohol.

items.name: Kalanchoe fedtschenkoi
items.growersTips:
Bring indoors before October frosts as this tender succulent cannot survive wet UK winter freezes
Water only when the top three centimetres of gritty compost are completely dry to prevent root rot
Prune leggy stems in late spring to encourage bushier growth and propagate the cuttings in sand
Grow in a terracotta pot using a fifty-fifty mix of peat-free compost and horticultural grit
Watch for mealybugs in leaf axils during winter when indoor heating creates dry stagnant air

items.name: Kalanchoe garambiensis
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds on the soil surface in early spring under glass as they need light to germinate.
Water only when the top two inches of compost are dry to prevent root rot in damp UK weather.
Bring pots indoors by September before the first autumn frost to protect this tender succulent.
Mix fifty percent grit with peat-free compost to ensure the sharp drainage this plant requires.
Pinch out the growing tips in late spring to encourage a bushier habit and more yellow flowers.

items.name: Kalanchoe gastonis-bonnieri
items.growersTips:
Bring indoors before first frost as this succulent cannot survive wet UK winters below ten degrees.
Propagate in summer by detaching the plantlets that form on leaf tips and potting them in grit sand.
Water only when the top two inches of gritty loam are dry to prevent root rot in humid UK weather.
Use a free-draining mix of two parts peat-free compost to one part perlite for outdoor summer pots.
Watch for mealybugs in leaf crevices during autumn when moving containers into indoor glasshouses.

items.name: Kalanchoe crenato-daigremontiana
items.growersTips:
Grow in gritty peat-free loam with fifty percent perlite to survive damp UK autumn humidity.
Water only when the top three centimetres of soil are bone dry, keeping completely dry in winter.
Keep indoors on a south-facing windowsill from October to May to protect from frost and wet rot.
Scrape off the tiny plantlets from leaf margins in spring to prevent them invading nearby pots.
Check leaf crevices weekly for mealybugs, treating infestations with an organic neem oil spray.

items.name: Kalanchoe longiflora
items.growersTips:
Bring indoors before October frosts as this succulent cannot survive wet cold UK winter conditions
Water only when the gritty compost dries out completely to prevent root rot in damp UK climates
Grow in a mix of two parts peat-free compost to one part horticultural grit for sharp drainage
Prune leggy stems in spring to encourage bushy growth and propagate the cuttings in dry soil
Place on a south-facing windowsill to maximise light and develop the signature red leaf margins

items.name: Kalanchoe luciae
items.growersTips:
Bring indoors before first frost as this succulent cannot survive wet UK winters below five degrees.
Grow in a gritty loam-based potting mix with fifty percent perlite or horticultural sand for drainage.
Water only when the soil is bone dry then drench fully, keeping the central leaf rosette dry.
Place on a south-facing windowsill to get maximum sunlight which triggers the red leaf margins.
Propagate in spring by taking leaf cuttings and letting them callus for three days before potting.

items.name: Copper Spoons
items.growersTips:
Bring indoors before first autumn frost as this succulent cannot survive wet UK winter freezes.
Water only when the gritty compost dries out completely to prevent root rot in damp UK climates.
Grow in a pots with fifty percent perlite or grit to ensure the rapid drainage this plant needs.
Place on a south facing windowsill to maximise light levels during dark British winter months.
Prune leggy stems in late spring to encourage bushier growth and maintain the bronze leaf colour.

items.name: Air plant
items.growersTips:
Grow in pots of peat-free grit mix so you can move them indoors before the first autumn frost hits.
Water only when the top two inches of soil are dry to prevent root rot in damp UK winters.
Propagate by placing a mature leaf flat on damp compost to trigger plantlets along the margins.
Keep in a south-facing conservatory or windowsill to maximise limited UK winter sunlight hours.
Watch for vine weevil grubs in the compost during spring and treat with beneficial nematodes.

items.name: Kalanchoe robusta
items.growersTips:
Bring indoors by late September to protect this frost-tender succulent from damp UK autumn chills.
Water only when the top three centimeters of gritty, free-draining loam soil is completely dry.
Sow seeds shallowly in early spring on the surface of damp compost under a clear polythene cover.
Position in your brightest south-facing windowsill or conservatory to prevent leggy, weak growth.
Watch for vine weevil grubs in containers and treat with UK-approved nematodes in late summer.

items.name: Bryophyllum
items.growersTips:
Bring potted mother of thousands indoors by October to survive the wet, freezing UK winter frosts
Water only when the top two inches of gritty, free-draining cactus compost are bone dry to touch
Pick off and discard the falling plantlets from leaves to stop them invading nearby garden pots
Provide maximum winter windowsill light to prevent leggy growth and weak stems in gloomy UK months
Watch for mealybugs in leaf crevices and dab them with a cotton bud dipped in rubbing alcohol

items.name: Kalanchoe suarezensis
items.growersTips:
Bring indoors by late September to protect this frost-tender succulent from cold UK winters.
Water only when the top two inches of gritty, free-draining cactus compost have dried out completely.
Grow in a terracotta pot rather than open soil to prevent root rot during wet British summers.
Position on a south-facing windowsill to ensure it receives the six hours of daily sun it requires.
Pick off the tiny plantlets that form on leaf margins to propagate new plants easily in spring.

items.name: White Lady
items.growersTips:
Grow in a gritty, free-draining loam-based compost with fifty percent perlite to prevent root rot.
Water only when the soil is bone dry, then drench thoroughly, keeping the central rosette dry.
Move indoors to a south-facing windowsill by October to protect from damp UK autumn frosts.
Position in maximum direct summer sun to trigger the vibrant red leaf margins on Flapjack foliage.
Propagate by taking leaf cuttings in late spring, allowing the wound to callus before potting.

items.name: Kalanchoe tomentosa
items.growersTips:
Grow in free-draining grit-heavy compost on a south-facing UK windowsill to maximise daily light.
Water only when the soil is bone dry, reducing to once a month during damp UK winter months.
Keep indoors year-round as this succulent cannot survive UK frost and needs temperatures above 10C.
Snip leggy stems in spring just above a leaf node to encourage a bushier, more compact habit.
Inspect the fuzzy silver leaves weekly for mealybugs which hide easily in the dense leaf hairs.

items.name: Kalmia latifolia
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist well-drained acidic soil using ericaceous compost and pine needles to lower the pH
Water with stored rainwater rather than tap water to maintain the low soil pH that kalmias require
Prune lightly immediately after flowering in June to avoid cutting off next year's developing buds
Shelter from cold dry winds by planting near camellias or rhododendrons in partial woodland shade
Watch for vine weevil larvae in autumn and drench the soil with parasitic nematodes to kill them

items.name: Kalmiopsis fragrans
items.growersTips:
Plant in ericaceous compost mixed with grit to mimic Oregon scree and prevent winter root rot.
Water with rainwater rather than tap water to maintain the essential acidic soil pH below five.
Grow in a terracotta pot to ensure sharp drainage and allow winter protection from heavy UK rain.
Prune lightly immediately after spring flowering to maintain its compact, dome-shaped habit.
Position in partial shade with morning sun to prevent leaf scorch during dry UK summer spells.

items.name: Kalmiopsis leachiana
items.growersTips:
Plant in acidic, gritty, ericaceous soil with plenty of pine bark and grit to ensure sharp drainage.
Position in a cool, partially shaded spot that mimics a damp UK rock garden, avoiding midday sun.
Water with rainwater only to keep the soil consistently moist but never waterlogged or soggy.
Protect from winter wet and heavy frosts using a rain shelter or alpine house to prevent root rot.
Prune very lightly immediately after spring flowering to maintain its compact, mounded shrub habit.

items.name: Karomia speciosa
items.growersTips:
Grow Karomia in pots using peat-free grit mix so you can move them indoors before winter frosts hit.
Water sparingly from autumn to spring to prevent root rot in damp, cold UK winter greenhouse soils.
Prune Karomia lightly in late spring after frost risk passes to shape and encourage bushier growth.
Position pots against a south-facing brick wall to maximise summer heat and mimic native warmth.
Feed monthly with a high-potassium liquid fertiliser from May to August to boost summer flowering.

items.name: Kickxia commutata
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn in free-draining gravelly loam to mimic dry Mediterranean coastal habitats.
Water sparingly only during prolonged summer droughts to prevent root rot in damp UK winters.
Position in full south-facing sun against a warm brick wall to maximise summer flowering.
Prune back dead stems in early spring just as new growth emerges from the perennial crown.
Grow alongside Thymus serpyllum in a raised bed to ensure the sharp drainage this species needs.

items.name: Sharpleaf cancerwort
items.growersTips:
Hand-weed this low-growing arable weed in spring before its delicate, trailing stems tangle in turf
Sow seeds in autumn just below the soil surface in well-drained, chalky loam to mimic UK cornfields
Water sparingly only during prolonged summer droughts as this plant thrives in dry, disturbed soil
Grow alongside wild pansy and field madder in a sunny wildflower border to prevent aggressive grass
Check trailing stems in June for powdery mildew and space plants fifteen centimetres apart for airflow

items.name: Kirengeshoma palmata
items.growersTips:
Plant in deep, moisture-retentive, acidic to neutral soil enriched with plenty of leaf mould.
Position in a sheltered, fully shaded or partially shaded border to prevent leaf scorch from sun.
Water copiously during dry summer spells to keep the soil consistently damp but never waterlogged.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic pellets or beer traps.
Cut the dead stems back to ground level in late winter before new growth begins in spring.

items.name: Kirengeshoma koreana
items.growersTips:
Plant in deep, moist, humus-rich acid to neutral soil in a sheltered, fully shaded woodland border.
Water deeply and regularly during dry UK summers to prevent the large, delicate leaves from crisping.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.
Mulch annually in late winter with leaf mould or composted bark to mimic its native forest floor.
Cut the dead stems back to ground level in early spring just before the new growth begins to emerge.

items.name: Kirengeshoma palmata
items.growersTips:
Plant in deep partial shade sheltered from cold UK winds to prevent delicate leaves from scorching.
Incorporate plenty of leafmould or well-rotted manure to mimic a damp woodland soil before planting.
Water deeply during dry summer spells to keep the soil consistently moist but never waterlogged.
Cut the dead stems back to ground level in late winter before new shoots emerge in early spring.
Apply a thick mulch of compost in autumn to protect the crown from severe UK winter frosts.

items.name: Klattia partita
items.growersTips:
Plant this South African bulb in a container of acidic, peat-free ericaceous compost mixed with grit.
Overwinter containers indoors in a frost-free greenhouse as this tender plant cannot survive UK frost.
Water with harvested rainwater rather than tap water to maintain the low pH soil it requires to grow.
Position in the sunniest spot of your garden or conservatory to mimic its native fynbos light levels.
Feed monthly in spring with a highly diluted, low-phosphorus liquid fertiliser to avoid root burn.

items.name: Red klattia
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender South African bulb in a gritty loam-based compost inside a frost-free greenhouse.
Water moderately during its winter growing season but keep the pot completely dry during summer.
Plant the corms 5cm deep in terracotta pots to ensure excellent drainage and prevent winter rot.
Position in full sun under glass to mimic the intense light of its native fynbos habitat.
Propagate by carefully separating offsets from the parent corm during its summer dormant period.

items.name: Kmeria septentrionalis
items.growersTips:
Plant Kmeria in acidic to neutral soil enriched with leaf mould to mimic UK woodland conditions.
Protect young Kmeria from late UK spring frosts using fleece to prevent damage to emerging buds.
Water deeply once a week during dry UK summers, ensuring the soil remains moist but never waterlogged.
Prune Kmeria minimally in mid-summer after flowering to remove dead wood without losing next year's buds.
Shelter Kmeria from cold, drying winds by planting it near a south or west-facing garden wall.

items.name: Knowltonia capensis
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist well-drained humus-rich acid to neutral soil in a sheltered partially shaded border
Protect the crown with a thick dry winter mulch of bark or leaf mould to survive wet UK frosts
Water consistently during dry summer spells to mimic its native damp woodland margin habitat
Propagate by sowing fresh seed in cold frames in autumn or divide established clumps in spring
Wear gloves when handling to avoid skin irritation from the toxic sap typical of Ranunculaceae

items.name: Knowltonia vesicatoria
items.growersTips:
Plant in partial shade under deciduous trees to mimic its native woodland margin habitat in the UK.
Incorporate leaf mould and grit into heavy clay soil to ensure excellent drainage and prevent rot.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells but keep the crown dry during wet UK winters.
Wear thick gloves when pruning dead leaves in spring to avoid painful blisters from the toxic sap.
Sow fresh seed in autumn in cold frames to allow natural winter chilling for successful germination.

items.name: Koompassia malaccensis
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in April at 2cm depth using bottom heat of 21C to counter cool UK spring soils.
Plant out in June after the last frost in a south-facing spot with grit added for sharp drainage.
Water deeply once a week at the base during dry summer spells, avoiding waterlogged soil conditions.
Watch for slugs and snails on young spring shoots, protecting them with copper tape or beer traps.
Grow alongside nitrogen-loving leafy greens to benefit from this legume's natural soil enrichment.

items.name: Koompassia excelsa
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in early spring at a depth of two centimetres using a heated propagator at twenty-one Celsius.
Grow in deep pots of sandy, acidic loam to accommodate the taproot before transplanting outdoors in June.
Water deeply once a week at the base during dry summer spells to mimic tropical wet-dry cycles.
Position in the sunniest, most sheltered south-facing spot to protect the foliage from cold UK winds.
Apply a potassium-rich liquid seaweed feed monthly in summer to boost resilience against damp autumns.

items.name: Koompassia malaccensis
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in April at a depth of two centimeters using bottom heat to mimic tropical warmth.
Water the soil deeply once a week during summer dry spells to simulate a monsoon wet-dry pattern.
Watch for glasshouse red spider mite when growing this tropical legume under glass in cool UK spring.
Incorporate grit and leaf mould into heavy clay soil to ensure the sharp drainage this species needs.
Grow alongside nitrogen-loving leafy greens to benefit from this legume's root nodule activity.

items.name: Krapfia weberbaueri
items.growersTips:
Plant in acidic, gritty loam that mimics Scottish scree slopes to ensure vital winter drainage.
Sow fresh seed in autumn in cold frames, as they require winter chilling to break dormancy.
Water with rainwater to keep the soil consistently damp but never waterlogged during dry summers.
Protect crown from winter wet using a cloche to prevent rot in damp UK winters.
Grow in a cool, semi-shaded rock garden or alpine house to shield from intense midday sun.

items.name: False dandeloin
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in autumn at a depth of two millimetres to mimic natural UK winter stratification.
Plant in poor, well-drained acidic soil to prevent this wildflower from being outcompeted by weeds.
Water seedlings weekly during dry spring spells but allow the soil to dry out completely between waterings.
Position near Campanula rotundifolia to create a naturalistic UK meadow aesthetic that attracts bees.
Deadhead spent orange blooms in midsummer to prevent aggressive self-seeding across your garden beds.

items.name: Dwarf dandelion
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at a depth of two millimetres in early spring using free-draining sandy loam.
Water sparingly once established to mimic dry meadows, allowing the top soil layer to dry fully.
Sow directly into final pots to avoid root disturbance, as this taprooted annual hates transplanting.
Position in full south-facing sun to prevent leggy growth in damp, overcast UK summer conditions.
Deadhead spent yellow blooms weekly to control self-seeding and prolong the summer flowering window.

items.name: Potato dandelion
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in spring at a depth of 2mm in well-drained, sandy loam to mimic native pineland soils.
Water sparingly once established, allowing the top 3cm of soil to dry out completely between feeds.
Position in full sun to light shade, ensuring protection from wet winter waterlogging using grit.
Sow alongside low-growing UK native grasses to provide structural support and prevent soil erosion.
Monitor closely for slugs and snails during wet British spring nights using beer traps or grit.

items.name: Krigia montana
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at a depth of two millimetres in autumn to mimic natural Appalachian exposure.
Keep the grit-heavy soil damp but never waterlogged during the cool, wet UK spring growing season.
Position containers in full morning sun but provide light afternoon shade during hot July spells.
Protect young spring rosettes from slugs and snails using organic iron phosphate pellets or beer traps.
Deadhead spent yellow blooms weekly in summer to prevent excessive self-seeding across gravel beds.

items.name: Krigia occidentalis
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds thinly in autumn on the soil surface of well-drained, sandy loam as they need light to grow
Water sparingly during damp UK winters to prevent root rot in this drought-tolerant annual wildflower
Position in full sun and protect young spring seedlings from slugs using organic grit barriers
Grow alongside low-growing native UK annuals like field pansy to prevent aggressive weed takeover
Allow the seed heads to dry on the plant in late summer to self-sow naturally for next spring

items.name: Dwarf dandelion
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in spring on the surface of well-drained, sandy soil as they require light to germinate.
Grow in a container to prevent this self-seeding annual from spreading aggressively in damp borders.
Water sparingly once established, allowing the gritty compost to dry out fully between waterings.
Position in full sun to mimic its native dry habitat and prevent the rosettes from rotting in UK rain.
Watch for slugs and snails during wet UK springs, protecting the delicate emerging basal rosettes.
items.description: Krigia virginica, also known as dwarf dandelion or Virginia dwarf dandelion, is a North American species of plants in the family Asteraceae. Its native range reaches from Maine to Florida and extends westward to central Texas. It is commonly found in disturbed areas, along roadsides, and within rocky woodlands.

items.name: Krigia wrightii
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at a depth of two millimetres in early spring to ensure vital light germination.
Grow in a well-drained sandy loam with low nutrients to mimic its native dry gravelly habitats.
Water sparingly only during dry spells to prevent root rot in damp UK autumn and winter climates.
Position in full sun alongside low-growing rockery companion plants like Sedum or Thymus.
Collect seed heads in late summer for indoor sowing to protect delicate seedlings from wet winters.
items.description: Krigia wrightii, known as Wright's dwarfdandelion, is a North American species of plants in the family Asteraceae. It is native to the southern Great Plains of the south-central United States.

items.name: Cape Cowslip
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs five centimetres deep in autumn using gritty, free-draining compost to prevent rot.
Keep pots in a frost-free greenhouse or sunny indoor windowsill as they cannot survive UK winters.
Water weekly once autumn shoots appear, but keep completely dry during their summer dormant phase.
Feed with a high-potassium liquid fertiliser every fortnight from winter until the flowers fade.
Watch for slugs and snails on the fleshy leaves during the damp UK winter growing season.
items.description: Lachenalia aloides is a species of flowering plant in the family Asparagaceae, native to the Western Cape of South Africa. It is a bulbous perennial growing to 15–28 cm (6–11 in) tall by 5 cm (2 in) broad, with strap-shaped spotted leaves and fleshy stems bearing pendent tubular yellow flowers, red at the tips, in winter and spring. The Latin aloides literally means "aloe-like"; though L. aloides, despite its similarity, does not belong to the same family of plants as aloes.

items.name: Lachenalia bulbifera
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs in autumn 5cm deep in gritty, free-draining compost to prevent winter waterlogging rot.
Keep pots in a frost-free greenhouse or sunny windowsill as they cannot survive harsh UK winters.
Water sparingly from September, increase as leaves grow, then stop completely when foliage dies back.
Watch for slugs and snails in early spring as they quickly ruin the succulent leaves and red flowers.
Feed with a high-potassium liquid fertiliser fortnightly once flower spikes appear in midwinter.
items.description: Lachenalia bulbifera, syn. L. pendula, is a species of flowering plant in the family Asparagaceae, native to the Western Cape of South Africa. It is a bulbous perennial growing to 30 cm (12 in) tall by 5 cm (2 in) broad, with strap-shaped spotted leaves and fleshy stems bearing pendent tubular orange or red flowers 3 cm long, in winter and spring. The Latin bulbifera literally means "bulb-bearing", and refers to the plant's habit of producing bulblets, which can be separated from the parent plant and grown on.

items.name: Lachenalia contaminata
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs in autumn at a depth of five centimetres in sharply draining gritty soil to prevent rot.
Grow in pots to easily move them under a cold glasshouse or porch to protect from wet UK winters.
Water sparingly from autumn to spring, then dry them out completely during their summer dormancy.
Watch for slugs and snails in early spring as they eagerly target the emerging grassy foliage.
Repot every three years in late summer using a mix of two parts grit to one part loam-based compost.
items.description: Lachenalia contaminata is a species of flowering plant in the family Asparagaceae, native to the Western Cape of South Africa. It is a bulbous perennial growing to 25 cm (10 in) tall, with grass-like leaves and fleshy stems bearing brushlike white flowers tipped with maroon in spring.

items.name: Lachenalia corymbosa
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs in autumn 8cm deep in gritty, sharply draining compost to survive wet UK winters.
Keep pots in a frost-free greenhouse or sunny cold frame as they will not survive hard UK frosts.
Water weekly from autumn leaf emergence until spring flowering, then stop completely for summer.
Bake the dormant bulbs in dry soil in a sunny greenhouse during summer to trigger next year's blooms.
Watch for aphids on new winter growth and apply organic soap spray immediately to prevent damage.
items.description: Lachenalia corymbosa, the corymbous Cape cowslip, is a species of flowering plant in the genus Lachenalia native to the southwest Cape Provinces of South Africa. It has gained the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit.

items.name: Lachenalia flava
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs in autumn five centimetres deep in extremely gritty, free-draining soil to prevent rot.
Keep pots in a frost-free greenhouse or sunny windowsill as they cannot survive wet UK winters.
Water weekly from autumn foliage emergence through flowering, then stop completely for summer dormancy.
Feed with a high-potash liquid fertiliser every two weeks during the winter active growing phase.
Check leaves regularly in winter for aphids and slugs which thrive in damp UK greenhouse conditions.
items.description: Lachenalia flava, the golden opal flower, is a species of flowering plant in the genus Lachenalia native to the southwest Cape Provinces of South Africa. It has gained the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit.

items.name: Lachenalia longituba
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs in autumn 8cm deep in gritty, free-draining compost using terracotta pots for drainage.
Keep pots in a frost-free greenhouse or sunny windowsill as this South African native is tender.
Water sparingly from autumn foliage emergence through winter, then stop completely when leaves yellow.
Protect emerging winter shoots from slugs and snails using organic bait or copper tape on pots.
Repot every three years in late summer during dormancy, separating offsets to propagate new plants.
items.description: Lachenalia longituba is a species of flowering plant in the genus Lachenalia, native to the Roggeveld plateau of South Africa. It has gained the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit.

items.name: Lachenalia mutabilis
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs in autumn at a depth of eight centimetres in extremely free-draining gritty compost.
Keep compost damp during winter growth but stop watering completely when leaves yellow in summer.
Overwinter pots in a frost-free greenhouse or sunny windowsill as they cannot survive UK freezes.
Feed fortnightly with a high-potash liquid fertiliser only while the active winter growth occurs.
Watch closely for aphids and slugs on the tender emerging flower spikes during early spring.
items.description: Lachenalia mutabilis is a plant species in the Lachenalia genus. Lachenalia mutabilis can be found in western South Africa.

items.name: Lachenalia quadricolor
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs in autumn 8cm deep in gritty, free-draining compost to prevent winter rot in wet UK soil.
Grow in pots to easily move them under glass or indoors before the first harsh UK winter frosts hit.
Water weekly from autumn growth until spring flowering, then stop completely for summer dormancy.
Position in a south-facing cold frame or conservatory to maximise scarce UK winter sunlight.
Watch for aphids on new shoots in early spring and treat immediately to prevent virus transmission.
items.description: Lachenalia quadricolor, the four‑coloured opal flower, is a species of flowering plant in the genus Lachenalia, native to the southwest Cape Provinces of South Africa. It has gained the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit.

items.name: Yellow Soldiers
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs in autumn at a depth of five centimetres in sharply draining gritty soil to prevent rot.
Grow in pots under glass or move indoors by October to protect them from wet UK winter frosts.
Water moderately during autumn and winter growth but keep completely dry during summer dormancy.
Position in full sun on a south-facing windowsill or cold frame to mimic South African light.
Watch for aphids on new winter shoots and treat immediately to prevent virus transmission.
items.description: Lachenalia reflexa is species of the genus Lachenalia endemic to lowland areas near Cape Town, South Africa.

items.name: Lachenalia unifolia
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs in autumn at a depth of eight centimetres in extremely gritty, free-draining compost.
Keep pots in a cold greenhouse or sunny cold frame to protect them from wet UK winter freezes.
Water sparingly from autumn emergence, then dry off completely in summer during their dormant phase.
Watch for slugs and snails in early spring as they quickly destroy the single, delicate leaf.
Grow in terracotta pots rather than open borders to easily manage the essential summer baking.
items.description: Lachenalia unifolia, the banded viooltjie, is the most common Lachenalia species in the Cape Floristic Region of South Africa.

items.name: Lachnostachys ferruginea
items.growersTips:
Grow woolly lambstail in a container with fifty percent grit to survive wet UK winter root rot.
Place pots against a south-facing brick wall in winter to maximise heat and shield from heavy rain.
Water only when the top five centimetres of soil is dry, keeping the woolly foliage completely dry.
Prune back leggy stems by one third in April using sharp shears to promote compact silver growth.
Position next to purple-leaved Heuchera in full sun to create a striking foliage colour contrast.
items.description: Lachnostachys is a genus of flowering plants in the mint family, Lamiaceae, first described in 1842 by William Jackson Hooker. The type species is Lachnostachys ferruginea. The genus name, Lachnostachys, comes from two Greek words/roots, lachnề ("wool") and -stachys, and thus describes the genus as having spiked woolly inflorescences. The entire genus is endemic to Western Australia

items.name: Lamprocapnos
items.growersTips:
Plant in partial shade in moisture-retentive, humus-rich soil to prevent early summer dormancy.
Incorporate well-rotted leafmould or compost into the planting hole to mimic British woodland soil.
Water consistently during dry spring spells to prolong the delicate heart-shaped pink blooms.
Cut back yellowing foliage to ground level in midsummer once the plant naturally dies back.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using beer traps or organic wool pellets.
items.description: Lamprocapnos spectabilis, commonly known as bleeding heart or Asian bleeding heart, is a species of flowering plant belonging to the fumitory subfamily (Fumarioideae) of the Papaveraceae. It is native to Northeast China and the Korean peninsula; however, it has been introduced by humans into a larger area of Northeast Asia, including parts of Siberia, Russia and Japan.

items.name: Lapeirousia plicata
items.growersTips:
Plant Lapeirousia laxa corms 5cm deep in autumn using gritty, free-draining soil to prevent winter rot.
