Grow them in pots to easily move them indoors to a frost-free greenhouse or cold frame by October.
Water weekly during spring growth but keep them completely dry during their summer dormant phase.
Position pots in the sunniest south-facing spot to mimic their native South African warmth.
Overwinter outdoors only in mild UK coastal zones under a thick 10cm layer of dry bark mulch.
items.description: Lapeirousia is a genus in the plant family Iridaceae. It is endemic to sub-Saharan Africa, about a third of the species occurring in fynbos.

items.name: Laphangium teydeum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at two millimetres deep in April using free-draining peat-free compost indoors
Transplant outdoors in late May after frosts into a sheltered south-facing spot with full sun
Water the base only when the top two centimetres of soil is dry to prevent stem rot in damp UK weather
Protect young spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic wool pellets or beer traps
Grow alongside thyme or rosemary in gravel gardens to mimic its natural dry, rocky habitat conditions
items.description:
Laphangium is a genus of plants in the family Asteraceae.SpeciesLaphangium affine (D.Don) Tzvelev - Turkey, Republic of Georgia
Laphangium luteoalbum (L.) Tzvelev - Europe, Middle East, North Africa
Laphangium teydeum Wildpret & Greuter - Canary Islands

items.name: Lappula occidentalis
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn at a depth of 3mm into gritty, free-draining soil to mimic UK winter chilling.
Position in full sun and water only during prolonged dry spells to prevent root rot in damp UK clay.
Watch for slugs on young spring rosettes and clear surrounding weeds to prevent damp microclimates.
Plant alongside thyme or sedum in gravel gardens to provide the sharp drainage this species craves.
Cut back the flowering stems in late summer before seed drop if you want to limit its self-seeding.
items.description: Lappula occidentalis, also known as flatspine stickseed, flatspine sheepburr, western stickseed, Lappula redowskii, or Redowski's stickseed, is a biennial forb native to North America and parts of Europe and Asia. It belongs to the family Boraginaceae. Variants include L. redowskii var. cupulata and L. redowskii var. redowskii, which differ in fruit morphology from the type specimen.

items.name: Bristly sheepbur
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at a depth of three millimetres in autumn to mimic natural UK winter chilling.
Grow in poor, sharply drained chalky soil to prevent the plant from becoming floppy and invasive.
Water sparingly only during prolonged summer droughts as this annual is highly rot-prone in wet soil.
Wear thick gloves when clearing dead summer plants to avoid the painful, hook-spined burr seeds.
Plant alongside wild marjoram in sunny borders to attract native UK pollinators to the blooms.
items.description: Lappula squarrosa is a species of flowering plant in the borage family known by several common names, including European stickseed, bur forget-me-not, bluebur, and bristly sheepbur. It is native to Europe and Asia, where it is common, and it is an introduced species in much of North America and Africa. It is well known as a noxious weed where it is naturalized and also in many parts of its native range. This is an annual herb producing an erect stem often with sprays of many long, bending branches, its form varying in different regions and climates. The plant may approach a meter in height. Th

items.name: Laxmannia squarrosa
items.growersTips:
Grow in a gritty loam-based compost with added horticultural sand to ensure the sharp drainage needed.
Position in a cold frame or unheated greenhouse to protect the crown from wet UK winter rot.
Water sparingly from spring to autumn, allowing the soil to dry out completely between waterings.
Propagate by carefully dividing the fibrous root clumps in early spring just as new growth begins.
Check regularly for slugs and snails which target the delicate grassy foliage in damp spring weather.
items.description: Laxmannia squarrosa is a species of Laxmannia, a genus of tufted perennial herbs in the family Asparagaceae, subfamily Lomandroideae, which is endemic to Western Australia. From 0.03 to 0.1 m high, it grows on gravel and lateritic sand, and its white flowers may be seen from September to November.

items.name: Layia carnosa
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in spring under glass using a gritty, free-draining compost to prevent dampening off.
Plant out in late May in full sun, choosing your poorest, sandiest soil to mimic its dune habitat.
Water sparingly only during prolonged dry spells, as this coastal annual is highly drought-tolerant.
Protect young seedlings from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps in spring.
Leave faded flower heads to self-seed naturally in gravel gardens to ensure plants return next year.
items.description: Layia carnosa is a species of flowering plant in the family Asteraceae known by the common name beach tidytips, or beach layia. It is endemic to California, where it lives in coastal habitat. It is known from several areas of mostly fragmented or relict sand dune habitat, and it was listed as an endangered species in California. On March 31, 2022, the category was changed from endangered species to threatened species by the US Department of the Interior Fish and Wildlife Service.

items.name: Layia chrysanthemoides
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at three millimetres deep in April after the last frost to ensure light germination
Grow in free-draining sandy soil to prevent root rot during wet UK summers and avoid heavy clay
Water sparingly only during dry spells once established as this annual dislikes waterlogged soil
Sow alongside Calendula to attract hoverflies that naturally control aphids on delicate stems
Deadhead spent yellow-and-white daisy blooms weekly in July to prolong flowering until first frost
items.description: Layia chrysanthemoides is a species of flowering plant in the family Asteraceae known by the common name smooth tidytips, or smooth layia.

items.name: Layia discoidea
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at a depth of three millimetres in April once the risk of frost has passed.
Grow in poor well-drained sandy soil to mimic its native habitat and prevent root rot in UK rain.
Water sparingly only during prolonged dry spells as this annual is highly drought-tolerant.
Position in full south-facing sun to encourage the unusual rayless yellow flower heads to bloom.
Sow alongside low-growing thyme or sedum to provide structural support for its sprawling stems.
items.description: Layia discoidea is a rare species of flowering plant in the family Asteraceae known by the common name rayless tidytips, or rayless layia.

items.name: Layia elegans
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in April directly into well-drained, gritty soil at a shallow depth of just three millimetres
Position in your garden's absolute fullest sun to prevent the weak, floppy stems common in UK damp
Water seedlings sparingly only during dry spells to avoid the root rot caused by typical wet summers
Deadhead faded daisy-like blooms weekly through July and August to prolong the yellow flowering season
Sow alongside poached egg plants to attract hoverflies that naturally control aphids on your Layia
items.description: Layia elegans is a species of flowering plants in the family Asteraceae. It is found in California.

items.name: Layia fremontii
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at three millimetres deep in April once the risk of UK spring frost has passed
Grow in sharply draining gritty soil to prevent root rot during wet British summer spells
Water sparingly only during dry spells as this California native dislikes soggy UK conditions
Deadhead faded yellow daisy flowers weekly in July and August to prolong the summer blooming period
Sow alongside companion plants like Eschscholzia californica to mimic a dry meadow aesthetic
items.description: Layia fremontii is a species of flowering plant in the family Asteraceae known by the common name Frémont's tidytips. Both its common name, and its specific epithet are derived from John C. Frémont.

items.name: Layia glandulosa
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in April directly into well-drained, gritty soil to avoid root disturbance from potting.
Choose a south-facing border with maximum sun to mimic its native dry, Californian habitat.
Water sparingly once established, only during prolonged dry spells to prevent root rot in UK damp.
Deadhead spent daisy-like blooms weekly in July and August to prolong the summer flowering window.
Watch for slugs and snails on young spring seedlings, using organic grit barriers to protect them.
items.description: Layia glandulosa is a species of flowering plant in the family Asteraceae known by the common names whitedaisy tidytips and white layia. It is native to western North America south from central Washington (state) to Baja California and east to Utah and Arizona, where it is common in a number of habitat types.

items.name: Layia heterotricha
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at three millimetres deep in April after the last frost to ensure germination.
Grow in free-draining sandy soil to prevent root rot during wet, cool United Kingdom summers.
Water only during prolonged dry spells once established, as this annual dislikes waterlogged soil.
Position in full south-facing sun to maximise the opening of the daisy-like yellow-tipped blooms.
Deadhead spent flowers weekly in July and August to prolong the display of scented blossoms.
items.description: Layia heterotricha is a species of flowering plant in the family Asteraceae known by the common name pale yellow tidytips, or pale yellow layia.

items.name: Layia hieracioides
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at a depth of three millimetres in April to avoid late UK spring frosts.
Grow in free-draining sandy loam to prevent root rot during wet British summer spells.
Water only when the top five centimetres of soil is dry to mimic its native drought tolerance.
Deadhead spent yellow blooms weekly in July and August to prolong the summer flowering display.
Sow alongside English lavender to attract pollinators while keeping the soil nutrient levels low.
items.description: Layia hieracioides is a species of flowering plant in the family Asteraceae known by the common name tall tidytips, or tall layia.

items.name: Jones' tidytips
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at three millimetres deep in April after the last frost to ensure germination.
Grow in sharply draining sandy soil to prevent root rot during wet United Kingdom summer spells.
Water sparingly once established, allowing the top five centimetres of soil to dry out completely.
Position in the brightest, most south-facing spot of your garden to maximise daily sun exposure.
Deadhead spent yellow-tipped daisy flowers weekly in July and August to prolong the blooming season.
items.description: Layia jonesii is a species of flowering plant in the family Asteraceae known by the common name Jones' tidytips, or Jones' layia.

items.name: Comanche Point tidytips
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at three millimetres deep in April once the risk of spring frost has passed.
Grow in sharply draining, gritty soil to prevent root rot during wet United States-like UK summers.
Water only during prolonged dry spells, letting the top five centimetres of soil dry out completely.
Sow alongside companion plants like English lavender to attract pollinators and deter garden pests.
Deadhead faded daisy-like flowers weekly in July and August to prolong the summer blooming period.
items.description: Layia leucopappa is a rare species of flowering plant in the family Asteraceae known by the common name Comanche Point tidytips, or Comanche Point layia.

items.name: Layia munzii
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at three millimetres deep in April after the last frost for best germination.
Grow in sharply draining sandy soil to prevent root rot during wet United Kingdom summer spells.
Water sparingly only when the top five centimetres of soil is dry to mimic its arid native habitat.
Protect young spring shoots from slugs and snails using beer traps or organic wool pellets.
Position in your sunniest south-facing border to maximise the daily opening of the daisy flowers.
items.description: Layia munzii is a rare species of flowering plant in the family Asteraceae known by the common name Munz's tidytips, or Munz's layia.

items.name: Layia pentachaeta
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at three millimetres deep in April once the risk of spring frost has passed
Grow in poor to moderately fertile sandy soil to prevent floppy growth in wet UK summers
Water sparingly only during prolonged dry spells to avoid root rot in damp British climates
Deadhead spent yellow blooms weekly in July and August to prolong the flowering season
Sow alongside English lavender to attract pollinators while keeping the soil dry and drained
items.description: Layia pentachaeta is a species of flowering plant in the family Asteraceae known by the common name Sierra tidytips, or Sierra layia.

items.name: Layia platyglossa
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds thinly in late spring directly into well-drained soil at a shallow depth of three millimetres
Grow in full sun and poor soil to prevent the plants from becoming floppy and producing fewer flowers
Water seedlings weekly until established then only during prolonged dry spells to avoid root rot
Deadhead spent yellow-and-white blooms regularly to prolong the flowering season through to autumn
Protect young shoots from slugs using organic grit barriers during damp UK spring weather conditions
items.description: Layia platyglossa, commonly called coastal tidytips, is an annual wildflower of the family Asteraceae, native to western North America.

items.name: Layia septentrionalis
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in April 1.5mm deep directly into well-drained, gritty soil in full, south-facing sun.
Water seedlings sparingly once a week, allowing the top 5cm of soil to dry out completely.
Protect young spring shoots from slugs using organic wool pellets or beer traps in damp weather.
Deadhead spent yellow-tipped daisy flowers weekly in July to prolong the summer blooming period.
Sow alongside California poppies in poor, sandy soil to replicate its dry native habitat.
items.description: Layia septentrionalis is an uncommon species of flowering plant in the family Asteraceae known by the common name Colusa tidytips, or Colusa layia.

items.name: Lecocarpus darwinii
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at three millimetres deep in early spring under glass with gentle bottom heat.
Grow in free-draining gritty loam to prevent root rot during wet, cool British summer periods.
Water only when the top two centimetres of soil are dry, as this Galapagos native hates wet feet.
Position in your sunniest south-facing border or a container to maximise scarce UK summer warmth.
Protect young plants from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers during damp spring nights.
items.description: Lecocarpus darwinii is a species of flowering plant in the family Asteraceae. It is found only in Galápagos Islands, Ecuador.

items.name: Lecocarpus pinnatifidus
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at three millimetres deep under glass in April to combat cool UK spring soil.
Water the base weekly to keep soil moist but never waterlogged to prevent root rot in damp climates.
Position in the sunniest south-facing border to maximise heat for this rare Galapagos native.
Protect young plants from slugs using beer traps during wet British spring and summer nights.
Grow in free-draining sandy loam mixed with grit to mimic its natural volcanic island habitat.
items.description: Lecocarpus pinnatifidus, the wing-fruited leocarpus, is a species of flowering plant in the family Asteraceae. It is found in only on the Floreana Island of the Galápagos Islands.

items.name: Leptarrhena pyrolifolia
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist, acidic peat-free compost mixed with grit to mimic Scottish highland bog conditions.
Position in partial shade to protect the evergreen leaves from scorching during dry UK summer heat.
Water with harvested rainwater rather than tap water to maintain the low soil pH this alpine needs.
Propagate by dividing the creeping rhizomes in early autumn before the first frost wet weather sets in.
Watch for vine weevil larvae in container-grown plants during damp British autumn and winter months.
items.description: Leptarrhena pyrolifolia is a species of flowering plants belonging to the family Saxifragaceae. It is the sole species in genus Leptarrhena.

items.name: Leptarrhena pyrolifolia
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist acidic humus-rich soil mimicking UK bog gardens using a mix of peat-free compost and sand
Position in partial shade to prevent the evergreen leathery foliage from scorching in midday sun
Water frequently during dry UK summers to keep the soil consistently damp but never waterlogged
Propagate by dividing the creeping rhizomes in early spring just as new growth begins to emerge
Grow alongside Astilbe or Primula japonica in a damp woodland border for compatible moisture needs
items.description: Leptarrhena pyrolifolia is a species of flowering plants belonging to the family Saxifragaceae. It is the sole species in genus Leptarrhena.

items.name: Sand lily
items.growersTips:
Plant in sharply draining grit-rich soil to prevent winter wet rot in damp UK climates.
Position in full sun in a raised bed or rockery to mimic its native dry mountain habitat.
Plant the fleshy roots five centimetres deep in autumn while the plant is dormant.
Withhold all watering during its summer dormant phase to prevent the crown from rotting.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers.
items.description: Leucocrinum montanum, commonly known as the common starlily, sandlily, or mountain lily, is the only species in the monotypic genus Leucocrinum, which was placed in the asparagus family in 2009. It is a common and widespread early spring wildflower on the shortgrass prairie, the central and southern Rocky Mountains, and the Intermountain West.

items.name: Leucophyta brownii
items.growersTips:
Plant in gritty, free-draining soil to prevent winter root rot in wet UK autumns.
Water sparingly, allowing the top two inches of compost to dry completely between drinks.
Position in full south-facing sun to maintain the intense silver foliage colour.
Trim lightly in midsummer to keep the cushion shape compact and prevent leggy growth.
Pair with purple-flowered heathers in autumn containers for a striking colour contrast.
items.description: Leucophyta is a plant genus which is endemic to Australia. The genus was first formally described by botanist Robert Brown in 1818.

items.name: Leucopogon collinus
items.growersTips:
Plant in acidic sandy loam with ericaceous compost to mimic their native dry Australian heathland.
Water with rainwater rather than tap water to keep soil pH low and prevent chlorosis in UK gardens.
Grow in pots to move indoors to a cold greenhouse before the first wet autumn frosts hit the UK.
Prune lightly immediately after spring flowering to maintain shape without cutting into old wood.
Ensure excellent drainage by mixing grit into the soil to prevent root rot during wet UK winters.
items.description: Leucopogon is a genus of about 150–160 species of shrubs or small trees in the family Ericaceae, in the section of that family formerly treated as the separate family Epacridaceae. They are native to Australia, New Zealand, New Caledonia, the western Pacific Islands and Malaysia, with the greatest species diversity in the south-west of Western Australia. Plants in this genus have leaves with a few more or less parallel veins, and tube-shaped flowers usually with a white beard inside.

items.name: Pau ferro
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in April at a depth of two centimeters using bottom heat to overcome UK cold.
Plant out in June after the last frost in a south-facing border with free-draining sandy soil.
Water deeply once a week at the base during dry summer spells to establish the taproot system.
Pinch out the growing tips in early July to encourage a bushier habit and more summer flowers.
Watch for glasshouse red spider mite when starting young plants under glass in early spring.
items.description: Libidibia is a genus of flowering plants in the family Fabaceae. It includes seven species of trees and shrubs native to the tropical Americas, ranging from northern Mexico to northern Argentina. Typical habitats include seasonally-dry tropical forest and scrub, thorn forest, and savanna woodland. It belongs to the subfamily Caesalpinioideae.

items.name: Pau ferro
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender Brazilian tree in a large pot so you can move it indoors before the first autumn frost
Plant in free-draining loam mixed with thirty percent grit to prevent root rot during wet UK winters
Water deeply only when the top five centimetres of soil dries out, reducing to monthly in winter
Prune lightly in late spring after new growth starts to maintain shape and remove any frost damage
Position in your sunniest south-facing spot or conservatory to maximise heat and mimic its homeland
items.description: Libidibia ferrea, formerly Caesalpinia ferrea, and commonly known as Brazilian ironwood, leopardtree or jucá, is a tree found in Brazil.

items.name: Libidibia paraguariensis
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in April at a depth of two centimeters using a heated propagator to boost warmth.
Grow in free-draining sandy loam enriched with grit to prevent winter root rot in damp UK soils.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells, allowing the top five centimeters to dry fully.
Position in your warmest south-facing border or against a brick wall to maximize limited UK sun.
Sow alongside nasturtiums to naturally deter aphids and blackfly from attacking the young foliage.
items.description:
Libidibia paraguariensis is a species of legume in the family Fabaceae.
It is found in Argentina, Bolivia, Brazil, and Paraguay.
It is threatened by habitat loss.
Guayacaú negro is used for timber in several Latin American countries, especially Argentina and Paraguay. Commercially it is marketed as Argentinian brown ebony, mistakenly as Brazilian ebony, and as a family group as partridgewood. The end use for this timber is typically high-end exotic hardwood flooring, cabinetry and turnings.

items.name: Lilieae
items.growersTips:
Plant Lilium bulbs in autumn at three times their depth to protect them from winter frost and wind.
Apply organic mulch in spring to keep roots cool and damp while keeping the foliage in UK sun.
Handpick bright red lily beetles and their grubs from spring onwards to prevent total defoliation.
Grow lilies in pots of ericaceous compost if your UK garden soil is alkaline to prevent yellowing.
Cut spent flower stems back to the base only in autumn after the foliage has turned completely brown.
items.description: The Lilieae are a monophyletic tribe of monocotyledon perennial, herbaceous mainly bulbous flowering plants in the lily family (Liliaceae).

items.name: Lilioideae
items.growersTips:
Plant Lilium bulbs in autumn at three times their depth in well-drained, acidic soil to avoid rot.
Handpick bright red lily beetles and their sticky larvae from April onwards to prevent defoliation.
Water container-grown lilies deeply from the base, keeping the compost moist but never waterlogged.
Apply a thick mulch of composted bark in winter to protect Fritillaria bulbs from hard UK frosts.
Stake tall Cardiocrinum stems early in spring using bamboo canes to withstand strong UK winds.
items.description: The Lilioideae are a subfamily of monocotyledonous perennial, herbaceous mainly bulbous flowering plants in the lily family, Liliaceae. They are found predominantly in the temperate and colder regions of the Northern Hemisphere, particularly East Asia and North America. The subfamily includes two tribes. They are of economic importance, particularly the lilies and tulips.

items.name: Loa kèn trắng
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs at three times their depth in acidic soil for Asiatic and alkaline for Madonna lilies.
Water deeply at the base in early morning to prevent botrytis blight in damp UK summer weather.
Handpick red lily beetles and their grubs from April onwards to protect emerging spring foliage.
Keep lily pots in a sheltered spot over wet UK winters to prevent the bulbs from rotting in cold mud.
Cut stems back to ground level only in autumn after the foliage has turned completely yellow.
items.description: Lilium is a genus of herbaceous flowering plants growing from bulbs, all with large and often prominent flowers. Lilies are a group of flowering plants which are important in culture and literature in much of the world. Most species are native to the Northern Hemisphere and their range is temperate climates and extends into the subtropics. Many other plants have "lily" in their common names, but do not belong to the same genus and are therefore not true lilies. True lilies are known to be highly toxic to cats.

items.name: Mountain lily
items.growersTips:
Plant in deep pots or borders at least 15 to 20cm deep in ericaceous compost as they are lime-haters.
Provide shade at the roots using low-growing companion plants while keeping the flower heads in sun.
Water with rainwater rather than tap water to maintain the acidic soil conditions they require to thrive.
Apply a thick layer of organic mulch in autumn to protect the bulbs from wet UK winter rot.
Watch for red lily beetles from spring onwards, removing them and their larvae by hand immediately.
items.description: Lilium auratum is one of the true lilies. It is native to Japan and is sometimes called the golden-rayed lily or the goldband lily.

items.name: Lilium bolanderi
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs in autumn at a depth of 10cm in gritty, ericaceous soil to mimic its native habitat.
Position in partial shade with its roots kept cool and damp while its head reaches into the sun.
Water with rainwater to keep soil moist in summer but ensure sharp drainage to prevent winter rot.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.
Avoid disturbing the roots once planted as this species resents transplanting and takes time to settle.
items.description: Lilium bolanderi is a rare North American species of plants in the lily family, known by the common name Bolander's lily. It is native to northwestern California and southwestern Oregon.

items.name: Brown's lily
items.growersTips:
Plant Lilium brownii bulbs 15-20cm deep in acidic to neutral soil to encourage strong stem roots.
In the wet UK winter, plant bulbs on their sides on a bed of sharp grit to prevent crown rot.
Watch for red lily beetles from April onwards and hand-pick them to protect the delicate foliage.
Keep the bulb in shade using low companion plants like hostas while keeping the flower head in sun.
Do not cut back yellowing stems until late autumn to allow the bulb to store energy for winter.
items.description: Lilium brownii is a species of lily native to mainland China, Hong Kong, Kinmen and Matsu Islands as well as northern and central Vietnam and Kachin of Myanmar. Its common names include Hong Kong lily and Brown's lily.

items.name: Lilium brownii viridulum
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs in autumn at least 15cm deep in acidic to neutral soil to protect stems from UK frosts.
Incorporate plenty of leafmould and grit to ensure excellent drainage in wet British winters.
Position in a spot where the base and roots are shaded by low shrubs but the flowers get morning sun.
Guard emerging spring shoots diligently from red lily beetles and slugs using organic nematodes.
Water thoroughly during the active summer growing season but keep the bulbs dry during winter dormancy.
items.description: Lilium brownii var. viridulum is a variety of Lilium brownii native to China.

items.name: Lilium catesbaei
items.growersTips:
Grow this bog lily in a highly acidic, nutrient-poor mix of wet peat moss and horticultural sand.
Keep the pot sitting in a shallow tray of rainwater year-round to mimic its native wetland habitat.
Provide full sun but protect the pot from freezing solid by overwintering it in a cold greenhouse.
Plant the small bulb very shallowly, with the nose sitting just below the soil surface.
Watch out for scarlet lily beetles and their larvae, removing them by hand immediately.
items.description: Lilium catesbaei, commonly known as Catesby's lily, pine lily, leopard lily, tiger lily, or southern-red lily is a species of lily native to the coastal plain of the American Southeast, from southeast Virginia to Florida, and west to Louisiana.

items.name: Lilium cernuum
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs in autumn at a depth of fifteen centimetres in gritty, sharply draining acidic soil.
Position in a spot that receives morning sun but keeps the bulb and roots shaded by low shrubs.
Water moderately during the spring growing season but keep the soil almost dry throughout winter.
Apply a thick layer of organic mulch in November to protect the shallow bulbs from severe UK frosts.
Check emerging spring shoots daily for scarlet lily beetles and handpick them to prevent damage.
items.description: Lilium cernuum is a species of lily native to Korea, the Primorye region of Russia, and northeastern China.

items.name: Lilium columbianum
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs in autumn at a depth of fifteen centimetres in moist but very well-drained acidic soil.
Position in dappled shade or mimicking woodland edges to keep the bulb cool and the flowers in sun.
Water weekly during dry spring spells but keep soil barely damp in winter to prevent bulb rot.
Apply organic mulch annually in spring to mimic natural forest leaf litter and retain acidity.
Search daily for red lily beetles and their larvae from April onwards to protect the foliage.
items.description: Lilium columbianum is a lily native to western North America. It is also known as the Columbia lily, Columbia tiger lily, or simply tiger lily.

items.name: Lilium concolor
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs in autumn at three times their depth in gritty, sharply draining acidic to neutral soil.
Water moderately in spring and summer, keeping the soil damp but never waterlogged to prevent rot.
Check regularly for bright red lily beetles and their larvae from April onwards, removing by hand.
Position in full sun to partial shade, keeping the base shaded by low-growing companion plants.
Apply a thick layer of dry mulch in winter to protect the bulbs from excessive UK winter wetness.
items.description: Lilium concolor is a species of flowering plant in the lily family which occurs naturally in China, Japan, Korea and Russia. Its relationship with other species is not clear, although it has some similarities to Lilium pumilum.

items.name: Lilium formosanum
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs 15cm deep in acidic to neutral, well-drained soil to protect them from UK winter frosts.
Sow seeds in spring as this fast-growing lily can flower in its first year from seed in the UK.
Apply a thick organic mulch in November to protect the bulb crown from wet and freezing UK winters.
Handpick red lily beetles and their grubs from spring onwards to prevent total foliage defoliation.
Grow in pots using ericaceous compost to easily move them under cover during severe winter freezes.
items.description: Lilium formosanum, also known as the Formosa lily or Taiwanese lily, is a plant species in the lily family, endemic to Taiwan. It is closely related to the Easter lily found in the Ryukyu Islands of Japan, eastern and northern Taiwan. Both species are cultivated for their showy, trumpet-shaped flowers. Lilium formosanum has become naturalized in scattered locations in Africa, Australia, and the Americas.

items.name: Lilium grayi
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs in autumn at a depth of 15cm in acidic, humus-rich soil that mimics wet UK woodland.
Keep the soil constantly moist but never waterlogged, especially during dry British summer spells.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.
Position in dappled shade or morning sun to keep the delicate red-orange blooms from bleaching.
Leave the flower stems to die back naturally in autumn to return vital nutrients to the bulb.
items.description: Lilium grayi is a perennial plant that is endemic to the eastern US states of North Carolina, Virginia, and Tennessee, growing in moist, acid soil in the Appalachian Mountains on higher elevation meadows, bogs, and seeps. The plant was introduced to Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew in 1890 and was featured in the Kew Bulletin in 1892.

items.name: Lilium humboldtii
items.growersTips:
Plant the bulbs deeply at twenty centimetres in autumn to protect them from hard UK winter frosts.
Grow in dappled shade under deciduous trees to mimic their native woodland edge habitat in the UK.
Provide acidic to neutral soil with leafmould and grit to ensure the sharp winter drainage they need.
Water deeply during active spring growth but keep the soil almost dry once the stems die back in autumn.
Handpick red lily beetles daily from April onwards to protect the emerging foliage from devastation.
items.description: Lilium humboldtii, or Humboldt's lily, is a species of lily native to the US state of California and the Mexican state of Baja California. It is named after naturalist and explorer Alexander von Humboldt. It is native to the South High Cascade Range, High Sierra Nevada, south Outer South Coast Ranges, and the Santa Monica Mountains and others in Southern California, growing at elevations from 600 metres (2,000 ft) to 1,200 metres (3,900 ft).

items.name: Lilium iridollae
items.growersTips:
Grow in wet acidic peat-free compost mixed with sand to mimic its native boggy seepage habitat
Keep soil consistently moist but never stagnant using rainwater rather than hard UK tap water
Plant bulbs shallowly with only two centimetres of soil covering the top of the bulb scales
Provide dappled shade to keep the soil cool while allowing the flower stems to reach for the sun
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps
items.description: Lilium iridollae is a species of "true lily". A perennial forb, it is one of nine known Lilium species native to the eastern North America. In 1940, this species was discovered by Mary Henry in its habitat. She named the lily in reference to a "pot of gold at the end of the rainbow".

items.name: Sasa yuri
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs 15cm deep in acidic, ericaceous soil as this woodland lily cannot tolerate any lime.
Provide dappled shade and shelter from strong winds, mimicking a British woodland edge environment.
Keep soil consistently moist but never waterlogged, especially during wet UK winters to avoid rot.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and red lily beetles using organic nematodes or handpicking.
Mulch annually with leaf mould in autumn to replicate natural forest debris and keep roots cool.
items.description: Lilium japonicum, the bamboo lily, is a species of flowering plant in the family Liliaceae. It is native to central and southern Japan. A cold-hardy bulbous geophyte growing to 50 to 100 cm tall, it is often found in association with bamboos of the genus Sasa, which it resembles in its stems and leaves. It is used in Shinto rites.

items.name: Lilium kesselringianum
items.growersTips:
Plant the bulbs deep at 15-20cm in autumn to encourage stem roots and protect from UK winter frosts.
Provide moist but sharp-draining, neutral to slightly alkaline soil, adding grit to heavy clay.
Position in dappled shade or morning sun to mimic its native Caucasian woodland edge habitat.
Apply a thick leaf-mould mulch annually in spring to keep the bulb cool and mimic forest soils.
Watch out for red lily beetles from April onwards, hand-picking them immediately to prevent damage.
items.description: Lilium kesselringianum is a large herbaceous member of the lily family. It is native to North and South Caucasus as well as northern Turkey. It grows from sea level along the Black Sea up into the mountains to subalpine level on forest edges, in brushlands, and in grassy meadows.

items.name: Lilium maculatum
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs in autumn at three times their depth in acidic to neutral, very well-drained gritty soil.
Position pots in full sun but shade the base with low-growing companion plants like hardy geraniums.
Handpick red lily beetles and their sticky larvae daily from early spring to protect the foliage.
Water thoroughly during the active summer growing season but keep bulbs almost dry throughout winter.
Apply a thick mulch of composted bark in late autumn to protect shallow roots from hard UK frosts.
items.description: Lilium maculatum  is a plant in the lily family native to Japan.

items.name: Lilium maritimum
items.growersTips:
Plant the bulbs in autumn at a depth of ten centimetres in acidic, humus-rich, well-draining soil.
Keep the soil constantly moist but never waterlogged, mimicking its native wet-meadow habitat.
Grow in partial shade to mimic coastal fog, protecting the delicate red blooms from hot midday sun.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.
Overwinter in pots of ericaceous compost if your garden soil is heavy clay or naturally alkaline.
items.description: Lilium maritimum is a species of lily known by the common name coast lily. It is endemic to California, where it is known only from the coastline north of San Francisco. It formerly occurred south of San Francisco, but these occurrences have all been extirpated. The species is now restricted to the North Coast from Marin County to Del Norte County, and is most common in Mendocino County. It grows in the California coastal prairie habitat, coniferous forests, and bogs amongst Drosera species.

items.name: Martagon lily
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs 15-20cm deep in autumn in well-drained, alkaline to neutral soil with added leaf mould.
Position in dappled shade or woodland edges, as they dislike the hot afternoon UK summer sun.
Keep soil moist but never waterlogged, watering deeply during dry spring spells before flowering.
Hand-pick red lily beetles and their grubs from April onwards to prevent total foliage ruin.
Leave the faded flower stems to die back naturally in autumn to feed the bulb for next summer.
items.description: Lilium martagon, the martagon lily or Turk's cap lily, is a Eurasian species of lily. It has a widespread native region extending from Portugal east through Europe and Asia as far east as Mongolia.

items.name: Lilium medeoloides
items.growersTips:
Plant in partial shade mimicking woodland edges using leafmould to keep soil acidic and moist.
Sow seeds in autumn in cold frames as they require winter chilling to trigger germination.
Plant bulbs deep at fifteen centimetres in well-drained grit to protect from UK winter wet.
Handpick scarlet lily beetles daily from April to prevent devastating foliage damage.
Water with rainwater rather than tap water to maintain the low soil pH this lily requires.
items.description: Lilium medeoloides is an East Asian herb in the lily family. It is native to southeast China, Jeju-do in Korea, Japan and eastern Russia, where it grows in forests and on grassy and rocky subalpine areas.

items.name: Lilium michauxii
items.growersTips:
Plant this bulb in autumn at a depth of fifteen centimetres in acidic, ericaceous soil mix.
Incorporate plenty of leafmould and grit to mimic its native woodland floor in wet UK winters.
Position in partial shade where the delicate orange blooms are sheltered from strong midday sun.
Water with rainwater to keep soil damp but never soggy, especially during dry summer spells.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and red lily beetles using organic nematodes or grit.
items.description: Lilium michauxii, commonly known as the Carolina lily, is a wildflower native to the southeastern United States, thriving in dry, sandy soils of upland forests and ridges. It is the only fragrant lily species native east of the Rocky Mountains. Known for its vibrant orange to red flowers adorned with dark spots, the Carolina lily blooms from July to October, providing nectar for pollinators such as butterflies.

items.name: Lilium michiganense
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs 15cm deep in autumn to protect them from hard UK winter frosts and support tall stems.
Incorporate leaf mould and grit to mimic native wet-meadow soil that drains well but stays damp.
Water consistently during dry spring spells to keep the soil moist but never waterlogged or soggy.
Apply organic mulch annually in spring to keep the bulb roots cool and mimic woodland floor cover.
Handpick bright red lily beetles and their larvae from spring onwards to prevent leaf defoliation.
items.description: Lilium michiganense is a species of true lily commonly referred to as the Michigan lily. It is a wildflower present in prairie habitats in the Great Lakes and Upper Mississippi Valley regions of the United States and Canada, from South Dakota through Ontario to New York, south to Georgia and Oklahoma.

items.name: Lilium nanum
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs 8cm deep in gritty, humus-rich, acidic soil to mimic their native Himalayan scree.
Position in a cool, north-facing rockery or raised bed to prevent summer soil from overheating.
Keep soil consistently moist during spring growth but ensure sharp winter drainage to prevent rot.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic pellets or copper tape.
Grow in pots of ericaceous compost mixed with perlite if your garden soil is alkaline or heavy clay.
items.description: Lilium nanum is a species belonging to the lily family (Liliaceae). The species is widespread throughout the Himalayas and is one of the genus's smallest species. Lilium nanum was discovered in 1845 on a journey by Prince Waldemar of Prussia. The name was first described in 1860.

items.name: Lilium nepalense
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs 15cm deep in acidic, humus-rich soil to mimic their native Himalayan woodland habitat.
Water generously during active spring growth but keep the soil almost dry during winter dormancy.
Grow in pots to easily move them under a cold frame or unheated greenhouse to prevent winter rot.
Provide deep shade for the roots using low ferns while allowing the stems to grow into morning sun.
Watch for the stoloniferous habit as stems often emerge a distance away from where you planted them.
items.description: Lilium nepalense, the lily of Nepal, is an Asian plant species in the lily family. It is native to the Himalayas and nearby regions: northern Thailand, northern Myanmar, Assam, Bhutan, Sikkim, Nepal, Uttarakhand, Tibet, and Yunnan. It can be found growing on wet forest borders at 1,200 to 3,000 m.

items.name: Lilium nobilissimum
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs in autumn at a depth of fifteen centimetres in acidic, ericaceous compost to avoid rot.
Provide winter protection in the UK by overwintering pots in a cold greenhouse or frost-free shed.
Water thoroughly during active growth but keep the soil barely moist during the winter dormancy.
Apply organic mulch in spring to keep the shallow roots cool and moist during dry UK summers.
Check daily for bright red lily beetles from spring onwards and remove them by hand immediately.
items.description: Lilium nobilissimum is a species of plant in the lily family Liliaceae. Endemic to the island of Kuchinoshima in Japan's Kagoshima Prefecture, it grows on the cliffs of the southwestern portion of the island. In floral breeding circles, the plant was used for the production of upright oriental lilies. Lilium nobilissimum was first described as a form of Lilium japonicum by Tomitaro Makino in 1902; it was elevated to full species status in 1914.

items.name: Lilium occidentale
items.growersTips:
Plant the bulbs 15cm deep in autumn in humus-rich, acidic soil to mimic their native boggy habitat.
Keep the soil consistently moist but never waterlogged, especially during the active spring growth.
Position in a sheltered spot with dappled shade to protect delicate stems from strong UK winds.
Apply a thick mulch of leafmould or composted pine needles annually in spring to maintain acidity.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic barriers or beer traps.
items.description: Lilium occidentale is a rare North American species of lily known by the common name western lily. Its species name 'Occidentale' means 'westernmost' and refers to its location along the West Coast. It is native to northwestern California and southwestern Oregon. It grows in coastal prairie habitat, swamps and stagnant bogs with Drosera species, bluffs and sandy cliffs, and seaside spruce forests. This rare wildflower is limited in distribution and directly endangered by a number of environmental factors. It is a federally listed endangered species and it is listed as endangered by the states

items.name: Lilium oxypetalum
items.growersTips:
Plant this alpine lily in acidic to neutral, humus-rich soil that mimics a cool Scottish scree.
Sow bulbs 8cm deep in autumn, surrounded by sharp grit to prevent winter rot in wet UK climates.
Position in partial shade with cool roots, using low ferns or dwarf rhododendrons as companions.
Water regularly in spring and summer to keep soil moist but never waterlogged during active growth.
Check daily in spring for red lily beetles and their larvae to protect the delicate yellow blooms.
items.description:
Lilium oxypetalum is a small to medium member of the Liliaceae family which grows to a height of 20–30 cm. It is native to the N. W. Himalayas.
It grows as a single stem from a bulb, preferring a cool, shady position in moist, acid soil. The green stem is tinged with purple and supports a scattering of linear to lanceolate leaves, sometimes in a whorl beneath the flowers. The leaves are up to 7 cm long. The yellow, semi-pendant, unscented flowers are produced in early summer in ones or twos on slender stems. The flowers are shaped like a shallow bowl, up to 5 cm across and have a scattering of

items.name: Lilium papilliferum
items.growersTips:
Plant this rare Idaho native bulb 10cm deep in extremely sharp-draining, gritty, alkaline soil.
Water sparingly only during spring growth, then keep the bulb completely dry during summer dormancy.
Protect the delicate, narrow foliage from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers in spring.
Grow in pots under a cold glasshouse or cold frame to shield the bulb from wet UK winter rot.
Position in full sun but keep the pot shaded or mulched to mimic its cool desert-basin root run.
items.description: Lilium papilliferum is a species of the lily genus (Lilium) in the Oriental hybrids division (VII). The species, about which little is known, has only been collected a few times and is native to north-central and south-central China. Its deep dark red flower color is unique in the genus.

items.name: Lilium pardalinum subsp. pitkinense
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs in autumn at a depth of fifteen centimetres in neutral to acid moisture-retentive soil
Position in partial shade mimicking its native boggy woodland edge to prevent the soil drying out
Water consistently during dry UK spring spells to keep the soil constantly damp but never waterlogged
Apply a thick annual mulch of leafmould in winter to mimic forest floor conditions and retain moisture
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps
items.description: Lilium pardalinum subsp. pitkinense, the Pitkin Marsh lily, is an endangered perennial herb of the family Liliaceae that is endemic to certain wetland areas in the northern California Coast Ranges of Sonoma County, California, United States. It is a subspecies of Lilium pardalinum.

items.name: Lilium pensylvanicum
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs in autumn at a depth of fifteen centimetres in acidic to neutral well-drained soil.
Keep soil consistently moist but never waterlogged during the active spring and summer growth.
Handpick bright red lily beetles and their larvae from leaves daily from early spring onwards.
Position pots in full sun but shade the base with low-growing violas to keep the bulbs cool.
Allow stems to die back completely in autumn before cutting them down to ground level in winter.
items.description: Lilium pensylvanicum is an Asian plant species of the family Liliaceae. Sometimes called the Siberian lily, it is native to a cold climate and needs frost in the winter. It is found in the wild form in Siberia, the Russian Far East, Mongolia, northeast China, Korea and Hokkaidō.

items.name: Lilium philadelphicum
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs in autumn at a depth of fifteen centimetres in acidic, sandy, very well-drained soil.
Water deeply once a week in dry spring weather but keep the soil dry during winter to prevent rot.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.
Do not cut back the stems until they have turned completely brown and died down in late autumn.
Grow in dappled shade alongside acid-loving heathers or ferns to keep the bulb roots cool and damp.
items.description: Lilium philadelphicum, also known as the wood lily, flame lily, Philadelphia lily, (wild) tiger lily, prairie lily, or western red lily, is a perennial species of lily native to North America.

items.name: Lilium philippinense
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs 15cm deep in autumn using grit at the base to prevent rot during wet UK winters.
Grow in pots of ericaceous compost as this species strictly requires acidic, lime-free soil.
Move pots to a frost-free greenhouse or cold frame from November to March to survive UK freezes.
Water with collected rainwater rather than tap water to maintain the essential low soil pH.
Handpick red lily beetles daily from April onwards to protect the delicate trumpet blooms.
items.description: Lilium philippinense, commonly known as the Benguet lily, or Philippine lily, is a lily native to Taiwan and to the Cordillera region, primarily to the province of Benguet, in the northern Philippines. This flower has several native names like us-usdong, kanyon and sabong ti bantay.

items.name: Lilium polyphyllum
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs 20cm deep in autumn to protect them from UK winter frosts and keep the roots cool.
Provide gritty, neutral to alkaline soil with leafmould to mimic their native Himalayan woodland.
Position in dappled shade under deciduous shrubs to shield delicate white flowers from midday sun.
Water moderately in spring but keep the soil almost dry during their dormant late summer period.
Check emerging shoots daily in spring for red lily beetles and handpick them to prevent defoliation.
items.description: Lilium polyphyllum is a species of lily endemic to montane environments in central Asia.

items.name: Lilium pyrenaicum
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs in autumn at a depth of 15cm in heavy, moisture-retentive clay soil that drains well.
Position in partial shade or north-facing borders to mimic its native cool Pyrenean woodland edge.
Handpick bright red lily beetles and their larvae daily from April to prevent total defoliation.
Apply an annual winter mulch of leafmould to keep the soil cool and acidic during hot UK summers.
Leave the pungent, musky-scented yellow flowers intact to set seed and naturalise in damp grass.
items.description: Lilium pyrenaicum is native to montane regions, mainly the Pyrenees, from Spain and eastwards, with the range extending into the Caucasus. It grows up to 1.3 m high. It bears up to 12 Turks-cap shaped flowers. These are yellow, orange or red, and has an unusual musky scent, which some people find unpleasant.

items.name: Lilium pyrophilum
items.growersTips:
Plant this rare wet-meadow lily in acidic, peat-free ericaceous compost mixed with plenty of grit.
Keep the soil constantly moist but free-draining, mimicking its native boggy seepage habitats.
Position the pot in full sun to partial shade but keep the compost cool by mulching with gravel.
Protect the emerging spring shoots from devastating scarlet lily beetles by hand-picking daily.
Overwinter the bulb in a cold greenhouse or cold frame to protect it from excessive winter wet.
items.description: Lilium pyrophilum, the sandhills lily or sandhills bog lily, is a North American species of plant in the lily family. It is endemic to the Sandhills region of southern Virginia, North Carolina and northern South Carolina, in the eastern United States.

items.name: Lilium rhodopeum
items.growersTips:
Plant this rare yellow lily in sharply draining neutral to slightly alkaline soil with added grit.
Position the bulb five inches deep in a spot with morning sun and light afternoon dappled shade.
Water moderately in spring but keep the soil relatively dry during its dormant late summer phase.
Protect the emerging spring shoots from red lily beetles by handpicking them off the foliage.
Grow in a raised bed or deep alpine pot to mimic its native Balkan mountain scree conditions.
items.description: Lilium rhodopeum is a European species of plants in the lily family. It is endemic to the Rhodopi Mountains of Bulgaria and Greece, where it is found in alpine meadows and on mountain slopes. It is as critically endangered and listed as an IUCN red list threatened species. This Balkan endemic can be found in Bulgaria and Greece where it is native to the Rhodopi mountains from which it takes it name.

items.name: Lilium rubescens
items.growersTips:
Plant this redwood lily bulb 15cm deep in acidic, leaf-mould enriched soil to mimic its forest home.
Provide dappled shade for the roots while allowing the flower stem to grow up into morning sunlight.
Water deeply during dry spring spells but keep the bulb virtually dry in winter to prevent rotting.
Protect emerging spring shoots from red lily beetles by hand-picking them daily in April and May.
Grow in a raised bed or sloped woodland border to ensure the rapid winter drainage this lily needs.
items.description: Lilium rubescens is an uncommon species of lily known by the common names redwood lily and chaparral lily. It is native to northwestern California and southwestern Oregon, where it is known from the Coast Ranges from Lane County to Santa Cruz Counties.

items.name: Lilium speciosum
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs 15-20cm deep in late autumn to allow stem roots to develop and anchor the tall stems.
Grow in ericaceous compost or acidic soil as this species cannot tolerate lime or alkaline conditions.
Position in partial shade with the base shaded by low shrubs to mimic its native woodland edge.
Watch for red lily beetles from spring onwards and hand-pick them immediately to prevent defoliation.
Keep soil consistently moist but never waterlogged during the active summer growing season.
items.description: Lilium speciosum is an East Asian species of plants in the lily family. It is native to southern Japan and southern China, where it can be found at elevations of 600–900 metres (2,000–3,000 ft). It is sometimes called the Japanese lily though there are other species with this common name.

items.name: Lilium superbum
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs in autumn at a depth of 15cm in moisture-retentive, humus-rich, acidic to neutral soil.
Position in a sheltered spot with the roots in cool shade and the flower heads in full morning sun.
Water deeply during dry UK summer spells to keep the soil consistently damp but never waterlogged.
Apply a thick annual mulch of leafmould or composted pine needles in spring to maintain soil acidity.
Handpick red lily beetles and their grubs daily from April onwards to prevent total defoliation.
items.description: Lilium superbum is a species of true lily native to the eastern and central regions of North America. Common names include Turk's cap lily, turban lily, swamp lily, lily royal, or American tiger lily. The native range of the species extends from southern New Hampshire, Massachusetts, and New York, west to Illinois, Missouri, and Arkansas, and south to Georgia, Alabama, Mississippi, and Florida.

items.name: Lilium tsingtauense
items.growersTips:
Plant this woodland lily in dappled shade to mimic its native forest home and prevent leaf scorch.
Plant bulbs deep at fifteen centimetres in humus-rich, acidic to neutral soil that drains freely.
Keep soil consistently moist but never waterlogged during the active spring and summer growth.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit or beer traps.
Leave the stems to die back naturally in autumn to return vital nutrients to the bulb for winter.
items.description: Lilium tsingtauense, also known as twilight lily, is an East Asian species of plants in the lily family. It is native to Korea and eastern China.

items.name: Lilium washingtonianum
items.growersTips:
Plant the bulbs deep at twenty centimetres in extremely free-draining, gritty, neutral to acid soil.
Position in dappled shade to mimic woodland edges, keeping the bulb cool and the flowers in sun.
Water moderately in spring but keep the soil almost dry during its dormant late summer period.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and red lily beetles using organic nematodes or grit.
Avoid moving established bulbs as this species resents root disturbance and takes years to recover.
items.description: Lilium washingtonianum is a North American plant species in the lily family. It is also known as the Washington lily, Shasta lily, or Mt. Hood lily. It is named after Martha Washington and not the state of Washington; in fact, as the northern range of the plant is near Mount Hood in Oregon, it does not naturally occur in the state of Washington.

items.name: Limbarda
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at a depth of two millimetres in free-draining sandy loam during early April
Water sparingly once a week only when the top five centimetres of soil has dried out completely
Position pots in full south-facing sun to mimic coastal cliffs and prevent damp winter root rot
Sow alongside sea lavender in gravel gardens to match natural salt-tolerant coastal conditions
Monitor young spring shoots closely for slug damage during typical wet UK April weather spells
items.description:
Limbarda is a genus of succulent, xerophytic plants in the daisy family.SpeciesLimbarda crithmoides (L.) Dumort. - - Mediterranean Region and British Isles
Limbarda salsoloides (Turcz.) Ikonn. - Mongoliaformerly included

items.name: Limnophila aquatica
items.growersTips:
Grow this tropical aquatic herb in a heated indoor aquarium as it cannot survive UK winter cold.
Plant stems two inches deep in nutrient-rich aquatic soil capped with gravel to prevent floating.
Provide intense LED lighting for ten hours daily to prevent the lower leaves from rotting away.
Prune the fast-growing stem tops weekly in summer using sharp aquascaping scissors to promote bushiness.
Inject carbon dioxide gas into the water to maintain the vibrant lime-green colour of the foliage.
items.description: Limnophila aquatica, known commonly as the giant ambulia, is a plant belonging to the family Plantaginaceae. Limnophila aquatica grows naturally in Asia, Sri Lanka and India and is characterised by its fine leaves and bushy, pine-like appearance. In the aquarium it grows best in medium or very high lighting, preferably in acidic conditions. It can grow to a height of 9-20 inches, and its width can vary from 3-6 inches.

items.name: Limnophila aromatica
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender herb in a heated greenhouse or indoor windowsill as it cannot survive UK winters.
Plant in a soil mix of acidic peat and sand kept constantly wet to mimic its native wetland habitat.
Provide at least six hours of direct supplemental grow lighting to maintain its purple leaf colour.
Pinch out the growing tips in late spring to encourage a bushier habit and prevent leggy growth.
Watch for aphids on new shoots during humid summer months and wash them off with a gentle water spray.
items.description: Limnophila aromatica, the rice paddy herb, is a tropical flowering plant in the family Plantaginaceae. It is native to Southeast Asia, where it flourishes in hot temperatures and grows most often in watery environments, particularly in flooded rice fields. It is called ngò ôm or ngò om or ngổ in Vietnam and used as an herb and also cultivated for use as an aquarium plant. The plant was introduced to North America in the 1970s due to Vietnamese immigration following the Vietnam War. It is called "ma om" (ម្អម) in Khmer. It is used in traditional Cambodian soup dishes and Southern Vietnamese cui

items.name: Limnophila repens
items.growersTips:
Grow in a heated indoor aquarium or warm greenhouse pond as this tropical herb cannot survive UK frost
Plant stems individually two centimetres deep in nutrient-rich aquatic soil using long tweezers
Prune the fast-growing stem tops weekly in summer to encourage bushy lateral growth and red leaves
Maintain high light levels and inject carbon dioxide to prevent the lower leaves from rotting away
Pair with slow-growing Cryptocoryne species to balance the tank layout and prevent nutrient spikes
items.description: Limnophila repens, the creeping marshweed, is a herbaceous plant belonging to the family Plantaginaceae. It grows up to 45 cm tall both in terrestrial and fresh water habitats. The plant has a strong aromatic smell. Stems are covered with fine hair. Leaves are subsessile opposite and oblong. Violet-pink(rarely yellow) flowers are axilary and solitary or in short racemes. Seeds are angular and brown. Flowering season: November to May.

items.name: Limnophila sessiliflora
items.growersTips:
Grow this aquatic herb submerged in a heated indoor aquarium as it cannot survive UK winter cold.
Plant stems individually spaced two centimeters apart in nutrient-rich aquarium soil to prevent rot.
Prune the fast-growing stems weekly from the top to encourage bushy lateral growth in your tank.
Provide high light and dose liquid carbon to prevent the delicate whorled leaves from shedding.
Keep water temperature between twenty and twenty-eight degrees Celsius using an aquarium heater.
items.description: Limnophila sessiliflora, known as dwarf ambulia, ambulis, and Asian marshweed is a flowering plant in the family Plantaginaceae, mostly found in southeast Asia.

items.name: Linaria algarviana
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds thinly in April directly into poor, well-drained soil to prevent floppy, weak stems.
Position in full sun and shelter from cold winds to mimic its native warm Portuguese coast.
Water sparingly only during prolonged dry spells, as this annual is highly susceptible to rot.
Watch for slugs and snails on young spring seedlings, protecting them with grit or beer traps.
Leave spent flower spikes in autumn to self-seed naturally for a display the following spring.
items.description: Linaria algarviana, commonly known as the Algarve toadflax, is a species of flowering plant in the family Plantaginaceae, endemic to the Algarve region of southern Portugal. It was first described by the Swiss botanist Édouard-Louis Chavannes in 1833.

items.name: Linaria alpina
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn on the surface of gritty, sharply draining soil to allow winter cold to break dormancy.
Position in full sun in a scree garden or wall crevice to mimic its native alpine gravel habitat.
Water sparingly only during dry spells to prevent root rot in the damp UK climate.
Leave faded flowers intact to allow the plant to self-seed freely and persist in your garden.
Protect young spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.
items.description: Linaria alpina, sometimes called alpine toadflax, is a purple-flowered plant native to mountainous areas of southern and central Europe. It belongs to the family Plantaginaceae family. It was first described by Carl Linnaeus, and given its exact name by Philip Miller.

items.name: Linaria amethystea
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds thinly in autumn or early spring directly into gritty, well-drained soil in full sun.
Cover seeds with just a very fine dusting of sharp sand as they need light to trigger germination.
Water seedlings sparingly only during dry spells to prevent root rot in damp UK spring weather.
Leave spent flower spikes in late summer to allow this annual to self-seed naturally for next year.
Grow alongside thyme or sedums in gravel gardens to provide the sharp drainage this species craves.
items.description: Linaria amethystea is a species of annual flowering plant in the family Plantaginaceae, native to the Iberian Peninsula and northwest Africa. It grows primarily in temperate biomes in Portugal, Spain, Morocco and Western Sahara.

items.name: Linaria arenaria
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn or early spring in a gritty, free-draining sandy loam to mimic coastal dunes.
Sow seeds shallowly at a depth of two millimetres and do not cover them, as they require light to germinate.
Position in the sunniest spot of your garden, such as a south-facing gravel bed or rockery.
Water seedlings sparingly during dry spells and avoid any watering once the plants are established.
Leave the faded flower spikes intact at the end of summer to allow self-seeding for next year.
items.description: Linaria arenaria, sometimes called sand toadflax or French toadflax, is a yellow-flowered member of the genus Linaria. It is found in sand-dunes and sandy grassland in western France, north-west Spain and Portugal and is thus a psammophyte plant. It is found casually in England and reliably at two sites. One is Braunton Burrows in north Devon where it was planted around 1893 and continues to grow, and the other, since 2004, is in north Somerset.

items.name: Linaria bipartita
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds thinly outdoors in April at a depth of three millimetres in a sunny, well-drained spot.
Water seedlings lightly twice a week until established, then only during prolonged dry UK summers.
Shear back the stems by half after the first flush of flowers in July to encourage a second bloom.
Sow alongside Nigella damascena to provide physical support for the slender, floppy Linaria stems.
Watch for slugs and snails on young spring shoots by using beer traps or organic wool pellets.
items.description: Linaria bipartita is a species of flowering plant in the plantain family known by the common name clovenlip toadflax. It is native to Morocco, but it can be found elsewhere as an introduced species and it is cultivated as an ornamental plant. It is an annual herb growing 10 to 30 centimeters tall with linear leaves 3 to 5 centimeters in length. The inflorescence is a raceme of flowers occupying the top of the stem. The flower is about 2 centimeters long with five lobes arranged into two lips with a spur at the end. The flower is often reddish purple in color, but flowers of many different colo

items.name: Linaria dalmatica
items.growersTips:
Plant in sharply draining gritty soil to prevent root rot during wet UK winters.
Sow seeds on the soil surface in spring as they require light to germinate.
Cut flower spikes to the base in August to prevent aggressive self-seeding in your garden.
Water only during prolonged summer droughts once the deep taproot is established.
Grow alongside Origanum or Stachys byzantina which thrive in the same dry, sunny borders.
items.description: Linaria dalmatica is a herbaceous, short-lived perennial plant native to western Asia and southeastern Europe that has become a weed in other areas. The family this plant now belongs to is the Plantaginaceae Family. Previously, it belonged to the Scrophulariaceae (Figwort) family. Its common names include Balkan toadflax, broadleaf toadflax, and Dalmatian toadflax. Linaria dalmatica has unique yellow flowers with an orange center that draw individuals to purchase them to display in their gardens. The distribution of L. dalmatica to North America can be attributed to use as a fabric dye, folk r

items.name: Linaria genistifolia
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in autumn or spring just pressing them into free-draining gritty soil for light.
Water sparingly only during prolonged summer droughts as this plant thrives in dry UK gravel gardens.
Cut back the faded flowering stems in late summer to encourage a second flush of autumn blooms.
Plant alongside companion plants like Thymus or Sedum that share its love for poor alkaline soils.
Watch for slugs and snails on young spring shoots especially during wet UK spring weather.
items.description: Linaria genistifolia is a species of flowering plant belonging to the family Plantaginaceae.

items.name: Linaria maroccana
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds thinly outdoors in April or May just 2mm deep as they need light to germinate in UK soil.
Grow in poor to moderately fertile well-drained soil to prevent floppy stems in wet UK summers.
Water seedlings lightly until established then leave to tolerate dry spells without extra watering.
Shear back the faded stems by half in midsummer to encourage a second flush of blooms by autumn.
Watch for slugs on young spring shoots and protect them using beer traps or organic wool pellets.
items.description: Linaria maroccana is a species of flowering plant in the plantain family known by the common names Moroccan toadflax and annual toadflax. It is native to Morocco, but it can be found elsewhere growing wild as an introduced species, such as California. It is a readily available ornamental plant for the flower garden. This is an annual herb growing erect to approach a maximum height of 50 cm (20 in), its stem with linear leaves 2–4 cm (0.8–1.6 in) long. The inflorescence is a raceme of flowers occupying the top of the stem. At the base of each flower is a calyx with five narrow, pointed lobes. T

items.name: Linaria purpurea
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in autumn onto well-drained grit to let UK winter cold trigger germination.
Grow in poor, sharply drained soil to prevent floppy stems and encourage self-seeding in gravel.
Cut flower spikes to the base in August to prompt a second flush and control prolific self-seeding.
Plant alongside dry-loving UK partners like Nepeta or Lavender in full sun to prevent root rot.
Watch for rosemary beetle damage in dry summers and hand-pick them off the purple flower spikes.
items.description: Linaria purpurea or purple toadflax is a purple-flowered plant native to Italy, part of the plantain family (Plantaginaceae). It is sometimes planted in gardens and is also an introduced weed in North America and other parts of Europe.

items.name: Linaria repens
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at two millimetres deep in autumn to allow winter cold to trigger germination.
Grow in poor, sharply drained chalky soil to prevent the plant from flopping and becoming invasive.
Water seedlings sparingly during dry UK springs, then leave established plants to rely on rainfall.
Cut back faded flower spikes in August to prevent excessive self-seeding in small cottage gardens.
Plant alongside wild marjoram or thyme in sunny gravel borders to support native UK pollinators.
items.description: Linaria repens, also known as pale toadflax or creeping toadflax in Europe and as striped toadflax in the US, is an herbaceous plant in the family Plantaginaceae, native to Europe.

items.name: Linaria ricardoi
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn in well-drained, gritty soil to mimic its native dry Mediterranean habitat.
Position in the sunniest, south-facing spot of your UK garden to maximize summer flowering potential.
Water sparingly only during prolonged dry spells, as this annual is highly prone to root rot in wet.
Protect young spring seedlings from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.
Allow the seed heads to dry on the plant in late summer to encourage self-seeding for next year.
items.description: Linaria ricardoi is a rare species of flowering plant in the family Plantaginaceae endemic to Portugal. Its scientific authority is Coutinho (Cout.). Locally known as "Linária dos Olivais" it blossoms from February to June.

items.name: Linaria triornithophora
items.growersTips:
Plant in spring at the same depth as the pot in free-draining soil to prevent winter root rot.
Water deeply once a week during dry UK summers, allowing the soil to dry out between waterings.
Cut back the spent flowering stems to ground level in autumn to encourage fresh basal growth.
Protect young spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.
Divide congested clumps every three years in early spring to maintain plant vigour and flowering.
items.description: Linaria triornithophora, commonly known as three bird toadflax, is a perennial plant in the family Plantaginaceae.

items.name: Linaria triphylla
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds thinly in April directly into poor, well-drained soil to prevent floppy, weak growth.
Water seedlings sparingly, only during dry spells, as this Mediterranean native hates wet roots.
Watch for slugs and snails on young spring shoots, protecting them with pet-safe organic grit.
Deadhead spent flower spikes weekly in summer to prolong the blooming season into early autumn.
Plant alongside thyme or sedums in gravel gardens to match its preference for dry, sunny spots.
items.description: Linaria triphylla is a species of plants in the family Plantaginaceae.

items.name: Linaria tristis
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in April by pressing them into a gritty, free-draining soil mix without covering.
Water seedlings sparingly only during dry spells to prevent root rot in damp UK spring weather.
Watch for slugs and snails on young shoots during wet British nights and protect with organic grit.
Plant alongside thyme or sedum in gravel gardens to provide the sharp drainage this species craves.
Deadhead spent blooms in midsummer to encourage a second flush of flowers before the autumn frosts.
items.description: Linaria tristis, the melancholy toadflax, is a species of annual flowering plant in the family Plantaginaceae, native to the western Mediterranean region and centered in the Iberian Peninsula. It inhabits open, dry environments on sandy or rocky substrates and is characteristic of disturbed ground in Mediterranean climates.

items.name: Linaria vulgaris
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in autumn or early spring directly into poor, well-drained sandy or gravelly soil.
Water seedlings sparingly during dry UK spells, then leave established plants to thrive on rainfall.
Cut back the faded flower stems in late summer to prevent aggressive self-seeding in small gardens.
Grow alongside wild marjoram or thyme in sunny borders to attract native UK pollinators and bees.
Watch for linaria pug moth caterpillars in summer and tolerate them as they are harmless to plants.
items.description: Linaria vulgaris, the common toadflax, is a species of flowering plant in the family Plantaginaceae, native to Europe, and northern, central and eastern Asia. It has also been introduced to North America and is now common there.

items.name: Liriodendron
items.growersTips:
Plant Chinese tulip shrub chinense in fertile deep loam sheltered from cold drying UK easterly winds
Water young shrubs deeply once a week during dry British summers to establish a deep root system
Prune Liriodendron only in late winter to avoid sap bleeding and preserve its natural shape
Grow in acidic to neutral soil as chalky UK soils cause leaf yellowing and stunt shrub growth
Mulch annually in spring with well-rotted manure to retain moisture in sandy UK garden soils
items.description: Liriodendron is a genus of two species of characteristically large trees, deciduous over most of their populations, in the magnolia family (Magnoliaceae).

items.name: Liriodendron chinense
items.growersTips:
Plant in deep moisture-retentive acidic to neutral soil in a sheltered spot to mimic woodland edges
Water young trees deeply once a week during dry UK summers to establish the sensitive root system
Prune only in late winter to remove damaged stems before the sap rises to prevent bleeding wounds
Protect young spring foliage from late frosts using horticultural fleece in colder northern UK regions
Position away from exposed windy corners to prevent the large characteristic leaves from shredding
items.description: Liriodendron chinense is Asia's native species in the genus Liriodendron. This native of central and southern China grows in the provinces of Anhui, Guangxi, Jiangsu, Fujian, Guizhou, Hubei, Hunan, Jiangxi, Shaanxi, Zhejiang, Sichuan and Yunnan, and also locally in northern Vietnam. Protected populations occur in the Tianmushan National Reserve, Huangshan, Wuyi Shan, and Badagongshan Nature Reserve.

items.name: Liriodendron tulipifera
items.growersTips:
Plant in deep fertile moisture-retentive acidic to neutral soil in a sheltered sun-drenched spot.
Water young trees deeply every week during dry UK summers until their root systems are established.
Prune only in winter to remove dead wood as spring pruning causes sap to bleed heavily and weaken.
Protect the brittle young branches from strong prevailing winds by staking securely at planting.
Watch for aphids on new spring growth and treat immediately to prevent disfiguring sooty mould.
items.description: Liriodendron tulipifera—known as the tulip tree, American tulip tree, tulipwood, tuliptree, tulip poplar, whitewood, fiddletree, lynn-tree, hickory-poplar, and yellow-poplar—is the North American representative of the two-species genus Liriodendron. It is native to eastern North America from Southern Ontario and possibly southern Quebec west to Illinois, and east to southwestern Massachusetts, then south to central Florida and Louisiana.

items.name: Lithodora
items.growersTips:
Plant in acidic soil with grit added to the planting hole to prevent winter wet root rot in UK rain.
Cut back by half immediately after flowering in July to keep the growth compact and prevent leggy stems.
Water only during prolonged dry summer spells once established as they prefer drought to damp soil.
Position in full sun to maximise the intensity of the blue flowers and prevent the foliage thinning.
Protect young plants from slugs in damp UK springs using organic grit barriers around the base.
items.description: Lithodora is a genus of flowering plants in the family Boraginaceae, native to southwestern Europe, southern Greece, Turkey and Algeria. They are low-growing, evergreen shrubs and subshrubs, producing 5-lobed blue or white flowers. The Greek lithodora literally means "stone gift", referring to the plant's preferred rocky habitats. The genus Glandora was split from Lithodora in 2008.

items.name: Lithodora fruticosa
items.growersTips:
Plant in sharply draining gritty soil or a raised bed to survive wet UK winters without root rot.
Position in full sun against a south-facing wall to mimic its native warm Mediterranean climate.
Prune lightly in late summer after flowering to prevent the woody stems from becoming leggy.
Water newly planted shrubs sparingly and only during prolonged dry spells once established.
Propagate by taking semi-ripe cuttings in midsummer to safeguard against severe winter losses.
items.description: Lithodora fruticosa, or the shrubby gromwell, is a small 15–60 cm high densely branched perennial shrub. Its erect young stems are covered with short white hairs, while Its older stems have peeling grey bark and are frequently gnarled and twisted.
