The up to 25 mm long alternate leaves have a covering of flattened hairs and as they grow older they often develop small raised nodules or tubercules particularly near their edges which are downturned. The flowers which are about 15 mm long, vary in colour from violet to an intense blue, with a long petal tube, corolla tubes hairless on outside and o

items.name: Lithophragma tenellum
items.growersTips:
Plant woodland stars in humus-rich, well-drained soil that mimics a damp British deciduous forest.
Sow bulbils just two centimetres deep in autumn to ensure they establish before the winter frosts.
Water weekly during spring growth but keep soil completely dry during their dormant summer phase.
Shed light shade over them by planting alongside native UK ferns and primroses in a woodland border.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.
items.description: Lithophragma is a genus of flowering plants in the saxifrage family containing about nine species native to western North America. These plants are known generally as woodland stars. The petals of the flowers are usually bright white with deep, long lobes or teeth. Each petal may look like three to five petals, when at closer inspection the lobes fuse into a single petal at its base. Most species reproduce via bulblets instead of seeds. L. maximum is a federally listed endangered species. Lithophragma specifically coevolved with moths of the genus Greya, who pollinate and only lay eggs on Lith

items.name: Lithophragma affine
items.growersTips:
Plant tubers in autumn three centimetres deep in humus-rich soil that drains rapidly during winter
Position under deciduous shrubs to mimic woodland shade and prevent summer baking during dormancy
Water weekly during spring growth but stop completely in summer when the foliage naturally dies back
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps
Combine with native wood anemones or primroses which share its preference for damp spring soil
items.description: Lithophragma affine is a species of flowering plant in the saxifrage family known by the common name San Francisco woodland star or fringed woodland star. It is native to the coast of western North America from Oregon to Baja California, where it grows in open habitat on mountain slopes, hills, and canyonsides up to an altitude of 6,600 feet (2,000 m).

items.name: Lithophragma cymbalaria
items.growersTips:
Plant bulblets 3cm deep in autumn in well-drained, gritty loam to mimic its native woodland habitat.
Water weekly in spring during active growth, then stop watering completely as it goes dormant in July.
Position in dappled shade under deciduous shrubs to protect delicate white blooms from midday sun.
Sow fresh seed in cold frames in autumn, allowing natural UK winter chills to trigger germination.
Guard emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.
items.description: Lithophragma cymbalaria is a species of flowering plant in the saxifrage family known by the common name mission woodland star.

items.name: Lithophragma glabrum
items.growersTips:
Plant bulblets 3cm deep in autumn in sharply draining gritty soil to mimic their native rocky slopes.
Water sparingly in spring, then keep completely dry during their summer dormancy to prevent bulb rot.
Sow in UK cold frames in autumn as seeds require winter chilling to break dormancy and germinate.
Grow in partial shade under deciduous shrubs to replicate their natural woodland edge habitat in UK.
Protect emerging spring foliage from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.
items.description: Lithophragma glabrum is a slender perennial western North American mountain plant in the Saxifrage family (Saxifragaceae), known by the common names bulbous woodland star, bulbiferous prairie-star, smooth woodland star, and smooth rockstar.

items.name: Lithophragma heterophyllum
items.growersTips:
Plant bulblets 3cm deep in autumn in gritty, well-drained soil under deciduous shrubs or trees.
Water only during dry spring spells, then keep the soil completely dry during summer dormancy.
Protect emerging spring foliage from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.
Do not prune the dying summer foliage; let it wither naturally to feed the underground bulbils.
Associate with native UK woodlanders like Primula vulgaris in partial shade to mimic its habitat.
items.description: Lithophragma heterophyllum, commonly known as hillside woodland star, is a species of flowering plant in the saxifrage family found in the western United States. It is native to the coastal mountain ranges of California, where it can generally be found in shady habitat. It is a rhizomatous perennial herb growing erect or leaning with a slender naked flowering stem. The leaves are located on the lower part of the stem, each divided into rounded lobes. The stem bears 3 to 12 flowers, each in a cuplike calyx of red or green sepals. The five petals are white, up to 1.2 centimeters long, and usuall

items.name: Lithophragma maximum
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist but well-drained acidic to neutral loam in partial shade to mimic its woodland edge.
Sow seeds shallowly in cold frames during autumn to benefit from natural UK winter stratifying.
Water consistently during spring growth but reduce watering in summer when the plant goes dormant.
Protect young spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.
Divide established clumps in early spring just as new growth appears to propagate successfully.
items.description: Lithophragma maximum, known by the common name San Clemente Island woodland star, is a rare species of flowering plant in the saxifrage family. It is endemic to San Clemente Island, one of the eight Channel Islands of California. It is known from only about four kilometers of rocky coastal cliffs on the edge of the island. The plant was thought to be extinct until a few specimens were rediscovered in 1979. Only 200 individuals were tallied in a 1996 survey. In 1997 the plant was listed as an endangered species on the federal level.

items.name: Smallflower woodland star
items.growersTips:
Plant in autumn using a gritty, free-draining loam mix to mimic its native dry woodland habitat.
Sow bulbils or seeds shallowly at a depth of two millimetres in cold frames during autumn.
Water moderately in spring but keep almost entirely dry during its summer dormant period.
Position in dappled shade under deciduous shrubs to protect from intense midday summer sun.
Watch for vine weevil grubs in containers and protect emerging spring foliage from slugs.
items.description: Lithophragma parviflorum is a species of flowering plant in the saxifrage family known by the common name smallflower woodland star. It is native to much of western North America from British Columbia to California to South Dakota and Nebraska, where it grows in several types of open habitat. It is a rhizomatous perennial herb growing erect or leaning with a naked flowering stem. The leaves are mainly located low on the stem, each cut into three lobes or divided into three lobed leaflets. The stem bears up to 14 flowers, each in a cuplike calyx of red or green sepals. The five petals are brigh

items.name: Lithophragma tenellum
items.growersTips:
Plant in autumn at a depth of 5cm in gritty, sharply draining soil to prevent winter bulb rot.
Position in dappled shade under deciduous shrubs to mimic its natural woodland edge habitat.
Water only during spring growth, then keep the soil almost entirely dry during summer dormancy.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using beer traps or physical barriers.
Propagate by carefully separating the tiny bulbils from the parent plant in late summer.
items.description: Lithophragma tenellum is a species of flowering plant in the saxifrage family known by the common name slender woodland star.

items.name: Red gromwell
items.growersTips:
Plant in sharply draining gritty soil to prevent winter root rot in wet UK climates.
Position in full sun to maximise the intense blue flowers of cultivars like Heavenly Blue.
Trim back lightly with shears immediately after summer flowering to keep the mound compact.
Water sparingly once established as this plant is highly drought-tolerant in dry summers.
Propagate by taking semi-ripe cuttings in midsummer to replace short-lived parent plants.
items.description: Lithospermum is a genus of plants belonging to the family Boraginaceae. The genus is distributed nearly worldwide, but most are native to the Americas and the center of diversity is in the southwestern United States and Mexico. Species are known generally as gromwells or stoneseeds.

items.name: Littorella americana
items.growersTips:
Grow this aquatic perennial in acidic to neutral sandy loam at the edge of a garden pond or bog garden.
Plant crowns in shallow water up to thirty centimetres deep or in wet mud that never dries out.
Expose to full sun to encourage the compact, lawn-like rosettes to spread via runners in summer.
Propagate in spring by carefully detaching rooted runners and replanting them directly into silt.
Watch for invasive pond weeds and manually clear filamentous algae to prevent smothering the leaves.
items.description: Littorella americana Is a species of flowering plant commonly called American shore plantain. It is a small aquatic plant native to Newfoundland and Nova Scotia to Minnesota.

items.name: Littorella uniflora
items.growersTips:
Plant in acidic to neutral, sandy or gravelly soil at the margins of a garden pond or bog garden.
Position in full sun to partial shade, ensuring the crown sits exactly level with the mud surface.
Submerge up to thirty centimetres deep or keep constantly wet in a boggy, damp UK soil zone.
Propagate in spring by gently detaching and replanting the runners that naturally spread outwards.
Grow alongside companion plants like Caltha palustris or Myosotis scorpioides in shallow water.
items.description: Littorella uniflora (vernacular name: (American) shoreweed) is a species of aquatic flowering plant native to the Azores, Morocco, most of Europe excluding the dry southeast, Iceland, and the Faroes. It prefers to live mostly submerged in nutrient-poor freshwater habitats. When submerged, it draws CO2 mostly through its roots and uses a mix of crassulacean acid metabolism (CAM) and C3 carbon fixation for photosynthesis. If the water level drops and exposes the roots, it ceases using CAM.

items.name: Loeflingia hispanica
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in April in a gritty, free-draining sandy loam to mimic dry Mediterranean conditions.
Place pots in the sunniest south-facing spot of your patio to maximise scarce UK summer warmth.
Water sparingly only when the top two inches of soil are dry to prevent root rot in damp climates.
Grow alongside Sedum or Thymus in rock gardens as companions that thrive in identical dry soils.
Scatter seeds directly on the soil surface and press lightly as they require light to germinate.
items.description: Loeflingia is a genus of plant in the family Caryophyllaceae occurring in North America, Europe, northern Africa, and southwestern Asia. Plants of the genus bear bristle-like stipules, as well as axillary, sessile flowers with awned sepals and no or vestigial petals. The fruit is a three-valved capsule.

items.name: Iron grass
items.growersTips:
Plant in free-draining grit-amended soil to prevent root rot during wet, cold UK winters.
Position in full sun against a south-facing wall to protect from frost below minus five Celsius.
Water deeply once a week during the first summer, then leave to rely solely on natural UK rainfall.
Comb through the clump with gloved hands in spring to pull out dead brown leaves and tidy the base.
Divide congested clumps in mid-spring using a sharp spade once the soil begins to warm up.
items.description: Lomandra banksii, commonly known as tropical mat rush, is a species of plant in the asparagus family Asparagaceae. It is native to New Guinea, New Caledonia and the state of Queensland, Australia.

items.name: Lomandra bracteata
items.growersTips:
Plant this Australian native in free-draining sandy loam to prevent winter root rot in wet UK soils.
Position in full sun against a south-facing wall to maximize summer heat and protect from hard frost.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells but keep completely dry during damp winter months.
Prune dead outer leaves individually in late spring rather than shearing the crown to avoid rot.
Grow in a terracotta pot with grit so you can move it into a cold greenhouse during freezing winters.
items.description: Lomandra bracteata is a species of plant in the Asparagaceae family, first described in 1962 by Alma Theodora Lee.

items.name: Lomandra confertifolia
items.growersTips:
Plant in free-draining grit-amended soil to prevent winter root rot in wet UK climates.
Position in full sun or light shade against a south-facing wall to protect from harsh frost.
Water deeply once a week during the first summer, then leave to rely on natural UK rainfall.
Prune back dead outer leaves individually in mid-spring rather than shearing the whole clump.
Grow in raised beds or containers to ensure the sharp drainage this Australian native requires.
items.description: Lomandra confertifolia is a species of perennial herbs in the genus Lomandra, Asparagaceae, subfamily Lomandroideae. It is native to Queensland, Australia. Although it appears grass-like, it is not in the grass family.

items.name: Lomandra cylindrica
items.growersTips:
Plant in free-draining grit-amended soil to prevent winter root rot in wet UK climates.
Position in full sun against a south-facing wall to mimic its native warm Australian habitat.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells, but keep completely dry throughout winter.
Prune dead outer leaves individually in mid-spring rather than shearing the entire clump.
Protect the crown with a dry straw mulch or fleece wrap when UK temperatures drop below -5C.
items.description: Lomandra cylindrica is a species of plant in the Asparagaceae family, first described in 1962 by Alma Theodora Lee.

items.name: Lomandra effusa
items.growersTips:
Plant in free-draining gravelly soil to prevent root rot during wet UK winters.
Position in full sun against a south-facing wall to mimic its warm Australian habitat.
Water deeply once a week during summer establishment, then leave dry once settled.
Comb out dead under-foliage in spring using gloved hands to maintain a tidy clump.
Protect the crown with a dry mulch of grit or straw before the first winter frost.
items.description: Lomandra effusa is a perennial, dioecious, rhizomatous herb native to Australia. It is a perennial tussock with bluish green, large, arching leaves which are distinctive by the two toothed leaf tip. It has white, cream or pink fragrant flowers during the months of June to October.

items.name: Lomandra filiformis
items.growersTips:
Plant in free-draining grit-amended soil to prevent winter root rot in wet UK climates.
Position in full sun to light dappled shade to maintain the dense tufted golden-green foliage.
Water weekly during the first summer then leave dry as they are highly drought-tolerant once set.
Comb through the clump with gloved hands in spring to remove dead thatch rather than cutting back.
Protect young crowns from slugs and snails in damp British springs using organic wool pellets.
items.description: Lomandra filiformis, commonly known as wattle mat-rush, is a tussock forming perennial herb that is native to Australia. It is sparsely tufted, with strap-like leaves and yellow flowers. It grows in dry sclerophyll forest and grassy woodland, usually on well-drained rocky or sandy soils.

items.name: Lomandra fluviatilis
items.growersTips:
Plant in free-draining sandy loam with grit to prevent winter root rot in wet UK soils.
Water deeply once a week during the first summer, then leave to rely on natural UK rainfall.
Prune back dead outer foliage in late spring using sharp shears to encourage fresh green growth.
Position in full sun to partial shade, ensuring shelter from freezing winter winds in cold regions.
Divide established clumps in mid-spring to propagate and maintain a neat, non-sprawling habit.
items.description: Lomandra fluviatilis is a perennial, rhizomatous herb found in the Australian state of New South Wales.

items.name: Lomandra gracilis
items.growersTips:
Plant in free-draining grit-amended soil to prevent root rot during wet UK winters.
Position in full sun to partial shade, ensuring shelter from freezing, drying winter winds.
Water deeply once a week during the first summer, then leave to rely on natural UK rainfall.
Comb out dead thatch by hand in spring using rubber gloves rather than cutting the crown back.
Protect young plants with fleece if temperatures are forecast to drop below minus five Celsius.
items.description: Lomandra gracilis is a perennial, rhizomatous herb that is found in New South Wales and Queensland in eastern Australia.

items.name: Lomandra hystrix
items.growersTips:
Plant in spring at the same depth as the pot in free-draining soil to prevent winter crown rot.
Water weekly during the first summer then leave dry as established plants tolerate UK droughts well.
Prune back to fifteen centimetres from the ground in late spring every three years to renew foliage.
Protect the crown with dry straw mulch in late autumn to survive severe wet UK winter frosts.
Divide mature clumps in spring using a sharp spade to propagate and maintain plant vigour.
items.description: Lomandra hystrix, commonly known as green mat-rush, or creek mat-rush, is a perennial, rhizomatous a tall herb of Northern NSW to North Queensland wet tropics, Australia.

items.name: Lomandra laxa
items.growersTips:
Plant in free-draining acidic to neutral soil to prevent root rot during wet UK winters.
Position in partial shade rather than full sun to mimic its native Australian forest understory.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells, but keep dry in winter to avoid crown rot.
Cut back dead foliage in early spring before new growth starts, using gloves to avoid sharp leaves.
Grow in a container to easily move indoors or to a greenhouse if temperatures drop below minus five.
items.description: Lomandra laxa is a perennial, rhizomatous herb found in the Australian states of New South Wales and Queensland.

items.name: Woolly Mat-rush
items.growersTips:
Plant in free-draining sandy loam with grit to survive wet UK winters and prevent root rot.
Position in full sun against a south-facing wall to mimic its native hot Australian climate.
Water deeply once a week during the first summer, then leave to rely solely on UK rainfall.
Prune back old brown foliage by one third in late spring once the risk of hard frost has passed.
Protect the crown with a dry straw mulch from November to March to shield it from severe freezes.
items.description: Lomandra leucocephala is a perennial, rhizomatous herb found in Australia. The plant is sometimes referred to as Irongrass because the plant is known to be tough and has a grass-like look.

items.name: Lomandra longifolia
items.growersTips:
Plant in well-drained soil with the crown exactly level with the soil surface to prevent wet rot.
Water weekly during the first UK summer, then transition to zero watering once fully established.
Cut back the entire clump to ten centimetres above the ground in late spring to clear winter damage.
Protect the root zone with dry straw mulch during prolonged sub-zero UK winter cold snaps.
Divide congested clumps in mid-spring by slicing the tough rootball with a sharp spade.
items.description: Lomandra longifolia, commonly known as spiny-head mat-rush, spiky-headed mat-rush, or basket grass, is a perennial, rhizomatous herb found throughout eastern Australia. The leaves are 40 cm to 80 cm long, and generally have a leaf of about 8 mm to 12 mm wide. It grows in a variety of soil types and is frost, heat and drought tolerant. Labillardiere described Lomandra longifolia from a specimen collected in Tasmania.

items.name: Lomandra micrantha
items.growersTips:
Plant in free-draining sandy loam with grit to prevent winter root rot in wet UK soils.
Water deeply once a week during the first summer, then leave to rely on natural UK rainfall.
Prune yellowing outer leaves individually in spring rather than shearing the whole clump back.
Position in full sun or light dappled shade to maintain the upright, needle-like foliage structure.
Protect the crown with a dry mulch of gravel in winter to shield it from persistent cold damp.
items.description: Lomandra micrantha commonly known as small-flower mat-rush, is a species of flowering plant in the family Asparagaceae.

items.name: Lomandra montana
items.growersTips:
Plant in free-draining acid to neutral soil with the crown level with the soil to prevent rot.
Water deeply once a week during dry UK summers until established, then rely on natural rainfall.
Protect the crown from severe winter frost below minus five Celsius using a thick dry straw mulch.
Prune back dead outer leaves in mid-spring by cutting them individually near the base of the plant.
Position in full sun or light dappled shade next to Heucheras to contrast the fine grass-like foliage.
items.description: Lomandra montana is a perennial, rhizomatous herb found in eastern Australia.

items.name: Lomandra multiflora
items.growersTips:
Plant in free-draining gravelly soil to prevent winter root rot in wet UK climates.
Protect young plants from frost with horticultural fleece during their first two UK winters.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells, but leave completely dry throughout winter.
Cut back dead outer foliage in late spring to encourage fresh green growth and tidy the clump.
Divide mature clumps in mid-spring when the soil warms up to propagate and maintain plant vigour.
items.description: Lomandra multiflora, also commonly known as many-flowered mat rush, mat rush and many flowered mat-lily, is a perennial, rhizomatous herb found in Australia and Papua New Guinea. The mat rush is distributed widely in the region and common within its preferred growing conditions. Its conservation status is considered not to be of concern and risk.

items.name: Lomandra nigricans
items.growersTips:
Plant this Australian native in free-draining gravelly soil to prevent winter root rot in UK wet.
Position in full sun against a south-facing wall to maximize summer heat and ensure winter survival.
Water deeply once a week during its first UK summer, then leave dry once the roots are established.
Prune dead outer leaves individually in late spring rather than shearing the whole clump back.
Protect the crown with a dry straw mulch or fleece wrap during prolonged UK winter frosts.
items.description: Lomandra nigricans is a species of flowering plant in the family Asparagaceae.

items.name: Lomandra obliqua
items.growersTips:
Plant in free-draining sandy loam or grit-amended clay to prevent winter root rot in wet UK soils.
Position in full sun or light dappled shade against a south-facing wall to mimic its native warmth.
Water weekly during the first summer then leave to rely solely on natural UK rainfall once settled.
Comb through the foliage with gloved hands in spring to remove dead straw-coloured leaves at the base.
Protect the crown with dry bracken or fleece during prolonged UK winter frosts below minus five.
items.description: Lomandra obliqua, known as fish bones and twisted mat-rush, is a small wiry ground-covering flowering plant found in eastern Australia. It is a widespread plant seen on the coast and tablelands. The foliage superficially resembles a fern, but creamy/yellow flowers form on clusters in spring. Leaves are two-ranked, somewhat glaucous and twisted.

items.name: Lomandra preissii
items.growersTips:
Plant in sharply draining sandy loam with grit to survive wet UK winters and prevent root rot.
Water deeply once a week during the first summer, then leave to rely on natural UK rainfall.
Prune back old brown foliage by one third in late spring to stimulate fresh bright green growth.
Position in full sun or light dappled shade to maintain its structural upright tufted habit.
Protect the crown with dry mulch or fleece during prolonged sub-zero winter freezes in cold regions.
items.description: Lomandra preissii is a species of perennial, herbaceous plant in the family Asparagaceae native to Southwest Australia. It grows to a heights of 20 cm (7.9 in) to 60 cm (24 in), and has flowers in green or yellow/purple from April till July.

items.name: Lomandra spicata
items.growersTips:
Plant in free-draining sandy loam with grit to prevent winter root rot in wet UK climates.
Water deeply once a week during the first summer, then leave to rely solely on natural UK rainfall.
Cut back old tattered foliage to five centimetres from the base in late spring to renew growth.
Protect the crown with dry bracken or fleece during prolonged sub-zero British winter freezes.
Divide congested clumps in mid-spring using a sharp spade when the soil begins to warm up.
items.description: Lomandra spicata is a rainforest flowering plant in the family Asparagaceae. It is found in eastern Australia.

items.name: Lomandra tropica
items.growersTips:
Plant this Australian native in free-draining gravelly soil to prevent winter root rot in UK wet.
Water deeply once a week during hot UK summers but keep completely dry during damp winter months.
Protect the crown with a thick dry mulch of bark or straw before the first sharp November frosts.
Prune back dead outer leaves individually in late spring rather than shearing the whole clump down.
Divide established clumps in April using a sharp spade to ensure quick establishment in warm soil.
items.description: Lomandra tropica is a perennial, rhizomatous herb found in northern Australia, in Western Australia and the Northern Territory.

items.name: Lopezia racemosa
items.growersTips:
Grow Lopezia coronata in free-draining loam mixed with grit to prevent winter root rot in wet UK soil.
Sow seeds shallowly at two millimetres deep in spring under glass with gentle bottom heat of fifteen C.
Overwinter these tender perennials in a frost-free greenhouse or conservatory kept above five degrees.
Prune back stems by half in early spring to encourage bushy growth and more mosquito-like flowers.
Water weekly in dry summer spells but allow the top three centimetres of compost to dry out first.
items.description: Lopezia is a genus of plants of the family Onagraceae, largely restricted to Mexico and Central America.

items.name: Lophospermum atrosanguineum
items.growersTips:
Plant in late May after frosts in free-draining soil mixed with grit to prevent winter root rot.
Water deeply once a week in summer, allowing the top two inches of compost to dry out completely.
Provide a sturdy trellis or obelisk immediately at planting to support its rapid twining stems.
Overwinter indoors in a frost-free greenhouse or conservatory kept at a minimum of five degrees.
Take softwood cuttings in late summer as insurance against wet UK winters which often kill the plant.
items.description: Rhodochiton atrosanguineus is a herbaceous perennial vine native to Mexico. It has been cultivated as an ornamental plant since at least 1836.

items.name: Lophospermum erubescens
items.growersTips:
Plant in late May after frosts in free-draining soil mixed with grit to prevent winter root rot.
Provide a sturdy trellis or obelisk at planting to support its rapid two-meter climbing habit.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells, allowing the top two inches of soil to dry out.
Take stem cuttings in August to overwinter indoors as insurance against wet UK winter losses.
Prune back hard to thirty centimeters in early spring only if overwintered in a heated greenhouse.
items.description: Lophospermum erubescens, known as Mexican twist or creeping gloxinia, is a climbing or sprawling herbaceous perennial plant, native to the Sierra Madre Oriental mountains of Mexico, where it is found along forest margins or canyon walls. It climbs by means of twining leaf stalks. Wild plants have pink and white tubular flowers, although other colours are found in cultivation. It has been cultivated as an ornamental plant since at least 1830. Although not frost-hardy, it will survive if its base and roots are protected from freezing in the winter. It has escaped from cultivation and become natu

items.name: Lophospermum purpusii
items.growersTips:
Overwinter indoors in a frost-free greenhouse or conservatory as this tender climber cannot survive UK winter frost.
Plant in free-draining loam-based compost with added grit to prevent root rot during wet UK summers.
Water deeply once a week in summer, allowing the top two inches of soil to dry out between waterings.
Prune back hard in early spring to encourage vigorous new flowering shoots from the base of the plant.
Provide a sturdy trellis or netting for the self-clinging leaf petioles to climb up in late spring.
items.description: Lophospermum purpusii is a scambling or climbing herbaceous perennial native to Mexico. It has tubular flowers, white at the base and red to violet elsewhere.

items.name: Lophospermum scandens
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in March at a depth of two millimetres using a heated propagator set to twenty degrees
Grow in pots of peat-free loam-based compost so you can move them into a frost-free greenhouse by October
Water copiously from June to September keeping soil damp but never allow the pot to sit in standing water
Provide a trellis or netting for the self-clinging leaf petioles to climb up as soon as shoots appear
Check young spring growth daily for aphids and glasshouse whitefly which thrive in sheltered UK patios
items.description: Lophospermum scandens is a scambling or climbing herbaceous perennial native to south central Mexico, with red-violet and white tubular flowers and toothed heart-shaped leaves. It grows at elevations between 1,400 and 2,400 m in dry habitats, including deciduous oak forests and recent lava flows. The long-tubed flowers are pollinated by hummingbirds. It has been used in gardens as an ornamental plant since the mid-19th century. Its roots require protection from frost in regions where this occurs in the winter. Hybrids of L. scandens are also grown.

items.name: Mexican primrose-willow
items.growersTips:
Grow Ludwigia palustris in boggy pond margins or wet soil under three inches of water in full sun.
Prune stems in midsummer by cutting just above a leaf node to encourage bushy, colorful side shoots.
Plant alongside Caltha palustris to provide spring color before Ludwigia reaches peak summer growth.
Bring container-grown plants indoors to a frost-free greenhouse or bright windowsill over winter.
Propagate in spring by taking four-inch stem cuttings and inserting them directly into wet compost.
items.description:
Ludwigia is the generic name of three groups of organisms. It can refer to:Animals
Ludwigia (ammonite)
Ludwigia (beetle) 
Plants
Ludwigia (plant)

items.name: Water Primrose
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender aquatic perennial in a basket submerged no deeper than fifteen centimetres in water
Overwinter plants indoors in a frost-free greenhouse as they will not survive a typical UK winter
Prune aggressive floating stems weekly in midsummer to prevent them from choking pond oxygenators
Plant in heavy clay loam topsoil without added organic compost to prevent pond water eutrophication
Pair with native Marsh Marigold to provide early spring structure before this late-starter emerges
items.description: Ludwigia adscendens, the water primrose, is a species of flowering plant in the evening primrose family. Its native distribution is unclear. It is now a common weed of rice paddies in Asia and occurs also in Australia and Africa, but may have originated in South America.

items.name: Bushy seedbox
items.growersTips:
Plant this native wet-loving perennial in heavy, moisture-retentive clay soil at a pond edge or bog.
Ensure the crown sits no deeper than five centimetres below water level to prevent winter crown rot.
Prune stems back to the base in late autumn to encourage bushy new growth and vibrant red stems.
Water daily in dry summer spells if planted in borders to maintain the essential boggy conditions.
Grow alongside Caltha palustris to provide early spring cover before this late-emerging plant wakes.
items.description: Ludwigia alternifolia, commonly known as seedbox, bushy seedbox, rattlebox, and square-pod water-primrose, is a herbaceous perennial plant of the family Onagraceae. It is native to central and eastern North America, growing in marshes, wet meadows, and swamps. It has yellow, four-petaled flowers and brown seed pods that are shaped like a cube.

items.name: Ludwigia glandulosa
items.growersTips:
Grow this marginal plant in a pond basket submerged no deeper than ten centimetres below the surface.
Propagate in late spring by taking five-inch stem cuttings and rooting them directly in wet compost.
Plant in a heavy clay-loam aquatic soil topped with pea gravel to prevent fish from digging it up.
Position in full sun to ensure the foliage develops its signature deep red and purple coloration.
Cut back dead stems to the water level in late autumn to prevent rotting vegetation in your pond.
items.description: Ludwigia glandulosa, the small-flowered seedbox or the cylindricfruit primrose-willow, is an amphibious plant from southeast United States. It can grow partially or fully submerged. It grows very slowly and needs carbon dioxide in order to grow well. The leaves of this plant will turn greener if insufficient light is provided.

items.name: Ludwigia hexapetala
items.growersTips:
Report sightings of this invasive weed to the GB Non-Native Species Secretariat as it is illegal to grow.
Do not plant this in UK garden ponds or waterways as it is a banned invasive species of concern.
If found on your property eradicate it completely by digging out all roots and drying them thoroughly.
Dispose of plant material by burning or landfill rather than composting to prevent vegetative spread.
Never transfer water or pond plants from an infested site to prevent spreading stem fragments.
items.description: Ludwigia hexapetala, the water primrose, is a herbaceous perennial plant of the family Onagraceae. Native to Central and South America, its habitat includes the margins of lakes, ponds, ditches, and streams. Its stems may be immersed or fully emergent. It is a noxious invader of aquatic ecosystems in North America.

items.name: Ludwigia hirtella
items.growersTips:
Grow in wet acidic soil or boggy pond edges using ericaceous compost to mimic its native habitat
Overwinter container plants indoors or in a heated greenhouse as this species cannot survive UK frost
Position in full sun to maximize the striking red stem coloration and yellow summer blooms
Prune leggy stems in late spring to encourage bushier growth and prevent the plant from becoming untidy
Check regularly for water lily beetles and sawfly larvae which damage foliage in damp UK gardens
items.description: Ludwigia hirtella, commonly called spindleroot, is a species of plant in the evening primrose family that is native to the south-central United States of America.

items.name: Ludwigia murchisonae
items.growersTips:
Grow in full sun in a clay-heavy, nutrient-rich soil to bring out the deep red foliage coloration.
Plant in shallow pond margins or bog gardens at a maximum water depth of ten centimeters.
Protect young shoots from late spring frosts using fleece if grown outside of a greenhouse.
Prune aggressively in late summer to maintain a bushy shape and prevent invasive leggy growth.
Propagate in spring by taking stem cuttings and rooting them directly in wet, muddy compost.
items.description: Ludwigia is an extinct genus of ammonites in the family Graphoceratidae, which lived during the Middle Jurassic.

items.name: Mexican primrose-willow
items.growersTips:
Grow in a pond basket filled with heavy loam and submerge no deeper than fifteen centimetres.
Overwinter indoors in a heated greenhouse or conservatory as this tropical plant cannot survive frost.
Water daily with harvested rainwater to keep the soil saturated if growing in a bog garden border.
Prune leggy stems by half in late spring to encourage bushier growth and more yellow flowers.
Check submerged foliage regularly for water snails and manually remove them to prevent leaf damage.
items.description: Ludwigia octovalvis is a species of flowering plant in the Onagraceae family known by the common name Mexican primrose-willow. Its native distribution is unclear, but can be found in Central America, Australia, South-East Asia, Tamilnadu (IND), the Middle East, the Central-West African regions and spreads easily to become naturalized. It is also cultivated as an aquatic plant. The plant is known for its anti-aging properties. The species is sometimes regarded as an invasive species and is classified by IUCN as of "least concern" with stable populations. An adult plant is one meter tall on aver

items.name: Ludwigia palustris
items.growersTips:
Plant in wet mud or submerged up to thirty centimetres deep at pond edges in full sun for red leaves.
Prune aggressively in midsummer by pinching stem tips to encourage bushy growth and prevent leggy stems.
Grow in acidic to neutral clay loam enriched with organic compost to mimic UK wetland conditions.
Pair with shallow-water companions like Caltha palustris to provide shade and suppress green algae.
Watch for water snails in late spring which rapidly consume the soft submerged foliage of this plant.
items.description: Ludwigia palustris is a species of flowering plant in the evening primrose family known by the common names marsh seedbox, Hampshire-purslane and water purslane. This is an aquatic or semiaquatic perennial herb which grows in moist to wet to flooded areas. It is sometimes a weed. The species epithet palustris is Latin for "of the marsh" and indicates its common habitat.

items.name: Creeping water-primrose
items.growersTips:
Keep this highly invasive weed strictly contained in sealed garden ponds to prevent environmental escape.
Prune stems aggressively in late summer to prevent the plant from smothering native pond oxygenators.
Overwinter a small stem cutting indoors in a jar of water to protect it from harsh UK winter frosts.
Plant in heavy clay loam within a submerged aquatic basket to restrict its rapid root spread.
Dispose of all excess plant material by burning or bagging it to comply with strict UK wildlife laws.
items.description: Ludwigia peploides is a species of flowering plant in the evening primrose family known by the common names floating primrose-willow and creeping water primrose. It is native to Australia, North America, and South America, but it can be found on many continents and spreads easily to become naturalized. It is well known as a troublesome aquatic noxious weed that invades water ecosystems and can clog waterways. This is perennial herb which grows in moist to wet to flooded areas. The stem can creep over 2 meters long, sometimes branching. It spreads to form mats on the mud, or floats ascending in

items.name: Ludwigia peruviana
items.growersTips:
Grow this invasive tender perennial in a submerged container to prevent aggressive spread in ponds.
Overwinter containers indoors or in a heated greenhouse as it cannot survive frost below five degrees.
Prune stems hard in late spring to encourage bushy growth and maximize the yellow summer blooms.
Plant in heavy clay loam with a slow-release aquatic fertilizer tablet to support rapid summer growth.
Check foliage weekly in summer for water lily aphid infestations and wash them off with a hose.
items.description: Ludwigia peruviana, with the common names Peruvian primrose-willow or Peruvian water primrose, is an aquatic, sometimes deciduous species of flowering plant in the evening primrose family. It can grow to approximately 12 feet (3.7 m) in height. While native to Peru, it has been introduced in many other countries for its attractive simple yellow flowers, it is now a common weed in swampy areas around the world.

items.name: Ludwigia polycarpa
items.growersTips:
Plant this marginal perennial in shallow water up to fifteen centimetres deep in a sunny garden pond.
Plant in heavy clay loam using aquatic baskets to prevent the roots from spreading invasively.
Propagate in midsummer by taking stem cuttings and inserting them directly into wet pond-side mud.
Cut the dying stems back to the pond basket level in late autumn to prevent winter water pollution.
Check foliage regularly in spring for water lily beetle larvae which skeletonise the green leaves.
items.description: Ludwigia polycarpa, common names many-fruited false-loosestrife and false loosestrife seedbox, is a plant found in North America. It is listed as a special concern and believed extirpated in Connecticut, and as endangered in Massachusetts, Pennsylvania and Vermont.

items.name: Creeping waterpurslane
items.growersTips:
Grow this aquatic perennial in UK garden ponds at a planting depth of fifteen to thirty centimetres.
Propagate in spring by snipping healthy stem cuttings and inserting them directly into clay soil.
Prune aggressively in midsummer to prevent the rapid growth from choking out slower pond plants.
Position in full sun to ensure the leaves develop their signature deep red autumn coloration.
Overwinter submerged below the UK pond ice line to protect the crown from severe winter freezes.
items.description: Ludwigia repens is a species of flowering plant in the evening primrose family known by the common name creeping primrose-willow. It is native to parts of the Americas and it has the potential to spread easily and become naturalized in many areas. It is known as an aquatic weed in some regions. It is also cultivated as an aquarium plant. This is a mat-forming perennial herb with a creeping stem up to 30 centimeters long, rooting at nodes which come in contact with wet substrate. The leaves are oppositely arranged and up to 4 or 5 centimeters long. The flower has four yellow colored petals no m

items.name: Ludwigia sedoides
items.growersTips:
Overwinter indoors in a heated tank or conservatory as this tropical plant cannot survive UK frosts.
Plant in heavy loam soil within a shallow aquatic basket submerged exactly five to fifteen centimeters.
Position in your pond's absolute brightest spot to ensure the foliage develops its red coloration.
Check regularly for water snails and aphids which quickly disfigure the delicate floating rosettes.
Group with deeper water lilies to provide wind protection and keep the floating mosaic stable.
items.description: Ludwigia sedioides, commonly known as mosaic flower and false loosestrife, is a herbaceous perennial plant of the family Onagraceae. It has yellow flowers that bloom from June to August. Native to Brazil and Venezuela, its habitat includes wet, swampy localities.

items.name: Ludwigia sphaerocarpa
items.growersTips:
Plant this aquatic perennial in a heavy clay loam soil enriched with iron-rich root tabs.
Keep water levels consistently above the crown or grow in a bog garden that never dries out.
Position in full sun to achieve the characteristic deep bronze-orange foliage in UK summers.
Prune the stems in late spring by pinching the growing tips to encourage a bushier habit.
Overwinter indoors or in a heated greenhouse as this species is tender and will not survive UK frost.
items.description:
Ludwigia sphaerocarpa, common names globe-fruited false-loosestrife, globefruit primrose-willow, round-fruited false-loosestrife, globe-fruited seedbox, globe-fruited ludwigia, spherical-fruited seedbox and round-fruited false loosestrife; is a plant in the Myrtales family Onagraceae found in North America. It is listed as endangered in Connecticut,
 
Indiana, Massachusetts and Rhode Island, and as threatened in Michigan and New York (state). It is listed as extirpated in Pennsylvania.

items.name: Lychnis apetala
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in April on damp compost and cover with a very fine layer of vermiculite.
Water young seedlings gently at the base twice a week to prevent dampening off in cool UK springs.
Watch for slugs and snails on tender new growth during wet May nights using organic beer traps.
Deadhead faded blooms weekly in July to prolong the flowering season until the first autumn frosts.
Grow alongside companion plants like Nigella or Briza media in free-draining, gritty UK soil.
items.description: Silene is a genus of flowering plants in the family Caryophyllaceae. Containing between 500 and 900 species, it is the largest genus in the family. Common names include campion and catchfly. Many Silene species are widely distributed, particularly in the northern hemisphere.

items.name: Lyonia fruticosa
items.growersTips:
Plant in highly acidic peat-free ericaceous compost mixed with pine needles to mimic its native soil.
Water only with stored rainwater as tap water contains calcium that will cause leaf chlorosis.
Position in full sun to partial shade in a sheltered spot to protect it from harsh UK winter winds.
Prune lightly in late spring after flowering only to remove dead wood and maintain its bushy shape.
Mulch annually with composted pine bark or leaf mould to retain moisture and keep the roots cool.
items.description: Lyonia fruticosa, the poor-grub or coastal plain staggerbush, is a plant species native to the US states of Florida, southern Georgia and the extreme southern part of South Carolina. It grows in pine woodlands and shrub bogs at elevations less than 100 meters.

items.name: Lyonia ligustrina
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist acidic soil with a pH of 4.5 to 6.0, incorporating peat-free ericaceous compost.
Position in full sun to partial shade, ensuring the soil remains consistently damp but not sodden.
Mulch annually in spring with pine needles or composted bark to retain moisture and maintain acidity.
Prune lightly immediately after summer flowering to shape the shrub and remove dead wood.
Water with harvested rainwater rather than tap water to prevent the soil pH from rising.
items.description: Lyonia ligustrina is a species of flowering plant in the family Ericaceae known by the common names maleberry and he-huckleberry. It is native to the eastern United States from Maine to Florida and west to Texas and Oklahoma.

items.name: Lyonia lucida
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist acidic soil with ericaceous compost and sulfur to keep pH strictly between 4.5 and 5.5
Water with stored rainwater rather than tap water to prevent lime-induced chlorosis in summer
Prune immediately after flowering in late spring to avoid cutting off next year's developing buds
Mulch annually with pine needles or composted bark to retain moisture and mimic forest floor acidity
Grow in a sheltered spot facing south or west to protect the evergreen foliage from cold UK winds
items.description: Lyonia lucida is a species of flowering plant in the family Ericaceae known by the common names fetterbush lyonia, hurrahbush, and staggerbush. Other plants may also be called fetterbush. This broadleaved evergreen plant grows on the coastal plain of the southeastern United States from Virginia to Florida to Louisiana. It also occurs in Cuba.

items.name: Lyonia mariana
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist acidic soil with a pH of 4.5 to 5.5, mixing in plenty of composted pine needles.
Water weekly with collected rainwater rather than tap water to maintain the required soil acidity.
Prune lightly in late winter to remove dead wood and shape the shrub before spring growth starts.
Mulch annually in autumn with leaf mould or composted bark to protect roots from UK winter frosts.
Position in partial shade to mimic its natural woodland edge habitat and prevent leaf scorch.
items.description: Lyonia mariana, the Piedmont staggerbush and staggerbush, is a perennial shrub that is native to the United States.

items.name: Lyonia ovalifolia
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist acidic soil enriched with pine needles or leaf mould to mimic UK woodland conditions.
Grow in partial shade sheltered from harsh winds to protect the delicate bell-shaped spring flowers.
Water with harvested rainwater rather than tap water to maintain the necessary low soil pH level.
Prune lightly in late winter only to remove dead wood as this slow-growing shrub needs minimal cuts.
Mulch annually with composted bark in autumn to protect shallow roots from hard UK winter frosts.
items.description: Lyonia ovalifolia is a species of plant in the family Ericaceae. This plant is Native to Himalaya, Nepal, China, Japan, Cambodia, Myanmar, Thailand, Vietnam and Malaysia. It is known as Anyaar in India and Angeri in Nepal.

items.name: Lyonia truncata
items.growersTips:
Plant in highly acidic, peaty, well-draining soil with a pH of 4.5 to 5.5 to prevent chlorosis.
Water exclusively with harvested rainwater to avoid raising soil pH with alkaline UK tap water.
Protect from harsh winter winds by planting in a sheltered, semi-shaded spot facing south or west.
Prune lightly in late spring after flowering to maintain shape and remove dead wood from frost.
Mulch annually with pine needles or composted bark to retain moisture and mimic forest floor soil.
items.description: Lyonia truncata is a species of flowering plant in the family Ericaceae known as Dominican staggerbush. It is a shrub or tree native to Hispaniola and Puerto Rico.

items.name: Lysidice brevicalyx
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in early April at a depth of two centimeters to combat the cool UK spring soil.
Water deeply once a week at the base rather than daily sprinkles to encourage deep taproot growth.
Watch for black bean aphid infestations on young shoots during humid British midsummer afternoons.
Incorporate well-rotted grit into heavy UK clay soils to prevent winter root rot in wet conditions.
Plant alongside sweet peas to maximize nitrogen fixation and attract essential UK pollinators.
items.description: Lysidice may refer to :

items.name: Macleania loeseneriana
items.growersTips:
Grow in ericaceous compost with perlite as this Andean shrub requires acidic, highly drained soil.
Overwinter indoors or in a heated greenhouse as it cannot survive UK frost below five degrees Celsius.
Water with rainwater rather than tap water to maintain the low soil pH this Ericaceae plant needs.
Prune lightly immediately after spring flowering to shape the shrub without cutting into old wood.
Position in bright, indirect light or dappled shade to mimic its natural cloud forest canopy home.
items.description: Macleania loeseneriana is a species of plant in the family Ericaceae. It is endemic to Ecuador.

items.name: Macleaya cordata
items.growersTips:
Plant Macleaya microcarpa Kelways Coral Plume in deep moist soil to prevent windburn in dry UK summers
Control aggressive underground runners in small gardens by planting inside a buried bottomless bucket
Cut the hollow stems right down to ground level in late autumn to prevent winter wet rotting the crown
Wear gloves when pruning to avoid skin irritation from the toxic orange sap typical of Papaveraceae
Stake the tall stems in spring using hazel twigs before the heavy summer rain bends them to the lawn
items.description: Macleaya, or plume poppy, is a genus of two or three species of flowering plants in the poppy family Papaveraceae, native to Japan and China. They are large rhizomatous herbaceous perennials with palmately lobed, frilly leaves of olive green or grey colour, 25 cm (10 in) long, and tall stems with airy plumes of petal-less, tubular, off-white or cream flowers.

items.name: Macleaya cordata
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist, well-drained soil in full sun or partial shade, sheltered from strong UK winds.
Control its invasive rhizomes by planting inside a buried, bottomless bucket or deep root barrier.
Cut the hollow stems right back to ground level in late autumn or winter using sharp secateurs.
Wear gloves when pruning to avoid skin irritation from the toxic, staining orange-yellow sap.
Propagate in spring by dividing the root clump or taking root cuttings before new growth starts.
items.description: Macleaya cordata, the five-seeded plume-poppy, is a species of flowering plant in the poppy family Papaveraceae, which is used ornamentally. It is native to China and Japan. It is a large herbaceous perennial growing to 2.5 m (8 ft) tall by 1 m (3 ft) or more wide, with olive green leaves and airy panicles of buff-white flowers in summer.

items.name: Macleaya microcarpa
items.growersTips:
Plant in deep, moist, well-drained loam in full sun or partial shade to reach its full height.
Install a root barrier at planting to contain its invasive, fast-spreading underground runners.
Wear gloves when cutting back dead stems in late winter to avoid irritation from the orange sap.
Propagate by taking root cuttings in late autumn or winter when the plant is dormant.
Stake the tall stems in late spring to protect them from strong winds in exposed UK gardens.
items.description: Macleaya microcarpa is a species of flowering plant in the poppy family, Papaveraceae. It is a vigorous, substantial herbaceous perennial growing to 2 m (7 ft) tall by 1 m (3 ft) or more wide, with grey-green felted leaves and loose panicles of buff flowers in midsummer.

items.name: Macledium spinosum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in April at a depth of five millimetres to protect them from late UK frosts.
Grow in sharply draining gritty soil to prevent root rot during wet British summer spells.
Water sparingly only when the top two inches of soil are dry to mimic its arid native habitat.
Position in the sunniest south-facing border or greenhouse to maximise essential summer warmth.
Deadhead faded blooms weekly in July and August to prolong the flowering display before autumn.
items.description: Macledium spinosum is a variable species of flowering plant in the family Asteraceae, that is endemic to the southern Cape regions of South Africa.

items.name: Doll's protea
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in early spring at a depth of five millimetres to combat the cool UK climate.
Grow in free-draining sandy loam with added grit to prevent root rot during wet British summers.
Water sparingly once established, allowing the top two inches of gritty soil to dry out completely.
Position in the sunniest south-facing border or greenhouse to maximise essential summer heat.
Protect young seedlings from slugs and snails using copper tape or beer traps in damp spring weather.
items.description: Macledium zeyheri is a species of flowering plant in the family Asteraceae. It is found in Southern Africa, ranging through South Africa's Cape Provinces, KwaZulu-Natal, and Northern Provinces to Eswatini and Mozambique. Its natural habitats are subtropical or tropical dry shrubland and plantations, particularly along the KwaZulu-Natal coast.

items.name: Macrolobium suaveolens
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in April at 2cm depth in peat-free compost using bottom heat of 21C to start early.
Plant out in June after frosts in a south-facing border with grit added to clay soil for drainage.
Water deeply at the base twice a week during dry July spells to prevent early pod drop in dry soil.
Watch for black bean aphid on young shoots in June and wash them off with a firm spray of water.
Grow alongside sweet alyssum to attract hoverflies that naturally control pests on the foliage.
items.description: Macrolobium is a legume genus in the subfamily Detarioideae. It is a tropical genus with about 80 species. Half occur in Brazil, where they are common in the floodplains of the Amazonian Basin. Members of the genus are used as ornamentals and for their wood.

items.name: Macrolobium pittieri
items.growersTips:
Grow this tropical legume in a heated conservatory or greenhouse to survive cold UK winters.
Plant in acidic to neutral loam mixed with orchid bark to mimic its native rainforest floor.
Water with tepid rainwater to keep the soil consistently moist but never waterlogged or soggy.
Prune lightly in late spring after new growth starts to maintain shape and remove dead wood.
Check regularly for glasshouse red spider mite and scale insects under the leaves in dry winter.
items.description: Macrolobium pittieri is a species of flowering plant in the family Fabaceae. It is a tree native to Colombia and Panama. It is threatened by habitat loss.

items.name: Bull bay
items.growersTips:
Plant in a sheltered spot away from cold winds to protect early spring buds from late frost damage.
Incorporate plenty of ericaceous compost into the planting hole to maintain the preferred acidic pH.
Water deeply during dry summer spells in the first three years to establish a strong root system.
Prune minimally and only in midsummer to late summer to prevent the cuts from bleeding sap.
Mulch annually in spring with composted bark to retain moisture and protect shallow surface roots.
items.description: Magnolia is a large genus of about 210 to 340 flowering plant species in the subfamily Magnolioideae of the family Magnoliaceae. The natural range of Magnolia species is disjunct, with a main center in east, south and southeast Asia and a secondary center in South America, Central America, the West Indies, and some species in eastern North America.

items.name: Magnolia 'Butterflies'
items.growersTips:
Plant in a sheltered spot away from cold UK winds to protect the delicate yellow spring blossoms.
Incorporate plenty of acidic to neutral leaf mould or peat-free compost to keep the soil moist.
Water deeply during dry summer spells for the first three years to establish the shallow root system.
Prune only in midsummer after flowering to prevent bleeding sap and allow wounds to heal quickly.
Apply a thick layer of bark mulch every spring to retain moisture and protect shallow roots from frost.
items.description: Magnolia 'Butterflies' is a hybrid Magnolia that is the offspring of a cross between the cucumbertree Magnolia acuminata and the Yulan magnolia Magnolia denudata. Its Plant Patent was granted in 1991.

items.name: White Champa
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender hybrid in a large pot of acidic loam to move indoors before first autumn frosts.
Water weekly with harvested rainwater to prevent leaf chlorosis caused by alkaline UK tap water.
Position in a sheltered south-facing sun trap to protect the delicate white blooms from cold winds.
Prune lightly only in midsummer after flowering to prevent sap bleeding and encourage next wood.
Mulch annually with composted pine needles to maintain the required acidic soil pH of 5.5 to 6.5.
items.description: Magnolia × alba, also known as the white champaca, white sandalwood, or white jade orchid tree, is a hybrid flowering plant that is commonly cultivated in Southeast Asia and tropical regions of East Asia. Although the exact origin is uncertain, it is considered to be a hybrid of Magnolia champaca and Magnolia montana.

items.name: Magnolia × brooklynensis
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist well-drained acidic to neutral soil enriched with plenty of composted pine bark.
Position in a sheltered spot facing south or west to protect early spring buds from harsh frost.
Water deeply weekly during dry summer spells for the first three years to establish deep roots.
Prune lightly only in midsummer after flowering to prevent bleeding sap and promote next year's buds.
Mulch annually in spring with composted bracken or leaf mould keeping the stem clear to retain moisture.
items.description: Magnolia × brooklynensis is a hybrid Magnolia that is the result of a cross between Magnolia acuminata (cucumbertree) and Magnolia liliiflora. It was developed in a breeding program at the Brooklyn Botanic Garden beginning in 1953 to create yellow-flowered varieties.

items.name: Magnolia × thompsoniana
items.growersTips:
Plant this magnolia at the exact same depth as its pot to prevent trunk rot in damp UK winters.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells to support its large, moisture-loving leaves.
Prune only in midsummer after flowering to prevent bleeding sap and allow cuts to heal quickly.
Incorporate acidic leaf mould into the planting hole to suit its preference for fertile, damp soil.
Shelter from strong winds to protect the large, fragrant white blooms from tearing and browning.
items.description: Magnolia × thompsoniana is a hybrid tree in the genus Magnolia and family Magnoliaceae. It is a semideciduous tree with large white fragrant flowers.

items.name: Magnolia × loebneri
items.growersTips:
Plant in a sheltered spot facing south or west to protect early spring buds from late UK frosts.
Incorporate plenty of composted pine needles or ericaceous compost to keep the soil slightly acidic.
Water deeply during dry summer spells in the first three years to establish a strong root system.
Prune only in midsummer after flowering is complete to prevent the stems from bleeding sap.
Mulch annually in spring with well-rotted manure, keeping it clear of the main woody stems.

items.name: Tulip magnolia
items.growersTips:
Plant in a sheltered spot facing south or west to protect early spring buds from late UK frosts.
Incorporate acidic peat-free compost or leaf mould into neutral to acid soil to prevent chlorosis.
Water deeply during dry summer spells in the first three years to establish a strong root system.
Prune only in midsummer after flowering to prevent bleeding sap and allow wounds to heal quickly.
Mulch annually in spring with well-rotted bark to retain moisture and protect shallow roots.
items.description: Magnolia × soulangeana, the saucer magnolia or sometimes the tulip tree, is a hybrid flowering plant in the genus Magnolia and family Magnoliaceae. It is a deciduous tree with large, early-blooming flowers in various shades of white, pink, and purple. It is one of the most commonly used magnolias in horticulture, being widely planted in the British Isles, especially in the south of England; and in the United States, especially the east and west coasts.

items.name: Magnolia × wieseneri
items.growersTips:
Plant this shallowly in moist, acidic to neutral soil, keeping the root flare level with the surface.
Mulch annually with composted pine needles to maintain the low soil pH and retain summer moisture.
Shelter from strong winds to prevent damage to the large, highly scented summer-blooming flowers.
Prune only in midsummer after flowering to prevent sap bleeding and allow wounds to heal quickly.
Water deeply during dry spells in July and August to support the development of next year's buds.

items.name: Cucumber tree
items.growersTips:
Plant in deep moist acidic to neutral soil enriched with leaf mould to mimic UK woodland conditions
Water deeply weekly during dry summer spells for the first three years to establish the taproot
Prune minimally only in midsummer to late summer to prevent bleeding sap and silver leaf disease
Mulch annually in spring with composted bark to retain moisture and protect shallow feeder roots
Shelter from strong winds in a south or west facing spot to prevent damage to the large leaves
items.description: Magnolia acuminata, commonly called the cucumber tree, cucumber magnolia or blue magnolia, is one of the largest magnolias, and one of the cold-hardiest. It is a large forest tree of the Eastern United States and Southern Ontario in Canada. It is a tree that tends to occur singly as scattered specimens, rather than in groves.

items.name: Magnolia amoena
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist well-drained acidic to neutral soil enriched with leaf mould to mimic woodland beds
Position in a sheltered spot facing south or west to protect early spring buds from harsh UK frosts
Water deeply with rainwater during dry summer spells in the first three years to establish roots
Prune only in midsummer after flowering to prevent sap bleeding and maintain its natural shrub form
Apply a thick mulch of composted pine needles or bark every autumn to protect shallow surface roots
items.description: Magnolia amoena is a species of plant in the family Magnoliaceae. It is endemic to China. It is threatened by habitat loss.

items.name: Ashe's Magnolia
items.growersTips:
Plant in a sheltered, frost-free spot with dappled shade to protect the huge leaves from wind damage.
Incorporate acidic leaf mould or peat-free ericaceous compost deeply into the planting hole.
Water weekly with rainwater during dry summer spells to keep the shallow root system moist.
Prune only in midsummer after flowering to prevent bleeding sap and allow wounds to heal.
Mulch annually in spring with pine needles or bark to maintain soil acidity and moisture.
items.description: Magnolia ashei is a species of flowering plant in the family Magnoliaceae, endemic to northwestern Florida. It is known commonly as Ashe's magnolia. It is sometimes considered to be a subspecies or variety of Magnolia macrophylla which occurs further north in the southeastern United States, but is now generally considered a distinct species. It was discovered in Okaloosa County, Florida by William Willard Ashe, and named after him by Charles Alfred Weatherby.

items.name: Magnolia biondii
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist well-drained acidic to neutral soil enriched with leaf mould to prevent chlorosis.
Sited in a sheltered south or west facing spot to protect early March buds from harsh UK frosts.
Water deeply weekly during dry summer spells for the first three years to establish deep roots.
Prune only in midsummer after flowering to prevent bleeding sap and allow wounds to heal quickly.
Mulch annually in spring with composted bark keeping the material clear of the main woody stem.
items.description: Magnolia biondii, or Biondi's magnolia, is a deciduous tree that flowers in late winter to early spring before leaf growth. Its early flowering nature gives it the name of the Hope for Spring Flower.

items.name: Magnolia blumei
items.growersTips:
Plant in acidic to neutral soil enriched with leaf mould to mimic their native forest floor.
Provide a sheltered south-facing spot to protect the delicate evergreen foliage from cold UK winds.
Water deeply with rainwater weekly during dry summer spells to keep the shallow root system moist.
Prune lightly only in midsummer after flowering to shape the shrub and avoid bleeding sap.
Mulch annually in spring with composted pine needles to maintain soil acidity and conserve moisture.
items.description: Magnolia sumatrana var. glauca is a variety of magnolia that is endemic to Indonesia. It is native to Sumatra, Java, the Lesser Sunda Islands, and Sulawesi.

items.name: Campbell's Magnolia
items.growersTips:

Provide deep, acidic to neutral soil enriched with leaf mould to mimic their native forest floor.
Water young trees deeply during dry summer spells to support flower bud development for next spring.
Prune only in midsummer to late autumn to prevent the tree from bleeding sap and attracting disease.
Mulch annually with composted bark to protect the shallow root system from winter freezing.
items.description: Magnolia campbellii, or Campbell's magnolia, is a species of Magnolia that grows in sheltered valleys in the Himalaya from eastern Nepal, Sikkim and Assam, India, east to southwestern China and south to northern Myanmar.

items.name: Magnolia caricifragrans
items.growersTips:
Plant in acidic to neutral soil enriched with leaf mould to prevent chlorosis in wet UK winters.
Shelter from cold easterly winds in spring to protect the delicate emerging flower buds from frost.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells in the first two years to establish the roots.
Prune lightly only in midsummer after flowering to avoid sap bleeding and encourage next year's buds.
Mulch annually in spring with composted pine needles to maintain the required acidic root environment.
items.description: Magnolia caricifragrans is a species of plant in the family Magnoliaceae. It is endemic to Colombia.

items.name: Golden Champa
items.growersTips:
Grow in a large pot with ericaceous compost so you can move it indoors to protect from winter frost
Water with tepid rainwater keeping soil consistently moist but never waterlogged to prevent root rot
Place in a sheltered conservatory or south-facing patio corner to maximise sun and block cold winds
Prune lightly only in late spring after flowering to shape the shrub and remove dead wood safely
Feed fortnightly in spring and summer with a high-potassium liquid fertiliser to boost flower buds
items.description: Magnolia champaca, known in English as champak, is a large evergreen tree in the family Magnoliaceae. It was previously classified as Michelia champaca. It is known for its fragrant flowers, and its timber used in woodworking.

items.name: Magnolia chapensis
items.growersTips:

Incorporate plenty of acidic leaf mould or peat-free ericaceous compost into the planting hole.
Water deeply with collected rainwater weekly during dry summer spells to keep the shallow roots moist.
Prune only in midsummer after flowering to prevent sap bleeding and allow wounds to heal quickly.
Apply a thick mulch of chipped pine bark each autumn to insulate roots from freezing UK winter soil.
items.description: Magnolia chapensis is a species of flowering plant in the family Magnoliaceae, native to southern China and northern Vietnam. A tree reaching 30 m (100 ft), it is hardy to USDA zone 7b. It has found wide use as a street tree in southern Chinese cities.

items.name: Magnolia coco
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender shrub in a pot of acidic ericaceous compost so you can move it indoors for winter.
Keep the compost consistently moist with tepid rainwater, never letting it dry out or waterlog.
Place the pot in a warm conservatory or near a bright south-facing window from October to April.
Prune lightly only in late spring after the first flush of flowers to maintain its compact shape.
Feed fortnightly from May to September with a liquid fertiliser formulated for acid-loving plants.
items.description: Magnolia coco, the coconut magnolia, is a species of flowering plant in the family Magnoliaceae, native to southern China, Taiwan, Cambodia and northern Vietnam. A small tree from 7–13 ft (2–4 m) in the garden, it is hardy to zone 9, and can also be kept as a houseplant. It is incorrectly called Magnolia pumila in some sources. In Thailand, it is called yi hoob flower [ยี่หุบ]. In Cambodia, it is call Yi hoop flower (យីហ៊ុប).

items.name: Magnolia compressa
items.growersTips:
Plant in acidic to neutral soil enriched with leaf mould to mimic their native woodland floor.
Shelter from cold UK winds by planting against a south or west-facing wall to protect early buds.
Water deeply with collected rainwater during dry summer spells to support autumn flower bud formation.
Prune lightly only in midsummer after flowering to prevent sap bleeding and maintain a neat shape.
Mulch annually in spring with composted pine needles to maintain the low soil pH this shrub craves.
items.description: Magnolia compressa is a species of flowering plant in the family Magnoliaceae, native to Yunnan, Taiwan, the Ryukyu Islands, and southwest Japan, and introduced to South Korea. A small tree when in cultivation, it is hardy only to USDA zone 10. It may be planted in containers and brought indoors in the winter.

items.name: Magnolia cylindrica
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist, acidic to neutral soil, adding composted pine bark to the planting hole to lower pH.
Position in a sheltered, west-facing spot to protect early spring buds from late UK frosts and wind.
Mulch annually in spring with leaf mould to keep shallow roots cool and moist during dry spells.
Prune only in midsummer after flowering to prevent bleeding sap and reduce the risk of dieback.
Water deeply with rainwater during dry summer weeks to ensure healthy bud formation for next spring.
items.description: Magnolia cylindrica, the Huangshan magnolia, is a species of plant in the family Magnoliaceae. It is endemic to southeastern China. It is threatened by habitat loss.

items.name: Magnolia dawsoniana

items.description: Magnolia dawsoniana, known as Dawson's magnolia, is a magnolia species native to the provinces of Sichuan and Yunnan in China, usually at altitudes of 1,400 to 2,500 m.

items.name: Magnolia dealbata
items.growersTips:

Mulch the root zone annually in autumn with composted bark to protect shallow roots from UK frosts.
items.description: Magnolia dealbata is a species of flowering plant in the family Magnoliaceae, native to Mexico. It is known commonly as the cloudforest magnolia and eloxochitl. It is sometimes considered to be a subspecies of Magnolia macrophylla, which is otherwise native to the southeastern United States.

items.name: Magnolia delavayi
items.growersTips:
Plant against a south or west-facing wall to shelter the evergreen foliage from cold UK winter winds.
Prune in midsummer after flowering to shape the shrub and prevent frost damage to new autumn cuts.

Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells to support the large, moisture-loving leathery leaves.
Apply a thick layer of bracken or bark mulch in late autumn to protect the shallow roots from frost.
items.description: Magnolia delavayi is a species of flowering plant in the genus Magnolia. It is known by the common names of Chinese evergreen magnolia or Delavay's magnolia. It was named after Father Delavay, French Catholic missionary in China, who collected it.

items.name: Lily tree
items.growersTips:
Plant in a sheltered spot facing south or west to protect early spring buds from frost and cold winds.

Apply a thick mulch of chipped bark each autumn to protect shallow roots from hard UK winter frosts.
items.description: Magnolia denudata, the lilytree or Yulan magnolia, is native to central and eastern China. It has been cultivated in Chinese Buddhist temple gardens since 600 AD. Its flowers were regarded as a symbol of purity in the Tang dynasty and it was planted in the grounds of the emperor's palace. It is the official city flower of Shanghai.

items.name: Magnolia dodecapetala
items.growersTips:
Plant in a site sheltered from cold UK winds to protect the early spring buds from frost damage.

Prune only in midsummer after flowering to prevent the cuts from bleeding sap and attracting pests.

items.description: Magnolia dodecapetala is a species of plant in the genus Magnolia, family Magnoliaceae. It was described by a French naturalist named Lamarck, and it obtained the name from a Belgian botanist named Rafaël Herman Anna Govaerts.

items.name: Sweet Michelia

Plant in a sheltered south-facing spot to protect early spring buds from late UK frosts and wind.
Incorporate plenty of acidic leaf mould or peat-free ericaceous compost into the planting hole.
Water deeply weekly with rainwater during dry summer spells to ensure next year's flower buds form.
Prune lightly only in midsummer after flowering to avoid sap bleeding and loss of next year's buds.
Mulch annually in spring with composted bark to retain moisture and protect shallow roots from cold.
items.description: Magnolia doltsopa is a large shrub or small tree native to the eastern Himalayan region and the Meghalaya subtropical forests in Northeastern India. The wood is fragrant.

items.name: Magnolia elegans

Position in a sheltered, south or west-facing spot to protect early spring buds from harsh UK frosts.
Water deeply weekly during dry summer spells for the first two years to establish the root system.
Prune only in midsummer after flowering to prevent sap bleeding and allow wounds to heal quickly.
Mulch annually in spring with composted bark to retain moisture and protect shallow roots from cold.

items.name: Magnolia figo

Plant in acidic to neutral, humus-rich soil, adding ericaceous compost to the planting hole.
Position in a sheltered, south or west-facing spot against a wall to protect from cold UK winds.

Prune lightly immediately after flowering in late spring to maintain shape and remove dead wood.
Mulch annually in spring with pine needles or composted bark to retain moisture and acidity.

items.name: Magnolia floribunda

items.name: Magnolia garrettii

items.name: Bull bay

items.description: Magnolia grandiflora, commonly known as the southern magnolia or bull bay, is a tree of the family Magnoliaceae native to the Southeastern United States, from Virginia to central Florida, and west to East Texas. Reaching 27.5 m (90 ft) in height, it is a large, striking evergreen tree, with large, dark-green leaves up to 20 cm long and 12 cm wide, and large, white, fragrant flowers up to 30 cm (12 in) in diameter.

items.name: Magnolia hernandezii
