Prune lightly after flowering in late summer to maintain a compact shape and prevent woody stems.

items.name: Metalasia serrata
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at two millimetres deep in early spring using a free-draining sandy loam mix.
Water sparingly once established, allowing the top five centimetres of soil to dry out completely.
Protect young plants from slugs and snails during wet UK springs using organic copper barriers.
Position in the sunniest south-facing spot to mimic its native South African light requirements.
Deadhead faded flower heads weekly in late summer to prolong the overall blooming period in the UK.

items.name: Metalasia tricolor
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at two millimetres deep in early spring under glass to protect from UK frosts.
Grow in sharply draining gritty soil with low nutrients to mimic its native South African habitat.
Water sparingly only when the top two inches of soil are dry to prevent root rot in damp UK weather.
Position in the sunniest south-facing spot of your garden to maximise summer flowering potential.
Deadhead spent blooms weekly in July and August to prolong the display of papery flower heads.

items.name: Mexipedium xerophyticum
items.growersTips:
Grow in a fine bark and perlite mix with limestone chippings to mimic their native alkaline cliffs.
Keep winter temperatures strictly above twelve degrees Celsius using a heated greenhouse or indoors.
Water with rainwater weekly in summer, keeping the roots damp but never allowing them to sit in water.
Position in bright, indirect east-facing light, shielding the foliage from direct UK summer sun.
Propagate by carefully dividing mature multi-growth clumps only when the pot is completely crowded.

items.name: Mezoneuron benthamianum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in April at a depth of 2cm using bottom heat of 20C to counter cool UK springs.
Plant out in June in a south-facing border with grit added to the soil to ensure sharp drainage.
Water deeply once a week at the base during dry summer spells to establish the taproot system.
Watch for slugs on young spring shoots and protect them using beer traps or copper tape barriers.
Grow alongside nitrogen-hungry leafy brassicas to benefit from this legume's soil enrichment.

items.name: Mezoneuron kauaiense
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in early spring at a depth of two centimeters using a heated propagator at twentyC
Grow in free-draining sandy loam amended with grit to prevent winter root rot in wet UK climates
Position in the warmest south-facing sheltered spot or greenhouse to maximise summer heat units
Water deeply only when the top five centimeters of soil feels dry to mimic its drought tolerance
Check foliage regularly for glasshouse red spider mite when growing under cover in dry UK summers

items.name: Micklethwaitia carvalhoi
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in April at a depth of two centimetres to protect young roots from late UK frosts.
Plant in free-draining chalky soil mixed with grit to prevent winter root rot in wet British clay.
Water deeply once a week at the base rather than daily misting to encourage deep drought-resistant roots.
Position next to lavender or rosemary to attract bumblebees needed for successful pod pollination.
Watch for early signs of black bean aphid on new shoots and spray with organic horticultural soap.

items.name: Micranthes stellaris
items.growersTips:
Grow in moist, gritty, acidic to neutral soil in a cool, partially shaded rock garden or scree bed.
Water consistently during dry UK spring spells to mimic natural alpine snowmelt without waterlogging.
Plant crowns exactly level with the soil surface and surround with a thick layer of grit to prevent rot.
Propagate by carefully detaching and potting up offsets in late summer after the flowering period.
Watch for vine weevil grubs in autumn, which target the roots of these compact alpine perennials.

items.name: Micranthes aprica
items.growersTips:
Plant in gritty, free-draining soil in a rock garden to prevent winter wet root rot in UK rain.
Position in partial shade or a north-facing crevice to protect from hot, drying summer afternoon sun.
Water moderately during spring growth but keep almost dry during damp, cold UK winter dormancy.
Propagate by carefully detaching offsets in late spring after flowering to increase your stock.
Watch for vine weevil grubs in containers, which eat the roots of these small alpine perennials.

items.name: Micranthes bryophora
items.growersTips:
Grow in gritty, free-draining acidic soil in a rock garden or alpine trough to mimic mountain scree.
Position in a north-facing site or partial shade to protect from hot, direct UK summer afternoon sun.
Water moderately in spring but keep dry in winter by using a rain shelter to prevent crown rot.
Propagate by carefully detaching the tiny vegetative bulbils that form in the leaf axils in autumn.
Protect from slugs and vine weevil grubs which target the fleshy foliage and roots in damp weather.

items.name: Micranthes californica
items.growersTips:
Plant in autumn in gritty, free-draining soil at a depth where the crown sits level with the surface.
Water only during dry spring spells, then stop watering in summer when the plant goes dormant.
Protect from winter wet by placing a layer of horticultural grit around the base of the rosette.
Grow alongside companion plants like dwarf ferns or Primula vulgaris in a cool, semi-shaded rockery.
Watch for vine weevil grubs in autumn and treat with nematodes if you notice notched leaf margins.

items.name: Micranthes ferruginea
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist acidic humus-rich soil in a cool north-facing rockery to mimic Scottish scree habitats
Water weekly during dry UK summers to keep the soil constantly damp but never waterlogged or stagnant
Surround the crown with granite grit to prevent winter wet rot during damp British winters
Propagate by gently detaching the small offsets produced in late summer and potting them in peat-free compost
Keep a vigilant watch for vine weevil grubs which frequently attack the roots of Saxifragaceae species

items.name: Micranthes hieraciifolia
items.growersTips:
Grow in a permanently moist, acidic peat-free compost mixed with grit to mimic UK mountain flushes.
Position in a cold, north-facing rockery or alpine trough to protect from hot UK summer afternoon sun.
Water using collected rainwater rather than tap water to maintain the low pH this alpine requires.
Sow seeds in autumn in a cold frame as they need winter chilling to break dormancy in UK climates.
Surround the crown with sharp grit to prevent winter wet rot during damp UK winters.

items.name: Micranthes integrifolia
items.growersTips:
Plant in moisture-retentive, gritty soil in a rock garden or scree bed to mimic alpine conditions.
Water consistently during dry UK spring months to keep the soil damp but never waterlogged.
Position in partial shade to protect the delicate foliage from strong afternoon summer sun.
Propagate by carefully dividing the rosettes in early autumn after the flowering period ends.
Protect young spring growth from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.

items.name: Micranthes micranthidifolia
items.growersTips:
Plant in a permanently wet, acidic bog garden or beside a garden stream in partial to deep shade.
Sow fresh seed in autumn in cold frames, leaving pots outdoors to experience winter chill for spring.
Keep soil consistently saturated year-round, mimicking its native Appalachian mountain seep habitat.
Protect young spring foliage from slugs and snails using organic beer traps or physical barriers.
Divide established clumps in early spring just as new growth begins to maintain plant vigour.

items.name: Dotted saxifrage
items.growersTips:
Plant in moisture-retentive, acidic to neutral soil in a cool, partially shaded rock garden spot.
Water consistently during dry UK summer spells to mimic its native damp, subarctic stream habitats.
Position away from aggressive spreading plants, using slow-growing dwarf conifers as companions.
Propagate by dividing the rosettes in early spring just as new growth begins to emerge.
Protect from slugs and snails in wet spring weather using organic beer traps around the foliage.

items.name: Micranthes nidifica
items.growersTips:
Plant in autumn at a depth equal to the root ball in gritty, free-draining acidic soil mix.
Water weekly during dry spring periods but keep the crown dry in winter to prevent rot.
Watch for vine weevil grubs in UK peat-free composts and treat with nematodes in late summer.
Position in a north-facing rockery or crevice to mimic alpine conditions and avoid midday sun.
Divide congested clumps immediately after flowering in early summer to maintain plant vigour.

items.name: Micranthes nivalis
items.growersTips:
Grow in a gritty, free-draining scree bed or alpine trough to mimic its native UK mountain habitat.
Water only during dry spring spells, then keep the crown dry in winter to prevent rot from wet cold.
Plant shallowly in autumn with the crown level with the soil, topped with a thick layer of grit.
Position in a cool, north-facing rock crevice to shield it from intense, direct summer afternoon sun.
Watch for vine weevil grubs in containers, which eat the roots and cause the rosette to collapse.

items.name: Micranthes occidentalis
items.growersTips:
Plant in gritty neutral to acid soil to mimic UK upland scree and prevent winter crown rot.
Position in a north-facing rockery or alpine trough to provide essential cool summer shade.
Water moderately during dry spring growth but keep almost dry during damp UK winter dormancy.
Sow fresh seed in autumn in cold frames to trigger germination via natural UK winter chills.
Protect emerging spring foliage from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.

items.name: Micranthes odontoloma
items.growersTips:
Grow in constantly moist humus-rich soil mimicking UK stream edges, never letting the roots dry out.
Position in partial to full shade, ideally on a north-facing slope or cool woodland garden spot.
Plant crown level with the soil surface in autumn to prevent winter waterlogging rot of the base.
Divide congested clumps in early spring just as new growth begins to maintain plant vigour.
Protect emerging spring foliage from slugs and snails using beer traps or organic wool pellets.

items.name: Bog saxifrage
items.growersTips:
Plant in permanently wet boggy soil or pond edges in full sun to mimic its native wetland habitat.
Sow seeds in autumn on the soil surface as they need winter cold stratification to germinate in UK.
Keep the crown at soil level when planting to prevent rot in the damp conditions it requires.
Watch for vine weevil grubs in container-grown plants and treat with nematodes in late summer.
Divide congested clumps in early spring just as new growth begins to maintain plant vigour.

items.name: Micranthes palmeri
items.growersTips:
Plant in gritty, free-draining acidic soil mimicking UK scree gardens to prevent winter crown rot.
Position in partial shade facing north or east to protect delicate foliage from harsh midday sun.
Water moderately during dry spring spells but keep virtually dry during dormant wet UK winters.
Surround the base with a thick layer of granite grit to keep foliage off wet soil and deter slugs.
Propagate by carefully detaching offsets in late spring after flowering has finished.

items.name: Micranthes pensylvanica
items.growersTips:
Plant in boggy neutral to acid soil near ponds to mimic its native North American wetland habitat
Sow seeds in cold frames during autumn as they require winter chill to germinate in the UK climate
Keep the soil consistently wet or saturated year-round never allowing this perennial to dry out
Position in partial shade to protect the lush foliage from scorching during hot dry UK summers
Divide the rhizomatous crown in early spring every three years to maintain plant vigour and health

items.name: Micranthes petiolaris
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist well-drained acidic soil using leafmould to mimic UK woodland floor conditions.
Position in partial to full shade to protect the delicate foliage from scorching UK summer sun.
Water consistently during dry spring spells to keep the soil damp but never waterlogged or soggy.
Propagate by carefully dividing the rosettes in early autumn after the flowering period ends.
Protect young spring growth from slugs and snails using organic barriers or beer traps in damp weather.

items.name: Micranthes rufidula
items.growersTips:
Plant in gritty, free-draining soil in a rock garden or alpine trough to survive wet UK winters.
Position in partial shade or a north-facing crevice to protect the foliage from hot summer sun.
Water moderately during spring growth but keep almost dry during the damp autumn and winter months.
Surround the plant crown with a layer of granite grit to prevent rot from contact with wet soil.
Propagate by carefully dividing the small rosettes in early spring just as new growth commences.

items.name: Micranthes scopularum
items.growersTips:
Plant in gritty, free-draining neutral to acid soil to mimic its native rocky alpine habitat.
Position in a partially shaded, north-facing rockery to protect it from hot UK summer midday sun.
Water moderately in spring but keep almost dry in winter to prevent the crown from rotting in wet.
Propagate by carefully detaching and potting up offsets in late spring after the flowering phase.
Protect from slugs and vine weevil grubs which target the fleshy foliage in damp British springs.

items.name: Micranthes stellaris
items.growersTips:
Plant in a permanently moist, acidic, gritty scree mix or a bog garden to mimic UK mountain rills.
Position in a cool, north-facing spot with shade from midday sun to prevent the foliage scorching.
Water frequently with rainwater rather than tap water to maintain the required low soil pH.
Propagate by carefully detaching and potting up the small offsets in late spring after flowering.
Protect the delicate rosettes from winter waterlogging by top-dressing the soil with granite grit.

items.name: Micranthes tolmiei
items.growersTips:
Plant in gritty, sharply draining acidic scree or alpine troughs to survive wet UK winters.
Position in a cool, north-facing rock crevice to shield the roots from hot summer afternoon sun.
Water with harvested rainwater rather than tap water to maintain the preferred low soil pH.
Top-dress the soil surface with a thick layer of granite grit to prevent crown rot from damp.
Propagate by carefully detaching rooted offsets in late spring after the main flowering flush.

items.name: Micranthes virginiensis
items.growersTips:
Plant in gritty, well-drained acidic to neutral soil to mimic its native rocky woodland habitat.
Position in partial shade under deciduous shrubs to protect the delicate foliage from hot UK sun.
Water consistently during dry spring spells but keep the crown dry in winter to prevent rot.
Propagate by carefully dividing the small rosettes in early autumn after the summer dormancy.
Sow seeds in autumn in cold frames to allow natural UK winter chilling for spring germination.

items.name: Microberlinia brazzavillensis
items.growersTips:
Grow zebrawood in a large pot with ericaceous compost to easily move it indoors before UK frosts.
Water deeply once a week in summer then keep the soil barely damp during the cold winter dormancy.
Prune lightly in late spring after new growth starts to maintain a compact shrub shape in patios.
Check the undersides of the leaves weekly for glasshouse red spider mite during hot dry UK summers.
Feed monthly from April to August with a high-potassium liquid fertilizer to boost root resilience.
items.description: Microberlinia is a genus of plants in the family Fabaceae. It includes two species of tree native to Cameroon and Gabon in west-central tropical Africa. The common name is zingana or zebrawood.

items.name: Microberlinia brazzavillensis
items.growersTips:
Grow in a heated conservatory or greenhouse as this tropical West African shrub cannot survive UK frost
Pot in free-draining acidic loam mixed with orchid bark to mimic its native rainforest floor soils
Water with tepid rainwater only when the top two inches of soil dry out to prevent root rot in winter
Prune lightly in late spring after new growth starts to maintain shape and manage its indoor height
Inspect regularly for spider mites and mealybugs which thrive in dry indoor winter heating drafts
items.description: Microberlinia brazzavillensis is a tree in the family Leguminosae, found in West Africa. It is also called zebrano, zingana, and allen ele, and is commonly sold in the US as zebrawood. The tree is tall and straight, growing up to 40 m in height with a diameter of up to 1 m. The flower has white petals and, as other legumes do, the tree produces pods.

items.name: Microcorys glabra
items.growersTips:
Grow in a free-draining gritty loam with a neutral to alkaline pH to mimic its native habitat
Overwinter in a cold greenhouse or conservatory to protect its roots from freezing UK winter wet
Water only when the top five centimetres of soil is dry to prevent root rot in damp climates
Prune lightly in late spring after frosts pass to maintain a compact shape and encourage blooms
Plant alongside rosemary or lavender in a sunny sheltered gravel garden to match its dry needs
items.description: Microcorys is a genus of flowering plants in the family Lamiaceae, first described in 1810. The entire genus is endemic to Australia.

items.name: Microparacaryum intermedium
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn in cold frames to allow winter chilling to break dormancy before spring growth.
Plant in sharply draining gritty soil to prevent root rot during wet UK winters and damp springs.
Position in full sun against a south-facing wall to mimic its native dry montane microclimate.
Water sparingly only during prolonged summer droughts once the deep taproot has established itself.
Protect young spring foliage from slugs and snails using beer traps or physical grit barriers.
items.description: Microparacaryum is a genus of flowering plants in the family Boraginaceae. It includes four species ranging from the eastern Mediterranean and Eritrea to the Arabian Peninsula, Iran, Central Asia, Afghanistan, Pakistan, and the western Himalayas.

items.name: Micropus amphibolus
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in April under glass at a depth of two millimetres using a gritty, free-draining compost
Plant out in May in a south-facing rockery or scree bed to maximise scarce British summer sun
Water sparingly only when the top two inches of soil are dry to prevent root rot in damp UK winters
Protect young spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps
Grow alongside Sedum or Thymus to provide the sharp drainage and low-nutrient soil this annual needs
items.description: Micropus amphibolus is a species of flowering plant in the family Asteraceae known by the common name Mount Diablo cottonseed.

items.name: Micropus californicus
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in spring at a depth of three millimetres in free-draining sandy loam to prevent rot.
Grow in full sun in a south-facing gravel garden or container to mimic dry California summers.
Water sparingly only during dry spells in spring and stop completely once flowering begins.
Protect young seedlings from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers during damp UK springs.
Position next to low-growing Sedum or Thymus species which share its need for dry, nutrient-poor soil.
items.description: Micropus californicus is a plant in the family Asteraceae which is known by the common name slender cottonweed. Its flowerheads resemble very small cotton balls, often rounded with cottony white hairs forming the pappus of each seed. The individual plants are known more informally as Q-tips due to their resemblance to the cotton swabs. It is found mostly in California, and into Oregon and northern Baja California. This plant is a resident of the vernal pool plant community.

items.name: Mikania micrantha
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in April at three millimetres deep to combat the cool UK spring temperatures.
Water the soil consistently to keep it damp but never soggy to prevent root rot in damp UK summers.
Pinch out the growing tips in early summer to encourage a bushier habit and more abundant flowers.
Watch for slugs and snails on young shoots during wet British spring nights using organic barriers.
Plant alongside marigolds to deter pests and complement the climbing habit of this annual vine.
items.description: Mikania is a genus of about 450 species of plants in the tribe Eupatorieae within the family Asteraceae.

items.name: Minuartia hybrida
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in autumn under a cold frame to mimic natural UK winter chilling for germination.
Grow in a gritty, free-draining soil mix with added limestone chippings to prevent winter wet rot.
Water sparingly only during dry summer spells, allowing the gritty substrate to dry out completely.
Position in full sun alongside Sempervivum in a raised rockery to ensure maximum light and drainage.
Watch for slugs during damp UK springs as they quickly consume the delicate, thread-like seedlings.
items.description: Minuartia is a genus of flowering plants commonly known as sandworts in the family Caryophyllaceae.

items.name: Minuartia bosniaca
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at two millimetres deep in early spring using a free-draining grit-based compost.
Water sparingly only when the top two centimetres of soil is dry to prevent root rot in UK damp.
Incorporate fifty percent horticultural grit into heavy UK clay soils to ensure sharp drainage.
Position in full south-facing sun to mimic its native Balkan habitat and prevent leggy growth.
Protect young seedlings from slugs using organic pellets during wet British spring nights.
items.description: Minuartia bosniaca, or Bosnian sandwort, in Bosnian bosanska mišjakinjica, is endemic plant at East Dinaric mountains. Itbelongs to family of Caryophyllaceae (carnations).

items.name: Minuartia glabra
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds thinly on the soil surface in spring as they need light to germinate in UK climates.
Mix grit into sandy soil to ensure the sharp drainage this alpine annual needs to prevent rot.
Water sparingly only during dry spells, allowing the gritty soil to dry out completely between times.
Position in full sun in a rock garden or raised bed to mimic its natural dry, exposed habitat.
Clear away surrounding weeds regularly to prevent this delicate, low-growing annual from being choked.
items.description: Geocarpon glabrum, commonly called Appalachian stichwort, is a species of flowering plant in the carnation family (Caryophyllaceae). It is native to the eastern United States, where it has a scattered distribution.

items.name: Minuartia rubella
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds thinly in early spring on the surface of a gritty, free-draining compost and do not cover.
Water sparingly from below to keep the soil damp but never soggy, preventing damp-off in wet UK weather.
Mix equal parts horticultural grit and loam to mimic its natural limestone scree habitat in the UK.
Position pots in full sun to maximise light levels and prevent the delicate stems from becoming leggy.
Watch closely for slugs and snails during damp British springs as they can quickly consume seedlings.
items.description: Sabulina rubella is a species of flowering plant in the family Caryophyllaceae known by several common names, including beautiful sandwort, mountain sandwort, Arctic sandwort, and boreal stitchwort.

items.name: Minuartia uniflora
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn in a cold frame to mimic natural UK winter chilling for optimal germination.
Plant in a gritty, sharply draining soil mix to prevent winter wet from rotting the delicate roots.
Water sparingly, allowing the top layer of grit to dry completely between drinks to avoid damp-off.
Position in full sun, ideally in a raised scree bed or alpine trough to maximize scarce UK light.
Sow alongside low-growing Sedums to provide physical support and prevent soil erosion around stems.
items.description: Geocarpon uniflorum, the one-flower stitchwort, is a species of flowering plant in the family Caryophyllaceae. It is native to the Southeastern United States where it is primarily found in the Piedmont. Its preferred habitat is sandy or granitic rock outcrops.

items.name: Minuria cunninghamii
items.growersTips:
Plant this Australian native in a raised bed or gravel garden to ensure the sharp winter drainage it needs.
Grow in a container to easily move it under a cold frame or unheated greenhouse during wet UK winters.
Prune back the woody stems by half in late spring after frosts pass to encourage fresh bushy growth.
Water sparingly only during dry summer spells once established as this plant is highly drought-tolerant.
Propagate by taking softwood cuttings in early summer to overwinter young plants as insurance backups.
items.description: Minuria cunninghamii commonly known as bush minuria, is a flowering plant in the family Asteraceae and grows on mainland Australia. It is a perennial shrub with white daisy-like flowers and a yellow centre.

items.name: Minuria leptophylla
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender Australian daisy in pots of gritty, free-draining soil to move indoors for winter.
Water sparingly from below only when the top two inches of soil are dry to prevent crown rot.
Position in your sunniest south-facing spot to mimic its native arid climate and boost flowering.
Prune back by half in late spring after the last frost to encourage bushy growth and more blooms.
Propagate by taking softwood cuttings in July to ensure backup plants survive the damp UK winter.
items.description: Minuria leptophylla commonly known as minnie daisy, is a flowering plant in the family Asteraceae. It is a small perennial herb with white daisy-like flowers. It is endemic to Australia and grows in all mainland states.

items.name: Minuria scoparia
items.growersTips:
Grow in free-draining gritty soil or raised beds to prevent winter root rot in wet UK climates.
Plant in full sun and shelter from cold winds, using a south-facing gravel garden or alpine house.
Water sparingly once established, allowing the soil to dry out completely between summer waterings.
Protect from slugs and snails in spring when tender new shoots emerge in damp British weather.
Propagate by taking softwood cuttings in late spring to ensure backup plants survive harsh winters.
items.description: Minuria scoparia is a flowering plant in the family Asteraceae. It is a small stiff, broom-like, perennial herb with white flowers, which are seen most of the year. It is endemic to Australia and found only on the north-western slopes of New South Wales.

items.name: Misopates calycinum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in April at a depth of two millimetres using a gritty, free-draining seed compost
Position in the sunniest south-facing spot to mimic its native Mediterranean light levels in the UK
Water sparingly once established, allowing the top two inches of soil to dry out completely between feeds
Watch for slugs and snails on young spring shoots, protecting them with copper tape or beer traps
Sow alongside low-growing thyme or sedum to provide structural support and prevent the stems splaying
items.description: Misopates calycinum is a species of annual herb in the family Plantaginaceae. They have simple leaves.

items.name: Weasel's snout
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in spring by pressing them lightly into gritty, well-drained soil in full sun.
Water sparingly once established as this drought-tolerant weed-like annual dislikes wet winter soil.
Watch for powdery mildew in damp UK summers and space plants fifteen centimetres apart for airflow.
Deadhead regularly to prolong flowering but leave some seed pods to self-sow for the following year.
Grow alongside thyme or sedum in gravel gardens to match its preference for low-nutrient, sandy soil.
items.description: Misopates orontium, known as weasel's snout, is a herbaceous annual plant in the family Plantaginaceae. It is a native of disturbed ground in Europe. It is also naturalised as a weed in other parts of the world such as North America. The pink flowers resemble a miniature snapdragon and are followed by a hairy green fruit which is said to resemble a weasel's snout.

items.name: Mitella trifida
items.growersTips:
Plant Mitella in moist acidic to neutral soil enriched with leafmould to mimic UK woodland floors
Position in deep or partial shade under deciduous shrubs to prevent summer leaf scorch from hot sun
Water weekly during dry UK summers to keep the soil consistently damp but never waterlogged
Divide overgrown clumps in early spring just as new growth begins to maintain plant vigour
Protect emerging spring foliage from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps
items.description: Mitella is a genus of flowering plants known as miterworts or bishop's caps. Mitella species are native to temperate and arctic North America and Asia.

items.name: Brewer's miterwort
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist humus-rich acidic soil in deep shade to mimic its native cool woodland habitat.
Water consistently during dry UK summers to keep the soil damp but avoid waterlogged winter pots.
Sow seeds in autumn in cold frames to allow natural winter chilling for spring germination.
Protect the delicate emerging spring foliage from slugs and snails using organic wool pellets.
Divide established clumps in early spring just as new growth begins to maintain plant vigour.
items.description: Brewerimitella breweri is a species of flowering plant in the saxifrage family, known by the synonyms Mitella breweri and Pectiantia breweri and by the common names Brewer's mitrewort and Brewer's bishop's cap. It is native to western North America from British Columbia to central California and Nevada, where it grows in moist meadows, woods, and mountain forests.

items.name: Mitella diphylla
items.growersTips:
Plant in moisture-retentive, humus-rich soil in deep or dappled shade to mimic UK woodland floors.
Water weekly during dry UK summers to keep the soil consistently damp but never waterlogged.
Sow seeds in cold frames during autumn to allow natural winter chilling for spring germination.
Divide mature clumps in early spring just as new growth appears to propagate and maintain vigour.
Plant alongside hostas and ferns to provide the humid microclimate this woodland perennial needs.
items.description: Mitella diphylla is a clump forming, open woodland plant native to northeast and midwest regions of North America.

items.name: Mitella nuda
items.growersTips:
Plant in partial to full shade using acidic, leaf-mould enriched soil to mimic UK woodland floors.
Keep soil consistently moist but free-draining, watering more during dry British summer spells.
Sow seeds shallowly in autumn, barely covering them, to allow natural winter cold stratification.
Protect young spring foliage from slugs and snails using beer traps or organic copper tape barriers.
Divide established clumps in early spring just as new growth begins to propagate and maintain vigour.
items.description: Mitella nuda, the naked bishop's cap or naked miterwort, is a species of flowering plant in the family Saxifragaceae. It is a perennial or rhizomatous geophyte native to temperate and subarctic regions of northern North America and northeastern Asia, ranging across Canada and the northern United States, and from Western Siberia through Mongolia and northern China to Korea, Japan, and the Russian Far East.

items.name: Mitella ovalis
items.growersTips:
Plant in moisture-retentive, humus-rich acidic soil in deep shade to mimic its native woodland.
Water weekly during dry UK summers to keep the soil consistently damp but never waterlogged.
Position under deciduous shrubs like Corylus to provide winter light and essential summer shade.
Mulch annually in autumn with leaf mould to protect shallow roots from hard UK winter frosts.
Divide congested clumps in early spring just as new growth begins to maintain plant vigour.
items.description: Brewerimitella ovalis is a species of flowering plant in the saxifrage family known by the common names coastal miterwort and oval-leaf miterwort. It is native to western North America from southwestern British Columbia, including Vancouver Island, to northern California as far south as Marin County. It grows in moist, shady habitat, such as coastal forests and streambanks.

items.name: Mitella pentandra
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist humus-rich acidic soil under deciduous trees to mimic native cool woodland conditions
Water weekly during dry UK summers to keep the shallow fibrous root system from drying out completely
Sow seeds in cold frames during autumn as they require winter chilling to trigger spring germination
Divide mature clumps in early spring just as new growth begins to maintain plant vigour and spread
Position away from aggressive ground cover to prevent this delicate species from being smothered
items.description: Pectiantia pentandra is a species of flowering plant in the Saxifrage Family (Saxifragaceae), known by the common names fivestamen miterwort or five-point bishop's cap.

items.name: Mitella trifida
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist humus-rich acidic soil in deep shade to mimic its native cool woodland habitat
Water consistently to keep soil damp but never waterlogged during dry British summer spells
Position away from aggressive ground cover and pair with delicate ferns or miniature hostas
Protect the tender emerging spring foliage from slugs and snails using organic beer traps
Divide the rhizomes in early autumn every three years to maintain plant vigour and prevent crowding
items.description: Ozomelis trifida is a species of flowering plant in the saxifrage family known by the common names threeparted miterwort and Pacific miterwort. It is native to western North America from Alaska to Montana to California, where it grows in wet wooded habitat types. It is a rhizomatous perennial herb growing up to about 45 centimeters tall. The leaves occur around the base of the stem. They have rounded blades up to 10 centimeters wide and lobed, round-toothed edges. The erect inflorescence bears up to 20 flowers, usually along one side of the stem. The distinctive flower is cup-shaped with five

items.name: Moehringia lateriflora
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at a depth of two millimetres in early spring using a free-draining grit mix.
Water sparingly from below to prevent dampening-off in the damp and cool UK spring climate.
Position in partial shade mimicking woodland edges to prevent the delicate foliage from scorching.
Mix grit and leaf mould into heavy clay soils to ensure the sharp drainage this alpine plant needs.
Watch out for slugs and snails during wet UK summers as they quickly consume the tender stems.
items.description: Moehringia is a genus of flowering plants in the family Caryophyllaceae. Members of this genus and of some other genera in Caryophyllaceae are commonly called sandworts. They are found only in the north temperate zone. The genus Moehringia was first formally named by Carl Linnaeus in 1753. It is named after the German naturalist Paul Möhring (1710–1792).

items.name: Erect Chickweed
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn directly onto well-drained, gritty soil to mimic UK wild gravelly habitats.
Keep soil barely damp during winter and avoid waterlogging to prevent damp-off in wet UK winters.
Position in full sun alongside low-growing Sedum to provide essential sharp drainage companions.
Do not prune or deadhead if you want this short-lived annual to self-seed for the following spring.
Scatter seeds on the soil surface without burying them as they require light to trigger germination.
items.description: Moenchia is a genus of plants in the family Caryophyllaceae with three species native to the Mediterranean region of southern Europe and naturalised in southern Africa and parts of North America and Australia. They are herbs, with an annual life span. They have slender roots and thin stems that are upright or ascending. Inflorescences are one- to three-flowered and terminally end the stems. The flowers are in spreading cymes or solitary, with bracts paired that are leaf like. Named after the 18th century German botanist Conrad Moench. A common name for the plants in this genus is upright chick

items.name: Moldenhawera nutans
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in April at a depth of two centimeters using free-draining peat-free compost.
Plant out in late May after the last frost in a sheltered south-facing spot with full sun.
Water deeply at the base once a week to establish the taproot while avoiding waterlogged soil.
Provide a sturdy trellis or hazel twigs early in June to support the climbing Fabaceae stems.
Watch for black bean aphid infestations on young shoots and wash them off with a sharp water spray.
items.description: Moldenhawera is a genus of flowering plants in the legume family, Fabaceae. It includes 12 species of trees and shrubs endemic to eastern Brazil. They grow in diverse habitats, including restinga, coastal dunes, wooded grassland (cerrado), low mountain scrub on sandstone-derived soils, and rocky montane grassland. It belongs to the subfamily Caesalpinioideae.

items.name: Moltkiopsis ciliata
items.growersTips:
Plant in sharply draining gritty soil or a raised scree bed to survive wet UK winters without rotting
Position in full south facing sun to mimic its native desert habitat and encourage summer flowering
Water sparingly only during active growth and keep completely dry during damp autumn and winter months
Protect from heavy UK winter rain using a cold frame or a glass cloche to prevent crown rot
Propagate by taking semi ripe cuttings in late summer to ensure backup plants against severe frosts
items.description: Moltkiopsis is a monotypic genus of flowering plants belonging to the family Boraginaceae. The only species is Moltkiopsis ciliata.

items.name: Monanthes laxiflora
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly on gritty compost in spring, barely covering them to ensure light germination.
Water only when the top two inches of gritty soil are dry, reducing to a trickle during damp autumns.
Grow in shallow terracotta pots with fifty percent grit to survive wet UK summers without root rot.
Bring pots indoors to a bright windowsill by October to protect this tender annual from UK frosts.
Sow Monanthes polyphylla seeds in early spring for the best dome-shaped rosettes in UK rockeries.
items.description:
Monanthes is a genus of small, succulent, subtropical plants of the family Crassulaceae. Most species in the genus are endemic to the Canary Islands, with one species also endemic to the Savage Islands and another to the High Atlas mountains of Morocco. Its center of diversity is Tenerife, with seven species occurring on this island. On Fuerteventura and Lanzarote, only M. laxiflora occurs.
Monanthes is a rare example where a species re-colonizes the continent from an island, after their ancestors have colonized the island from the continent.

items.name: Moneses
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist acidic pine leaf mould under deep shade to mimic native Caledonian pine forest soils.
Sow seeds directly next to mature heather or blueberry to establish essential mycorrhizal fungi.
Water with rainwater only to keep the soil consistently damp and maintain the required low pH.
Protect the delicate single wintergreen stems from slugs using organic copper tape around pots.
Do not prune this slow-growing dwarf shrub as it relies on intact evergreen leaves for survival.
items.description: Moneses uniflora, the one-flowered wintergreen, single delight, wax-flower, shy maiden, star of Bethlehem (Aleutians), St. Olaf's candlestick (Norway), wood nymph, or frog's reading lamp, is a plant of the family of Ericaceae, that is indigenous to moist coniferous forests in temperate regions of the Northern Hemisphere from Spain to Japan and across North America. It is the sole member of genus Moneses.

items.name: Monotropa hypopitys
items.growersTips:
Do not sow seeds in soil but scatter them near mature beech or pine trees to find essential fungi.
Never apply any fertiliser or organic compost as this disrupts the delicate mycorrhizal network.
Keep the planting site constantly damp and shaded to mimic a cool British woodland floor.
Do not attempt to transplant wild specimens because they cannot survive without their host fungi.
Avoid digging or hoeing near established patches to protect the underground fungal connections.
items.description: Monotropa is a genus of five species of herbaceous perennial flowering plants. The genus was formerly classified in the family Monotropaceae and presently classified in Ericaceae. They are native to temperate regions of the Northern Hemisphere and are generally rare. Unlike most plants, they do not have chlorophyll and therefore are non-photosynthetic; they are myco-heterotrophs that obtain food through parasitism on subterranean fungi. Because they do not need any sunlight to live, they can live in very dark sites such as the floor of deep forest. The name "Monotropa" is Greek for "one turn"

items.name: Monotropa coccinea
items.growersTips:
Grow this rare red mycoheterotroph in deep shade under mature beech trees to mimic UK woodland.
Do not plant in soil; instead, transplant a plug of host-tree roots and mycorrhizal fungi intact.
Keep the planting site constantly damp with rainwater, never letting the woodland leaf litter dry.
Avoid all chemical fertilisers and soil disturbances that destroy the essential host fungal network.
Protect emerging summer stems from slugs using organic wool pellets around the host tree root zone.
items.description: Monotropa coccinea, sometimes called red Indian pipe, is a species of obligately parastic plant occurring in the Neotropical realm. It belongs to the family Ericaceae.

items.name: Monotropa hypopitys
items.growersTips:
Do not plant seeds or bare roots; instead, transplant a containerised host pine or beech tree.
Never apply any fertiliser or organic manure, as this disrupts the essential mycorrhizal fungi.
Plant in deep shade under mature beech, pine, or birch trees in highly alkaline, chalky soils.
Keep the soil consistently damp but never waterlogged, mimicking a damp British woodland floor.
Leave the decaying flower stems intact over winter to allow natural self-seeding in leaf litter.
items.description: Monotropa hypopitys, syn. Hypopitys monotropa, also known as yellow bird's nest in Britain and Ireland, pinesap and false beechdrops in Canada and the United States, is a herbaceous perennial plant of the Monotropoideae subfamily of the family Ericaceae. It is native to temperate regions of the Northern Hemisphere and is scarce within its range. M. hypopitys is a mycotrophic plant which means it obtains nutrients and fixed carbon by parasitizing the mycorrhizal networks of trees. It lacks chlorophyll and does not photosynthesize. The species name, M. hypopitys, is from Latinized Greek hypo-, "

items.name: Monotropa uniflora
items.growersTips:
Do not plant seeds or move wild specimens as they rely on a complex mycorrhizal network to survive.
Establish host trees like beech or oak to provide the essential fungal partners this plant needs.
Maintain a thick natural leaf mulch to keep the soil constantly damp and mimic a UK woodland floor.
Avoid applying any chemical fungicides or fertilizers which destroy the vital underground fungi.
Position in deep damp shade where other plants fail to grow to match its natural forest habitat.
items.description: Monotropa uniflora, also known as the American Indian ghost pipe plant, is a herbaceous, parasitic, non-photosynthesizing, perennial flowering plant native to temperate regions of Asia, North America, and northern South America, but with large gaps between areas. The plant is waxy white, but some specimens have been described as having black flecks or pale pink coloration. Rare variants may have a deep red color. The name "Monotropa" is Greek for "one turn" and "uniflora" is Latin for "one flowered" as there is one sharply curved stem for each single flower. M.uniflora is commonly found growin

items.name: Monotropastrum
items.growersTips:
Grow in deep shade under beech or oak trees using leaf mould to mimic UK woodland soil conditions.
Do not fertilize this plant as it lacks chlorophyll and relies entirely on mycorrhizal fungi.
Keep soil consistently damp but never waterlogged during dry British summer spells to protect roots.
Plant container-grown specimens in autumn at the exact same soil depth as they were in their pot.
Avoid digging or hoeing near the base to prevent damaging the delicate underground fungal network.
items.description: Monotropastrum is a small genus of myco-heterotrophic plants in the family Ericaceae. As currently circumscribed the group includes three species.

items.name: Monotropastrum humile
items.growersTips:
Grow this non-photosynthetic mycorrhizal parasite near beech or oak to exploit their fungal networks.
Never apply standard fertilizers as chemical nutrients will destroy the delicate host mycorrhizae.
Keep the planting site constantly damp and heavily mulched with leaf mould to mimic UK woodlands.
Do not prune this herbaceous perennial; despite the prompt label, it is not a woody shrub at all.
Plant fresh seed capsules immediately in autumn directly over active mycelium of Russula mushrooms.
items.description: Monotropastrum humile is a species of myco-heterotrophic plant of the family Ericaceae, distributed throughout eastern Asia, from the Himalayas to the Islands of Japan.

items.name: Monsonia
items.growersTips:
Grow in a gritty mix of two parts pumice to one part loam to prevent root rot in wet UK winters.
Water only when the soil is bone dry from May to September then keep almost completely dry in winter.
Overwinter indoors on a south-facing windowsill or heated greenhouse kept above eight degrees Celsius.
Propagate by taking root cuttings in late autumn when the plant enters its active winter growth phase.
Watch for mealybugs in the deep leaf crevices and treat immediately with an organic neem oil spray.
items.description: Monsonia is a genus of plants in the family Geraniaceae. It is named after Lady Anne Monson, 1714–76, known for her botanical knowledge and plant collecting in the Cape.

items.name: Monsonia emarginata
items.growersTips:
Grow in a gritty, free-draining loam-based compost with fifty percent perlite or horticultural grit.
Keep completely dry in winter indoors and water only when the soil is dry during the summer growth.
Overwinter on a south-facing windowsill or heated greenhouse keeping the temperature above five Celsius.
Sow seeds shallowly in spring using a heated propagator and maintain a constant twenty degrees Celsius.
Monitor closely for mealybugs and glasshouse red spider mites in the leaf axils during dry summer spells.
items.description: Monsonia emarginata is a species of plant in the family Geraniaceae native to southern Africa.

items.name: Monticalia
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at two millimetres deep in April using a heated propagator to combat UK chills.
Water the base weekly during dry summer spells, keeping soil moist but never waterlogged or soggy.
Watch for slugs and snails on young spring shoots, using beer traps or organic wool pellets to deter.
Deadhead faded daisy-like flowers weekly in July and August to prolong the summer blooming display.
Incorporate grit into heavy clay soils before planting to ensure the sharp drainage this plant needs.
items.description: Monticalia is a genus of flowering plants in the family Asteraceae.

items.name: Mora
items.growersTips:
Sow Mora seeds indoors in April at a depth of two centimetres to protect them from late UK frosts.
Grow Mora in a south-facing spot with grit-amended soil to prevent root rot during wet UK summers.
Water Mora deeply once a week at the base to keep the soil moist but avoid waterlogging the roots.
Protect young Mora seedlings from slugs and snails using copper tape or beer traps in damp spring.
Apply a potassium-rich liquid seaweed feed every three weeks in summer to boost Mora flower production.
items.description: Mora may refer to:

items.name: Moraea aristata
items.growersTips:
Plant the bulbs in autumn at a depth of five centimetres in a sharply draining gritty loam soil
Grow this tender South African bulb in a container to easily move it into a frost-free greenhouse
Water weekly during the winter growing season but keep the soil completely dry during summer dormancy
Position the pot in the most sun-drenched south-facing spot to mimic its native Cape habitat
Watch for aphids on the emerging winter foliage and wash them off to prevent viral infections
items.description: Moraea aristata is a species of flowering plant in the family Iridaceae. It is referred to by the common names blue-eyed uintjie or Blouooguintjie in Afrikaans. It is endemic to the city of Cape Town and is considered to be critically endangered.

items.name: Moraea bellendenii
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs 8cm deep in autumn using a gritty compost mix to ensure sharp winter drainage in UK wet.
Grow in pots to easily move them under glass or a cold frame to protect from wet UK winter frosts.
Water moderately during spring growth but keep the soil completely dry during summer dormancy.
Position in the sunniest south-facing spot possible to mimic South African light and heat levels.
Watch for aphids on new spring shoots and treat immediately to prevent virus transmission.
items.description: Moraea bellendenii is a species of plant in genus Moraea that was named after John Bellenden, the English botanist.

items.name: Moraea bituminosa
items.growersTips:
Plant this South African bulb five centimetres deep in autumn using a gritty, free-draining compost.
Grow in a container to easily move it into a frost-free greenhouse or cold frame for UK winters.
Water weekly during its active winter growth but keep the soil bone dry throughout summer dormancy.
Position in your sunniest south-facing spot to mimic its native hot, dry summer baking period.
Top-dress the pot with horticultural grit to prevent wet soil from rotting the delicate collar.
items.description: Moraea bituminosa is a species of the genus Moraea in family Iridaceae.

items.name: Moraea collina
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs 5cm deep in autumn using pots of gritty compost to protect them from wet UK winters.
Move pots to a frost-free greenhouse or cold frame from November to March to prevent winter rot.
Water weekly during the spring growing season but keep completely dry once summer dormancy begins.
Position in the sunniest south-facing spot possible to mimic South African winter-rainfall warmth.
Watch for aphids on emerging spring flower buds and squash them by hand to prevent virus spread.
items.description: Moraea collina is a species of the genus Moraea, in the family Iridaceae. It was formerly known as Homeria collina.

items.name: Moraea sisyrinchium
items.growersTips:
Plant the bulbs in autumn at a depth of eight centimetres in sharply draining, gritty, alkaline soil.
Grow in a south-facing terracotta pot to easily move them under glass to dry out during summer.
Withhold all water from July to September to mimic the dry Mediterranean summer dormancy period.
Protect the winter foliage from severe UK frosts using a cold frame or horticultural fleece.
Position near low-growing Mediterranean herbs like thyme to ensure they are not shaded out.
items.description: Moraea sisyrinchium, commonly the Barbary nut, is a species of flowering plant that belongs to the tribe Irideae. It is native to southern Europe and the Mediterranean region.

items.name: Moraea viscaria
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs in autumn five centimetres deep in sharply draining grit-heavy soil to prevent winter rot.
Grow in pots to easily move them under a cold glasshouse or porch to protect from wet UK winters.
Water sparingly from autumn to spring only when the top soil dries out then keep completely dry.
Position in the sunniest south-facing spot possible to mimic their native South African climate.
Watch for aphids on new spring shoots and treat immediately to prevent viral transfer to bulbs.
items.description: Moraea viscaria is the type species of the genus of Moraea in the family Iridaceae that is named after the sticky secretion on the stem and branches.

items.name: Moullava
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in April at 2cm depth using bottom heat of 20C to overcome cool UK spring soils
Plant in free-draining sandy loam enriched with grit to prevent winter root rot in wet UK climates
Water deeply once a week at the base during dry summer spells to support the rapid annual growth
Position in your warmest south-facing border against a brick wall to maximize limited UK sunshine
Sow alongside nasturtiums to divert aphids away from the tender young Fabaceae foliage in June
items.description: Moullava is a genus of flowering plants in the legume family, Fabaceae. It includes four species of lianas or scrambling shrubs native to tropical Africa from Cameroon to Tanzania and Angola, and to tropical Asia from India to Indochina, southern China, and western Malesia. Typical habitat includes forest margins of semi-evergreen seasonal tropical forest. It belongs to the subfamily Caesalpinioideae.

items.name: Moullava spicata
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in April at 2cm depth using bottom heat to overcome the cool UK spring temperatures.
Grow in free-draining sandy loam mixed with grit to prevent winter root rot in wet British soils.
Position in your warmest south-facing border or against a brick wall to maximise essential sunlight.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells rather than daily shallow sprinkles to aid roots.
Watch for aphids and slugs on young spring shoots using beer traps or organic sprays to protect them.
items.description: Moullava spicata is an endemic species of creeper found in the Western Ghats of India.

items.name: Mukdenia
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist but well-drained humus-rich acid to neutral soil in dappled shade to prevent leaf burn.
Water consistently during dry UK summer spells to keep the soil evenly damp but never waterlogged.
Protect emerging spring foliage from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.
Divide congested clumps in early spring just as new growth appears to maintain plant vigour.
Plant alongside Astilbes or Hostas in woodland borders for contrasting foliage textures and colours.
items.description: Mukdenia rossii is a species of flowering plant in the saxifrage family, Saxifragaceae. It is the sole species in genus Mukdenia. It is a perennial native to Korea and northeastern China.

items.name: Mukdenia rossii
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade, mimicking UK woodland edges to prevent leaf scorch.
Water consistently during dry summer spells to keep soil damp, as drought triggers early dormancy.
Protect emerging spring foliage from slugs and snails using organic grit or beer traps in damp UK.
Divide congested clumps in early spring just as new growth starts, replanting at the original depth.
Pair with hostas or ferns to shield Mukdenia from midday sun and highlight its autumn red foliage.
items.description: Mukdenia rossii is a species of flowering plant in the saxifrage family, Saxifragaceae. It is the sole species in genus Mukdenia. It is a perennial native to Korea and northeastern China.

items.name: Muniria
items.growersTips:
Grow in free-draining gritty loam to prevent root rot during wet, cold United Kingdom winters.
Position in full south-facing sun against a warm wall to mimic its native hot Australian climate.
Protect from frost using a thick dry mulch of gravel or horticultural fleece from November to March.
Water deeply but infrequently during summer, allowing the soil to dry out completely between waterings.
Prune lightly in late spring after the last frost to shape the shrub and encourage fresh new growth.
items.description: Muniria is a genus of four species of flowering plants in the mint family, Lamiaceae and is endemic to the Northern Territory in Australia. Plants in this genus are woolly shrubs with five petals joined to form a tube-shaped flower with four stamens of unequal lengths. These species are similar to those in the genus Pityrodia except that the branches are distinctly 4-angled in cross section and the fruit has calluses or ridges.

items.name: Myosotis
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds outdoors in July for robust spring-flowering plants that survive wet UK winters easily.
Plant bareroot Myosotis in autumn at a depth where the crown sits exactly level with the soil surface.
Water young plants twice weekly during dry spring spells to prevent powdery mildew on the foliage.
Cut stems back to ground level in June after flowering to prevent excessive self-seeding in borders.
Interplant with late-season tulips to mask the dying Myosotis foliage as it yellows in May.
items.description: Myosotis is a genus of flowering plants in the borage family Boraginaceae. In the Northern Hemisphere, they are colloquially known as forget-me-nots or scorpion grasses. The forget-me-not is the official flower of Alaska.

items.name: Myosotis alpestris
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at two millimetres deep in June for strong roots before winter frosts arrive.
Grow in moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to mimic their native cool UK woodland habitat.
Water consistently at the base during dry summer spells to prevent powdery mildew on the foliage.
Cut back faded stems in July to prevent excessive self-seeding and keep your borders tidy.
Plant alongside spring bulbs like yellow daffodils to create a classic British colour contrast.
items.description: Myosotis alpestris or alpine forget-me-not is a herbaceous perennial plant in the flowering plant family Boraginaceae. The alpine forget-me-not is the county flower of Westmorland in the United Kingdom.

items.name: Myosotis arvensis
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at a depth of 2mm in late summer for robust spring-flowering plants.
Water consistently during dry UK spring spells to prevent powdery mildew on the foliage.
Cut back spent stems in July to encourage a second flush of blooms and control self-seeding.
Plant alongside spring bulbs like yellow daffodils to create a classic British cottage garden contrast.
Grow in moist, well-drained soil with partial shade to mimic its natural UK woodland edge habitat.
items.description: Myosotis arvensis or field forget-me-not is a herbaceous annual to short lived perennial flowering plant in the family Boraginaceae. It is native to Europe, Turkey, the Caucasus, Siberia, the western Himalayas, and northwestern Africa. The plant is annual to perennial, erect, to 40 centimetres (16 in) and patent-hairy. The flowers are grey-blue, 3–5 millimetres across, saucer shaped in profile, the sepal tube with hooked hairs. The mature fruits are dark brown, shiny nutlets. In the British Isles the plant is an archaeophyte, common throughout the isles on open, well-drained ground.

items.name: Myosotis discolor
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in late summer directly into damp, weeded soil to mimic the natural UK autumn germination.
Grow in dappled shade under deciduous shrubs to prevent the delicate yellow-to-blue flowers fading.
Water weekly during dry spring spells to keep the shallow roots moist in sandy or acidic UK soils.
Leave faded flower heads intact until July so the plant can self-seed freely across your borders.
Interplant with wild strawberries or primroses to create a low-growing, weed-suppressing groundcover.
items.description: Myosotis discolor is a species of forget-me-not known by the common name changing forget-me-not. It is native to Europe, and it can also be found throughout eastern and western North America, where it is an introduced species. It grows in many types of habitat, including disturbed areas such as roadsides.

items.name: Myosotis dissitiflora
items.growersTips:
Plant in early autumn in moist but well-drained soil enriched with leaf mould to mimic woodland beds.
Sow seeds shallowly at a depth of five millimetres in June for strong winter-hardy spring blooms.
Water consistently during dry summer spells to prevent powdery mildew, a common UK fungal issue.
Cut back faded stems to ground level in July to encourage fresh foliage and potential autumn rebloom.
Divide established clumps in autumn every three years to maintain vigour and prevent overcrowding.
items.description: Myosotis dissitiflora is a species of forget-me-not native to the Caucasus. It is one of the largest-flowered species in Myosotis. There used to be a dozen of ornamental cultivars during the late 19th and early 20th centuries, but they are all lost now. Currently there exist two known cultivars, namely 'Baby Blue' and 'Myomark'.

items.name: Myosotis pansa subsp. pansa
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at two millimetres deep in late summer for strong roots before winter frosts.
Grow in moist but well-drained humus-rich soil in partial shade to mimic its coastal cliff habitat.
Water consistently during dry summer spells to prevent powdery mildew on the delicate foliage.
Divide mature clumps in early autumn every three years to maintain vigour and prevent overcrowding.
Plant alongside native ferns or primroses which thrive in the same cool damp British shade conditions.
items.description: Myosotis pansa subsp. pansa, also known as the Waitakere forget-me-not, is a subspecies of flowering plant in the family Boraginaceae, endemic to the North Island of New Zealand. Lucy Moore described the variety M. petiolata var. pansa in 1961, and it was transferred to a subspecies of M. pansa by Heidi Meudt, Jessica Prebble, Rebecca Stanley and Michael Thorsen in 2013. Plants of this species of forget-me-not are perennial rosettes with ebracteate inflorescences and white corollas with exserted stamens.

items.name: Myosotis pansa subsp. praeceps
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist well-drained soil enriched with leaf mould to mimic its native coastal cliff habitat
Sow seeds shallowly in summer at a depth of two millimetres for natural spring flowering the next year
Position in partial shade to protect the delicate foliage from scorching in dry UK summer spells
Watch for powdery mildew in late summer and space plants thirty centimetres apart to improve airflow
Divide established clumps in autumn every three years to maintain vigor and prevent overcrowding
items.description: Myosotis pansa subsp. praeceps is a subspecies of flowering plant in the family Boraginaceae, endemic to the North Island of New Zealand. Lucy Moore described the variety M. petiolata var. pansa in 1961, and it was transferred to a subspecies of M. pansa by Heidi Meudt, Jessica Prebble, Rebecca Stanley and Michael Thorsen in 2013. Plants of this species of forget-me-not are perennial rosettes with partially bracteate inflorescences and white corollas with exserted stamens.

items.name: Myosotis retrorsa
items.growersTips:
Plant in damp acidic soil near pond edges or bog gardens to mimic its native wet habitats.
Sow seeds shallowly at a depth of two millimetres in late summer for natural spring germination.
Water consistently during dry UK summers to keep the soil constantly moist but not stagnant.
Divide the perennial clumps in autumn every three years to maintain vigour and prevent overcrowding.
Watch for slugs and snails in spring as they target the tender new foliage in damp garden spots.
items.description: Myosotis retrorsa is a species of flowering plant in the family Boraginaceae, endemic to the South Island of New Zealand. Heidi Meudt, Jessica Prebble and Rowan Hindmarsh-Walls described the species. Plants of this species of forget-me-not are perennial with a prostrate habit, bracteate inflorescences, and white corollas.

items.name: Myosotis stricta
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at two millimetres deep in late summer for natural spring flowering in the UK.
Grow in gritty, free-draining sandy loam to mimic its native UK dry gravelly habitat and avoid rot.
Water sparingly once established, allowing the soil to dry out completely between light waterings.
Watch for powdery mildew in humid UK summers and space plants fifteen centimetres apart for airflow.
Plant alongside early-flowering Sedum or wild pansies which thrive in the same dry, nutrient-poor soil.
items.description: Myosotis stricta is a plant species of the genus Myosotis. Common names include strict forget-me-not and blue scorpion grass.

items.name: Myosoton
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn 5mm deep in damp UK soil to mimic natural winter stratification for spring growth.
Water the soil base consistently during dry summer spells to keep the shallow root system hydrated.
Watch for slugs and snails on young spring shoots during damp British mornings and use beer traps.
Clear surrounding weeds in early spring to prevent them smothering this delicate low-growing annual.
Plant alongside moisture-loving UK native ferns or primroses which share its damp woodland habitat.
items.description: Stellaria is a genus of about 190 species of flowering plants in the family Caryophyllaceae, with a cosmopolitan distribution. Common names include starwort, stitchwort and chickweed.

items.name: Myosurus
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn directly into damp, heavy clay soils to mimic natural UK wetland margins.
Keep the soil consistently boggy and wet during spring to support the unique green mousetail blooms.
Position in full sun alongside companion plants like Caltha palustris to prevent taller weed takeover.
Allow the annual seed heads to dry and self-sow naturally on bare mud to ensure next year's crop.
Avoid any nitrogen-rich fertilisers which cause excessive foliage growth and ruin the tiny flowers.
items.description: The genus Myosurus, or mousetail, belongs to the family Ranunculaceae. It comprises about 15 species of annual scapose herbs. These herbs are nearly cosmopolitan, with a center of diversity in western North America. The flowers are easily recognised by bearing 6 stamens with numerous ovaries on a stalk.

items.name: Nanorrhinum
items.growersTips:
Plant in gritty, sharply draining soil in full sun to prevent winter wet rot in damp UK climates.
Sow seeds shallowly on the soil surface in spring, pressing lightly without burying them deep.
Water sparingly once established, allowing the gritty compost to dry out fully between waterings.
Cut back faded stems in autumn to encourage a compact habit and prevent the plant from flopping.
Grow alongside Sedums or Sempervivums in rock gardens to match their low-water, high-drainage needs.
items.description: Nanorrhinum is a genus of flowering plants in family Plantaginaceae. It includes 29 species ranging from the Sahara and Sahel of northern Africa to the Arabian Peninsula, Iran, the Indian subcontinent, and Myanmar.

items.name: Naravelia
items.growersTips:
Grow Naravelia in a large pot of loam-based compost so you can move it into a heated greenhouse for winter
Water deeply once a week in summer but keep the compost barely damp from November to March to prevent rot
Prune stems back by half in April to encourage bushy growth and more yellow-green flowers on new wood
Provide a sturdy trellis in a sheltered south-facing spot to support its leaf-tip climbing tendrils
Watch for clematis slime flux on damaged stems in wet UK springs and prune out affected wood immediately
items.description: Clematis is a genus of about 380 species within the buttercup family, Ranunculaceae. Their garden hybrids and cultivars have been popular among gardeners, beginning with Clematis 'Jackmanii', a garden staple since 1862. More cultivars are being produced constantly, mainly of Chinese and Japanese origin.

items.name: Nemosenecio nikoensis
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds on the soil surface in spring as they need light to germinate in the cool UK climate.
Grow in moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade to mimic its native Japanese woodland habitat.
Water consistently to keep soil damp but not waterlogged, especially during dry UK summer spells.
Protect young seedlings from slugs and snails which target tender Asteraceae foliage in damp spring.
Plant alongside hostas or ferns in a woodland border to provide the dappled shade it requires.
items.description: Nemosenecio nikoensis is a species of flowering plant in the aster family (Asteraceae). It is endemic to Japan, where it is widespread and found on all four main islands. Its natural habitat is in wet forests in the mountains, where it grows along streamsides.
